Software Engineering — Self-Paced Bachelor’s Guide 40 chapters · 277 topics · 165 code samples · works offline

Welcome — How to Use This Course

This opening section explains how to get the most out of the self-paced course before you begin. It sets expectations about pacing, exercise habits, and the recommended workflow, and tells you what software you should have installed. Skimming it before diving into Chapter 1 prevents confusion and helps you build a sustainable learning routine from day one.

How this course is organisedThe right mindsetTools you will use all course long

This is a complete, self-paced guide that walks you through the knowledge a Bachelor’s degree in Software Engineering / Computer Science gives you — from absolute beginner ("I don’t know anything") to advanced, scalable systems engineering.

How this course is organised

This section explains the navigational structure of the course so you can study it efficiently. Work through the chapters in order, complete every hands-on exercise, and use the contents pane to jump back to earlier material when a concept reappears. Because later chapters assume earlier ones, following the sequence matters more than rushing ahead.

  • Chapters follow a real curriculum order. Each chapter builds on the one before it. Read them top to bottom.
  • Every chapter has explanations, real code examples, tables, warnings and exercises. Do the exercises — that’s where learning actually happens.
  • Use the table of contents on the left to navigate and to jump back to anything. It is searchable.
  • Toggle dark/light mode with the button in the top-right. Your preference is saved.
  • Your last-read position and theme are saved locally, so you can continue where you left off.

    • Three routes through it, and how to choose

    The chapters are ordered so that each one depends only on what came before, which means there are three genuinely different ways through and choosing one is the first useful decision. The degree route is all thirty-two chapters in order, and it is the right route if your time horizon is measured in years and your goal is a broad foundation. Its cost is that it front-loads material you will not need for two years — virtual memory, compilers, linear algebra — and its benefit is that you never hit a chapter that says "you must already know this" and do not. The job route is four to seven chapters chosen for a specific role, taken in dependency order and skipping everything else: front-end, back-end, databases, networking and testing for a web developer; cloud, containers and delivery for a platform engineer; databases, consistency and data engineering for a data engineer. Its benefit is that you reach competent work in months rather than years. Its cost is that the gaps are real and you will discover them as a specific kind of confusion — you will be using a word whose definition is chapter 11 and you will not know it. The reference route is not reading but searching: use the search box, land in a chapter, read the section and the exercises, and leave. This works and it is how a large fraction of readers will use the library, and the one thing to know about it is that a chapter read out of order is roughly half as useful, because the depth of each section assumes the vocabulary the earlier chapters established. Then how to actually work through a chapter, because this is where the depth is either realised or wasted. Read the prose, not the code. The code samples are dense and compressed — they show a shape, not a tutorial — and a reader who starts with them gets the shape without the reason and cannot adapt when the reason matters. Write the exercises out in full, not in your head. Every exercise is designed to produce something, and a chapter you read and did not produce anything from has been read and not learned; the debugging chapter's finding is that producing an artefact is what makes it retrievable, and an exercise done mentally leaves nothing to retrieve. When you get stuck, do not skip. A skipped exercise is a hole that later exercises assume is filled, and the symptom is not feeling stuck in chapter nine but feeling confused in chapter fourteen. And come back. The single highest-value thing about a reference route is that the chapters are written to be re-readable, and a chapter that made no sense in month one often makes complete sense in month nine once you have met the problem it is about.

    The conventions, and what each label means

    The library uses a small set of labels consistently across all thirty-two chapters, and knowing them means you can tell what kind of thing you are reading and what kind of thing you are being asked to do without the text having to say so each time. Numbering runs chapter, section, subsection — chapter 14, section 14.3, subsection 14.3.2 — and every one of those is a linkable address, which means a specific claim can be pointed at rather than paraphrased, and that matters for a book of this size because the discussions refer back to each other constantly. A code sample is a specification, not a tutorial. It is written to be correct and complete in isolation and to be read, not run; it shows a shape or a mechanism, and the prose around it is where the explanation lives. A callout is a category. A tip is a practice that will save you time, stated without argument because it is uncontroversial. A warn is a mistake that is common, expensive, and invisible — the ones worth the most attention, because a mistake you would notice is a mistake you will fix. A note is context: something true that is not part of the argument, a caveat, a version-specific detail. Reading them selectively is reasonable; reading only the tips is not, because the warnings are where the mistakes are. An exercise block is the specification of something you should build, and it is marked as a distinct block so it is visually obvious where the reading stops and the work starts — a chapter you have not exercised is a chapter you have read. Then the properties of the thing itself, which are worth knowing because they change what you can do with it. It works from disk with no server. Every page is a single HTML file plus two shared assets, which means it opens by double-clicking, works on a plane, works on a locked-down machine where installing anything is not possible, and never stops working because a service is down or a URL changed. It is searchable across all chapters at once, and the search is client-side, so it is instant and it works offline. Your position and your theme are stored locally in your browser, which is why a page you closed is where you left it when you come back, and it also means the state is per-browser — clearing site data resets it, and there is no account and nothing stored anywhere else. And no page depends on a third party. There is no CDN, no web font fetched from a font service, no analytics and no script from another origin, which means a page renders identically on a machine with no outbound network access at all, and which is also why it works eight years from now without anyone maintaining it.

The right mindset

This section frames programming as a practiced skill rather than a memorisation task. Study a little every day, expect confusion as normal and even useful, and cement each idea by explaining it aloud or writing it out in your own words. That spaced, active practice is what actually converts reading into ability.

The rule hidden in this whole degree: programming is not about memorising syntax — it is about breaking problems into small, solvable pieces and communicating ideas precisely. Everything else (languages, frameworks, tools) is just vocabulary.

  • Practice > watching. Type every example yourself. Then change it and break it on purpose.
  • Read error messages like they matter — they usually tell you the exact line and reason.
  • Confusion is progress. The moment you struggle is the moment your brain is wiring new circuits.
  • Repetition with spacing. Revisit chapters after 1 day, 7 days, 30 days. This is how memory becomes permanent.
  • Teach to learn. Explain each topic to an imaginary student aloud. If you can’t explain it, you haven’t learned it yet.

Practice the basic workflow of editing a file, running a command, and committing a change until it feels automatic. Fluency here makes every subsequent exercise dramatically easier.

Exercise 0 — Set your 10-week rhythm

A realistic bachelor’s pace: 3–4 focused hours per day. Structure each study day as: 30 min review of yesterday → 60 min new lesson → 60 min hands-on exercises → 30 min write a summary + glossary entry. Write summaries in your own words; it forces understanding.

1 · How Computers and Code Actually Work

This chapter explains the fundamental way machines store and process information, from binary digits up to the CPU executing instructions. It covers how human-readable source code is translated into machine language through compilation or interpretation. This foundation supports every later topic, so the concepts here recur constantly throughout the course.

1.1 Bits and bytes — the atoms of information1.2 The four main hardware parts1.3 From human language to machine language1.4 Key terms you’ll meet forever

Before you write a single line of code, understand the machine you’re talking to. Everything in software engineering eventually reduces to this layer.

1.1 Bits and bytes — the atoms of information

Bits and bytes are the smallest units of digital information, with a bit holding a single 0 or 1 and a byte grouping eight bits. Text, numbers, and images are all encoded into these binary patterns, for example through character encodings like ASCII and UTF-8. Understanding how values are represented as binary helps you reason about data types, storage limits, and file formats.

A computer stores everything as binary: a stream of 0s and 1s. Each single 0 or 1 is called a bit (from binary digit). A group of 8 bits is a byte.

Why binary? Physically, a bit is something like a tiny switch — is there voltage or not? Is the tiny magnet polarised north or south? On/off states are cheap, reliable and endlessly repeatable.

  • 1 bit → 2 possibilities (0 or 1)
  • 1 byte → 2⁸ = 256 possibilities
  • 4 bytes → 2³² ≈ 4.3 billion possibilities (this is why a 32-bit number maxes out there)

Numbers in binary: 0 = 0, 1 = 1, 2 = 10, 3 = 11, 4 = 100, 5 = 101. Each digit’s place value doubles: …64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.

Letter = number. Text is stored as numbers using a code table. Two you must know: ASCII (7-bit, 128 chars — old but everywhere) and Unicode/UTF-8 (covers every writing system on Earth; the default for the modern web). In UTF-8 the letter "A" is byte 65.

Why eight, and what the choice actually bought

A byte is eight bits because eight is the smallest power of two above the handful of states early hardware could distinguish cheaply — and choosing a power of two is not an accident of convenience, it is the reason bits are added rather than multiplied. A bit can distinguish two states, two bits four, three bits eight, and because each doubling requires one more physical element, the size of a representable value grows exactly when hardware doubles, so no value ever wastes a combination. It is also why the usual sizes are multiples of eight and why 2^8 = 256 keeps appearing: the range of a uint8 is 0 to 255 because the zero is included in the count. That last detail is the single most common off-by-one in a beginner's mental model — 256 combinations is 256 distinct values starting at zero, not 256 values above zero.

Then how the same eight bits mean different things, which is the real content of the topic and the reason it is not merely arithmetic. A byte is a unit of storage; its meaning is assigned by whatever program interprets it. The number 65 is the same eight bits whether it is the letter A, a temperature, a command byte, or one pixel's red channel — and nothing in the bits records which. So every format is a convention that pairs a layout with a meaning: ASCII assigns the first 128 slots to characters, UTF-8 extends that encoding to the whole Unicode range using more bytes when a character needs them, a floating-point format uses the bits for a sign, an exponent and a mantissa, and a compressed format uses them for whatever its algorithm decides. Consequence worth internalising: two programs agree on a file only if they agree on the convention, which is why an off-by-one in a length prefix, a text file saved as UTF-8 and read as Latin-1, and a JPEG header interpreted by the wrong decoder all produce garbage rather than an error.

/* Why eight bits. */
const WHY_EIGHT = {
  reason: 'the smallest power of two above what early hardware could distinguish cheaply',
  critical: 'a power of two, because it is why bits are ADDED rather than multiplied',
  mechanism: 'each doubling of states needs exactly one more physical element, so the
    representable range grows exactly when hardware doubles and no value wastes a combination',
  sizings: 'the usual sizes are multiples of eight, and 2^8 = 256 keeps appearing',
  offByOne: 'uint8 spans 0 to 255 - 256 combinations is 256 distinct values STARTING AT ZERO',
};

/* A byte is a storage unit; meaning is assigned by whoever interprets it. */
const SAME_BITS = {
  example: 'the number 65 is the same eight bits as the letter A, a temperature,
    a command byte, or one pixels red channel',
  nothingInTheBitsRecordsWhich: true,
  therefore: 'a format is a convention pairing a layout with a meaning',
  conventions: {
    ascii: 'the first 128 slots are characters',
    'utf-8': 'extends ASCII, using more bytes when a character needs them',
    float: 'sign, exponent and mantissa',
    compressed: 'whatever the algorithm decides',
  },
  consequence: 'two programs agree on a file only if they agree on the convention',
  garbageRatherThanAnError: ['an off-by-one in a length prefix',
    'a UTF-8 file read as Latin-1', 'a JPEG header given to the wrong decoder'],
};

Bytes as a unit of measurement, and the arithmetic that trips people

Once bytes are a unit, prefixes apply, and the arithmetic is worth doing carefully because a factor-of-1024 slip produces a bug that works on the developer's data. One kilobyte is 1024 bytes, because a storage device addresses bytes in binary and the next addressable step up is a power of two — the prefix here describes the addressing, not a decimal quantity. Megabyte, gigabyte, terabyte follow the same rule, which is why a "500 GB" disk shows as about 465 GB in an operating system: 500 000 000 000 bytes divided by 1024 three times. The exception is that manufacturers use decimal prefixes for capacity and operating systems use binary ones, so the mismatch is permanent and the honest response is to know both numbers rather than to suspect a bug. Characters are not bytes. One ASCII character is one byte; one character in the basic multilingual plane in UTF-8 is two or three bytes; an emoji outside it is four. So "a string of 10 000 characters" tells you nothing about the bytes unless you know the encoding, which is why a database column sized in characters can overflow one sized in bytes — a real and recurring bug when a column is sized for Latin text and receives Greek, Japanese or emoji.

Then the three places the difference bites and how to reason about each. Rates versus sizes. A transfer rate is bits per second and a file size is bytes, so the download time is bytes * 8 / bits-per-second; a "100 megabit" connection moves 12.5 MB per second, not 100, and forgetting the factor of eight is the classic estimate error. Memory addresses versus file sizes. An address counts elements, and whether an element is a byte, a word or a cache line depends on the machine and the operation — so "100 million units" is meaningless without saying units. Bits versus bytes in a data structure. A bit can hold two states and is the right unit for a flag or a permission; a boolean in most languages occupies far more than a bit because of alignment and because the language must be able to represent an unset state; and a set of eight independent booleans packed into one byte is a real technique that turns eight bytes into one. Then the practical discipline this chapter is for: when a program allocates, know which it is doing — len(s) in Python is characters, len(s.encode('utf-8')) is bytes, and the difference is the bug you will meet.

/* Prefixes describe addressing, not decimal quantity. */
const PREFIXES = {
  kb: '1024 bytes', mb: '1024 KB', gb: '1024 MB', tb: '1024 GB',
  why: 'a storage device addresses bytes in binary, so the next addressable step is a power of two',
  permanentMismatch: 'manufacturers use decimal, operating systems use binary',
  example: '500 000 000 000 bytes shows as about 465 GB',
  response: 'know both numbers rather than suspecting a bug',
};

/* Characters are not bytes. */
const ENCODING_SIZES = {
  ascii: '1 byte per character',
  'utf-8 basic multilingual plane': '2 or 3 bytes per character',
  'utf-8 outside the BMP (emoji)': '4 bytes per character',
  consequence: 'a string of 10000 characters says nothing about the bytes',
  realBug: 'a column sized in characters, sized for Latin text, overflowing on Greek, Japanese or emoji',
};

/* Three places the difference bites. */
const BITES = [
  { c: 'rates versus sizes',
    fact: 'a rate is bits per second, a size is bytes',
    formula: 'seconds = bytes * 8 / bits_per_second',
    classicError: 'a 100 megabit connection moves 12.5 MB per second, not 100' },
  { c: 'memory addresses versus file sizes',
    fact: 'an address counts elements, and an element may be a byte, a word or a cache line',
    conclusion: '100 million units is meaningless without saying units' },
  { c: 'bits versus bytes in a data structure',
    oneBit: 'right for a flag or a permission',
    booleanReality: 'occupies far more than a bit - alignment, plus the language must represent unset',
    packing: 'eight independent booleans in one byte is a real technique: eight bytes become one' },
];
const DISCIPLINE = 'when a program allocates, know which it is doing - len(s) in Python is characters, len(s.encode(utf-8)) is bytes, and the difference is the bug you will meet';

Exercise 1.1

Convert these to decimal: 1010, 1111, 100000 (hint: 2⁵=32). Then convert decimal 42 to binary. Answers at the end of the chapter.

1.2 The four main hardware parts

This topic covers the four core hardware components shared by every computer: the CPU that executes instructions, RAM that holds working data, storage for persistent files, and input and output devices. Each part has a distinct speed and purpose, which explains why programs spend time waiting on disk or memory. Knowing these roles helps you reason about performance before you even write code.

The four parts and the one number that orders them

CPU, memory, storage, input/output — and the number that makes them comparable is latency, not speed. The parts differ by one to five orders of magnitude, and keeping them straight in your head is what lets you answer "why is this slow" without running a profiler. Roughly: CPU registers and cache are measured in nanoseconds; main memory in tens of nanoseconds; SSD in hundreds of microseconds; spinning disk or network in milliseconds. So a CPU can perform hundreds of memory operations in the time one SSD read takes, and a program that touches every element once per pass is bound by memory bandwidth rather than by arithmetic — which is why an O(n log n) sort on a million elements can be faster than an O(n) pass that reads each element from disk. Time to read 1 MB, as a mental constant, is about 100 microseconds from RAM and about 10 milliseconds from an SSD: a factor of a hundred, on a single operation, with no code change at all.

Then what each part is actually responsible for, because the misconceptions here cause bad designs. The CPU executes instructions from a program counter and has a small, very fast cache hierarchy feeding it; its performance is limited by instruction count, by how often it stalls waiting for memory, and by branch misprediction. Memory is volatile, is addressed directly, is managed by the hardware for capacity but by the language runtime for lifetime, and is where the working set lives — so a data structure's real cost is usually its memory footprint and locality, not its arithmetic. Storage is persistent, is accessed in blocks rather than bytes, and is dramatically faster when sequential than when random, which is why index structure and page layout dominate database design and why a scan of contiguous data beats an indexed lookup of scattered data at small sizes. Input and output is where a user feels the system: a display refresh at 60 Hz is 16.7 milliseconds, and a design that requires three sequential round trips to the server to draw a frame has spent more time waiting than a display frame costs — the arithmetic that makes 100 milliseconds feel slow and 16 milliseconds not.

/* The number that orders the parts is latency, not speed. */
const LATENCY = {
  'cpu register and cache': 'nanoseconds',
  'main memory': 'tens of nanoseconds',
  ssd: 'hundreds of microseconds',
  'spinning disk or network': 'milliseconds',
  consequence: 'the CPU performs hundreds of memory operations in the time one SSD read takes',
  therefore: 'touching every element once per pass is bound by memory bandwidth, not arithmetic',
  paradox: 'O(n log n) on a million elements can beat an O(n) pass that reads each element from disk',
  mentalConstant: { read1mbFromRam: 'about 100 microseconds', read1mbFromSsd: 'about 10 milliseconds',
    factor: 100, codeChangeRequired: 'none' },
};

/* What each part is responsible for. */
const PARTS = [
  { p: 'cpu', does: 'executes instructions from a program counter',
    fedBy: 'a small, very fast cache hierarchy',
    limitedBy: ['instruction count', 'stalls waiting for memory', 'branch misprediction'] },
  { p: 'memory', is: 'volatile, directly addressed',
    managedBy: 'hardware for capacity, language runtime for lifetime',
    holds: 'the working set',
    consequence: 'a data structures real cost is usually memory footprint and locality, not arithmetic' },
  { p: 'storage', is: 'persistent, accessed in blocks not bytes',
    asymmetry: 'dramatically faster sequential than random',
    drives: ['index structure', 'page layout', 'why a scan beats an indexed lookup at small sizes'] },
  { p: 'input and output', is: 'where the user feels the system',
    arithmetic: 'a 60Hz display frame is 16.7ms, so three sequential server round trips to draw a frame cost more than a frame',
    consequence: '100ms feels slow and 16ms does not',
  },
];

How the parts interact, and the four questions that explain almost all slowness

Components are not independent and the interactions explain most real performance problems. The memory hierarchy is the whole story of cache. When the CPU reads a value it checks L1, then L2, then L3, then memory — each larger and slower — and a cache miss costs roughly as much as a hundred hits, which is why an algorithm's constant factor is usually dominated by memory access pattern and not by arithmetic. A loop that reads an array sequentially is almost free in cache terms; the same loop with a stride larger than a cache line touches every cache line for one useful element, and the ratio is the reason a nested-loop matrix routine can be twenty times slower with no change in the algorithm. Storage is slower still, and is batched. A single 4 KB disk read is a seek plus a rotation plus a transfer; a thousand 4 KB reads cost a thousand seeks, while one 4 MB sequential read costs a handful — so batching reads is worth far more than making them individually faster, and it is the principle behind every buffer, page cache and write-coalescing design in existence.

Then the four questions, in the order they resolve a symptom fastest, because this is the diagnostic sequence this chapter is really for. Is the program CPU-bound or waiting? A profiler's utilisation number answers it: high CPU means arithmetic; low CPU with a slow operation means I/O, a lock, or a sleep. Which operation, and how many times? A thousand small calls that each cost a millisecond is a different problem from one call costing a second, and the fix is entirely different — batching in the first case, optimising the query in the second. What is the access pattern? Sequential, random, or strided, because only the first one is cheap and the difference is two orders of magnitude. And how much data is resident? A working set larger than cache turns every pass into a stream from memory, which is where the classic fix is to make the data smaller rather than the code faster: fewer bytes per element, better locality, or processing in blocks. And the habit worth forming: measure first, because each of those four questions has a different answer and guessing wrong means optimising the wrong one — and a change that made the code shorter and the product slower is a real outcome that ships.

/* Cache is the story of memory behaviour. */
const CACHE = {
  chain: 'L1, then L2, then L3, then memory - each larger and slower',
  missCost: 'roughly as much as a hundred hits',
  therefore: 'a constant factor is usually dominated by memory access pattern, not arithmetic',
  sequence: 'sequential array reads are almost free in cache terms',
  stride: 'a stride larger than a cache line touches every line for one useful element',
  example: 'a nested-loop matrix routine twenty times slower with no algorithm change',
};

/* Batching beats faster primitives. */
const BATCHING = {
  cost: 'one 4KB disk read is a seek plus a rotation plus a transfer',
  vs: 'a thousand 4KB reads cost a thousand seeks, while one 4MB sequential read costs a handful',
  therefore: 'batching is worth far more than making each operation faster',
  underlies: ['buffers', 'page cache', 'write coalescing'],
};

/* Four questions, in resolution order. */
const DIAGNOSE = [
  { q: 'is it CPU-bound or waiting', answer: 'profiler utilisation',
    read: 'high CPU means arithmetic; low CPU with a slow operation means I/O, a lock or a sleep' },
  { q: 'which operation, how many times', why: 'a thousand 1ms calls and one 1s call are different problems',
    fixDiffers: 'batching versus optimising the query' },
  { q: 'what is the access pattern', values: ['sequential', 'random', 'strided'],
    fact: 'only the first is cheap, and the difference is two orders of magnitude' },
  { q: 'how much data is resident', symptom: 'a working set larger than cache makes every pass a stream from memory',
    fix: 'make the data smaller rather than the code faster - fewer bytes per element, better locality, or processing in blocks' },
];
const HABIT = 'measure first: each question has a different answer, and guessing wrong means optimising the wrong one - and a change that made the code shorter and the product slower is a real outcome that ships';
PartAnalogyJobNotes
CPU (Central Processing Unit)The chef in a kitchenExecutes instructions one at a timeFast but can only keep a handful of values in reach (registers)
RAM (Memory)The counter-top workspaceHolds running programs + their dataFast, but wiped when power is lost (volatile)
Storage (SSD / hard disk)The pantry/cupboardsKeeps files permanentlySlow-ish but non-volatile
I/O devicesCustomers & deliveriesTalk to the outside world (keyboard, screen, network)Handled via buses and device drivers

A program runs by being copied from storage into RAM, then the CPU fetches instructions one by one and executes them (this is the famous fetch-decode-execute cycle, repeated billions of times per second).

"Programs are data too." A compiled program sitting on disk is just a very long sequence of bytes. The CPU is a machine that reads those bytes as instructions; your photo files are bytes it reads as pictures. Same storage, different interpretation.

1.3 From human language to machine language

This section traces how source code becomes executable machine code. Compiled languages translate the entire program ahead of time into machine code, while interpreted languages translate and run it line by line through a runtime. Concepts like compilation, interpretation, bytecode, and just-in-time compilation differentiate these paths and shape each language’s behaviour.

Humans write high-level code. CPUs only understand machine code. Between them travel several layers:

  1. High-level language (Python, Java, C, JavaScript) — readable by humans.
  2. Assembly — barely-readable mnemonic version of machine code (mov eax, 5).
  3. Machine code — raw bytes the CPU executes.

Two ways to travel that distance:

The spectrum, and why the compiled/interpreted split is the wrong axis

Almost everybody learns this as two categories, and the split is a useful first approximation that becomes actively misleading once you need to reason about performance. The better model is a spectrum of how much work is done before the first line runs and when translation happens. A compiler that emits native machine code ahead of time does all translation up front. A runtime that compiles to bytecode and then interprets that does translation when the program starts and executes the translator's output. A just-in-time compiler does translation while the program runs, compiling a function the first time it is hot. A hybrid compiles some code ahead of time and JITs the rest. The labels "compiled" and "interpreted" describe the endpoint of a process rather than a property of a language, and JavaScript, Java, C#, Python and PHP all sit in the middle rather than on one side.

Then what the model is actually for, because the model predicts four things that matter and nothing else. Startup time — ahead-of-time compilation pays a cost before the first line; an interpreter pays a smaller one but a larger per-operation cost; a JIT pays the largest up front cost and then operates at near-native speed, which is why the first call in a hot path is slow and the hundredth is not. Peak throughput — the JIT and AOT ends win, and the margin over an interpreter is between ten and fifty times on numerical work. Portability — bytecode is the portable form, which is why a JVM or a .NET runtime can execute the same artefact on any platform with that runtime. Where errors surface. A compile-time error is found before anything runs, an interpreter finds it when the line is reached, and a JIT finds it the first time the function executes — which is why "it worked until somebody hit that path" is a normal and predictable property of a dynamically compiled runtime rather than a defect.

/* Compiled versus interpreted is the wrong axis. */
const SPECTRUM = [
  { m: 'ahead-of-time native compilation', when: 'all translation before the program runs' },
  { m: 'bytecode plus interpretation', when: 'translation at start; the translators output is executed' },
  { m: 'just-in-time compilation', when: 'a function is compiled the first time it becomes hot' },
  { m: 'hybrid', when: 'some code ahead of time, the rest JITed' },
];
const MIDDLE_SITTING_LANGUAGES = ['JavaScript', 'Java', 'C#', 'Python', 'PHP'];
const LABELS_DESCRIBE = 'the endpoint of a process, not a property of a language';

/* What the model predicts. */
const PREDICTS = [
  { p: 'startup time',
    aot: 'pays a cost before the first line',
    interpreted: 'pays a smaller one, but a larger per-operation cost',
    jit: 'pays the largest cost up front, then operates near-native',
    explains: 'the first call in a hot path is slow and the hundredth is not' },
  { p: 'peak throughput', winner: 'AOT and JIT',
    margin: 'ten to fifty times over an interpreter on numerical work' },
  { p: 'portability', mechanism: 'bytecode is the portable form',
    consequence: 'a JVM or .NET runtime executes the same artefact on any platform with that runtime' },
  { p: 'where errors surface', ranked: ['compile time - before anything runs',
    'interpretation - when the line is reached',
    'JIT - the first time the function executes'],
    reframes: 'it worked until somebody hit that path is a normal property of a dynamic runtime, not a defect' },
];

What each choice costs you, and the hybrid that won

The three pure designs each lose something specific, and the losses explain why the industry converged. AOT-only pays startup and compile time on every deploy, cannot respond to the workload's actual shape, and makes reflection and dynamic loading awkward — it is the right choice for a predictable, long-running, latency-sensitive binary and a poor one for anything whose load pattern is unknown. Interpreter-only has the best startup and the worst throughput, which is fine for a shell, a small script or a system whose time is dominated by I/O, and unacceptable for anything doing real computation in a loop. JIT-only gets both throughput and startup at the cost of a warm-up period during which the code runs slowly, of compiling code that may turn out to run once, and of a compiler being a full part of the runtime with its own bugs, its own memory usage and its own deoptimisation paths when an assumption it made turns out to be wrong.

Then the hybrid that nearly everything now uses, and the specific reason each part is where it is. AOT for the code that is known and hot — the standard library, the module loader, the parts that run on every invocation — because compiling it once per install beats compiling it per launch. Bytecode as the distribution format, because it is portable and because it is a stable, compact form that a runtime can verify and cache. A JIT for code that becomes hot, because the only way to know what deserves optimising is to watch what actually runs, and a profile from production beats any static guess. And a deoptimisation escape hatch, because a JIT's optimisations rest on assumptions, and when one breaks it must be able to back out and re-enter the interpreter — which is why the worst performance surprises in these runtimes happen on the third call rather than the first, and why a benchmark that calls a function once measures the wrong thing. The practical takeaway for choosing a language for a project: decide which of the four things you are optimising — startup, throughput, portability, or error-timing — and pick the design that wins it, because that is the only question the spectrum answers.

/* What each pure design loses. */
const TRADE = [
  { d: 'ahead-of-time only',
    loses: ['compile time on every deploy', 'responding to the workloads actual shape',
            'reflection and dynamic loading'],
    rightFor: 'a predictable, long-running, latency-sensitive binary',
    wrongFor: 'anything whose load pattern is unknown' },
  { d: 'interpreter only',
    has: ['best startup', 'worst throughput'],
    fineFor: ['a shell', 'a small script', 'a system whose time is dominated by I/O'],
    unacceptable: 'anything doing real computation in a loop' },
  { d: 'JIT only',
    gains: ['throughput', 'good startup after warm-up'],
    costs: ['a warm-up period where code runs slowly',
            'compiling code that may run once',
            'a full compiler inside the runtime with its own bugs, memory and deoptimisation paths'] },
];

/* The converged hybrid, part by part. */
const HYBRID = [
  { part: 'ahead-of-time for known-hot code', instances: ['the standard library', 'the module loader'],
    why: 'compiling once per install beats compiling per launch' },
  { part: 'bytecode as the distribution format', why: ['portable', 'stable and compact',
    'verifiable and cacheable by a runtime'] },
  { part: 'a JIT for code that becomes hot',
    why: 'the only way to know what deserves optimising is to watch what runs - a production profile beats any static guess' },
  { part: 'a deoptimisation escape hatch',
    why: 'JIT optimisations rest on assumptions, and a broken one must back out and re-enter the interpreter',
    symptom: 'worst performance surprises happen on the third call rather than the first',
    benchmarkTrap: 'a benchmark calling a function once measures the wrong thing' },
];
const CHOOSING = 'decide which of startup, throughput, portability or error-timing you are optimising, and pick the design that wins it - that is the only question the spectrum answers';
Compiled (e.g. C, C++, Go, Rust)Interpreted (e.g. Python, JS, Ruby)
Translation stepA compiler converts the whole program to machine code before runningAn interpreter reads and runs source line-by-line (or via a virtual machine)
SpeedUsually faster at run timeUsually slower, but portable
Error timingMany errors caught at compile timeErrors appear at run time
Dev loopEdit → compile → runEdit → run

Python is technically bytecode-compiled then interpreted by its virtual machine. For now, "interpreted, edit-and-run" is the mental model you need.

1.4 Key terms you’ll meet forever

This section defines the vocabulary every later chapter assumes: the operating system that manages resources, a process as a running program, and abstraction as hiding complexity behind a simple interface. These terms are the shared language of software engineering. Understanding them early means you never have to pause later chapters over basic wording.

  • Operating system — the boss program that manages hardware and runs other programs, protecting them from each other.
  • Process — one running instance of a program.
  • Instruction set — the fixed list of operations a CPU knows (add, load, store, branch, …).
  • Compiler / Interpreter — translation tools (above).
  • Abstraction — hiding messy detail behind a clean interface. Computer science is essentially the art of stacking abstractions.

The vocabulary, stated so it survives contact with a real system

These terms are worth defining precisely, because the imprecision is what produces arguments that cannot be resolved. The operating system is the program that owns the hardware and arbitrates access to it: it schedules processes onto cores, gives each an address space, provides the file and socket abstractions, and enforces whatever isolation the protection model provides. It is a resource manager and an isolation boundary, and every one of its jobs is a place where two programs that wanted the same thing must be made to wait or be prevented. A process is a running program together with its own address space, its own file descriptors, and its own copy of everything it has allocated. A thread is an execution context inside a process, sharing that process's address space and files. That single sentence contains most of what is confusing: two threads in one process can read and write the same memory without any system call, which is why shared state is cheap and why the resulting bugs have no memory barrier to stop them. Abstraction is hiding complexity behind an interface that is easier to reason about, and its whole purpose is to let a programmer be wrong about the layer underneath without consequence — which is a property with a failure mode, because an abstraction leaks exactly when its assumptions are violated.

Then the four terms that carry the most weight later in the book, because everything from databases to compilers depends on them. Resource is anything finite that a program consumes and that someone must decide how to divide — a lock, a file handle, a connection, a block of memory. The reason this matters is that resource exhaustion is the failure mode that turns a small bug into an outage, and the discipline is that every resource is acquired in exactly one place and released in exactly one place, including on the error path. State is anything a future result depends on, and the distinction that carries the most weight is between visible and hidden state: visible state is what a caller can observe and must be told about, hidden state is what a program remembers and keeps to itself, and a design in which both are entangled cannot be reasoned about because any change to either might change the other. Concurrency is more than one thing happening at the same time, and its entire difficulty is ordering: without ordering guarantees, two operations that appear simultaneous produce a result dependent on timing, and a result that depends on timing is a result nobody can test. And the runtime — the environment a program executes in, as distinct from the language it is written in — which is where global state like a clock, a random source, a network connection, the filesystem and the environment variables actually live, and which is why testing gets easier the moment you notice which of those a function touches.

/* Defined precisely, because imprecision produces unresolvable arguments. */
const OS = {
  is: 'the program that owns the hardware and arbitrates access to it',
  jobs: ['schedules processes onto cores', 'gives each an address space',
         'provides file and socket abstractions', 'enforces the isolation the protection model provides'],
  nature: 'a resource manager and an isolation boundary',
  consequence: 'every job is a place where two programs wanting the same thing must wait or be prevented',
};
const PROCESS_VS_THREAD = {
  process: 'a running program plus its own address space, file descriptors and allocations',
  thread: 'an execution context inside a process, sharing its address space and files',
  singleSentenceConsequence: 'two threads can read and write the same memory with no system call',
  whyThatMatters: 'shared state is cheap, and the resulting bugs have no memory barrier to stop them',
};

/* The four terms everything later depends on. */
const CORE = [
  { t: 'resource', is: 'anything finite a program consumes that someone must divide',
    instances: ['a lock', 'a file handle', 'a connection', 'a block of memory'],
    why: 'resource exhaustion turns a small bug into an outage',
    discipline: 'every resource acquired in exactly one place and released in exactly one place, including on the error path' },
  { t: 'state', is: 'anything a future result depends on',
    distinctionThatCarriesTheWeight: 'visible (a caller can observe it and must be told) versus hidden (the program remembers it)',
    consequence: 'a design where both are entangled cannot be reasoned about, because any change to either might change the other' },
  { t: 'concurrency', is: 'more than one thing at the same time',
    entireDifficulty: 'ordering',
    withoutOrdering: 'two apparently simultaneous operations produce a timing-dependent result',
    consequence: 'a timing-dependent result is a result nobody can test' },
  { t: 'runtime', is: 'the environment a program executes in, as distinct from the language it is written in',
    livesThere: ['a clock', 'a random source', 'a network connection', 'the filesystem', 'environment variables'],
    whyItMatters: 'testing gets easier the moment you notice which of those a function touches' },
];

/* The nature of abstraction. */
const ABSTRACTION = {
  is: 'hiding complexity behind an interface that is easier to reason about',
  purpose: 'letting a programmer be wrong about the layer underneath without consequence',
  failureMode: 'it leaks exactly when its assumptions are violated',
};

The pairs that are constantly confused, and how to tell them apart

Several of these terms get used interchangeably in conversation and are not the same thing, and the confusion causes arguments that cannot be resolved by assertion. A program versus a process. The program is the bytes on disk — the artefact you ship. The process is that artefact brought to life by the operating system, with an address space, open files, environment variables, a working directory and credentials. The same program run twice is two processes with different state, which is why "the app crashed" can be true of one and not the other, and why a restart is a real fix rather than a superstition. A thread versus a process. A thread is a unit of execution inside a process and shares everything; a process shares nothing and needs explicit communication. The consequence is a straight trade: threads are cheap to create and expensive to get right, processes are expensive to create and safe by default — which is why runtimes default to one thread and why every concurrent design is a decision somebody made deliberately. An API versus an interface. An interface is the shape a thing has; an API is the set of calls it offers. A library can have a rich interface and a single-function API, and callers of the API are insulated from everything behind it, which is the entire point of having one. An interpreter versus a virtual machine. An interpreter executes source directly; a virtual machine executes an intermediate representation for a specific instruction set. The distinction matters mainly because a VM has an instruction set you can inspect, profile and optimise for, and because "runs on the JVM" is a portability promise that "runs on an interpreter" is not.

Then the terms whose real content is a property rather than a noun, because describing a language with them is a category error. Compiled versus interpreted code. The point to internalise is that compilation is a translation, not a speed-up: a compiler is a program whose output is another program, and the eventual speed comes from having done the translation once rather than on every run. Object-oriented versus functional. These describe how a program is composed — around mutable objects exchanging messages, or around functions and immutable data — and real programs are mostly one with a bit of the other, so treat the label as a description of the dominant style rather than a property of the language. Static versus dynamic typing. Not a spectrum of safety but a placement of the check: before the program runs, or at the point of use. The honest comparison is not "one is safe" but "one moves a class of error earlier and pays for it in verbosity". And a bug versus a feature is not a technical distinction at all — which is exactly why it is worth naming that it is a business decision, and why the two get confused inside a team that has not agreed who decides.

/* Pairs used interchangeably that are not the same thing. */
const PROGRAM_VS_PROCESS = {
  program: 'the bytes on disk - the artefact you ship',
  process: 'that artefact brought to life by the operating system',
  processCarries: ['an address space', 'open files', 'environment variables',
                   'a working directory', 'credentials'],
  consequence: 'the same program run twice is two processes with different state',
  reframe: 'the app crashed can be true of one process and not the other, so a restart is a real fix rather than a superstition',
};
const THREAD_VS_PROCESS = {
  thread: 'a unit of execution inside a process, sharing everything',
  process: 'shares nothing, needs explicit communication',
  trade: ['threads are cheap to create and expensive to get right',
          'processes are expensive to create and safe by default'],
  whyItMatters: 'runtimes default to one thread, so every concurrent design is a deliberate decision',
};
const API_VS_INTERFACE = {
  interface: 'the shape a thing has',
  api: 'the set of calls it offers',
  illustration: 'a library can have a rich interface and a single-function API',
  point: 'API callers are insulated from everything behind it, which is the entire point',
};
const INTERPRETER_VS_VM = {
  interpreter: 'executes source directly',
  virtualMachine: 'executes an intermediate representation for a specific instruction set',
  whyItMatters: 'a VM has an instruction set you can inspect, profile and optimise for',
  promise: 'runs on the JVM is a portability promise; runs on an interpreter is not',
};

/* Terms whose content is a property, not a noun. */
const PROPERTIES = [
  { t: 'compiled versus interpreted', realContent: 'compilation is a translation, not a speed-up',
    detail: 'a compiler is a program whose output is another program; the speed comes from translating once rather than on every run' },
  { t: 'object-oriented versus functional', describes: 'how a program is composed',
    sides: ['mutable objects exchanging messages', 'functions and immutable data'],
    reframe: 'real programs are mostly one with a bit of the other - a description of dominant style, not a property of the language' },
  { t: 'static versus dynamic typing', notA: 'spectrum of safety',
    actually: 'placement of the check - before the program runs, or at the point of use',
    honestComparison: 'one moves a class of error earlier and pays for it in verbosity' },
