2 · Setting Up Your Development Environment

This chapter walks you through installing and configuring the professional toolkit used for the whole course. You will set up a capable code editor, learn your way around a terminal, and install Python correctly so it runs from anywhere. A solid, verified setup removes the common beginner stumbling blocks before any real programming begins.

2.1 Your editor or IDE2.2 The terminal — your second home2.3 Install Python correctly2.4 Your first program — say hello three ways2.5 How to read an error — the superpower

Professionals almost never use websites to run code. You’ll set up the real toolkit a developer uses every day — and it’s the same trio in every company on Earth.

2.1 Your editor or IDE

This topic advises choosing one code editor or IDE and learning it thoroughly rather than switching constantly. Features like syntax highlighting, code completion, extensions, and keyboard shortcuts boost daily productivity. The power comes from deep familiarity with one tool, so invest time in its shortcuts and workspace customisation.

An IDE (Integrated Development Environment) bundles an editor, compiler, debugger and tools. You need one great editor, not five average ones.

ToolTypeGreat for
VS CodeEditor + extensionsEverything; the default choice of most engineers today (recommended)
PyCharmFull IDEPython-only work, academic courses
IntelliJ IDEAFull IDEJava / Kotlin
Vim / NeovimTerminal editorSpeed once you master it (optional, later)

What an editor is for, and why the defaults are wrong

An editor's job is not to let you type text — that is a text field. Its job is to make the error visible before you run it, and every feature of a good editor serves that. The defaults of a fresh install are wrong for that purpose for a specific reason: they assume you know what to look for. A formatter that reformats on save means the file is always in one style, so a diff shows only your logic and never an indentation argument. A linter that flags an unused import, a shadowed name, a comparison that is always true, or a bare exception catches the class of mistake that a compiler cannot — a except: that swallows every error, a variable assigned and never read, a mutable default argument — and it does so while you are typing rather than three weeks later. An interpreter or REPL attached to the editor means a variable's value is one click away, which converts a debugging session into an inspection. And version control integration means the diff is not a separate ritual: it is what you see every time you save.

Then the four settings worth changing on day one, each for a reason that will pay off within the week. Format on save, with a formatter configured — otherwise the file drifts between styles and every review begins with whitespace. Enable whitespace rendering, because indentation is syntax in Python and a stray space is an error you cannot see without it. Turn on error checking for the language, with the language server rather than the built-in syntax highlighting, because the language server knows what a name resolves to across files and can tell you a typo before you run anything. And set the interpreter explicitly if more than one is installed, because a virtual environment nobody selected produces ModuleNotFoundError for a package that is plainly installed — and it is the single most common confusing error in a first month. Then what to learn later rather than now: a proper debugger with breakpoints and stepping, because the workflow of guessing, running, reading a traceback, editing and repeating is slower than setting a breakpoint and looking at six variables; and a code formatter's own options, because it will reformat your code according to its opinions and fighting it wastes an afternoon.

/* The editors job. */
const EDITOR_JOB = {
  isNot: 'letting you type text - that is a text field',
  is: 'making the error visible before you run it',
  whyDefaultsAreWrong: 'they assume you already know what to look for',
  features: [
    { f: 'formatter on save', why: 'the file is always in one style, so a diff shows only logic' },
    { f: 'linter', catchesWhatTheCompilerCannot: ['a bare except that swallows every error',
      'a variable assigned and never read', 'a mutable default argument', 'a shadowed name'],
      when: 'while typing rather than three weeks later' },
    { f: 'attached interpreter or REPL', why: 'converts a debugging session into an inspection' },
    { f: 'version control integration', why: 'the diff is not a separate ritual, it is what you see on save' },
  ],
};

/* Day-one settings. */
const SETTINGS = [
  { s: 'format on save', with: 'a configured formatter', why: 'otherwise files drift and every review starts with whitespace' },
  { s: 'render whitespace', why: 'indentation is syntax in Python and a stray space is invisible without it' },
  { s: 'language server error checking', not: 'built-in syntax highlighting',
    why: 'the server resolves names across files and catches a typo before you run anything' },
  { s: 'set the interpreter explicitly', when: 'more than one is installed',
    symptom: 'ModuleNotFoundError for a package that is plainly installed',
    rank: 'the single most confusing error in a first month' },
];

/* Later, not now. */
const LATER = [
  { t: 'a real debugger', why: 'guessing, running, reading a traceback, editing and repeating is slower than a breakpoint and six variables' },
  { t: 'the formatters own options', why: 'it will reformat according to its opinions, and fighting it wastes an afternoon' },
];

What a real debugging session looks like with the right setup

With the settings above in place a bug investigation becomes a sequence rather than a guess, and it is worth walking one end to end because the sequence is the skill. Put the breakpoint where the value is first wrong, not where it was computed. This single choice removes most of the work, because the difference between the last correct value and the first incorrect one is exactly the question you were trying to answer. Then run and inspect: look at the variable, look at its type, look at two or three neighbours. A value that is None three frames up where it should be an object identifies the function that failed to return; a value that is right but of the wrong type identifies a conversion that never happened; a value that is correct here and wrong later identifies an in-place mutation nobody expected. Then step rather than print — each step costs milliseconds and shows the whole state, whereas each print costs a rerun and shows one value, so twenty prints and two steps is twenty reruns against one. And when the answer is not visible in the current function, break in the function that owns the data instead: ownership is almost always where the defect is, because that is where the invariant was established and then broken by somebody else's assumption.

Then the three editor capabilities that pay for themselves within a week and that beginners routinely postpone. Refactoring. Rename-symbol changes a name everywhere it is used and writes the files back, which turns a four-file, forty-occurrence rename from an afternoon into a keystroke — and, more usefully, removes the temptation to leave a variable called data2 behind. Extract-function turns a selected block into a named function, and doing it as a habit is what stops a function growing to two hundred lines. Go-to-definition and find-references. These are how you read code you did not write: definition answers "what does this name actually resolve to", and references answers "who else depends on this" — which is the question you need before changing a shared function, and the one that turns an hour of reading into two minutes. Version control integration. A diff view with blame on a line is the fastest way to answer "why is this like this": blame gives you the commit, the message and the author, and in a mature codebase the answer is usually already there. The discipline that makes all three worth having is small, frequent, explained commits, because a commit that changes one thing is reviewable and revertable while a commit that changes forty is neither — and the size of the commit is decided at the moment you make it, not afterwards.

/* A debugging session with the right setup, as a procedure. */
const DEBUG_SESSION = [
  { step: 1, do: 'put the breakpoint where the value is first wrong, not where it was computed',
    why: 'the gap between last correct and first incorrect is exactly the question you were trying to answer' },
  { step: 2, do: 'run and inspect - the variable, its type, and two or three neighbours',
    reads: [
      'None three frames up where an object belongs -> the function that failed to return',
      'right value, wrong type -> a conversion that never happened',
      'correct here and wrong later -> an in-place mutation nobody expected' ] },
  { step: 3, do: 'step rather than print',
    why: 'a step costs milliseconds and shows the whole state; a print costs a rerun and shows one value',
    arithmetic: 'twenty prints and two steps is twenty reruns against one' },
  { step: 4, do: 'when the answer is not visible in the current function, break in the function that owns the data',
    why: 'ownership is almost always where the defect is - where the invariant was established, then broken' },
];

/* Three capabilities beginners postpone. */
const CAPABILITIES = [
  { c: 'refactoring', items: ['rename-symbol', 'extract-function'],
    renameWins: 'a four-file, forty-occurrence rename from an afternoon into a keystroke',
    renameAlso: 'removes the temptation to leave a variable called data2 behind',
    extractWhy: 'doing it as a habit stops a function growing to two hundred lines' },
  { c: 'go-to-definition and find-references',
    definition: 'what does this name actually resolve to',
    references: 'who else depends on this - the question you need BEFORE changing a shared function',
    payoff: 'an hour of reading becomes two minutes' },
  { c: 'version control integration', feature: 'diff view with blame on a line',
    answers: 'why is this like this',
    mechanism: ['the commit', 'the commit message', 'the author'],
    note: 'in a mature codebase the answer is usually already there' },
];
const COMMIT_DISCIPLINE = {
  rule: 'small, frequent, explained commits',
  why: 'a commit that changes one thing is reviewable and revertable; one that changes forty is neither',
  timing: 'the size of the commit is decided at the moment you make it, not afterwards',
};
Minimum setup in VS Code for this course: install the Python extension and the Prettier formatter. Learn these shortcuts early: Ctrl+S save, Ctrl+/ comment line, Ctrl+P open file, Ctrl+F search in file.

2.2 The terminal — your second home

This topic introduces the terminal as the fastest and most scriptable way to interact with a computer. You learn core commands for navigating directories, listing and copying files, and running programs, such as cd, ls, cp, and mv, alongside commands that invoke the interpreter. These basics are used constantly throughout every later chapter.

The terminal takes text commands (ls, cd…) and runs them. It looks hostile, but it’s the fastest, most scriptable, and most powerful tool you have.

Essential commands (Windows PowerShell / Linux / macOS share these):

pwd            # print the folder you're in
ls / dir       # list files
cd folder      # change into a folder
cd ..          # go up one level
mkdir newdir   # create a folder
touch file.txt # create an empty file
rm file.txt    # delete a file
cat file.txt   # print a file's contents
python --version   # check Python installed
python hello.py    # run a Python program

Six commands that cover most of what a beginner does

The terminal is not a programming language and should not be learned as one. It needs a dozen concepts and six commands cover almost all beginner use. pwd prints the working directory, and the single most useful habit in the shell is running it whenever a command behaves unexpectedly — nearly every "it cannot find the file" is a wrong-directory problem. ls lists, and ls -la adds hidden files and details; the detail that matters is ls -l's permissions column, which is how a permission error becomes legible. cd changes directory, and the flag worth knowing is cd -, which returns to the previous one — worth more than it sounds, because the mistake it fixes is the one everybody makes. mkdir creates a directory, and the habit worth forming immediately is to create it and then enter it, because an empty directory that was never entered is a directory whose name was guessed. cat prints a file, and the pair of flags that changes everything are head and tail — a log file is conventionally large, and tail -f on one is the single most useful command in operations. And cp copies while mv moves, with cp -r for directories; the flag that matters is mv's refusal to overwrite, because a silent overwrite of the wrong file is unrecoverable.

Then the three concepts that turn the terminal from a list into a tool, and each of them removes a class of repetitive work. Pipes. One command's standard output becomes the next's standard input, so cat access.log | grep ERROR | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head answers "which errors are most common" without a script — and the discipline is that each stage must be independently runnable, so you can pipe the first two stages to head to see what is actually flowing before adding more. Redirection. > writes standard output to a file and truncates it, >> appends, 2> sends standard error and &> sends both — and the distinction between the first two is the one that produces the bug where an analysis script's output overwrote the input. Globbing. The shell expands *, ? and [] against filenames before the program ever sees them, which is why rm *.log is faster than a loop and why quoting matters: rm "*" is the command that deletes everything in a directory, and the fact that it requires quotation marks is the only thing standing between a beginner and a catastrophe.

Writing the command down, and the habits that keep a terminal safe

The habit that makes a terminal usable long after the six commands are learned is writing commands down. A plain text file of the commands that worked, one per line with a comment saying what each produced, is worth more than a notes application: it is searchable, it is diffable, it survives a reinstall, and it is the substrate for turning a sequence into a script. The progression is type it, then note it, then script it, and skipping the middle step produces a person who has scripts they cannot modify and notes they cannot find. Related, and worth forming at the same time: check before you act. ls before rm, cat before head -1 > — because the second of those writes a file that does not exist and destroys the one that does, and no confirmation prompt appears.

Then the safety habits, in the order they matter. Never run a command you cannot predict. Not do not run unknown commands — run them when you need to, but understand what they do first, which means reading the help. Every program worth using has a --help, and five minutes of reading is cheaper than an afternoon of recovering. Understand wildcards before using them. rm *.txt expands to every matching filename, so a typo in the pattern is a mass deletion; the safe habit is to run the expansion through a harmless command first, so you see exactly what matched before anything is deleted. Do not use sudo as a habit. It hides the permission problem rather than solving it, and the files created with it are then unwritable by the account that owns the project. Quote paths. A directory with a space in it breaks every unquoted command, and the resulting error message points at the last argument rather than at the space. And keep a clean working directory. A directory with six thousand files is a directory where rm * is catastrophic and where searching for a file takes a minute, so projects get one directory each and generated files get one directory each.

/* Six commands, and the habit that goes with each. */
const SIX = [
  { c: 'pwd', why: 'nearly every it-cannot-find-the-file is a wrong-directory problem' },
  { c: 'ls', flag: '-la', adds: 'hidden files and details', detail: 'ls -l permissions make a permission error legible' },
  { c: 'cd', flag: '-', why: 'returns to the previous directory, which fixes the mistake everybody makes' },
  { c: 'mkdir', habit: 'create it and then enter it',
    why: 'an empty directory never entered is one whose name was guessed' },
  { c: 'cat', with: ['head', 'tail'], mostUseful: 'tail -f on a log file' },
  { c: 'cp and mv', flags: ['cp -r', 'mv refuses to overwrite'],
    why: 'mv refusing is important - a silent overwrite is unrecoverable' },
];

/* Three concepts that remove repetitive work. */
const CONCEPTS = [
  { c: 'pipes', is: 'one commands stdout becomes the next stdin',
    example: 'cat access.log | grep ERROR | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head',
    answers: 'which errors are most common',
    discipline: 'each stage must be runnable on its own - pipe the first two to head to see what is flowing before adding more' },
  { c: 'redirection', tokens: ['> truncates a file', '>> appends', '2> sends stderr', '&> sends both'],
    classicBug: 'the second of the first two - an analysis script overwriting its input' },
  { c: 'globbing', expands: ['*', '?', '[]'],
    note: 'the shell expands before the program sees anything, which is why rm *.log beats a loop',
    danger: 'rm "*" deletes everything in a directory, and the quotation marks are the only thing preventing it' },
];

/* The habit that makes it usable later. */
const WRITE_IT_DOWN = {
  format: 'a plain text file, one command per line, a comment saying what each produced',
  why: ['searchable', 'diffable', 'survives a reinstall', 'the substrate for turning a sequence into a script'],
  progression: 'type it, then note it, then script it',
  consequenceOfSkippingTheMiddle: 'scripts you cannot modify and notes you cannot find',
  related: 'check before you act - ls before rm, cat before head -1 >, because the second writes a file that does not exist and destroys the one that does, with no prompt',
};

/* Safety habits, in order. */
const SAFETY = [
  { h: 'never run a command you cannot predict', not: 'do not run unknown commands',
    rather: 'run them when needed, but understand them first',
    how: 'read the --help; five minutes is cheaper than an afternoon of recovering' },
  { h: 'understand wildcards before using them',
    why: 'rm *.txt expands to every match, so a typo in the pattern is a mass deletion',
    safeHabit: 'run the expansion in a harmless command first, so you see what matched' },
  { h: 'do not use sudo as a habit', why: 'it hides the permission problem rather than solving it',
    consequence: 'files created with it are then unwritable by the account that owns the project' },
  { h: 'quote paths', why: 'a space in a path breaks every unquoted command and the error points at the last argument, not the space' },
  { h: 'keep a clean working directory', why: 'six thousand files makes rm * catastrophic and searching take a minute',
    practice: ['one directory per project', 'one directory for generated files'] },
];
Your daily terminal vocabulary: navigate folders, list and manipulate files, and run Python — mostly the same in PowerShell, Linux, and macOS.

Absolute vs relative paths. An absolute path is complete from the root (C:\Users\you\repo\app.py); a relative path is from where you currently are (app.py or src/app.py). A huge share of beginner frustration is simply being in the wrong folder when you run a command.

2.3 Install Python correctly

This topic explains how to install Python correctly so it is available from the terminal. The key steps are adding Python to your PATH, choosing the right installer for your operating system, and creating a virtual environment (venv) per project to isolate dependencies. Getting this right avoids the classic frustrations of running the wrong interpreter or version.

  1. Download Python from python.org (choose Python 3, current stable).
  2. Windows: tick "Add Python to PATH" during install — this is the step everyone forgets.
  3. Verify: open a terminal and run python --version. You should see something like Python 3.12.x.
  4. Best practice: keep code in one dedicated folder, e.g. C:\Users\you\code\.

Why Python first, and what it does not teach you

Python is a good first language for reasons that are specific rather than general. It has no ceremony. A program is a sequence of statements at module level; there is no main function, no type declaration, no class declaration required to run something. The feedback loop is short. The interpreter reports the exact line and the exact expression, so a beginner's errors are about the program rather than about the tooling. The built-in types are genuinely enough. A list, a dictionary, a string and a set cover a large fraction of real programming, so early exercises are about the problems rather than about the workarounds. Everything returns a value. Expressions compose in a way that makes a one-liner legible rather than merely clever. And it is used professionally, which means the skills transfer rather than being a training language discarded after the course.

Then what it does not teach you, because these are the gaps that are filled later and are better filled deliberately than discovered. Static types. Python will happily add a string to an integer and fail three lines later, which means a beginner never builds the habit of stating what a value is; this is the single biggest thing to pick up afterwards, and picking it up is easier than it would have been. Memory management. Allocation is invisible, so a beginner does not learn that a list copy is a copy or that a large list in a loop is a cost. Concurrency. The GIL means a beginner's first instinct — a thread per task — is the wrong answer for CPU work in CPython, and this should be taught rather than discovered as a mystery. Concurrency safety. Nothing stops two parts of a program from disagreeing about a value; no compiler catches it, so the habit has to be built deliberately. Interoperability and the boundaries. Calling into C, using a compiled extension, or dealing with a memory-mapped buffer all assume knowledge Python deliberately hides. And deployment. Installing a dependency and shipping the result are two real skills and neither is taught by learning the language.

/* Why Python first, specifically. */
const GOOD_FIRST = [
  { r: 'no ceremony', detail: 'a program is a sequence of statements at module level - no main function, no type declaration, no required class' },
  { r: 'short feedback loop', detail: 'the interpreter reports the exact line and expression, so errors are about the program rather than the tooling' },
  { r: 'the built-in types are enough', detail: 'list, dict, string and set cover a large fraction of real programming',
    consequence: 'early exercises are about the problems, not the workarounds' },
  { r: 'everything returns a value', detail: 'expressions compose so a one-liner stays legible rather than merely clever' },
  { r: 'used professionally', detail: 'the skills transfer rather than being a training language discarded after the course' },
];

/* What it does not teach, and the fix for each. */
const GAPS = [
  { gap: 'static types', symptom: 'adding a string to an integer fails three lines later',
    consequence: 'a beginner never builds the habit of stating what a value is',
    note: 'the single biggest thing to pick up afterwards, and easier to pick up later than to have had' },
  { gap: 'memory management', symptom: 'allocation is invisible',
    consequence: 'no instinct that a list copy is a copy, or that a big list in a loop is a cost' },
  { gap: 'concurrency', symptom: 'the GIL makes a thread per task the wrong answer for CPU work in CPython',
    fix: 'teach it rather than let it be discovered as a mystery' },
  { gap: 'concurrency safety', symptom: 'nothing stops two parts of a program disagreeing about a value, and no compiler catches it',
    fix: 'build the habit deliberately' },
  { gap: 'interoperability boundaries', instances: ['calling into C', 'using a compiled extension', 'a memory-mapped buffer'],
    note: 'all assume knowledge Python deliberately hides' },
  { gap: 'deployment', instances: ['installing a dependency', 'shipping the result'],
    note: 'two real skills, neither taught by the language' },
];

What to learn deliberately, in the order that pays off

Four things, in this order, and each one is a small addition to what a beginner already writes rather than a replacement of it. Functions with parameters and return values, including default and keyword arguments — because the moment a function takes arguments, code stops being copy-and-paste and starts being reusable, and the keyword form is what makes a call site readable. Modules and imports, because a program that lives in one file cannot be organised and the import is the only concept needed. Reading a traceback from the bottom up, which is a specific skill with a specific order: the last line is the error, the line above it is where it happened, and the frames above that are how you got there — most beginners read it top-down and see only their own file. And reading someone else's code, which is the one that separates people who can write from people who can work: pick a library you use, find one function, and read it without running it, working out what it does from the names, the shape and the tests. That exercise builds the ability to enter an unfamiliar codebase, which is the most-used skill in the profession and the one no course teaches.

Then the three things to establish as habits rather than facts, because they are what a reviewer notices first. Name things after what they mean, not what they are. user_list rather than l, retry_count rather than n, because the next reader is you in three months and the name is the only documentation that cannot go out of date. Handle the empty case explicitly — an empty list, a zero, a missing key, a failed call — because a program that assumes its input is well-formed fails on somebody else's data and the stack trace points at your code rather than at the cause. And make the failure path as considered as the success path, because the majority of real code is error handling, and a program written to assume success has an except: at the top that hides everything, which converts a small bug into an unexplained outage. Those three habits are worth more than any language feature, and they are the reason the rest of this book is arranged around them.

/* Four things to learn deliberately, cheapest first. */
const LEARN = [
  { t: 'functions with parameters and returns', detail: 'including default and keyword arguments',
    effect: 'the moment a function takes arguments, code stops being copy-and-paste',
    whyKeywords: 'the keyword form makes a call site readable' },
  { t: 'modules and imports', why: 'a program in one file cannot be organised, and the import is the only concept needed' },
  { t: 'reading a traceback bottom-up',
    order: ['the last line is the error', 'the line above is where it happened', 'the frames above are how you got there'],
    mistake: 'most beginners read top-down and see only their own file' },
  { t: 'reading someone elses code', method: 'pick a library you use, find one function, read it without running it',
    deriveFrom: ['names', 'shape', 'tests'],
    why: 'builds the ability to enter an unfamiliar codebase - the most-used skill in the profession and the one no course teaches' },
];

/* Habits, because they are what a reviewer notices first. */
const HABITS = [
  { h: 'name things after what they mean, not what they are',
    examples: ['user_list not l', 'retry_count not n'],
    why: 'the next reader is you in three months, and a name is the only documentation that cannot go out of date' },
  { h: 'handle the empty case explicitly', items: ['an empty list', 'zero', 'a missing key', 'a failed call'],
    why: 'a program assuming well-formed input fails on somebody elses data, and the traceback points at your code rather than the cause' },
  { h: 'make the failure path as considered as the success path',
    fact: 'the majority of real code is error handling',
    failure: 'a program written to assume success ends with a bare except that hides everything, converting a small bug into an unexplained outage',
    note: 'this is why the rest of this book is arranged around them' },
];

Virtual environments (venv). Different projects need different package versions. Later in the course we always use python -m venv .venv per project so projects don’t fight over libraries. Remember the concept now — it reappears in Ch. 18 and 22.

2.4 Your first program — say hello three ways

This topic proves your whole toolchain works by running a hello world program several different ways, such as in the interpreter, in a script file, and from the editor. Each route exercises the connection between editor, terminal, and Python interpreter. Confirming all paths end to end early prevents mystery failures later.

# hello.py — save this file, then run:  python hello.py
greeting = "Hello, Software Engineer!"
print(greeting)  # print the string to the console

A two-line program: store a string in a variable, then print it, and run it from the terminal with python hello.py.

Run it from the terminal with python hello.py. Then try the interactive shell — type python alone and write code directly:

>>> 2 + 2
4
>>> name = "Ada"
>>> print("Hi " + name)
Hi Ada
>>> exit()

Why a REPL is a real tool and not a toy

An interactive prompt is not a beginner convenience — it is a development environment with the edit-compile cycle removed, and the properties it gives are the reason it survives in professional work. Feedback is immediate, so the loop from idea to evidence is under a second rather than minutes. State persists between statements, so you can construct a value once and interrogate it repeatedly instead of rebuilding it in every script. And errors arrive at the statement that caused them, with the interpreter's state still intact, so you can inspect the half-built object and find out where it went wrong instead of re-reading your own code. The three things it is genuinely bad at are equally real: nothing is saved, so a session that found the answer loses it; nothing is checked, so a typo in a line you did not execute is invisible; and the history is linear, so there is no way to re-run one statement from the middle of a construction after fixing an earlier one. The habit worth forming is to treat the prompt as a place to find out and immediately write down what you found.

What to do in the first hour, in order

A sequence that produces something useful rather than something that merely types things, because the goal of a first hour is to learn how to ask the machine questions. Values and types. Type a number, a string, a list, a dictionary, and ask each what type it is — then discover that 4/2 is 2.0 in Python 3 and that this catches everybody once. Printing and formatting. Learn that a value must be converted to text to be printed with it, and meet f-strings, because every later exercise needs them. Collections. Build a list of five names, index it, slice it, append to it, and then notice that a dictionary maps a key to a value and that the difference is what you are actually choosing when you pick a data structure. Control flow. Write a loop that prints numbers one to ten, then the same loop with a filter, then a comprehension — and notice that the comprehension is the same thing written more densely. Functions. Write one that takes two arguments and returns a value, then call it with a keyword argument and notice nothing changed, which is the point. An error on purpose. Divide by zero, index past the end of a list, and read the traceback carefully, because a traceback read properly tells you the line, the call chain and often the intended type — and reading them is a skill this hour is for. Then a small program that does something. Twenty lines: read a list of numbers, drop the negatives, report the mean, handle the empty case. That last part is the habit that matters more than the arithmetic.

/* What the prompt is good and bad at. */
const REPL = {
  isNot: 'a beginner convenience',
  is: 'a development environment with the edit-compile cycle removed',
  good: ['feedback in under a second rather than minutes',
         'state persists between statements, so a value is built once and interrogated repeatedly',
         'errors arrive at the statement that caused them, with state intact'],
  bad: ['nothing is saved, so a session that found the answer loses it',
        'nothing is checked, so a typo in an unexecuted line is invisible',
        'history is linear, so you cannot re-run one statement after fixing an earlier one'],
  habit: 'treat the prompt as a place to find out, and immediately write down what you found',
};

/* The first hour, in order. */
const FIRST_HOUR = [
  { step: 'values and types', do: ['type a number, a string, a list, a dictionary',
    'ask each what type it is', 'discover that 4/2 is 2.0 in Python 3'],
    note: 'this catches everybody once' },
  { step: 'printing and formatting', do: ['learn that a value must be converted to text to print with it',
    'meet f-strings'], why: 'every later exercise needs them' },
  { step: 'collections', do: ['build a list of five names, index it, slice it, append',
    'notice that a dictionary maps a key to a value'],
    insight: 'the difference is what you are choosing when you pick a data structure' },
  { step: 'control flow', do: ['a loop printing 1 to 10', 'the same loop with a filter', 'a comprehension'],
    notice: 'the comprehension is the same thing written more densely' },
  { step: 'functions', do: ['write one taking two arguments and returning a value',
    'call it with a keyword argument and notice nothing changed'], why: 'that is the point' },
  { step: 'an error on purpose', do: ['divide by zero', 'index past the end of a list', 'read the traceback carefully'],
    gains: ['the line', 'the call chain', 'often the intended type'],
    note: 'reading a traceback is the skill this hour is for' },
  { step: 'a small program that does something',
    spec: 'twenty lines: read a list of numbers, drop negatives, report the mean, handle the empty case',
    why: 'the empty case is the habit that matters more than the arithmetic' },
];
This is the interactive Python shell: each line is evaluated immediately and the result appears under the prompt — ideal for experimenting.

2.5 How to read an error — the superpower

This topic teaches you to treat an error traceback as useful information instead of a failure. You learn to read a traceback from the bottom up, following the chain of calls to find the real cause. Reproducing the error, isolating the smallest failing case, and testing fixes turns debugging into a fast learning loop.

A traceback (Python’s error report) is a map, not a slap. Read it bottom-up:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "hello.py", line 3, in <module>
    print(unsomething)   <-- your line
NameError: name 'unsomething' is not defined   <-- the type of error + cause

Python’s traceback names the exact file and line, and the bottom line tells you the error type — read it last line first.

The last line names the problem type. Learn these three first: NameError (typo / not defined), TypeError (wrong kind of value), IndexError (list index out of range). Copy the exact error into Google — you are never the first person to hit it.

The method, stated as a procedure

Debugging is not talent and it is not staring harder. It is a procedure, and the procedure has a shape: reproduce, isolate, hypothesise, test, fix, verify. Each step exists because skipping it is what makes debugging take a day. Reproduce — get it to fail reliably, every time, with the smallest input that still fails. An intermittent bug with no reproduction is not debuggable yet, and the effort belongs in making it deterministic rather than in watching it. Isolate — narrow it to the smallest piece of code that still misbehaves, by cutting things out rather than by reasoning about what might be wrong. Bisection works: comment out half, run; if the failure persists, the cause is in the other half. Hypothesise — write down, in a sentence, what you believe is happening and why. This is the step people skip and it is the one that pays: a written hypothesis that turns out to be wrong has still eliminated a possibility, whereas no hypothesis has eliminated nothing. Test — one change, one prediction. If you make two changes and the symptom disappears you have learned nothing about either. Fix — and this is the part with a real rule: fix the cause, not the symptom. Adding a retry to hide a race, a null check to hide an uninitialised value, or a try to hide an exception each make the symptom go away and leave the defect, and each is the origin story of an outage. Verify — confirm the original case no longer fails, and confirm nothing else did, because a fix that changes behaviour somewhere else has traded a bug for a different bug.

The tools, in the order they become useful

Four tools, each of which supersedes the one before it for a class of problem. Printing. Genuinely sufficient for a surprising number of bugs, and the discipline is to print the type and the identity as well as the value — because the bug that looks like a wrong value is often the right value of the wrong object, and printing an identifier alongside reveals it where printing the value does not. Logging. For anything that runs more than once, a logger beats print because it has levels, timestamps, a destination that survives a crash, and structured fields; the two habits that matter are logging where decisions are made rather than only where things fail, and logging the inputs and outputs of a boundary rather than the internals. A debugger. Breakpoints, stepping, and inspecting live variables, which changes the cost model entirely: instead of adding a print, rerunning, and reading, you stop at the interesting line and look at six values at once — and this is where beginners should move as soon as they are comfortable, because the guessing loop is the slowest thing about their work. Assertions and tests. An assertion stating an invariant converts "sometimes it is wrong" into "fails here, deterministically", and a test is the only tool that keeps a fixed bug fixed; the pairing worth forming is to write the test that reproduces the bug before fixing it, because a test written afterwards tests the fix rather than the defect.

/* The procedure, and why each step exists. */
const METHOD = [
  { s: 'reproduce', do: 'fail reliably, every time, with the smallest input that still fails',
    why: 'an intermittent bug with no reproduction is not debuggable yet',
    effortGoes: 'into making it deterministic, not into watching it' },
  { s: 'isolate', do: 'narrow to the smallest piece that still misbehaves, by cutting rather than reasoning',
    technique: 'bisection: comment out half, run; if it persists the cause is in the other half' },
  { s: 'hypothesise', do: 'write one sentence saying what you believe is happening and why',
    whyItPays: 'a wrong written hypothesis still eliminates a possibility; none eliminates nothing' },
  { s: 'test', rule: 'one change, one prediction',
    why: 'two changes that remove the symptom teach you nothing about either' },
  { s: 'fix', rule: 'fix the cause, not the symptom',
    antiPatterns: ['a retry to hide a race', 'a null check to hide an uninitialised value',
      'a try to hide an exception'],
    why: 'each makes the symptom vanish, leaves the defect, and is the origin story of an outage' },
  { s: 'verify', do: ['the original case no longer fails', 'nothing else did'],
    why: 'a fix that changes behaviour elsewhere trades a bug for a different bug' },
];

/* Tools, in the order they become useful. */
const TOOLS = [
  { t: 'printing', sufficientFor: 'a surprising number of bugs',
    discipline: 'print the type and the identity as well as the value',
    catches: 'the bug that looks like a wrong value is often the right value of the wrong object' },
  { t: 'logging', beats: 'print', because: ['levels', 'timestamps',
    'a destination that survives a crash', 'structured fields'],
    habits: ['log where decisions are made, not only where things fail',
             'log inputs and outputs at a boundary, not internals'] },
  { t: 'a debugger', does: ['breakpoints', 'stepping', 'inspecting live variables'],
    changesTheCostModel: 'instead of print, rerun, read - stop at the interesting line and look at six values at once',
    moveHere: 'as soon as comfortable, because the guessing loop is the slowest part of a beginners work' },
  { t: 'assertions and tests', assertionDoes: 'converts sometimes-it-is-wrong into fails-here-deterministically',
    testDoes: 'the only tool that keeps a fixed bug fixed',
    pairing: 'write the reproducing test BEFORE the fix, because one written afterwards tests the fix rather than the defect' },
];

3 · Programming Fundamentals (Python)

This is the core chapter of the course, covering Python fundamentals you will reuse every day: values and types, control flow, functions, data structures, modules, files, and regular expressions. Each topic builds a tool you combine freely in real programs. Mastery here makes the rest of the course far smoother.

3.1 Values and types3.2 Input, output, and f-strings3.3 Making decisions: if / elif / else3.4 Loops: for and while3.5 Lists, indexing, slicing3.6 Functions — packaging reusable logic3.7 Dictionaries and tuples3.8 A methodical debugging recipe3.9 Modules, imports and the standard library3.10 Files and JSON — making data persist3.11 Regular expressions: the text-processing superpower

This is the biggest and most important chapter of the first semester. Everything later — data structures, algorithms, OOP, web backends — leans on exactly these ideas.

3.1 Values and types

Every value in Python carries a type that determines which operations are legal, such as integers, floats, strings, booleans, and lists. Python’s dynamic typing assigns types automatically, which is friendly but puts responsibility on you to keep types consistent. You can inspect types with the type function and convert between them explicitly.

Programs manipulate values. Every value has a type that says what you can do with it and how it’s stored. The core ones:

TypeExample valueNotes
int (integer)42, -7Whole numbers, arbitrary size in Python
float3.14, 2.5e3Numbers with decimals; beware binary rounding
str (string)"hi", 'bye'Text. Immutable: you can’t change a string, only build new ones
boolTrue / FalseThe only two truth values
list[1, 2, 3]Ordered, changeable collection
dict{"name": "Ada"}Key → value lookup table
NoneNone"No value here" — crucial for missing data
age = 21                 # int  -> assigned a value
price = 19.99            # float
name = "Ada Lovelace"    # str
is_student = True        # bool
scores = [85, 90, 78]    # list
user   = {"name": "Ada", "age": 21}   # dict

print(type(age))     # <class 'int'>   type() tells you the type
print(age + 1)       # 22
print(name.upper())  # "ADA LOVELACE" — strings have methods

Each variable holds a value of a given type; type() reveals it, and ints, strings, lists, and dicts each carry their own operations.

Values, objects, and names — the three things that get confused

Almost every confusing bug in a beginner's Python comes from conflating three distinct ideas. A value is what a thing is: the number 42, the text hello, the list [1,2,3]. An object is the runtime container that holds a value, carrying a type, an identity, and any data attached to it — so [1,2,3] in two places in your program can be two objects that happen to be equal. A name is a label you bind to an object, and the binding can be changed at any time without touching the object. That is why x = [1,2] followed by y = x followed by x.append(3) makes y also contain the 3: the two names point at the same object, and mutating through one name mutates what the other name refers to. Almost every "Python changed my list without me asking" bug is this, and the mental model that prevents all of them is names are labels stuck onto objects — not boxes that contain values.

Then what follows from that model and surprises people next. Assignment never copies. It rebinds a name. To copy you must ask for a copy: b = a.copy() for a list, b = a[:] for a list or tuple, copy.deepcopy(a) for nested structures, and in Python 3.8+ the | operator merges dictionaries into a new one. A shallow copy of a nested list shares the inner lists, so mutating them affects the original — and the fix is a deep copy, which is one of the few genuinely surprising behaviours in the language. Equality versus identity. == asks whether two objects have the same value; is asks whether they are the same object. == is what you almost always want, and is on a list or a string is nearly always a bug — except for the specific check x is None, where is is required because None is a singleton and there is only one of it. Mutability. Lists, dictionaries and sets can change; tuples, strings and numbers cannot, and the practical consequence is that a tuple can be a dictionary key and a list cannot, and that passing a mutable object to a function lets that function change something you did not expect it to.

/* Three ideas that get conflated. */
const THREE = {
  value: 'what a thing is - the number 42, the text hello, the list [1,2,3]',
  object: 'the runtime container holding a value, carrying a type, an identity and attached data',
  name: 'a label bound to an object, rebindable at any time without touching the object',
  consequence: 'two names can point at one object, so mutating through one mutates what the other refers to',
  mentalModel: 'names are labels stuck onto objects, not boxes containing values',
  classicBug: 'x = [1,2]; y = x; x.append(3) - y now also contains the 3',
  rule: 'almost every Python-changed-my-list-without-me-asking bug is this',
};

/* What follows from the model. */
const FOLLOWS = [
  { c: 'assignment never copies', it: 'rebinds a name',
    copyWith: ['b = a.copy() for a list', 'b = a[:] for a list or tuple',
               'copy.deepcopy(a) for nested structures', 'a | b merges dicts into a new one (3.8+)'],
    surprise: 'a shallow copy of a nested list shares the inner lists' },
  { c: 'equality versus identity',
    doubleEquals: 'do two objects have the same value',
    isOperator: 'are they the same object',
    rule: '== is what you almost always want; is on a list or string is nearly always a bug',
    exception: 'x is None - required, because None is a singleton' },
  { c: 'mutability',
    mutable: ['list', 'dict', 'set'],
    immutable: ['tuple', 'str', 'number'],
    consequences: ['a tuple can be a dictionary key and a list cannot',
                   'passing a mutable object to a function lets it change something you did not expect'] },
];

Types, and what dynamic typing costs you in practice

Python decides types at run time from the value itself, which buys a beginner a great deal: no declaration ceremony, a variable can be rebound to a different type, and the interpreter's error messages point at the line rather than at a mismatch in a type signature. What it costs is the thing that bites later. Errors move downstream and lose their location. Adding a string to an integer does not fail at the point of the mistake; the variable holding a string simply travels three functions further, and the exception arrives where the arithmetic happens, pointing at innocent code. Nothing catches an unused value. You can assign a value, never use it, and get no warning; a linter will warn, which is one of the reasons to use one. Nothing catches a shape change. A function that received a list and now receives a dictionary fails at the first subscript, and a function that received ten fields and now receives nine fails when it reads the tenth. And nothing catches the reconnection. If a function is supposed to return a list and one branch returns a single item because of a typo, the caller unpacks it into a character — and the type error, if any, is in the caller.

Then the practices that recover the missing safety without leaving the language, and each is cheap. Say what you mean in names. A variable called user_list documents its type to every reader including yourself, and this costs nothing. Check the empty case where the type makes it possible. An empty list, a zero, a missing key, a None: four checks that prevent the majority of real bugs, and the four the interpreter will not do for you. Use assertions for invariants. assert isinstance(x, list) at a boundary converts "sometimes it is wrong" into "fails here, immediately, with a clear message" — and because an assertion can be disabled, use a real check for anything security-relevant. And accept that a static checker is a separate tool. Type hints plus a checker give back exactly what the interpreter gave up, with no change to the language's behaviour at run time, and a signature also makes a function's contract readable at the definition rather than at the call site fifty lines later.

/* What dynamic typing buys and costs. */
const BUYS = [
  'no declaration ceremony',
  'a variable can be rebound to a different type',
  'errors point at the line rather than at a type signature',
];
const COSTS = [
  { c: 'errors move downstream and lose their location',
    mechanism: 'adding a string to an integer fails three functions later, at the arithmetic',
    symptom: 'the exception arrives where the arithmetic happens, pointing at innocent code' },
  { c: 'nothing catches an unused value',
    workaround: 'a linter warns - one of the reasons to use one' },
  { c: 'nothing catches a shape change',
    examples: ['a function that received a list now receives a dict and fails at the first subscript',
               'a function that received ten fields now receives nine and fails when it reads the tenth'] },
  { c: 'nothing catches the reconnection',
    mechanism: 'a function meant to return a list has one branch return a single item',
    symptom: 'the caller unpacks it into a character; any type error is in the caller' },
];

/* Practices that recover the safety, cheapest first. */
const RECOVERS = [
  { p: 'say what you mean in names', how: 'user_list documents its type to every reader', cost: 'nothing' },
  { p: 'check the empty case where the type makes it possible',
    items: ['an empty list', 'zero', 'a missing key', 'None'],
    why: 'four checks preventing the majority of real bugs, and the four the interpreter will not do for you' },
  { p: 'assertions for invariants', how: 'assert isinstance(x, list) at a boundary',
    gain: 'converts sometimes-it-is-wrong into fails-here-immediately-with-a-clear-message',
    caveat: 'an assertion can be disabled - use a real check for anything security-relevant' },
  { p: 'accept that a static checker is a separate tool',
    how: 'type hints plus a checker, with no change to run-time behaviour',
    bonus: 'a signature makes a contract readable at the definition rather than at a call site fifty lines later' },
];

Dynamic typing. Python figures out types for you and lets a variable change type. That’s flexible but means you are responsible for keeping track — the type system can’t catch your mistakes at compile time (unlike Java/C). Great for learning, and a trade-off to reconsider in Ch. 18.

3.2 Input, output, and f-strings

Programs talk to users through input and output. The input function reads a line from the user and always returns a string, while print writes text to the screen. F-strings, marked with an f before the quotes, embed expressions inside curly braces as in f"Hello {name}", making formatted output concise and readable.

name = input("What's your name? ")
age  = int(input("How old are you? "))   # input() always gives a string!
years = 100 - age

# f-strings: put values directly into text
print(f"Hello {name}, you have {years} years until you're 100.")
print(f"In 2036 you'll be {age + 10}.")

input() returns a string, so the age is wrapped in int(); f-strings then inject variables and even expressions straight into the printed text.

Input, output, and the string trap that catches everyone

input() returns a string, always, and this is not a detail — it is the origin of the most common first-program crash, because "21" + 1 is a TypeError while 21 + "1" silently produces "211" in some languages and an error in others. The consequence is that a program which reads a number, adds one, and prints has three places where the type is wrong, and the correct habit is to convert immediately at the boundary — read, convert, then work — rather than carrying a string through twenty lines and converting at the point of use, where the failure message points at the arithmetic instead of at the input. The conversion functions worth knowing are int() for a whole number, float() for a decimal, and bool() for a truth test — plus the fact that int("21.5") raises rather than truncating, which surprises people who expected the truncation they would get from a cast in another language.

Then the two ways to take input and when each is right. input() prompts on one line and is right for anything a person types at a terminal. sys.stdin.read() reads the whole stream, and sys.stdin.readline() reads one line, which is what you want for a script reading a data file or a piped stream — and the distinction matters because input() strips the trailing newline and prompts, whereas reading sys.stdin does neither, so a loop built on input() cannot consume a file and a loop built on readline() must handle the final line that has no newline at all. And then splitting the result, which is the second half of the boundary problem: input().split() turns one line into a list of strings, and if you expected numbers you must map the conversion across the list rather than convert the list, because int(list) is meaningless.

/* The string trap. */
const INPUT_STRING = {
  fact: 'input() returns a string, always',
  notADetail: 'it is the origin of the most common first-program crash',
  crash: '"21" + 1 is a TypeError',
  silent: '21 + "1" produces "211" in some languages and an error in others',
  consequence: 'a program that reads a number, adds one and prints has three places the type is wrong',
  habit: 'convert IMMEDIATELY at the boundary - read, convert, then work',
  why: 'carrying a string through twenty lines and converting at point of use makes the error point at the arithmetic instead of at the input',
  conversions: ['int() for a whole number', 'float() for a decimal', 'bool() for a truth test'],
  surprise: 'int("21.5") raises rather than truncating',
  expectation: 'people expect the truncation they would get from a cast in another language',
};

/* Two ways to take input. */
const WAYS_IN = [
  { way: 'input()', does: 'prompts on one line', rightFor: 'anything a person types at a terminal' },
  { way: 'sys.stdin.read()', does: 'reads the whole stream' },
  { way: 'sys.stdin.readline()', does: 'reads one line',
    rightFor: 'a script reading a data file or a piped stream' },
  { whyTheDistinctionMatters: [
    'input() strips the trailing newline and prompts',
    'sys.stdin does neither',
    'so a loop on input() cannot consume a file',
    'a loop on readline() must handle the final line that has no newline at all' ],
  splitting: 'input().split() turns one line into a list of strings',
  trap: 'if you expected numbers, map the conversion across the list - int(list) is meaningless',
};

Output, formatting, and where output should actually go

print() is a function that writes to standard output, and its flexibility is worth knowing precisely because it replaces a formatting language most beginners do not know exists. Multiple values, separated automatically — print("a", "b") puts a space between them, and print("a", "b", sep=", ") changes it. end= controls what follows, and its default of a newline is why a progress indicator uses end="\r" to overwrite the same line. f-strings interpolate expressions directly into a string: print(f"{name} is {age}"), which is more readable than concatenation and more readable than format or percent-style formatting, and which also allows a format specification after a colon — {value:.2f} for two decimal places, {count:,} for thousands separators, {name:>10} for right-alignment in a column. That last one is what turns a loop into a readable table, and it is the feature that gets discovered last and used every day.

Then the question that matters more than any of it: where should output go? For a person watching, standard output is right. For a program whose results another program reads, output is a data format, and a data format needs to be stable, delimited, and quoted — and hand-built string concatenation produces a format that breaks the moment a value contains the delimiter, which is the classic CSV bug where a name with a comma in it shifts every column after it. The fix is a library: the csv module for delimited output, json for structured output, and both handle quoting, escaping and encoding for you. Then the discipline: progress and diagnostics do not belong in the data stream. A progress message printed into a file that something else parses will eventually be parsed as data, and the failure surfaces in a different program, which is why serious tools send diagnostics to standard error and keep standard output for the result. And the final point for a chapter that has just covered files: flushing. Buffered output is faster and will not appear when you expected it — which is why a progress indicator needs an explicit flush, and why output that disappeared before a crash is a buffering artefact rather than a bug in your code.

/* What print() gives you, replacing a whole formatting language. */
const PRINT = [
  { f: 'multiple values, separated automatically', detail: 'print("a", "b") puts a space between them', control: 'sep=", "' },
  { f: 'end=', detail: 'controls what follows', default: 'a newline',
    use: 'a progress indicator uses end="\r" to overwrite the same line' },
  { f: 'f-strings', example: 'f"{name} is {age}"',
    why: 'more readable than concatenation, format and percent-style',
    specifications: ['{value:.2f} for two decimal places', '{count:,} for thousands separators',
      '{name:>10} for right-alignment in a column'],
    payoff: 'right-alignment turns a loop into a readable table',
    note: 'discovered last and used every day' },
];

/* Where output should go. */
const WHERE = [
  { q: 'a person watching', answer: 'standard output' },
  { q: 'another program reading the results', answer: 'output is a DATA FORMAT',
    requires: ['stable', 'delimited', 'quoted'],
    handBuiltFailure: 'a value containing the delimiter breaks the format',
    classicBug: 'the CSV bug where a name with a comma in it shifts every column after it',
    fix: 'the csv module for delimited output, json for structured - both handle quoting, escaping and encoding' },
  { q: 'progress and diagnostics', rule: 'they do not belong in the data stream',
    why: 'a progress message printed into a file something else parses will eventually be parsed as data',
    symptom: 'the failure surfaces in a different program',
    practice: 'diagnostics to standard error, standard output for the result' },
  { q: 'flushing', fact: 'buffered output is faster and will not appear when you expected it',
    consequence: 'a progress indicator needs an explicit flush',
    reframe: 'output that disappeared before a crash is a buffering artefact, not a bug in your code' },
];

input() returns a string. If you need a number, convert it with int(...) or float(...) — otherwise "21" + 1 raises a TypeError.

3.3 Making decisions: if / elif / else

Conditional statements branch program flow based on boolean expressions. The if keyword runs a block only when its condition is true, elif chains additional checks, and else catches everything remaining. Python signals code blocks by indentation, so consistent spacing is mandatory and not merely stylistic.

score = int(input("Score: "))

if score >= 90:
    grade = "A"
elif score >= 80:
    grade = "B"
elif score >= 70:
    grade = "C"
else:
    grade = "F"

print(f"Grade: {grade}")

# comparison operators:  == !=  < >  <= >=
# logical operators:     and  or  not
if score >= 90 and score <= 100:
    print("Perfect range")

Chained if/elif/else maps scores to grades, and comparison and logical operators combine conditions; the colon plus indentation defines each block.

Indentation is not cosmetic in Python — it is the block structure. Four spaces, consistently, for the whole file.

The three shapes and the trap inside each

A conditional has only three shapes, and every bug in one is a variant of the same mistake. The simple form — if condition: — has no trap, but has one frequent design error: testing something that is already implied by the branch you are in. The two-branch form — if ... else — has the trap that else attracts everything, including the case you did not think about, and the fix is a habit: write the else first, as "and in all other cases the value is X", and let the if earn the exception. The chain — if / elif / else — has the trap that the chain is evaluated in order and the first match wins, so an overlapping condition placed later is dead code; the discipline is to make the ranges provably disjoint, and the way to prove it is to write each bound twice, once as the lower limit and once as the upper, which makes an overlap visible on the page rather than in a bug report. Then match, which pattern-matches a value against shapes and is genuinely clearer than an elif chain when you are comparing a value against several literal or structural alternatives — and its real subject is destructuring, not equality.

Then the comparison operators and the truthiness rules, because these are where the surprises live. Chained comparison. 0 < x < 10 is a single condition in Python, not two, and it is both more readable and faster than x > 0 and x < 10 — worth knowing because it is the one place a language's syntax is strictly better. Equality on collections. == compares contents and order for lists, so [1,2] == [2,1] is false, while a set comparison ignores order — and comparing two large lists is O(n) each time, so do not put a list comparison inside a loop over items. Truthiness. An empty container, zero, an empty string, None, and False are all falsey; everything else is truthy, including the string "0" and the number 0.0 in some languages' habits but not Python's. The practical rules that follow: never write if x: when you mean "if x is not None", because a valid empty string or zero would take the wrong branch; prefer is None over == None; and write if items is not None and len(items) > 0 rather than a compound truthiness test when the difference matters.

/* Three shapes, one trap each. */
const SHAPES = [
  { shape: 'if condition:',
    trap: 'none syntactically',
    designError: 'testing something already implied by the branch you are in' },
  { shape: 'if / else',
    trap: 'else attracts everything, including the case you did not think about',
    fix: 'write the else first as "and in all other cases the value is X", let the if earn the exception' },
  { shape: 'if / elif / else',
    trap: 'evaluated in order, first match wins, so an overlapping condition placed later is dead code',
    discipline: 'make the ranges provably disjoint by writing each bound twice - once as a lower limit, once as an upper' },
  { shape: 'match',
    when: 'comparing a value against several literal or structural alternatives',
    win: 'genuinely clearer than an elif chain',
    realSubject: 'destructuring, not equality' },
];

/* Comparison and truthiness. */
const COMPARISON = {
  chained: '0 < x < 10 is ONE condition in Python, not two',
  why: 'more readable and faster than x > 0 and x < 10',
  note: 'the one place the syntax is strictly better',
  collections: '== compares contents, and order for lists, so [1,2] == [2,1] is false',
  setContrast: 'a set comparison ignores order',
  cost: 'comparing two large lists is O(n) each time - do not put it inside a loop over items',
};
const TRUTHINESS = {
  falsey: ['an empty container', 'zero', 'an empty string', 'None', 'False'],
  truthy: 'everything else',
  rules: [
    'never write if x: when you mean if x is not None - a valid empty string or zero takes the wrong branch',
    'prefer is None over == None',
    'write if items is not None and len(items) > 0 when the difference matters' ],
};

The bugs that come specifically from indenting the block

Because indentation is the block structure in Python, the compiler cannot tell a block that ended early from one that was never started, and this produces a family of errors that look like logic bugs and are not. A line that should be inside the if sits one level out. The branch executes, the code beneath it always executes, and the symptom is a value that changes when the condition is false. A line that should be outside sits one level in. The symptom is code that silently never runs — and worse, it is invisible when the condition happens to be true in testing and appears in production. An elif at the wrong indentation becomes an independent if, so both branches run when both conditions hold, and the second silently overwrites the first. A one-line if followed by an indented block is a syntax error, because Python's one-line form accepts only a single simple statement — the message points at the end of the line, which is not where the mistake is. And mixed tabs and spaces produces an IndentationError that looks like a phantom character problem, because the two have different widths on screen and the file looks consistent to you and not to the interpreter.

Then what to do about it, since each prevention is cheaper than each diagnosis. Four spaces, one style, everywhere. Pick it and never deviate, and let the formatter enforce it rather than your attention. Render whitespace in the editor, which turns the phantom space into a visible dot — and this one feature prevents more Python bugs than any other setting. Never rely on a one-line if for anything but the shortest case, because the moment it grows the transform is not obvious and the diff is unreadable. Prefer early returns to nested blocks. A function with three if-return pairs at one indentation level has no nesting at all and can be read top to bottom; the same logic as nesting reaches four levels by the last branch and nobody can hold it. And make each condition do one thing. if user and user.is_active and user.balance > 0: is one line containing three decisions, and when it fails you do not know which; three named flags computed on the lines above are three lines you can print and find the answer in. That is the whole design lesson of this section: conditionals are where logic becomes visible, and the cost of making it visible is the indentation discipline the language forces you to learn anyway.

/* Errors that look like logic bugs and are not. */
const INDENT_FAULTS = [
  { fault: 'a line that should be inside the if sits one level out',
    symptom: 'the branch executes, the code beneath always executes',
    presents: 'a value that changes when the condition is false' },
  { fault: 'a line that should be outside sits one level in',
    symptom: 'code silently never runs',
    whyWorse: 'invisible when the condition is true in testing, appears in production' },
  { fault: 'an elif at the wrong indentation',
    becomes: 'an independent if',
    symptom: 'both branches run when both conditions hold, the second overwrites the first' },
  { fault: 'a one-line if followed by an indented block',
    is: 'a syntax error - the one-line form accepts only a single simple statement',
    whyConfusing: 'the message points at the end of the line, which is not where the mistake is' },
  { fault: 'mixed tabs and spaces',
    symptom: 'an IndentationError that looks like a phantom character problem',
    why: 'the two have different widths on screen, so the file looks consistent to you and not to the interpreter' },
];

/* Prevention, cheapest first. */
const PREVENTS = [
  { p: 'four spaces, one style, everywhere', how: 'let the formatter enforce it rather than your attention' },
  { p: 'render whitespace in the editor', why: 'turns the phantom space into a visible dot',
    claim: 'this one feature prevents more Python bugs than any other setting' },
  { p: 'never rely on a one-line if except for the shortest case',
    why: 'the moment it grows the transform is not obvious and the diff is unreadable' },
  { p: 'prefer early returns to nested blocks',
    good: 'three if-return pairs at one indentation level, readable top to bottom',
    bad: 'the same logic nested reaches four levels by the last branch' },
  { p: 'make each condition do one thing',
    bad: 'if user and user.is_active and user.balance > 0 - one line containing three decisions',
    symptom: 'when it fails you do not know which',
    good: 'three named flags computed on the lines above - three lines you can print' },
];

Exercise 3.3

Write a program that asks for a temperature in Celsius and prints "Cold" (< 10), "Mild" (10–25), or "Hot" (> 25).

3.4 Loops: for and while

Loops repeat a block of work. The for loop iterates over a sequence such as a list or a range of numbers, while while keeps running as long as its condition holds. The keywords break and continue exit the loop early or skip to the next iteration, giving precise control over execution.

# for loop — iterate over a sequence
for i in range(5):                     # 0,1,2,3,4
    print("Counting:", i)

for name in ["Ada", "Grace", "Alan"]:
    print("Hello", name)

# while loop — repeat while condition is true
n = 10
while n > 0:
    print(n)
    n -= 1          # n = n - 1
print("Liftoff!")

# break exits the loop; continue skips to the next iteration
for i in range(10):
    if i == 3:
        continue
    if i == 8:
        break
    print(i)        # prints 0 1 2 4 5 6 7

for loops walk over ranges and lists, while repeats until a condition fails, and break and continue steer the flow; something must change each iteration.

Choosing the loop, and the question that decides it

Python has two loops and the decision between them has a rule that is worth stating once and then never thinking about again: if you know how many times, or you are walking a sequence, use for; if the number of repetitions depends on a condition that only the body can satisfy, use while. That is the whole rule. The reason it matters is that a for loop over a sequence is driven by the sequence itself, so it cannot run forever, cannot forget to advance, and stops correctly if the sequence is emptied mid-loop — whereas a while loop is driven by a condition you write, and every failure mode of while comes from that condition not changing. Three forms of for cover nearly everything: over a range of numbers, over a sequence directly, and over the sequence with index via enumerate. And the single most important property of the for loop is that it asks the sequence how long it is, once, at the start — which is why modifying the list's length during the loop is a bug, and why for x in list(iterable) is the correct way to walk a list while mutating it.

Then break, continue, else, and the loop variable, because each has a specific use and each is misused often. break exits the innermost loop — and note innermost, because break inside a nested loop leaves the outer one running, which is the mechanism behind most "the outer loop ran too many times" reports. continue skips the rest of the current iteration and starts the next, and the trap is using it as a substitute for wrapping the body in an if, which adds an indentation level and hides the real structure; when more than one continue exists in a loop the if version is almost always clearer. else on a loop runs when the loop finished without a break, which is a genuinely useful way to express "search succeeded" without a flag variable — though it confuses most readers, so a comment saying # else: not found earns its place. And the loop variable leaks after the loop in Python, which is occasionally convenient and more often the reason two functions in the same scope interfere with each other.

/* The deciding question. */
const CHOOSE_LOOP = {
  rule: 'if you know how many times, or you are walking a sequence, use for; if the count depends on a condition only the body can satisfy, use while',
  why: 'a for loop over a sequence is driven by the sequence, so it cannot run forever',
  forLoopGuarantees: ['cannot run forever', 'cannot forget to advance',
    'stops correctly if the sequence is emptied mid-loop'],
  whileLoopDanger: 'driven by a condition you write - every failure mode comes from that condition not changing',
  forForms: ['over a range of numbers', 'over a sequence directly', 'over the sequence with index via enumerate'],
  keyProperty: 'for asks the sequence how long it is, ONCE, at the start',
  consequences: ['modifying the list length during the loop is a bug',
                 'for x in list(iterable) is the correct way to walk a list while mutating it'],
};

/* break, continue, else, and the loop variable. */
const CONTROLS = [
  { k: 'break', does: 'exits the INNERMOST loop',
    trap: 'inside a nested loop it leaves the outer one running',
    whyItMatters: 'the mechanism behind most outer-loop-ran-too-many-times reports' },
  { k: 'continue', does: 'skips the rest of the current iteration and starts the next',
    trap: 'used as a substitute for wrapping the body in an if',
    cost: 'adds an indentation level and hides the real structure',
    rule: 'with more than one continue in a loop, the if version is almost always clearer' },
  { k: 'else on a loop', does: 'runs when the loop finished WITHOUT a break',
    use: 'expresses search-succeeded without a flag variable',
    caveat: 'confuses most readers - a comment saying else: not found earns its place' },
  { k: 'the loop variable', does: 'leaks after the loop in Python',
    upside: 'occasionally convenient',
    downside: 'the reason two functions in the same scope interfere with each other' },
];

The cost model, and the three loop bugs that are really design bugs

Loops are where programs become slow, and the reason is almost never the loop itself. Iterating over indices to reach back into the sequence is the classic mistake — for i in range(len(a)): when for x in a: would do — because it does two lookups where one would do and reads worse; where it is genuinely necessary, because the loop body must modify several elements at the same index or skip ahead, enumerate and zip are the readable forms. Membership tests inside loops are quadratic. if x in some_list: inside a loop over a thousand items is a million comparisons, and the fix is a set, which makes it a thousand lookups — this is the single highest-value performance change available to a beginner and it is one line. Appending in a loop where accumulation would do builds an intermediate structure nobody needs. And string concatenation in a loop is quadratic because each + copies the whole string; the join function on a list of pieces is linear, and joining once at the end is the correct shape even when the loop is short enough that the difference does not show.

Then three bugs that are not performance problems but look like them. Modifying a collection while iterating it. Removing the current item from a list skips the next one, because every index shifts left; the correct forms are to iterate over a copy, to build a list of what to remove and remove it afterwards, or to collect into a new list. The same rule governs dictionaries and sets. Looping forever because nothing changed. A while that tests a condition the body never touches is an infinite loop, and the two ways to prevent it are to make the state change explicit in the body and to add a bound — an iteration counter with a sane maximum, so a logic error becomes a wrong answer instead of a hung process that eats a core until somebody notices. And the off-by-one at the boundary. range(len(a)) excludes the last index; range(1, len(a)) excludes the first; and a slice's stop is exclusive, so an index that "looks right" against a list is wrong against a range. The habit worth forming is to say out loud which of the two you mean, because Python gives you both conventions and neither is wrong on its own.

/* Where programs actually become slow. */
const SLOW = [
  { mistake: 'iterating over indices to reach back into the sequence',
    example: 'for i in range(len(a)): where for x in a: would do',
    costs: ['two lookups where one would do', 'reads worse'],
    whenActuallyNeeded: 'the body must modify several elements at the same index, or skip ahead',
    readableForms: ['enumerate', 'zip'] },
  { mistake: 'membership tests inside loops',
    example: 'if x in some_list inside a loop over a thousand items',
    arithmetic: 'a million comparisons',
    fix: 'a set - a thousand lookups',
    claim: 'the single highest-value performance change available to a beginner, and it is one line' },
  { mistake: 'appending in a loop where accumulation would do',
    symptom: 'builds an intermediate structure nobody needs' },
  { mistake: 'string concatenation in a loop',
    why: 'each + copies the whole string, so it is quadratic',
    fix: ''.join(parts) is linear - join once at the end',
    note: 'the correct shape even when the loop is short enough that the difference does not show' },
];

/* Three bugs that are design problems. */
const BUGS = [
  { bug: 'modifying a collection while iterating it',
    detail: 'removing the current item skips the next, because every index shifts left',
    correctForms: ['iterate over a copy', 'build a list of what to remove, remove it afterwards',
                   'collect into a new list'],
    generalises: 'the same rule governs dictionaries and sets' },
  { bug: 'looping forever because nothing changed',
    detail: 'a while testing a condition the body never touches',
    prevention: ['make the state change explicit in the body',
                 'add a bound - an iteration counter with a sane maximum'],
    payoff: 'a logic error becomes a wrong answer instead of a hung process eating a core' },
  { bug: 'the off-by-one at the boundary',
    facts: ['range(len(a)) excludes the last index',
            'range(1, len(a)) excludes the first',
            'a slices stop is exclusive'],
    reframe: 'an index that looks right against a list is wrong against a range',
    habit: 'say out loud which of the two you mean - Python gives you both conventions and neither is wrong' },
];

A while loop whose condition never becomes false runs forever and hangs your program. This is the classic infinite-loop bug — always ask "what changes each iteration, and will it eventually exit?"

3.5 Lists, indexing, slicing

A list is an ordered, mutable sequence of values accessed by index, starting at zero. Slicing with a colon extracts contiguous sublists, and methods like append, insert, and remove modify the list in place.
