Because nearly every program works with collections, these operations are essential daily tools.

scores = [80, 90, 75, 95]

print(scores[0])      # 80    <-- indexes start at 0!
print(scores[-1])     # 95    last element
print(scores[1:3])    # [90, 75]   slice: from index 1 up to (not including) 3

scores.append(88)     # add to the end
scores.insert(0, 70)  # add at the front
scores.remove(90)     # remove by value
scores[2] = 100       # change in place -- lists ARE changeable

print(len(scores))    # how many items
print(sum(scores))    # handy built-ins for numbers

Lists are indexed from zero, support slicing and negative indexes, and mutate in place via append, insert, remove, and direct assignment.

Indexing, slicing, and the off-by-one family of bugs

A list is an ordered, mutable sequence, and indexing counts from zero — so the first element is at 0 and the last is at len - 1. Zero-based indexing is not an arbitrary cruelty: it makes i the number of elements before an item, which is exactly what you need for computing a position in a slice or an offset, and a one-based scheme would force a subtraction at every use. Negative indexes count from the end, with -1 being the last element, which exists because "the last three items" is a common request and list[-3:] is the way to say it. Slicing is list[start:stop:step] where stop is excluded — and the exclusion is the second thing that catches everybody, because it is what makes slicing composable: two adjacent slices a[:i] and a[i:] partition the list exactly, with no overlap and nothing lost, which is only true if the boundary is shared and exclusive. Three related facts follow from that design, and they are worth having as statements: a slice returns a new list, so a[:] is a shallow copy; a slice with an out-of-range index does not error but clamps; and a step of -1 reverses, which turns a sorted list into a descending one and is the idiom for reversal.

Then mutation, and the specific consequences. append adds to the end, insert(i, x) inserts before index i — the other classic off-by-one, since insert(1, x) puts the item second — and remove(x) removes by value, raising ValueError if absent, which is a different failure mode from a bad index. pop(i) removes by position and returns it, whereas pop() removes the last; sort() sorts in place and returns nothing, which surprises people who write x = x.sort() and lose the list entirely; and extend appends every element of another iterable while append adds the iterable as one element. That last pair is the single most common list bug in real code: append([4,5]) nests, extend([4,5]) concatenates, and the resulting shape differs by a bracket. Underneath all of it is the cost model that matters more than the syntax: insert and remove at the front or middle are O(n) because every later element must shift, so a loop that inserts at position zero inside a loop over a large list is quadratic, and the fix is to append and reverse, or to use a deque when you need both-ends access.

/* Indexing, slicing and the off-by-one family. */
const INDEXING = {
  base: 'zero - the first element is 0, the last is len - 1',
  whyZeroBased: 'i is the number of elements BEFORE an item, which is what a slice offset needs',
  oneBasedCost: 'a one-based scheme would force a subtraction at every use',
  negative: 'counts from the end, with -1 being the last',
  whyNegative: 'the last three items is a common request and list[-3:] is how to say it',
};
const SLICING = {
  form: 'list[start:stop:step]',
  stopIs: 'EXCLUDED',
  whyExcluded: 'it makes slicing composable - a[:i] and a[i:] partition the list exactly',
  threeFacts: ['a slice returns a NEW list, so a[:] is a shallow copy',
    'an out-of-range index clamps rather than erroring',
    'a step of -1 reverses - the idiom for reversal'],
};
const MUTATION = [
  { op: 'append(x)', does: 'adds to the end' },
  { op: 'insert(i, x)', does: 'inserts BEFORE index i', trap: 'insert(1, x) puts the item second' },
  { op: 'remove(x)', does: 'removes by VALUE',
    failure: 'ValueError if absent - a different failure mode from a bad index' },
  { op: 'pop(i)', does: 'removes by POSITION and returns it', note: 'pop() removes the last' },
  { op: 'sort()', does: 'sorts in place and returns nothing',
    trap: 'x = x.sort() loses the list entirely' },
  { op: 'extend vs append', does: 'extend appends every element; append adds the iterable as one element',
    trap: 'the most common list bug - append([4,5]) nests, extend([4,5]) concatenates' },
];

/* The cost model, which matters more than the syntax. */
const COST = {
  fact: 'insert and remove at the front or middle are O(n) - every later element must shift',
  consequence: 'inserting at position zero inside a loop over a large list is quadratic',
  fixes: ['append and reverse', 'use a deque when you need both-ends access'],
};

Nested lists, copying, and the built-ins worth knowing by heart

Lists containing lists are how you represent a table, a matrix, a graph, and a ragged structure, and the mechanics are worth being precise about because two operations that look symmetrical are not. a[i][j] indexes twice: take the i-th element, which is itself a list, then take its j-th. a[i] = [...] replaces the whole row, so it works regardless of length; a[i].append(x) mutates the row in place, and the rows are shared references, so mutating one row changes it everywhere that row is referred to. a[i][j] = x mutates the innermost value. That asymmetry — replace the container, or mutate through it — is the reason a copy of a table of lists is not a copy. And a genuinely useful trick: a list of tuples is not a table, but zip(*rows) transposes one, which converts rows-to-columns and is the two-line way to pivot a matrix.

Then the built-ins, which are worth learning by trying them with surprising inputs rather than by reading them once. len for length — and note it is O(1) on a list because the size is stored, but O(n) on a generator, which is the difference between a loop that is instant and one that takes a minute. sum, min, max for aggregation, all of which skip an empty list by raising rather than returning. sorted for a new sorted list versus sort for in place, which is the difference between a value and an effect. enumerate to get index and value together — and the reason to prefer it over range(len(a)) is not brevity but that it does not break if the list changes length, which matters if the loop body appends. zip to walk several iterables together, whose one sharp edge is that it stops at the shortest, so zip silently truncating two lists of different lengths is a real and confusing bug. any and all for a truth question, which short-circuit — a detail that matters when the expression is an expensive call or a generator. And reversed rather than list[::-1] when you only need to iterate once, because it does not build a copy.

/* Nested lists: two operations that look symmetrical are not. */
const NESTING = {
  reads: 'a[i][j] - take the i-th element, which is itself a list, then its j-th',
  replaceRow: 'a[i] = [...] replaces the whole row, so it works regardless of length',
  mutateRow: 'a[i].append(x) mutates the row in place',
  theCatch: 'the rows are shared references, so mutating one row changes it everywhere it is referred to',
  mutateCell: 'a[i][j] = x mutates the innermost value',
  asymmetry: 'replace the container, or mutate through it',
  whyItMatters: 'a copy of a table of lists is not a copy',
  trick: 'zip(*rows) transposes - rows to columns, in two lines',
};

/* Built-ins worth learning by trying surprising inputs. */
const BUILTINS = [
  { fn: 'len', note: 'O(1) on a list because the size is stored',
    trap: 'O(n) on a generator - the difference between an instant loop and a minute-long one' },
  { fn: 'sum, min, max', trap: 'all raise rather than return on an empty list' },
  { fn: 'sorted vs sort', note: 'a new list versus in place - the difference between a value and an effect' },
  { fn: 'enumerate', note: 'index and value together',
    whyNotRange: 'not brevity - it does not break if the list changes length, which matters if the body appends' },
  { fn: 'zip', note: 'walk several iterables together',
    sharpEdge: 'it stops at the shortest, so zip on two different-length lists silently truncates' },
  { fn: 'any and all', note: 'a truth question', detail: 'they short-circuit - matters when the expression is expensive or a generator' },
  { fn: 'reversed', note: 'instead of list[::-1] when you only iterate once',
    why: 'it does not build a copy' },
];

Useful built-ins this semester: len, sum, max, min, sorted, enumerate, range, zip. Learn them by opening an interactive shell and trying each with surprising inputs.

3.6 Functions — packaging reusable logic

A function packages reusable logic behind a name, accepting inputs through parameters and returning results with the return keyword. Breaking programs into small, well-named functions reduces duplication and makes code testable and readable. Parameter defaults and explicit arguments are key concepts for flexible function signatures.

A function is a named block that takes inputs (parameters), does work, and often returns a result. Functions are the single most important tool for taming complexity.

def greet(name, loud=False):
    """Return a greeting string. loud makes it uppercase."""  # docstring
    msg = "Hello " + name
    return msg.upper() if loud else msg

print(greet("Ada"))            # Hello Ada
print(greet("Grace", True))    # HELLO GRACE

def average(nums):
    return sum(nums) / len(nums)

print(average([10, 20, 30]))   # 20.0

def packages logic behind a name with parameters and an optional return; the default argument loud=False lets one function serve both calls.

  • Parameters = the names the function accepts; arguments = the values you pass.
  • A function without return returns None.
  • Variables created inside a function don’t leak out (that’s scope).

Parameters, arguments, and the five ways a call can bind them

A function is a name for a block of code plus the parameters it accepts, and the whole design rests on one decision made at the call site: which value goes to which parameter. Python has five ways to do it, and confusion between them is the source of most "it did not do what I expected" reports. Positional binds by order — f(a, b) means the first argument is a. Keyword binds by name — f(b=2, a=1) is the same call as f(1, 2), and this is the single most valuable readability feature the language offers, because a call with three arguments of similar type is unreadable positionally and self-documenting by keyword. Default supplies a value used when the argument is omitted — def f(a, b=10) — and the rule that makes defaults a frequent source of bugs is that a default is evaluated once, when the function is defined, not on each call. That is why the classic mutable-default bug exists: def f(items=[]) shares one list across every call that omits the argument, and the second caller sees the first caller's data. The fix is def f(items=None) followed by items = items or [] inside. Variadic *args collects any number of extra positional arguments into a tuple, and variadic keyword **kwargs collects any number of named ones into a dictionary — and the real use of both is not convenience but forwarding, where a wrapper passes *args, **kwargs to the function it wraps so it never needs to know that function's signature.

Then what actually makes a function good, which is not the same as what makes it short. One reason to exist. If a function needs a comment saying what it also does, it is two functions. A name that is a phrase. calculate_total_tax, not do_it; the name is the first line of the documentation and the only part of it that cannot go stale. Few parameters, and a limit worth enforcing. Three is comfortable, five is a smell, seven means the abstraction is doing too many jobs — and the practical consequence of too many is that every caller must remember an ordering, which is memory work that should not be necessary. Return early. A function with four if-return pairs at one indentation level can be read top to bottom; the same logic nested reaches four levels by the last branch and nobody can hold it in their head. Return a value, or raise — never both. A function that returns None on failure makes every caller check, and a function that raises on one path and returns on another makes the callers inconsistent. And do not mutate an argument you were given. Sorting a list in place inside a function changes the caller's data invisibly, which is why sorted(x) and x.sort() both existing is a genuine design decision rather than redundancy.

/* Five ways a call can bind arguments. */
const BINDING = [
  { k: 'positional', does: 'binds by order - f(a, b) means the first argument is a' },
  { k: 'keyword', does: 'binds by name - f(b=2, a=1) is the same call as f(1, 2)',
    why: 'the most valuable readability feature the language offers',
    gain: 'a call with three similar-typed arguments is unreadable positionally and self-documenting by keyword' },
  { k: 'default', does: 'supplies a value used when the argument is omitted',
    rule: 'a default is evaluated ONCE, when the function is defined, not on each call',
    bug: 'def f(items=[]) shares one list across every call that omits the argument',
    symptom: 'the second caller sees the first callers data',
    fix: 'def f(items=None), then items = items or [] inside' },
  { k: 'variadic *args', does: 'collects extra positional arguments into a tuple' },
  { k: 'variadic keyword **kwargs', does: 'collects extra named arguments into a dict' },
  { realUseOfBoth: 'forwarding - a wrapper passes *args, **kwargs to the function it wraps
    so it never needs to know that functions signature',
};

/* What makes a function good, which is not the same as short. */
const QUALITY = [
  { r: 'one reason to exist', test: 'if it needs a comment saying what it also does, it is two functions' },
  { r: 'a name that is a phrase',
    example: 'calculate_total_tax, not do_it',
    why: 'the first line of documentation and the only part that cannot go stale' },
  { r: 'few parameters', numbers: '3 comfortable, 5 a smell, 7 means the abstraction is doing too many jobs',
    consequence: 'every caller must remember an ordering - memory work that should not be necessary' },
  { r: 'return early',
    good: 'four if-return pairs at one indentation level, readable top to bottom',
    bad: 'the same logic nested reaches four levels by the last branch' },
  { r: 'return a value, or raise - never both',
    why: 'returning None on failure makes every caller check; mixing makes callers inconsistent' },
  { r: 'do not mutate an argument you were given',
    mechanism: 'sorting a list in place inside a function changes the callers data invisibly',
    note: 'why both sorted(x) and x.sort() existing is a design decision rather than redundancy' },
];

Scope, the two kinds of default, and returning more than one thing

Scope in Python is mostly not what beginners expect. Functions create scope; blocks do not. An if or a for inside a function does not introduce a new scope, so a variable assigned there exists afterwards — which is why a loop variable leaks and why a name assigned inside an if can be read outside it and be undefined on the other path, producing an NameError on exactly one branch. Names are looked up at use time, not definition time. A function body referring to a global reads whatever that global is when the line executes, which is why a global changed later in the file changes the function's behaviour, and why a global read inside a hot loop is both a correctness hazard and a performance one. Assignment anywhere in a function makes the name local throughout. Reading a global before assigning to it in the same function raises UnboundLocalError, and this is the single most confusing error in the language for a beginner: the message says local variable and there is no local variable anywhere. The fix is to declare the intent — read it, mutate it, and write it back, or read the global explicitly — never to add an assignment to silence it.

Then three design decisions that come up constantly. Default values are evaluated once, which was covered above and is the mutable-default bug's whole cause. Mutable defaults versus None sentinels: when you genuinely need a per-call empty list, the None-then-assign pattern is the correct form, and the discipline is to use a name that reads as a sentinel rather than a magic value. Returning more than one thing. Python can return a tuple, and unpacking min_height, min_width = image_size(img) is genuinely pleasant — but the moment a caller does not need both, or the order matters, a tuple is an unnamed contract and the correct move is an object with named attributes, because result.width survives a refactor and result[1] does not. The same reasoning explains why a function that returns a bare boolean makes a caller's if line unreadable: the name is_valid says what the True means and if check(x): does not. And the practical rule for the whole section: a function is a module of one, and it should be readable on its own page without the rest of the file.

/* Scope is mostly not what beginners expect. */
const SCOPE = [
  { fact: 'functions create scope; blocks do not',
    consequence: 'an if or a for inside a function introduces no new scope',
    symptom: 'a variable assigned in an if can be read outside it and be undefined on the other path',
    error: 'NameError on exactly one branch' },
  { fact: 'names are looked up at use time, not definition time',
    consequence: 'a function reading a global reads whatever it is when the line executes',
    why: 'a global changed later changes the functions behaviour',
    cost: 'a global read inside a hot loop is a correctness hazard and a performance one' },
  { fact: 'assignment anywhere in a function makes the name local throughout',
    error: 'reading a global before assigning to it in the same function raises UnboundLocalError',
    confusing: 'the message says local variable and there is no local variable anywhere',
    fix: 'declare the intent - read, mutate, write back, or read the global explicitly - never add an assignment to silence it',
];

/* Three design decisions. */
const DECISIONS = [
  { d: 'default values evaluated once', covered: 'the whole cause of the mutable-default bug' },
  { d: 'mutable defaults versus None sentinels',
    when: 'you genuinely need a per-call empty list',
    correctForm: 'the None-then-assign pattern',
    discipline: 'use a name that reads as a sentinel rather than a magic value' },
  { d: 'returning more than one thing',
    nice: 'min_height, min_width = image_size(img)',
    whenItStopsBeingNice: 'a caller does not need both, or the order matters',
    fix: 'an object with named attributes - result.width survives a refactor, result[1] does not',
    alsoExplains: 'why a function returning a bare boolean makes an if line unreadable',
    example: 'if is_valid(x) says what the True means; if check(x) does not' },
];
const MODULE_OF_ONE = 'a function is a module of one, and it should be readable on its own page without the rest of the file';

Exercise 3.6

Write is_even(n) returning True/False. Then write fizzbuzz(n) that prints numbers 1..n, but "Fizz" for multiples of 3, "Buzz" for 5, "FizzBuzz" for both. FizzBuzz is a famous interview warm-up.

3.7 Dictionaries and tuples

A dictionary maps keys to values, enabling fast lookups by key, while a tuple is an immutable, ordered collection of items. You build dicts with braces and colons, access values by key, and use tuples to group related values that must not change. Both structures appear in almost every real program.

user = {"name": "Ada", "age": 21, "skills": ["Python", "SQL"]}

print(user["name"])            # Ada  (lookup by key)
user["city"] = "London"        # add a new key
user["age"] = 22               # update
if "email" in user:            # check existence
    print(user["email"])

for key, value in user.items():   # iterate through all entries
    print(f"{key} = {value}")

# tuple: like a list but immutable (can't change after creation)
point = (10, 20)
x, y = point                   # unpacking
print(x, y)                    # 10 20

Dictionaries give fast key lookup, grow by assignment, and iterate as key-value pairs; tuples are immutable ordered pairs you can unpack.

Choosing the right container, which is the real content of this section

A dictionary is a lookup table: a set of keys, each mapped to a value, with lookup by key in roughly constant time regardless of size. What makes it more than a convenience is what it requires of a key. A key must be hashable — its hash must be computable and it must compare equal to itself — which is why strings, numbers and tuples can be keys and lists and dictionaries cannot. The second requirement is subtler and causes the bug everybody hits once: the key must not change while it is in the dictionary. A hash is usually derived from the key's contents, so mutating a key in place makes it unfindable, and the entry is silently leaked rather than reported. Then insertion order is preserved, which makes a dictionary usable as an ordered mapping where a sorted structure would have been needed otherwise, and duplicate keys overwrite — {'a': 1, 'a': 2} is {'a': 2} and no warning, which is the classic bug when a literal is written with a repeated key by mistake.

Then the decision that this section really exists to make: which container for which job. Use a dictionary when the thing is a lookup with a natural identity. A user by id, a setting by name, a column by name, a route by path, a count by word. Use a list when order matters and the items are interchangeable. A sequence of records processed in order, a queue, a result set you will page through. Use a tuple when the shape is fixed and meaningful — a coordinate pair, a database row, a return value — because the fixed arity is documentation and immutability makes it hashable and safe to share. Use a set when you only care about membership. Removing duplicates, tracking what has been seen, and testing membership in constant time rather than by scanning. The decision procedure is short: if you would reach for index, use a list or a tuple; if you would reach for .index() to find something, use a set or a dictionary; if two items at the same key must never both exist, a set or a dictionary is enforced by the container rather than by your discipline.

/* What makes a dictionary more than a convenience. */
const DICT = {
  is: 'a lookup table - keys mapped to values, constant-time lookup regardless of size',
  keyRequirement: 'hashable - its hash must be computable and it must compare equal to itself',
  hashable: ['str', 'number', 'tuple'],
  notHashable: ['list', 'dict'],
  subtleRequirement: 'the key must not change while it is in the dictionary',
  why: 'the hash is derived from the contents, so mutating a key in place makes it unfindable',
  silentFailure: 'the entry is leaked rather than reported',
  insertionOrder: 'preserved - a dictionary is usable as an ordered mapping',
  duplicateKeys: "last one wins, with no warning - {'a': 1, 'a': 2} is {'a': 2}",
  classicBug: 'a literal written with a repeated key by mistake',
};

/* Choosing the container: the decision this section exists to make. */
const CHOOSE = [
  { use: 'dictionary', when: 'a lookup with a natural identity',
    instances: ['a user by id', 'a setting by name', 'a column by name', 'a route by path', 'a count by word'] },
  { use: 'list', when: 'order matters and the items are interchangeable',
    instances: ['records processed in order', 'a queue', 'a result set you will page through'] },
  { use: 'tuple', when: 'the shape is fixed and meaningful',
    instances: ['a coordinate pair', 'a database row', 'a return value'],
    why: 'the fixed arity is documentation, and immutability makes it hashable and safe to share' },
  { use: 'set', when: 'you only care about membership',
    instances: ['removing duplicates', 'tracking what has been seen'],
    win: 'constant-time membership rather than a scan' },
];
const PROCEDURE = [
  'if you would reach for index, use a list or a tuple',
  'if you would reach for .index() to find something, use a set or a dictionary',
  'if two items at the same key must never both exist, a set or a dictionary enforces it rather than your discipline',
];

The operations worth memorising, and the failure modes worth knowing

Six operations cover almost everything a beginner needs, and it is worth having them on the fingers rather than looking them up. d[key] requires the key and raises KeyError without it; d.get(key, default) returns a default instead, and this is the single most useful difference in the container — it turns a crash into a decision. key in d tests membership without the cost of fetching. for key, value in d.items() iterates both at once rather than indexing each time. d.keys() and d.values() give the two halves when you only need one. del d[key] removes, and d.pop(key, default) removes and returns — which is how you consume a key from a mapping exactly once. Then the operations that reach for nested data: d.get('config', {}).get('timeout', 30) chains safely through missing levels, and it is worth understanding that it is safe because of the defaults, not because the nesting is shallow.

Then the four failure modes, because they are what a dictionary causes and none of them is about the dictionary. Iterating while modifying. Adding or removing a key inside a loop over that same dictionary raises an error, and the correct shape is to build a second collection of changes and apply them afterwards — which generalises to a rule about all mutation-during-iteration, not just dictionaries. Mixing key types. d[1] and d['1'] are different entries, and a lookup that used the wrong type returns nothing with no error, because nothing is missing — the key you wanted is simply under a different representation. Assuming a default. d.get(k, []) returns a fresh empty list each call, so mutating it silently discards the mutation, whereas d.setdefault(k, []) stores that list and returns it, which is the version people reach for and the reason for the classic "why did my append vanish" bug. And the unhashable key. Passing a list as a key fails immediately and clearly, which is a good failure — but passing a mutable custom object as a key fails silently and much later, which is the reason the hashable requirement exists.

/* Six operations worth having on the fingers. */
const OPS = [
  { op: 'd[key]', behaviour: 'requires the key, raises KeyError without it' },
  { op: 'd.get(key, default)', behaviour: 'returns a default instead',
    why: 'the most useful difference in the container - it turns a crash into a decision' },
  { op: 'key in d', behaviour: 'tests membership without the cost of fetching' },
  { op: 'for key, value in d.items()', behaviour: 'iterates both at once rather than indexing each time' },
  { op: 'd.keys() and d.values()', behaviour: 'the two halves when you only need one' },
  { op: 'd.pop(key, default)', behaviour: 'removes and returns - how you consume a key exactly once',
    also: 'del d[key] removes without returning' },
];
const NESTED = "d.get('config', {}).get('timeout', 30) chains safely through missing levels";
const NESTED_WHY = 'safe BECAUSE OF THE DEFAULTS, not because the nesting is shallow';

/* Four failure modes, none of which is about the dictionary. */
const FAILURES = [
  { f: 'iterating while modifying',
    symptom: 'adding or removing a key inside a loop over that dictionary raises an error',
    correctShape: 'build a second collection of changes and apply them afterwards',
    generalises: 'a rule about all mutation-during-iteration, not just dictionaries' },
  { f: 'mixing key types', detail: "d[1] and d['1'] are different entries",
    whyItHurts: 'a lookup with the wrong type returns nothing with no error',
    reframe: 'nothing is missing - the key you wanted is simply under a different representation' },
  { f: 'assuming a default',
    detail: 'd.get(k, []) returns a FRESH empty list each call',
    symptom: 'mutating it silently discards the mutation',
    contrast: 'd.setdefault(k, []) stores that list and returns it',
    classicBug: 'why did my append vanish' },
  { f: 'the unhashable key',
    goodFailure: 'passing a list as a key fails immediately and clearly',
    badFailure: 'passing a mutable custom object as a key fails silently and much later',
    note: 'the reason the hashable requirement exists' },
];

Why care about immutability now? Chapter 4 will live in it: immutability makes code easier to reason about and is core to functional style and to concurrency in Ch. 23.

3.8 A methodical debugging recipe

This topic gives a repeatable recipe for fixing bugs: reproduce the problem, read the error and surrounding code, form a hypothesis about the cause, and test it with a small experiment. Using print statements or a debugger to inspect values at key points narrows the search. The methodical loop turns mystifying failures into quick fixes.

  1. Reproduce the bug with the smallest input possible.
  2. Read the error message and the line it points at.
  3. Print intermediate values (print("DEBUG x =", x)) or use the debugger. Treat print-debugging as fine, but remove it before "done".
  4. Form a hypothesis about the cause, fix it, and test again.
  5. If stuck, explain the bug out loud — rubber-duck mode — or simplify the code until it’s obviously correct.

What debugging actually is, and the loop that makes it work

Debugging is not staring harder at the code. It is a loop of five steps, and the value of naming them is that a stuck debugger is usually stuck at one identified step rather than "stuck". Reproduce. Make it fail, reliably, with the smallest input that still fails. An intermittent bug you cannot reproduce is not debuggable yet, and the effort belongs in making it deterministic — logging every input, freezing the data, running it in a loop — rather than in watching it. Isolate. Narrow to the smallest piece that still misbehaves, and the tool for this is removal: comment out half and run. If the failure persists, the cause is in the other half; that is four runs to localise a fault to a half, and eight to a quarter, which is faster than any amount of reading. Hypothesise. Write one sentence: "I believe the value is wrong because X". This is the step almost everybody skips and the one that pays, because a written hypothesis that turns out to be wrong has still eliminated a possibility, while no hypothesis eliminates nothing. Test. One change, one prediction. Two changes that together remove the symptom tell you nothing about either. Fix, then verify. Fix the cause rather than the symptom — a retry over a race, a null check over an uninitialised value, a try block over an exception each make the symptom vanish and leave the defect — and then confirm the original case is fixed and nothing else broke, because a fix that changed behaviour elsewhere has traded one bug for another.

Then the traceback, which is the artefact a beginner reads worst and which contains the answer in a fixed order. Read it bottom-up. The last line is the error type and message; the line directly above it is where it happened, with the file and line number; the frames above that are the call chain that got you there. Reading top-down shows you the outermost caller — which is usually your own main — and teaches you nothing. The three lines at the bottom are the answer; everything above is the path. Two specific readings make it much faster: the exception type narrows the search before you read anything else, because a TypeError is a type problem and a KeyError is a lookup problem, and the type tells you which half of your program to look at; and the last frame in your own code, which is where the defect usually is, since library frames are usually innocent.

/* Five steps, and naming them means a stuck debugger is stuck at ONE step. */
const DEBUG_LOOP = [
  { s: 'reproduce', do: 'fail reliably, with the smallest input that still fails',
    why: 'an intermittent bug you cannot reproduce is not debuggable yet',
    effort: 'into making it deterministic - logging every input, freezing the data, running in a loop - rather than watching' },
  { s: 'isolate', tool: 'removal - comment out half and run',
    arithmetic: 'four runs to localise a fault to a half, eight to a quarter',
    why: 'faster than any amount of reading' },
  { s: 'hypothesise', do: 'write one sentence - I believe the value is wrong because X',
    everyoneSkipsIt: true,
    whyItPays: 'a written hypothesis that turns out wrong has still eliminated a possibility; none eliminates nothing' },
  { s: 'test', rule: 'one change, one prediction',
    why: 'two changes that together remove the symptom tell you nothing about either' },
  { s: 'fix, then verify', rule: 'fix the cause, not the symptom',
    antiPatterns: ['a retry over a race', 'a null check over an uninitialised value', 'a try over an exception'],
    verification: ['the original case is fixed', 'nothing else broke'],
    why: 'a fix that changed behaviour elsewhere has traded one bug for another' },
];

/* Reading the traceback bottom-up. */
const TRACEBACK = {
  rule: 'read it bottom-up',
  order: ['the last line is the error type and message',
    'the line directly above is where it happened, with file and line number',
    'the frames above are the call chain that got you there'],
  whyTopDownFails: 'it shows the outermost caller, usually your own main, and teaches nothing',
  reframe: 'the three lines at the bottom ARE the answer; everything above is the path',
  speedUpOne: 'the exception type narrows the search before you read anything else',
  byType: ['TypeError is a type problem', 'KeyError is a lookup problem'],
  speedUpTwo: 'the last frame in your own code is where the defect usually is',
  because: 'library frames are usually innocent',
};

Debuggers, print statements done right, and the bugs that resist all of it

A real debugger changes the cost model of the work. Instead of adding a print, rerunning, reading, removing the print and repeating, you set a breakpoint and inspect six variables at the moment they matter — and the two capabilities that matter most are conditional breakpoints, which stop only when a condition holds rather than on every one of a thousand iterations, and watch expressions, which evaluate something on every stop without a print. Both turn a thousand reruns into one. Then the print statement, done properly, because it is still the right tool for a script you are about to run once and for anything where a debugger is inconvenient. The rules are specific. Print the type and the identity, not just the value. The bug that looks like a wrong value is frequently the right value of the wrong object, and printing id(x) or type(x) beside x reveals it where printing x does not. Print where decisions are made — inside every if, at the branch decision itself — rather than only where things go wrong, because an else branch that should not have been taken produces no error at all. Print the boundary, the inputs and outputs of a function that crosses into another system, rather than the internals of either. And make failures loud during development: an assertion or an explicit raise in code that "cannot happen" turns a silent wrong value three steps later into an immediate failure where it happened.

Then three classes of bug that all of this does not catch, and each needs its own technique. Heisenbugs — the bug disappears when you look at it — are usually a race, an uninitialised value or an uninitialised struct member, and the technique is not more logging but changing the timing deliberately: insert a sleep, or move the breakpoint, and see whether the bug changes shape. A bug that changes when you change the schedule is a concurrency bug, and you have just learned that in ten seconds what would otherwise have taken a day. Bohlen bugs — the bug is worse the more you look — are usually an exception handler that swallows everything, or a test that asserts on something the code was not supposed to change, or a retry that papers over the cause. The technique is to remove the defensive code and see what was being hidden; the answer is always more interesting than the symptom. And bugs in code you did not write and cannot change — in a library, in the interpreter, in a dependency — where the technique is to isolate: construct the smallest input that reaches the failure, determine whether the contract is being violated or the contract is wrong, and if the latter, wrap it. Each of these is a different investigation, and naming them is what stops you from applying "add a print" to all three.

/* What a debugger changes. */
const DEBUGGER = [
  { f: 'breakpoint', replaces: 'add a print, rerun, read, remove, repeat',
    gain: 'inspect six variables at the moment they matter' },
  { f: 'conditional breakpoint', does: 'stops only when a condition holds rather than on every one of a thousand iterations',
    payoff: 'a thousand reruns become one' },
  { f: 'watch expression', does: 'evaluates on every stop without a print',
    payoff: 'a thousand reruns become one' },
];
const PRINTS_DONE_RIGHT = [
  { rule: 'print the type and the identity, not just the value',
    catches: 'the bug that looks like a wrong value is often the right value of the wrong object',
    how: 'print id(x) or type(x) beside x',
    why: 'reveals what printing x alone does not' },
  { rule: 'print where decisions are made', detail: 'inside every if, at the branch decision itself',
    notEnough: 'only where things go wrong',
    why: 'an else branch that should not have been taken produces no error at all' },
  { rule: 'print the boundary', detail: 'inputs and outputs of a function crossing into another system',
    notThis: 'the internals of either side' },
  { rule: 'make failures loud during development',
    how: 'an assertion or an explicit raise in code that cannot happen',
    gain: 'a silent wrong value three steps later becomes an immediate failure where it happened' },
];

/* Three classes all of this misses. */
const RESISTANT = [
  { bug: 'Heisenbug', detail: 'the bug disappears when you look at it',
    usually: ['a race', 'an uninitialised value', 'an uninitialised struct member'],
    technique: 'not more logging - change the timing deliberately',
    how: ['insert a sleep', 'move the breakpoint', 'see whether the bug changes shape'],
    finding: 'a bug that changes when you change the schedule is a concurrency bug, learned in ten seconds what would take a day' },
  { bug: 'Bohlen bug', detail: 'the bug is worse the more you look',
    usually: ['an exception handler that swallows everything',
      'a test asserting on something the code was not supposed to change',
      'a retry papering over the cause'],
    technique: 'remove the defensive code and see what was being hidden',
    finding: 'the answer is always more interesting than the symptom' },
  { bug: 'a bug in code you did not write and cannot change',
    where: ['a library', 'the interpreter', 'a dependency'],
    technique: ['construct the smallest input that reaches the failure',
      'decide whether the contract is violated or the contract is wrong',
      'if the latter, wrap it'],
    note: 'each is a different investigation, and naming them stops you applying add-a-print to all three' },
];

Ruby-duck debugging is real. Explaining your code line-by-line to an inanimate object forces you to notice the assumption your brain silently skipped.

3.9 Modules, imports and the standard library

Modules let you split code into separate files and reuse them with the import statement. Python ships a large standard library with modules for file handling, math, JSON, regular expressions, and more, so you rarely need to write common tools from scratch. Organising code into modules keeps large programs maintainable.

As programs grow, split them into modules (files). Python’s standard library is a treasure chest — "batteries included" — and most real problems have a ready tool.

# main.py  <-- one module importing another
import math                      # a standard library module
from random import randint       # import just the pieces you need
from my_utils import greet       # your OWN module, same folder

print(math.floor(3.99))          # 3
print(randint(1, 6))             # dice roll
print(greet("Ada"))

imports pull in whole standard-library modules, individual functions, or your own files — the mechanism that keeps code split and reusable.

ModuleWhat it gives you
mathfloor, sqrt, pi, log, trig
randomrandom numbers, choice, sample, shuffle
datetimedates and times, timezone math — timestamps everywhere in logs/APIs
jsonload/dump JSON — the web’s data format (Ch. 18)
reregular expressions — pattern matching in text (Ch. 25 formalises them)
collectionsdeque, Counter, defaultdict — the data-structure extras (Ch. 8)
os / pathlibfilesystem and paths (Ch. 3.10)
urllib / requestsfetching URLs (Ch. 14, 18)
unittest / pytesttesting (Ch. 16)

For anything not in the standard library: pip install <package> (PyPI = the Python package index). Your project’s dependency list should be reproducible — we’ll store it in requirements.txt and later in containers (Ch. 22).

Why modules exist, and the three things every file needs

A module in Python is just a file with .py on the end, and the reason to have one is not organisation for its own sake — it is that a file is the unit of testing, of importing, and of naming. The second reason matters more than it first appears: a module is a namespace. Two projects can both have a utils.py with a parse() in it, because a module's name is what identifies it, and that is the entire mechanism preventing one project's helper from shadowing another's. This is the same reasoning that later produces packages and, much further on, containers and namespaces at the operating-system level: the problem is always the same — two unrelated things want the same name — and the fix is always the same, a level of scoping that gives each a distinct identity.

Then the three things every file needs, in this order, and the reasons are what make this a habit rather than a style preference. if __name__ == "__main__": at the bottom. When a file is run directly, __name__ is "__main__"; when it is imported, it is the module's own name. Without the guard, importing a file runs its demonstration code, which is why a script that works when you run it can break an unrelated program that imports it — and the error message points at the imported file, in somebody else's project, which makes it close to undebuggable without knowing this mechanism. A docstring at the top — a triple-quoted string on line one, describing what the module is for. It costs one line, it is what help(module) prints, and unlike a comment it is part of the object. A blank line, then imports. The blank line separates the module docstring from the code, and the grouping is the convention worth knowing: standard library first, then third-party, then your own — because that ordering tells a reader, in three seconds, what this file depends on, and dependencies are what you need to know first when something breaks.

Then the import syntax and the one thing not to do. import x gives you the module; you reach things through x.y, which is verbose and completely unambiguous. from x import y brings in a specific name, which reads better and is fine when the name is specific and unusual. from x import y as z is for when two modules both call something json or logging, and the alias says which. from x import * is the one to avoid, and the reason is precise: it copies every public name into your namespace, so you no longer know where any name came from, a collision is resolved by whichever import ran last rather than by an error, and a reader cannot tell what the file depends on by looking at it. The cost is not style — it is that the file stops being checkable, which is why a linter flags it and why every codebase you have read has a rule against it.

/* A module is a file with .py on the end. */
const MODULE = {
  is: 'a file with .py on the end',
  whyNotOrganisation: 'a file is the unit of testing, of importing, and of naming',
  realReason: 'a module is a NAMESPACE',
  namespacePoint: 'two projects can both have a utils.py with a parse() in it, because the modules name identifies it',
  generalises: 'packages, and much later containers and OS namespaces - two unrelated things want the same name, and the fix is a level of scoping giving each a distinct identity',
};

/* Three things every file needs. */
const FILE_NEEDS = [
  { need: 'if __name__ == "__main__": at the bottom',
    mechanism: 'run directly gives __main__; imported gives the modules own name',
    whyItExists: 'without it, importing a file runs its demonstration code',
    symptom: 'a script that works when you run it breaks an unrelated program that imports it',
    whyUndebuggable: 'the error points at the imported file in somebody elses project' },
  { need: 'a docstring at the top',
    form: 'a triple-quoted string on line one',
    cost: 'one line',
    gains: ['what help(module) prints', 'it is part of the object, unlike a comment'] },
  { need: 'a blank line, then imports',
    grouping: 'standard library, then third-party, then your own',
    payoff: 'the ordering tells a reader in three seconds what this file depends on',
    why: 'dependencies are what you need to know first when something breaks' },
];

/* Import syntax, and the one to avoid. */
const IMPORTS = [
  { form: 'import x', gives: 'the module; you reach things through x.y',
    verdict: 'verbose and completely unambiguous' },
  { form: 'from x import y', gives: 'a specific name',
    verdict: 'reads better, fine when the name is specific and unusual' },
  { form: 'from x import y as z', when: 'two modules both call something json or logging',
    gain: 'the alias says which' },
  { form: 'from x import *', avoid: true,
    mechanism: 'copies every public name into your namespace',
    problems: ['you no longer know where any name came from',
      'a collision is resolved by whichever import ran last rather than by an error',
      'a reader cannot tell what the file depends on by looking at it'],
    cost: 'the file stops being checkable',
    note: 'every codebase you have read has a rule against it' },
];

Running, importing, and the circular import

Three run modes, and knowing which one you are in explains most "works when I run it" bugs. Running a script sets __name__ to "__main__" and puts the script's own directory at the front of the import path, so a module in that same directory is importable. Importing a module loads it once, caches it, and gives it its own name — and the caching is the detail worth internalising, because a module's code runs once per process, no matter how many files import it. That is why a print at module level appears once when a program starts and nowhere near as many times as the program imports it, and why a module-level variable set at import time is shared state that every importer sees. The practical rule that follows: never put work at module level that you would not want done once at import, and never rely on import order. Running a package entry point sets __name__ to "__main__" too, but through a console-script wrapper rather than by naming a file directly, which is why installed programs take a command rather than a path.

Then the circular import, because it is the failure everybody meets once and the error message actively misleads. It happens when module A imports B at the top and B imports A at the top: whichever is imported first begins loading, reaches its import of the other, which begins loading, reaches its import back to the first, and finds it in a state where it exists but is not finished — so a name it expected is not there yet. Depending on language and version the symptom is an ImportError naming a name you can plainly see defined, or a partially-initialised module warning, or in the worst case an AttributeError: module X has no attribute Y raised from a third file. The fixes, in order of preference: move the shared code into a third module that both import, which is the right answer and also the better design, since two modules needing the same thing is a signal that thing should be its own module. Move the import inside the function that needs it, which defers it until the module is fully loaded — cheap and effective, at the cost of an import on every call unless cached. And restructure so one side does not import the other, usually by passing the object in as an argument, which is the direction the rest of this book takes anyway. The underlying lesson is that the failure is not about imports at all — it is that a module whose top-level code reaches outward in a cycle has no valid initial order, and any structure that removes the cycle removes the error.

/* Three run modes, and which one you are in explains most works-when-I-run-it bugs. */
const RUN_MODES = [
  { m: 'running a script',
    name: '__main__',
    path: 'puts the scripts own directory at the front of the import path',
    gain: 'a module in that same directory is importable' },
  { m: 'importing a module', does: 'loads once, caches, gives its own name',
    keyFact: 'a modules code runs ONCE per process, no matter how many files import it',
    consequences: ['a print at module level appears once at startup, not once per importer',
      'a module-level variable set at import time is shared state every importer sees'],
    rule: 'never put work at module level you would not want done once at import, and never rely on import order' },
  { m: 'running a package entry point', name: '__main__',
    difference: 'through a console-script wrapper rather than by naming a file directly',
    why: 'why installed programs take a command rather than a path' },
];

/* The circular import. */
const CIRCULAR = {
  happens: 'module A imports B at the top and B imports A at the top',
  sequence: ['whichever is imported first begins loading',
    'reaches its import of the other, which begins loading',
    'reaches its import back to the first, which exists but is not finished',
    'so a name it expected is not there yet'],
  symptoms: ['an ImportError naming a name you can plainly see defined',
    'a partially-initialised module warning',
    'AttributeError: module X has no attribute Y, raised from a third file'],
  whyMisleading: 'the error points at a missing name rather than at the cycle',
  fixesInOrder: [
    { fix: 'move the shared code into a third module both import',
      verdict: 'the right answer and the better design',
      why: 'two modules needing the same thing is a signal that thing should be its own module' },
    { fix: 'move the import inside the function that needs it',
      mechanism: 'defers until the module is fully loaded',
      cost: 'an import on every call unless cached' },
    { fix: 'restructure so one side does not import the other, usually by passing the object in as an argument',
      note: 'the direction the rest of this book takes anyway' },
  ],
  lesson: 'the failure is not about imports - a module whose top-level code reaches outward in a cycle has no valid initial order',
};

Import style rules that keep code maintainable: imports at the top of the file, one import per region: standard library → third-party → your own modules; avoid from x import * (it dumps names into your scope and causes collisions).

3.10 Files and JSON — making data persist

Programs persist data across sessions by reading and writing files and JSON. The with statement opens a file and guarantees it is closed automatically even when an error occurs. JSON, Python’s favoured serialisation format, converts between text and native data structures through the json module’s load, loads, dump, and dumps functions.

Programs that forget everything when they exit are toys. Reading and writing files (and JSON, the lingua franca of data) is the same skill repeated a thousand times in a real job.

# Writing text
with open("notes.txt", "w") as f:      # "w" overwrites; "a" appends; "r" reads
    f.write("Hello disk\n")

# Reading text back
with open("notes.txt", "r") as f:
    text = f.read()
print(text)

# Structured data: JSON in, JSON out
import json
data = {"name": "Ada", "scores": [85, 90, 78]}

with open("user.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(data, f, indent=2)         # write with pretty formatting

with open("user.json", "r") as f:
    loaded = json.load(f)
print(loaded["scores"][0])               # 85

The with-block opens and auto-closes files; text round-trips through write and read, and JSON dictionaries round-trip via dump and load.

Why with-blocks? They guarantee the file is closed even if the code throws an exception — no leaked handles, no corrupted files. This "resource management" idea returns as context managers and in Go/Java with defer/try-with-resources.

The three modes, and the bug that only happens in one of them

Reading a file requires choosing a mode and a reason, and the reason matters more than the letter. 'r' reads and fails if the file is missing — which is correct, because a missing input file is not a condition to recover from, it is a mistake worth stopping on. 'w' writes and truncates: if the file exists, its contents are gone before the first byte is written. This is the single most destructive thing in the language and it does it silently — the whole reason to open a file for writing is to lose the previous version. 'a' appends, which is what you want for a log and the wrong choice for a rewrite. Then the two that catch people: 'r+' requires the file to exist and 'w+' creates it and truncates, so 'w+' is 'w' with extra permissions nobody wanted. And the practical rule that prevents the worst outcome: when writing, write to a new name and replace afterwards, so an interrupted write leaves the original intact. A crash halfway through a 'w' write leaves a truncated file and no way back.

Then the context manager, which is not a style preference but a correctness mechanism. with open(path) as f: guarantees the file is closed when the block ends — including when it ends because of an exception, which is the case that matters, because an unclosed file holds a lock on Windows, leaks a descriptor on Linux, and means the buffered content may never reach disk. The deeper reason the with form is the idiom is that it removes the need to reason about cleanup at all: there is no path through the function that can forget, because the language performs the close rather than the programmer. This generalises, and the generalisation is worth more than the file case — every resource in programming should be acquired inside a construct that guarantees release, which is why database connections, locks and sockets all have the same shape and why the discipline is called RAII in C++ and context management everywhere else. And the small thing that saves the most time: always use a with block, even for a single read.

/* Reading requires a mode and a reason, and the reason matters more than the letter. */
const MODES = [
  { m: 'r', does: 'reads, fails if missing',
    why: 'a missing input file is not a condition to recover from, it is a mistake worth stopping on' },
  { m: 'w', does: 'writes and TRUNCATES', order: 'contents are gone before the first byte is written',
    whyDangerous: 'the most destructive thing in the language, done silently',
    reframe: 'the whole reason to open for writing is to lose the previous version' },
  { m: 'a', does: 'appends', rightFor: 'a log', wrongFor: 'a rewrite' },
  { m: 'r+', does: 'reads and writes', requirement: 'the file must exist' },
  { m: 'w+', does: 'reads and writes', requirement: 'creates and truncates',
    reframe: 'w+ is w with extra permissions nobody wanted' },
];
const WRITE_SAFELY = {
  rule: 'when writing, write to a new name and replace afterwards',
  why: 'so an interrupted write leaves the original intact',
  consequenceOfIgnoring: 'a crash halfway through a w write leaves a truncated file and no way back',
};

/* The context manager is a correctness mechanism, not a style preference. */
const WITH_BLOCK = {
  form: 'with open(path) as f:',
  guarantees: 'the file is closed when the block ends, INCLUDING when it ends because of an exception',
  whyThatCaseMatters: ['an unclosed file holds a lock on Windows', 'leaks a descriptor on Linux',
    'the buffered content may never reach disk'],
  deeperReason: 'it removes the need to reason about cleanup at all - no path through the function can forget',
  generalises: ['database connections', 'locks', 'sockets'],
  name: 'RAII in C++, context management everywhere else',
  habit: 'always use a with block, even for a single read',
};

Paths, encodings, and the file formats worth knowing

Three things about paths that are correct on one platform and wrong on another, which is why code that works on the machine you wrote it does not work on the server. A path separator is not a slash. Windows uses \, and the correct fix is pathlib.Path with its / operator, which is not sugar — it produces the right separator for the platform it runs on. An absolute path is not portable. A path that starts with C:\Users\you\... works on exactly one machine, and the discipline is to build paths relative to the file that contains them, which Path(__file__).parent makes possible and which is why installed programs never hard-code an installation directory. Text mode versus binary mode. 'r' decodes bytes into text using an encoding; 'rb' does not and gives you bytes. Choosing wrongly produces either a UnicodeDecodeError or a string full of meaningless characters, and the rule is: binary for images, archives, audio and anything where the bytes are the data, text for anything a person wrote.

Then formats, because "just save it as a file" has a specific answer. Plain text — human-readable, diffable, and the right answer for configuration, for anything a person will edit, and as a fallback for everything else. CSV for tabular data, through the csv module rather than by joining strings, because values containing commas, quotes or newlines will otherwise corrupt the file; and the dialect is a real decision, since separators differ by locale. JSON for structured data exchanged between programs, and its limits are worth knowing: no comments, and no date type, so a date becomes a string and its format becomes a decision somebody must document. Pickle — and here the warning is the point: it serialises arbitrary Python objects including their code paths, so loading a pickle from an untrusted source executes code. It is fast and correct for your own data and unsafe for anything you received, which is a distinction every professional has internalised once. And then the operational habit that prevents data loss entirely: a format you cannot read is data you have lost. If your program's output is the only copy of something, store it in a form a person can open, because a future maintainer with a broken runtime cannot open a pickle either.

/* Three things about paths that are right on one platform and wrong on another. */
const PATHS = [
  { fact: 'a path separator is not a slash',
    platform: 'Windows uses a backslash',
    fix: 'pathlib.Path with the / operator',
    why: 'not sugar - it produces the right separator for the platform it runs on' },
  { fact: 'an absolute path is not portable',
    example: 'a path starting with a drive letter and a user directory works on exactly one machine',
    discipline: 'build paths relative to the file that contains them',
    how: 'Path(__file__).parent',
    note: 'why installed programs never hard-code an installation directory' },
  { fact: 'text mode versus binary mode',
    text: 'decodes bytes using an encoding', binary: 'rb gives you bytes',
    wrongChoices: ['a UnicodeDecodeError', 'a string full of meaningless characters'],
    rule: 'binary for images, archives, audio and anything where the bytes ARE the data; text for anything a person wrote' },
];

/* Formats: just-save-it-as-a-file has specific answers. */
const FORMATS = [
  { f: 'plain text', rightFor: ['configuration', 'anything a person will edit'],
    note: 'also a perfectly good fallback for everything else', quality: ['human-readable', 'diffable'] },
  { f: 'CSV', rightFor: 'tabular data',
    through: 'the csv module, not by joining strings',
    why: 'values containing commas, quotes or newlines corrupt the file otherwise',
    realDecision: 'the dialect - separators differ by locale' },
  { f: 'JSON', rightFor: 'structured data exchanged between programs',
    limits: ['no comments', 'no date type - a date becomes a string and its format becomes a decision somebody must document'] },
  { f: 'pickle', good: ['serialises arbitrary objects including their code paths', 'fast', 'correct for your own data'],
    warning: 'loading a pickle from an untrusted source EXECUTES code',
    rule: 'unsafe for anything you received - a distinction every professional has internalised once' },
];
const OPERATIONAL_HABIT = 'a format you cannot read is data you have lost - if a programs output is the only copy of something, store it so a person can open it, because a maintainer with a broken runtime cannot open a pickle either';

Opening a file that doesn’t exist for reading raises FileNotFoundError; saving into a folder that doesn’t exist raises FileNotFoundError. Learn graceful handling early: try/except OSError around file work, or create folders with os.makedirs(..., exist_ok=True).

3.11 Regular expressions: the text-processing superpower

Regular expressions match patterns in text, letting one expression handle searches, validation, and extraction that would otherwise take many lines. You use the re module’s functions like search, match, findall, and sub with patterns built from metacharacters, character classes, and quantifiers. This skill turns painstaking string handling into compact one-liners.

A regular expression is a tiny pattern-matching language. Once you can read the syntax, tasks that look like "write a program" become one-liners — searching logs, validating input, extracting data, renaming files.

import re

text = "Orders: ABC-123, abc-456, X9Z-999, and a typo ABX-1234"
# \b word boundary, [A-Z]{3} exactly three capitals, \d{3} three digits
found = re.findall(r"\b[A-Z]{3}-\d{3}\b", text)
print(found)                      # ['ABC-123', 'ABC-456'? -- no! 'ABC-123', 'X9Z-999']

# Capture groups let you USE the parts, not just find whole matches:
m = re.search(r"([A-Z]{3})-(\d{3})", text)
print(m.group(1), m.group(2))     # 'ABC', '123'

# Replace + function transforms text with logic:
def fix(part):
    country, num = part.group(1), part.group(2)
    return f"US-{country}-{num}"
print(re.sub(r"\b([A-Z]{3})-(\d{3})\b", fix, text))
# The same skill powers grep/ripgrep: find "py3\.\d+ errors" in 2M log lines

re.findall locates matches, capture groups extract their parts, and re.sub rewrites matches with logic — the regex toolchain in three moves.

PatternMeans
.any single character
* + ?0+, 1+, 0-or-1 of previous
^ $start / end of line
[a-z] [^0-9]character class / negated class
\d \w \sdigit, word char, whitespace
(...) (?:...)capture group / non-capturing group

Greedy vs lazy: .* matches as much as possible, so <.*> on <a>x</a><b> grabs the whole string. Use .*? (lazy) to stop at the first >. And beware catastrophic backtracking: (a+)+ on pathological input can hang the CPU — prefer a simpler pattern or a parser.

Chapter 3 consolidation project

What a regular expression is, and what it is not

A regular expression is a small language for describing strings. It is not a programming language, and the boundary it cannot cross is worth stating first: a regular expression cannot count. It cannot match balanced parentheses, cannot tell whether a string of brackets is well-formed, and cannot decide whether an if has a matching else — because matching balanced delimiters requires remembering an unbounded stack, and a regular expression has no memory. Anything needing nesting, counting or cross-line structure is a job for a parser, and reaching for a regular expression to do it produces a pattern nobody can maintain. This is not a limitation to work around; it is the boundary of the tool, and knowing it is what lets you trust it everywhere else.

Then the parts, in the order worth learning. Literals match themselves. Character classes — square brackets — match any one of a set, with ranges and negation: [abc], [0-9], [^0-9]. Quantifiers say how many: * zero or more, + one or more, ? zero or one, {3} exactly three, {2,5} between two and five. Anchors — ^ and $ — anchor to the start and end rather than matching anywhere, which is the difference between finding a substring and validating a whole line. Groups — parentheses — capture part of a match so you can use it later, and alternation is |. Two properties of the design explain every surprise. Quantifiers are greedy: they take as much as they can and then give back the minimum needed for the rest of the pattern to match, which is why <.+> against <a><b> matches the whole thing rather than the first tag — and <.+?>, made lazy with a question mark, fixes it. And there is no backslash-free way to mean a literal special character, so the dot, the plus, the brackets and the backslash itself must be escaped — and the escaping is not optional in any engine, which is why a pattern pasted from a web page can fail for no visible reason.

/* What a regex is, and the boundary it cannot cross. */
const WHAT_IT_IS = 'a small language for describing strings - not a programming language';
const CANNOT_COUNT = {
  fact: 'a regular expression cannot count',
  examples: ['cannot match balanced parentheses',
    'cannot tell whether a string of brackets is well-formed',
    'cannot decide whether an if has a matching else'],
  why: 'matching balanced delimiters needs an unbounded stack, and a regex has no memory',
  rule: 'anything needing nesting, counting or cross-line structure is a job for a parser',
  consequence: 'reaching for a regex to do it produces a pattern nobody can maintain',
  reframe: 'not a limitation to work around - it is the boundary of the tool, which is what lets you trust it elsewhere',
};

/* The parts, in the order worth learning. */
const PARTS = [
  { p: 'literals', matches: 'themselves' },
  { p: 'character classes', form: 'square brackets',
    does: 'match any one of a set, with ranges and negation', examples: ['[abc]', '[0-9]', '[^0-9]'] },
  { p: 'quantifiers', means: ['* zero or more', '+ one or more', '? zero or one',
    '{3} exactly three', '{2,5} between two and five'] },
  { p: 'anchors', forms: ['^', '$'],
    does: 'anchor to start and end rather than matching anywhere',
    keyDistinction: 'the difference between finding a substring and validating a whole line' },
  { p: 'groups', form: 'parentheses',
    does: 'capture part of a match so you can use it later',
    alternation: '|' },
];

/* Two properties that explain every surprise. */
const SURPRISES = [
  { property: 'quantifiers are greedy',
    mechanism: 'take as much as possible, then give back the minimum needed for the rest to match',
    example: '<.+> against <a><b> matches the whole thing rather than the first tag',
    fix: 'make it lazy with a question mark - <.+?>' },
  { property: 'there is no way to mean a literal special character without escaping',
    mustEscape: ['the dot', 'the plus', 'the brackets', 'the backslash itself'],
    consequence: 'not optional in any engine',
    symptom: 'a pattern pasted from a web page fails for no visible reason' },
];

Using one safely, and the catastrophic backtracking trap

Three things make a regular expression safe to use, and each corresponds to a specific failure. Match with a boundary you chose deliberately. A find that scans the whole string can match in the middle of a word, so validation patterns anchor with ^ and $ — and using the full-match function rather than a search function is the habit that prevents a password validator accepting password1xyz. Bound every repetition. * and + have no upper limit, so a pattern applied to a megabyte of text can run effectively forever; {1,100} says what you actually mean and makes the cost predictable. Compile it once. A regex compiled inside a loop is recompiled on every iteration, which is a measurable cost in a hot path, and the fix is one line.

Then the trap that matters more than all of it. Catastrophic backtracking happens when a pattern has nested or adjacent unbounded quantifiers, so the engine must try exponentially many ways to satisfy a match that ultimately fails. (a+)+b against a string of thirty as and no b does not take thirty steps — it takes a billion, because for every way of splitting the run of as between the outer and inner repetitions, the engine tries the b, fails, and backtracks. The symptom is a program that hangs on a long input and runs instantly on a short one, which is the opposite of what people expect and therefore gets misdiagnosed for hours. Three preventions, all of them the same habit: prefer a specific, bounded pattern over a general one — match [a-zA-Z0-9_]+ rather than w+ when you know the shape, and avoid a nested quantifier entirely. Bound what can be repeated, so the number of ways to fail is bounded. And never nest a repetition inside a repetition, which is the rule that removes the entire class. Add to that a fourth, operational point: never run an untrusted pattern against untrusted input in a backtracking engine, because the cost is controlled by the pattern and the input together, and this is the mechanism behind a family of denial-of-service bugs in real applications.

/* Three things that make a regex safe, each fixing a specific failure. */
const SAFE = [
  { p: 'match with a boundary you chose deliberately',
    why: 'a find that scans the whole string can match in the middle of a word',
    fix: 'anchor with ^ and $, and use the full-match function rather than search',
    symptom: 'a password validator accepting a string that merely contains the password' },
  { p: 'bound every repetition',
    why: '* and + have no upper limit',
    symptom: 'a pattern applied to a megabyte of text running effectively forever',
    fix: '{1,100} says what you actually mean and makes the cost predictable' },
  { p: 'compile it once',
    why: 'a regex compiled inside a loop is recompiled on every iteration',
    cost: 'measurable in a hot path',
    fix: 'one line' },
];

/* The trap that matters more than all of it. */
const CATASTROPHIC = {
  name: 'catastrophic backtracking',
  happens: 'a pattern with nested or adjacent unbounded quantifiers, so the engine tries exponentially many ways to satisfy a match that ultimately fails',
  example: '(a+)+b against thirty as and no b',
  arithmetic: 'not thirty steps - a billion, because every way of splitting the run between the outer and inner repetitions is tried, the b fails, and it backtracks',
  symptom: 'hangs on a long input and runs instantly on a short one',
  whyMisdiagnosed: 'the opposite of what people expect',
  prevention: [
    { p: 'prefer a specific, bounded pattern over a general one',
      example: '[a-zA-Z0-9_]+ rather than \w+ when you know the shape',
      note: 'avoid a nested quantifier entirely' },
    { p: 'bound what can be repeated', gain: 'the number of ways to fail is bounded' },
    { p: 'never nest a repetition inside a repetition', claim: 'this removes the entire class' } ],
  operational: 'never run an untrusted pattern against untrusted input in a backtracking engine',
  why: 'the cost is controlled by the pattern and the input together - the mechanism behind a family of denial-of-service bugs',
};
Write a single script mini_quiz.py that: keeps a dict of 5 questions→answers, asks the user each one via input(), scores them, loops while the user wants to replay, defines at least two functions, and prints the final percentage. This one small project uses every concept in this chapter.

4 · Data Structures I & Algorithm Thinking

This chapter introduces algorithm thinking: how to measure performance with Big-O, choose the right data structure, and apply classic techniques. It covers sorting, searching, recursion, two pointers, and the trade-off between time and memory. These mental models determine whether programs run in microseconds or hours.

4.1 Why this matters (the elevator case study)4.2 Big-O notation — how algorithms scale4.3 Two workhorse structures: array vs list vs dict4.4 Recursion — a function that calls itself4.5 Searching: linear vs binary4.6 Sorting: from terrible to classic4.7 Two pointers and sliding windows4.8 The time-space trade-off4.9 Binary search & the power of halves

Data structures are ways to organise data so operations are fast. Algorithms are step-by-step recipes that use data. Together they are the heart of computer science. This chapter builds the mental model; Chapter 8 and 9 go deep.

4.1 Why this matters (the elevator case study)

The elevator pitch, and the number that makes it concrete

A building has two lifts. One serves the first ten floors; the other serves all fifty. Both take the same roughly forty seconds to start, travel and stop. The question — which is better? — is not answerable until you say for what, and the answer inverts entirely depending on the trip. In the morning, everyone is going from the ground floor to their desk, so the local lift is useless above ten and the express is exactly right: you wait once and you arrive. In the evening, everyone comes down, so the express delivers everybody to the lobby and then has nothing further to do, while the local lift carries forty people a floor at a time. The same two lifts are optimal in one direction and wasteful in the other, and nothing about the lifts changed. What changed was the distribution of requests.

Now the arithmetic that makes this a lesson about software rather than a parable. Assume thirty seconds of fixed cost and one second per floor. Express to floor fifty: 30 + 50 = 80 seconds. Local, in ten-floor batches, to floor fifty: 30 + 10, then 30 + 10, four more times — roughly 30 + 5 × 40 = 230 seconds. So the express is about three times faster for the express-shaped trip, and about five times slower for a floor-ten trip, because it stops only once. Both numbers are small; both would be invisible in a journey of a few buildings. At two hundred floors the express takes 230 seconds and the local takes 30 + 20 × 40 = 830 — and now the gap is a coffee break rather than a walk. The distance between the two designs grows with the size of the problem, which is the entire subject of this chapter in one sentence.

/* Two lifts, 30s fixed, 1s per floor, building of 50. */

  building: 50,

  morning: { direction: 'ground floor to desk', distribution: 'everyone going up',
    express: '30 + 50 = 80s', local: 'the local serves only the first ten floors',
    verdict: 'express is exactly right' },

  evening: { direction: 'desk to lobby', distribution: 'everyone coming down',
    express: 'delivers everybody to the lobby and then has nothing further to do',
    local: 'carries forty people a floor at a time',
    verdict: 'local wins' },

  keyPoint: 'the same two lifts are optimal in one direction and wasteful in the other,
    and nothing about the lifts changed - the distribution of requests changed',
};

What the case is actually about

The lesson is not "pick the fast one". It is that algorithmic complexity is a property of how a problem grows, not a measurement of how fast a program runs. A program can be fast on small data and unusable on large data, and nothing in a stopwatch at n = 100 reveals it. Two programs can both complete instantly on today's data and diverge by a factor of a billion at ten times the input — and the only way to know in advance which one you have is to ask how the work grows. That reframing has a practical consequence: you choose data structures and algorithms against the size you expect, not the size you have. A contact list of forty people and a contact list of forty million have different correct implementations of "find this person", and the code for the second is not a faster version of the first — it is a different structure with a different cost model. The same applies to the question "which database should we use" and "should we cache this": those are complexity questions wearing product language.

Then the three consequences that follow for how you work, and they are worth stating because most people arrive at the conclusion differently. Measurement at one size does not generalise. If you benchmark at n = 1000 you learn which of two implementations is faster at 1000, which is not the same question as which you want at 10 million — the one with the better asymptote can lose at the small size and win everywhere above a crossover point. The constant factor is real but bounded. A constant-factor improvement — a tighter loop, an in-place operation, avoiding an allocation — buys you a fixed multiple, typically two to ten times, and it never changes the shape. An asymptotic improvement buys you a factor that grows without limit. This is why the asymptotic win is usually worth the extra complexity and the constant-factor win is usually worth taking anyway, because they are complementary rather than exclusive: do both, and be honest about which one you are relying on. The input that matters is the one you did not test. Every complexity class assumes something about the input — sorted, random, uniform, adversarial — and the gap between the assumption and reality is where the production incident lives. A binary search is O(log n) only on sorted input; a hash table is O(1) only until the keys collide; a cache is O(1) only while the hit rate is high. Those are not footnotes, they are the terms of the guarantee, and holding the terms is what makes the guarantee usable.
