This section motivates algorithm analysis with a concrete case study, such as an elevator control problem, where the choice of data structure and algorithm changes a lookup from a million steps to a handful. It shows that organising data well can beat raw hardware speed. The lesson is to reason about costs before coding.

Imagine a phone book with a million names, unsorted, kept as one enormous list. To find "Zoe" you might scan 999,999 entries — about a million steps. Even on a fast computer, that’s a cost.
Now sort the book (a cost paid once). To find a name you can open the middle: if "Zoe" > the middle name, discard the entire left half, repeat. That’s binary search: ~20 steps instead of a million. The same task, radically different speed, because of how the data is organised and which algorithm you choose. That contrast — a million vs twenty steps — is exactly what this field studies.

4.2 Big-O notation — how algorithms scale

Big-O notation describes how an algorithm’s runtime or memory grows as the input size increases. Common classes are constant, logarithmic, linear, linearithmic, quadratic, and exponential time, written like O(1), O(log n), O(n), and O(n log n). It gives a universal vocabulary for comparing and communicating algorithm efficiency.

Big-O measures how runtime grows as input size n grows. We ignore constants and small terms and keep the "shape" of growth:

What Big-O actually says, and the three things it deliberately ignores

Big-O describes how the number of operations grows as the input grows, above a threshold and ignoring constants. All three of those qualifications are load-bearing. "Grows" means it is about the trend, not the value: an O(n²) algorithm on ten items is faster than an O(n log n) one, because ten squared is a hundred and ten log ten is thirty-three comparisons but with far more constant overhead. "Above a threshold" means Big-O is a statement about asymptotics and nothing about small inputs, which is why real libraries frequently use a quadratic algorithm below a cutoff of about fifty elements and a divide-and-conquer one above — the crossover is a measured fact, not a contradiction. And "ignoring constants" means Big-O cannot tell you that one algorithm is four times faster; it can only tell you which one eventually wins, and the ratio between them either stays bounded or grows without limit. Everything else follows from those three facts.

Then the classes worth knowing, ordered, with the intuition that makes each memorable rather than a table to memorise. O(1) — a hash lookup, an array index, a stack push. The cost does not depend on the size, because it computes an address rather than searching. O(log n) — binary search, a balanced tree, heap operations. Each step eliminates half of what remains, so 1,000 items takes ten steps and a billion takes thirty. O(n) — a single pass. You touch everything once and there is no way to touch less if the answer depends on every element. O(n log n) — sorting well. Grows like a linear pass times a logarithm, and it is the practical floor for comparison-based sorting, because deciding the order of n items requires about n log n comparisons and no cleverer scheme escapes it. O(n²) — comparing everything with everything. Doubling the input quadruples the work, which is what makes it fatal at scale and merely annoying in a tutorial. And O(2ⁿ) and O(n!) — the classes to recognise on sight, because a problem whose solution is exponential is usually one where you have not yet found the right question.

/* Big-O says exactly three things, and all three are load-bearing. */
const BIG_O = {
  says: 'how the number of operations grows as the input grows',
  qualifications: [
    { q: 'grows', means: 'about the trend, not the value',
      consequence: 'O(n^2) on ten items can beat O(n log n), because ten squared is a hundred while ten log ten is only thirty-three comparisons with far more constant overhead' },
    { q: 'above a threshold', means: 'a statement about asymptotics and nothing about small inputs',
      consequence: 'real libraries use a quadratic algorithm below a cutoff of about fifty elements and divide-and-conquer above - the crossover is measured, not a contradiction' },
    { q: 'ignoring constants', means: 'Big-O cannot tell you one algorithm is four times faster',
      canTell: 'only which one eventually wins',
      consequence: 'the ratio either stays bounded or grows without limit' },
  ],
};

Space complexity, the lower bounds, and how to read a complexity claim

Space complexity is Big-O over memory, and the same classes apply, but two terms are specific to memory. In-place versus copy — an algorithm that rearranges the input with one extra variable is O(1) space, and one that builds a second array is O(n), and for a large input that is the difference between fitting in memory and not. The recursion stack counts. A recursive solution to a problem with n levels of nesting uses O(n) stack even when it allocates nothing else, which is why a naive recursive tree walk can exhaust a stack that an iterative one handles comfortably. And the fourth term people forget: the output often dominates. An algorithm returning all n! permutations is O(n!) space before you write a line of it, and no cleverness in the auxiliary space changes that.

Then the lower bounds, which are the reason some algorithms exist and which save you from trying to beat an impossibility. Sorting requires about n log n comparisons in the comparison model, because the information-theoretic argument is clean: n! orderings are possible and each comparison is one bit, so you need log₂(n!) ≈ n log n of them. That is why quicksort, merge sort and heapsort are all the same class and why an O(n) comparison sort does not exist — but a radix sort does, because it does not compare; it buckets by digit, which leaves the model entirely. Searching an unsorted list requires n steps in the worst case, because the last element examined may be the answer. Hash lookups are O(1) only on average, because a collision forces a probe, and the worst case is linear. And some problems have no known subexponential algorithm and may have none — recognising those is a legitimate and valuable skill, because it converts an afternoon of optimisation into a design conversation about approximations, heuristics or constraints.

Finally, how to read a complexity claim in the wild, because the claims are usually incomplete in one specific way. Ask four questions. Worst case, average case, or best case? Quicksort is O(n log n) average and O(n²) worst, and the difference is entirely about pivot choice. Over what input size range? A claim of O(n log n) for a sort is often an average over random data and a different shape for nearly-sorted data. What is being counted — operations, comparisons, memory accesses, or network round trips? A hash lookup is one memory access and one hash computation, which are not the same cost. And what is the constant? An O(n log n) algorithm with a large constant loses to O(n²) until the crossover, which is measured rather than assumed. A complexity claim without those four qualifications is not wrong, exactly; it is incomplete in the way that produces a bad decision.

/* Space complexity, with two terms specific to memory. */
const SPACE = [

    whyItMatters: 'for a large input, the difference between fitting in memory and not' },
  { term: 'the recursion stack counts',
    detail: 'a recursive solution with n levels of nesting uses O(n) stack even allocating nothing else',
    consequence: 'a naive recursive tree walk can exhaust a stack an iterative one handles comfortably' },
  { term: 'the output often dominates',
    example: 'an algorithm returning all n! permutations is O(n!) space before you write a line',
    reframe: 'no cleverness in auxiliary space changes that' },
];

Read the table like a physicist: a n² algorithm on a million items does roughly a trillion steps — minutes or hours. Log-linear does ~20 million — well under a second. Constant does ~1. Choosing the right structure/algorithm is worth more than a faster CPU.

4.3 Two workhorse structures: array vs list vs dict

Arrays, lists, dicts, and sets charge different costs for different operations. Indexing an array or list is constant time, searching a list is linear, and key lookups in a dict are near constant time. Choose a structure based on which operations your program performs most, balancing insertion, lookup, and memory costs.

The cost model of each structure, side by side

The reason to learn array versus list versus dictionary is not that one is better — it is that each answers a different question and each has a different cost for the two operations that dominate real programs: look something up and find something. A dynamic array — an array, a Python list, a vector, a JavaScript Array — gives O(1) lookup by position and O(n) search by value, because finding an element means scanning until it matches. Its growth is amortised O(1) per append: it allocates spare capacity, doubles when full, and copies once — so the total cost of n appends is O(n) even though individual appends occasionally cost O(n). That last point is worth internalising because "append is O(1)" is true on average and false for any particular append, and the difference shows up as occasional latency spikes. A linked list, by contrast, gives O(1) insert and delete once you have the node — which is why it appears in every textbook — and O(n) lookup by position, because reaching position 500 means walking 500 links, each of which is a pointer dereference into a memory location you cannot predict. Almost nobody should use a linked list in application code, and the reason is not the asymptotics — those are fine — it is that cache locality dominates: an array walks memory in one direction and the hardware prefetcher loves it, while a linked list jumps randomly and every step is a likely cache miss.

Then a dictionary, which is a different answer to a different question. A hash table gives O(1) lookup, insert and delete by key, on average, in exchange for three costs. Space overhead — a table with n entries typically allocates more than n slots, and for small entries that overhead can be a factor of two or three. No ordering — iteration order is arbitrary in principle and stable in practice, which is why relying on it is a bug waiting for a version change. Hashable keys only — a key must have a computable, stable hash, which is a real constraint on what you can use as an identifier. And the failure mode that matters: collisions degrade the average case into the worst case, so an adversary who can choose your keys can make a hash table behave like a linked list, which is the mechanism behind a class of denial-of-service attacks on web frameworks. The defence is a keyed hash — a seed chosen at random per process — so the adversary cannot predict which keys collide. This is a good example of a general principle: average-case performance is a promise about the inputs you expect, and anything an adversary controls is not an input you should be relying on an average for.

Choosing between them, and the structures that fall out of that choice

A short decision procedure, which is the thing worth memorising. Do you access by position, or iterate in order? Array. Do you look up by an identifier? Dictionary. Do you need sorted order, or a range query? Neither of the above — a balanced tree, or a sorted array if you sort once and query many. Do you only need membership? Set. Do you need both ends? A deque rather than an array, so both operations are O(1). Do you need the smallest or largest item repeatedly? A heap — which is the structure behind a priority queue, a Dijkstra run, and every "top k" query. Every more exotic structure is one of these plus a constraint: a trie is a dictionary keyed by prefix, which turns a string lookup into work proportional to the key's length rather than its number of characters compared; a union-find is a set with a merge operation, which makes "are these two in the same group" nearly free; a graph is a dictionary of adjacency lists; and a B-tree is the database's answer to the same trade-off — sorted, searchable, and shallow enough that a disk read is not a wild guess.

Then the two questions that decide most real choices, both of which are about the shape of the access rather than its count. What is the read-to-write ratio? If you write once and read a million times, pay for the write — build an index, precompute, sort it. If you read once and write a million times, do not: an index you must update on every write costs more than the lookups it saves. This is the pre-processing idea the next-but-one section is about, and it is the single most consequential performance decision in most systems, because it is not about constants. How local is the access? If you need the whole set, streaming through an array beats jumping to arbitrary rows in a hash table; if you need one element, the reverse. And the practical tiebreaker that overrides all of it: start with the structure whose cost is easiest to predict — an array or a dictionary — and move to something exotic when a measurement, not a hunch, says you must. The most common performance mistake in application code is choosing an exotic structure for a problem that never needed one, paying its constant factor and its complexity forever, in exchange for a complexity class that was never the bottleneck.

  { q: 'need the smallest or largest item repeatedly', answer: 'a heap',

];

# WRONG for this job: scanning a list for a person
people = [("ada", 21), ("grace", 35)]
for name, age in people:
    if name == "grace":
        print(age)          # O(n) every time

# RIGHT: a dict gives O(1) lookup
people = {"ada": 21, "grace": 35}
print(people["grace"])      # 35

Scanning a list for a name costs O(n) every time; the same lookup through a dict key is O(1) — choose the structure to match how you query.

4.4 Recursion — a function that calls itself

Recursion solves a problem by having a function call itself with a smaller or simpler input, guided by a base case that stops the chain. Every recursive call must move toward the base case or the function overflows the stack. It pairs naturally with divide-and-conquer and tree traversal problems.

Recursion solves a problem by solving a smaller version of itself. Two parts: a base case (stop condition) and a recursive case (shrink toward the base).

def factorial(n):
    if n <= 1:               # base case — stops the chain
        return 1
    return n * factorial(n - 1)   # recursive case

print(factorial(5))   # 120 = 5*4*3*2*1

def count_down(n):
    print(n)
    if n >= 1:
        count_down(n - 1)

count_down(3)   # 3 2 1 ? - note the base-case shape for n=... base case is n < 1

factorial calls itself with n-1 until the base case stops the chain; the two parts — a base case and a recursive case — are plain to see.

def count_down2(n):
    print(n)
    if n == 0:               # clean base case
        return
    count_down2(n - 1)

A cleaner recursive countdown: each call prints, then recurses, and the explicit n == 0 base case guarantees the chain terminates.

What recursion is, and the two parts it needs

A recursive function is one that calls itself on a smaller version of the same problem, and every correct one has exactly two parts. The base case — a condition under which it returns an answer without recursing, which stops the descent. The recursive case — the part that calls itself on strictly smaller input, which guarantees termination. That is the whole theory. Everything else is consequence, and the consequences are where the bugs live. The most common failure is a missing or wrong base case, which produces infinite recursion and, in Python, a RecursionError once the stack is exhausted — the symptom that looks like a hang and is actually thousands of frames deep. The second is a base case that is never reached, which is subtler: it looks correct on the inputs you tried and diverges on an input you did not, because the recursion went off in a direction you did not exercise. The third is recursing on the same input — the classic bug where the recursive call receives the original problem rather than a smaller one, which is a stack overflow wearing a disguise.

Then the mental model, because a wrong mental model is why people find recursion hard. Recursion is not "the function calling itself". Recursion is a function making a call, and each call gets its own frame: its own parameters, its own local variables, its own position in the chain. The call stack is a stack of those frames, and it behaves exactly like a stack of plates — you add to the top and you must remove from the top. When function A calls B, B's frame goes on top; when B returns, B's frame is discarded and A continues. This gives you the two things you need to reason about a recursive function. To know what a call returns, evaluate from the bottom up. For factorial of 4: the call with 1 returns 1 because it hits the base case; the call with 2 is 1 × 2; the call with 3 is 2 × 3; the call with 4 is 6 × 4. Each frame's answer is computed from the answer of the frame below it, and that is exactly why the base case must be first in your reasoning and last in your execution. To know how much memory it uses, count the depth. Depth-first recursion on a tree is O(height), which is O(log n) on a balanced tree and O(n) on a list-shaped one — which is the entire reason recursive tree walks blow the stack on real data and iterative ones do not.

/* Recursion has exactly two parts. */
const TWO_PARTS = [
  { p: 'the base case', does: 'returns an answer without recursing', purpose: 'stops the descent' },
  { p: 'the recursive case', does: 'calls itself on strictly smaller input', purpose: 'guarantees termination' },
];
const THEORY = 'that is the whole theory; everything else is consequence, and the consequences are where the bugs live';
const FAILURES = [
  { f: 'a missing or wrong base case', symptom: 'infinite recursion',
    appearsAs: 'a RecursionError once the stack is exhausted',
    note: 'looks like a hang, is actually thousands of frames deep' },
  { f: 'a base case that is never reached', whySubtle: 'it looks correct on the inputs you tried',
    symptom: 'diverges on an input you did not try, because the recursion went off in a direction you did not exercise' },
  { f: 'recursing on the same input', classic: 'the recursive call receives the original problem rather than a smaller one',
    appearsAs: 'a stack overflow wearing a disguise' },
];

/* The mental model. */
const MODEL = {
  notThis: 'the function calling itself',
  actually: 'a function making a CALL',
  perCall: 'each call gets its own frame - its own parameters, local variables, and position in the chain',
  theStack: 'a stack of frames behaving exactly like a stack of plates - add to the top, remove from the top',
  sequence: 'A calls B, Bs frame goes on top; when B returns its frame is discarded and A continues',
  twoThingsYouCanReasonAbout: [
    { t: 'what a call returns', direction: 'evaluate from the BOTTOM UP',
      worked: 'factorial of 4 - the call with 1 returns 1; with 2 is 1x2; with 3 is 2x3; with 4 is 6x4',
      consequence: 'the base case must be FIRST in your reasoning and LAST in your execution' },
    { t: 'how much memory it uses', measure: 'the depth',
      worked: 'depth-first on a tree is O(height) - O(log n) balanced, O(n) list-shaped',
      consequence: 'the entire reason recursive tree walks blow the stack on real data and iterative ones do not' },
  ],
};

When recursion is the right tool, and the tail-call caveat

Three situations where recursion is not merely acceptable but clearly right. The problem is defined in terms of itself. A directory tree, a JSON document, an expression parser, a file system, an HTML document — none of these has a fixed depth known in advance, and writing them iteratively requires an explicit stack that duplicates the call stack's job. The structure is recursive. Tree traversals, divide and conquer, traversals of arbitrary graphs, and the recursive descent parsers that every language implementation of an expression grammar is built from. It is clearer, and clarity has a cost worth paying. A quicksort written recursively is shorter and more obviously correct than the iterative version with an explicit stack and an index, and this is the honest trade: an explicit stack buys stack depth and costs readability. The rule is to prefer recursion when the depth is bounded by the shape of ordinary data — hundreds, not hundreds of thousands — and to reach for an explicit stack when you cannot promise that.

Then the caveat that belongs here because it surprises people from other languages, and the three problems recursion creates. Tail-call optimisation. Some languages — and some Python interpreters, historically — optimise a call in tail position, reusing the current frame instead of adding one, so a tail-recursive function runs in constant stack space. This is not guaranteed in Python and must not be relied on; the tail-recursive formulation of an algorithm does not make it safe here. Stack depth. Every frame costs memory, so deep recursion exhausts the stack, and the limit is low — a thousand in Python by default, which is far below the depth of a real directory tree or a deeply nested JSON document from an untrusted source. Function call overhead. A call is not free, so a recursive solution to a problem with millions of base cases is measurably slower than the iterative version, sometimes by a large factor. The trade, stated so it can be made deliberately: recursion costs memory proportional to depth and time per frame, and buys you code that matches the shape of the problem. Use it when the shape match is worth the cost — which for a tree traversal almost always is — and flatten it into a loop when you have measured that the cost is real.

/* Three situations where recursion is clearly right. */

  { s: 'the problem is defined in terms of itself',
    examples: ['a directory tree', 'a JSON document', 'an expression parser',

    why: 'none has a fixed depth known in advance',
    cost: 'writing them iteratively requires an explicit stack that duplicates the call stacks job' },
  { s: 'the structure is recursive',

      'the recursive descent parsers every expression grammar implementation is built from'] },

];

Every recursive call needs stack memory, and Python limits recursion depth. A missing (wrong) base case → RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded. When you meet trees and graphs in Ch. 8, recursion is the natural tool again.

4.5 Searching: linear vs binary

Linear search scans every element until it finds a match, costing linear time. Binary search instead repeatedly compares the middle element and discards half of a sorted range each step, reaching the answer in logarithmic time. The huge difference in cost is why sorting data before many searches pays off.

def linear_search(items, target):
    """O(n): check every element."""
    for i, item in enumerate(items):
        if item == target:
            return i
    return -1

def binary_search(sorted_items, target):
    """O(log n): halve the range each step. items MUST be sorted."""
    low, high = 0, len(sorted_items) - 1
    while low <= high:
        mid = (low + high) // 2
        if sorted_items[mid] == target:
            return mid
        elif sorted_items[mid] < target:
            low = mid + 1          # discard left half
        else:
            high = mid - 1         # discard right half
    return -1

print(binary_search([2, 5, 8, 12, 99], 12))   # 3

linear_search checks every element in O(n), while binary_search repeatedly halves a sorted range — O(log n) — by moving low and high past the midpoint.

Linear search, and why it is not the stupid option

Linear search — check each element until you find a match — looks primitive and is actually the correct answer more often than beginners expect. It is optimal when the data is not sorted, because there is no information to exploit; any algorithm that claims to do better is relying on a property the data does not have. It is optimal when the data is small, because the constant factor of anything cleverer exceeds its advantage at that size — this is not a compromise, it is arithmetic, and it is why real libraries use brute force below a cutoff. It is optimal when the search is one-off over data you will not search again: sorting costs n log n to save one O(n) scan, which is a net loss. And it is optimal when the container does not support indexing — a generator, a stream, a file being read line by line — where there is no random access at all, so "scan through it" is not a choice but the only option. Add to that a fifth: it is optimal for the occasional hit near the front, because the expected cost of a linear scan is n/2 for a random hit while the setup cost of an index is paid in full even if you search once.

Then how to write it well, since if you are going to scan, scan properly. Return the position, not just a yes. A find that returns True forces the caller to scan again to get the index, which doubles the work and is the single most common way linear search is implemented badly. Handle the not-found case explicitly. Returning -1 is a convention; returning None is Pythonic; but the real requirement is that absence is a value the caller must handle, not an exception that propagates. Use the container's own method when one exists, because it is implemented in a lower-level language, may be vectorised, and is the version that has been profiled by everybody who uses it — list.index(), in, dict.get. And know the membership test's cost, because it is a trap. x in some_list is a linear scan, so if x in some_list inside a loop over a thousand items is a million comparisons where a set makes it a thousand. That single change — list to set — is the most valuable one-line optimisation available to a beginner, and it is invisible until the data grows.

/* Linear search is optimal more often than beginners expect. */

  { when: 'the data is not sorted', why: 'there is no information to exploit',

  { when: 'the data is small', why: 'the constant factor of anything cleverer exceeds its advantage at that size',

  { when: 'the search is one-off over data you will not search again',

  { when: 'the container does not support indexing',
    examples: ['a generator', 'a stream', 'a file read line by line'],

  { when: 'hits are occasional and near the front',
    arithmetic: 'expected cost of a linear scan is n/2 for a random hit, while index setup is paid in full even if you search once' },
];

    why: 'a find returning True forces the caller to scan again for the index',
    cost: 'doubles the work',
    note: 'the most common way linear search is implemented badly' },

    requirement: 'absence is a VALUE the caller must handle, not an exception that propagates' },
  { r: "use the container's own method when one exists", list: ['list.index()', 'in', 'dict.get'],
    why: ['implemented in a lower-level language', 'may be vectorised',
      'the version profiled by everybody who uses it'] },
  { r: 'know what a membership test costs',
    trap: 'x in some_list is a linear scan',
    symptom: 'a membership test inside a loop over a thousand items is a million comparisons',
    fix: 'a set makes it a thousand',
    claim: 'the most valuable one-line optimisation available to a beginner, and invisible until the data grows' },
];

When a scan is not enough, and the shapes that need something else

Four situations where linear search is genuinely insufficient, each with the reason. Sorted data, repeated lookups. One sort makes every subsequent search O(log n); the break-even is roughly three searches on the same data, which is far fewer than people assume — if you search the same collection three times, sorting first already wins. Frequent membership tests. As above: build the set once, and every test becomes O(1). The general principle is that when the same question is asked repeatedly about the same data, the answer is to preprocess rather than to repeat the work, and that is the whole content of the pre-processing idea later in this chapter. Prefix questions. "How many items start with 'ma'?" answered by scanning is O(n); answered with a sorted list and a binary search for the two boundaries it is O(log n), because all the matching items are contiguous once sorted. This is why indexes make range queries fast in databases, and it is a shape — contiguity after sorting — that a scan cannot exploit. Nearest-neighbour questions. "Which element is closest to this value?" on unsorted data is a full scan with a comparison per element; on sorted data it is a binary search for the insertion point plus one comparison on each side, which is O(log n) and a completely different program.

Then the practical habit, because the right instinct here is subtle and getting it wrong costs more than picking a slow algorithm. Do not optimise what you have not measured. A linear search over a thousand items takes microseconds and no user will ever notice; replacing it with a binary search adds an invariant, a sort, and a second thing to keep in sync, in exchange for a saving nobody can perceive. That trade is almost never worth it. The rule that follows is the one worth internalising: optimise when the cost is user-visible or the data is unbounded, and not before — because the complexity you add is permanent and the saving is only worth what it was worth on the day you measured it. There is one exception, and it is worth knowing because it is the case that bites hardest: optimise the data structure choice, not the loop. Choosing a set over a list inside a loop is a one-line change that converts a quadratic into a linear, and it is not premature — it is correcting a choice that was wrong at any size. Tuning a constant factor in a loop that runs once is premature; picking the right container is not.

    fix: 'build the set once; every test becomes O(1)',

    without: 'O(n)',
    with: 'sorted list plus a binary search for the two boundaries, O(log n)',
    why: 'all matching items are contiguous once sorted',
    generalises: 'why indexes make range queries fast in databases' },

    without: 'a full scan with a comparison per element',

];

Trace binary_search([2,5,8,12,99], 12) by hand with pencil and paper. Half the battle of "getting" algorithms is literally playing the computer with a pen.

4.6 Sorting: from terrible to classic

Sorting arranges data in a defined order and is the classic training ground for algorithm design. Simple approaches like bubble sort and selection sort are easy but slow, while divide-and-conquer algorithms like merge sort and quicksort reach n log n time. Understanding sorting teaches comparisons, recursion, and trade-offs you reuse everywhere.

Two extremes on one table (full treatment in Ch. 9):

def bubble_sort(items):
    """O(n²) average — simple, educational, slow on big data."""
    n = len(items)
    for i in range(n):
        swapped = False
        for j in range(n - i - 1):
            if items[j] > items[j+1]:
                items[j], items[j+1] = items[j+1], items[j]   # swap
                swapped = True
        if not swapped:
            break
    return items

def merge(a, b):
    """Combine two sorted lists into one sorted list."""
    res, i, j = [], 0, 0
    while i < len(a) and j < len(b):
        if a[i] <= b[j]:
            res.append(a[i]); i += 1
        else:
            res.append(b[j]); j += 1
    res.extend(a[i:]); res.extend(b[j:])
    return res

def merge_sort(items):
    """O(n log n) — divide, sort halves, merge."""
    if len(items) <= 1:
        return items
    mid = len(items) // 2
    return merge(merge_sort(items[:mid]), merge_sort(items[mid:]))

print(merge_sort([9, 3, 7, 1, 4]))   # [1, 3, 4, 7, 9]

The two shapes, and what separates them

Every sorting algorithm is a trade among three things: speed in the average case, how much extra memory it needs, and how it behaves when the input is nearly sorted, reversed, or full of duplicates — and the third is the one that decides real production outcomes. Bubble sort and selection sort are O(n²) and belong in a textbook. Insertion sort is O(n²) worst-case but O(n) on nearly-sorted data, which makes it genuinely useful and gives it a place in real hybrid implementations. Merge sort is O(n log n) guaranteed, needs O(n) extra space, and is stable. Heapsort is O(n log n) guaranteed with O(1) extra space but is not stable. Quicksort is O(n log n) average with O(log n) stack, is fast in practice because of cache behaviour, but is O(n²) on bad pivots.

Two definitions first, because they are what the trade is made of. Stability means equal elements keep their relative order. It matters whenever the sort key is not the whole record — sorting people by surname must not shuffle first names, and a database doing a partial sort on one column of several depends on it. In-place means using O(1) extra space. It matters when the data is large relative to memory, which is the normal case for sorting in a database or on a machine you do not own. And the fourth property, adaptivity — how much faster the sort gets when the input is nearly sorted — which is the property that distinguishes insertion sort, Timsort and Shell sort from the rest, and which is why Python's built-in sort and Java's are both hybrid: run insertion sort on small runs and merge sort on large ones, because each is optimal in the regime the other is bad at. That hybrid is not a compromise; it is the correct answer, and it is why the theoretical best algorithm is not what ships.

/* Every sort trades among three things. */
const THE_TRADE = ['speed in the average case', 'how much extra memory it needs',
  'how it behaves on nearly-sorted, reversed or duplicate-heavy input'];
const WHY_THE_THIRD_WINS = 'the third is the one that decides real production outcomes';

/* The sorts. */

];

/* Two definitions the trade is made of. */

  { d: 'stability', means: 'equal elements keep their relative order',

    examples: ['sorting people by surname must not shuffle first names',
      'a database doing a partial sort on one column of several'] },
  { d: 'in-place', means: 'O(1) extra space',
    mattersWhen: 'the data is large relative to memory',
    normalCase: 'sorting in a database, or on a machine you do not own' },
  { d: 'adaptivity', means: 'how much faster the sort gets when the input is nearly sorted',
    distinguishes: ['insertion sort', 'Timsort', 'Shell sort'],
    whyItMatters: 'why Pythons built-in sort and Javas are both hybrid',
  },
];
const THE_HYBRID = {
  shape: 'insertion sort on small runs, merge sort on large ones',
  why: 'each is optimal in the regime the other is bad at',
  reframe: 'not a compromise - the correct answer, and the reason the theoretical best is not what ships',
};

The three sorts worth being able to write, and when to reach for each

Insertion sort, because it is nine lines and it teaches the idea that makes hybrid sorts work. It keeps a sorted prefix and, for each new element, shifts every larger element right and drops the new one into place — and the reason it is O(n) on nearly-sorted data is that each element shifts zero times. Merge sort, because it is the clearest example of divide-and-conquer: split, sort each half, merge. The merge is the interesting half and the part worth being able to write — two sorted lists merged by repeatedly taking the smaller head, which is O(n) because every element is moved exactly once — and the insight is that after splitting a list in half repeatedly you have n sublists of one element, and each is already sorted, so you only ever have the merge left to solve. Quicksort, because it is the one you will meet in interview and production code: partition around a pivot, recurse on each side. The partition is a loop and the base case is trivial, and the whole algorithm is perhaps twelve lines. Its one real weakness is pivot choice, and the fix is not cleverness but randomness or the median-of-three — because the O(n²) case is exactly "every pivot is the smallest or largest element remaining", and any pivot rule that can be predicted can be fed that input.

Then the practical selection, which is the part that saves time. Do not write a sort. Every language has one, and it is implemented in the language you are running and tuned for the machine you are on. What you write instead, when a sort looks necessary, is a key function — and the mistakes there are worth knowing: returning a compound comparison instead of a key, comparing tuples when you meant to compare one field, mixing types so the comparison raises halfway through, or using a comparison that is not a valid total order, which produces an implementation-specific result rather than an error. Then sorting when you did not need to. If you only need the smallest k items, a heap of size k is O(n log k) and uses O(k) memory, where sorting is O(n log n) and O(n) — and for "the ten largest errors in a million-line log" that is the difference between feasible and not. If you only need to find one item, sorting is entirely unnecessary and a single pass beats it. And if the same collection is sorted repeatedly, sorting once and maintaining the order is nearly free, which is the pre-processing idea again.
