Two sorts of the same problem: bubble sort swaps neighbouring pairs in O(n²), while merge sort divides, sorts halves, and merges in O(n log n).

4.7 Two pointers and sliding windows

Two-pointer and sliding window techniques replace naive nested loops with a single pass over the data. Two pointers move from opposite ends or at different speeds to find pairs, while a sliding window maintains a moving subrange for substring and subarray problems. Both are standard ways to reach linear time.

Two of the most reused "move indices cleverly" patterns in interviews and real code. They convert a naive O(n²) scan into a single O(n) pass — exactly the Big-O payoff from 4.2.

# TWO POINTERS on a SORTED array: find two numbers that sum to target
def two_sum_sorted(nums, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        s = nums[lo] + nums[hi]
        if s == target:
            return (lo, hi)
        elif s < target:
            lo += 1          # need a bigger pair -> move left up
        else:
            hi -= 1          # need a smaller pair -> move right down
    return None

print(two_sum_sorted([1, 3, 5, 8, 12], 15))   # (2, 4) : 5 + 12

Two pointers walk toward each other across a sorted array, adjusting one end at a time to find a target sum in a single pass.

# SLIDING WINDOW: max sum of any k consecutive elements
def max_window_sum(nums, k):
    if len(nums) < k:
        return None
    window = sum(nums[:k])
    best = window
    for i in range(k, len(nums)):
        window += nums[i] - nums[i - k]       # slide: add new, drop old
        best = max(best, window)
    return best

print(max_window_sum([4, 2, 1, 7, 8, 1, 2, 8, 1, 0], 3))   # 16 (7+8+1)

The window keeps one running sum: each step adds the incoming element and drops the outgoing one, keeping every update O(1).

Two pointers, and why the trick is narrowing rather than cleverness

The two-pointer technique is not a family of tricks; it is one idea applied twice. One pointer is at the end and one is at the start. Compare the values; the comparison tells you which pointer can be discarded entirely rather than which one to advance by one. That elimination is the whole trick: each step removes one element from consideration, so a problem that looks like a nested loop over n² pairs becomes a single pass. Both pointers move forward through overlapping ranges. Maintain a window, extend it when the running value is too small, shrink it when too large — again, each step discards information irreversibly, so the total work is O(n) rather than O(n²). In both cases the win comes from the same thing: a monotonicity property that makes one comparison decisive. Without that property, moving either pointer discards nothing useful and you are back to quadratic. This is why the technique works on sorted input and generally does not on unsorted input — the sortedness is what makes the answer to "can I discard this element" a definite yes or no.

Then the canonical problems, which are worth knowing by shape because the shape is the recognition method. Two-sum on a sorted array: start at both ends, and if the sum is too small the left pointer must advance (nothing to its left could sum with anything to make it larger); if too large, the right retreats. Two-sum on an unsorted array: different algorithm — the answer is to put the values in a hash map and look up the complement, which is O(n) but needs O(n) extra space, so the sorted version trades space for time instead. Find the pair with a target difference in a sorted array, the same shape with a different comparison. Three-sum to zero: sorted input, one outer loop plus a two-pointer inner scan, and a skip rule to avoid duplicate triples — O(n²) where the naive version is O(n³). Counting pairs whose sum is below a threshold, which is two pointers plus a running total rather than a target. Removing duplicates in place from a sorted array: one read pointer, one write pointer, and the read pointer decides when the write pointer advances. And the container-with-most-water problem, which looks like a puzzle and is the purest statement of the principle: move the shorter side, because moving the taller side cannot improve a container limited by the shorter one.

/* One idea applied twice. */
const THE_TRICK = {
  form1: 'one pointer at the end, one at the start',
  rule1: 'the comparison tells you which pointer can be DISCARDED ENTIRELY, not which to advance by one',
  gain: 'each step removes one element from consideration, turning an apparent n^2 nested loop into a single pass',
  form2: 'both pointers move forward through overlapping ranges',
  rule2: 'maintain a window - extend when too small, shrink when too large',
  gain2: 'each step discards information irreversibly, so total work is O(n) rather than O(n^2)',
  commonRoot: 'a MONOTONICITY PROPERTY that makes one comparison decisive',
  withoutIt: 'moving either pointer discards nothing useful and you are back to quadratic',
  whySortedMatters: 'sortedness is what makes discard-this-element a definite yes or no',
};

/* Canonical problems, known by shape. */
const CANONICAL = [
  { p: 'two-sum on a sorted array',
    shape: 'start at both ends',
    rule: 'if the sum is too small the left pointer advances - nothing to its left could sum to more; if too large the right retreats' },
  { p: 'two-sum on an unsorted array', differentAlgorithm: true,
    method: 'put the values in a hash map and look up the complement',
    cost: 'O(n) time, O(n) extra space',
    versusSorted: 'the sorted version trades space for time instead' },
  { p: 'pair with a target difference', shape: 'the same shape with a different comparison' },
  { p: 'three-sum to zero',
    shape: 'one outer loop plus a two-pointer inner scan, with a skip rule for duplicate triples',
    gain: 'O(n^2) where the naive version is O(n^3)' },
  { p: 'counting pairs whose sum is below a threshold',
    difference: 'two pointers plus a running total rather than a target' },
  { p: 'removing duplicates in place',
    mechanics: ['one read pointer', 'one write pointer', 'the read pointer decides when the write advances'] },
  { p: 'container with most water',
    looksLike: 'a puzzle',
    is: 'the purest statement of the principle',
    rule: 'move the shorter side, because moving the taller side cannot improve a container limited by the shorter one' },
];

Sliding window, and the two variants

A sliding window is a contiguous range that you move across the data, and it solves the same class of problems for a different reason: not "find the pair", but "find the range with the best property". The shape is always the same — right pointer extends, left pointer shrinks, and a running value is updated on both moves — and the decision of when to shrink is where the two variants differ. The shrinking window finds the longest range satisfying a constraint: extend the right edge, and while the window violates the constraint, move the left edge until it does not; the answer is the largest window seen. Because each pointer only ever moves forward, the total work is O(n) even though you are examining every possible window. The growing window finds the shortest range satisfying a constraint: extend the right edge, and while the window already satisfies it, shrink from the left and record the length; then keep extending. Same pointers, opposite stopping condition, and confusing the two variants is the most common mistake in this family.

Then the specific problems, each of which the shape should trigger. Longest substring without repeating characters — a shrinking window over a set of seen characters. Longest substring with at most k distinct — identical, with the constraint changed. Minimum window substring — the growing variant, where the constraint is that the window must contain all the characters of a target and you shrink while it still does. Minimum size subarray with sum at least k, which needs the sum being positive, because then shrinking the window can only reduce the sum — and that positivity is precisely why the two-pointer approach works there and the ordinary growing-window shape does not apply to a general target-sum problem. That last one is worth dwelling on: the technique applies when the problem is monotone under shrinking, and when it is not, you need prefix sums and a different algorithm entirely. Anagram search — a window of fixed length, compared by a running count vector. Permutation in string — the same thing with a different constraint. And the longest subarray with sum divisible by k, which is not a sliding window at all — it is a prefix-sum-and-modulo trick, and recognising that the sliding window does not apply is part of the skill.

Finally, the practical note that makes these techniques worth reaching for. The O(n²) version is the specification. Write the nested loop first, because it says exactly what the problem is and it is obviously correct; then ask whether the comparison lets you discard anything, and if so collapse it. This order matters — people who try to invent a two-pointer solution in their head tend to produce something that works on the examples and is subtly wrong, because they never wrote down the invariant. And the invariant is what to write down. For two pointers: "any solution using the discarded element is impossible, because of the comparison we just made". For a window: "the current window is the longest valid window ending at the right pointer". If you can state that sentence, the algorithm is right; if you cannot, you have a pattern you do not understand and it will fail on input you did not consider.

/* A sliding window solves find-the-range-with-the-best-property. */
const WINDOW_SHAPE = ['right pointer extends', 'left pointer shrinks', 'a running value is updated on both moves'];
const DECIDING_FACTOR = 'when to shrink - which is where the two variants differ';

const VARIANTS = [
  { v: 'shrinking window', finds: 'the LONGEST range satisfying a constraint',
    loop: 'extend the right edge; while the window violates the constraint, move the left edge until it does not; record the largest seen',
    whyLinear: 'each pointer only ever moves forward, so total work is O(n) despite examining every possible window' },
  { v: 'growing window', finds: 'the SHORTEST range satisfying a constraint',
    loop: 'extend the right edge; while the window already satisfies it, shrink from the left and record the length; then keep extending',
    relation: 'same pointers, opposite stopping condition',
    mostCommonMistake: 'confusing the two variants' },
];

/* The problems each shape should trigger. */
const WINDOW_PROBLEMS = [
  { p: 'longest substring without repeating characters', shape: 'a shrinking window over a set of seen characters' },
  { p: 'longest substring with at most k distinct', note: 'identical, with the constraint changed' },
  { p: 'minimum window substring', variant: 'growing',
    constraint: 'the window must contain all the characters of a target; shrink while it still does' },
  { p: 'minimum size subarray with sum at least k',
    requires: 'the sum being positive, because then shrinking can only reduce the sum',
    consequence: 'which is why the two-pointer approach works there and the ordinary growing-window shape does not apply to a general target-sum problem',
    generalRule: 'the technique applies when the problem is MONOTONE UNDER SHRINKING' },
  { p: 'anagram search', mechanics: 'a window of fixed length, compared by a running count vector' },
  { p: 'permutation in string', note: 'the same with a different constraint' },
  { p: 'longest subarray with sum divisible by k',
    notASlidingWindow: true, is: 'a prefix-sum-and-modulo trick',
    skill: 'recognising that the sliding window does not apply is part of the skill' },
];

/* How to work these problems. */
const METHOD = [
  { step: 'the O(n^2) version is the SPECIFICATION',
    why: 'write the nested loop first - it says what the problem is and it is obviously correct',
    then: 'ask whether the comparison lets you discard anything, and collapse it if so',
    whyOrderMatters: 'inventing a two-pointer solution in your head produces something that works on the examples and is subtly wrong, because the invariant was never written down' },
  { step: 'write down the invariant',
    twoPointer: 'any solution using the discarded element is impossible, because of the comparison we just made',
    window: 'the current window is the longest valid window ending at the right pointer',
    test: 'if you can state that sentence the algorithm is right; if you cannot, you have a pattern you do not understand and it will fail on input you did not consider' },
];

Instincts: "sorted array + pair/triple target" → two pointers. "any contiguous subarray/substring with a length bound or sum threshold" → sliding window. Both are O(n) — the whole point.

4.8 The time-space trade-off

The time-space trade-off states that speeding up an algorithm usually costs extra memory, and saving memory often slows it down. Caching results, precomputing tables, or using hash maps reduce time at the price of storage. It is the standard answer when someone asks how to make a program faster.

Speed and memory pull in opposite directions. You can often buy O(1) lookups by paying O(n) extra memory: precompute a hash table, sort once, or cache results.

# Find duplicates: two philosophies for the same problem
def has_duplicates_quadratic(items):        # O(n²) time, O(1) space
    for i in range(len(items)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(items)):
            if items[i] == items[j]:
                return True
    return False

def has_duplicates_linear(items):           # O(n) time, O(n) space
    seen = set()
    for x in items:
        if x in seen:                        # O(1) hash lookup
            return True
        seen.add(x)
    return False

The same problem solved two ways: nested loops are O(n²) time with no memory, while a set is O(n) time at the price of O(n) space.

Another instance you already met: memoization (Ch. 9.4) — recursion collapses from exponential time by paying polynomial memory. When an interviewer says "can you do better?", the phrase they want to hear is: "Trade a bit of memory for speed."

What the trade-off actually is, and the three forms it takes

Time-space trade-off is not "you can have speed or memory, never both". It is a more specific claim: you can often convert time into space, and occasionally space into time, by storing something you could otherwise recompute. The classical example is a lookup table — a sorted array plus a hash index is more memory and less time; a list scanned linearly is less memory and more time. Three forms cover almost every real instance. Memoisation and caching. Store the result of an expensive computation keyed by its inputs, so the second identical call is a dictionary lookup instead of the work. Precomputation and indexing. Sort once, or build an index, so that many subsequent queries are cheap — and the essential condition is that the data must not change often, because every change invalidates the precomputation. Trading space for time with a sentinel or a lookup table. A finite set of states can be precomputed into an array, turning a branch into an index. And the direction is not always space-to-time: streaming is time-for-space, processing a large input in constant memory instead of loading it, which is why every tool that must handle more data than fits in memory is written as a stream rather than a list.

Then the two conditions that decide whether a trade is worth taking, and they are where this goes wrong in practice. How many times will it be paid for? The amortised cost of memoising is one extra lookup per call in exchange for eliminating the work entirely on a repeat. If the input never repeats, you have paid for a dictionary and gained nothing — which is why memoisation on a function whose arguments are all distinct is pure overhead, and why a cache keyed on something that is not actually shared between callers never hits. What is the lifetime of the validity? This is the one people skip. A cache is correct only while its inputs are unchanged; an index is correct only while the table is not written; a precomputed table is correct only while the function being precomputed has not been redefined. Every one of those is a staleness problem rather than a performance problem, and it is the reason a cached value is the single most common source of a bug that only appears in production: it was correct when it was stored, the thing it depends on changed, and nothing invalidated it. The rule that follows is short and absolute: a cache is correct only if you can name the thing that invalidates it. If you cannot name it, you have not built a cache, you have built a bug with a performance benefit.

/* Not "speed or memory, never both". */
const THE_TRADE = {
  claim: 'you can often convert TIME into space, and occasionally space into time, by storing something you could otherwise recompute',
  classical: 'a sorted array plus a hash index is more memory and less time; a list scanned linearly is less memory and more time',
};
const THREE_FORMS = [
  { f: 'memoisation and caching', does: 'store the result of an expensive computation keyed by its inputs',
    gain: 'the second identical call is a dictionary lookup instead of the work' },
  { f: 'precomputation and indexing', does: 'sort once or build an index so many subsequent queries are cheap',
    essentialCondition: 'the data must not change often, because every change invalidates the precomputation' },
  { f: 'trading space for time with a sentinel or lookup table', does: 'a finite set of states precomputed into an array',
    gain: 'turns a branch into an index' },
];
const REVERSE_DIRECTION = {
  form: 'streaming',
  trades: 'time for space',
  does: 'processes a large input in constant memory instead of loading it',
  why: 'why every tool that must handle more data than fits in memory is written as a stream rather than a list',
};

/* Two conditions that decide whether a trade is worth taking. */
const CONDITIONS = [
  { c: 'how many times will it be paid for',
    amortised: 'one extra lookup per call in exchange for eliminating the work on a repeat',
    whenItDoesNotPay: 'if the input never repeats you have paid for a dictionary and gained nothing',
    consequences: ['memoising a function whose arguments are all distinct is pure overhead',
      'a cache keyed on something not actually shared between callers never hits'] },
  { c: 'what is the lifetime of the validity',
    whySkipped: 'it is the one people skip',
    is: 'a STALENESS problem rather than a performance problem',
    instances: ['a cache is correct only while its inputs are unchanged',
      'an index is correct only while the table is not written',
      'a precomputed table is correct only while the function has not been redefined'],
    whyItMatters: 'the single most common source of a bug that only appears in production - it was correct when stored, its dependency changed, and nothing invalidated it',
    absoluteRule: 'a cache is correct only if you can NAME THE THING THAT INVALIDATES IT; if you cannot name it, you have built a bug with a performance benefit' },
];

When to take the trade, and how to know if you did

Three questions that settle it, in order. Is it measured? A cache added to a function that accounts for two per cent of runtime has made the program harder to reason about and faster by nothing. Will it be reused? The break-even for memoisation is roughly three repetitions, because each one costs a lookup and each saving is a full computation — and the reuse rate of a real request path is usually knowable, so this is a question you can answer rather than guess. How expensive is the invalidation? A cache whose lifetime is the life of the process is simple and safe; one that must be invalidated on every write is a distributed-systems problem wearing a performance costume, and if that is what you are building then you want a proper caching layer with a stated consistency model rather than a dictionary in a function.

Then how to tell whether the trade worked, because the failure is usually silent. Measure the hit rate, not the speed. A cache with a five per cent hit rate is slower than no cache, and the speed measurement alone may not reveal it because the added work is small. Watch memory. A memo table that grows without bound is a memory leak with a performance rationale; bounding it — by size, by age, or by scope — is part of building it, not an optimisation to add later. Measure both sides. The honest comparison is total time including the cost of the lookup and the maintenance, against total time without, on the workload you actually have. And then the last point, which is the one that keeps this section honest: the trade is a design decision before it is an optimisation. Deciding at the outset that a lookup will be hot enough to deserve an index is different from noticing later that it is hot — because the first is a change to the shape of the code and the second is a patch onto code that was written assuming otherwise. Whichever you do, the invariant is the same, and it is the same invariant that makes it debuggable: if you cannot state what makes the stored value stale, you cannot know whether it is stale.

/* Three questions that settle it, in order. */
const SETTLE = [
  { q: 'is it measured',
    counterexample: 'a cache added to a function accounting for two per cent of runtime has made the program harder to reason about and faster by nothing' },
  { q: 'will it be reused',
    breakEven: 'roughly three repetitions, because each costs a lookup and each saving is a full computation',
    reframe: 'the reuse rate of a real request path is usually knowable, so this is answerable rather than a guess' },
  { q: 'how expensive is the invalidation',
    spectrum: ['a cache whose lifetime is the life of the process is simple and safe',
      'one that must be invalidated on every write is a distributed-systems problem wearing a performance costume'],
    conclusion: 'if that is what you are building, use a proper caching layer with a stated consistency model rather than a dictionary in a function' },
];

/* How to tell whether the trade worked. */
const TELLING = [
  { measure: 'the hit rate, not the speed',
    why: 'a cache with a five per cent hit rate is slower than no cache',
    catch: 'the speed measurement alone may not reveal it, because the added work is small' },
  { measure: 'memory',
    failure: 'a memo table that grows without bound is a memory leak with a performance rationale',
    requirement: 'bounding it by size, by age or by scope is part of building it, not an optimisation to add later' },
  { measure: 'both sides',
    honestComparison: 'total time including lookup and maintenance, against total time without, on the workload you actually have' },
];
const DESIGN_FIRST = {
  claim: 'the trade is a design decision before it is an optimisation',
  early: 'deciding at the outset that a lookup will be hot enough to deserve an index changes the shape of the code',
  late: 'noticing later that it is hot patches onto code written assuming otherwise',
  invariant: 'if you cannot state what makes the stored value stale, you cannot know whether it is stale',
};

Preprocessing changes the game. "Sort the input once, then every query is fast" and "build the index once, then lookups are instant" are the same idea — and it returns as database indexes (Ch. 13) and build steps (Ch. 17).

4.9 Binary search & the power of halves

Binary search exploits sorted data by repeatedly discarding half of the remaining search space, reaching any answer in logarithmic steps. Beyond searching, the same halving mindset applies to finding ranges, peaks, and satisfiable values. Rooting your thinking in halves converts many hard problems into easy ones.

Binary search finds an item in a sorted array in O(log n) — the first "exponentially powerful" algorithm you learn. It’s also a frame of mind: repeatedly halving a search space solves many problems (finding thresholds, roots, the first element that satisfies a predicate).

def binary_search(arr, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(arr) - 1                 # invariant: answer in [lo, hi]
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if arr[mid] == target: return mid
        elif arr[mid] < target: lo = mid + 1
        else:                 hi = mid - 1
    return -1

print(binary_search([1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11], 7))   # 3

# The "answer a question" version: find FIRST index where f(i) is True
def first_true(n, f):
    lo, hi = 0, n
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if f(mid): hi = mid         # could be the answer; don't skip it
        else:      lo = mid + 1
    return lo
print(first_true(20, lambda i: i * i >= 10))    # 4  (sqrt floor)

# In real projects: from bisect import bisect_left, insort  -- C-speed,
# and bisect is the hidden engine of many "range query" interview solutions.

Binary search pinpoints a value in sorted data in logarithmic steps, and the first_true variant finds the first index where a predicate turns true.

The off-by-one is the entire bug class: decide whether your hi is inclusive or exclusive and stay consistent. The first_true loop above uses exclusive hi and never excludes a candidate — memorize the pattern and you’ll never write the buggy variant again.

Exercises 4

  1. Time your own bubble vs merge sort on a random list of 1,000 and 10,000 numbers (import random; random.sample(range(1_000_000), n)). Measure with time.time() around each call.
  2. Rewrite binary_search recursively.
  3. For each Big-O class, give one real operation from your daily life that matches it.

    4. Why binary search beats linear search, and the exact amount

    The arithmetic is worth doing because it is the whole case. On one million sorted elements, a linear search averages about 500,000 comparisons and worst-cases at 1,000,000. Binary search needs about 20 — because each comparison halves what remains, and 2²⁰ ≈ 1,048,576. On a billion elements it is about 30. So the saving is not a factor of two, it is a factor of fifty thousand and it grows without limit, which is the characteristic that makes this the canonical example of an algorithmic win. What you give up is equally clear: the data must be sorted, and staying sorted is not free. Insert into the middle of a sorted array is O(n) because everything after it must shift. So binary search is not "faster than linear search" in general — it is a trade: one O(log n) lookup against an O(n) cost to maintain the invariant that makes it possible.

    Then the algorithm itself, and the invariant is the thing to understand rather than the arithmetic. The invariant: if the target is in the array, it is between low and high, inclusive. Every line of the implementation exists to preserve it. Compare the middle element: if it equals the target, done. If it is smaller, the target cannot be to the left, so raise low. If it is larger, lower high. The loop ends when low > high, which is the signal for absence — and that signal is the thing everyone gets wrong, because an implementation that loops until low == high will hang on a missing element forever. The three failure modes to know in advance are all boundary errors: using < where you need <=, which either loops forever or skips the last element; mixing inclusive and exclusive bounds, which is the single most common source of an off-by-one here, because high = len - 1 with an inclusive comparison and high = len with an exclusive one are both correct and differ by one iteration; and overflow in the midpoint, (low + high) // 2, which is safe in Python but overflows in a fixed-width language — the correct form is low + (high - low) // 2, and knowing why is the point.

    /* The arithmetic, which is the whole case. */
const BINARY_ARITHMETIC = {
  size: 'one million sorted elements',
  linear: 'averages about 500,000 comparisons, worst case 1,000,000',
  binary: 'about 20, because each comparison halves what remains and 2^20 is about 1,048,576',
  billion: 'about 30',
  saving: 'not a factor of two - a factor of fifty thousand, growing without limit',
  whyCanonical: 'it is the textbook example of an algorithmic win rather than a constant-factor one',
  theCost: 'the data must be sorted, and staying sorted is not free',
  insertCost: 'O(n) in the middle of a sorted array, because everything after it shifts',
  reframe: 'not faster than linear search in general - a trade of one O(log n) lookup against an O(n) cost to maintain the invariant',
};

/* The algorithm, understood through its invariant. */
const INVARIANT = {
  statement: 'if the target is in the array, it is between low and high, inclusive',
  why: 'every line of the implementation exists to preserve it',
  steps: ['compare the middle element',
    'equal to the target, done',
    'smaller, the target cannot be to the left, raise low',
    'larger, lower high'],
  endsWhen: 'low > high',
  theSignalEveryoneGetsWrong: 'an implementation looping until low == high hangs on a missing element forever',
};
const FAILURE_MODES = [
  { f: 'using < where you need <=', symptom: 'either loops forever or skips the last element' },
  { f: 'mixing inclusive and exclusive bounds',
    why: 'the single most common source of an off-by-one here',
    detail: 'high = len - 1 with an inclusive comparison, and high = len with an exclusive one, are both correct and differ by one iteration' },
  { f: 'overflow in the midpoint', expression: '(low + high) // 2',
    safeIn: 'Python', unsafeIn: 'a fixed-width language',
    correctForm: 'low + (high - low) // 2',
    why: 'knowing why is the point' },
];

    Binary search variants worth knowing

    Three variants cover nearly every problem that a binary search solves, and each is a small change to the loop rather than a different algorithm. Lower bound returns the first index at which a value could be inserted while keeping order — which is the first element not less than the target, and is also the answer to "where do all the duplicates end". Upper bound returns the first index strictly greater than the target, which is the first of the duplicates. The pair together give a count and a range: upper_bound(x) - lower_bound(x) is how many of them there are, and together they bracket every element equal to x. This is the form used in every serious implementation because it does not stop at the first match, which is almost never what you want. Then searching on the answer — the pattern where instead of searching for a value, you binary-search over a monotone predicate: the smallest capacity that makes a function true, the lowest page on which a name appears. The loop asks "is the predicate true at index m?" and moves low or high; the answer is not found but bracketed. This is the most transferable idea in the chapter, because a monotone predicate is extremely common — "can this be done in t time" is monotone in t — and the technique turns "guess and check" into O(log n) instead of a binary search over a number range anyway.

    Then two things that are easy to get wrong and expensive to debug. The off-by-one at the ends. Whether the target can equal the first or last element decides whether low starts at 0 and high at len - 1, or whether high starts at len, and getting this wrong produces a bug that appears only on the boundary values — which are the values a hand-written test most often omits, because you reach for a middle element when writing a test. Testing binary search properly. Write a brute-force version first, then compare on random inputs including empty, single-element, all-duplicate, and missing arrays. The technique of testing an algorithm against a slow obviously-correct version on random inputs finds in minutes what reading the code will not find in an hour, and it generalises to every algorithm in this chapter and beyond.

    /* Three variants, each a small change to the loop. */
const VARIANTS = [
  { v: 'lower bound', returns: 'the first index at which a value could be inserted while keeping order',
    equivalently: 'the first element not less than the target',
    bonus: 'also the answer to where do all the duplicates end' },
  { v: 'upper bound', returns: 'the first index strictly greater than the target',
    equivalently: 'the first of the duplicates' },
  { v: 'the pair together',
    count: 'upper_bound(x) - lower_bound(x) is how many of them there are',
    range: 'together they bracket every element equal to x',
    whyThisIsTheRealForm: 'it does not stop at the first match, which is almost never what you want' },
];

/* Searching on the answer: the most transferable idea here. */
const SEARCH_ON_ANSWER = {
  pattern: 'instead of searching for a value, binary-search over a monotone predicate',
  examples: ['the smallest capacity that makes a function true', 'the lowest page on which a name appears'],
  loop: 'ask is the predicate true at index m, then move low or high',
  keyDifference: 'the answer is not found but BRACKETED',
  whyTransferable: 'a monotone predicate is extremely common - can this be done in t time is monotone in t',
  payoff: 'turns guess-and-check into O(log n) instead of a binary search over a number range anyway',
};

/* Two things that are easy to get wrong. */
const BOUNDARY = [
  { f: 'the off-by-one at the ends',
    rule: 'whether the target can equal the first or last element decides the starting bounds',
    detail: 'low = 0 and high = len - 1, or high starting at len',
    symptom: 'a bug that appears only on the boundary values',
    whyItSurvives: 'boundary values are what a hand-written test most often omits, because you reach for a middle element when writing a test' },
  { f: 'testing binary search properly',
    method: ['write a brute-force version first',
      'compare on random inputs including empty, single-element, all-duplicate and missing arrays'],
    why: 'testing against a slow obviously-correct version on random inputs finds in minutes what reading the code will not find in an hour',
    generalises: 'every algorithm in this chapter and beyond' },
];

5 · Object-Oriented Programming

Object-oriented programming bundles data and the behaviour that operates on it into objects. The four pillars, encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, and polymorphism, are the foundation of most production codebases. Master them and you can both write maintainable systems and read almost any real-world code.

5.1 Classes and instances — blueprints and objects5.2 The four pillars5.3 Dunder methods — teach objects Python’s syntax5.4 Modelling with UML — the engineer’s sketchbook5.5 Hands-on: a tiny bank system5.6 dataclasses, abstract classes and composition

As programs grow, plain functions over loose variables start to fight each other. OOP bundles related data and the functions that operate on it into objects. OOP is one of the two giant paradigms you’ll master (the other is functional, Ch. 19).

5.1 Classes and instances — blueprints and objects

A class is a blueprint that defines attributes and methods, and an instance is a concrete object created from it. You create instances by calling the class as a constructor, and each instance stores its own attribute values. The self parameter binds methods to the specific instance that calls them.

A class is a blueprint; an instance/object is one concrete thing made from it. The blueprint defines attributes (data every instance has) and methods (behaviour every instance has).

class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name, age):   # constructor: runs when object is created
        self.name = name             # self = "the current object I'm building"
        self.age = age

    def bark(self):
        print(f"{self.name} says Woof!")

    def birthday(self):
        self.age += 1                # methods can mutate the object

milo = Dog("Milo", 3)    # __init__ runs -> Milo.bark()
milo.bark()              # Milo says Woof!
milo.birthday()
print(milo.age)          # 4

Defines a Dog class with a constructor, methods and instance attributes; notice the self parameter threading through every method.

self is pure Python convention: the object itself. Every method receives it automatically as the first argument.

Class versus instance, and what self is actually doing

Two terms to be precise about. The class is the template: a description of what every instance will have, plus the behaviour that behaviour available on all of them. An instance is one object built from that template, with its own copy of the data. When you write d = Dog("Rex"), Dog is not an object — it is the thing that makes objects; d is the object. This is the same relationship as a class and an object in every object-oriented language, and the confusion between them is what produces the mistake of treating a class as if it were a single shared instance.

Then self, which is the parameter that makes the whole thing work and the one thing to understand before writing anything else. self is the instance the method was called on. Not the class, not a keyword, not magic — an ordinary first parameter that Python passes automatically, and every method's body starts by referring to self.attribute to mean "this particular object's attribute". The reason it exists is that a method is shared by every instance, so it needs to know which one it is operating on; passing it explicitly makes that dependency visible, and the rule that follows is simply never call a method with self supplied by you — d.bark() passes d as self, and writing d.bark(d) is a type error at best. And the class-level operation Dog.count accesses an attribute on the class itself rather than on an instance, which is how you keep a registry or a counter that is shared by every object rather than duplicated a thousand times. The distinction between a class attribute and an instance attribute is worth being careful with, because an assignment inside __init__ creates an instance attribute while an assignment in the class body creates a shared one — and the resulting bug, where mutating a list class attribute, appends to the same list for everybody, is a classic first encounter with shared mutable state.

/* Class versus instance. */
const TERMS = {
  theClass: 'the template - a description of what every instance will have, plus the behaviour available on all of them',
  anInstance: 'one object built from that template, with its own copy of the data',
  worked: 'd = Dog("Rex") - Dog is not an object, it is the thing that MAKES objects; d is the object',
  generalises: 'the same relationship as class and object in every object-oriented language',
  theConfusion: 'treating a class as if it were a single shared instance',
};

/* What self is. */
const SELF = {
  is: 'the instance the method was called on',
  notAnyOf: ['the class', 'a keyword', 'magic'],
  actually: 'an ordinary first parameter that Python passes automatically',
  whyItExists: 'a method is shared by every instance, so it needs to know which one it is operating on',
  gain: 'passing it explicitly makes that dependency visible',
  bodyRule: 'every methods body starts with self.attribute to mean this particular objects attribute',
  theRule: 'never call a method with self supplied by you - d.bark() passes d as self',
  counterExample: 'writing d.bark(d) is a type error at best',
  classLevelAccess: 'Dog.count accesses an attribute on the class itself rather than on an instance',
  whyUseful: 'keeps a registry or counter shared by every object rather than duplicated a thousand times',
};
const ATTRIBUTE_DISTINCTION = {
  inInit: 'an assignment inside __init__ creates an INSTANCE attribute',
  classBody: 'an assignment in the class body creates a SHARED one',
  classicBug: 'mutating a list class attribute appends to the same list for everybody',
  lesson: 'a classic first encounter with shared mutable state',
};

Why classes at all, and what they cost

The honest reason to use a class is not "to organise code" — modules and functions do that. It is that a class lets you attach data and the operations valid on that data together, and guarantee they travel as one unit. A bank account's balance is not a number you pass around; it is a number plus the three operations that are allowed to change it. Binding them means no code anywhere can set the balance directly without going through validation, which is a property you cannot get from a tuple of (balance, deposit, withdraw) that a caller is free to take apart. This is the encapsulation argument and it is real: the value of a class is that it makes illegal states unrepresentable, not that it saves typing. The three reasons, in order of how often they actually matter. Invariant enforcement — a class can refuse a negative deposit. Shared behaviour without repetition — one describe() for every object rather than one per class. Substitutability — a function written against an interface works on anything that implements it, which is what makes collections of different types usable together.

Then the costs, because a class that is used where a function would do is worse than either. Coupling. A class is a contract; anyone can construct one, call any method, and depend on any attribute. That surface area is why a large class is hard to change — a refactor to it breaks callers you never find. Inheritance coupling. A subclass depends on its parent's internals, so a change in the parent breaks children in ways the type system does not catch. Mutable shared state. Two references to the same object mutate together, which is harmless in a single-threaded script and a data race in a concurrent one. Ceremony. A class with one method and two attributes is a dictionary with extra steps. And the wrong altitude. Classes modelled on nouns produce an object graph with no behaviour anywhere — entities that hold data and pass it to functions, which is the most common object-oriented failure and is worse than no objects at all because it carries the cost without the benefit. The test worth applying: a class earns its place when there is an invariant to protect, or when the same behaviour genuinely applies to many different data shapes. Otherwise a function with named parameters is more readable, more testable, and cheaper to change.

/* The honest reason to use a class. */
const REASON = {
  notThis: 'to organise code - modules and functions do that',
  actually: 'attach data and the operations valid on that data together, and guarantee they travel as one unit',
  example: 'a bank balance is not a number you pass around; it is a number plus the three operations allowed to change it',
  whyThatMatters: 'no code can set the balance directly without going through validation',
  notAvailableFromATuple: 'a tuple of (balance, deposit, withdraw) can be taken apart by a caller',
  argument: 'the value of a class is that it makes ILLEGAL STATES UNREPRESENTABLE, not that it saves typing',
  threeReasons: [
    { r: 'invariant enforcement', example: 'a class can refuse a negative deposit' },
    { r: 'shared behaviour without repetition', example: 'one describe() for every object rather than one per class' },
    { r: 'substitutability', example: 'a function written against an interface works on anything implementing it - what makes collections of different types usable together' },
  ],
};

/* The costs. */
const COSTS = [
  { c: 'coupling', detail: 'a class is a contract; anyone can construct one, call any method, depend on any attribute',
    consequence: 'a large class is hard to change, because a refactor breaks callers you never find' },
  { c: 'inheritance coupling', detail: 'a subclass depends on its parents internals',
    consequence: 'a change in the parent breaks children in ways the type system does not catch' },
  { c: 'mutable shared state', detail: 'two references to the same object mutate together',
    context: 'harmless in a single-threaded script, a data race in a concurrent one' },
  { c: 'ceremony', detail: 'a class with one method and two attributes is a dictionary with extra steps' },
  { c: 'the wrong altitude', detail: 'classes modelled on nouns produce an object graph with no behaviour anywhere',
    why: 'entities that hold data and pass it to functions',
    verdict: 'the most common object-oriented failure - worse than no objects at all, because it carries the cost without the benefit' },
];
const EARNED = {
  test: 'a class earns its place when there is an INVARIANT to protect, or when the same behaviour genuinely applies to many different data shapes',
  otherwise: 'a function with named parameters is more readable, more testable and cheaper to change',
};

Class vs instance attributes. Put shared, fixed values on the class; put per-object values in __init__. Rule of thumb: if every instance must have its own copy, it lives in __init__.

5.2 The four pillars

The four pillars of OOP shape reusable design. Encapsulation hides internal state behind methods, abstraction presents simple interfaces over complex detail, inheritance lets classes reuse and extend each other, and polymorphism lets different classes respond to the same interface. Knowing what each protects and enables guides better design choices.

PillarMeaningWhy it matters
EncapsulationBundle data + methods; hide internals behind a public interfaceCallers can’t accidentally corrupt internal state; you can change internals freely
AbstractionExpose "what it does", hide "how it does it"Reuse and decouple: other code depends on the contract, not the implementation
InheritanceA class inherits behaviour from a parent classReuse common code; model "is-a" relationships
PolymorphismDifferent classes respond to the same method name differentlyOne loop / one interface works on many object types
# Inheritance + polymorphism
class Animal:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
    def speak(self):
        raise NotImplementedError   # "override me"

class Dog(Animal):
    def speak(self):
        return f"{self.name} says Woof!"

class Cat(Animal):
    def speak(self):
        return f"{self.name} says Meow!"

# Polymorphism: one interface (speak), many behaviours
pets = [Dog("Milo"), Cat("Bella")]
for p in pets:
    print(p.speak())        # works for both classes

Inheritance plus polymorphism: one speak interface, two behaviours, and a single loop that works on both classes.

The four pillars, each as a specific mechanism rather than a slogan

Abstraction is hiding detail behind a name that says what it does rather than how. The mechanism is not "keep it private"; it is that the caller is able to be wrong about the implementation without consequence. A function that sums a list lets you not know whether it is a loop, a recursion, or a library call, and that is the point — the abstraction is valuable precisely because it can be replaced without the caller changing. The failure mode is leakage: an abstraction that leaks forces the caller to know about the layer underneath, and the usual cause is promising more than the implementation can support. Encapsulation is making illegal states unrepresentable, and the mechanism is a rule about who may write to what. The encapsulate is not a keyword — it is the set of operations through which mutation happens. A balance that can only change via deposit and withdraw has an invariant that is enforced by construction, not by discipline. In Python there is no real privacy, so the honest statement is: a single leading underscore is a convention that says this is internal, and the class does nothing to stop you; what stops you is that the only supported way in is a method, and tests that go around it are the defect.

Then inheritance, which is both the useful one and the overused one. Its mechanism is a substitutability guarantee: if a subclass satisfies the parent's contract, code written against the parent works on the child without knowing it exists. What it actually gives you is the opposite of what most people use it for — it does not primarily save code, it guarantees a relationship. And the two failure modes are the reason the rule "prefer composition" exists: the fragile base class problem, where a change to the parent breaks every child in ways nobody anticipated, and the wrong-hierarchy problem, where a Car extends Engine because it is convenient rather than because a car is an engine. Polymorphism is the mechanism by which the same code handles different types: the function calls a method, and each object supplies its own version. It is what makes a collection of mixed types usable, and its practical payoff is the reason to care — a loop that says do the thing rather than if this type, then that. The test for whether you have it: if your if statement is branching on type, you have not used polymorphism yet, and the branch is a place a new type will be forgotten.

/* Abstraction and encapsulation. */
const ABSTRACTION = {
  is: 'hiding detail behind a name that says what it does rather than how',
  notThis: 'keep it private',
  mechanism: 'the caller is ABLE TO BE WRONG about the implementation without consequence',
  value: 'a function that sums a list lets you not know whether it is a loop, a recursion or a library call',
  point: 'the abstraction is valuable precisely because it can be replaced without the caller changing',
  failureMode: 'leakage - an abstraction that leaks forces the caller to know about the layer underneath',
  usualCause: 'promising more than the implementation can support',
};
const ENCAPSULATION = {
  is: 'making illegal states unrepresentable',
  mechanism: 'a rule about who may write to what',
  theEncapsulate: 'NOT a keyword - it is the set of operations through which mutation happens',
  worked: 'a balance changeable only via deposit and withdraw has an invariant enforced by construction, not by discipline',
  inPython: 'there is no real privacy',
  honestStatement: 'a single leading underscore is a CONVENTION that says this is internal, and the class does nothing to stop you',
  whatStopsYou: 'the only supported way in is a method, and tests that go around it are the defect',
};

/* Inheritance and polymorphism. */
const INHERITANCE = {
  is: 'both the useful one and the overused one',
  mechanism: 'a substitutability guarantee - if a subclass satisfies the parents contract, code written against the parent works on the child without knowing it exists',
  actuallyGives: 'the OPPOSITE of what most people use it for - it does not primarily save code, it guarantees a relationship',
  failureModes: [
    { f: 'the fragile base class problem', detail: 'a change to the parent breaks every child in ways nobody anticipated' },
    { f: 'the wrong-hierarchy problem', example: 'a Car extends Engine because it is convenient, not because a car IS an engine',
      note: 'the reason prefer-composition exists' },
  ],
};
const POLYMORPHISM = {
  is: 'the mechanism by which the same code handles different types',
  mechanism: 'the function calls a method and each object supplies its own version',
  payoff: 'a collection of mixed types becomes usable',
  theRealBenefit: 'a loop that says DO THE THING rather than if this type, then that',
  theTest: 'if your if statement is branching on type, you have not used polymorphism yet',
  whyItMatters: 'the branch is a place a new type will be forgotten',
};

Choosing between the four, and the rule that resolves most of it

The four are not alternatives to pick from; they are layers, and knowing which one a problem is actually about is most of the skill. Is the problem "this data must stay valid"? Encapsulation — write one class that owns the invariant, and every operation that could break it goes through a method. Is the problem "this code has grown branches on type"? Polymorphism — define the behaviour once on each type, and let the shared code call it without asking. Is the problem "this function has grown parameters and callers who must remember the order"? Abstraction — wrap the parameter cluster into one object, and callers now pass a thing rather than remembering four things. Is the problem "these types share behaviour that genuinely varies"? Inheritance, but check first whether a shared interface plus composition would serve — because if the shared part is an implementation detail rather than a contract, inheritance is the wrong tool even when it works. That last distinction is the one worth keeping: inherit for a contract, compose for an implementation.

Then the rule that resolves most cases, and the failure mode each pillar produces when misapplied. Abstraction misapplied produces a layer that adds indirection without adding safety — a wrapper with one method that delegates everything, which makes every read of the code a redirect and protects nothing. Encapsulation misapplied produces a class with fifteen private fields and no public method that uses them together, so every operation is a getter-setter pair and the invariant is enforced nowhere. Inheritance misapplied produces a five-level hierarchy where the leaf classes are the only ones anyone can reason about and no two of them can be substituted for one another — which is not polymorphism at all, despite the syntax. Polymorphism misapplied produces an interface with twenty methods where a caller uses two, so every implementation must implement eighteen it does not care about — which is why a narrow interface is worth more than a complete one. And the practical review question that catches all four: can you name the invariant this class protects? If yes, the class is earning its keep. If you find yourself describing what the class contains rather than what it guarantees, you have written a bag of fields.

/* The four are layers, not alternatives. */
const LAYERS = [
  { problem: 'this data must stay valid', pillar: 'encapsulation',
    action: 'write one class that owns the invariant, and every operation that could break it goes through a method' },
  { problem: 'this code has grown branches on type', pillar: 'polymorphism',
    action: 'define the behaviour once on each type and let the shared code call it without asking' },
  { problem: 'this function has grown parameters and callers who must remember the order', pillar: 'abstraction',
    action: 'wrap the parameter cluster into one object, so callers pass a thing rather than remembering four things' },
  { problem: 'these types share behaviour that genuinely varies', pillar: 'inheritance - but check composition first',
    check: 'if the shared part is an implementation detail rather than a contract, inheritance is the wrong tool even when it works' },
];
const RULE = 'inherit for a CONTRACT, compose for an IMPLEMENTATION';

/* Misapplication, and the failure each pillar produces. */
const MISAPPLIED = [
  { pillar: 'abstraction', produces: 'a layer that adds indirection without adding safety',
    shape: 'a wrapper with one method delegating everything',
    cost: 'every read of the code is a redirect, and it protects nothing' },
  { pillar: 'encapsulation', produces: 'a class with fifteen private fields and no public method that uses them together',
    cost: 'every operation is a getter-setter pair and the invariant is enforced nowhere' },
  { pillar: 'inheritance', produces: 'a five-level hierarchy where only the leaves are reason-about-able',
    sting: 'no two of them can be substituted for one another - not polymorphism at all, despite the syntax' },
  { pillar: 'polymorphism', produces: 'an interface with twenty methods where a caller uses two',
    cost: 'every implementation must implement eighteen it does not care about',
    lesson: 'a narrow interface is worth more than a complete one' },
];
const REVIEW_QUESTION = {
  q: 'can you name the invariant this class protects',
  yes: 'the class is earning its keep',
  instead: 'if you find yourself describing what the class CONTAINS rather than what it GUARANTEES, you have written a bag of fields',
};

Prefer composition over inheritance in modern design: a Car has an Engine rather than Car extends Engine. Deep inheritance trees (5+ levels of "…extends…extends") become rigid and confusing — Chapter 19 revists this through SOLID.

5.3 Dunder methods — teach objects Python’s syntax

Dunder (double underscore) methods hook your classes into Python’s own syntax and built-ins. Methods like __init__, __str__, __lt__, and __eq__ control construction, printing, comparison, and equality, while __add__ enables the plus operator on your objects. Implementing them makes custom classes behave like native ones.

Methods with double underscore (dunder) let your classes participate in Python’s own features.

class Money:
    def __init__(self, amount):
        self.amount = amount
    def __repr__(self):                     # how it looks in the debugger
        return f"Money({self.amount})"
    def __str__(self):                      # how print() shows it
        return f"${self.amount}"
    def __add__(self, other):               # lets you write a + b
        return Money(self.amount + other.amount)
    def __eq__(self, other):                # lets you compare ==
        return self.amount == other.amount

print(Money(5) + Money(7))     # $12
print(Money(5) == Money(5))    # True

Dunder methods, and the principle behind all of them

A dunder method — a method whose name is wrapped in double underscores — is a method Python calls on your behalf. len(x) is not asking your object for its length; it is calling x.__len__(), and the language chose that name for you. a + b calls a.__add__(b). print(x) calls x.__str__(). That is the whole principle: the operators you already know are just names for methods, and defining the method is how you make your own type work with syntax other code already uses. The name is dunder because Python reserves the double-underscore namespace for itself — names like __init__, __len__, __str__ are looked up by the interpreter, not called by you directly, and defining your own ones is how you hook into that.

Then the set worth knowing, grouped by what you are trying to make work. Construction: __init__ runs after the object exists and is where you set up state; __new__ controls creation itself and is what a metaclass or an immutable type uses; __del__ runs at teardown and is why explicit resource management is better than relying on it. Representation: __repr__ returns something you could paste back into the interpreter, for you to read, and __str__ returns something for a person — and the rule is that __repr__ should be unambiguous and __str__ should be readable, because they are used in different places and the debugger uses __repr__ while a printed value uses __str__. Comparison: __eq__, __lt__ and the rest, and the detail that catches people is that defining __eq__ without __hash__ makes the object unhashable, which is why such a class suddenly cannot go in a set. Arithmetic: __add__, __mul__, and so on — and the design question is whether + on your type means the same thing as it means on the types people already know. Containers: __len__, __getitem__, __contains__, __iter__, and defining the last three together makes your object work in a for loop and an in check for free. Context management: __enter__ and __exit__, which is how an object becomes usable in a with block — and how one object guarantees another's cleanup.

/* The principle. */
const PRINCIPLE = {
  is: 'a method Python calls on your behalf',
  notThis: 'asking your object for its length',
  actually: 'len(x) is calling x.__len__(); a + b is calling a.__add__(b); print(x) is calling x.__str__()',
  payoff: 'defining the method is how you make your own type work with syntax other code already uses',
  whyTheName: 'Python reserves the double-underscore namespace for itself - the interpreter looks these up rather than you calling them',
};

/* The set worth knowing, grouped by intent. */
const SET = [
  { group: 'construction',
    methods: ['__init__ - after the object exists, sets up state',
      '__new__ - controls creation itself; what a metaclass or immutable type uses',
      '__del__ - runs at teardown'],
    consequence: 'why explicit resource management is better than relying on it' },
  { group: 'representation',
    methods: ['__repr__ - something you could paste back into the interpreter, for YOU',
      '__str__ - something for a PERSON'],
    rule: '__repr__ unambiguous, __str__ readable',
    whyItMatters: 'the debugger uses __repr__ while a printed value uses __str__' },
  { group: 'comparison', methods: ['__eq__', '__lt__', 'and the rest'],
    trap: 'defining __eq__ without __hash__ makes the object UNHASHABLE',
    symptom: 'such a class suddenly cannot go in a set' },
  { group: 'arithmetic', methods: ['__add__', '__mul__', 'and so on'],
    designQuestion: 'does + on your type mean the same thing it means on the types people already know' },
  { group: 'containers', methods: ['__len__', '__getitem__', '__contains__', '__iter__'],
    payoff: 'defining the last three together makes your object work in a for loop and an in check for free' },
  { group: 'context management', methods: ['__enter__', '__exit__'],
    gain: 'how an object becomes usable in a with block, and how one object guarantees anothers cleanup' },
];

The rules for using them, and the three ways to avoid them

Four rules, each of which exists because breaking it produces something confusing. Never call a dunder method directly. Write len(x), not x.__len__() — the direct call bypasses every layer that might handle it, including subclass overrides and library conventions. Never invent your own dunder names. The double-underscore namespace belongs to the language; a method called __total__ that you define yourself is something nobody else will call, and it invites the assumption that it is part of a protocol it is not. Do not confuse __str__ with __repr__ in logs. A log line is read by a person and often parsed by a machine, so a representation that is readable but ambiguous — "User Bob" rather than User(id=4, name='Bob') — is the wrong choice for anything structured. And keep the operator's meaning honest. If __add__ on your type concatenates two things of different units, every future reader is misled, and the fix is a named method: scale_by() rather than __mul__.

Then three cases where you should not write them, which is the more useful half of the guidance. When a function would do. A dunder method is a public interface that every caller depends on; a function is one call site. When a dataclass or a named tuple would do. If the type is data with no invariants, a dataclass gives you construction, representation, equality and the whole dunder surface for a fraction of the code, and generated correctly — which is the fastest way to stop hand-writing __repr__ and getting it subtly wrong. When the operator does not mean what it means elsewhere. Python's operators carry arithmetic and sequence semantics; a __add__ that means "and also" or "send a message" is a clever use of a syntax whose entire value is that everyone reads it the same way. The cost of that cleverness is paid by every future reader, and the benefit accrues only to the author. And the one thing worth doing regardless: write a class's dunder methods by running them. Print the object, put it in a set, sort it, use it in a with block — the failures are almost always found in three minutes of interaction rather than by reading the code, which is the testing lesson from chapter three appearing again in a different context.

/* Four rules, each because breaking it produces something confusing. */
const RULES = [
  { r: 'never call a dunder method directly', write: 'len(x)', notThis: 'x.__len__()',
    why: 'the direct call bypasses every layer that might handle it, including subclass overrides and library conventions' },
  { r: 'never invent your own dunder names', why: 'the double-underscore namespace belongs to the language',
    symptom: 'a method called __total__ that you define is something nobody else will call, and it invites the assumption that it is part of a protocol it is not' },
  { r: 'do not confuse __str__ with __repr__ in logs',
    why: 'a log line is read by a person and often parsed by a machine',
    wrong: 'User Bob', right: 'User(id=4, name=Bob)',
    rule2: 'anything structured wants the unambiguous one' },
  { r: "keep the operator's meaning honest",
    test: 'if __add__ concatenates two things of different units, every future reader is misled',
    fix: 'a named method - scale_by rather than __mul__' },
];

/* Three cases where you should not write them. */
const AVOID = [
  { when: 'a function would do',
    reason: 'a dunder method is a public interface every caller depends on; a function is one call site' },
  { when: 'a dataclass or a named tuple would do',
    condition: 'the type is data with no invariants',
    gain: 'construction, representation, equality and the whole dunder surface for a fraction of the code, generated correctly',
    payoff: 'the fastest way to stop hand-writing __repr__ and getting it subtly wrong' },
  { when: "the operator does not mean what it means elsewhere",
    detail: 'Python operators carry arithmetic and sequence semantics',
    badUse: 'a __add__ that means and also, or send a message',
    why: 'the entire value of that syntax is that everyone reads it the same way',
    whoPays: 'every future reader pays; only the author benefits' },
];
const REGARDLESS = 'write a class dunder methods by RUNNING them - print the object, put it in a set, sort it, use it in a with block';
const WHY_REGARDLESS = 'the failures are almost always found in three minutes of interaction rather than by reading the code - the testing lesson from chapter three in a different context';

Dunder methods make Money printable, addable and comparable with plain operators instead of method calls.

5.4 Modelling with UML — the engineer’s sketchbook

UML class diagrams sketch a design on paper before code exists, showing classes, their attributes and methods, and the relationships between them. Different arrow styles represent inheritance, composition, and association. Drawing the diagram first clarifies interviews, code reviews, and your own planning at almost no cost.

UML class diagrams let you draw the structure before writing code. Core notation:

+----------------------+
|        Animal        |
+----------------------+
| -name: str           |     - private   (hidden)
+----------------------+
| +speak() -> str      |     + public    (interface)
+----------------------+
         ^
         |   (inheritance: hollow arrow to parent)
+------------+  +------------+
|    Dog     |  |    Cat     |
+------------+  +------------+
| +speak()   |  | +speak()   |
+------------+  +------------+

What UML is for, and the notation that actually gets used

UML — the Unified Modelling Language — started as a way to specify systems before building them, and its useful survivors are much narrower. What a diagram is genuinely good for is making a design argument visible so it can be criticised. The value is not the notation; it is that a class diagram forces you to answer questions that prose lets you skip: what data does this thing hold, which of those are other things rather than primitives, what can it do, and what is allowed to substitute for what. Those four questions are the ones that surface design mistakes before three hundred lines of code exist. And the second real use is communication across a boundary — a diagram is language-independent in a way prose is not, which makes it the right artefact when you need a backend developer and a frontend developer to agree on a shape.

Then the notation that actually gets used, and the honest statement that most of UML is not. Class diagrams — three compartments: name, attributes, methods. Visibility markers — + public, − private, # protected, ~ package-private. Relationships, four kinds. Association — "knows about", drawn as a plain line with optional multiplicities at each end. Inheritance — "is a", drawn as a solid line with a hollow triangle arrowhead pointing at the parent. Composition — "owns, and the owner defines its lifetime", drawn as a filled diamond at the whole end. Aggregation — "has, but the parts live independently", drawn as a hollow diamond. The distinction between composition and aggregation is the one worth being able to state precisely, because it is a lifetime question: if deleting the parent should make the child unreachable, it is composition; if the child can be shared and outlive the parent, it is aggregation. Beyond that: sequence diagrams for how objects interact over time, with vertical lifelines and arrows, which are excellent for the hard cases — a login flow, a payment, anything with retries — and the two that are mostly decoration — state machine diagrams and package diagrams — which earn their place only in specific circumstances and are usually a sign that a diagram was drawn because it was expected rather than because it answered a question. The rule of thumb: draw the diagram when a disagreement is likely, not to demonstrate you know the notation.

/* What UML is for. */
const PURPOSE = [
  { use: 'making a design argument VISIBLE so it can be criticised',
    notTheValue: 'the notation',
    isTheValue: 'a class diagram forces you to answer questions prose lets you skip',
    theQuestions: ['what data does this thing hold',
      'which of those are other things rather than primitives',
      'what can it do',
      'what is allowed to substitute for what'],
    payoff: 'the four questions that surface design mistakes before three hundred lines of code exist' },
  { use: 'communication across a boundary',
    why: 'a diagram is language-independent in a way prose is not',
    forWhom: 'a backend developer and a frontend developer agreeing on a shape' },
];

/* The notation that actually gets used. */
const NOTATION = {
  classDiagrams: 'three compartments - name, attributes, methods',
  visibility: { '+': 'public', '-': 'private', '#': 'protected', '~': 'package-private' },
  relationships: [
    { r: 'association', means: 'knows about',
      drawn: 'a plain line with optional multiplicities at each end' },
    { r: 'inheritance', means: 'is a',
      drawn: 'a solid line with a hollow triangle arrowhead pointing at the parent' },
    { r: 'composition', means: 'owns, and the owner defines its lifetime',
      drawn: 'a filled diamond at the whole end' },
    { r: 'aggregation', means: 'has, but the parts live independently',
      drawn: 'a hollow diamond' },
  ],
  compositionVsAggregation: {
    worthBeingPreciseAbout: true,
    because: 'it is a LIFETIME question',
    composition: 'if deleting the parent should make the child unreachable',
    aggregation: 'the child can be shared and outlive the parent' },
  sequenceDiagrams: { for: 'how objects interact over time', marks: 'vertical lifelines and arrows',
    excellentFor: ['a login flow', 'a payment', 'anything with retries'] },
  mostlyDecoration: ['state machine diagrams', 'package diagrams'],
  whyTheyAreDecoration: 'they earn their place only in specific circumstances',
    symptom: 'usually a sign that a diagram was drawn because it was expected rather than because it answered a question',
  ruleOfThumb: 'draw the diagram when a disagreement is likely, not to demonstrate you know the notation',
};

Using it without ceremony, and the mistakes it catches

Four rules for using a diagram in practice. One class per diagram at medium size. Not one class per box on a wall — a diagram of thirty boxes is a picture nobody reads, and the exercise it was supposed to prompt happens at five. Show the relationships, not the methods. The relationships are the part that generates the discussion; a diagram listing twelve method signatures is a code dump with worse readability. Draw it after the code, once, when the design has settled — or draw it first, badly, for five minutes, as a thinking tool. Both work. Do not maintain it. A diagram that must be updated with the code always lags, and a stale diagram is worse than none because it is trusted; an automatically-generated one from the code has the opposite problem, that it shows structure without showing intent. Keep it as a design document and let it go stale deliberately.

Then the mistakes it catches, which is the argument for having it at all. Cyclic dependencies — A knows B and B knows A — which no single class can reveal and which makes every unit of code hard to test in isolation. Too many relationships to one class. One class drawn with fifteen arrows to fifteen others is a class that has several responsibilities, and the diagram says so in a way a file listing does not. Relationships you did not intend. The most valuable outcome: drawing the arrows reveals an association you wrote by accident, usually because two classes both reached for a shared third one. The wrong direction of a relationship. If your class holds a reference to the thing that owns it, you have inverted the dependency and will get a lifecycle bug you cannot see otherwise. And an inheritance tree drawn honestly. If the diagram shows four levels and you cannot name what each level adds, that hierarchy is not earning its depth — which is exactly the point the next chapter makes about preferring composition, now visible instead of argued. The summary is short enough to be worth stating as a rule: draw the boxes and the arrows, ask one question — is every arrow something I chose deliberately? If yes, the design is defensible. If any arrow makes you hesitate, that is the conversation to have before writing the code.

/* Four rules for practice. */
const RULES = [
  { r: 'one class per diagram at medium size',
    notThis: 'one class per box on a wall',
    why: 'a diagram of thirty boxes is a picture nobody reads, and the exercise happens at five' },
  { r: 'show the relationships, not the methods',
    why: 'relationships are the part that generates the discussion',
    bad: 'a diagram listing twelve method signatures is a code dump with worse readability' },
  { r: 'draw it after the code, once, when the design has settled - or draw it first, badly, for five minutes as a thinking tool',
    note: 'both work' },
  { r: 'do not maintain it',
    failure1: 'a diagram that must be updated with the code always lags',
    whyWorse: 'a stale diagram is worse than none because it is trusted',
    failure2: 'an automatically generated one shows structure without showing intent',
    practice: 'keep it as a design document and let it go stale deliberately' },
];

/* What it catches - the argument for having it. */
const CATCHES = [
  { c: 'cyclic dependencies', example: 'A knows B and B knows A',
    whyHidden: 'no single class can reveal it',
    cost: 'makes every unit of code hard to test in isolation' },
  { c: 'too many relationships to one class', evidence: 'one class drawn with fifteen arrows to fifteen others',
    meaning: 'a class with several responsibilities',
    whyVisible: 'the diagram says so in a way a file listing does not' },
  { c: 'relationships you did not intend',
    whyMostValuable: true,
    mechanism: 'drawing the arrows reveals an association written by accident',
    usualCause: 'two classes both reached for a shared third one' },
  { c: 'the wrong direction of a relationship',
    symptom: 'your class holds a reference to the thing that owns it',
    consequence: 'an inverted dependency producing a lifecycle bug invisible otherwise' },
  { c: 'an inheritance tree drawn honestly',
    test: 'if the diagram shows four levels and you cannot name what each level adds, the hierarchy is not earning its depth',
