const SUMMARY_RULE = 'draw the boxes and the arrows, ask one question - is every arrow something I chose deliberately? yes means defensible; any arrow that makes you hesitate is the conversation to have before writing the code';

An ASCII UML class diagram: private fields with a minus, public methods with a plus, and a hollow arrow meaning inheritance.

Relationships: inheritance (hollow triangle arrow, "is-a"), association (plain line, "has-a/uses"). You’ll redraw these diagrams constantly in senior courses and on whiteboards in interviews.

5.5 Hands-on: a tiny bank system

This hands-on section builds a tiny bank system that ties the chapter’s concepts together. Encapsulation matters most here: the balance stays private behind methods, and deposits and withdrawals expose a clean, validated interface. Building it teaches how the four pillars feel when applied to real code.

class BankAccount:
    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0):
        self.owner = owner
        self._balance = balance          # underscore = "internal, don't touch"

    def deposit(self, amount):
        if amount <= 0:                  # guard against negative deposits
            raise ValueError("Deposit must be positive")
        self._balance += amount

    def withdraw(self, amount):
        if amount > self._balance:
            raise ValueError("Insufficient funds")
        self._balance -= amount

    def get_balance(self):
        return self._balance             # read through a method, don't poke field

acc = BankAccount("Ada", 100)
acc.deposit(50)
acc.withdraw(30)
print(acc.owner, acc.get_balance())      # Ada 120

Encapsulation as a mechanism, not a naming convention

Encapsulation is not the underscore. The underscore is a signal; encapsulation is the property that there is exactly one way to change a value, and that way validates. Consider what happens without it. account.balance = -500 is one assignment and it succeeds, and now the account violates the invariant it was supposed to guarantee; the class was described as protecting the balance, and it did not, because nothing stopped the assignment. The reason a class helps is that it can put the check in one place and make the raw field unreachable by convention — and the correctness of the whole design depends on nothing outside the class reaching past it. This is worth understanding precisely because the mechanism is social as much as technical: Python will not stop you, and what makes the class correct is that every other piece of code in the codebase chooses the method. The class provides the only legitimate path; the codebase's discipline is what makes it the only path taken.

Then the shape of a well-encapsulated class, and each element has a reason. Validation at the boundary where the value enters. Not in the constructor only — in every method that changes the value, because a class with a validated constructor and an unvalidated setter has an invariant that is one call away from being false. Reject rather than silently correct. A deposit of −50 that quietly becomes 0 hides a bug in the caller; a deposit of −50 that raises points at it. The general principle is that an error the caller can fix should be reported rather than absorbed, because a silently corrected bad value becomes a wrong value three steps later. No public access to the raw field. A get_balance() that returns a copy of a mutable value, rather than a direct reference to it, so the caller cannot mutate the interior without going through the class — and if the value is immutable, the getter can return it directly. Read-only accessors. If only one operation should change the value, expose that operation and a read method, and make everything else private. And a name that says what the method guarantees: withdraw(amount) that raises on insufficient funds is a better name than debit(amount) that returns a boolean, because the second makes the caller handle a case the class has already decided.

/* Encapsulation is not the underscore. */
const WHAT_IT_IS = {
  notThis: 'the underscore - that is a signal',
  actually: 'the property that there is EXACTLY ONE WAY to change a value, and that way validates',
  withoutIt: 'account.balance = -500 is one assignment, it succeeds, and the invariant is now violated',
  irony: 'the class was described as protecting the balance and did not, because nothing stopped the assignment',
  mechanism: 'the class puts the check in one place and makes the raw field unreachable by convention',
  crucialDetail: 'the mechanism is social as much as technical - PYTHON WILL NOT STOP YOU',
  whatMakesItCorrect: 'every other piece of code in the codebase chooses the method',
  restated: 'the class provides the only legitimate path; the codebase discipline makes it the only path taken',
};

/* The shape of a well-encapsulated class. */
const SHAPE = [
  { element: 'validation where the value ENTERS',
    notJustTheConstructor: 'every method that changes the value',
    why: 'a validated constructor with an unvalidated setter has an invariant one call away from being false' },
  { element: 'reject rather than silently correct',
    example: 'a deposit of -50 that quietly becomes 0 hides a bug in the caller; one that raises points at it',
    principle: 'an error the caller can fix should be reported rather than absorbed',
    why: 'a silently corrected bad value becomes a wrong value three steps later' },
  { element: 'no public access to the raw field',
    how: 'get_balance() returns a COPY of a mutable value rather than a reference to it',
    why: 'so the caller cannot mutate the interior without going through the class',
    exception: 'if the value is immutable, the getter can return it directly' },
  { element: 'read-only accessors',
    rule: 'if only one operation should change the value, expose that operation plus a read method',
    everythingElse: 'private' },
  { element: 'names that say what the method guarantees',
    good: 'withdraw(amount) that raises on insufficient funds',
    worse: 'debit(amount) that returns a boolean',
    why: 'the second makes the caller handle a case the class has already decided' },
];

Where encapsulation goes wrong, and the test that catches it

Three failure modes, each of which feels reasonable at the time. The getter-setter class. Every field private, a getter and a setter for each, and every setter assigns with no validation — which is the worst of both worlds: the ceremony of encapsulation with none of the safety, and now a caller has no way to tell whether setBalance checks anything. If a class has a setter that only assigns, delete it; a public attribute is more honest, because a public attribute cannot be mistaken for a validated one. Validation in the caller. The check lives where the data is entered rather than where the value is owned, so the second caller — a script, an API handler, a test — does not get it. This is the failure that produces "but the check is there" bug reports, and the fix is always the same: move the check to the class that owns the value, so there is one place rather than several that must all remember. Returning internals. A method returning self._items hands the caller a live reference, and the caller appends to it — so the class's invariant is now bypassable through its own getter, and the bug looks like a mysterious change somewhere else. The fix is a copy, or an iterator, or making the field a frozen structure.

Then the test that catches all three, and it is a single question: can you name every way the value can change, and is that list short enough to check? If the answer is "the setter, the deposit method, and the periodic recalculation job", you have an invariant with three doors and you can test each. If the answer involves a list comprehension over the internals, an attribute assignment somewhere in a different package, or a serialiser that can reconstruct the object from a dictionary, you do not have encapsulation at all — you have a public field with extra steps, and no test can prove otherwise because there is no bounded set of entry points to check. The second test is equally short and catches the remaining cases: write the test that tries to break the invariant from outside, and confirm it cannot. A class whose invariant survives an attempt to violate it from every accessible angle is encapsulated; one where the test cannot even be written has told you the design is not finished.

/* Three failure modes, each reasonable at the time. */
const FAILURES = [
  { f: 'the getter-setter class',
    shape: 'every field private, a getter and setter for each, every setter assigning with no validation',
    verdict: 'the worst of both worlds - the ceremony of encapsulation with none of the safety',
    why: 'a caller has no way to tell whether setBalance checks anything',
    fix: 'if a setter only assigns, delete it - a public attribute is more honest because it cannot be mistaken for a validated one' },
  { f: 'validation in the caller',
    where: 'the check lives where data is entered rather than where the value is owned',
    symptom: 'the second caller - a script, an API handler, a test - does not get it',
    reports: 'this produces the but-the-check-is-there bug report',
    fix: 'move the check to the class that owns the value, so there is one place rather than several that must all remember' },
  { f: 'returning internals',
    mechanism: 'a method returning self._items hands the caller a live reference',
    consequence: 'the caller appends to it, so the invariant is bypassable through the class own getter',
    symptom: 'looks like a mysterious change somewhere else',
    fixes: ['return a copy', 'return an iterator', 'make the field a frozen structure'] },
];

/* Two tests that catch all three. */
const TESTS = [
  { t: 'can you name every way the value can change, and is that list short enough to check',
    good: 'the setter, the deposit method and the periodic recalculation job - three doors, each testable',
    bad: 'a list comprehension over the internals, an attribute assignment in another package, a serialiser that reconstructs the object from a dict',
    verdictWhenBad: 'you do not have encapsulation at all - a public field with extra steps',
    why: 'no test can prove otherwise because there is no bounded set of entry points to check' },
  { t: 'write the test that tries to break the invariant from outside, and confirm it cannot',
    reads: 'a class whose invariant survives an attempt to violate it from every accessible angle is encapsulated',
    unreadable: 'one where the test cannot even be written has told you the design is not finished' },
];

Encapsulation in action: the underscore-prefixed balance is protected by deposit, withdraw and get_balance methods, plus validation.

5.6 dataclasses, abstract classes and composition

This topic covers three everyday design tools. Dataclasses remove boilerplate by auto-generating init, repr, and comparison methods from the field annotations. Abstract base classes define contracts that subclasses must implement, and composition wires flexible systems by giving objects other objects rather than inheriting behaviour.

Three everyday hammer-and-nails of Python OOP: @dataclass to write plain data holders without boilerplate, abc to design clean interfaces, and composition to build flexible systems.

# dataclass: free __init__, __repr__, == And more, from ONE line
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Money:
    amount: float
    currency: str = "USD"      # field with a default

a = Money(19.99)               # default currency kicks in
b = Money(19.99, "USD")
print(a)                       # Money(amount=19.99, currency='USD')
print(a == b)                  # True  (value equality, not identity!)
print(a.amount)

One @dataclass line buys __init__, __repr__ and value equality, and a field with a default keeps call sites short.

# Abstract base class: define a contract, force implementations
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Exporter(ABC):            # ABC = abstract contract, no direct instantiation
    @abstractmethod
    def export(self, data) -> str:
        """Return data formatted for one format."""
        pass                            # subclasses MUST implement this

class JsonExporter(Exporter):   # concrete implementation of the contract
    def export(self, data) -> str:
        return json.dumps(data)

class CsvExporter(Exporter):
    def export(self, data) -> str:
        return ",".join(str(x) for row in data for x in row)

An abstract base class forces every exporter to implement export, so callers can rely on the contract.

# Composition over inheritance: a Report HAS an exporter
class Report:
    def __init__(self, rows, exporter: Exporter):
        self.rows = rows
        self.exporter = exporter        # injected ("dependency injection")

    def generate(self) -> str:
        return self.exporter.export(self.rows)

# Same Report, two behaviours, zero inheritance...
print(Report([[1, 2], [3, 4]], JsonExporter()).generate())
print(Report([["a", "b"]], CsvExporter()).generate())
# ...and adding MarkdownExporter later changes NOTHING here.

The Report has an injected exporter, so swapping formats changes nothing inside Report — the same class, different behaviour.

This is the dependency-inversion idea (Ch. 19 SOLID) in its simplest, most useful form: make classes depend on an interface you inject, not on a concrete implementation they construct. It’s what makes code testable with fakes (Ch. 16).

Choosing between the three, and the test that settles it

Three ways to get a shared shape, and the reason the choice is consequential is that it decides what the compiler will let you get wrong later. A dataclass is generated behaviour. The declaration says what the fields are and the language supplies the constructor, the representation, the equality and the string form — which means a dataclass is the right answer when the thing is its data. A record of a transaction, a configuration value, a point: the fields are the entire meaning, nothing needs to be enforced, and generated code is strictly better than hand-written code because it cannot drift. A plain class with __init__ is explicit behaviour with a data shape. You write the initialisation because there is something to say about it — a derived field computed once, a validation that rejects an invalid combination, a normalisation of a value that arrived in the wrong form. This is the right answer when the invariant matters, because the invariant is in the constructor where every path through it goes. An abstract base class is enforced behaviour. It exists to declare that subclasses must provide something and to let a caller depend on that declaration rather than on a concrete class; its value is not the reuse but the substitutability, and its cost is real: every subclass must satisfy the contract whether or not it needs the shared behaviour. So the test, and it is worth memorising because it decides most cases. If the subclass only needs to fill in a name, you wanted an abstract method — a base class. If the subclass needs to hold different state but obey the same rules, you wanted a base class with the rules in it. If the subclass is just a convenient initialisation of the same fields, you wanted composition or nothing at all. And then composition, which is the answer that the "is-a" test is designed to make you consider. A dataclass that holds an object rather than extending it — a SavingsAccount with an Account field, or better, with an InterestStrategy field — changes nothing about what you can do and gains two things: the held object can be swapped, so one class serves several behaviours; and the composed class has no obligation to pretend it is the composed type, so it cannot be used where the composed type's invariants are assumed. That last point is the important one and it is the reason the design chapter prefers composition: inheritance couples two things that have no reason to change together, because a change to the base class silently changes every subclass, including the one somebody else wrote.

/* The three, and what each is for. */const THREE = [  { k: 'a DATACLASS',    is: 'GENERATED BEHAVIOUR',    supplies: ['the CONSTRUCTOR', 'the REPRESENTATION', 'EQUALITY', 'the STRING FORM'],    rightWhen: 'the thing IS ITS DATA',    examples: ['a RECORD of a transaction', 'a CONFIGURATION VALUE', 'a point'],    whyBetter: 'because GENERATED CODE CANNOT DRIFT' },  { k: 'a PLAIN CLASS with a constructor',    is: 'EXPLICIT BEHAVIOUR with a data shape',    rightWhen: 'there is SOMETHING TO SAY about initialisation',    instances: ['a DERIVED FIELD computed once',      'a VALIDATION that rejects an invalid combination',      'a NORMALISATION of a value that ARRIVED IN THE WRONG FORM'],    why: 'because the INVARIANT IS IN THE CONSTRUCTOR where EVERY PATH THROUGH IT GOES' },  { k: 'an ABSTRACT BASE CLASS',    is: 'ENFORCED BEHAVIOUR',    existsTo: ['DECLARE that subclasses must PROVIDE something',      'let a CALLER DEPEND on that declaration rather than on a CONCRETE CLASS'],    value: 'not the REUSE but the SUBSTITUTABILITY',    cost: 'EVERY SUBCLASS MUST SATISFY THE CONTRACT whether or not it needs the shared behaviour' },];/* The test. */const TEST = [  { if: 'the subclass ONLY NEEDS TO FILL IN A NAME', then: 'you wanted an ABSTRACT METHOD - a BASE CLASS' },  { if: 'the subclass needs to HOLD DIFFERENT STATE but OBEY THE SAME RULES',    then: 'you wanted a BASE CLASS with THE RULES IN IT' },  { if: 'the subclass is just a CONVENIENT INITIALISATION of the same fields',    then: 'you wanted COMPOSITION or NOTHING AT ALL' },];/* Composition. */const COMPOSITION = {  is: 'a DATACLASS THAT HOLDS AN OBJECT rather than extending it',  example: 'a savings account with an interest strategy FIELD',  changes: 'NOTHING about what you can do',  gains: ['the HELD OBJECT CAN BE SWAPPED, so ONE CLASS serves SEVERAL behaviours',    'the COMPOSED CLASS has NO OBLIGATION TO PRETEND IT IS the composed type'],  whyThatLastMatters: 'so it CANNOT BE USED where the composed types INVARIANTS ARE ASSUMED',  is: 'the reason the design chapter PREFERS COMPOSITION',  coupling: 'INHERITANCE COUPLES TWO THINGS THAT HAVE NO REASON TO CHANGE TOGETHER',  because: 'a CHANGE TO THE BASE CLASS SILENTLY CHANGES EVERY SUBCLASS, including the one SOMEBODY ELSE WROTE',};

  2. Draw the UML diagram for your bank system first, then code it.
