6 · Git & Version Control

Git is the distributed version control system used by nearly every software team to track, share, and review code. You record snapshots of your work as commits, share them with remotes, and review changes through branches and pull requests. Fluency in the basic workflow pays off every single day of your career.

6.1 The mental model6.2 Your first repository6.3 Travel through history safely6.4 Branches: parallel universes6.5 GitHub: collaboration workflow (Pull Requests)6.6 Don’t commit junk: .gitignore6.7 Fixing mistakes: reset, reflog, bisect & stash

Version control records every version of your files, lets you branch ideas safely, and is how teams of any size collaborate. Git is the industry standard; GitHub is the most used hosting service. You will use it every single day as an engineer.

6.1 The mental model

Git is best understood as a handful of ideas: a repository holds history, a commit is a saved snapshot, staging selects changes, a branch is a moving pointer, and a remote is a shared copy. Holding this model in mind makes every Git command intuitive, because each one manipulates those few pieces.

  • Repository (repo) — a project folder versioned by Git (a hidden .git folder holds all history).
  • Commit — a saved snapshot of your whole project at a moment, with a message. Like a save-point.
  • Working tree — the files you’re editing now (uncommitted changes).
  • Stage (index) — the "box" you put chosen changes into before committing.
  • Branch — an independent line of work. Main/master is the default; feature branches power teamwork.
  • Remote — a copy elsewhere (e.g. GitHub) you push to and pull from.
# Lifecycle — the one flow you'll repeat forever:
git status                        # what's different? (use it constantly)
git add file.py                   # 1) stage the file (or: git add . whole folder)
git commit -m "Add fee calculation"   # 2) snapshot it with a message
git push origin main              # 3) send to remote
git pull                          # 4) bring remote changes back

What Git actually stores, and why that explains all its behaviour

Most confusion about Git dissolves once you know what it stores. Git stores a series of snapshots. Not a diff between two versions — a complete copy of every file at each commit. That sounds wasteful and is enormously important: because each commit is complete, checking out any version is trivial, and a diff between any two commits is a computation rather than a stored artefact. Git stores objects in a content-addressed store. Every file's content is hashed, and the hash is its name — so identical content is stored once no matter how many commits contain it, and a file whose content did not change is literally the same object in the next commit. This is why Git is fast, why repositories stay small even with a long history, and why the hash appears in every commit id. Commits point at parents. Each commit records the hashes of its own content, its metadata, and its parent commits — so the history is a directed acyclic graph, and a branch is not a copy of anything, it is a movable pointer to a commit. A commit has a tree of blobs. One commit may reference many trees if you record deletes and renames that way, but normally a commit has one tree, and a tree maps paths to blobs.

Then the three places you work, and they are what make Git feel unusual. The working tree — the files you edit. The staging area (index) — a snapshot you have selected but not yet committed, and this is the part almost nobody understands and everybody gets wrong. The repository — committed history. Staging is not automatic: when you git add a file, Git records that file's current content in the index, so if you edit it again and commit, only the staged version is committed and your newer edit remains unstaged. This is not a quirk, it is what makes partial commits possible — staging three of the eight files you changed is a deliberate act, and the ability to do it is why Git users can keep a commit to one concern. The mental model that makes the whole thing stick: commit is not "save my files", it is "record the snapshot in the index", and everything else follows from that sentence.

/* What Git stores. */
const WHAT = [
  { f: 'snapshots', detail: 'a complete copy of every file at each commit, NOT a diff',
    soundsWasteful: true,
    whyImportant: 'each commit is complete, so checking out any version is trivial',
    consequence: 'a diff between any two commits is a COMPUTATION rather than a stored artefact' },
  { f: 'a content-addressed store', detail: 'every files content is hashed and the hash is its name',
    effects: ['identical content is stored once no matter how many commits contain it',
      'a file whose content did not change is literally the same object in the next commit'],
    explains: ['why Git is fast', 'why repositories stay small with a long history',
      'why the hash appears in every commit id'] },
  { f: 'commits point at parents',
    detail: 'each commit records hashes of its content, its metadata and its parent commits',
    structure: 'a directed acyclic graph',
    branch: 'not a copy of anything - a MOVABLE POINTER to a commit' },
  { f: 'a commit has a tree of blobs', detail: 'the tree maps paths to blobs',
    note: 'normally one tree per commit; a commit may reference many if you record deletes and renames that way' },
];

/* The three places you work. */
const THREE_PLACES = [
  { p: 'the working tree', is: 'the files you edit' },
  { p: 'the staging area (index)', is: 'a snapshot you have selected but not yet committed',
    note: 'the part almost nobody understands and everybody gets wrong' },
  { p: 'the repository', is: 'committed history' },
];
const STAGING_MECHANICS = {
  notAutomatic: 'when you git add a file, Git records THAT FILES CURRENT CONTENT in the index',
  consequence: 'edit it again and commit - only the staged version is committed, and the newer edit remains unstaged',
  notAQuirk: 'this is what makes partial commits possible',
  use: 'staging three of the eight files you changed is a deliberate act',
  whyItMatters: 'the ability to do it is why Git users can keep a commit to one concern',
  theModel: 'commit is not save my files - it is RECORD THE SNAPSHOT IN THE INDEX',
  everythingElse: 'everything else follows from that sentence',
};

Uncommitted versus untracked, and the three states every file can be in

The vocabulary matters because git status uses it precisely and the distinctions drive the commands. A file is untracked when Git has never seen it: it exists on disk and Git does not know it exists at all. It is modified when it is tracked, its content differs from the last commit, and the difference is not staged. It is staged when the current content is recorded in the index and differs from HEAD. It is committed when it matches HEAD. These are four states and a file can be in two of them at once — staged and modified being the one that confuses people, and it is entirely normal: you staged a version, then edited again, so the index holds one version and your disk holds another. git diff shows the working tree against the index; git diff --staged shows the index against HEAD; and git status shows which is which. Learning to read those three outputs is worth more than memorising commands, because almost every "Git did the wrong thing" report is really "I did not know which of the two diffs I was looking at".

Then HEAD and the branch model, which is one pointer and not a copy. HEAD is a pointer to the commit you have checked out, and the branch you are on is itself a pointer. Checking out a branch moves HEAD to point at that branch, so HEAD is one level of indirection above wherever you actually are — which is why detached HEAD exists and why it is safe: you are just pointed at a commit rather than at a name. Almost everything you have been taught about Git's model is wrong in one specific way: branches are not containers and merging does not combine files. Merging walks both histories to find their common ancestor, applies the changes on each side since that point, and produces a commit with two parents. That is why merges can conflict even when no file was edited by both — if two branches changed nearby lines, Git cannot decide, and the conflict markers are Git asking you to decide. And tags and branches differ only in intent. A branch moves; a tag is meant to stay, and is how you mark a release. The underlying mechanism is identical, which is why you can check out a tag to look at old code and even create a branch from one.

/* The four states, and the one that confuses people. */
const STATES = [
  { s: 'untracked', means: 'Git has never seen it - it exists on disk and Git does not know it exists' },
  { s: 'modified', means: 'tracked, content differs from the last commit, difference NOT staged' },
  { s: 'staged', means: 'the current content is in the index and differs from HEAD' },
  { s: 'committed', means: 'matches HEAD' },
];
const TWO_AT_ONCE = {
  which: 'staged AND modified',
  whyNormal: 'you staged a version, then edited again',
  state: 'the index holds one version and your disk holds another',
  theThreeOutputs: ['git diff - the working tree against the index',
    'git diff --staged - the index against HEAD',
    'git status - which is which'],
  whyWorthLearning: 'almost every Git-did-the-wrong-thing report is really I-did-not-know-which-diff-I-was-looking-at',
};

/* HEAD and the branch model. */
const HEAD = {
  is: 'a pointer to the commit you have checked out',
  indirection: 'the branch you are on is itself a pointer, so HEAD is one level above wherever you actually are',
  whyDetachedHeadIsSafe: 'you are pointed at a commit rather than at a name',
  theWrongThingAlmostEverythingTeaches: 'branches are not containers and merging does not combine files',
  whatMergingActuallyDoes: ['walk both histories to find their common ancestor',
    'apply the changes on each side since that point',
    'produce a commit with two parents'],
  whyConflictsHappenWithoutOverlap: 'if two branches changed nearby lines, Git cannot decide',
  conflictMarkersAre: 'Git asking you to decide',
  tagsVsBranches: { differOnlyInIntent: true, branch: 'moves', tag: 'meant to stay - how you mark a release',
    consequence: 'you can check out a tag to look at old code and create a branch from one' },
};

The everyday loop: status, add, commit, push, pull. Run status constantly; it narrates everything Git is doing.

6.2 Your first repository

This topic turns an ordinary folder into a versioned repository. You run git init, set your name and email with git config, add files with git add, and record them with git commit, always with a clear message. Committing early and often creates a history you can revisit and share.

git init                          # turn the current folder into a repo
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email you@example.com

# ... add your first file, then:
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit"
git status                        # should show "nothing to commit, working tree clean"

Initialises a repo, sets your Git identity once, then makes the first commit; status confirms a clean tree.

The setup that prevents the two errors everybody hits

Two configuration items, set once, that between them prevent the most common first-day problems. Your name and email. Every commit records who made it, and without these set, a commit either fails outright or — far more often — records your machine's default identity, which is why a project ends up with commits attributed to a user nobody recognises. The command sets it globally, and the habit is to check it once per machine rather than per repository, because the failure is invisible until somebody asks why the history is wrong. Your default branch name. Newer Git asks at init time; older versions assume master. Either is fine, but the point is to know what yours is, because every command that says "go to the default branch" depends on it. And a third item worth adding on day one, which nobody mentions and everybody needs: your editor. Git opens an editor for commit messages and for merge conflicts, and if you have not configured one it launches vi, in which the first thing you must do is press i, and this single fact accounts for a large fraction of beginner confusion with a tool that appears frozen.

Then the sequence itself, and what each step actually does. Initialise. This creates the .git directory — the entire repository — and does not touch your files. Check status. Before the first add, this tells you what Git sees, which is the moment to notice something you did not expect: a generated file, a large binary, a folder of dependencies that should never have been committed. Add selectively. Adding everything on the first commit is how a repository acquires a thousand dependency files and a twenty-megabyte database dump, so the practice worth forming is adding by intent — the source files, the readme, the ignore file — and watching status to confirm. Commit with a real message. And then the piece that matters most for everything after this chapter: write the commit message for the person who has to understand this change at 3am, which in practice means yourself in six months. That person needs to know what changed, why, and what would be affected — not what the diff shows, which they can read.

/* Two settings that prevent the most common first-day problems. */
const SETUP = [
  { s: 'your name and email',
    why: 'every commit records who made it',
    withoutIt: 'a commit either fails outright or records your machines default identity',
    symptom: 'a project ends up with commits attributed to a user nobody recognises',
    habit: 'check it once per MACHINE rather than per repository',
    whyThere: 'the failure is invisible until somebody asks why the history is wrong' },
  { s: 'your default branch name',
    detail: 'newer Git asks at init time; older versions assume master',
    stance: 'either is fine, but KNOW what yours is',
    why: 'every command that says go to the default branch depends on it' },
  { s: 'your editor', whyMentioned: 'nobody mentions it and everybody needs it',
    detail: 'Git opens an editor for commit messages and merge conflicts',
    withoutIt: 'it launches vi, where the first thing you must do is press i',
    claim: 'this single fact accounts for a large fraction of beginner confusion with a tool that appears frozen' },
];

/* The sequence, and what each step does. */
const SEQUENCE = [
  { step: 'initialise', does: 'creates the .git directory - the entire repository',
    note: 'does not touch your files' },
  { step: 'check status', when: 'before the first add',
    gain: 'tells you what Git sees',
    theMomentToNotice: 'a generated file, a large binary, a folder of dependencies that should never have been committed' },
  { step: 'add selectively', bad: 'adding everything on the first commit',
    consequence: 'how a repository acquires a thousand dependency files and a twenty-megabyte database dump',
    practice: 'add by intent - the source files, the readme, the ignore file - and watch status to confirm' },
  { step: 'commit with a real message' },
  { step: 'write the message for the person reading at 3am', inPractice: 'yourself in six months',
    theyNeed: ['what changed', 'why', 'what would be affected'],
    notThis: 'what the diff shows, which they can read' },
];

Commit messages as documentation, and the commit that is easy to review

A commit message has a structure that pays for itself, and it is worth knowing that a summary line, a blank line, and a body are three different things. The summary is one line, imperative mood, under about fifty characters, and it must stand alone — because it is what appears in a log listing, in a pull-request title, and in the blame view of the line you are currently looking at, all of which show nothing else. "Fixed bug" fails at all three. "fix: validate email format on signup (#142)" passes: what, where, and which issue. Then the body answers why, in prose, in the past tense, because the code already says what changed and the only thing the code cannot say is the reasoning — what was tried, what constraint forced this approach, what would break it. Wrap at about seventy-two columns, not for aesthetics but because a single long line is unreadable in a review comment and because the tooling that will eventually render it assumes it.

Then what makes a commit reviewable, which is a property of the change rather than the message and matters more. One concern. A commit that fixes a bug and reformats a file cannot be reviewed, because the reviewer must check two unrelated things and the reformatting hides the fix in the noise — this is the practical reason the "do not mix changes" advice exists, and it is why every codebase has a separate formatting commit. One reason to revert it. If reverting the commit would leave the system in a working state, it is one concern; if not, it contains work that belongs together and cannot be split. It builds. A commit that leaves the tests failing is not a state anyone can resume from, so if it must not build, say so explicitly in the message and make it obvious in history. And it is small enough to describe. If the summary line needs the word "and", that is the signal. Finally, the convention that helps in every project: a type prefix. A short prefix — fix:, feat:, refactor:, docs:, test: — makes a fifty-commit branch readable at a glance and lets tooling filter history, and the cost is four characters per commit.

/* The three parts of a commit message. */
const STRUCTURE = [
  { part: 'summary line', constraints: ['imperative mood', 'under about fifty characters', 'must stand alone'],
    whereItAppears: ['git log listing', 'a pull-request title', 'the blame view of the line you are looking at'],
    allShowNothingElse: true,
    bad: 'Fixed bug - fails at all three',
    good: 'fix: validate email format on signup (#142) - passes, because it gives what, where and which issue' },
  { part: 'blank line' },
  { part: 'body', answers: 'why',
    tense: 'past tense',
    why: 'the code already says what changed; the only thing it cannot say is the reasoning',
    shouldCover: ['what was tried', 'what constraint forced this approach', 'what would break it'],
    wrap: 'about seventy-two columns',
    whyWrap: 'not aesthetics - a single long line is unreadable in a review comment, and the tooling that renders it assumes it' },
];

/* What makes a commit reviewable. */
const REVIEWABLE = [
  { p: 'one concern', symptom: 'a commit that fixes a bug and reformats a file cannot be reviewed',
    why: 'the reviewer must check two unrelated things, and the reformatting hides the fix in the noise',
    note: 'the practical reason do-not-mix-changes advice exists, and why every codebase has a separate formatting commit' },
  { p: 'one reason to revert it', test: 'if reverting the commit leaves the system in a working state it is one concern',
    else: 'if not, it contains work that belongs together and cannot be split' },
  { p: 'it builds', symptom: 'a commit that leaves the tests failing is not a state anyone can resume from',
    exception: 'if it must not build, say so explicitly in the message and make it obvious in history' },
  { p: 'it is small enough to describe', signal: 'if the summary line needs the word and, that is the signal' },
  { p: 'a type prefix', examples: ['fix:', 'feat:', 'refactor:', 'docs:', 'test:'],
    gain: 'a fifty-commit branch is readable at a glance and tooling can filter history',
    cost: 'four characters per commit' },
];

Write good commit messages. "Fixed bug" is useless. "fix: validate email format on signup (#142)" tells a colleague (or you, in 6 months) what and why. Use present-tense, imperative style: Add, Fix, Refactor, Update tests.

6.3 Travel through history safely

This topic teaches you to explore and undo past work safely. git log lists history, git diff shows changes, and git show displays a single commit. For undoing, prefer safe additive operations like git revert and git restore over rewriting shared history, since they preserve the record for teammates.

git log --oneline        # compact history
git diff                 # uncommitted changes (what did I edit?)
git diff HEAD            # full diff vs last commit
git show <commit-hash>   # what one commit changed
git checkout <hash> -- file.py   # restore one file from history
git revert <hash>        # add a NEW commit that undoes an old one (team-safe)

Reads history with log and diff, plus branch-safe undos with show, checkout and revert.

Reading history, and what each log flag is actually for

Four commands answer almost every question about the past, and it is worth knowing what each one is for rather than learning the flags. git log is the history itself, and the default view is one commit per entry with the hash, author, date and message. The flags worth knowing: --oneline for a compact list, -p to add the diff of each commit, --stat for the diff summary of which files changed, --graph for the branch structure drawn as ASCII art — which is the fastest way to understand a tangled merge history — and --author or --since to narrow. git show is for one specific commit, and it is strictly more useful than log -p for a single one because it defaults to showing the diff with surrounding context. git diff is for uncommitted changes, and the two invocations people need are the plain one (working tree against the index) and --staged (index against HEAD) — and knowing which one you are looking at is the difference between understanding what you are about to commit and being surprised by it. git blame answers "when and why did this line become like this", one line at a time, and for a line that looks wrong it is the fastest route to the discussion that explains it.

Then the safe undos, and the distinction the whole area turns on. git restore (or checkout, in older Git) discards uncommitted changes to a file — it is safe precisely because those changes are not in history, so nothing is lost that was ever shared. git revert creates a new commit that undoes an old one; history is preserved and the reversal is recorded, which is why it is the correct undo on any branch other people have. git reset moves the current branch pointer, and its three modes are the thing to know: --soft moves the pointer and leaves the index and working tree alone, so your changes become staged; --mixed moves the pointer and resets the index, so your changes become unstaged but survive; --hard moves the pointer and discards the index and working tree too, so your changes are gone. That last one is the only command in ordinary Git use that destroys work, which is why the rule is to check status first — and better, to make a branch before you do it, so the old state is still reachable.

/* Four commands, and what each is for. */
const FOUR = [
  { c: 'git log', is: 'the history itself',
    default: 'one commit per entry with hash, author, date and message',
    flags: ['--oneline for a compact list', '-p to add the diff of each commit',
      '--stat for a summary of which files changed',
      '--graph for branch structure drawn as ASCII art',
      '--author or --since to narrow'],
    bestFor: '--graph is the fastest way to understand a tangled merge history' },
  { c: 'git show', is: 'for one specific commit',
    whyBetterThanLogP: 'it defaults to showing the diff with surrounding context' },
  { c: 'git diff', is: 'for uncommitted changes',
    twoInvocations: ['plain - working tree against the index', '--staged - index against HEAD'],
    whyItMatters: 'knowing which one you are looking at is the difference between understanding what you are about to commit and being surprised by it' },
  { c: 'git blame', answers: 'when and why did this line become like this, one line at a time',
    bestFor: 'a line that looks wrong - the fastest route to the discussion that explains it' },
];

/* Safe undos. */
const SAFES = [
  { u: 'git restore (or checkout, older Git)', does: 'discards uncommitted changes to a file',
    whySafe: 'those changes are not in history, so nothing is lost that was ever shared' },
  { u: 'git revert', does: 'creates a new commit that undoes an old one',
    effect: 'history is preserved and the reversal is recorded',
    rule: 'the correct undo on any branch other people have' },
  { u: 'git reset', does: 'moves the current branch pointer',
    modes: [
      { m: '--soft', does: 'moves the pointer, leaves the index and working tree alone',
        effect: 'your changes become STAGED' },
      { m: '--mixed', does: 'moves the pointer and resets the index',
        effect: 'your changes become UNSTAGED but survive' },
      { m: '--hard', does: 'moves the pointer and discards the index and working tree too',
        effect: 'your changes are GONE' } ],
    onlyDestroyer: 'the only command in ordinary Git use that destroys work',
    rule: 'check status first - and better, make a branch before you do it, so the old state is still reachable',
  },
];

The bisect command, and what history is actually good for

git bisect is the tool that most people do not know exists and that turns a two-hour hunt into a two-minute one. The problem it solves: given a history where the bug exists now and did not exist at some earlier point, find the commit that introduced it. The manual approach is binary search by hand — check out the midpoint, test, halve — and on a history of five hundred commits that is nine rounds. Bisect does exactly this, and because each round is a test you run anyway, the time cost is the tests themselves. The usage: mark the last known-good commit and the current known-bad one, and Git checks out the midpoint and asks whether the bug is present; you answer good or bad and it halves again. When it converges it names the commit and shows the diff, so you get not just the culprit but the change. Two ways to make it better: mark intermediate commits as you discover good ones during a bisect of your own bug, which shrinks the range immediately; and use it to find not just bugs but anything that changed — a performance regression, a log line that appeared, a behaviour that differs between two environments. And the caveat: bisect assumes the bug was introduced by one commit and that the intermediate history was testable, which is true for a regression and false for a bug that appeared because of an interaction with something outside the repository.

Then the broader point, because the value of version control is not the individual commands. History answers four questions that nothing else can. What was the code when it worked? What changed between the version that worked and the one that did not? Who introduced this and when? And what else was in the same commit as this change — which is the question that finds the actual bug, because a bug is rarely in the commit that changed the line it appears on, and the line it appears on is usually the last thing to have been touched. That last one is why "look at the last commit that touched this" is frequently the wrong first move and "look at the commits around the time it started" is frequently the right one. And history as evidence: a bug report that says "worked in version X, broken in version Y" is dramatically more actionable than one that describes a symptom, because it converts an unbounded search into nine bisect rounds. When you file or receive a bug, asking for the last known-good version is not bureaucracy; it is the single highest-value question you can ask.

/* git bisect. */
const BISECT = {
  solves: 'given a history where the bug exists now and did not exist earlier, find the commit that introduced it',
  manualApproach: 'binary search by hand - check out the midpoint, test, halve',
  arithmetic: 'on five hundred commits that is nine rounds',
  howItWorks: 'Git checks out the midpoint and asks whether the bug is present; you answer good or bad and it halves again',
  payoff: 'it converges, names the commit, and shows the diff - so you get the culprit AND the change',
  timeCost: 'each round is a test you run anyway',
  twoWaysToMakeItBetter: ['mark intermediate commits as you discover good ones during a bisect of your own bug, shrinking the range immediately',
    'use it to find not just bugs but ANYTHING that changed - a performance regression, a log line that appeared, a behaviour differing between environments'],
  caveat: ['it assumes the bug was introduced by one commit',
    'and that the intermediate history was testable - true for a regression, false for a bug caused by an interaction with something outside the repository'],
};

/* What history is actually for. */
const HISTORY_ANSWERS = [
  { q: 'what was the code when it worked' },
  { q: 'what changed between the version that worked and the one that did not' },
  { q: 'who introduced this and when' },
  { q: 'what else was in the same commit as this change',
    whyMostValuable: true,
    detail: 'a bug is rarely in the commit that changed the line it appears on, and that line is usually the last thing to have been touched',
    consequence: ['look at the last commit that touched this is frequently the WRONG first move',
      'look at the commits around the time it started is frequently the RIGHT one'] },
];
const AS_EVIDENCE = {
  contrast: ['a report saying worked in version X, broken in version Y is dramatically more actionable',
    'than one describing a symptom'],
  why: 'it converts an unbounded search into nine bisect rounds',
  practice: 'when you file or receive a bug, asking for the last known-good version is not bureaucracy - it is the single highest-value question you can ask',
};

git reset --hard deletes history — never use it on shared branches, and only after you truly understand it. When in doubt, make new commits that undo old ones (revert) instead of rewriting history.

6.4 Branches: parallel universes

Branches are independent lines of development that can be merged back together. You create a branch with git branch or a checkout command, switch with git checkout or git switch, and later merge it with git merge, resolving conflicting changes by hand. This makes experimentation and parallel features safe.

git branch -M main              # name the default branch "main"
git checkout -b feature/pricing # create AND switch to a new branch
# ... work, commit ...
git checkout main               # jump back to main
git merge feature/pricing       # bring the feature into main
                           # or:      git branch -d feature/pricing

Creates a feature branch, commits on it, then merges it back into main and deletes it.

A merge conflict happens when two branches changed the same lines. Git is not broken — it’s asking you to decide. The conflicted file shows:

<<<<<<< HEAD
price = 10
=======
price = 12
>>>>>>> feature/pricing

What a branch is, and why switching is instant

The reason branching is fast is worth understanding, because it is the fact that makes the whole workflow practical. A branch is a 41-byte file containing a commit hash. Creating one writes a file; switching moves a pointer. There is no copying of files, no branch manifest, nothing to synchronise with a server beyond pushing the new ref. This is why a repository with a hundred branches costs essentially nothing extra, and why branching per change is a free decision rather than an architectural one to be argued about. It also explains the one thing that surprises everybody: committing on a branch does not record that you were on a branch. A commit records a parent and a tree, nothing about names or labels — so git log --oneline on a merged branch shows exactly the same commits as any other branch that contained them, and merging two branches produces one commit whose parents are the tips of both. Nothing in the history says "this was a feature"; that story is told by the commit messages and the pull request, not by Git.

Then the workflow and the reason for each step. Branch from an up-to-date base, not from wherever you are. If you start a branch while your main is three commits behind, your feature branch contains three unrelated changes and the merge is a conflict waiting to happen — so the habit is to pull before branching. One branch per change, named for the change. Not dev2, not my-branch: a name that says what is on it, because the name appears in every command and in every review. Commit continuously on the branch. This is the part that makes rebase safe and bisect possible: a history of twenty small commits is both reviewable and bisectable, while one giant commit is neither, and you cannot retroactively create the boundary you did not make. Merge when it is ready and verified, and then delete the branch — deletion is safe because the commits are reachable from main now, and keeping hundreds of merged branches is a form of litter that makes branch listings useless.

/* Why branching is fast. */
const WHY_FAST = {
  is: 'a 41-byte file containing a commit hash',
  operations: ['creating one writes a file', 'switching moves a pointer'],
  noSuchThings: ['copying of files', 'a branch manifest', 'anything to synchronise with a server beyond pushing the ref'],
  consequence: 'a repository with a hundred branches costs essentially nothing extra',
  reframe: 'branching per change is a free decision, not an architectural one to be argued about',
  surprise: 'committing on a branch does NOT record that you were on a branch',
  whatACommitRecords: 'a parent and a tree - nothing about names or labels',
  visible: 'git log --oneline on a merged branch shows exactly the same commits as any other branch that contained them',
  mergeShape: 'one commit whose parents are the tips of both',
  nothingSaysThisWasAFeature: 'that story is told by the commit messages and the pull request, not by Git',
};

/* The workflow, and the reason for each step. */
const WORKFLOW = [
  { step: 'branch from an up-to-date base, not from wherever you are',
    symptom: 'starting a branch while main is three commits behind',
    consequence: 'the feature branch contains three unrelated changes and the merge is a conflict waiting to happen',
    habit: 'pull before branching' },
  { step: 'one branch per change, named for the change',
    bad: ['dev2', 'my-branch'],
    why: 'the name appears in every command and in every review' },
  { step: 'commit continuously on the branch',
    whyThisMatters: 'a history of twenty small commits is reviewable and bisectable',
    contrast: 'one giant commit is neither',
    cannotRetroactive: 'you cannot retroactively create the boundary you did not make' },
  { step: 'merge when it is ready and verified, then delete the branch',
    whySafe: 'the commits are reachable from main now',
    litter: 'keeping hundreds of merged branches makes branch listings useless' },
];

Merge versus rebase, and the conflicts both produce

Two ways to combine, and the difference is what the history looks like afterwards, which matters because people read history. Merge takes both branches, finds their common ancestor, applies what changed on each side, and records a commit with two parents. The graph shows a branch splitting and rejoining — which is truthful: both lines of work really happened, and the merge commit is an honest record that two lines converged. Rebase takes your commits off your branch and replays them on top of the other branch, producing new commit ids. The graph becomes a straight line, which is nicer to read — but it is a rewrite, and the old commits become unreachable, which is why the rule about rebasing is absolute: rebase commits you have not pushed. Rebasing published history means that anyone who already fetched your commits has a history that no longer matches yours, and they will find out at the worst possible moment. The general principle underneath both is worth stating because it generalises past Git: history is a record of what happened, and rewriting it is a claim that something else happened. Merge keeps the claim honest; rebase makes the record cleaner. Choose merge for shared history and rebase for your own unpushed work.

Then conflicts, because the first time you hit one is a bad time to learn. A conflict means Git cannot decide, not that something is broken — the mechanism is that both sides changed the same region and there is no rule that says which is right. Common markers: <<<<<<< marks the start of your version, ======= separates the two, >>>>>>> marks the other. To resolve: read both sides, decide what the result should be — sometimes it is one, sometimes the other, sometimes both — edit the file to contain only the resolved content with all markers removed, stage it, and continue. Four things people get wrong. Leaving the markers in and committing, which puts visible garbage into the file. Choosing a side wholesale without reading, which silently discards work. Resolving the same conflict repeatedly because one file was conflicted at several places. And avoiding the cause — the biggest cause is long-lived branches diverging far from main, so the practical prevention is to rebase or merge main into your branch regularly while you work, rather than merging once after three weeks.

/* Merge versus rebase. */
const TWO_WAYS = [
  { m: 'merge', does: ['takes both branches', 'finds their common ancestor',
    'applies what changed on each side', 'records a commit with two parents'],
    graph: 'a branch splitting and rejoining',
    whyGood: 'TRUTHFUL - both lines of work really happened, and the merge commit honestly records that two lines converged' },
  { m: 'rebase', does: 'takes your commits off your branch and replays them on top of the other branch, producing new commit ids',
    graph: 'a straight line, which is nicer to read',
    but: 'it is a REWRITE, and the old commits become unreachable' },
];
const REBASE_RULE = {
  statement: 'rebase commits you have NOT PUSHED',
  whyAbsolute: 'rebasing published history means anyone who already fetched your commits has a history that no longer matches yours',
  whenTheyFindOut: 'the worst possible moment',
  principle: 'history is a record of what happened, and rewriting it is a claim that something else happened',
  mergeKeeps: 'the claim honest', rebaseMakes: 'the record cleaner',
  choose: 'merge for shared history, rebase for your own unpushed work',
};

/* Conflicts. */
const CONFLICT = {
  means: 'Git cannot decide - not that something is broken',
  mechanism: 'both sides changed the same region and there is no rule that says which is right',
  markers: ['<<<<<<< start of your version', '======= separates the two', '>>>>>>> the other'],
  toResolve: ['read both sides', 'decide what the result should be - sometimes one, sometimes the other, sometimes both',
    'edit the file to contain only the resolved content with all markers removed', 'stage it', 'continue'],
  mistakes: [
    { m: 'leaving the markers in', consequence: 'visible garbage committed into the file' },
    { m: 'choosing a side wholesale without reading', consequence: 'silently discards work' },
    { m: 'resolving the same conflict repeatedly', cause: 'one file was conflicted at several places' },
    { m: 'avoiding the cause',
      biggestCause: 'long-lived branches diverging far from main',
      prevention: 'rebase or merge main into your branch regularly while you work, rather than merging once after three weeks' },
  ],
};
These markers are Git asking you to choose the right lines; edit, remove the markers, then add and commit.

Edit to the correct final result, remove the marker lines, then git add + git commit. Conflict resolution is a core skill, not a disaster.

6.5 GitHub: collaboration workflow (Pull Requests)

GitHub Flow is the collaborative loop at the centre of modern teams: create a branch, commit, push it, open a pull request, discuss and review, then merge. Code reviews happen on pull requests before changes land on the main branch. A profile of active, reviewed contributions doubles as your resume.

The industry’s default loop is called GitHub Flow:

  1. Create a branch: git checkout -b feature/x.
  2. Commit changes with clear messages.
  3. Push the branch: git push -u origin feature/x.
  4. Open a Pull Request (PR) on GitHub: "merge my branch into main, please review".
  5. Team reviews → addresses comments → CI tests pass.
  6. Merge, then delete the branch.

What a remote is, and the three operations everything else builds on

Git is local; a remote is a copy of your repository on a server, and exactly three operations connect them. Push sends commits from your local repository to the remote — and the reason push can be refused is worth stating, because it is the single most common confusion: a push is rejected when the remote has commits you do not have, because pushing would overwrite them. That is Git refusing to lose work, and the resolution is never to force it without understanding; it is to fetch first, see what arrived, integrate it, and then push. Fetch downloads commits and refs without changing your working tree — safe, always, and the right first move when you are confused. Pull is fetch followed by merge, or fetch followed by rebase if configured to; it is the convenience command, and it is where the surprise lives, because a merge performed by pull can produce conflict markers without you asking. Knowing the three separately makes the whole model legible: push is the only one that can lose work, fetch is the only one that cannot, and pull is the one that does both in a single word.

Then the two flows people need on day one. Cloning copies a remote repository to your machine and checks out its default branch — and it is not the same as "download", because it carries the full history, which means you can check out any commit, create branches, and push back. Forking is a copy of somebody else's repository into your own account on the server, which is how you contribute to code you cannot write to; you then push to your fork and open a pull request against the original. The distinction is worth having straight: clone for your own work, fork to contribute to theirs, and a fork is a server-side concept while a clone is local. Then two things that surprise people: authentication, where GitHub stopped accepting account passwords for Git operations and requires a token or an SSH key — so if a push prompts for a username and password and fails, that is why, and the fix is a personal access token or an SSH key rather than a more careful password. And private repositories, which are private by default and free, and which are the right answer to "should I put my project on GitHub" for anything with a client in it — a public repository holding a client's name is a disclosure, regardless of your intentions.

/* Three operations, and what each costs. */
const THREE_OPS = [
  { op: 'push', does: 'sends commits from your local repository to the remote',
    refusedWhen: 'the remote has commits you do not have, because pushing would overwrite them',
    why: 'Git refusing to lose work',
    resolution: 'never force without understanding - fetch first, see what arrived, integrate, then push' },
  { op: 'fetch', does: 'downloads commits and refs without changing your working tree',
    safety: 'safe, always, and the right first move when you are confused' },
  { op: 'pull', does: 'fetch followed by merge, or fetch followed by rebase if configured to',
    surprise: 'a merge performed by pull can produce conflict markers without you asking' },
];
const MODEL = 'push is the only one that can lose work, fetch is the only one that cannot, and pull is the one that does both in a single word';

/* Two flows for day one. */
const FLOWS = [
  { f: 'cloning', does: 'copies a remote repository to your machine and checks out its default branch',
    notDownload: 'it carries the full history',
    gain: 'you can check out any commit, create branches, and push back' },
  { f: 'forking', does: 'a copy of somebody elses repository into your own account on the server',
    for: 'contributing to code you cannot write to',
    flow: 'push to your fork, then open a pull request against the original',
    scope: 'a fork is a SERVER-SIDE concept while a clone is local' },
];
const DISTINCTION = 'clone for your OWN work, fork to CONTRIBUTE TO THEIRS';

/* Two things that surprise people. */
const SURPRISES = [
  { s: 'authentication',
    detail: 'GitHub stopped accepting account passwords for Git operations and requires a token or an SSH key',
    symptom: 'a push prompts for a username and password and fails',
    fix: 'a personal access token or an SSH key, rather than a more careful password' },
  { s: 'private repositories',
    detail: 'private by default and free',
    answers: 'should I put my project on GitHub',
    rule: 'anything with a client in it',
    why: 'a public repository holding a clients name is a DISCLOSURE, regardless of your intentions' },
];

Pull requests, and the repository as a portfolio

A pull request is a request to merge one branch into another, and the parts worth writing deliberately are small in number and large in effect. The title is read in a list of forty open requests, so it must state the change and nothing else — "fix: handle empty cart on checkout", not "update". The description answers what and why, in prose, because the diff answers what mechanically and a reviewer needs the reasoning. Linking the issue is what connects the change to the reason it exists, and closing the issue automatically on merge is a small habit that makes a project's history navigable. Requesting review from a person rather than a team, because a team gets notified and a person reads it. And responding to review comments with commits rather than with text, where the reviewer's suggested change is pushed so the diff shows it — this is what keeps a review thread and a code history the same thing.

Then the repository as a portfolio, which is worth thinking about deliberately rather than incidentally. What a reader sees, in order: the profile — the pinned repositories, which is where you decide what the first impression is. The readme, which is the one file that matters most and the one most people write worst: it needs a title, a sentence on what the project is, a screenshot or two, an explicit "how to run this", and a licence. A repository with a good readme and thin code reads better than the reverse, because the readme is what tells a reader the project exists and what shape it has. The commit history, which is read as a signal of how you work: small focused commits with real messages read as a professional; one weekly commit reading "WIP" reads as someone who does not finish. The contributions graph, which is only meaningful if it is real. And whether the repository builds. A project that cannot be run is documentation of itself, and the honest version of a learning project — a project built while learning — is fine, provided the readme says so and the run instructions are correct. The compounding effect is the real point: a repository is a portfolio piece you maintain rather than a CV line you write, and the difference shows in the first question asked in an interview, which is "walk me through something you built".

/* Pull request parts worth writing deliberately. */
const PR = [
  { part: 'title', context: 'read in a list of forty open requests',
    must: 'state the change and nothing else',
    good: 'fix: handle empty cart on checkout', bad: 'update' },
  { part: 'description', answers: 'what and why, in prose',
    why: 'the diff answers what mechanically and a reviewer needs the reasoning' },
  { part: 'linking the issue', does: 'connects the change to the reason it exists',
    bonus: 'closing the issue automatically on merge makes a projects history navigable' },
  { part: 'requesting review', from: 'a person rather than a team', why: 'a team gets notified, a person reads it' },
  { part: 'responding to review with commits rather than text',
    mechanism: 'push the reviewers suggested change so the diff shows it',
    gain: 'keeps a review thread and a code history the same thing' },
];

/* The repository as a portfolio, in reading order. */
const PORTFOLIO = [
  { s: 'the profile', detail: 'the pinned repositories', decides: 'what the first impression is' },
  { s: 'the readme', mostImportant: true, worstWritten: true,
    needs: ['a title', 'a sentence on what the project is', 'a screenshot or two',
      'an explicit how to run this', 'a licence'],
    asymmetry: 'a repository with a good readme and thin code reads better than the reverse',
    why: 'the readme tells a reader the project exists and what shape it has' },
  { s: 'the commit history', readAs: 'a signal of how you work',
    good: 'small focused commits with real messages, reading as professional',
    bad: 'one weekly commit reading WIP, reading as someone who does not finish' },
  { s: 'the contributions graph', onlyMeaningfulIf: 'real' },
  { s: 'whether the repository builds', detail: 'a project that cannot be run is documentation of itself',
    honest: 'a project built while learning is fine, provided the readme says so and the run instructions are correct' },
];
const COMPOUNDING = 'a repository is a portfolio piece you MAINTAIN rather than a CV line you write - and the difference shows in the first interview question, which is walk me through something you built';

A GitHub profile is your resume’s centrepiece. Every project you build from now on should live in a repo: a good README (what/why/how to run it), LICENSE, and tidy commit history. Recruiters look.

6.6 Don’t commit junk: .gitignore

A .gitignore file tells Git which files to leave out of the repository: secrets, caches, build output, and dependencies. It uses plain patterns to match file names and directories, so you commit source only. Keeping junk out of the repo protects sensitive data and keeps history clean.

# .gitignore — files to NEVER commit
__pycache__/
*.pyc
.venv/
node_modules/
.env                 # secrets! never version these
.DS_Store

What ignore is for, and the four categories that matter

Git tracks files, not file types, so the ignore file is the only mechanism that says this file should not be a thing I know about. Its job is to keep three specific things out of the repository, and it is worth separating them because they have different consequences when they go wrong. Generated artefacts — build output, compiled binaries, compiled CSS, packaged output. These are reproducible from the source, so committing them doubles the repository for no benefit and creates merge conflicts on a file nobody edits by hand. Dependencies — node_modules, vendor, a Python virtual environment, a compiled dependency directory. The reason is not size alone: a lockfile plus a manifest is enough to reproduce them exactly, and committing the installed tree means every merge is thousands of files, every clone is enormous, and two machines that installed on different days have different trees. Local configuration and secrets — a .env, a local database file, credentials, a machine-specific path. This is the category that matters most, because it is the one that cannot be undone: once a secret is in the history it is in the history, and every clone of every fork has it. Editor and OS noise — .DS_Store, Thumbs.db, swap files, a folder of screenshots. Harmless individually, corrosive in aggregate, because a repository full of churn has no useful history to read.

Then the syntax, which is small and has two rules that surprise people. Patterns use glob syntax, not regular expressions: * matches anything except a slash, ** matches across directories, ? matches one character, and a trailing / means a directory only. Negation with ! re-includes a path that a broader pattern excluded, and the order matters — later lines win — so the usual shape is a broad exclusion followed by the specific inclusions you need. The two things that surprise everybody: a leading slash anchors the pattern to the ignore file's directory, so /build ignores only the top-level build folder while build ignores every folder named build anywhere. And an ignore file only affects untracked files — a file already in the repository stays tracked, so adding a pattern does nothing until you remove the file from the index. That is not a bug; it is the design, because silently untracking committed files would be a far worse surprise.

/* Four categories, and the consequence of getting each wrong. */
const CATEGORIES = [
  { c: 'generated artefacts', instances: ['build output', 'compiled binaries', 'compiled CSS', 'packaged output'],
    rule: 'reproducible from the source',
    wrongWhy: 'committing them doubles the repository for no benefit and creates merge conflicts on a file nobody edits by hand' },
  { c: 'dependencies', instances: ['node_modules', 'vendor', 'a Python virtual environment', 'a compiled dependency directory'],
    notJustSize: 'a lockfile plus a manifest is enough to reproduce them exactly',
    wrongConsequences: ['every merge is thousands of files', 'every clone is enormous',
      'two machines that installed on different days have different trees'] },
  { c: 'local configuration and secrets', instances: ['a .env', 'a local database file', 'credentials', 'a machine-specific path'],
    whyMostImportant: 'it is the one that CANNOT BE UNDONE',
    detail: 'once a secret is in the history it is in the history, and every clone of every fork has it' },
  { c: 'editor and OS noise', instances: ['.DS_Store', 'Thumbs.db', 'swap files', 'a folder of screenshots'],
    aggregate: 'harmless individually, corrosive in aggregate',
    why: 'a repository full of churn has no useful history to read' },
];

/* Syntax, and the two rules that surprise people. */
const SYNTAX = {
  patterns: 'glob, NOT regular expressions',
  tokens: ['* matches anything except a slash', '** matches across directories',
    '? matches one character', 'a trailing / means a directory only'],
  negation: { token: '!', does: 're-includes a path that a broader pattern excluded',
    orderMatters: 'later lines win',
    usualShape: 'a broad exclusion followed by the specific inclusions you need' },
  surprises: [
    { s: 'a leading slash anchors the pattern to the ignore files directory',
      detail: '/build ignores only the top-level build folder, while build ignores every folder named build anywhere' },
    { s: 'an ignore file only affects UNTRACKED files',
      detail: 'a file already in the repository stays tracked, so adding a pattern does nothing until you remove the file from the index',
      notABug: 'it is the design, because silently untracking committed files would be a far worse surprise' },
  ],
};

The mistakes that turn a repository into a mess, and how to recover

Four mistakes, and the recovery for each because all four will happen. Committing secrets. Recovery has an order: remove the file from the current state, commit that, then rewrite history to purge it — because removing it in a new commit leaves it in the old ones, and a repository whose history contains a key must have the history rewritten before the key is rotated. Committing dependencies or build output. Recovery: add the patterns, then remove the files from the index with git rm --cached so they stay on disk while Git stops tracking them, and commit that. The repository does not shrink immediately — the blobs are still in history — so if size matters, a history rewrite is the only thing that reduces it, and that is a strong reason to set the ignore file up front rather than clean up later. Adding a pattern for a file that is already tracked, then being confused that nothing changed; the fix is the --cached removal above, and the habit of checking git status to see what Git currently considers tracked rather than what is on disk. And one enormous first commit, which is not a mistake so much as a missed opportunity: history you can bisect, review and read is worth real money later, and the cost of producing it is simply committing as you go.

Then the two disciplines that prevent all of it. Start the repository with an ignore file before the first commit, not after — this takes two minutes and eliminates the majority of recovery work. And know the difference between a file that is secret and a file that is ignored. .gitignore prevents a file from being added; it does nothing for a file already added, and it does nothing about a file deliberately committed in the past. That distinction is the whole reason the recovery procedure for secrets has three steps rather than one, and it is worth internalising before it is needed, because the moment it is needed is the moment it is urgent.

/* Four mistakes, each with its recovery - because all four will happen. */
const MISTAKES = [
  { m: 'committing secrets',
    recoveryOrder: ['remove the file from the current state', 'commit that', 'rewrite history to purge it'],
    whyNotJustRemove: 'removing it in a new commit leaves it in the old ones',
    absolute: 'a repository whose history contains a key must have the history rewritten BEFORE the key is rotated' },
  { m: 'committing dependencies or build output',
    recovery: ['add the patterns', 'git rm --cached the files', 'commit that'],
    whyCached: 'so they stay on disk while Git stops tracking them',
    sizeNote: 'the repository does not shrink immediately - the blobs are still in history',
    consequence: 'only a history rewrite reduces it, which is why the ignore file belongs up front',
  },
  { m: 'adding a pattern for a file that is ALREADY tracked',
    symptom: 'nothing changes',
    fix: 'the --cached removal above',
    habit: 'check git status to see what Git currently considers tracked rather than what is on disk' },
  { m: 'one enormous first commit',
    notAMistakeExactly: 'a missed opportunity',
    costOfAvoiding: 'history you can bisect, review and read is worth real money later',
    effortRequired: 'simply committing as you go' },
];

/* Two disciplines that prevent all of it. */
const DISCIPLINES = [
  { d: 'start the repository with an ignore file BEFORE the first commit',
    cost: 'two minutes', gain: 'eliminates the majority of recovery work' },
  { d: 'know the difference between a file that is SECRET and a file that is IGNORED',
    detail: ['.gitignore prevents a file from being added',
      'it does nothing for a file already added',
      'it does nothing about a file deliberately committed in the past'],
    whyItMatters: 'that distinction is the whole reason the recovery for secrets has three steps rather than one',
    when: 'internalise it before it is needed, because the moment it is needed is the moment it is urgent' },
];

A .gitignore keeping caches, dependencies and especially .env secrets out of the repository.

6.7 Fixing mistakes: reset, reflog, bisect & stash

This topic covers Git’s stronger repair tools. git reset moves or discards commits, git reflog recovers work that seems lost, git stash temporarily shelves uncommitted changes, and git bisect runs a binary search through history to find the commit that introduced a bug. Together they make nearly every mistake recoverable.

Git’s real power is that almost nothing is permanent. Learn the recovery toolkit and "I broke git" becomes "let me find the hash".

# Two different "undo" verbs -- know when to use each:
git reset --soft HEAD~1     # uncommit, KEEP changes staged   (fix the commit)
git reset --hard HEAD~1     # uncommit AND discard changes    (nuke it)
git revert HEAD             # NEW commit that undoes the last (safe on shared branches!)

# Safety net: reflog records every HEAD move -- rescue anything.
git reflog                  # find the hash of the state you want
git checkout <hash> -- file

# Find the commit that BROKE something (half the debugging time):
git bisect start
git bisect good <old-good-hash>   # known-good
git bisect bad  HEAD              # known-bad
# git checks out middle commits; you answer good/bad; two dozen steps later
# you have the one commit responsible. It is binary search on history.

# Sideline uncommitted work without losing it:
git stash push -m "wip"     # put changes away
git stash list; git stash pop   # bring them back

The recovery toolkit: soft and hard reset, team-safe revert, reflog for rescued commits, bisect’s binary search, and stash for sideline work.

A rule to live by: revert on shared branches, reset only before you’ve pushed. Never hard-reset before checking git status for uncommitted work — or better, use git switch -c backup/<today> first and let the branch be your time machine.

Exercises 6

  1. Put your mini_quiz.py into a new repo; practise the full stage→commit→push loop.
  2. Create a branch, break something, commit, then merge it back with git log --oneline showing both lines.
  3. Push to GitHub, then clone it on the same machine into a second folder (git clone <url>) to prove your history travelled.

    4. The recovery toolkit, ordered by how much it destroys

    Six tools, and the useful thing about them is that they form a ladder from least to most destructive, so you can choose by asking how much you are willing to lose. Undo uncommitted changes — git restore discards work in progress; free, because nothing was ever shared. Undo a commit you have not pushed — git reset --soft keeps the changes staged, --mixed keeps them unstaged, --hard loses them; all three are safe locally and all three are why you should be able to explain the difference without looking it up. Undo a commit you have pushed — git revert, which records the reversal rather than hiding the original; this is the only option on a shared branch and it is correct there too, because a history that says "this was wrong and here is why we reversed it" is more useful than one where the mistake never appears. Recover something you destroyed — git reflog, which records every position HEAD has held, including ones no branch points at, and is the reason a hard reset is genuinely recoverable rather than merely reversible. Find which commit broke something — git bisect, covered above. Set work aside temporarily — git stash, which stores your uncommitted changes and restores a clean tree, and which is the correct answer to "I need to switch branches but I am mid-thought".

    Then the rules that make this safe rather than dangerous, and each exists because of a specific accident. Never rewrite shared history. Rebase and force-push on a branch other people have fetched produce a state where their local history and the remote no longer agree, and they find out at the worst moment. Check status before anything destructive. The command costs a second; the mistake costs an afternoon. Make a branch before a reset. git switch -c backup/<what-you-are-about-to-do> before a hard reset means the old state is a branch rather than a reflog entry you have to remember existed. Prefer revert on anything shared, always, without exception; the cost is a slightly noisier history and the benefit is that nobody's local repository breaks. And know that reflog has a retention window — it is not a backup, and entries expire, which is the distinction between "I can get this back" and "I can get this back for about ninety days".

    /* Six tools as a ladder from least to most destructive. */
const LADDER = [
  { t: 'undo uncommitted changes', cmd: 'git restore',
    costs: 'work in progress', free: 'nothing was ever shared' },
  { t: 'undo a commit you have not pushed', cmd: 'git reset',
    modes: ['--soft keeps the changes staged', '--mixed keeps them unstaged', '--hard loses them'],
    safeLocally: true,
    note: 'all three are why you should be able to explain the difference without looking it up' },
  { t: 'undo a commit you have pushed', cmd: 'git revert',
    mechanism: 'records the reversal rather than hiding the original',
    onlyOption: 'on a shared branch',
    alsoCorrectThere: 'a history that says this was wrong and here is why we reversed it is more useful than one where the mistake never appears' },
  { t: 'recover something you destroyed', cmd: 'git reflog',
    does: 'records every position HEAD has held, including ones no branch points at',
    why: 'the reason a hard reset is genuinely recoverable rather than merely reversible' },
  { t: 'find which commit broke something', cmd: 'git bisect', coveredAbove: true },
  { t: 'set work aside temporarily', cmd: 'git stash',
    does: 'stores uncommitted changes and restores a clean tree',
    rightAnswerTo: 'I need to switch branches but I am mid-thought' },
];

/* The rules, each because of a specific accident. */
const RULES = [
  { r: 'never rewrite shared history',
    command: 'rebase and force-push on a branch other people have fetched',
    consequence: 'their local history and the remote no longer agree, and they find out at the worst moment' },
  { r: 'check status before anything destructive', cost: 'a second', mistake: 'an afternoon' },
  { r: 'make a branch before a reset', cmd: 'git switch -c backup/<what-you-are-about-to-do>',
    gain: 'the old state is a branch rather than a reflog entry you have to remember existed' },
  { r: 'prefer revert on anything shared, always, without exception',
    cost: 'a slightly noisier history',
    benefit: "nobody's local repository breaks" },
  { r: 'know that reflog has a retention window',
    notABackup: true,
    distinction: 'I can get this back versus I can get this back for about ninety days' },
];

    The workflow habits that stop you needing recovery

    Six habits, ordered by how much trouble they prevent, and each is small enough that there is no excuse. Commit before you experiment. One commit — labelled wip, committed to a scratch branch if necessary — means every subsequent mistake is recoverable with a checkout, and it costs four seconds. This single habit eliminates the majority of the situations people reach for reflog to escape. Read status before every commit. Not out of caution: because the diff you are about to commit is not always the diff you think you made, and the status output is where you see the file you did not intend to touch, the change you forgot to stage, and the change you staged and then edited again. Stage by file, not by git add .. The habit is mildly inconvenient and it is the one that stops a debug print, a comment, and a half-finished function from travelling together into a commit whose message says "fix login bug". Commit at the end of each coherent unit rather than at the end of the day — the value is not organisational, it is that each commit is then a reviewable unit and a bisectable point. Make a branch per change, so the history after merging tells the story of the work rather than the story of a person. And push frequently, not because pushing is safe but because an unpushed branch is a branch that exists on exactly one machine, and the most common way to lose work is losing the machine.

    Then the summary that is worth keeping, because it compresses the chapter into something usable: commit often, one concern per commit, message it for the person at 3am, branch per change, push often, and revert rather than rewrite anything shared. Every rule in this chapter exists to support one of those, and the reason they are all small is that Git's design makes the safe path the easy one — the staging area exists so you can compose a precise commit, commits are cheap so you can make one often, and the fact that branches are pointers is what makes experimenting unremarkable rather than frightening. Where the safe path stops being available — a destructive command, a force-push, a history rewrite — the rules above are the guard rails, and the reason they are stated as absolute is that they are the cases where the tool cannot help you afterwards.

    /* Six habits, ordered by how much trouble they prevent. */
const HABITS = [
  { h: 'commit before you experiment',
    how: 'one commit, labelled wip, on a scratch branch if necessary',
    cost: 'four seconds',
    gain: 'every subsequent mistake is recoverable with a checkout',
    claim: 'this single habit eliminates the majority of the situations people reach for reflog to escape' },
  { h: 'read status before every commit',
    notCaution: 'because the diff you are about to commit is not always the diff you think you made',
    catches: ['the file you did not intend to touch', 'the change you forgot to stage',
      'the change you staged and then edited again'] },
  { h: 'stage by file, not by git add .',
    cost: 'mildly inconvenient',
    prevents: 'a debug print, a comment and a half-finished function travelling together into a commit whose message says fix login bug' },
  { h: 'commit at the end of each coherent unit rather than at the end of the day',
    value: 'not organisational - each commit is then a reviewable unit and a bisectable point' },
  { h: 'make a branch per change',
    gain: 'the history after merging tells the story of the work rather than the story of a person' },
  { h: 'push frequently',
    notBecauseSafe: 'because an unpushed branch exists on exactly one machine',
    claim: 'the most common way to lose work is losing the machine' },
];

/* The compression. */
const RULES_SUMMARY = [
  'commit often',
  'one concern per commit',
  'message it for the person at 3am',
  'branch per change',
  'push often',
  'revert rather than rewrite anything shared',
];
const WHY_SMALL = {
  claim: 'every rule exists to support one of those',
  reason: ["Git's design makes the safe path the easy one - the staging area exists so you can compose a precise commit, commits are cheap so you can make one often, and branches being pointers is what makes experimenting unremarkable rather than frightening"],
  whereSafetyEnds: ['a destructive command', 'a force-push', 'a history rewrite'],
  theRulesThere: 'the guard rails, and the reason they are stated as absolute is that they are the cases where the tool cannot help you afterwards',
};

7 · Discrete Mathematics for Computer Science

Discrete mathematics studies countable structures such as sets, graphs, and logic, in contrast to continuous calculus. It is the mathematical bedrock of algorithms, databases, machine learning, and cryptography. The chapter builds the reasoning skills you need to analyse correctness and efficiency rigorously.

7.1 Propositional logic — the grammar of reasoning7.2 Sets — containers of distinct things7.3 Counting — combinatorics7.4 Proof by induction — the programmer’s proof7.5 Probability — the language of uncertainty7.6 Boolean algebra + truth tables in code — a bridge to Ch. 10

Computer science is "discrete" math: it deals in countable, separate things — integers, sets, states, edges — not continuous curves. Any serious algorithms course, and any machine-learning or proofs-heavy CS course, assumes you know this chapter.

7.1 Propositional logic — the grammar of reasoning

Propositional logic combines statements with logical operators like AND, OR, NOT, and implication to formalise reasoning. Truth tables define exactly when each compound statement is true, and laws such as De Morgan’s laws simplify expressions. These connect to boolean conditions in code and keep resurfacing throughout your career.

A proposition is a statement that’s either true or false. Combine them with connectives:

OperatorSymbolMeansTruth table (p, q)
AND (conjunction)p ∧ qboth trueT F F F
OR (disjunction)p ∨ qat least one trueT T T F
NOT¬poppositeF T
IMPLIESp → q"if p then q"T F T T (only false when p true, q false)
IFFp ↔ qsame truth valueT F F T

Rules worth memorising now (they reappear as "boolean-algebra" and in SQL):

De Morgan's laws:   not (A and B) == (not A) or (not B)
                    not (A or B)  == (not A) and (not B)

Double negation:    not (not A) == A

De Morgan and double negation identities: the exact rules you apply when simplifying boolean conditions in code.

Implication, equivalence, and the operators nobody reads correctly

Implication — A → B, read "if A then B" — is the operator most often misread, and the misreading causes real logic errors. The correct reading is a material conditional: it is false only when A is true and B is false. When A is false the implication is vacuously true — "if the moon is made of cheese, then two plus two is four" is a true statement. This vacuous-truth rule is what makes implication awkward in code and why it is rarely used there: if x: y() is not an implication at all, because the if only says y() runs when x is true and says nothing about the other case. Equivalence — A ↔ B — is true only when A and B agree, and it is the operator to be careful with because if A == B in code means something different from it: for booleans the two happen to coincide, and for non-booleans they do not, which is why x == y where both are lists is a value comparison rather than an identity comparison. XOR — true when exactly one of A and B is true — has no direct Python operator and is written as (A and not B) or (not A and B), or as != on booleans. It is the operator behind checking "exactly one field was filled in", and it is the one where the mistake is silently accepting both.

Then the three things about logic in code that are worth stating as rules. Every expression must have a type, and a condition must be a boolean. In Python any truthy value works in an if — which is convenient and is exactly why if items: and if items is not None: are different expressions with different behaviour on an empty list, and why a function returning None on failure silently takes the false branch at every call site. De Morgan's rewrites are the primary debugging tool for conditions. When a condition is not firing and you cannot see why, rewrite it into the other form and read it as a sentence: not (a and b) as (not a) or (not b) almost always reveals a misplaced negation, because the second is a list of disqualifiers and the first is a thing that must be true. And propositions compose in ways that are worth exploiting. A conjunction of independent conditions is better written as separate guard clauses than as one long condition, because each can then carry its own error message, and the reason is distributivity: (A and B) and C is the same proposition as three separate checks, and three separate checks can each fail differently.

/* The operators nobody reads correctly. */
const IMPLICATION = {
  form: 'A implies B',
  correctReading: 'material conditional - FALSE ONLY WHEN A is true and B is false',
  vacuousTruth: 'when A is false the implication is vacuously true',
  example: 'if the moon is made of cheese, then two plus two is four is a true statement',
  whyAwkwardInCode: 'if x: y() is NOT an implication - it only says y() runs when x is true and says nothing about the other case',
  rarity: 'rarely used in code for exactly this reason',
};
const EQUIVALENCE = {
  form: 'A iff B', is: 'true only when A and B agree',
  trap: 'if A == B in code means something different from it',
  coincidence: 'for booleans the two coincide; for non-booleans they do not',
  example: 'x == y where both are lists is a VALUE comparison rather than an identity comparison',
};
const XOR = {
  is: 'true when exactly one of A and B is true',
  inPython: 'no direct operator - written as (A and not B) or (not A and B), or != on booleans',
  behind: 'checking exactly one field was filled in',
  mistake: 'the one where the mistake is silently accepting BOTH',
};

/* Three rules about logic in code. */
const RULES = [
  { r: 'every expression has a type, and a condition must be a boolean',
    detail: 'in Python any truthy value works in an if',
    consequences: ['if items: and if items is not None: are different expressions',
      'they behave differently on an empty list',
      'a function returning None on failure silently takes the false branch at every call site'] },
  { r: 'De Morgan rewrites are the PRIMARY debugging tool for conditions',
    how: 'when a condition is not firing and you cannot see why, rewrite it and read it as a sentence',
    detail: 'not (a and b) as (not a) or (not b)',
    whyItWorks: 'the second is a list of disqualifiers and the first is a thing that must be true, which reveals a misplaced negation' },
  { r: 'propositions compose in ways worth exploiting',
    detail: 'a conjunction of independent conditions is better written as separate guard clauses than one long condition',
    reason: 'distributivity - (A and B) and C is the same proposition as three separate checks',

Proving things about code, and the three forms a proof can take

You do not need to be a mathematician to benefit from this, but you should know that there are three things you do with logic in programming, and it helps not to conflate them. Finding counterexamples. To show a program is wrong you need one input where it fails, and logic tells you how to search for one systematically — by enumerating a small input space exhaustively, or by asking which condition must be false for the bug to occur and choosing values that make it false. This is refutation and it is usually cheaper than proof. Proving a program correct. Harder than it looks and usually not worth it for whole programs, but the per-function version is cheap and is where the value is: if you can state the preconditions of a function and show the postconditions, then every caller that meets the preconditions gets the postconditions, and the reasoning composes. That is the real content of the "check the boundary" discipline from earlier chapters, and it is why preconditions are worth writing down. Reasoning about equivalence and transformation. Showing that two expressions are logically the same, which is what refactoring is: replacing a condition with an equivalent one, or replacing a loop with a comprehension, requires believing they agree for every input — and that belief is only justified by a proof or an exhaustive check over the input space.

Then three practical habits that come out of this and that pay off immediately. Check the boundary cases deliberately, in a list, every time. Empty, zero, one, negative, the maximum, the maximum plus one, null, the largest and smallest values the type allows. Every one of these is a place a general argument stops being valid and a specific bug lives — the classic being an algorithm that handles n items and does something nonsensical for n = 0, because every step it takes was correct "for a nonempty input" and the empty case was never considered. State preconditions where they are non-obvious. Not in the code for code's sake, but in the test, because an untested precondition is an assumption, and assumptions become bugs when the input changes. And when a bug is non-obvious, find the counterexample before fixing it. The counterexample is the test you keep, and finding it first means your fix is verified rather than merely applied. That is the discipline from the debugging section and it is the same discipline: a fix without a reproducing case is a guess that happens to have stopped the symptom.

/* Three things you do with logic in programming. */
const THREE_USES = [
