    method: ['enumerate a small input space exhaustively',
      'ask which condition must be false for the bug to occur, and choose values that make it false'],
    name: 'REFUTATION',
    note: 'usually cheaper than proof' },
  { u: 'proving a program correct',
    scope: 'whole programs are hard and usually not worth it; the PER-FUNCTION version is cheap',
    how: 'state the preconditions of a function and show the postconditions',
    composes: 'every caller meeting the preconditions gets the postconditions, and the reasoning composes',
    connection: 'the real content of the check-the-boundary discipline, and why preconditions are worth writing down' },
  { u: 'reasoning about equivalence and transformation',
    applies: ['replacing a condition with an equivalent one', 'replacing a loop with a comprehension'],
    requires: 'believing they agree for every input',

Reading logic as code: not (x > 0 and y > 0) is exactly equivalent to x <= 0 or y <= 0. Practising De Morgan rewrites directly improves your if conditions.

Exercise 7.1

Build the full truth table for (p → q) ↔ (¬p ∨ q). You’ll find it’s ALWAYS true — a tautology. That’s why engineers "simplify" implication into not-Or form.

7.2 Sets — containers of distinct things

A set is a container of distinct, unordered items, supporting operations like union, intersection, and difference. These ideas map directly onto Python’s set type, with operators and methods that mirror the mathematical notation. Sets are the tool of choice for de-duplication and membership testing.

Sets have no order and no duplicates. Operations match Python’s set exactly:

  • Union A ∪ B — everything in either.
  • Intersection A ∩ B — everything in both.
  • Difference A − B — in A but not B.
  • Complement ¬A — everything in the universe not in A.
  • Subset A ⊆ B — all of A lives inside B.
A = {1, 2, 3}
B = {3, 4, 5}
print(A | B)          # union        {1,2,3,4,5}
print(A & B)          # intersection {3}
print(A - B)          # difference   {1,2}
print(B - A)          # difference   {4,5}
print(A <= B)         # subset?      False
print(3 in A)         # membership   True  (O(1))

What a set is, and the two properties that make it different from a list

A set is an unordered collection of unique elements, and the two defining properties are what everything else follows from. No duplicates. Adding an element that is already present changes nothing, which means a set answers "have I seen this" without any extra bookkeeping, and it means a list of things-that-should-be-unique is a bug waiting to be found by somebody who needed the uniqueness. No order. This one is more consequential than it looks: a set gives no promise about iteration order, so for x in my_set producing the same sequence on two runs of the same program is a bug waiting for a different Python version, a different machine, or a change in hash seed. The corollary is that a set is the wrong structure for anything where order carries meaning — a playlist, a ranked list, a display order — and the right one for membership, deduplication and grouping.

Then the operations, and the reason each exists. Membership is the reason sets exist: x in s is a hash lookup, so it is constant time regardless of size, where the same test on a list is a scan. This is the operation that changes a program's complexity, and it is the reason the idiom if x not in seen: exists — it turns an O(n²) algorithm into an O(n) one in a single line. Union combines two sets into everything in either; intersection into everything in both; difference into what is in one and not the other. The set identities behind them are worth having because they let you simplify conditions: the complement of a union is the intersection of the complements, and the complement of an intersection is the union of the complements — which is De Morgan again, in set clothing. Subset and superset tests answer "is every element of A also in B", which is a different question from "do A and B share anything" and the two are constantly confused. And set operations on strings — where a string is treated as a collection of characters — which is occasionally what you want and frequently a sign you should have used a set of words.

/* Two defining properties. */
const SET = {
  is: 'an unordered collection of unique elements',
  p1: { name: 'no duplicates',
    consequence: 'adding an element already present changes nothing',
    gain: 'a set answers have-I-seen-this without any extra bookkeeping',
    bugItPrevents: 'a list of things-that-should-be-unique is a bug waiting for somebody who needed the uniqueness' },
  p2: { name: 'no order', moreConsequentialThanItLooks: true,
    detail: 'a set gives no promise about iteration order',
    bug: 'for x in my_set producing the same sequence on two runs is a bug waiting for a different Python version, a different machine, or a change in hash seed',
    corollary: 'the wrong structure for anything where order carries meaning - a playlist, a ranked list, a display order',
    rightFor: ['membership', 'deduplication', 'grouping'] },
};

/* Operations, and why each exists. */
const OPS = [
  { op: 'membership', whyTheSetExists: true,
    detail: 'x in s is a hash lookup, constant time regardless of size, where the same test on a list is a scan',
    consequence: 'this is the operation that changes a programs complexity',
    idiom: 'if x not in seen: turns an O(n^2) algorithm into an O(n) one in a single line' },
  { op: 'union, intersection, difference',
    meanings: ['everything in either', 'everything in both', 'what is in one and not the other'],
    identity: 'the complement of a union is the intersection of the complements',
    connection: 'and the complement of an intersection is the union of the complements - De Morgan in set clothing' },
  { op: 'subset and superset tests', answers: 'is every element of A also in B',
    confusedWith: 'do A and B share anything',
    note: 'the two are constantly confused' },
  { op: 'set operations on strings', detail: 'treating a string as a collection of characters',
    verdict: 'occasionally what you want, frequently a sign you should have used a set of words' },
];

Where sets belong in program design, and the operations that are easy to get wrong

Four places sets earn their keep, and three of them are algorithmic. Deduplication, and making uniqueness structural rather than a promise in a comment. Seen-tracking in a loop, which is the single most valuable algorithmic use and the one worth reaching for by reflex whenever a loop has a nested scan. Grouping — a dictionary keyed by a group value with a set as each value — which is the shape almost every "group these by" requirement wants. And the membership test that replaces a linear scan, which is the same as the second but worth separating because it also applies to a fixed collection you never modify, where a set built once and reused beats converting per call. Then the correctness point that matters more than any of them: sets require elements to be hashable and, crucially, immutable in their hash. A mutable custom object as a set element works until you mutate it, at which point the element is unfindable and its entry is silently leaked. This is the same constraint as a dictionary key and it is the same reason.

Then the operations that are easy to get wrong, each with a specific reason. Mutating a set while iterating it raises, and the correct forms are to iterate a copy, to build the additions and apply them after, or to collect into a new set — the same rule as for lists and dictionaries. Assuming a set has an order, which is covered above and produces the bug where output order changes between runs and nobody can reproduce it. The empty-set falsy trap: if s: is false for an empty set, so a function returning an empty set to signal "no results" takes the false branch at every caller — the identical trap to None and to the empty list, and all three are worth remembering as one rule: be explicit about the difference between "absent" and "empty", because Python will not. And set operations on a generator, which consume it: calling two set operations on the same generator gives the second one nothing, and that produces a set of half the expected size with no error — one of the quieter bugs in the language.

/* Four places sets earn their keep. */
const EARN = [
  { use: 'deduplication', gain: 'makes uniqueness STRUCTURAL rather than a promise in a comment' },
  { use: 'seen-tracking in a loop', algorithmic: true,
    note: 'the most valuable algorithmic use',
    habit: 'reach for it by reflex whenever a loop has a nested scan' },
  { use: 'grouping', shape: 'a dictionary keyed by a group value with a set as each value',
    why: 'the shape almost every group-these-by requirement wants' },
  { use: 'the membership test that replaces a linear scan',
    distinctBecause: 'also applies to a fixed collection you never modify',
    gain: 'a set built once and reused beats converting per call' },
];
const CORRECTNESS = {
  rule: 'sets require elements to be HASHABLE and, crucially, immutable in their hash',
  customObjectBug: 'a mutable custom object as a set element works until you mutate it, at which point the element is unfindable and its entry is silently leaked',
  connection: 'the same constraint as a dictionary key, and the same reason',
};

/* The operations that are easy to get wrong. */
const TRAPS = [
  { t: 'mutating a set while iterating it', symptom: 'raises',

    note: 'the same rule as for lists and dictionaries' },
  { t: 'assuming a set has an order', coveredAbove: true,
    symptom: 'output order changes between runs and nobody can reproduce it' },
  { t: 'the empty-set falsy trap',
    detail: 'if s: is false for an empty set',
    consequence: 'a function returning an empty set to signal no results takes the false branch at every caller',

Python set operators map directly onto set theory: union, intersection, difference and subset checks.

Cardinality is the size (|A| = 3). "Set-breaking duplicates" is a classic coding pattern: list(set(words)).

7.3 Counting — combinatorics

Combinatorics counts arrangements and selections of items, covering the multiplication principle, permutations, and combinations. These counts seed probability theory, the analysis of hash collisions, and password and security reasoning. Being able to count possibilities is a prerequisite for measuring likelihood.

  • Multiplication rule: choose 1 of 3 starters and 1 of 4 mains → 3 × 4 = 12 meals.
  • Permutation P(n,k): order matters, n! / (n−k)!. 3 people on 3 chairs in order: 3! = 6.
  • Combination C(n,k): order doesn’t matter, n! / (k! (n−k)!). Choosing a committee of 2 from 4: 6 ways.
import itertools, math
print(math.comb(4, 2))                    # 6   combinations
print(math.perm(4, 2))                    # 12  permutations
print(list(itertools.combinations("abcd", 2)))   # all pairs, 6 of them
print(len(list(itertools.combinations(range(52), 2))))   # 1326 pokerish pairs

Counting versus choosing, and why the distinction is the whole subject

Combinatorics is about how many ways something can be arranged or chosen, and the first decision is always the same: does order matter? If it does you are counting permutations; if it does not, combinations. That single question determines every formula that follows, and getting it wrong produces a number that is wrong by a factor that grows with n, which is the most confusing way for a bug to present. Permutations of n things taken r at a time is n! / (n-r)! — arrangements of r chosen items where first and second positions are different. Combinations of n taken r is n! / (r! (n-r)!) — the same selection where first and second are not different. The relationship is that combinations are permutations divided by r!, and the division by r! is precisely the orderings you no longer count. Factorials grow explosively — 20 factorial is about 2.4 × 10¹⁸, which exceeds a 64-bit integer — and this is why nCr with large n is computed multiplicatively, not by dividing factorials, since n! / r! as separate values overflows long before the answer does. The practical warning is the one to remember: any algorithm whose runtime is factorial is not an algorithm for real data, and a combinatorial count that comes out above about 10⁹ is telling you that enumerating the possibilities is not a plan.

Then the four counts worth being able to compute on sight. Power set — 2ⁿ, because every element is independently in or out; this is also why a truth table over n variables has 2ⁿ rows, and why the same number appears for subsets, for coin-flip outcomes and for all possible feature subsets. Balls into bins, distinguishable balls into distinguishable bins is nᵏ — n choices, independently, k times. Indistinguishable balls into distinguishable bins is (n+k-1 choose k-1), which is the stars-and-bars formula and the answer to "how many ways to distribute these identical items", and it is the one that surprises people because the count is small when it feels like it should be large. Distinguishable balls into indistinguishable bins is the Stirling-number family, and it is worth knowing the name because it is the honest answer when the partitions are what you actually want. And derangements — permutations with nothing in its original place — which have a beautiful closed form involving a constant near one divided by e, and which appear whenever the question is "in how many ways can this go wrong in every possible way".

/* The first decision, and it determines every formula. */
const COUNTS = {
  firstQuestion: 'DOES ORDER MATTER',
  ifYes: 'permutations', ifNo: 'combinations',
  costOfGettingItWrong: 'a number wrong by a factor that grows with n - the most confusing way for a bug to present',
  permutations: { formula: 'n! / (n-r)!', means: 'arrangements of r chosen items where first and second positions are DIFFERENT' },
  combinations: { formula: 'n! / (r! (n-r)!)', means: 'the same selection where first and second are NOT different' },
  relationship: 'combinations are permutations divided by r!, and the division by r! is precisely the orderings you no longer count',
};

/* Factorials, and the overflow trap. */
const FACTORIALS = {
  grows: '20 factorial is about 2.4 x 10^18, which exceeds a 64-bit integer',
  consequence: 'nCr with large n must be computed MULTIPLICATIVELY, not by dividing factorials',
  why: 'n! / r! as separate values overflows long before the answer does',
  warning: 'any algorithm whose runtime is factorial is not an algorithm for real data',
  signal: 'a combinatorial count above about 10^9 is telling you that enumerating the possibilities is not a plan',
};

/* Four counts worth computing on sight. */
const ON_SIGHT = [
  { c: 'power set', value: '2^n', why: 'every element is independently in or out',
    alsoIs: ['the rows of a truth table over n variables', 'coin-flip outcomes', 'all possible feature subsets'] },
  { c: 'balls into bins, distinguishable into distinguishable', value: 'n^k', why: 'n choices, independently, k times' },
  { c: 'indistinguishable balls into distinguishable bins', value: '(n+k-1 choose k-1)',
    name: 'stars and bars', for: 'how many ways to distribute these identical items',
    surprise: 'the count is small when it feels like it should be large' },
  { c: 'distinguishable balls into indistinguishable bins', family: 'Stirling numbers',
    note: 'worth knowing the name because it is the honest answer when partitions are what you want' },
  { c: 'derangements', is: 'permutations with nothing in its original place',
    form: 'a closed form involving a constant near one divided by e',
    appears: 'whenever the question is in how many ways can this go wrong in every possible way' },
];

Counting versus enumerating, and why this matters in code

The practical reason this section exists: counting is cheap, enumerating is not. If a problem asks "how many ways", compute it with a formula and you are done in microseconds. If it asks "find one way" or "find all ways", and the count is combinatorial, you are writing an exponential search — and the difference between 3.6 million combinations and three operations is the difference between a solved problem and a timeout. Three consequences follow. Use the library. Every language has a combinatorial function that computes nCr exactly and correctly, including the large-value cases, because getting the multiplication order right is fiddly and there is no reason to get it wrong. Enumerate with a generator, not a list. A generator produces items one at a time so that a search which finds what it wants early never pays for the rest, and the failure mode of not doing this — building a list of every combination of ten things when you only wanted the first — is a memory blow-up that looks like a random crash. And use counting as an early-exit test. If the number of combinations is zero or one, you can often answer without searching; if it is 10¹², you know immediately that the approach is wrong before you write it.

Then the three counting mistakes that reach production code. Confusing combinations with permutations, the chapter's first point, which produces a wrong-by-a-factor-of-r! result. Counting ordered pairs when the relation is symmetric — if a is friends with b then b is friends with a, so an unordered pair count is n(n-1)/2 and not n(n-1), and doubling every friendship in your output is the symptom. And counting the structure rather than the instances: when two different inputs produce the same output shape, they are the same case for the purposes of counting, and a formula that treats them as distinct is off by exactly the number of duplicates. Each of these has a corollary that makes them findable: verify the count on a small case by brute force. Write the enumeration for n = 5, run it, count, and compare with the formula. If they differ, the formula is wrong in a way you can find with a five-line test that you will write once and never have to debug again — which is the same advice as testing binary search against a brute-force version, and it generalises to every closed form in this chapter.

/* Counting is cheap, enumerating is not. */
const DISTINCTION = {
  principle: 'COUNTING IS CHEAP, ENUMERATING IS NOT',
  cheapCase: 'if a problem asks how many ways, compute it with a formula and you are done in microseconds',
  expensiveCase: 'if it asks find one way or find all ways and the count is combinatorial, you are writing an exponential search',
  arithmetic: 'the difference between 3.6 million combinations and three operations is the difference between a solved problem and a timeout',
};
const CONSEQUENCES = [
  { c: 'use the library', why: 'every language has a combinatorial function that computes nCr exactly and correctly, including large-value cases',
    reason: 'getting the multiplication order right is fiddly and there is no reason to get it wrong' },
  { c: 'enumerate with a GENERATOR, not a list',
    gain: 'produces items one at a time so a search that finds what it wants early never pays for the rest',
    failureMode: 'building a list of every combination of ten things when you only wanted the first',
    symptom: 'a memory blow-up that looks like a random crash' },
  { c: 'use counting as an early-exit test',
    zeroOrOne: 'if the number of combinations is zero or one you can often answer without searching',
    huge: 'if it is 10^12 you know immediately that the approach is wrong BEFORE you write it' },
];

/* Three counting mistakes that reach production code. */
const MISTAKES = [
  { m: 'confusing combinations with permutations', consequence: 'a wrong-by-a-factor-of-r! result' },
  { m: 'counting ordered pairs when the relation is symmetric',
    detail: 'if a is friends with b then b is friends with a',
    correct: 'an unordered pair count is n(n-1)/2, not n(n-1)',
    symptom: 'doubling every friendship in your output' },
  { m: 'counting the STRUCTURE rather than the INSTANCES',
    detail: 'when two different inputs produce the same output shape they are the same case for counting purposes',
    consequence: 'a formula treating them as distinct is off by exactly the number of duplicates' },
];
const VERIFICATION = {
  method: 'verify the count on a small case by brute force',
  steps: ['write the enumeration for n = 5', 'run it', 'count', 'compare with the formula'],
  payoff: 'a five-line test you write once and never have to debug again',
  generalises: 'the same advice as testing binary search against a brute-force version - it applies to every closed form in this chapter',
};

Computes combinations and permutations with math.comb and perm, and generates the actual pairs with itertools.

Why care? Counting is the nuts-and-bolts of probability (Ch. 7.5), of hashing (average-case complexity), and of password-security math (permutations explode quickly).

7.4 Proof by induction — the programmer’s proof

Mathematical induction proves a statement for every natural number with two steps: a base case showing it holds at the start, and an inductive step showing that truth for one case implies truth for the next. The structure mirrors recursion and loop invariant proofs exactly. Programmers who master induction debug subtle loops better.

To prove a statement P(n) for all n ≥ 1:

  1. Base case: prove P(1).
  2. Inductive step: assume P(k) (the induction hypothesis); prove P(k+1).

Induction is the same shape as recursion and as loop invariants — the way we prove algorithms correct. Example: prove that the sum 1+2+…+n = n(n+1)/2. Base n=1: 1 = 1(2)/2 ✓. Step: assume true for k; then for k+1, the sum is [k(k+1)/2] + (k+1) = (k+1)(k+2)/2, which is the formula for k+1. ✓ Done.

Why induction exists, and its two halves

Mathematical induction is a proof technique that looks backwards and is the foundation of essentially every correctness argument in computer science. The shape is: prove the base case — that the statement holds for n = 1 (or n = 0); then prove the inductive step — that if it holds for n = k, then it holds for n = k+1. That is all. And it works for a reason that is genuinely surprising: the two halves combined form a chain from a known start to every number. The base case anchors the chain; each application of the step extends it by one; and since every natural number is a finite number of steps from 1, the statement is true for all of them. Nothing about a case that is infinitely far away is assumed — which is the thing that makes induction feel circular and is not, because the step does not assume "k+1 implies k+2"; it assumes "k implies k+1", which is a rule for producing the next truth from the previous one.

Then why this is a programming technique and not just a mathematics one, which is the part worth stating carefully. Loop invariants are inductive proofs. An invariant for a loop has exactly three parts: it holds before the loop starts, it holds after one iteration assuming it held before, and it holds when the loop ends. Those three statements are a base case, an inductive step and a conclusion. And the consequence is real and useful: if you cannot state the invariant, you cannot prove the loop correct, and a loop whose correctness you cannot argue is a loop whose termination and output you do not actually know. Recursive functions are proved by induction. To prove a recursive function correct you show it correct for the base case, then show that if the recursive call is correct for a smaller input, the enclosing computation is correct — and that is a complete proof, structurally identical to the mathematical version. Structural induction covers data types. A claim about a list or a tree is proved by proving it for the empty structure and then showing that if it holds for the parts, it holds for the whole built from them, which is induction over structure rather than over a number. And the induction principle is why the loop is trustworthy. Every bounded loop is a finite chain of applications of its step; that is the reason a loop that runs a known number of times terminates, and it is the reason "prove it by induction" and "prove the loop correct" are the same request.

/* The shape. */
const INDUCTION = {
  shape: ['prove the base case - the statement holds for n = 1 (or n = 0)',
    'prove the inductive step - if it holds for n = k, then it holds for n = k + 1'],
  thatIsAll: true,
  whyItWorks: 'the two halves combined form a chain from a known start to every number',
  theChain: ['the base case anchors it', 'each application of the step extends it by one',
    'every natural number is a finite number of steps from 1'],
  notCircular: 'the step does not assume k+1 implies k+2; it assumes k implies k+1, a rule for producing the next truth from the previous one',
  resolves: 'nothing about an infinitely distant case is assumed',
};

/* Why this is a programming technique. */
const IN_PROGRAMMING = [
  { p: 'loop invariants are inductive proofs',
    has: ['it holds before the loop starts', 'it holds after one iteration assuming it held before',
      'it holds when the loop ends'],
    areExactly: ['a base case', 'an inductive step', 'a conclusion'],
    consequence: 'if you cannot state the invariant you cannot prove the loop correct',
    sting: 'a loop whose correctness you cannot argue is a loop whose termination and output you do not actually know' },
  { p: 'recursive functions are proved by induction',
    method: ['show it correct for the base case',
      'show that if the recursive call is correct for a smaller input, the enclosing computation is correct'],
    complete: true, identicalTo: 'the mathematical version, structurally' },
  { p: 'structural induction covers data types',
    over: ['a list', 'a tree'],
    method: 'prove it for the empty structure, then show that if it holds for the parts it holds for the whole built from them',
    name: 'induction over STRUCTURE rather than over a number' },
  { p: 'the induction principle is why the loop is trustworthy',
    detail: 'every bounded loop is a finite chain of applications of its step',
    consequence: 'the reason a loop running a known number of times terminates',
    identity: 'prove it by induction and prove the loop correct are the same request' },
];

Applying it: loop invariants, and the two halves people skip

Writing a loop invariant is a specific skill with a specific format, and the format is what makes it work. State it as a fact about the state at the top of the loop, not about the code. "At the start of each iteration, total equals the sum of the elements seen so far" is an invariant; "we add each item to the total" is a description of the code. Include what the loop has consumed and what it has produced. An invariant that mentions only the accumulator says nothing about the index, so it cannot rule out an index bug — and the common form is a conjunction: "the first k elements have been summed into total, and k is the index of the next element to read." That single sentence catches an off-by-one, a wrong start value, and a skipped element, which three separate tests might not. Check it in all three places, and the two people skip are the last two. Everyone checks before the loop. Almost nobody checks that the step preserves it, and almost nobody checks what it guarantees at exit — and those are the two that are actually informative, because the first is satisfied by construction and the second is the postcondition you actually want.

Then what this buys, and the three mistakes it prevents. The invariant proves partial correctness — that if the loop terminates, the answer is right — and the loop's guard plus a decreasing measure proves termination. Those are two separate claims and both are needed, which is why a loop with a correct invariant and no argument that it ends is only half-proved. The mistakes it prevents are the ones from earlier chapters made catchable by a single sentence: an off-by-one at the boundary, because the invariant names both the consumed prefix and the next index and they cannot both be wrong; a loop that mutates the collection it walks, because "the first k elements have been processed" is false the moment the prefix changes underneath you; and an accumulator initialised wrongly, because the pre-loop check of the invariant catches a wrong seed immediately rather than at the third iteration. And the practical payoff is worth stating plainly, because it is the whole reason: writing the invariant takes five minutes and it is the only way to know the loop is right rather than that it appears to be right on the three cases you tried.

/* The format that makes writing an invariant work. */
const FORMAT = [
  { rule: 'state it as a fact about the STATE at the top of the loop, not about the code',
    invariant: 'at the start of each iteration, total equals the sum of the elements seen so far',
    notInvariant: 'we add each item to the total - that is a description of the code' },
  { rule: 'include what the loop has CONSUMED and what it has PRODUCED',
    why: 'an invariant mentioning only the accumulator says nothing about the index, so it cannot rule out an index bug',
    commonForm: 'a conjunction - the first k elements have been summed into total, and k is the index of the next element to read',
    catches: ['an off-by-one', 'a wrong start value', 'a skipped element',
      'which three separate tests might not'] },
  { rule: 'check it in all three places, and the two people skip are the last two',
    checked: 'before the loop - by construction and therefore uninformative',
    skipped: ['that the step preserves it', 'what it guarantees at exit'],
    whyThoseTwo: 'they are the ones that are actually informative' },
];

/* What it buys, and what it prevents. */
const BUYS = [
  { t: 'partial correctness', means: 'if the loop terminates, the answer is right', provedBy: 'the invariant' },
  { t: 'termination', means: 'the loop ends', provedBy: "the loop's guard plus a decreasing measure" },
  note: 'two separate claims and both are needed',
  consequence: 'a loop with a correct invariant and no argument that it ends is only half-proved',
];
const PREVENTS = [
  { m: 'off-by-one at the boundary',
    caughtBecause: 'the invariant names both the consumed prefix and the next index, and they cannot both be wrong' },
  { m: 'a loop that mutates the collection it walks',
    caughtBecause: 'the first k elements have been processed is false the moment the prefix changes underneath you' },
  { m: 'an accumulator initialised wrongly',
    caughtBecause: 'the pre-loop check of the invariant catches a wrong seed immediately rather than at the third iteration' },
];
const PAYOFF = 'writing the invariant takes five minutes and it is the only way to know the loop is right rather than that it appears to be right on the three cases you tried';

Exercise 7.4

Prove by induction that 2ⁿ > n for all n ≥ 1. (Hint for the step: 2·2ᵏ > 2k ≥ k+1 for k ≥ 1.)

7.5 Probability — the language of uncertainty

Probability quantifies uncertainty as ratios of outcomes, with key concepts like sample spaces, conditional probability, independence, and Bayes' theorem. Bayes' theorem updates beliefs given new evidence and powers spam filters, medical tests, and machine learning. It is the language in which decisions under uncertainty are expressed.

  • P(event) = favourable / total, when outcomes are equally likely.
  • Independent events: P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B). Roll two dice: P(6 and 6) = 1/6 · 1/6 = 1/36.
  • Union: P(A or B) = P(A)+P(B) − P(A and B) (avoid double counting).
  • Conditional: P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B). Bayes' theorem re-expresses P(A|B) in terms of P(B|A) — the basis of modern spam filters and machine learning.
import random
random.seed(42)                      # seed = reproducible randomness
print(random.randint(1, 6))          # dice roll
print(random.choice(["A", "B", "C"]))
print(random.sample(range(52), 5))   # poker hand

# Monte Carlo: estimate P(sum of two dice == 7) by simulation
hits = sum(
    1 for _ in range(100_000)
    if random.randint(1,6) + random.randint(1,6) == 7
)
print(hits / 100_000)   # about 0.167 = 6/36

The rules, and why independence is the assumption people forget

Programming with probability needs only four rules, and the one that causes every bug is the last. Addition: mutually exclusive outcomes add — the probability of a 1 or a 6 on a die is 1/6 + 1/6, and this is only valid because they cannot both happen. Multiplication for independent events: two coin tosses both heads is 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. Addition of complements: the probability of not A is 1 minus the probability of A, which is correct always and is the most reliable arithmetic in the subject — most conditional probability problems are easier when you compute the complement. And conditional probability: P(A given B) is P(A and B) / P(B), the probability of A restricted to the cases where B holds. It is the only genuinely new idea here and the one that trips people, because the conditioning does not multiply — it divides, and the intuition that a condition makes things more likely or less likely without accounting for how likely it was is what produces wrong answers.

Then independence, stated precisely because it is almost never true by assumption. Two events are independent when knowing one tells you nothing about the other, and that is a claim about the situation, not a default. Two coin tosses are independent. Two cards drawn from a deck are not — knowing the first was an ace changes the odds for the second, which is why a blackjack double-counts aces. A user's height and their basketball skill are not independent, and neither are two measurements of the same quantity. And the consequence that matters: conditional probability equals the product only under independence, so every place you multiply probabilities is a place you are asserting independence, and the assertion is wrong far more often than people assume. Two practical corollaries. Bayes' theorem is conditional probability rearranged — solving for the reverse direction — and it is the shape of every "I observed this, what are the odds" question: given a positive test and a 1 per cent base rate, the probability of having the condition is nowhere near 99 per cent, because the base rate was multiplied in the numerator too and nobody remembered it. And with two overlapping symptoms the probability of both is not the product unless the symptoms are independent, which symptoms usually are not — which is why "how likely is it that I have both" is a question with a much larger answer than intuition suggests.

/* Four rules, and the one that causes every bug. */
const RULES = [
  { r: 'addition', for: 'mutually exclusive outcomes', example: 'a 1 or a 6 on a die is 1/6 + 1/6',
    validBecause: 'they cannot both happen' },
  { r: 'multiplication', for: 'INDEPENDENT events', example: 'two coin tosses both heads is 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4' },
  { r: 'complements', formula: 'P(not A) = 1 - P(A)', alwaysCorrect: true,
    note: 'the most reliable arithmetic in the subject - most conditional probability problems are easier when you compute the complement' },
  { r: 'conditional probability', formula: 'P(A given B) = P(A and B) / P(B)',
    onlyGenuinelyNewIdea: true, whatTripsPeople: true,
    theKey: 'the conditioning does NOT MULTIPLY, it DIVIDES',
    wrongIntuition: 'that a condition makes things more likely or less likely without accounting for how likely it was' },
];

/* Independence, stated precisely. */
const INDEPENDENCE = {
  is: 'two events are independent when knowing one tells you nothing about the other',
  isAClaimAbout: 'the situation, not a default',
  examples: {
    independent: ['two coin tosses'],
    notIndependent: ['two cards from a deck - knowing the first was an ace changes the odds for the second',
      'a users height and their basketball skill',
      'two measurements of the same quantity'],
    consequence: 'why blackjack double-counts aces' },
  consequence: 'conditional probability equals the product ONLY under independence',
  therefore: 'every place you multiply probabilities is a place you are asserting independence',
  reality: 'the assertion is wrong far more often than people assume',
};
const COROLLARIES = [
  { c: 'Bayes theorem', is: 'conditional probability rearranged to solve for the reverse direction',
    shapeOf: 'every I observed this, what are the odds question',
    worked: 'given a positive test and a 1 per cent base rate, the probability of having the condition is nowhere near 99 per cent',
    why: 'the base rate was multiplied in the numerator too, and nobody remembered it' },
  { c: 'two overlapping symptoms',
    notTheProduct: 'the probability of both is not the product unless the symptoms are independent',
    reality: 'symptoms usually are not independent',
    result: 'how likely is it that I have both is a question with a much larger answer than intuition suggests' },
];

Simulation, and the four ways randomness breaks code

There is a legitimate technique here that deserves its own name: Monte Carlo estimation — run the experiment many times with random inputs and count how often an outcome occurs. The estimate converges to the true probability as the square root of the number of trials, so a hundred thousand runs gets you roughly three decimal places of accuracy, which is often plenty and is much better than deriving the closed form. It is genuinely the right tool for a probability too tangled to derive and too small to enumerate, and it appears in real work in performance estimation, reliability analysis and Monte Carlo integration. But four properties of randomness cause bugs, and all four are avoidable. Seed the generator when you need reproducibility. A seeded generator gives the same sequence every run, so a failure can be reproduced — and this is not optional for any test involving randomness, because a test that fails once in a hundred runs is a test you cannot use. Do not use randomness for security. random is not a cryptographically secure generator; its output is predictable from a small amount of observed output, which makes it useless for tokens, passwords, session identifiers and nonces. Use the operating system's generator for those, always. Do not seed with the clock on purpose. The same seed in two processes running at the same moment produces the same sequence, and if it matters at all, that is a bug — and the case where it genuinely matters is tests, which is why "seeded, deterministic" is the correct default and "seeded from the clock" is the correct default for genuinely independent runs. Do not confuse a probability with a count. A simulation tells you the frequency an outcome occurred, not that the next one is more or less likely — and code that returns "the most common observed result" is reading a frequency as if it were a mechanism, which is the single most common statistical error in otherwise competent code.

/* The legitimate technique. */
const MONTE_CARLO = {
  is: 'run the experiment many times with random inputs and count how often an outcome occurs',
  convergence: 'the estimate converges to the true probability as the SQUARE ROOT of the number of trials',
  arithmetic: 'a hundred thousand runs gets roughly three decimal places',
  rightToolWhen: 'a probability too tangled to derive and too small to enumerate',
  appearsIn: ['performance estimation', 'reliability analysis', 'Monte Carlo integration'],
};

/* Four ways randomness breaks code, all avoidable. */
const BREAKS = [
  { f: 'not seeding when you need reproducibility',
    fix: 'a seeded generator gives the same sequence every run, so a failure can be reproduced',
    notOptional: 'for any test involving randomness, because a test that fails once in a hundred runs is a test you cannot use' },
  { f: 'using randomness for security',
    detail: 'random is not a cryptographically secure generator; its output is predictable from a small amount of observed output',
    wrongFor: ['tokens', 'passwords', 'session identifiers', 'nonces'],
    fix: 'the operating systems generator, always' },
  { f: 'seeding with the clock on purpose',
    detail: 'the same seed in two processes at the same moment produces the same sequence',
    whereItMatters: 'if it matters at all, that is a bug',
    genuinelyRightCase: 'tests',
    defaults: ['seeded and deterministic is the correct default',
      'seeded from the clock is the correct default for genuinely independent runs'] },
  { f: 'confusing a probability with a count',
    detail: 'a simulation tells you the frequency an outcome occurred, not that the next one is more or less likely',
    symptom: 'code that returns the most common observed result is reading a frequency as if it were a mechanism',
    claim: 'the single most common statistical error in otherwise competent code' },
];

A seeded random generator plus a 100,000-roll Monte Carlo that lands near the true 6/36 probability of rolling a seven.

7.6 Boolean algebra + truth tables in code — a bridge to Ch. 10

Boolean algebra reasons over true and false using AND, OR, NOT, and XOR, guided by laws such as De Morgan’s. It is the logic inside CPUs and also the logic behind your if conditions and bitwise operations in code. Truth tables let you use code to evaluate every combination, verifying your reasoning and previewing Chapter Ten.

Booleans ARE the bit logic inside CPUs (and in if/while). Build truth tables in code to check your own logic — a habit that saves real bugs:

def truth_table(fn):                 # fn: (p, q) -> bool
    for a in (True, False):
        for b in (True, False):
            print(a, b, "->", fn(a, b))

def implies(p, q):                   # p implies q, in not/or form
    return (not p) or q

truth_table(implies)
# True True -> True
# True False -> False
# False True -> True
# False False -> True   <- matches p -> q table in 7.1

truth_table prints every input combination for a function — same idea as the 7.1 tables, but generated by code.

The laws, and why they are worth memorising

Boolean algebra is not a curiosity — it is the algebra that your if statements are written in, and knowing its laws is what lets you take a condition you cannot reason about and turn it into one you can. The core is five identities and everything else is derived from them. Identity: A and true is A, A or false is A. Domination: A or true is true, A and false is false. Idempotence: A and A is A, A or A is A. Complement: A and not A is false, A or not A is true. Associativity, commutativity, distributivity: brackets can be rearranged within an operator, the operands of an operator can be swapped, and A and (B or C) equals (A and B) or (A and C) in both directions. Then the two that carry the most practical weight: absorption — A and (A or B) is just A, and A or (A and B) is just A — and De Morgan's laws, which say not (A and B) is (not A) or (not B) and not (A or B) is (not A) and (not B).

Then why this matters in practice, which is not about writing elegant expressions but about seeing things. Short-circuit evaluation is absorption in action. A and f(A) does not call f when A is false, because false and anything is false — and this is not an optimisation the language applies, it is the meaning of the operator, and it is why if obj is not None and obj.value > 0 is safe while if obj.value > 0 and obj is not None raises. Distributivity lets you restructure a test. (A or B) and C is (A and C) or (B and C), which means a guard clause at the top of a function is literally the same condition as an extra and clause, and the guard form is better because it can return early. De Morgan turns a negated conjunction into a disjunction, which is almost always the readable direction: not (status == 'paid' and amount > 0) is status != 'paid' or amount <= 0, and the second reads as a list of things that disqualify rather than as a double negative. And idempotence explains a common bug: if x in seen and x in seen: is the same test twice, and if you wrote something like that expecting it to mean "seen twice", the boolean algebra says it can only ever mean "in seen" — which is the actual mechanism behind a whole family of logic bugs where a repeated condition was expected to count occurrences.

/* Core identities, and everything else is derived from these. */
const LAWS = {
  identity: 'A and true is A; A or false is A',
  domination: 'A or true is true; A and false is false',
  idempotence: 'A and A is A; A or A is A',
  complement: 'A and not A is false; A or not A is true',
  associative: 'brackets can be rearranged within an operator',
  commutative: 'the operands of an operator can be swapped',
  distributive: 'A and (B or C) equals (A and B) or (A and C), in both directions',
  heavyweights: {
    absorption: 'A and (A or B) is just A; A or (A and B) is just A',
    deMorgan: ['not (A and B) is (not A) or (not B)',
      'not (A or B) is (not A) and (not B)'],
  },
};

/* Why this matters: seeing, not elegance. */
const IN_PRACTICE = [
  { c: 'short-circuit evaluation is absorption in action',
    detail: 'A and f(A) does not call f when A is false, because false and anything is false',
    notAnOptimisation: 'this is the MEANING of the operator',
    safe: 'if obj is not None and obj.value > 0',
    unsafe: 'if obj.value > 0 and obj is not None raises' },
  { c: 'distributivity lets you restructure a test',
    detail: '(A or B) and C is (A and C) or (B and C)',
    consequence: 'a guard clause at the top of a function is literally the same condition as an extra and clause',
    whyGuardIsBetter: 'it can return early' },
  { c: 'De Morgan turns a negated conjunction into a disjunction',
    detail: 'not (status == paid and amount > 0) is status != paid or amount <= 0',
    whyReadable: 'the second reads as a list of things that disqualify rather than as a double negative' },
  { c: 'idempotence explains a common bug',
    detail: 'if x in seen and x in seen is the same test twice',
    expectedWrongly: 'that it means seen twice',
    reality: 'it can only ever mean in seen',
    consequence: 'the actual mechanism behind a family of logic bugs where a repeated condition was expected to count occurrences' },
];

Truth tables, and the classification that makes them useful

A truth table is every input combination with the output for each, and there are exactly 2ⁿ rows for n variables — which is why they stay useful for two or three variables and stop being useful at six. Its real value is not arithmetic but classification, because a Boolean function's whole character is determined by which of four kinds it is. A tautology is always true regardless of input; a condition that is a tautology is dead code that will never fire, and a test expecting it to catch something is broken. A contradiction is always false, which is how you recognise unreachable code and a condition that can never hold. A contradiction's dual, a contingency, is true for some inputs and false for others — the ordinary case, and the only one whose behaviour depends on the data. And a contradiction in the form of a condition whose negation is a tautology is one of the pairings worth recognising, because implication is defined as not A or B and that is why the equivalence in the exercise is always true. Two consequences in code. Enumerating small truth tables finds bugs you cannot see. With two booleans there are sixteen cases and you can check all of them; a condition that looks right on the four cases you tried can be wrong on a fifth. This is a genuinely practical technique — write the condition, generate the table, and read the output for rows where the answer is obviously wrong. And tautologies and contradictions are dead code that should be deleted, because a condition that is always true or always false is telling the reader something about the code that the code does not otherwise say, and every future reader must work it out again.

/* Classification: a Boolean functions whole character is which of four kinds it is. */
const KINDS = [
  { k: 'tautology', is: 'always true regardless of input',
    inCode: 'dead code that will never fire',
    symptom: 'a test expecting it to catch something is broken' },
  { k: 'contradiction', is: 'always false',
    recognises: 'unreachable code, and a condition that can never hold' },
  { k: 'contingency', is: 'true for some inputs and false for others',
    note: 'the ordinary case, and the only one whose behaviour depends on the data',
    dualOf: 'contradiction' },
];
const IMPLICATION_NOTE = 'implication is DEFINED AS not A or B, which is why the equivalence in the exercise is a tautology - always true';
const CONSEQUENCES = [
  { c: 'enumerate small truth tables to find bugs you cannot see',
    fact: 'with two booleans there are sixteen cases and you can check all of them',
    whyItWorks: 'a condition that looks right on the four cases you tried can be wrong on a fifth',
    practice: ['write the condition', 'generate the table', 'read the output for rows where the answer is obviously wrong'] },
  { c: 'tautologies and contradictions are dead code that should be deleted',
    why: 'a condition that is always true or always false tells the reader something the code does not otherwise say',
    cost: 'every future reader must work it out again' },
];
const ROWS = 'exactly 2^n rows for n variables - which is why they stay useful at two or three variables and stop being useful at six';

De Morgan keeps striking. When a condition seems backwards, apply De Morgan: rewrite not (A and B) as (not A) or (not B), then re-read the sentence in English. It consistently un-blocks bugs.

8 · Data Structures II — The Core Toolbox

This chapter completes the core data structure toolbox: hash tables, stacks, queues, linked lists, trees, heaps, graphs, tries, the LRU cache, and union-find. For each structure you learn its operations, costs, and the problems it suits. Interviewers love these topics, and they sit behind almost everything you will build.

8.1 Hash tables — the magic O(1) box8.2 Stack and queue — the two simple workhorses8.3 Linked lists8.4 Trees and binary search trees8.5 Heaps — fast min/max8.6 Graphs — networks of everything8.7 Tries — the string specialist8.8 The LRU cache — your first mini design problem8.9 Union-Find (disjoint sets)

These are the structures behind almost everything: stacks, queues, linked lists, trees, hash tables, and graphs. Learn the operations, the costs, and when to reach for each — this is the "aha" that data-structure courses are really about.

8.1 Hash tables — the magic O(1) box

A hash table maps keys to values by running each key through a hash function that picks a bucket, giving near-constant-time insert, lookup, and delete. Collisions are handled by chaining or open addressing. Python’s dict and set are hash tables, making them the first tool for counting and duplicate checks.

A hash table (Python dict) stores key→value. The trick: a hash function converts any key (string, int, …) into a numeric bucket. To look up a key you hash it → go straight to its bucket → O(1).

def hash_str(text, size=10):
    """A toy hash: add char codes, mod size -- real hashes are much better."""
    return sum(ord(c) for c in text) % size   # buckets = codes wrapped to range

print(hash_str("milo"))     # some bucket number
print(hash_str("bella"))

A toy hash adds character codes and takes the remainder; notice how collisions are handled by real hash tables.

Collisions happen when two keys hash to the same bucket — real hash tables handle them with chaining (a tiny list per bucket) or open addressing. A bad hash function (e.g. all keys → bucket 3) collapses the table into one big list → O(n). That’s why good hashing matters.

How it works, and the three numbers that define its behaviour

A hash table is an array of buckets plus a hash function that maps a key to a bucket index, and understanding the mechanism makes the behaviour predictable rather than magical. The hash function must be fast and must spread keys. It must be cheap — it runs on every operation — and its output must distribute keys across buckets, because every pathology below follows from a hash that clusters. Collisions are certain, not possible. There are more possible keys than buckets, so two keys will hash to the same slot; the question is only what happens then. Two answers: separate chaining, where each bucket holds a small list of entries and a lookup scans it, or open addressing, where the table holds entries only and a collision probes for the next free slot. Chaining is simpler and degrades more gracefully; open addressing has better cache behaviour and requires a good probe sequence. The load factor is the ratio of entries to buckets, and it is the number that determines everything: it should stay below about 0.75 for chaining and 0.5 for open addressing, and when it is exceeded the table must grow and rehash every entry, which is why a table's worst case is a sudden pause rather than a gradual slowdown. That rehash is amortised — over many operations the cost per insertion is constant — but it is a real cost with a real memory spike, and it is why a table built once from a known size is faster than one grown.

Then the complexity claims, stated with their conditions, because the conditions are what people forget. Lookup, insert and delete are O(1) on average and O(n) in the worst case — the worst case is every key colliding into one bucket, which reduces the table to a list. Enumeration is O(n + capacity), not O(n), because you must visit every bucket including the empty ones — a detail that makes iterating a large sparse table surprisingly expensive. Order is not defined. Modern Python's dict preserves insertion order as a documented property, but hash-set iteration order follows the hash values and will differ between processes with different hash seeds, so never write code whose output depends on set order — sort before you output, or use a dict if you need order. And resizing invalidates nothing but costs a lot. Growing the table rehashes every key, so pre-sizing a table you know will hold a million entries is a real and worthwhile optimisation, and building one by repeated addition is a real and avoidable cost.

/* The mechanism. */
const MECHANISM = {
  is: 'an array of buckets plus a hash function mapping a key to a bucket index',
  whyUnderstandIt: 'it makes the behaviour predictable rather than magical',
  hashFunction: { mustBe: 'fast and must spread keys',
    fastWhy: 'it runs on every operation',
    spreadWhy: 'every pathology below follows from a hash that clusters' },
  collisions: { certain: 'not possible - CERTAIN', why: 'more possible keys than buckets, so two keys will hash to the same slot',
    question: 'only what happens then',
    twoAnswers: [
      { a: 'separate chaining', does: 'each bucket holds a small list of entries and a lookup scans it',

      { a: 'open addressing', does: 'the table holds entries only and a collision probes for the next free slot',
        traits: 'better cache behaviour, requires a good probe sequence' } ] },
  loadFactor: { is: 'the ratio of entries to buckets', determinesEverything: true,

    whenExceeded: 'the table must grow and rehash every entry',
    whyWorstCase: 'a sudden pause rather than a gradual slowdown',
    amortised: 'over many operations the cost per insertion is constant',
    butReal: 'a real cost with a real memory spike',
    consequence: 'a table built once from a known size is faster than one grown' },
};

/* Complexity, with the conditions. */
const COMPLEXITY = [
  { op: 'lookup, insert, delete', avg: 'O(1)', worst: 'O(n)',
    worstBecause: 'every key colliding into one bucket reduces the table to a list' },
  { op: 'enumeration', cost: 'O(n + capacity), NOT O(n)',
    why: 'you must visit every bucket including the empty ones',
    consequence: 'iterating a large sparse table is surprisingly expensive' },
  { op: 'order', notDefined: true,
    nuance: 'modern Pythons dict preserves insertion order as a documented property',
    but: 'hash-SET iteration order follows the hash values and differs between processes with different hash seeds',
    rule: 'never write code whose output depends on set order - sort before you output, or use a dict if you need order' },
  { op: 'resizing', invalidatesNothing: true, costsALot: true,
    optimisation: 'pre-sizing a table you know will hold a million entries is real and worthwhile',
    avoidable: 'building one by repeated addition' },
];

The requirements, the problems, and where a dictionary is the wrong answer

Three requirements any hash-based structure has, and violating them is where the subtle bugs come from. Keys must be hashable — Python enforces this, so a list key raises immediately, which is a good failure. Keys must not change while stored — this is the one Python does not enforce, and a mutable key becomes unfindable the moment it mutates, with its entry silently leaked. Equality must agree with hashing: two keys that compare equal must hash equal, and if they do not, a lookup can fail for a key that is demonstrably in the dictionary. This is why a class defining __eq__ should also define __hash__, and why inheriting from str and overriding __eq__ without __hash__ silently makes your class unhashable.

Then where a dictionary is the wrong answer, which is worth stating because reach-for-a-dict is a reflex that should sometimes be overridden. When you need order plus range queries — a dict gives no range lookup, so "all users created this month" is a full scan and an ordered structure answers it in O(log n). When you need the smallest or largest key, a dict gives no min without a scan, and a sorted structure answers it directly. When the data is adversarial — a keyed hash defends against it, but if you cannot choose the hash, an attacker controlling the keys can force O(n) behaviour and this is a real denial-of-service vector in web frameworks. When keys are not naturally unique — a dict overwrites, so two records with the same key lose one silently, and a list of pairs does not. And when memory is the constraint — a dict carries per-entry overhead that a sorted array does not, which matters at tens of millions of entries.

/* Three requirements, and which are enforced. */
const REQUIREMENTS = [
  { r: 'keys must be hashable', enforced: true,
    goodFailure: 'a list key raises immediately' },
  { r: 'keys must NOT CHANGE while stored', enforced: false,
    symptom: 'a mutable key becomes unfindable the moment it mutates, with its entry silently leaked',
    note: 'the one Python does not enforce' },
  { r: 'equality must agree with hashing', rule: 'two keys that compare equal must hash equal',
    symptom: 'otherwise a lookup can fail for a key that is demonstrably in the dictionary',
    corollaries: ['a class defining __eq__ should also define __hash__',
      'inheriting from str and overriding __eq__ without __hash__ silently makes your class unhashable'] },
];

/* Where a dictionary is the wrong answer. */
const WRONG_WHEN = [
  { when: 'you need order plus range queries', example: 'all users created this month',
    dictCost: 'a full scan', betterCost: 'O(log n) with an ordered structure' },
  { when: 'you need the smallest or largest key',
    dictCost: 'no min without a scan', better: 'a sorted structure answers it directly' },
  { when: 'the data is adversarial',
    defence: 'a keyed hash defends against it',
    withoutIt: 'an attacker controlling the keys can force O(n) behaviour',
    reality: 'a real denial-of-service vector in web frameworks' },
  { when: 'keys are not naturally unique',
    dictBehaviour: 'overwrites, so two records with the same key lose one silently',
    better: 'a list of pairs' },
  { when: 'memory is the constraint',
    detail: 'a dict carries per-entry overhead a sorted array does not',
    magnitude: 'matters at tens of millions of entries' },
];

Usable immediately: any "count occurrences", "detect duplicates", "memoise results" problem → reach for a dict/set first. Practice rewiring "scan every element" instincts into "dict lookup".

8.2 Stack and queue — the two simple workhorses

A stack removes items in last-in-first-out order, while a queue removes them first-in-first-out. Stacks sit behind undo, function call stacks, and backtracking; queues drive scheduling and breadth-first search. If you only know two data structures, know these two and where each applies.

StructurePolicyAnalogyReal uses
StackLIFO — Last In, First OutStack of platesUndo (Ctrl+Z), function call stacks, expression evaluation, "back" in browsers
QueueFIFO — First In, First OutWaiting lineTask scheduling, print queues, BFS graph traversal, message queues in servers
# Python list makes a fine stack
stack = []
stack.append(1); stack.append(2); stack.append(3)
print(stack.pop())    # 3  (LIFO)
print(stack)          # [1, 2]

# deque (double-ended queue) makes a proper queue
from collections import deque
q = deque()
q.append("ada"); q.append("grace"); q.append("linus")
print(q.popleft())    # ada  (FIFO)
print(q.popleft())    # grace

A Python list doubles as a LIFO stack, while deque gives the efficient FIFO queue for real workloads.

The abstraction, and why it is called an ADT

A stack and a queue are abstract data types: a specification of what operations exist and what they guarantee, with no statement of how they are implemented. That separation is the entire reason they are worth learning separately from the arrays that implement them, and it is the distinction that makes the code portable — a stack backed by a list and a stack backed by an array are interchangeable at every call site, because the caller never knew which it was using. The guarantee is about behaviour, not structure: a stack is last-in-first-out, which means the most recent thing added is the next thing removed, and every valid implementation preserves that order; a queue is first-in-first-out, the oldest thing added is the next removed. Everything else about them is implementation. The three operations are push/pop and enqueue/dequeue, both O(1) — and the third operation is what makes them more than a bag: peek, which reports the next element without removing it, and which is what makes a stack usable for anything that needs to inspect before committing.

Then what stacks and queues are actually for, because this is the part that turns a data structure into a tool. A stack models nested scope. Function calls push a frame and return pops it, which is precisely why a recursive function whose recursion never ends overflows: the language's call stack is a real stack, and the frames are real entries. The same structure explains why a syntax parser works — nested brackets, nesting in expressions, and nesting in markup are all balanced, and a stack is the structure that verifies balance. A queue models fairness and order of arrival. Request handling, print jobs, work distribution to servers, and breadth-first traversal all process items in the order they arrived, which is exactly the guarantee a queue provides. A deque extends a queue to both ends, which is what sliding-window algorithms need — add on the right, remove from the left — and it is also what makes a stack-with-a-faster-tail possible. And a priority queue is a different thing entirely: it is not a queue but a heap, where the next element out is the largest or smallest rather than the oldest, and confusing the two is the source of most scheduling bugs.

/* Abstract data type: a specification with no statement of implementation. */
const ADT = {
  is: 'a specification of what operations exist and what they guarantee, with no statement of how they are implemented',
  whySeparate: 'that separation is the entire reason they are worth learning separately from the arrays that implement them',
  portability: 'a stack backed by a list and one backed by an array are interchangeable at every call site',
  guaranteeIs: 'about BEHAVIOUR, not structure',
  stack: { is: 'last-in-first-out', means: 'the most recent thing added is the next thing removed',
    invariant: 'every valid implementation preserves that order' },
  queue: { is: 'first-in-first-out', means: 'the oldest thing added is the next removed' },
  operations: ['push and pop', 'enqueue and dequeue', 'all O(1)'],
  thirdOperation: { peek: 'reports the next element without removing it',
    whyItMatters: 'what makes a stack usable for anything that needs to inspect before committing' },
};

/* What they are for. */
const FOR = [
  { s: 'a stack models NESTED SCOPE', how: 'function calls push a frame and return pops it',
    evidence: 'why a recursive function that never ends overflows - the languages call stack is a real stack with real entries',
    sameStructure: ['nested brackets', 'nesting in expressions', 'nesting in markup'],
    consequence: 'a stack is the structure that verifies balance' },
  { s: 'a queue models FAIRNESS AND ORDER OF ARRIVAL', instances: ['request handling', 'print jobs',
    'work distribution to servers', 'breadth-first traversal'] },
  { s: 'a deque extends a queue to BOTH ends', how: 'add on the right, remove from the left',
    neededBy: 'sliding-window algorithms',
    alsoEnables: 'a stack-with-a-faster-tail' },
  { s: 'a priority queue is a DIFFERENT THING',
    isNot: 'a queue - it is a heap',
    rule: 'the next element out is the largest or smallest rather than the oldest',
    consequence: 'confusing the two is the source of most scheduling bugs' },
];

The implementation choice, and the bugs each one has

Three implementation choices, and the decision between them is a memory-versus-speed trade with a specific answer. A stack on an array with the top at the end: push and pop are O(1) and nothing is wasted, but the array must grow, and growing means copying — so pushes are amortised O(1) and occasionally O(n), which is the same doubling trick as a dynamic array and the same latency-spike consequence. A stack on a linked list: no resize, and if you keep a pointer to both ends, both push and pop are O(1) with no amortisation caveat — at the cost of a pointer per element and terrible cache behaviour. A queue on an array: the trap. Removing from the front of an array is O(n) because everything shifts, so a naive queue on an array is O(n) per dequeue — which is not a queue at all, it is a slow list. The standard fix is a circular buffer: keep head and tail indices and treat the array as wrapping, so dequeue advances an index rather than shifting anything, and O(1) for everything. Alternatively a linked list with a tail pointer, which is O(1) and conceptually clearer but allocates a node per element.

Then the bugs, and each is a specific consequence of the structure. Off-by-one in the circular buffer. Full and empty are the same state unless you keep a count or leave one slot unused — the single most common bug in the whole family, and the fix is to be explicit about which convention you chose. Popping an empty stack. O(1) data structures have no bounds check unless you write one, so the failure is an index error or an exception rather than a clean return, and code that pops without checking is one refactor away from crashing on an edge case. Losing the tail. The singly-linked-list queue whose enqueue is O(n) because it walks to the end every time — adding a tail pointer turns it O(1) and is the difference between a queue that works and one that does not. Reusing a deque for two purposes. Pushing the right and popping the left is the sliding-window shape; mixing in a pop-the-right somewhere makes every reasoning about the contents wrong. And treating a queue as ordered storage. A queue gives insertion order, not sort order — the data comes out as it went in, and if you need it sorted that is a different problem requiring a different structure.

    cost: 'a pointer per element and terrible cache behaviour' },
