Exercise 8.2 — balanced brackets

Write is_balanced(s) that returns True if parentheses/brackets are properly nested: (()) ✓, ([{}]) ✓, (] ✗, ) ✗. Classic interview problem. Push openers onto a stack; on a closer, the top must match. (Solution hint in the appendix.)

8.3 Linked lists

A linked list chains nodes where each holds a value and a pointer to the next, so insertion and deletion at the front are constant time but indexing is linear. They teach pointer thinking, but arrays win in practice because of cache behaviour and memory layout. You mostly learn linked lists for interviews and foundational understanding.

A linked list is a chain of nodes; each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node.

class Node:
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value
        self.next = None

class LinkedList:
    def __init__(self):
        self.head = None

    def prepend(self, value):              # add at front: O(1)
        node = Node(value)
        node.next = self.head
        self.head = node                   # new node becomes the front

    def search(self, target):
        cur = self.head
        while cur:
            if cur.value == target:
                return True
            cur = cur.next
        return False                       # O(n)

    def as_list(self):
        out, cur = [], self.head
        while cur:
            out.append(cur.value); cur = cur.next   # collect in order
        return out

ll = LinkedList()
ll.prepend(3); ll.prepend(2); ll.prepend(1)
print(ll.as_list())      # [1, 2, 3]
print(ll.search(2))      # True

A hand-rolled linked list with O(1) front insertion and an O(n) walk for search — the pointer thinking that interviewers want to see.

Array (Python list)Linked list
Index accessO(1) — instantO(n) — walk the chain
Insert at frontO(n) — must shift everythingO(1) — point a pointer
Cache-friendlinessExcellent (contiguous memory)Poor (nodes scattered)
Real-world useDefault everywhereHash-table buckets, LRU caches, some OS lists

The trade, stated as a table

A linked list is a chain of nodes, each holding a value and a pointer to the next. Its virtues and its costs follow from one fact: the nodes are separate objects in memory, wherever the allocator put them. O(1) insert and delete once you have the node — you change two pointers, and nothing else moves, which is the genuine advantage and the reason every textbook shows it. O(n) access by position — to reach index 500 you walk 500 links. O(n) search — no random access, so finding is a walk. No allocation on append if the nodes were pre-allocated, and O(n) extra memory for the pointers themselves — every node costs a value plus a pointer, so a list of small values uses noticeably more memory than an array of the same values. And bad locality — which is the fact that decides the whole question in practice. An array walks memory in ascending order and the CPU prefetcher anticipates it; a linked list jumps to addresses chosen by an allocator and every step is a likely cache miss. The honest summary: the linked list is asymptotically fine and practically slower, and that gap is the reason almost nobody writes one in application code.

Then the three variants, because each exists to fix a specific weakness. The singly linked list is the basic chain, and its weakness is that removing a node requires knowing its predecessor — so a walk to find it, which makes deletion O(n) even in the middle. The doubly linked list adds a backward pointer, and that one extra pointer per node buys the ability to delete a node when you have only that node: go to the previous, fix its next, fix the node's own previous. Deletion becomes O(1) and backward traversal becomes possible, at the cost of eight more bytes per node and the invariant burden of maintaining two links. The circular linked list connects the last node back to the first, which turns "the end" into something you can reach from anywhere — the mechanism behind a round-robin scheduler, a circular buffer and the tail pointer of a queue. And the discipline that makes all three safe to write: the removal cases. Removing the head, removing the tail, removing the only node, and removing the middle are four distinct cases with four distinct pointer updates, and code that handles the middle and forgets the tail is the normal outcome. Write all four explicitly, in that order, and test them all — this is the single best argument for writing linked-list code by hand once.

/* The trade, following from one fact. */
const ONE_FACT = 'the nodes are separate objects in memory, wherever the allocator put them';
const TRADE = {
  insertDelete: 'O(1) once you have the node - two pointers change and nothing else moves',
  accessByPosition: 'O(n) - reaching index 500 means walking 500 links',
  search: 'O(n) - no random access, so finding is a walk',
  memory: 'O(n) extra for the pointers - every node costs a value plus a pointer, so a list of small values uses noticeably more than an array',
  locality: 'BAD - an array walks memory in ascending order and the prefetcher anticipates it; a linked list jumps to allocator-chosen addresses and every step is a likely cache miss',
  summary: 'asymptotically fine and practically slower - that gap is why almost nobody writes one in application code',
};

/* Three variants, each fixing a specific weakness. */
const VARIANTS = [
  { v: 'singly linked', shape: 'the basic chain',
    weakness: 'removing a node requires knowing its PREDECESSOR, so a walk to find it',
    consequence: 'deletion is O(n) even in the middle' },
  { v: 'doubly linked', adds: 'a backward pointer',
    buys: ['O(1) deletion when you have only that node - go to the previous, fix its next, fix the nodes previous',
      'the ability to traverse backward'],
    costs: ['eight more bytes per node', 'the invariant burden of maintaining two links'] },
  { v: 'circular', adds: 'the last node connects back to the first',
    buys: 'the end is reachable from anywhere',
    behind: ['a round-robin scheduler', 'a circular buffer', 'the tail pointer of a queue'] },
];
const DISCIPLINE = {
  what: 'the removal cases',
  howMany: 'four distinct cases with four distinct pointer updates',
  normalOutcome: 'code that handles the middle and forgets the tail',
  how: ['write all four explicitly, in that order: head, tail, only node, middle', 'test them all'],
  claim: 'the single best argument for writing linked-list code by hand once',
};

Reality check: in most modern languages arrays win for most jobs; linked lists are taught because pointer thinking and structural thinking are core skills, and they’re essential to many interviews and to systems like GCs, caches, and OS queues.

8.4 Trees and binary search trees

A tree is a hierarchy of nodes, and a binary search tree keeps smaller values on the left and larger on the right of each node, giving logarithmic search, insert, and delete. The catch is that inserting sorted data degrades the tree into a linear chain. Balanced variants like AVL and red-black trees fix that weakness.

A tree is a hierarchy: a root with children, each child with its own children. Binary search tree (BST): every node’s left subtree is smaller, right subtree larger — giving O(log n) search if balanced.

class BSTNode:
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def insert(node, value):
    if node is None:
        return BSTNode(value)              # hang new node in the empty slot
    if value < node.value:                 # smaller values go left
        node.left = insert(node.left, value)
    else:
        node.right = insert(node.right, value)
    return node

def contains(node, value):
    if node is None:
        return False
    if node.value == value:
        return True
    if value < node.value:                 # narrow search to the left half
        return contains(node.left, value)
    return contains(node.right, value)

root = None
for v in [8, 3, 10, 1, 6, 14]:
    root = insert(root, v)
print(contains(root, 6))    # True
print(contains(root, 7))    # False

Insertions and lookups recurse left or right, which yields O(log n) only when the tree stays balanced.

Traversals — visit every node in order. The three canonical orders: in-order (left, self, right — a BST in-order yields sorted output!), pre-order, post-order. In-order of the tree above prints 1 3 6 8 10 14.

def in_order(node):
    if node:
        yield from in_order(node.left)     # left subtree, then value, then right
        yield node.value
        yield from in_order(node.right)

print(list(in_order(root)))   # [1, 3, 6, 8, 10, 14]  -- sorted!

In-order traversal yields a BST’s values in sorted order, which is exactly why BSTs power ordered containers.

The three traversals, and why the order matters more than the code

A binary tree has no natural order, and the traversal order is something you choose to satisfy a purpose — which means picking the wrong order is the single most common tree bug and it looks like a data bug rather than an algorithm bug. Pre-order visits the node, then the left subtree, then the right. Use it when the answer is per-node: copying a tree, serialising it, computing a value that depends on a node and its children — and the rule of thumb is root first whenever the parent must act before its children, which covers the majority of tree problems. In-order visits the left subtree, the node, then the right — and its defining property is the reason it is worth knowing separately: on a binary search tree it yields the values in sorted order. That is not a coincidence to memorise but a consequence to understand: an in-order walk always puts smaller things to the left of the node, so the output is ascending. Post-order visits the children, then the node — and its property is the mirror: use it when children must be computed before the parent acts, which is every case where the node's value depends on its children's values, every case involving freeing or deleting a tree (you must free the children before the parent), and every case where a subtree must be completed before you can decide anything about it. The confusion worth internalising: pre-order is "act now, then children", post-order is "children, then act now", and if you can remember that phrase the order question is answered without memorising three names.

Then the binary search tree and its promise, and the promise's exact condition. A BST keeps smaller values in the left subtree and larger in the right, and when the tree is balanced, search, insert and delete are all O(log n) — because each comparison discards half the tree. The condition is doing all the work, and it fails in a specific, predictable way: inserting already-sorted data produces a tree that is a linked list, because each new value is the largest and goes right every time, so the height is n and every operation is O(n). That is not a hypothetical; it is what happens whenever data arrives in order, which sorted data, incrementing ids, timestamps and index-ordered reads all are. The fix is a self-balancing tree, and the two classical families differ in how they rebalance. AVL trees maintain a strict height balance at every node, giving the shortest possible height and therefore the fastest lookup — at the cost of more rotations on insert and delete, so they suit read-heavy workloads. Red-black trees allow a looser balance with colour rules, giving faster updates at a cost of up to one extra level of height, so they suit mixed workloads. Both give O(log n) worst case, which is the guarantee that matters, and the practical consequence is that a library's ordered map is one of these rather than a plain BST.

/* Three traversals; the order is chosen to satisfy a purpose. */
const TRAVERSALS = [
  { t: 'pre-order', order: 'node, left subtree, right subtree',
    use: 'when the answer is PER-NODE',
    instances: ['copying a tree', 'serialising it', 'computing a value that depends on a node and its children'],
    ruleOfThumb: 'ROOT FIRST whenever the parent must act before its children',
    covers: 'the majority of tree problems',
    phrase: 'act now, then children' },
  { t: 'in-order', order: 'left subtree, node, right subtree',
    definingProperty: 'on a binary search tree it yields the values in SORTED order',
    notMemoriseBut: 'understand it - an in-order walk always puts smaller things left of the node, so the output is ascending' },
  { t: 'post-order', order: 'children, then node',
    property: 'the mirror of pre-order',
    use: 'when children must be COMPUTED BEFORE the parent acts',
    instances: ['every case where the nodes value depends on its childrens values',
      'every case involving freeing or deleting a tree - you must free the children before the parent',
      'every case where a subtree must be completed before you can decide anything about it'],
    phrase: 'children, then act now' },
];
const PHRASE_TRICK = 'if you can remember act now, then children versus children, then act now, the order question is answered without memorising three names';

/* The BST and the exact condition on its promise. */
const BST = {
  invariant: 'smaller values in the left subtree, larger in the right',
  promise: 'WHEN BALANCED, search, insert and delete are all O(log n)',
  why: 'each comparison discards half the tree',
  conditionDoesAllTheWork: true,
  howItFails: 'inserting already-sorted data produces a tree that is a LINKED LIST',
  mechanism: 'each new value is the largest and goes right every time, so the height is n and every operation is O(n)',
  notHypothetical: 'it is what happens whenever data arrives in order',
  realSources: ['sorted data', 'incrementing ids', 'timestamps', 'index-ordered reads'],
};
const BALANCED = [
  { t: 'AVL', maintains: 'a strict height balance at every node',
    gain: 'the shortest possible height and therefore the fastest lookup',
    cost: 'more rotations on insert and delete', suits: 'read-heavy workloads' },
  { t: 'red-black', maintains: 'a looser balance with colour rules',
    trade: 'faster updates at a cost of up to one extra level of height', suits: 'mixed workloads' },
];
const GUARANTEE = 'both give O(log n) WORST CASE, which is the guarantee that matters';
const CONSEQUENCE = 'a librarys ordered map is one of these rather than a plain BST';

The tree problems, and the two that look alike and are not

Six problem shapes, and each is recognisable by what it asks for. Depth-first search — reach every node, follow children before siblings; pre-order for a per-node answer, post-order when children matter first. Breadth-first search — reach every node, level by level; use it when you want the shortest path in an unweighted graph, because the first time you reach a node is via the fewest edges, and when you want to search level by level for a shallow match. Find the lowest common ancestor, which is the ancestor deepest in the tree that has both nodes beneath it, and which is O(n) by a post-order walk or O(log n) on a balanced BST with depth information — the difficulty is the definition, not the code. Validate a binary search tree, which is a trap: checking each node against its parent is wrong because a node must satisfy the bounds from all its ancestors, so the correct check threads a lower and upper bound down the walk. Serialize and deserialize — usually to a string — which needs an encoding that cannot be ambiguous, and a delimiter or a length prefix is required precisely because "1,11" and "11,1" both parse to different trees with a naive comma encoding. And tree diameter: the longest path between two nodes, which is the deepest node plus the deepest node through the root in a single post-order pass, and which is a good exercise precisely because the two branches must be combined rather than maximised independently.

Then two problems that look alike and are not, because confusing them costs more than the effort of knowing. Dijkstra's algorithm is for a graph whose edges have different weights, and it uses a priority queue: pop the cheapest node, relax its edges, push any improvement. It is wrong if edges have negative weights. Breadth-first search is for a graph whose edges all have the same weight — or, more precisely, a graph where every edge counts as one step — and it gives correct shortest paths with no priority queue at all. The rule: unweighted graph, use BFS; weighted non-negative graph, use Dijkstra; weighted with possible negative weights, use Bellman-Ford, and the reason is not preference but that Dijkstra's greedy choice of the currently-cheapest node is only sound because no path can later become cheaper through a node it has already skipped — which fails the moment an edge is negative. And the practical note on both: mark nodes visited at enqueue time for BFS and at pop time for Dijkstra, because marking a node visited when you discover it rather than when you process it will skip shorter paths that arrive later.

/* Six shapes, recognisable by what they ask for. */
const PROBLEMS = [
  { p: 'depth-first search', rule: 'reach every node; children before siblings',
    pre: 'per-node answer', post: 'children matter first' },
  { p: 'breadth-first search', rule: 'reach every node; level by level',
    use: 'when you want the SHORTEST path in an unweighted graph',
    why: 'the first time you reach a node is via the fewest edges',
    also: 'searching level by level for a shallow match' },
  { p: 'lowest common ancestor', is: 'the ancestor deepest in the tree that has both nodes beneath it',
    cost: 'O(n) by a post-order walk, or O(log n) on a balanced BST with depth information',
    difficulty: 'the DEFINITION, not the code' },
  { p: 'validate a binary search tree', trap: true,
    wrongWay: 'checking each node against its parent',
    whyWrong: 'a node must satisfy the bounds from ALL its ancestors',
    correctWay: 'thread a lower and upper bound down the walk' },
  { p: 'serialize and deserialize', usually: 'to a string',
    requirement: 'an encoding that cannot be ambiguous',
    whyDelimiters: 'a naive comma encoding makes "1,11" and "11,1" parse to different trees',
    fix: 'a delimiter or a length prefix' },
  { p: 'tree diameter', is: 'the longest path between two nodes',

];

/* Two that look alike and are not. */

  dijkstra: { for: 'a graph whose edges have DIFFERENT weights',

    steps: ['pop the cheapest node', 'relax its edges', 'push any improvement'],

  bfs: { for: 'a graph whose edges all have the SAME weight, or where every edge counts as one step',

A BST’s O(log n) promise dies if you insert sorted data (1,2,3,4,…) — the tree degenerates into a linked list and search becomes O(n). From this crisis comes balanced trees (AVL, Red-Black) and their self-balancing cousins — Python’s sortedcontainers and database indexes know this well (Ch. 13).

8.5 Heaps — fast min/max

A heap is a tree-shaped structure that always exposes the smallest or largest element while staying balanced, giving logarithmic insert and extract-min. Priority queues and schedulers run on heaps, and Python’s heapq provides an in-place heap over lists. Heaps also underlie heap sort.

A binary heap keeps the smallest (or largest) element always at the top and stays balanced. Insert and extract-min are both O(log n). Used by priority queues, schedulers, and heapq.

import heapq
tasks = []
heapq.heappush(tasks, (3, "low priority"))        # smaller cost = higher priority
heapq.heappush(tasks, (1, "HIGH priority"))
heapq.heappush(tasks, (2, "medium"))
while tasks:
    print(heapq.heappop(tasks))   # always pops the smallest (priority 1 first)

The invariant, and why it buys better than linear

A heap is a complete binary tree, usually stored as a plain array, with one invariant: every parent is at least as large as each of its children (a max-heap), or at most (a min-heap). That is the whole definition — it is not sorted, it is not a tree you can search, and the only thing it guarantees is that the extreme element is always at the root, and finding it is O(1). That sounds like a weak guarantee for a serious data structure, and the strength is entirely in the operations built on top. Insert appends at the end and then sifts the new element up: O(log n), because the height of a complete tree is log n. Remove the extreme swaps the root with the last element, removes the last, and sifts the new root down: O(log n), again because of the tree height. And the killer property is that the whole sequence of operations is O(n log n) — that is, n pushes plus n pops costs n log n, not n log n plus n log n plus a sorting pass. That is the whole reason a heap is used instead of sorting: you do not need the data sorted, you need to consume it in priority order, and sorting then indexing does strictly more work than a heap ever will.

Then why "better than linear" is the claim to hold, and it is worth verifying because it is the least intuitive result in the chapter. The naive heapify — treat an arbitrary array as a heap and fix it — is O(n) if done bottom-up: the nodes near the bottom have small subtrees to sift, and summing the work over all levels is a convergent series, so the bottom half of the array costs about n/2 total, the level above n/4, and so on, summing to less than n. That is not a trick, it is arithmetic: sift-down cost is proportional to the subtree height, and the number of nodes at height h is n/2^(h+1), so the total is n·Σ h/2^(h+1), which converges. So build in linear time from an existing array, then do n extractions at O(log n) each, and you have a sort in O(n log n) with the useful property that you can stop early and still have consumed the top k. That is exactly what makes a heap the right tool for "the ten largest items in a million" and the wrong tool for "the sorted list of a million".

/* The invariant, and the guarantee. */
const HEAP = {
  is: 'a complete binary tree, usually stored as a plain array',
  invariant: 'every parent is at least as large as each of its children (max-heap), or at most (min-heap)',
  notThese: ['not sorted', 'not a tree you can search'],
  guarantee: 'the extreme element is always at the root, found in O(1)',
  looksWeak: 'it does, and the strength is entirely in the operations built on top',
  operations: [
    { op: 'insert', how: 'append at the end, then sift the new element up', cost: 'O(log n)',

    { op: 'remove the extreme', how: 'swap the root with the last element, remove the last, sift the new root down',
      cost: 'O(log n)', why: 'again because of the tree height' },
    { op: 'the sequence', cost: 'n pushes plus n pops is n log n',
      killerProperty: 'not n log n plus n log n plus a sorting pass' },
  ],
  whyNotSorting: 'you do not need the data SORTED, you need to CONSUME IT in priority order',
  conclusion: 'sorting then indexing does strictly more work than a heap ever will',
};

/* Why heapify is linear. */
const LINEAR_HEAPIFY = {
  method: 'treat an arbitrary array as a heap and fix it BOTTOM-UP',
  cost: 'O(n)',
  argument: ['nodes near the bottom have small subtrees to sift',
    'the bottom half of the array costs about n/2 total, the level above n/4, and so on',
    'summing over all levels is a convergent series, so the total is less than n'],
  notATrick: 'it is arithmetic',
  theSum: 'sift-down cost is proportional to the subtree height, and the number of nodes at height h is n/2^(h+1), so the total is n times the sum of h/2^(h+1), which converges',
  therefore: ['build in linear time from an existing array', 'then do n extractions at O(log n) each',
    'and you have a sort in O(n log n) with the useful property that you can stop early and still have consumed the top k'],
  rightTool: 'the ten largest items in a million',
  wrongTool: 'the sorted list of a million',

The three places heaps are the answer, and the problems heaps create

Three uses, and each is recognisable. Top-k from a larger collection, where the heap of size k beats sorting on time and on memory, and where the correctness detail is that you can stop after k extractions — which means for k = 10 out of a million you do 90 per cent of the work of a full sort and use a thousandth of the memory. Priority queues in scheduling, where the next item to run is by priority rather than by arrival, and which is why task schedulers, Dijkstra's algorithm, event simulation and operating-system scheduling are all heap-based. Dijkstra's algorithm, where the frontier is a priority queue and the priority is the current distance — and the requirement that matters is that a node may be re-inserted when a shorter path is found, which a heap supports cheaply and a sorted list does not.

Then the problems, and they are worth knowing because a heap is a structure with no search and that limitation leaks. No search. Finding an arbitrary element is O(n), because the invariant says nothing about where a specific value is. No order among siblings. The children of a node can be in any relative order, so "give me the second smallest" is not a supported operation — you must pop the first and look at the new root. Finding the minimum of a min-heap is O(1) but finding the maximum is O(n), which is the asymmetry that surprises people and which is why the library usually provides both and why converting the sign is the standard trick. Duplicate handling is unspecified. Two equal elements have no defined relative order, so any code that depends on which one comes out first is relying on an implementation detail. And heap operations are O(log n) but not free — each sift does several comparisons and swaps on array elements, so a heap is slower than it looks in interpreted code, and for small n a sorted list with a pointer beats it. The practical rule that covers all of this: use a heap when you will consume items in priority order and never need to look at them again; use a sorted list when you will iterate over everything more than once.

A heap keeps tasks ordered by priority; heappop always returns the smallest, so scheduling is automatic.

8.6 Graphs — networks of everything

A graph models networks as nodes connected by edges, representing maps, social networks, and dependencies with directed or undirected links. Two traversals dominate: depth-first search using a stack or recursion, and breadth-first search using a queue. Weighted graphs, adjacency representations, shortest paths, and connectivity all build on these.

A graph is nodes (vertices) plus edges. Maps, social networks, package dependency graphs, and web links are all graphs. Two mainstream representations:

# Adjacency list — easiest & most common: node -> list of neighbours
graph = {
    "A": ["B", "C"],
    "B": ["A", "D"],
    "C": ["A", "D"],
    "D": ["B", "C"],
}
print(graph["A"])     # neighbours of A: ['B','C']

A dict of node-to-neighbour lists, the most common graph representation; graph['A'] lists A’s neighbours directly.

Traversals (the two every interview expects):

def bfs(graph, start):
    """Breadth-first: explore layer by layer (uses a queue)."""
    seen, queue = {start}, [start]
    order = []
    while queue:
        node = queue.pop(0)
        order.append(node)
        for nb in graph[node]:
            if nb not in seen:
                seen.add(nb)
                queue.append(nb)
    return order

def dfs(graph, start):
    """Depth-first: dive deep before backtracking (uses a stack / recursion)."""
    seen = set()
    def visit(node):
        seen.add(node)
        for nb in graph[node]:
            if nb not in seen:
                visit(nb)
    visit(start)
    return list(seen)

print(bfs(graph, "A"))   # layer-by-layer order
print(dfs(graph, "A"))   # deep order

Two representations, and the decision between them is about what you will do

A graph is a set of vertices and a set of edges. The theory is identical either way; the implementation is not, and the representation determines which operations are cheap. Adjacency list — a dictionary from vertex to the list of its neighbours — costs O(V + E) memory and gives you O(1) lookup of a vertex's neighbours, O(deg) to walk them, and O(V + E) for a full traversal. Adjacency matrix — a two-dimensional array where m[u][v] is the edge — costs O(V²) memory and gives O(1) edge-existence tests and O(V) to walk a vertex's neighbours. The decision is mechanical: sparse graph, use a list; dense graph, use a matrix, with the crossover somewhere around a quarter of all possible edges, since the matrix wastes space on absent edges below that and wastes time scanning above it. The cases that push toward a matrix are "is there an edge between these two" asked often, and Floyd-Warshall, which is meaningless without one. The cases that demand a list are everything else, which is nearly everything. And the representation must record direction: a directed graph has a→b without b→a, and an undirected one adds the reverse edge — a detail that is easy to omit and produces a traversal that quietly ignores half the graph.

Then the properties that make a graph a graph rather than a structure, because each has an algorithm attached and each also disqualifies algorithms. Directed versus undirected — whether edges point one way. Cyclic versus acyclic — whether a path can return to where it started; a directed acyclic graph is worth recognising because it implies no cycles, which makes topological ordering possible and which underlies every build system, every spreadsheet dependency and every task scheduler. Connected versus disconnected — whether every vertex is reachable from every other; traversal algorithms that assume connectivity and are given a disconnected graph silently process half of it. Weighted versus unweighted — whether edges carry costs, which decides BFS versus Dijkstra as covered above. Tree versus general — a tree is a connected acyclic graph, and treating a tree as a general graph works but costs a factor of V in memory and forfeits the parent pointers that make tree algorithms linear. And the property most likely to cause a wrong answer: a graph may not be connected and may contain cycles, and an algorithm that does not handle both will appear to work on small clean examples.

/* Two representations; the representation determines which operations are cheap. */
const REPS = {
  adjacencyList: { memory: 'O(V + E)', neighbourLookup: 'O(1)', walkingNeighbours: 'O(deg)',
    fullTraversal: 'O(V + E)' },
  adjacencyMatrix: { memory: 'O(V^2)', edgeExistenceTest: 'O(1)', walkingNeighbours: 'O(V)' },
  decision: 'sparse graph, use a list; dense graph, use a matrix',
  crossover: 'around a quarter of all possible edges - below that the matrix wastes space on absent edges, above it wastes time scanning',
  matrixCases: ['is there an edge between these two, asked often', 'Floyd-Warshall, which is meaningless without one'],
  listCases: 'everything else, which is nearly everything',
  mustRecord: { direction: 'a directed graph has a-to-b without b-to-a; an undirected one adds the reverse edge',
    omissionConsequence: 'a traversal that quietly ignores half the graph' },
};

/* The properties, each with an algorithm attached. */
const PROPERTIES = [
  { p: 'directed versus undirected', q: 'whether edges point one way' },
  { p: 'cyclic versus acyclic',
    aCycle: 'whether a path can return to where it started',
    dag: 'a directed acyclic graph implies no cycles, which makes TOPOLOGICAL ORDERING possible',
    appearsIn: ['every build system', 'every spreadsheet dependency', 'every task scheduler'] },
  { p: 'connected versus disconnected',
    traversalNote: 'algorithms that assume connectivity and are given a disconnected graph SILENTLY PROCESS HALF OF IT' },
  { p: 'weighted versus unweighted', decides: 'BFS versus Dijkstra' },
  { p: 'tree versus general',
    is: 'a connected acyclic graph',
    cost: 'treating a tree as a general graph costs a factor of V in memory and forfeits the parent pointers that make tree algorithms linear' },
];
const WRONG_ANSWER_PROPERTY = 'a graph may not be connected and may contain cycles, and an algorithm that does not handle both will APPEAR to work on small clean examples';

Traversal, components, and topological order

Depth-first search uses a stack — or recursion, which is a stack — and is the right tool when you need to explore fully, detect cycles, find connected components, or do a computation that depends on finishing a subtree before you act on its parent. Breadth-first search uses a queue and is the right tool when you need the shortest path in an unweighted graph, the levels, or a shallowest-first search. The structural difference that matters: DFS marks a node visited when it is popped and explores one direction to exhaustion; BFS marks visited when enqueued and processes in waves. That distinction is not academic — marking visited at enqueue in DFS is wrong in a cyclic graph because a node can be reached twice through different branches before either is expanded. Both share one essential implementation detail: you must have a visited set, and you must mark visited on the way in, because a graph with a cycle will otherwise traverse forever. And both have the same failure mode when applied to a large graph: recursion depth. A DFS implemented recursively over a graph with a million vertices exhausts the stack, which is why the iterative form with an explicit stack is the one to use on anything whose size you do not know.

Then the three graph problems beyond traversal, each with a recognisable shape. Connected components — run a traversal from an unvisited vertex, count it, repeat; the count is the answer, and the detail is that forgetting to loop is what produces a graph that reports one component when it has five. Shortest path unweighted — BFS, and the answer is the distance recorded at first visit, because BFS visits in order of path length. Shortest path weighted — Dijkstra with a priority queue, where the correct implementation relaxes a node's edges every time it is popped and skips it if it has already been finalised, and where the negative-weight restriction from the last section applies. And topological sort — an ordering of a directed acyclic graph where every edge goes forward in the order — produced by repeated DFS with a post-order push, or by Kahn's algorithm with in-degrees, and the existence of a topological order is the test that a directed graph is acyclic: if you cannot produce one, there is a cycle, and the vertices left are the ones in it.

/* Traversal. */
const TRAVERSAL = [
  { t: 'depth-first search', uses: 'a stack, or recursion which is a stack',

      'a computation that must finish a subtree before acting on its parent'] },
  { t: 'breadth-first search', uses: 'a queue',

];

};

BFS explores layer by layer with a queue, DFS dives deep with recursion — the two canonical traversals.

BFS finds shortest path in unweighted graphs; DFS powers maze solving, topological sort, and cycle detection. Weighted shortest path → Dijkstra (Ch. 9). Bipartite/related graph tricks come later — for now, recognise any network problem as "it’s a graph".

8.7 Tries — the string specialist

A trie is a tree whose paths spell out strings, so lookup cost is proportional to word length rather than the size of the dictionary. Each node holds a letter and marks word endings. It powers autocomplete, spell checking, and IP routing prefixes.

A trie (pronounced "try") is a tree whose paths spell out strings; letters live on edges, and nodes mark where words end. Lookup is O(word length) regardless of how many words are stored — the shape of autocomplete, dictionaries, and IP routers.

class TrieNode:
    def __init__(self):
        self.children = {}
        self.is_end = False

class Trie:
    def __init__(self):
        self.root = TrieNode()

    def insert(self, word):
        node = self.root
        for ch in word:
            node = node.children.setdefault(ch, TrieNode())  # walk, creating nodes on demand
        node.is_end = True                     # final letter ends a word

    def search(self, word):
        node = self._walk(word)
        return bool(node) and node.is_end

    def starts_with(self, prefix):
        return self._walk(prefix) is not None       # "any word begins with..."

    def _walk(self, s):
        node = self.root
        for ch in s:
            node = node.children.get(ch)
            if node is None:
                return None
        return node

t = Trie()
t.insert("cat"); t.insert("car"); t.insert("dog")
print(t.search("cat"))          # True
print(t.starts_with("ca"))      # True  (autocomplete engine!)
print(t.search("c"))            # False (inserted words, not prefixes)

Inserting, searching and prefix-checking walk nodes by character; the shared prefixes make autocomplete cheap.

How it works, and the number that makes it linear

A trie is a tree of prefixes: each node represents a character position, and each edge is one possible character. Walking a string is walking down one path, and the cost is therefore proportional to the length of the string — O(L) — rather than to the number of strings stored. That single property is the entire reason the structure exists, and it is why a trie is the right answer when your cost model is dominated by the key's length rather than by how many keys you have. The consequence is worth stating as a range: O(L) is bounded by the key length, which is usually short. A trie beats a balanced tree when the key length is bounded and the number of keys is large, and loses badly when keys are long, because the memory is proportional to the total characters stored, not the number of entries. Each node usually holds an array of child pointers indexed by character — 26 for lowercase letters, 256 for bytes — and that fixed-width array is what makes traversal a single array index rather than a search, at the cost of memory. A dictionary-per-node variant trades memory for flexibility, which is what makes tries practical for arbitrary characters and Unicode.

Then what they are genuinely for, because the list is shorter than people expect. Prefix queries — "all keys starting with 'ma'" — which is a subtree walk and takes time proportional to the results rather than to the number of keys stored, and which no other structure does as cheaply. Autocomplete and search suggestions, the same operation. Exact lookup with a known key length, where the O(L) guarantee is a real win over hashing when the length is fixed. Longest-prefix matching — route tables, longest-match firewall rules, and the longest-prefix-match lookup a network router does for every packet, which is the structure's most important real deployment. And validation and parsing — a trie of valid keywords validates a token in O(L) with no false positives, where a list scan is O(n) and a hash set gives you membership but not "was this a prefix of something valid".

/* How it works. */
const STRUCTURE = {
  is: 'a tree of prefixes - each node represents a character position, each edge one possible character',
  cost: 'proportional to the length of the string, O(L), rather than to the number of strings stored',
  whyItExists: 'that single property is the whole reason',
  rightWhen: 'the cost model is dominated by the KEY LENGTH rather than by how many keys you have',
  bound: 'O(L) is bounded by the key length, which is usually short',
  comparison: ['beats a balanced tree when key length is bounded and the number of keys is large',
    'loses badly when keys are long'],
  memoryCost: 'proportional to the total CHARACTERS stored, not the number of entries',
  nodeLayout: 'usually an array of child pointers indexed by character - 26 for lowercase, 256 for bytes',
  whyArray: 'traversal becomes a single array index rather than a search',
  tradeoff: 'a dictionary-per-node variant trades memory for flexibility, which is what makes tries practical for Unicode',
};

/* What they are for. */
const USES = [
  { u: 'prefix queries', example: 'all keys starting with ma',
    cost: 'proportional to the RESULTS rather than the number of keys stored',
    claim: 'no other structure does it as cheaply' },
  { u: 'autocomplete and search suggestions', note: 'the same operation' },
  { u: 'exact lookup with a known key length', why: 'the O(L) guarantee is a real win over hashing when the length is fixed' },
  { u: 'longest-prefix matching', instances: ['route tables', 'longest-match firewall rules',
    'the longest-prefix-match lookup a network router does for every packet'],
    claim: 'the structures most important real deployment' },
  { u: 'validation and parsing', detail: 'a trie of valid keywords validates a token in O(L) with no false positives',
    contrast: ['a list scan is O(n)', 'a hash set gives membership but not was this a prefix of something valid'] },
];

The variants, the costs, and how to know you needed one

Four variants, and the differences are practical. A plain trie with a flag on each node marking whether a word ends there — the standard form, and the flag is what distinguishes a prefix from a word, which is why omitting it makes "is 'ma' a word or just a prefix" unanswerable. A compressed trie collapses chains, so a long single-branch path becomes one node; this makes the trie proportional to the number of distinct keys rather than to total characters, which matters when the alphabet is large or the keys share long prefixes. A radix trie, where the edges are strings rather than characters. A double-array trie, which is the memory-efficient representation used in Japanese and in compact dictionaries, where node overhead rather than character storage is the constraint. Separately, a ternary search trie is a different structure again — each node has three children, left, middle and equal — and it balances a trie against a tree.

Then the costs, stated honestly, because tries are over-used. Memory is the binding constraint and it is much worse than it looks: a million short strings can occupy more memory as a trie than as a hash set, because a hash set stores the string once and a trie stores a node per character plus a pointer per possible character per node. Constant factors in the cache — a trie walk is a pointer chase per character, which is a cache miss per character where a hash lookup is one miss total. The alphabet size multiplies the node size, so an array of 256 children per node is enormous and a dictionary per node is smaller but slower. And the decision test, which is the honest version: do you need prefix queries? If yes, a trie is right and the memory cost is justified. If no — if you only need exact lookup — a hash set is faster and smaller and you should use one. The signal that a trie is being chosen for the wrong reason is that nobody in the discussion has mentioned prefixes, and the other signal is a memory profile that grew unexpectedly after the change.

/* Four variants, with practical differences. */

  { v: 'compressed trie', does: 'collapses chains, so a long single-branch path becomes one node',
    gain: 'proportional to the number of distinct KEYS rather than total characters',
    mattersWhen: ['a large alphabet', 'keys sharing long prefixes'] },
  { v: 'radix trie', differs: 'the edges are strings rather than characters' },
  { v: 'double-array trie', does: 'the memory-efficient representation used in Japanese and compact dictionaries',
    constraint: 'node OVERHEAD rather than character storage' },
  { v: 'ternary search trie', isDifferent: true, shape: 'three children per node - left, middle and equal',

];

When a trie? Many strings sharing prefixes (dictionaries, contact lists, search suggestions). Time O(L) per operation almost regardless of n; the cost is memory for all those child pointers — a classic time/space trade-off (4.8).

8.8 The LRU cache — your first mini design problem

The least-recently-used cache keeps a fixed number of hot items and evicts the one used longest ago when full. The classic design pairs a hash map with a doubly linked list: the map finds keys in constant time, and the list tracks recency order. Implementing it is a classic interview and mini design problem.

"Least Recently Used" caches pop up in DBs, browsers and OS memory managers: keep N items; when full, evict the one unused the longest. The interviewer-famous version pairs a hash map (O(1) lookup) with a doubly linked list (O(1) move-to-front).

# Python's OrderedDict HAS the doubly-linked-list semantics built in:
from collections import OrderedDict

class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.data = OrderedDict()        # map + "order of use" in one

    def get(self, key):
        if key not in self.data:
            return -1
        self.data.move_to_end(key)       # touching it = recently used
        return self.data[key]

    def put(self, key, value):
        if key in self.data:
            self.data.move_to_end(key)
        self.data[key] = value
        if len(self.data) > self.capacity:
            self.data.popitem(last=False) # evict the LEAST recently used

c = LRUCache(2)
c.put("a", 1); c.put("b", 2)
print(c.get("a"))                        # 1  ('a' now most recent)
c.put("c", 3)                            # capacity full -> evicts 'b'
print(c.get("b"))                        # -1 (evicted)

OrderedDict keeps keys in use order; get and put both move the key to the end, and overflow evicts the least recent entry.

The problem, and the two questions that solve any variation of it

An LRU cache is a fixed-capacity cache that evicts the least recently used item when full. On its own it is a small problem; what makes it a teaching problem is that the shape of the solution is the shape of a large family of real design problems, and the shape is this: one operation needs to be fast for search and another needs to be fast for ordering, and you satisfy both by giving each its own structure and connecting them. A hash table gives you lookup by key in constant time but no notion of order. A linked list gives you perfect order maintenance — remove and insert at a known position in constant time — but no lookup. Combine them and you get both. That is the whole solution, and it generalises: a least-recently-used cache, a most-recently-used one, a cache with a size limit, an access-ordered eviction policy, and a "least frequently used" variant are all the same two-structure solution with different rules for where to move an element on access. So the useful thing to take away is not the code, it is the pattern: when one requirement is about finding and another is about order, do not try to make one structure do both — build each and link them by a key.

Then the design in detail, because every part has a reason. A doubly linked list holding the entries in recency order, with the most recent at the head and the least recent at the tail; doubly rather than singly because every operation needs to remove a node when you have only that node, and a singly linked list would make that O(n). A hash table mapping each key to its list node, which is what turns "find the entry" from O(n) into O(1) and what makes eviction possible: to evict, read the tail, and the table tells you nothing about the tail, so you read the node off the list and delete it from both structures. Get looks up the node, moves it to the head, and returns its value. Put either updates an existing node and moves it to the head, or creates a new one at the head; and if the cache is over capacity, remove the tail node from both the list and the table. Both structures must be updated together on every operation, and the failure mode to know is desynchronisation — a node in the list that is not in the table, or an entry in the table pointing to a node already removed, which produces a use-after-remove or a leak rather than an error, and which is why the correct implementation keeps the two in one class with no way to touch one directly.

/* The problem, and the shape that makes it worth learning. */
const PROBLEM = {
  is: 'a fixed-capacity cache evicting the least recently used item when full',
  shape: 'one operation needs to be FAST FOR SEARCH and another FAST FOR ORDERING, and you satisfy both by giving each its own structure and connecting them',
  theTwoStructures: [
    { s: 'a hash table', gives: 'lookup by key in constant time', lacks: 'any notion of order' },
    { s: 'a linked list', gives: 'perfect order maintenance - remove and insert at a known position in constant time',
      lacks: 'lookup' },
  ],
  generalisesTo: ['a least-recently-used cache', 'a most-recently-used one', 'a cache with a size limit',
    'an access-ordered eviction policy', 'a least-frequently-used variant'],
  howTheVariantsDiffer: 'they are the same two-structure solution with different rules for where to move an element on access',
  theTakeaway: 'when one requirement is about FINDING and another about ORDER, do not try to make one structure do both - build each and link them by a key',
};

/* The design, part by part. */
const DESIGN = [
  { part: 'a doubly linked list in recency order', order: 'most recent at the head, least recent at the tail',
    whyDoubly: 'every operation needs to remove a node when you have only that node, and a singly linked list would make that O(n)' },
  { part: 'a hash table mapping each key to its list node',
    gain: 'turns finding the entry from O(n) into O(1)',
    makesEvictionPossible: 'to evict, read the tail; the table tells you nothing about the tail, so you read the node off the list and delete it from both structures' },
  { part: 'get', does: ['look up the node', 'move it to the head', 'return its value'] },
  { part: 'put', does: ['update an existing node and move it to the head, or create a new one at the head',
    'if over capacity, remove the tail node from both the list and the table'] },
];
const SYNCHRONISATION = {
  rule: 'both structures must be updated together on every operation',
  failureMode: 'DESYNCHRONISATION - a node in the list that is not in the table, or an entry pointing to a node already removed',
  symptom: 'a use-after-remove or a leak rather than an error',
  prevention: 'keep the two in one class with no way to touch one directly',
};

The variations, the complexity table, and the traps

Then the complexity, which is worth having as a table because it is the argument for the design. Get is O(1) — a hash lookup plus a list splice, both constant. Put on a non-full cache is O(1) — same. Put that triggers eviction is O(1) too, because reading the tail is O(1) and removing a known node is O(1) with a doubly linked list. Capacity change is O(n), which is the one operation that is not constant and the reason capacity is set at construction rather than adjusted. Space is O(capacity), bounded and predictable. Every operation being O(1) is the design working as intended, and it is worth contrasting with the naive alternative — evict by scanning the whole cache for the oldest timestamp — which is O(n) per eviction and turns a cache into a performance problem.

Then the traps, which are the same for every cache and worth knowing once. Off-by-one on capacity. Whether the cache holds capacity or capacity + 1 items is decided at the point you write the eviction check, and getting it wrong means an off-by-one memory leak or an eviction one item too early. Evicting on insert but not on access. A cache that does not record reads is not an LRU cache; it is an insertion-order cache, and the difference is observable. Forgetting to update the table on eviction, which is the desynchronisation above and is the single most common bug in this family — the list is correct and the table still points at the removed node. Caching something that changes, which is not a bug in the cache at all: a cached value with no invalidation is a correctness bug that presents as staleness, and the test is whether you can name what makes it stale. And an unbounded cache, which stops being a cache and becomes a memory leak with a lookup table; every cache needs a size limit and every eviction policy needs a reason.

/* The complexity table, which is the argument for the design. */
const COMPLEXITY = {
  get: 'O(1) - a hash lookup plus a list splice, both constant',
  putNotFull: 'O(1) - same',
  putWithEviction: 'O(1) too - reading the tail is O(1) and removing a known node is O(1) in a doubly linked list',
  capacityChange: 'O(n) - the one operation that is not constant',
  whyThatMatters: 'capacity is set at construction rather than adjusted',
  space: 'O(capacity) - bounded and predictable',
  takeaway: 'every operation being O(1) is the design working as intended',
  contrast: 'evicting by scanning the whole cache for the oldest timestamp is O(n) per eviction and turns a cache into a performance problem',
};

/* Traps, the same for every cache. */
const TRAPS = [
  { t: 'off-by-one on capacity',
    decidedAt: 'the point you write the eviction check',
    wrong: ['an off-by-one memory leak', 'an eviction one item too early'] },
  { t: 'evicting on insert but not on access',
    consequence: 'a cache that does not record reads is not an LRU cache - it is an insertion-order cache, and the difference is observable' },
  { t: 'forgetting to update the table on eviction', isTheDesync: true,
    symptom: 'the list is correct and the table still points at the removed node',
    rank: 'the single most common bug in this family' },
  { t: 'caching something that changes',
    notACacheBug: 'a cached value with no invalidation is a CORRECTNESS bug that presents as staleness',
    test: 'whether you can name what makes it stale' },
  { t: 'an unbounded cache',
    consequence: 'stops being a cache and becomes a memory leak with a lookup table',
    rule: 'every cache needs a size limit and every eviction policy needs a reason' },
];

Yes, the real interview solution uses a linked list you implement by hand so the interviewer can watch you reason about pointers. The insight to carry away: two structures cooperate — a hash map for search, a linked list for ordering. "Two structures, one trade" is a recurring design move.

8.9 Union-Find (disjoint sets)

Union-find, also called disjoint sets, tracks a collection of groups and answers whether two items are connected in near-constant amortised time. The find operation locates a group’s representative, and union merges two groups. Path compression and union by rank keep the tree shallow and fast, powering connectivity queries and Kruskal’s algorithm.

Union-Find tracks which items belong to which group, and merges groups — answering "are A and B connected?" in near-constant time. With path compression + union by rank its operations are amortized O(α(n)) — effectively constant.

class UnionFind:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.parent = list(range(n))     # each node starts as its own root
        self.rank = [0] * n

    def find(self, x):                       # path compression
        if self.parent[x] != x:
            self.parent[x] = self.find(self.parent[x])
        return self.parent[x]

    def union(self, a, b):                   # union by rank
        ra, rb = self.find(a), self.find(b)
        if ra == rb: return False
        if self.rank[ra] < self.rank[rb]: ra, rb = rb, ra
        self.parent[rb] = ra
        if self.rank[ra] == self.rank[rb]: self.rank[ra] += 1
        return True

uf = UnionFind(6)
uf.union(0, 1); uf.union(1, 2); uf.union(3, 4)
print(uf.find(0) == uf.find(2))     # True  (same component)
print(uf.find(0) == uf.find(3))     # False

# Uses: connected components in graphs, Kruskal's MST (Ch.9),
# "accounts merge", dynamic connectivity, image segmentation.

find compresses paths and union merges by rank, so connectivity checks run in effectively constant time.

Exercises 8

  1. Implement dfs iteratively with an explicit stack instead of recursion.
  2. Write count_components(graph) returning how many disconnected pieces the graph has (loop all nodes with a seen-set, counting fresh traversals).
  3. Use a dict to find the most frequent word in a long text (split on spaces, count, print top 3).

    4. The operations, and why this is the one structure nobody invents

    A disjoint-set, or union-find, maintains a partition of n elements into disjoint sets, supporting exactly two things: union, which merges two sets, and find, which reports which set an element belongs to. That is the entire interface, and its appeal is that both operations are essentially constant time after an optimisation that took a page of mathematics — which is why the question "what data structure should I use" so often has the answer "the most specialised one available". The way to think about it: it is not a general-purpose structure. It is a set of sets with a merge operation and a query, and it is the right answer only when those are exactly your two needs. If you also need to know the members of a set, or delete from a set, or iterate, you need something else — because union-find deliberately throws that information away to make merge cheap.

    Then the two optimisations, which are the whole technique and are worth understanding rather than memorising because they are the same idea applied twice. Union by rank or size. When two sets merge, attach the smaller to the larger rather than the other way round, so the tree height stays logarithmic instead of becoming linear. Without it, merging a chain of elements one at a time produces a tree of depth n and every find is O(n) — which is precisely the mistake that makes people conclude union-find is slow. Path compression. During a find, make every node on the path point directly to the representative, so subsequent finds on the same nodes are shorter. The consequence is the celebrated inverse Ackermann function: with both optimisations, the amortised cost of any operation is O(α(n)), where α is effectively a constant for any n you will ever build — it grows so slowly that α(n) is under 5 for n in the range of the entire universe. Without path compression the bound is logarithmic; without union by rank it also degrades; with neither it is linear. This is the closest thing computer science has to a linear-time solution, and it is why union-find is used wherever the operation really is "are these two in the same group, and if not make them so".

    /* The interface. */
const INTERFACE = {
  maintains: 'a partition of n elements into disjoint sets',
  operations: ['union - merges two sets', 'find - reports which set an element belongs to'],
  thatIsAll: true,
  appeal: 'both operations are essentially constant time after an optimisation that took a page of mathematics',
  whyItComesUp: 'the question what data structure should I use so often has the answer the most specialised one available',
  notGeneralPurpose: true,
  detail: 'it is a set of sets with a merge operation and a query',
  rightWhen: 'those are exactly your two needs',
  wrongWhen: 'you also need to know the members of a set, to delete from one, or to iterate',
  why: 'union-find deliberately THROWS THAT INFORMATION AWAY to make merge cheap',
};

/* Two optimisations, the same idea applied twice. */
const OPTIMISATIONS = [
  { o: 'union by rank or size', does: 'attach the smaller to the larger rather than the other way round',
    gain: 'tree height stays LOGARITHMIC instead of becoming linear',
    withoutIt: 'merging a chain of elements one at a time produces a tree of depth n and every find is O(n)',
    whyItMatters: 'this is the mistake that makes people conclude union-find is slow' },
  { o: 'path compression', does: 'during a find, make every node on the path point directly to the representative',
    gain: 'subsequent finds on the same nodes are shorter' },
];
const BOUND = {
  name: 'the inverse Ackermann function',
  withBoth: 'amortised cost of any operation is O(alpha(n))',
  whatAlpha: 'effectively a CONSTANT for any n you will ever build',
  magnitude: 'alpha(n) is under 5 for n in the range of the entire universe',
  withoutCompression: 'logarithmic',
  withoutRank: 'also degrades',
  withoutEither: 'linear',
  claim: 'the closest thing computer science has to a linear-time solution',
  usedWhen: 'the operation really is are these two in the same group, and if not make them so',
};

    The applications, and the trap that catches everyone

    Five applications, each recognisable by its shape. Grouping — the canonical one: given pairs of things that belong together, merge and then ask which group each is in. Detecting cycles in a graph, which is the Kruskal variant: for every edge, if its two endpoints are already in the same set, that edge closes a cycle; and the useful output is the set of edges that did not, which is exactly a minimum spanning tree when the edges are weighted and sorted. Kruskal's minimum spanning tree follows from that: sort the edges by weight, add each one whose endpoints are in different sets, and stop when one tree spans everything. Image processing — labelling connected regions, where adjacent same-valued pixels are unioned and the resulting set identifiers are the labels. Accounts and permissions — transitive access, where being in a group implies the group's permissions, and a permission change on a group requires no change on its members. Then the trap that catches everyone, which is worth stating before anything else because it invalidates a naive implementation: find does not identify the group's members, it identifies the group. Two elements are in the same set if their find results are equal, and you cannot obtain the members by asking a single element. Code that tries — by walking up the tree and assuming the nodes below the root are the members — gets the set structure rather than the set, and then reports a group that is missing almost everything in it. If you need the members, you need to track them separately, and the structure to use is a list of members per root that you maintain on merge.

    /* Five applications, each recognisable by its shape. */

  { a: 'image processing', does: 'labelling connected regions',

];

  statement: 'FIND DOES NOT IDENTIFY THE GROUPS MEMBERS, it identifies the GROUP',
  test: 'two elements are in the same set if their find results are EQUAL',
  impossible: 'you cannot obtain the members by asking a single element',
  naiveAttempt: 'walking up the tree and assuming the nodes below the root are the members',
  whatThatGets: 'the set STRUCTURE rather than the set',
  symptom: 'a group reported that is missing almost everything in it',

9 · Algorithms — Divide, Conquer, Optimise

This chapter turns data structures into real solutions through families of algorithm techniques. You learn divide and conquer, greedy strategies, dynamic programming, graph algorithms, and backtracking, alongside the analysis that justifies them. Knowing which technique fits a problem is what separates strong engineers from most new graduates.

9.1 Divide and conquer9.2 Analysing D&C: the Master Theorem (the short version)9.3 Greedy algorithms — take the best step now9.4 Dynamic programming — recursion with a memory9.5 Graph algorithms that matter9.6 Backtracking — explore, undo, try the next

Now we turn the toolbox (Ch. 8) into technique. The three big families: divide & conquer, greedy, and dynamic programming. Plus the classic graph algorithms. This chapter is the ceiling of most algorithm-focused interview prep — get it right and you’re in the top tier of new graduates.

9.1 Divide and conquer

Divide and conquer splits a problem into smaller subproblems, solves each recursively, then combines the answers. Merge sort and quicksort follow it for sorting, and fast exponentiation uses repeated squaring. The approach turns many hard problems into simple recursion plus a combine step.

Break a problem into smaller identical problems, solve them recursively, combine. You already know the premier example: merge sort (Ch. 4.6) — split in half, sort halves, merge two sorted halves in O(n).

# Classic D&C: exponentiation by squaring -- O(log n) multiplications
def power(x, n):
    if n == 0: return 1
    half = power(x, n // 2)          # solve the smaller twin once
    if n % 2 == 0:
        return half * half
    return x * half * half

print(power(2, 10))    # 1024
print(power(3, 0))     # 1

Exponentiation by squaring halves n each recursion, doing O(log n) multiplications instead of n of them.

Quick sort is D&C with an in-place partition: pick a pivot, move smaller left / larger right, sort the two sides recursively. O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst — but with random pivots the worst is improbable, which is why quicksort underpins sort() in most languages.

def quicksort(items):
    if len(items) <= 1:
        return items
    pivot = items[0]
    smaller = [x for x in items[1:] if x <= pivot]   # left side: smaller values
    larger  = [x for x in items[1:] if x >  pivot]
    return quicksort(smaller) + [pivot] + quicksort(larger)

print(quicksort([9, 1, 8, 2, 7, 3]))   # [1,2,3,7,8,9]

Exponentiation by squaring, the clearest divide-and-conquer in existence

Start with the slowest possible algorithm and then ask what structure it has. x^n by repeated multiplication is O(n) multiplications. But x^(2k) is (x^k)² and x^(2k+1) is (x^k)² · x — so you can halve the exponent at every step and square instead of multiplying. That is O(log n) multiplications: thirty-one for a billion, rather than a billion. The pattern is the whole method. Divide: split the problem into subproblems. Conquer: solve each recursively until the subproblems are trivially base cases. Combine: merge the answers, and the merge must be cheaper than the original work — otherwise you have done nothing. Quicksort divides by partitioning an array around a pivot, sorts the halves, and concatenates. Merge sort divides by halving, sorts, and merges by repeatedly taking the smaller head. Binary search divides by comparing against the middle and discarding half. FFT divides the transform into even and odd samples, recurses, and combines — and it is the one where the combine step is the actual mathematics, because the naive divide-and-conquer FFT is still O(n²) and only the clever combination makes it O(n log n). Karatsuba divides a multiplication into four smaller multiplications and then recombines using five, which is fewer than the four you'd expect because the two cross terms can be recovered from the difference — and that trick, using algebra to replace a computation, is the mark of a good divide-and-conquer solution.

Then when to use it, and the condition that must hold. The subproblems must be independent. If solving one subproblem requires the answer to another, you have dynamic programming instead, and using divide and conquer produces a duplicated-work bug that is invisible until timing. The combination must be linear in the number of subproblems, or the recursion tree's bottom level costs as much as the work it saved. The base case must be trivial, and the recursion depth is bounded by how many times you can divide before reaching it — which is why the depth of a quicksort recursion is log n while a linked-list traversal written recursively is n and blows the stack. And a warning that catches people: divide and conquer does not always win. Quicksort's worst case is O(n²), merge sort's worst case is still O(n log n) with a worse constant factor, and for small inputs a hand-written insertion sort is faster than either because of the constant overhead of recursion — which is why real sorts are hybrids that switch below a cutoff of around a dozen elements.

/* Exponentiation by squaring: start slow, then find the structure. */
const SLOW: 'x^n by repeated multiplication is O(n)';

  { identity: 'x^(2k+1) is (x^k) squared times x' },
];

The three failure modes, and why they all present the same way

All three present as "it got slow on real data", which is why they are grouped. Unbalanced splitting. Quicksort's O(n log n) is an average over pivot choices; the worst case is a pivot that is always the smallest or largest, which turns the recursion into a chain of depth n and O(n²) work. Three fixes, in increasing order of robustness: always pick a random pivot, which makes the worst case vanishingly unlikely even against an adversary who knows your algorithm; pick the median of three; or use a guaranteed O(n log n) sort. The first is what production implementations do, and the reason it is not a third option is that randomness gives a probabilistic guarantee rather than an absolute one, which is a real and usually acceptable trade. Duplicated work from dependent subproblems. If two subproblems both compute the same answer you have built an exponential algorithm with good manners, and the fix is the memoisation cache from dynamic programming — which is why the two families are sometimes used together and why the boundary between them is really about whether the subproblems repeat, not about which section of the book you read. Expensive combination. If merging is superlinear, the divide-and-conquer buys nothing: divide in halves, spend n log n at each of log n levels, and you are back to where you started. This is why the combine step is where the design work goes, and it is why the FFT's combination is the interesting part of the FFT rather than the recursion.

Then what to do about it in practice, which is mostly measurement. Count the recursion depth and the number of leaf calls. Depth × leaves is the total work, and it is visible in a debug print of two counters — which finds an unbalanced partition in seconds, where reading the code does not. Compare against a known-good alternative on real data. If your quicksort is slower than Python's built-in sort, that is because Python's is a tuned hybrid and yours is not, and that comparison is more informative than any amount of reading. Test with adversarial input. Sorted, reverse-sorted, all-equal, and "many duplicates" are four inputs that break different implementations and none of which your random test data will produce. And remember that the library usually wins. Every general-purpose sort in every language is written in a lower-level language, tuned for the specific processor, with cache-aware pivot selection, a hybrid cutoff and hand-optimised inner loops. Writing your own is the correct move for an interview, for a constraint the library cannot meet, and for understanding — and writing your own in production code because it "should be faster" is a decision made without the one piece of information that would justify it.

A recursive quicksort partitions around a pivot and sorts the two halves; simple and it practically runs in O(n log n).

9.2 Analysing D&C: the Master Theorem (the short version)

The Master Theorem classifies divide-and-conquer recurrences into complexity classes quickly. Given a recurrence of the form T(n) = aT(n/b) plus f(n), comparing f(n) against n raised to the power log of a over log of b picks out the runtime class directly. It instantly matches binary search, merge sort, and friends to their big-O.

For a recurrence like "T(n) = a·T(n/b) + O(n^d)", the cost is dominated by whichever is bigger: the recursion tree’s branching or the per-level work. The practical takeaways, in plain words:

The five families, and the two questions that choose between them

Algorithm design is not a bag of tricks to memorise; it is five families, and two questions pick the family almost every time. Question one: is there a rule that lets you commit to a locally best choice with no way to be wrong? If yes, it is a greedy algorithm, and you are done — the whole difficulty is proving the rule is safe, not finding it. Question two: does the problem have overlapping subproblems, so that the answer for a large case is built from the answers to smaller cases of the same shape? If yes, it is dynamic programming. If the subproblems are non-overlapping but naturally split, it is divide and conquer. If the answer must be found by trying candidates and rejecting them, it is backtracking. And if the objects have relationships — nodes and edges — it is a graph algorithm, where the family is chosen by what the edges mean. The reason this framing is useful is that it converts "what algorithm does this problem want" from a recall question into a two-question question, and it is a question you can ask yourself in thirty seconds on an unfamiliar problem.

Then why the families exist at all, which is the more interesting half. Each family exploits a different structural property, and the property is what you are looking for when you read a problem. Greedy exploits a matroid-like property — an independence system where the locally best choice is globally optimal, which is rare and worth memorising the cases of: Huffman coding, Kruskal and Prim for spanning trees, activity selection, Dijkstra on non-negative weights, and interval scheduling. Divide and conquer exploits a problem that decomposes cleanly into independent halves with a cheap combination step: quicksort, merge sort, binary search, FFT, Karatsuba multiplication. Dynamic programming exploits state — a situation describable by a small number of parameters, where the future depends only on the present, so a computed answer can be reused; the constraint is what makes it work, and it is the reason DP is not applicable to problems with cycles or with unbounded state. Backtracking exploits combinatorial search with pruning: the space is huge but most branches can be shown hopeless early. And graph algorithms exploit connectivity with weights, where BFS covers the unweighted case, Dijkstra the non-negative weighted case, and Bellman-Ford and Floyd-Warshall the rest at higher cost.

/* Two questions that choose the family. */
const Q1 = {

  difficultyIs: 'PROVING THE RULE IS SAFE',
};
const Q2 = {

  yes: 'dynamic programming',
  nonOverlappingButSplittable: 'divide and conquer',
  combinatorialSearchWithPruning: 'backtracking',
  objectsWithRelationships: 'a graph algorithm, with the family chosen by what the edges mean',
};
const WHY = 'it converts what-algorithm-does-this-problem-want from a recall question into a two-question question you can ask in thirty seconds';

Recognising a problem, and the four questions that make it recognisable

Before choosing a family you have to see the structure, and four questions do most of the work. Does the problem decompose? If you can write the answer for size n in terms of the answers for n/2 with a cheap combination, divide and conquer is available and is often the simplest correct thing. Do the subproblems repeat? If computing the answer for n requires the answer for n−1, n−2 and n−3, all of which will themselves want the same smaller answers, you have overlapping subproblems and dynamic programming applies. Does a locally best choice exist? If you can name the rule, use it; the difficulty is proving it safe. Does the answer require exploring alternatives? If you must try options and reject most, that is backtracking, and the value you add is the pruning. Then three more that decide the harder cases. Is there a bottleneck that repeats? If a solution repeatedly solves "which part do I break first", that is dynamic programming, and the subproblem is usually the prefix or the interval rather than the whole. Is there a natural sort order on the choices? If the answer is "the smallest lexicographically" or "the one that sorts first", you have a candidate for either greedy-with-proof or a search. Is there an exchange argument? If you can show that any optimal solution can be modified to include the greedy choice without getting worse, greedy is correct — and that argument, not the algorithm, is what you are actually looking for. That is the real test, and it is the reason greedy problems are hard: a greedy algorithm without an exchange argument is a guess that happens to work on the examples.

Then the four failure modes of problem recognition, which are the ways people pick the wrong family. Treating a dynamic programming problem as greedy, which is the most common and produces code that passes the small cases and fails at scale — the coin problem above is exactly this. Using greedy where a proof is required and assuming the examples suffice, which is the same error with more confidence. Applying divide and conquer where the halves are not independent, which doubles the work silently and is caught only by timing. And memoising something that is not a pure function of its arguments, which produces a cache of wrong answers and is the specific way dynamic programming gets blamed for a bug that is actually in the function. The mitigation for all four is the same and it is unglamorous: write the brute-force solution first and keep it. Not to ship — to compare against. A brute-force version over a small input space is the only practical way to know that a fast algorithm is correct, and the comparison is what caught the coin problem in this chapter's own exercise. It is also the technique from chapter four's binary-search section, and the reason it keeps coming up is that it is the only verification available for algorithms whose whole value is that you cannot check their output by hand on real data.

/* Four questions that make the structure visible. */
