Monolithic versus microkernel, and why the debate never ends

Two architectures, and the argument is about where the trust boundary goes. A monolithic kernel puts drivers, the file system, networking and process management all in kernel space with direct access to everything — one address space, one privilege level, fast calls between subsystems because there is no transition. It is what Linux, Windows and macOS are. Its problem is that the trusted base is enormous: every device driver is kernel code, and drivers are the least trustworthy code in any system, written against undocumented hardware by people who did not design the kernel. A microkernel keeps only the minimum in kernel space — thread management, IPC, address-space primitives — and puts the file system and drivers in user mode as servers communicating by message passing. Its problem is that a message-passing call costs a context switch, and file system operations become thousands of them, which is why every microkernel has ended up shipping performance workarounds that blur the line back towards monolithic.

Then the four factors that actually decide the choice, because the architecture follows from the constraints. Performance requirement: if the dominant workload is system-call-heavy, transitions dominate and microkernels lose unless the transitions are very cheap. Driver ecosystem: most driver code is written for a monolithic model, and porting it to a microkernel is real work. Security goals: the narrower the trusted base the smaller the compromise surface, and this is the argument microkernels have been making for forty years. And codebase reality: the deciding factor in practice is whether you are starting fresh or modifying something that exists, because the microkernel advantages are all about a small trusted core and the monolithic advantages are all about a large body of working code. The honest modern position is a hybrid: a small kernel with a narrow trusted base and most drivers in user space where the architecture allows, which is roughly what both Linux and Windows converged on independently. The lesson worth taking is the general one: the architecture follows from what must be trusted and what must be fast, and any answer that does not name both is an argument from preference.

/* Two architectures; the argument is where the trust boundary goes. */

Kernel vs user space. The kernel is the trusted core that touches hardware. User programs run "in user mode", and every privileged action (open a file, send network data, allocate memory) goes through a system call (read(), write(), fork()...) — a controlled gateway. This design is why your buggy program can’t wreck the whole machine.

11.2 Process vs thread — the concurrency split

Processes are isolated, expensive to create, and crash-safe, each with its own address space. Threads share memory within a process, are cheap to create, and are the main source of race conditions. This split shapes every concurrency decision, since threads communicate easily but need synchronisation.

# Processes: you can see them right now in your OS
#   (In PowerShell):  Get-Process
#   (In Linux/mac):   ps aux | less

Two one-liners that surface every running process on Windows and Linux/macOS — your OS is full of living evidence, so go look.

The one difference that matters, and everything it causes

A process has its own address space: its own memory, its own open files, its own environment variables, its own current directory. A thread is a unit of execution inside a process, and it shares all of that with its siblings. Everything else — the cost of creating one, the cost of communicating, the failure modes — follows from this single fact, and it is worth being able to state it without hesitation because every question about threading reduces to it. Processes are expensive and safe; threads are cheap and dangerous. Creating a process costs a new address space and a page table, which on a modern system with copy-on-write is on the order of tens of microseconds; creating a thread costs a stack, which is on the order of a microsecond. So a server handling ten thousand connections uses threads or an event loop, never one process per connection — not because processes are wrong but because ten thousand address spaces is more memory than the machine has. And communication has no shared state, which is why process-based systems need explicit channels: pipes, sockets, message queues, and shared memory if you are willing to give up the safety. A thread needs no channel and has no isolation, and that is the entire trade: cost and safety on one side, cost and convenience on the other, with the same underlying fact producing both.

Then what each is actually for, because the honest answer is that you should use threads for the wrong-looking reasons and processes for the right-looking ones. Use threads when the work is genuinely parallel and shares a lot of state — a server handling many requests where passing the data through would cost more than the sharing risks; a numeric program over a shared array; anything where the alternative is copying a large data structure per task. Use processes when the tasks are independent — running many separate jobs, where isolation means one crashing does not take the others down, and where a memory leak in one is bounded because its memory is reclaimed when it exits. Use processes when you are running untrusted code. And use a hybrid, which is what most large systems do: a few processes for isolation, many threads or an event loop within each for concurrency, because the two mechanisms have genuinely different costs and the boundary between them is a real design decision rather than a style preference.

  },

  whyNot: 'ten thousand address spaces is more memory than the machine has',

    threads: 'need no channel and have no isolation',

Context switching, and what the operating system is actually doing

Every thread is not running. The operating system is multiplexing them onto a fixed number of cores, and the mechanism is the context switch: save the current thread's register state, its stack pointer and its program counter somewhere the thread will find them, load the next thread's state, and resume it. The cost is not the arithmetic — it is that the working set is now cold. The new thread's code and data are not in cache, the branch predictor has no history for it, and the memory it needs must come from somewhere slower than where the previous thread left the cache. So a context switch costs far more than its instruction count suggests, on the order of a microsecond plus cache-miss time, and this is why a thread that is switched out and back in immediately is measurably more expensive than one that runs for a while. That fact drives the scheduling policy in the next section, and it is why every scheduler has a time slice rather than switching at every opportunity: switching more often than necessary is pure overhead.

Then the three costs that people budget wrongly. Memory per thread. Each thread needs its own stack, and the stack is reserved at a substantial default — a megabyte or more per thread is normal — so a thousand idle threads can reserve a gigabyte of address space of which almost none is touched. Lock contention. Threads sharing a lock serialise, so N threads contending on one lock are slower than one thread doing the work serially, and the cure is fewer threads or a better decomposition rather than more threads. Cache effects. Threads on the same core evict each other's data; threads on different cores do not share cache lines, so two threads writing to the same data on different cores cause cache-line ping-pong that costs far more than the writes. Then the practical sizing guidance, which is the thing to take away: for I/O-bound work, many threads is correct, because a thread blocked on I/O costs the system nothing. For CPU-bound work, the right number is close to the core count, because more threads than cores adds switching overhead and contention without adding throughput. And for anything else, measure — because the number that is right depends on the ratio of waiting to working, and that ratio differs per workload and per day.

11.3 Scheduling — who gets the CPU

The scheduler decides which process or thread gets the CPU next, balancing fairness, throughput, and response time. Classic policies include first-come-first-served, round-robin, priority scheduling, and multilevel feedback queues, which adapt priority to observed behaviour. Each policy trades off latency, overhead, and the risk of starvation.

When many processes want the (few) CPUs, the OS scheduler decides. Algorithms you should know at a name level:

The trade, and why it is not a single number

Scheduling is deciding which thread runs on which core, and the objectives are in direct conflict. Throughput wants as much work done per second as possible, which means long-running threads and few switches. Latency wants every request answered quickly, which means short time slices and frequent switching so nothing waits behind a long job. Fairness wants every thread making progress, which means no thread is starved — and fairness costs throughput, because the scheduler is deliberately interrupting productive work. Priority wants the important work first, which conflicts with fairness: a high-priority thread that never yields starves everything below it, which is why every priority scheduler also has ageing, where a waiting thread's effective priority rises until nothing is starved. So there is no single number that is optimal, and the reason is not that the designers were undecided: it is that the right answer depends on the workload, and a scheduler is a policy about which of these four you are sacrificing. An interactive desktop wants latency and fairness; a batch job wants throughput; a server wants a mix, weighted by what its users notice. That is why every modern scheduler supports multiple queues with different policies and lets the workload be assigned to the right one.

Then the four classical policies and the failure mode of each, because knowing the failure tells you when a policy is right. First-come-first-served: fair, simple, and catastrophic under a long job — one request that takes five seconds delays everything behind it, which is why a naive queue produces a tail latency that grows with load. Shortest job first: optimises average wait and is the theoretically optimal policy for that, and it is impossible to implement exactly because you do not know how long a job will take before it runs — so real systems approximate it with a decaying estimate per process, which is what the operating system's scheduler largely does. Round robin: gives every thread a slice, which is fair and predictable and costs a switch per slice, so a slice that is too short makes the system spend its time switching and a slice that is too long reintroduces the starvation. Multilevel feedback queues, which is the real answer and is worth describing because it is what almost every scheduler is: multiple queues at different priorities, a new thread starts high and is demoted if it does not use its slice, and any thread that blocks on I/O is promoted back up. The demotion is the insight — CPU-bound processes end up at the bottom and interactive processes end up at the top, without anybody having to say which is which. That is why a machine is not frozen by one runaway job while also remaining responsive to a keystroke, and it is the single best idea in this chapter.

/* The objectives are in direct conflict. */
const OBJECTIVES = [
  { o: 'throughput', wants: 'as much work per second as possible', means: ['long-running threads', 'few switches'] },
  { o: 'latency', wants: 'every request answered quickly', means: ['short time slices', 'frequent switching so nothing waits behind a long job'] },
  { o: 'fairness', wants: 'every thread making progress', means: 'no thread is starved',
    costs: 'throughput - the scheduler is deliberately interrupting productive work' },
  { o: 'priority', wants: 'the important work first', conflictsWith: 'fairness',
    resolution: 'AGEING - a waiting threads effective priority rises until nothing is starved' },
];
const NO_SINGLE_NUMBER = {

  reframe: 'a scheduler is a policy about which of these four you are sacrificing',
  byWorkload: ['an interactive desktop wants latency and fairness', 'a batch job wants throughput',
    'a server wants a mix, weighted by what its users notice'],
  consequence: 'why every modern scheduler supports multiple queues with different policies',
};

Measuring it, and the practical failures

Then how you tell whether scheduling is the problem, because most "the system is slow" reports are not. Throughput tells you about the average; percentiles tell you about the user. Average latency hides the worst case entirely, and a queue's behaviour is almost entirely in the tail — so report p50, p95, p99 and the maximum, and treat any service where p99 is many times p50 as having a problem regardless of the average. Load versus latency is a curve with a shape. As offered load rises, latency rises slowly, then sharply near saturation, then unboundedly because queues grow without limit — and that sharp knee is where a system goes from "a bit slow" to "down", and finding it is a capacity-planning question rather than an optimisation one. Utilisation should not be at one hundred per cent. A queue at 100 per cent utilisation has no capacity for a burst, and the time to recover from overload grows without bound as utilisation approaches one; running at 80 per cent is not pessimism, it is leaving room for the burst that will inevitably arrive.

Then the four practical failures, and each has a distinctive signature. Convoy effect: a short-running thread waits behind a long one because it arrived just after it, so a FIFO queue's average wait exceeds its best possible by a lot, and the fix is a shorter slice or priority for short jobs. Priority inversion: a high-priority thread is blocked on a resource held by a low-priority thread which is itself waiting for something, and the counterintuitive cure is that the low-priority thread's priority is temporarily raised — the classic solution being a priority inheritance protocol where the low-priority thread borrows the high one's priority while holding the resource. Starvation: a low-priority thread never runs because higher-priority work never stops; the cure is ageing, and the fact that every production scheduler has it is evidence that without it the problem is routine. And thundering herd: a resource held by a thread that goes to sleep wakes every waiter at once, all but one immediately re-sleeping, which is why a condition variable wake-up is unconditional — the woken thread must re-check the condition, and the herd is the price of not losing a wake-up.

11.4 Virtual memory — the great illusion

Virtual memory gives every process its own full, private address space through paging and page tables. Address translation maps virtual pages to physical frames on demand, with pages swapped to disk under memory pressure. This isolation is also the safety boundary keeping one process from reading another’s data.

Every process gets a private, full address space, even if RAM is small. The trick: paging. Virtual pages map to physical pages via a page table. Only pages currently in use sit in RAM; the rest live on disk in the swap area.

  • Accessing a page not in RAM → page fault → OS loads it from disk (slow!) → resume.
  • Thrashing: when the working set doesn’t fit, the system pages constantly and throughput collapses. You’ll see "swap usage 100%" dashboards do exactly this.

It’s also the foundation of safety:

Three abstractions, and what each one actually is

Virtual memory is three ideas that are usually taught as one, and separating them makes the whole thing coherent. Abstraction: each process is given an address space that appears to be its own, contiguous, starting at zero. Isolation: the mapping from those virtual addresses to physical memory is kept in a structure the process cannot modify — a page table, maintained by the operating system and written only in kernel mode. This is why one process cannot see another's memory, and it is worth being precise that this is not a courtesy: the page table is a kernel data structure and a user program has no instruction for writing it. Efficiency: the mapping is not all of physical memory. Each block of virtual memory — a page, typically four kilobytes — is either backed by a physical page or not present at all, and when it is not present the reference causes a fault that the kernel handles by finding the data somewhere else, possibly on disk. That indirection is the whole mechanism: a virtual address is not an address, it is a lookup key, and the page table is the lookup.

Then what you get, in order of how often it matters. Isolation: a bug in one program cannot corrupt another's data or read its secrets, and this is the reason the whole design exists — a 1980s program that wrote past the end of its array would corrupt other programs, which was the specific problem virtual memory solved. More memory than you have: a program can address sixteen terabytes on a machine with eight gigabytes, because the address space is a mapping rather than a physical claim, and pages that are never touched cost nothing. Shared libraries: two processes using the same library have the same physical pages mapped into both address spaces, which is why fifty instances of the same program cost the memory once for the code. Efficient allocation: a program can allocate and free freely, and the kernel reclaims what is unused — and because physical pages need not be contiguous, a process's memory does not have to fit in one run of free physical memory, which is the difference between virtual memory being possible and being merely convenient. Fast process creation: a new process gets a fresh address space in microseconds by copying a page table structure, because pages are shared copy-on-write until one of them is written to. And swap: inactive pages are pushed to disk so active ones fit in RAM.

/* Three abstractions usually taught as one. */
const THREE = [
  { i: 'abstraction', means: 'each process is given an address space that appears to be its own, contiguous, starting at zero' },
  { i: 'isolation', means: 'the mapping from virtual addresses to physical memory is kept in a structure the process cannot modify - a page table, maintained by the OS, writable only in kernel mode',
    whyNotCourtesy: 'the page table is a kernel data structure and a user program has no instruction for writing it' },
  { i: 'efficiency', means: 'the mapping is not ALL of physical memory',
    detail: 'each block of virtual memory - a page, typically four kilobytes - is either backed by a physical page or not present at all',
    whenAbsent: 'the reference causes a fault the kernel handles by finding the data elsewhere, possibly on disk',
    theMechanism: 'a virtual address is not an address, it is a LOOKUP KEY, and the page table is the lookup' },
];

/* What you get, in order of importance. */
const GETS = [
  { g: 'ISOLATION', detail: 'a bug in one program cannot corrupt anothers data or read its secrets',
    whyTheDesignExists: 'a 1980s program that wrote past the end of its array would corrupt other programs' },
  { g: 'more memory than you have', example: 'sixteen terabytes addressed on a machine with eight gigabytes',
    why: 'the address space is a mapping rather than a physical claim',
    consequence: 'pages that are never touched cost nothing' },
  { g: 'shared libraries', detail: 'two processes using the same library have the same physical pages mapped into both',
    gain: 'fifty instances of the same program cost the memory once for the code' },
  { g: 'efficient allocation', detail: 'a program can allocate and free freely and the kernel reclaims what is unused',
    keyFact: 'physical pages need not be contiguous, so a processs memory does not have to fit in one run of free physical memory',
    significance: 'the difference between virtual memory being possible and being merely convenient' },
  { g: 'fast process creation', detail: 'a new process gets a fresh address space in microseconds by copying a page table structure',
    how: 'pages are shared COPY-ON-WRITE until one is written to' },
  { g: 'swap', does: 'inactive pages are pushed to disk so active ones fit in RAM' },
];

Page faults, swapping, and why memory management has a cliff in it

A page fault is normal. Two kinds. A minor fault: the page is valid but not resident — the kernel pulls it from the page cache, which was almost certainly holding it already, and the cost is a memory read. A major fault: the page is not in memory at all, and the kernel must read it from disk, which is a hundred thousand times slower. This is worth internalising because it means a program's startup time is dominated by major faults, and that is why every runtime ships a precompiled or preloaded form of its standard library — the files are already in memory, so the faults are minor. Then swapping, and the modern version is not really swapping. The current mechanism is: the kernel watches memory pressure and evicts the least recently used pages, writing dirty ones to disk first. Nothing "swaps in" a whole process; the pages come back on demand. This distinction matters because the old model — swapping a whole process out and back — is what caused the thrashing disaster where a machine spent all its time paging and made no progress, and the fix was admission control, which is to say refusing to run so many processes that the working set cannot fit.

Then the cliff, which is the thing that makes memory management feel strange and is worth knowing before it happens to you. When the working set exceeds physical memory, performance collapses rather than degrading. Because every additional process adds page-table overhead and its pages compete for cache and for disk bandwidth, the total throughput goes down as you add processes past the point of fit. This is not a slow degradation; it is a cliff, and it is why a machine with 8 GB running nine browsers can be slower than one with 4 GB running four. And the four knobs that turn it, in the order worth trying. Reduce the working set. A smaller program needs less memory, and the fix is usually in the application rather than the system. Increase physical memory. Reduce swapping — usually a symptom, not a fix. Add cores. Which sounds wrong and is not: more cores means more processes running concurrently, which usually means a larger aggregate working set, which makes the cliff more likely rather than less. That last point is a real operational trap and it is the reason that "add cores" is frequently the wrong response to a memory-bound workload.

/* Two kinds of page fault. */
const FAULTS = {
  minor: { is: 'the page is valid but NOT RESIDENT', cost: 'the kernel pulls it from the page cache, which was almost certainly holding it already - a memory read' },
  major: { is: 'the page is not in memory at all', cost: 'the kernel must read it from disk - a hundred thousand times slower' },
  consequence: 'a programs startup time is dominated by major faults',
  whyRuntimesShipPrecompiled: 'the standard library files are already in memory, so the faults are minor',
};

/* Modern swapping is not swapping. */
const SWAPPING = {
  currentMechanism: ['the kernel watches memory pressure', 'evicts the least recently used pages',
    'writes dirty ones to disk first'],
  whatDoesNotHappen: 'nothing swaps in a WHOLE PROCESS; the pages come back on demand',
  whyItMatters: 'the old model is what caused the thrashing disaster',
  thrashing: 'a machine spent all its time paging and made no progress',
  fix: 'admission control - refusing to run so many processes that the working set cannot fit',
};

/* The cliff. */
const CLIFF = {
  fact: 'when the working set exceeds physical memory, performance COLLAPSES rather than degrading',
  why: ['every additional process adds page-table overhead',
    'its pages compete for cache and for disk bandwidth',
    'total throughput goes DOWN as you add processes past the point of fit'],
  notThis: 'not a slow degradation',
  example: 'a machine with 8 GB running nine browsers can be slower than one with 4 GB running four',
};
const KNOBS = [
  { k: 'reduce the working set', best: true, note: 'a smaller program needs less memory, and the fix is usually in the application rather than the system' },
  { k: 'increase physical memory' },
  { k: 'reduce swapping', isASymptom: true, note: 'usually a symptom, not a fix' },
  { k: 'ADD CORES', soundsWrong: true, isNotWrong: true,
    why: 'more cores means more processes running concurrently, which usually means a larger aggregate working set, which makes the cliff MORE likely rather than less',
    consequence: 'a real operational trap, and the reason add-cores is frequently the wrong response to a memory-bound workload' },
];
one process cannot see another’s memory because each has its own page table — the mapping is supervised by the OS.

11.5 File systems

A file system maps human-readable names to disk blocks through directories, inodes, and permissions. Features like hard and symbolic links, as well as journaling for crash safety, appear across every vendor-specific format. The concepts outlive any particular filesystem, so the mental model transfers everywhere.

A file system places bytes of your files onto disk blocks and keeps a directory structure. Concepts that outlive every vendor:

  • Directories map names → inodes (metadata blobs holding size, owner, block pointers).
  • Permissions: read/write/execute for owner/group/other (chmod 755 means owner rwx, others rx).
  • Hard links vs symbolic links: a hard link is another name for the same file; a symlink is a shortcut that can point anywhere (and can dangle).

  • Files, inodes, and why a filesystem is two namespaces

    The thing to understand is that a Unix-like file system is two independent structures, and most of its behaviour follows from keeping them separate. A file is a sequence of bytes with a name. That is all a file is at this layer — no type, no structure, no metadata beyond length and permissions, which is why a file can be a database, an image, an executable and a text document without the file system knowing or caring. An inode is the file's metadata record: its size, owner, permissions, timestamps, link count, and a list of where its blocks live on disk. A directory is a mapping from name to inode number. It is not a list of files; it is a table of name-to-inode pairs, and that distinction explains almost everything surprising about file systems. It is why a directory can contain an entry pointing to an inode that no longer has any blocks. It is why two names can refer to one file — a hard link — so removing one name leaves the file alive. It is why a symbolic link stores a path rather than an inode, so it can point to a file that does not exist yet and can point outside the tree. And it is why renaming a directory with a million files inside is fast while moving a million files is not: renaming changes one entry in one directory; moving is a rename per file.

    Then how the bytes are actually stored, because this is where the performance surprises live. Blocks. A file is divided into fixed-size blocks — typically four kilobytes — and each is stored wherever on the disk there is room. Block allocation strategies, and each one's cost: contiguous allocation gives the best read performance because one seek reads sequentially and a file's extent can be described in one entry, but it fragments and cannot grow a file without moving it. Linked allocation gives every block a pointer to the next, so the file grows freely with no external fragmentation, but reading block n means following n pointers, and one damaged pointer loses the rest of the file. FAT allocation keeps a linked list in a table at the start of the disk, which makes the pointers cacheable and the chain traversable without seeking back to the block itself — at the cost of a table that must be read and cached. Indexed allocation gives each file an index block listing its data blocks, which is the practical compromise: one extra read to get the index, then random access to any block, and the file grows freely. Modern file systems are indexed allocation with extent records, which is indexed allocation with contiguous runs recorded together so that a sequential read of a large file stays sequential.

    Then the layer above the disk, and the reason "delete" is complicated. The cache. Reads and writes go through a page cache, because a disk read is a hundred thousand times slower than a memory read and almost every read is followed by another read of nearby data. Write-back versus write-through. Write-back means the write goes to the cache and is acknowledged immediately, so it is fast and it is also lost if the power fails before the flush; write-through means the write goes to the disk before being acknowledged, so it is slow and it is durable. Recovery. A journal — a log of intended operations written before they are applied — means a crash leaves a log that says what was in progress, so the file system replays or rolls back rather than guessing; this is what journaling file systems do, and it is the difference between a machine that reboots and a machine that has to be reformatted.

    /* A Unix-like file system is TWO independent structures. */
const TWO_STRUCTURES = [
  { s: 'a file', is: 'a sequence of bytes with a name',
    detail: 'no type, no structure, no metadata beyond length and permissions',
    consequence: 'a file can be a database, an image, an executable and a text document without the file system knowing' },
  { s: 'an inode', is: 'the files METADATA record',
    holds: ['size', 'owner', 'permissions', 'timestamps', 'link count', 'where its blocks live on disk'] },
  { s: 'a directory', is: 'a mapping from NAME TO INODE NUMBER',
    notThis: 'not a list of files',
    explains: ['a directory can contain an entry pointing to an inode with no blocks',
      'two names can refer to one file - a hard link - so removing one name leaves the file alive',
      'a symbolic link stores a PATH rather than an inode, so it can point to a file that does not exist yet and can point outside the tree',
      'renaming a directory with a million files inside is fast while moving a million files is not',
      'renaming changes one entry in one directory; moving is a rename per file'] },
];

/* How bytes are stored. */
const BLOCKS = {
  what: 'a file is divided into fixed-size blocks - typically four kilobytes - stored wherever there is room',
};
const ALLOCATION = [
  { m: 'contiguous', pro: 'best read performance - one seek reads sequentially and a files extent is described in one entry',
    cons: ['fragments', 'cannot grow a file without moving it'] },
  { m: 'linked', does: 'every block has a pointer to the next',
    pros: ['the file grows freely with no external fragmentation'],
    cons: ['reading block n means following n pointers', 'one damaged pointer loses the rest of the file'] },
  { m: 'FAT', does: 'keeps a linked list in a table at the start of the disk',
    pros: ['pointers are cacheable', 'the chain is traversable without seeking back to the block itself'],
    cons: 'a table that must be read and cached' },
  { m: 'indexed', does: 'each file has an index block listing its data blocks',
    pros: ['one extra read to get the index, then random access to any block', 'the file grows freely'],
    compromise: 'the practical choice' },
  { m: 'modern: indexed with extent records', does: 'indexed allocation with contiguous runs recorded together',
    gain: 'a sequential read of a large file stays sequential' },
];

/* The layer above the disk. */
const LAYER = [
  { p: 'the cache', does: 'reads and writes go through a page cache',
    why: 'a disk read is a hundred thousand times slower than a memory read, and almost every read is followed by another read of nearby data' },
  { p: 'write-back versus write-through',
    writeBack: 'the write goes to the cache and is acknowledged immediately - fast, and lost if power fails before the flush',
    writeThrough: 'the write goes to the disk before being acknowledged - slow, and durable' },
  { p: 'recovery via a journal',
    does: 'a log of intended operations written BEFORE they are applied',
    gain: 'a crash leaves a log saying what was in progress, so the file system replays or rolls back rather than guessing',
    significance: 'the difference between a machine that reboots and a machine that has to be reformatted' },
];

    The operations, and the traps in each

    Four operations, and each has a trap that every file system has to solve. Open — find the name in the directory, get the inode, check permissions, load an entry into the per-process table of open files. Read and write — translate the file offset into a block number via the allocation scheme, go through the page cache, and handle a read or write past the end of the file, where a write extends the file and a read returns nothing rather than failing. Rename — two cases, because renaming within a directory is just an entry change and renaming across directories means moving the entry and possibly updating an inode reference; and the reason a cross-directory rename of a large file is expensive while a within-directory one is instant. Delete — and this is the interesting one. Deleting does not remove anything. It decrements the link count, and when that reaches zero the inode and its blocks are reclaimed. Which means a file can be deleted and still readable, by any process that already had it open, until that process closes it — the reason that on a running system deleting a file being executed works, and the reason disk space is not reclaimed until the last handle closes. This is the detail that surprises everyone once and that explains why "I deleted it but the space did not come back" is a question with a real answer.

    Then the traps, and they are worth naming because each is a real operational surprise. Permission bits are checked at open time, not at read time. You open a file with permission and it stays open even if the permissions are subsequently changed — which is why revoking access to a file does not affect a process that already has it open. Deleting an open file keeps the data until the last close. Renaming a file does not affect processes with it open, for the same reason, and this is how atomic replacement works: write a new file, rename it over the old one, and every process sees either the whole old file or the whole new one and never a half-written one. Case-insensitive and case-sensitive file systems are different systems and code written on one behaves differently on the other. A path is resolved every time. A symlink's target, a mount point's location and a directory's permissions are all re-checked on each access, so a file that is fine now may not be fine in an hour. And the file system is not durable against power loss unless it is told to flush — a call whose name varies by language and which most code never makes, and which is why a sudden power cut loses recently written files even though the program said it wrote them.

    /* Four operations, each with a trap. */
const OPS = [
  { op: 'open', steps: ['find the name in the directory', 'get the inode', 'check permissions',
    'load an entry into the per-process table of open files'] },
  { op: 'read and write', steps: ['translate the file offset into a block number via the allocation scheme',
    'go through the page cache', 'handle a read or write past the end of the file'],
    atEnd: 'a write EXTENDS the file and a read returns nothing rather than failing' },
  { op: 'rename', cases: ['within a directory: just an entry change',
      'across directories: moving the entry and possibly updating an inode reference'],
    cost: 'a cross-directory rename of a large file is expensive while a within-directory one is instant' },
  { op: 'delete', is: 'the interesting one', whatItDoes: 'DECREMENTS THE LINK COUNT',
    then: 'when it reaches zero the inode and its blocks are reclaimed',
    consequence: 'a file can be deleted and still readable by any process that already had it open, until that process closes it',
    explains: ['why deleting a file being executed works on a running system',
      'why disk space is not reclaimed until the last handle closes'],
    surprise: 'I deleted it but the space did not come back is a question with a real answer' },
];

/* Traps, each a real operational surprise. */
const TRAPS = [
  { t: 'permission bits are checked at OPEN time, not at read time',
    consequence: 'you open a file with permission and it stays open even if permissions are subsequently changed',
    operational: 'revoking access does not affect a process that already has it open' },
  { t: 'deleting an open file keeps the data until the last close' },
  { t: 'renaming a file does not affect processes with it open', whyItMatters: 'this is how atomic replacement works',
    how: 'write a new file, rename it over the old one',
    guarantee: 'every process sees either the whole old file or the whole new one and never a half-written one' },
  { t: 'case-insensitive and case-sensitive file systems are different systems',
    consequence: 'code written on one behaves differently on the other' },
  { t: 'a path is RESOLVED EVERY TIME',
    rechecked: ['a symlinks target', 'a mount points location', 'a directorys permissions'],
    consequence: 'a file that is fine now may not be fine in an hour' },
  { t: 'the file system is not DURABLE against power loss unless it is told to flush',
    detail: 'a call whose name varies by language and which most code never makes',
    symptom: 'a sudden power cut loses recently written files even though the program said it wrote them' },
];
    Journaling / durability:     before changing data, the OS logs the plan — so a crash mid-write doesn’t corrupt the whole disk.

11.6 Concurrency: locks, race conditions, deadlock

When threads share data, interleavings can corrupt it, which is a race condition. Locks serialise critical sections, but acquiring locks in inconsistent order can cause deadlock, and contention can starve threads. The tools of the trade are locks, mutexes, semaphores, and condition variables plus careful ordering discipline.

Preview of Ch. 23 but the core idea belongs here. When two threads share data, interleaving can corrupt it — a race condition.

import threading

balance = 100
lock = threading.Lock()          # the mutex: only one thread holds it

def spend(amount):
    global balance
    for _ in range(1000):           # make the race likely
        with lock:                  # atomic section: only one thread at a time
            balance -= amount

a = threading.Thread(target=spend, args=(1,))
b = threading.Thread(target=spend, args=(1,))
a.start(); b.start(); a.join(); b.join()
print(balance)   # 0 if locked correctly; racy garbage if lock is removed

Two threads decrement the same balance 1000 times each, guarded by a lock; remove the lock and the final value becomes racy garbage — the classic race-condition demo.

  • Lock (mutex) — ensures mutual exclusion.
  • Deadlock — two threads each hold a lock the other needs. Prevent by a fixed global order when acquiring locks.
  • Modern alternatives: atomics, lock-free data structures, or better — design without shared mutable state (message passing).

Why shared state needs protection, and what the guarantee has to be

When two threads share memory, three things can go wrong, and they are not the same problem. A race condition is the general case: the result depends on the relative timing of two operations, so the program is correct for one interleaving and wrong for another. A data race is the specific, nasty case: two threads access the same memory location, at least one writes, and there is no ordering between the accesses. It is undefined behaviour in most languages, which means the compiler may reorder, cache, or eliminate the access entirely — so it is not "usually fine", it is unspecified, and the specification permits something you would not have predicted. A deadlock is when nothing progresses because each thread holds what the other needs. The distinction between the first two is the important one and it is the one beginners get wrong: a race is about logic and a data race is about memory visibility, and fixing logic does not fix visibility. Two threads each incrementing a counter has a race; it may also be a data race. Two threads checking a flag before doing expensive work has a race that might not be a data race, and the answer is different — a lock for one, atomics for the other.

Then the three guarantees a correct concurrent program needs, and each answers a different question. Mutual exclusion: only one thread is inside a critical section at a time, so no two threads interleave their reads and writes of shared state. This is what a lock provides. Atomicity: an operation appears to happen all at once from another thread's perspective, with no partial visibility — which is what an atomic instruction provides, and which is a strictly weaker guarantee than a lock and much cheaper. Visibility and ordering: a write by one thread is guaranteed to be seen by another, in the order the program wrote them. This is the guarantee that plain reads and writes do not provide, which is why a value written by one thread can be read indefinitely by another as the old value — the compiler cached it in a register, or reordered the read before the write — and why "it works" on one core and fails on another is the characteristic symptom. And the fourth, implied by all three: ordering is transitive. If A happens-before B and B happens-before C, then A happens-before C, which is what makes the whole thing composable rather than requiring pairwise guarantees everywhere.

/* Three things that go wrong, and they are not the same problem. */
const PROBLEMS = [
  { p: 'a RACE CONDITION', is: 'the general case',
    detail: 'the result depends on the relative timing of two operations, so the program is correct for one interleaving and wrong for another' },
  { p: 'a DATA RACE', is: 'the specific, nasty case',
    detail: 'two threads access the same memory location, at least one writes, and there is no ordering between the accesses',
    status: 'UNDEFINED BEHAVIOUR in most languages',
    whatThatPermits: 'the compiler may reorder, cache, or eliminate the access entirely',
    notThis: 'not usually fine - it is unspecified, and the specification permits something you would not have predicted',
    example: 'two threads each incrementing a counter' },
  { p: 'a DEADLOCK', is: 'nothing progresses because each thread holds what the other needs' },
];
const DISTINCTION = 'a RACE is about LOGIC and a DATA RACE is about MEMORY VISIBILITY - fixing logic does not fix visibility';
const EXAMPLE = 'two threads checking a flag before doing expensive work has a race that might not be a data race, and the answer differs - a lock for one, atomics for the other';

/* Three guarantees, each answering a different question. */
const GUARANTEES = [
  { g: 'mutual exclusion', means: 'only one thread is inside a critical section at a time',
    provides: 'a lock',
    protectsAgainst: 'two threads interleaving their reads and writes of shared state' },
  { g: 'atomicity', means: 'an operation appears to happen all at once from another threads perspective, with no partial visibility',
    provides: 'an atomic instruction',
    comparison: 'strictly WEAKER than a lock and much cheaper' },
  { g: 'visibility and ordering', means: 'a write by one thread is guaranteed to be seen by another, in the order the program wrote them',
    notProvidedBy: 'plain reads and writes',
    symptom: 'a value written by one thread can be read indefinitely by another as the OLD value - the compiler cached it in a register, or reordered the read before the write',
    characteristic: 'it works on one core and fails on another' },
  { g: 'implied by all three', is: 'ORDERING IS TRANSITIVE',
    detail: 'if A happens-before B and B happens-before C, then A happens-before C',
    whyItMatters: 'makes the whole thing composable rather than requiring pairwise guarantees everywhere' },
];

The tools, in the order to reach for them, and their costs

Four tools, and the order matters because each is more expensive than the last and using the wrong one is the commonest performance mistake in concurrent code. Do nothing. Most shared state is avoidable: pass data rather than share it, use a local variable rather than a field, use an immutable value so there is nothing to protect, and make the ownership clear so only one thread touches it. Immutability. If a value never changes after construction there is nothing to synchronise, and this is why functional-style code with immutable data is dramatically easier to run concurrently — not because it is faster but because most concurrency bugs are impossible. Atomics. A compare-and-swap or a fetch-add, which gives atomicity on a single value at roughly the cost of a memory write, and which is enough for a great deal: reference counts, counters, flags, and lock-free stacks built from a compare-and-swap. Locks. A mutex, which gives mutual exclusion over anything, and which is the right answer when the state you need to protect is more than one variable or has an invariant spanning them. Condition variables, for waiting rather than spinning — and the discipline that goes with them is the single most important rule in this chapter: always wait in a loop, and always re-check the condition inside the loop. A wait with a bare condition will return spuriously, or return because of a different signal, and the code that does not loop is the code that will eventually miss a wake-up.

Then the costs, which are the reason the order above is the order. Contention: a lock held by a thread doing real work blocks everyone else, so a lock's cost is not its acquisition but the wait behind it, which grows with utilisation. Convoy and priority inversion: the failure modes from the last section, both possible with locks and neither possible with an atomic. Cost under no contention: an uncontended lock is cheap — a few tens of nanoseconds — and an uncontended atomic is cheaper; what is expensive is a lock that is occasionally contended, because the occasional acquisition is enormously expensive and the average hides it. Read locks are not free either, because the shared state still invalidates cache lines and readers still slow writers. And the deadlock risk rises with the number of locks. The ordering rule — always acquire in the same global order — eliminates the deadlock cycle, but it is a rule a code reviewer has to enforce and a human has to remember, which is why the modern preference is to have few locks, or none.

/* Four tools, in the order to reach for them. */
const TOOLS = [
  { t: 'DO NOTHING', covers: 'most shared state is avoidable',
    how: ['pass data rather than share it', 'use a local variable rather than a field',
      'use an immutable value so there is nothing to protect', 'make ownership clear so only one thread touches it'] },
  { t: 'IMMUTABILITY', means: 'if a value never changes after construction there is nothing to synchronise',
    why: 'functional-style code with immutable data is dramatically easier to run concurrently - not faster, but most concurrency bugs are impossible' },
  { t: 'ATOMICS', does: 'a compare-and-swap or a fetch-add',
    cost: 'atomicity on a single value at roughly the cost of a memory write',
    enoughFor: ['reference counts', 'counters', 'flags', 'lock-free stacks built from a compare-and-swap'] },
  { t: 'LOCKS', does: 'a mutex giving mutual exclusion over anything',
    rightWhen: 'the state you need to protect is more than one variable, or has an invariant spanning them' },
  { t: 'CONDITION VARIABLES', for: 'waiting rather than spinning' },
];
const THE_RULE = {
  statement: 'always wait in a LOOP, and always re-check the condition INSIDE the loop',
  why: 'a wait with a bare condition will return spuriously, or return because of a different signal',
  consequence: 'code that does not loop is code that will eventually miss a wake-up',
  rank: 'the single most important rule in this chapter',
};

/* The costs, which explain the order above. */
const COSTS = [
  { c: 'contention', detail: 'a lock held by a thread doing real work blocks everyone else',
    notTheCost: 'acquisition', theRealCost: 'the wait behind it, which grows with utilisation' },
  { c: 'convoy and priority inversion', note: 'both possible with locks and neither possible with an atomic' },
  { c: 'cost under NO contention', detail: 'an uncontended lock is a few tens of nanoseconds, and an uncontended atomic is cheaper',
    theProblem: 'what is expensive is a lock that is OCCASIONALLY contended, because the occasional acquisition is enormously expensive and the average hides it' },
  { c: 'READ locks are not free either',
    why: 'the shared state still invalidates cache lines and readers still slow writers' },
  { c: 'deadlock risk RISES with the number of locks',
    rule: 'always acquire in the same global order eliminates the cycle',
    burden: 'a rule a code reviewer has to enforce and a human has to remember',
    modernPreference: 'few locks, or none' },
