12 · Databases I — Relational & SQL

Relational databases and SQL hold most of the world’s structured data. This chapter covers the relational model, entity relationship design, joins, normalisation, and the ACID guarantees that keep transactions safe. It gives you the SQL fluency interviewers assume you already have.

12.1 The relational model — tables, rows, keys12.2 Designing with an ERD first12.3 SQL in five verb families12.4 Joins — connecting tables12.5 Normalization — no redundant truth12.6 Transactions & ACID12.7 SQL that interviewers assume you know12.8 Reading query plans with EXPLAIN

Almost every system on Earth keeps its truth in a database. Relational databases (with SQL) are the oldest, most reliable, and most battle-tested family. Master these chapters and you can build the data layer of any app.

12.1 The relational model — tables, rows, keys

The relational model organises data into tables of columns and rows. A primary key uniquely identifies each row, and foreign keys represent relationships between tables. A fixed schema with well-chosen keys and constraints keeps the data consistent and queryable.

Data lives in tables (relations). Each table has columns (attributes) and rows (records). Rules that keep data sane:

  • Primary key (PK): a column (or combo) uniquely identifying each row — never NULL, never duplicated.
  • Foreign key (FK): a column referencing another table’s PK, wiring tables together.
  • Schema: the fixed shape — table names, columns, types, constraints.
-- A small university schema
CREATE TABLE students (
    id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
    name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    email VARCHAR(150) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    enrolled_on DATE NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE courses (
    code VARCHAR(10) PRIMARY KEY,
    title VARCHAR(150) NOT NULL,
    credits INT DEFAULT 3
);

-- many-to-many: a student takes many courses; a course has many students
CREATE TABLE enrollments (
    student_id INT NOT NULL,
    course_code VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,
    grade VARCHAR(2),
    PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_code),
    FOREIGN KEY (student_id) REFERENCES students(id),
    FOREIGN KEY (course_code) REFERENCES courses(code)
);

Entities, attributes, keys, and how a table becomes a design

Relational modelling turns a real-world thing into a table, and the transformation has steps. An entity is a thing you would use a noun for — a student, a course, an order — and it becomes a table. An attribute is a fact about one entity — a name, a date, a total — and it becomes a column. A key is the attribute or attributes that uniquely identify a row, and it becomes a primary key. A relationship is a verb or a preposition — a student enrols in a course — and it becomes a foreign key or a junction table. That last step is where modelling goes wrong, and the reason is worth stating as a rule: relationships are not stored as columns on either side. The instinct is to put course_id on the student, or student_id on the course, and both are wrong for a many-to-many relationship, because a student can take many courses and a course can have many students, and one column can only hold one value. The correct structure is a third table, and it is worth understanding exactly what that table contains because it does more than link two tables.

Then the junction table in detail, since it is the pattern behind every many-to-many relationship and it is worth being able to build one on sight. It has a foreign key to each side — student_id and course_id. Its primary key is the pair, a composite key of both columns, and that is what prevents a duplicate enrolment, because the database will refuse a second row with the same two values. It may hold attributes of the relationship itself, which is the part people miss: an enrolment has a date and a grade, and those belong to the relationship, not to the student and not to the course. Putting grade on the student is a genuine modelling error because it implies every student has one grade, rather than one grade per course. And it may be a table you query directly, which is a useful reframing: the many-to-many relationship is itself an entity, it just happens not to have a name in the domain until you look at what you need to store about it. Three real examples of the same shape: an order and the products on it, with quantity and unit price; a user and a role, with granted-by and granted-at; an author and a book, with contribution percentage.

/* The transformation, step by step. */
const STEPS = [
  { s: 'entity', is: 'a thing you would use a NOUN for', instances: ['a student', 'a course', 'an order'], becomes: 'a table' },
  { s: 'attribute', is: 'a fact about one entity', instances: ['a name', 'a date', 'a total'], becomes: 'a column' },
  { s: 'key', is: 'the attribute or attributes that uniquely identify a row', becomes: 'a primary key' },
  { s: 'relationship', is: 'a VERB or a PREPOSITION', example: 'a student enrols in a course', becomes: 'a foreign key or a junction table' },
];
const RULE = 'RELATIONSHIPS ARE NOT STORED AS COLUMNS ON EITHER SIDE';
const WHY_RULE = {
  instinct: 'put course_id on the student, or student_id on the course',
  whyWrong: 'a student can take many courses and a course can have many students, and one column can only hold one value',
  correctStructure: 'a third table',
};

/* The junction table, in detail. */
const JUNCTION = [
  { has: 'a foreign key to each side', example: 'student_id and course_id' },
  { has: 'a COMPOSITE primary key of both columns',
    why: 'what prevents a duplicate enrolment - the database refuses a second row with the same two values' },
  { has: 'attributes of the RELATIONSHIP ITSELF',
    instances: ['a date', 'a grade'],
    example: 'an enrolment has a date and a grade, and those belong to the relationship - not to the student and not to the course',
    modellingError: 'putting grade on the student implies every student has one grade rather than one grade per course' },
  { has: 'direct queryability',
    reframing: 'the many-to-many relationship is ITSELF AN ENTITY, it just happens not to have a name in the domain until you look at what you need to store about it' },
];
const SAME_SHAPE = [
  { junction: 'order and the products on it', attributes: 'quantity and unit price' },
  { junction: 'user and a role', attributes: 'granted-by and granted-at' },
  { junction: 'author and a book', attributes: 'contribution percentage' },
];

Keys, in all their forms, and what each constraint buys

Then the key types, and each one is a different choice with a different cost. A surrogate key — an auto-generated integer with no business meaning — is the right default. It never changes, it is never reused, and it makes foreign keys narrow and indexes small. Its cost is that it carries no information, so a row is meaningless without a lookup. A natural key — a real-world identifier such as a national insurance number or a product code — is meaningful and self-documenting, and its cost is that real-world identifiers are not unique in practice, get reassigned, get mistyped, and sometimes change, and a primary key that changes means every foreign key referencing it must be updated. A composite key — several columns together — is unavoidable for a junction table and occasionally correct elsewhere. And a candidate key — any attribute set that is unique — means a table may have several and you pick one as primary and optionally enforce the others with a unique constraint, which is the mechanism behind "email addresses must be unique".

Then the constraints, and what each is really for, because they are the schema's contract and most of the value is in the ones people skip. NOT NULL: a column that cannot be unknown, which is the constraint that turns "possibly absent" into a compile error at insert time rather than a runtime surprise. UNIQUE: which is not only about uniqueness but is also how the database builds the index that makes lookups fast, so choosing which columns are unique is choosing what will be quick. FOREIGN KEY: which enforces that a referenced row exists, and which is the constraint that stops a table silently containing the identifier of a thing nobody has — the most common form of relational garbage. CHECK: a domain rule the database enforces, which is the right place for anything that is true regardless of application — a quantity that must be positive, a status that must be one of an enumerated set. DEFAULT: which is convenience, not validation. And the ON DELETE rule, which is the one nobody sets and everybody should: when a row that is referenced is deleted, does the reference become null, is it deleted too, or is the deletion refused? Each is a statement about what the relationship means, and picking it at the schema level means it cannot be decided inconsistently by ten different application code paths.

/* Key types; each is a different choice with a different cost. */
const KEYS = [
  { k: 'SURROGATE key', is: 'an auto-generated integer with no business meaning', default: true,
    gains: ['never changes', 'never reused', 'makes foreign keys narrow and indexes small'],
    cost: 'carries no information, so a row is meaningless without a lookup' },
  { k: 'NATURAL key', is: 'a real-world identifier such as a national insurance number or a product code',
    gains: ['meaningful', 'self-documenting'],
    costs: ['real-world identifiers are not unique in practice', 'they get reassigned', 'they get mistyped',
      'they sometimes change, and a primary key that changes means every foreign key referencing it must be updated'] },
  { k: 'COMPOSITE key', is: 'several columns together',
    when: 'unavoidable for a junction table and occasionally correct elsewhere' },
  { k: 'CANDIDATE key', is: 'any attribute set that is unique',
    detail: 'a table may have several; you pick one as primary and optionally enforce the others with a unique constraint',
    mechanism: 'which is how email addresses must be unique is expressed' },
];

/* Constraints, and what each is really for. */
const CONSTRAINTS = [
  { c: 'NOT NULL', is: 'a column that cannot be unknown',
    gain: 'turns possibly-absent into an error at insert time rather than a runtime surprise' },
  { c: 'UNIQUE', isNotJust: 'uniqueness - it is also how the database builds the index that makes lookups fast',
    gain: 'choosing which columns are unique is choosing what will be quick' },
  { c: 'FOREIGN KEY', enforces: 'that a referenced row exists',
    gain: 'stops a table silently containing the identifier of a thing nobody has - the most common form of relational garbage' },
  { c: 'CHECK', is: 'a domain rule the database enforces',
    rightPlace: 'anything true REGARDLESS of application',
    examples: ['a quantity that must be positive', 'a status that must be one of an enumerated set'] },
  { c: 'DEFAULT', is: 'convenience, not validation' },
  { c: 'ON DELETE rule', whyNobodySetsIt: true,
    options: ['the reference becomes null', 'it is deleted too', 'the deletion is refused'],
    eachMeans: 'a statement about what the relationship means',
    gain: 'picking it at the schema level means it cannot be decided inconsistently by ten different application code paths' },
];

A small university schema: students and courses with primary keys, plus an enrollments junction table whose composite key and two foreign keys wire the many-to-many relationship.

12.2 Designing with an ERD first

An entity-relationship diagram models a database design before any DDL is written, showing entities, attributes, and the cardinality of their relationships such as one-to-many or many-to-many. Sketching the diagram first forces you to think through how data connects. The cardinality you choose early decides how painful the schema feels years later.

Before writing DDL, draw an entity-relationship diagram: entities (tables) as boxes, relationships as labelled lines with cardinality (1:1, 1:N, N:M).

  students -----< enrollments >------ courses
   (1)          (N, bridging)         (1)
   "a student    "a student joins     "a course is
    has many      many courses"        taken by many"
    enrollments"                      enrollments"

Rules to remember:
- Put a foreign key on the "many" side of a 1:N relationship.
- N:M needs a junction/bridge table (enrollments above).
- 1:1 can merge into one table (or FK one side).

An ERD sketch: students and courses bridged by an enrollments table, plus the rules for putting foreign keys on the many side and using junction tables for N:M.

What an ERD is for, and the notation that matters

An entity-relationship diagram is a picture of the data model that is not the schema, and the distinction matters because the two answer different questions. The schema says what is stored; the ERD says what the relationships are and what each one means. Its value is that it forces the modelling conversation before the tables exist, when changing your mind costs nothing — and the specific things it makes visible are the ones a list of tables hides: the cardinalities (one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many), which determine the entire table structure; the optionality of each relationship, which determines whether a foreign key is nullable; and where the data actually lives, which is the question that decides whether a table is a table or a view over two others. The notation worth knowing is Crow's foot, and it is worth learning because it is compact and unambiguous. A circle means optional; a crow's foot means many; a single line means exactly one; a double line means mandatory. So the symbol at each end of a line states the cardinality from that end's perspective, and reading the diagram requires reading both ends — which is why a one-to-many is a crow's foot on the many side and a single line on the one, and why reading it backwards gives the wrong answer if you are not careful.

Then the four cardinalities and the table structure each one forces, because this mapping is the practical content of the section. One-to-one: the foreign key goes on either side, and the decision is a real one — the side that would exist alone gets the nullable foreign key, so the optional entity can exist without the mandatory one. The classic use is to extend an existing table with attributes that only apply to some rows, which avoids a nullable column on the main table and a permanent null-check everywhere it is used. One-to-many: the foreign key goes on the many side, always, because the many side is the one that repeats — a department has many employees, so department_id is on the employee. Many-to-many: a junction table, as the last section established. And the optionality, which is a separate axis from cardinality and is encoded by the circle: a customer may have zero orders, so customer_id on the order is nullable; a customer with an order must have a customer, so it is not.

Then how to review one, because a diagram is a design argument and the review questions are the deliverable. Does every relationship have both ends specified? A line with a crow's foot on one end and nothing on the other is under-specified and will be implemented by guesswork. Does every many-to-many have a named junction? And does that junction have its own name, rather than being called "the join table" — because if it has attributes, it is an entity and needs a name. Is every nullable foreign key deliberate? Nullable columns in foreign keys are the single most common sign of a relationship that was not thought about. Does every entity have a key that is stable? And is there any table here that is really a view? A table that is always derived from others, never written independently, is a view, and modelling it as a table creates two sources of truth that will drift. Finally, the question with the highest ratio of value to effort: can you say out loud what each table represents in one sentence? If any table needs two sentences, it is probably two tables.

/* An ERD is a picture of the DATA MODEL, not the schema. */
const WHY = {
  schemaSays: 'what is stored',
  erdSays: 'what the RELATIONSHIPS are and what each one means',
  value: 'it forces the modelling conversation before the tables exist, when changing your mind costs nothing',
  makesVisible: ['the cardinalities - one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many',
    'the optionality of each relationship, which determines whether a foreign key is nullable',
    'where the data actually lives, which decides whether a table is a table or a view over two others'],
};

/* Crow's foot notation. */
const CROW = {
  circle: 'optional',
  crowsFoot: 'many',
  singleLine: 'exactly one',
  doubleLine: 'mandatory',
  readsFrom: 'the perspective of that end',
  mustReadBothEnds: true,
  consequence: 'reading it backwards gives the wrong answer',
  example: 'a one-to-many is a crow foot on the MANY side and a single line on the ONE',
};

/* Four cardinalities and the table structure each forces. */
const CARDINALITIES = [
  { c: 'one-to-one', fk: 'on either side',
    decisionIsReal: true,
    rule: 'the side that would exist alone gets the nullable foreign key, so the optional entity can exist without the mandatory one',
    classicUse: 'extending an existing table with attributes that only apply to some rows',
    gain: ['avoids a nullable column on the main table', 'avoids a permanent null-check everywhere it is used'] },
  { c: 'one-to-many', fk: 'on the MANY side, always',
    why: 'the many side is the one that repeats',
    example: 'a department has many employees, so department_id is on the employee' },
  { c: 'many-to-many', structure: 'a junction table' },
  { c: 'OPTIONALITY', isA: 'separate axis from cardinality', encodedBy: 'the circle',
    example: ['a customer may have zero orders, so customer_id on the order is NULLABLE',
      'a customer with an order must have a customer, so it is not'] },
];

/* Review questions - the review questions are the deliverable. */
const REVIEW = [
  { q: 'does every relationship have both ends specified',
    consequenceOfNo: 'a line with a crow foot on one end and nothing on the other is implemented by guesswork' },
  { q: 'does every many-to-many have a NAMED junction',
    detail: 'and does the junction have its own name rather than being called the join table',
    why: 'if it has attributes it is an entity and needs a name' },
  { q: 'is every nullable foreign key DELIBERATE',
    note: 'nullable foreign keys are the single most common sign of a relationship that was not thought about' },
  { q: 'does every entity have a key that is STABLE' },
  { q: 'is there any table here that is really a VIEW',
    detail: 'a table always derived from others and never written independently is a view',
    consequence: 'modelling it as a table creates two sources of truth that will drift' },
  { q: 'can you say out loud what each table represents in ONE SENTENCE',
    ifNot: 'it is probably two tables',
    value: 'the highest ratio of value to effort' },
];

Design BEFORE data. Reshaping a live table that millions of rows depend on is expensive and dangerous. The ERD you draw on a napkin in week one determines the pain you feel in year three.

12.3 SQL in five verb families

SQL divides into five verb families: CREATE for schema, INSERT for adding rows, UPDATE for changing rows, DELETE for removing rows, and SELECT for querying. The SELECT clause order is fixed: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT. Two classic traps are forgetting WHERE on an UPDATE or DELETE, which then affects every row.

-- CREATE (DDL - shape)
CREATE TABLE ...;

-- INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE (DML - change data)
INSERT INTO students (name, email) VALUES ('Ada', 'ada@uni.edu');
UPDATE students SET name = 'Ada L.' WHERE id = 1;
DELETE FROM students WHERE email = 'spam@x.com';   -- ALWAYS use WHERE!

CREATE shapes the schema; INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE change data. The rule to live by: a DELETE or UPDATE without WHERE hits every row.

UPDATE/DELETE without WHERE hits every row. This is the "oops I deleted the whole table" story in every company. Run SELECT first, confirm the rows, then do it.

-- SELECT (read data)  -- the heart of SQL
SELECT id, name
FROM students
WHERE enrolled_on >= '2025-01-01'
ORDER BY name
LIMIT 10;

SELECT COUNT(*) AS total, YEAR(enrolled_on) AS yr
FROM students
GROUP BY YEAR(enrolled_on)
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;    -- HAVING filters groups (WHERE can't)

The logical order of execution, which is not the order you write

SQL is declarative: you state what you want and the database decides how. Almost every confusion about SQL comes from forgetting that the database's order of operations is fixed and is not the order the clauses appear in. The actual order is: FROM and the joins, then WHERE, then GROUP BY, then HAVING, then SELECT, then DISTINCT, then ORDER BY, then LIMIT. Three consequences follow immediately and each of them explains a specific confusion. You cannot use a select-list alias in WHERE. WHERE total > 100 is invalid when total is a column alias from the SELECT line, because WHERE is evaluated before the select list exists. The fix is either to repeat the expression or to use a subquery. You cannot use a select-list alias in GROUP BY either, in most databases, for the same reason — and this is why GROUP BY sometimes looks redundant when the same expression is repeated in the select list. You can use an alias in ORDER BY, because ORDER BY runs after the select list, which is why ordering by a computed name works while filtering by one does not. Knowing this one ordering resolves most of the "why does my query error or ignore my filter" reports, and it also explains why an aggregate in the select list forces a GROUP BY: the database must know which rows form a group before it can compute an aggregate over them.

Then the five clauses and what each one is actually for, which is not obvious because the names are verbs that suggest filtering. FROM names the source rows, possibly several, joined together. WHERE filters rows before grouping, so it may reference columns but not aggregates. GROUP BY partitions rows into groups defined by the listed expressions; it collapses many rows into one. HAVING filters groups, so it may reference aggregates, which is the only difference from WHERE and the reason both exist. SELECT chooses and computes the output columns. And then ORDER BY and LIMIT shape the result set after it has been computed. The relationship worth holding onto: WHERE narrows rows, HAVING narrows groups, ORDER BY shapes, and LIMIT truncates — and because of the execution order, filtering with WHERE is always cheaper than filtering with HAVING, because fewer rows enter the grouping. That is not just a style preference: a WHERE filter can use an index and a HAVING filter generally cannot.

/* SQL is declarative; the database's order of operations is FIXED. */
const ORDER = ['FROM and the joins', 'WHERE', 'GROUP BY', 'HAVING', 'SELECT', 'DISTINCT', 'ORDER BY', 'LIMIT'];
const CONSEQUENCES = [
  { consequence: 'you CANNOT use a select-list alias in WHERE',
    why: 'WHERE is evaluated before the select list exists',
    bad: 'WHERE total > 100 when total is a column alias from the SELECT line',
    fixes: ['repeat the expression', 'use a subquery'] },
  { consequence: 'you CANNOT use a select-list alias in GROUP BY either, in most databases',
    why: 'the same reason',
    explains: 'why GROUP BY sometimes looks redundant when the same expression is repeated in the select list' },
  { consequence: 'you CAN use an alias in ORDER BY',
    why: 'ORDER BY runs after the select list',
    explains: 'why ordering by a computed name works while filtering by one does not' },
  { consequence: 'an aggregate in the select list forces a GROUP BY',
    why: 'the database must know which rows form a group before it can compute an aggregate over them' },
];
const ONE_ORDERING = 'knowing this single ordering resolves most why-does-my-query-error-or-ignore-my-filter reports';

/* Five clauses and what each is actually for. */
const CLAUSES = [
  { c: 'FROM', does: 'names the source rows, possibly several, joined together' },
  { c: 'WHERE', filters: 'rows BEFORE grouping',
    mayReference: ['columns', 'not aggregates'] },
  { c: 'GROUP BY', does: 'partitions rows into groups defined by the listed expressions; collapses many rows into one' },
  { c: 'HAVING', filters: 'GROUPS', mayReference: 'aggregates',
    onlyDifferenceFromWhere: 'it may reference aggregates - which is why both exist' },
  { c: 'SELECT', does: 'chooses and computes the output columns' },
  { c: 'ORDER BY and LIMIT', does: 'shape the result set after it has been computed' },
];
const SUMMARY = 'WHERE narrows rows, HAVING narrows groups, ORDER BY shapes, LIMIT truncates';
const COST_NOTE = {
  fact: 'WHERE is always CHEAPER than HAVING, because fewer rows enter the grouping',
  reason: 'a WHERE filter can use an index and a HAVING filter generally cannot',
  notJustStyle: true,
};

The writing rules that prevent data loss

Four rules, and every one exists because of a real accident. Always write the WHERE clause first, then the rest of the query, then go back and run it without the other clauses to see how many rows it will touch. This is the single most effective habit in database work and it is not a convention — it is the technique that turns an accidental mass update into a harmless experiment. A DELETE or UPDATE without a WHERE clause affects every row in the table. Not "probably every row" — every row, and it commits unless you are in a transaction. Test the SELECT before the DELETE. The safest form of a delete in a production system is to run the corresponding select first, look at the count, and only then run the delete with the identical predicate. Wrap multi-statement changes in a transaction. A transaction gives you all-or-nothing: either every statement in it took effect or none did, and a failure rolls back. This is what makes it safe to run a migration in production, because a migration that fails half way leaves the schema in a consistent state rather than half-converted.

Then the other three writing practices, which are less about damage and more about reviewability. Explicit column names in INSERT, never INSERT INTO t VALUES (...). The bare form depends on the column order in the table, so adding a column breaks every call site that used it, and a statement that worked yesterday fails today with no change to the statement. Never SELECT * in application code. It is tempting because it is shorter and it breaks for three reasons: the result changes shape when somebody adds a column, a query that reads one column of a wide table still reads the whole row, and you get a class of bug where a renamed column is invisible until runtime. Qualify ambiguous column names. When two joined tables both have an id, an unqualified reference is an error in standard SQL and a silent wrong-answer in some databases. And then the two questions that catch design problems early: is this query going to be correct for an empty table, and for one with a single row? Aggregates return one row even over no rows — COUNT returns 0 while SUM returns NULL — and code that assumes the row exists is a bug that only appears in production.

/* Four rules, each because of a real accident. */
const SAFETY = [
  { r: 'write the WHERE clause FIRST, then the rest, then run it WITHOUT the other clauses to see how many rows it will touch',
    claim: 'the single most effective habit in database work',
    notAConvention: 'it is the technique that turns an accidental mass update into a harmless experiment' },
  { r: 'a DELETE or UPDATE without a WHERE clause affects EVERY row in the table',
    detail: 'not probably every row - every row, and it commits unless you are in a transaction' },
  { r: 'test the SELECT before the DELETE',
    safestForm: 'run the corresponding select first, look at the count, then run the delete with the IDENTICAL predicate' },
  { r: 'wrap multi-statement changes in a TRANSACTION',
    gives: 'all-or-nothing - either every statement took effect or none did, and a failure rolls back',
    why: 'what makes it safe to run a migration in production, because a migration that fails half way leaves the schema consistent rather than half-converted' },
];

/* Three more practices, about reviewability. */
const PRACTICE = [
  { p: 'explicit column names in INSERT, never INSERT INTO t VALUES (...)',
    reason: 'the bare form depends on the column order in the table',
    consequence: 'adding a column breaks every call site that used it, and a statement that worked yesterday fails today with no change to the statement' },
  { p: 'never SELECT * in application code',
    temptingBecause: 'it is shorter',
    threeReasons: ['the result changes shape when somebody adds a column',
      'a query that reads one column of a wide table still reads the whole row',
      'a renamed column is invisible until runtime'] },
  { p: 'qualify ambiguous column names',
    detail: 'when two joined tables both have an id, an unqualified reference is an error in standard SQL and a silent wrong-answer in some databases' },
];
const EARLY_QUESTIONS = [
  'is this query going to be correct for an EMPTY table, and for one with a SINGLE ROW',
  detail: 'aggregates return one row even over no rows - COUNT returns 0 while SUM returns NULL',
  consequence: 'code that assumes the row exists is a bug that only appears in production',
];
The heart of SQL in one read: WHERE narrows rows, ORDER BY and LIMIT shape output, while COUNT with GROUP BY and HAVING summarises across groups.

Clause order in SELECT: SELECT → FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → ORDER BY → LIMIT. Everything you write must let the engine keep that order.

12.4 Joins — connecting tables

A JOIN combines rows from two tables by matching a key such as a foreign key, returning one result set that spans both. INNER JOIN keeps only matching rows, while LEFT JOIN keeps every left row and fills NULLs where the right side has none; RIGHT and FULL behave symmetrically. Write the ON condition explicitly, alias tables, and inspect the execution plan when the engine picks a costly hash, merge, or nested loop join.

-- Who has enrolled in what?  (inner join = only matching rows)
SELECT s.name, c.title, e.grade
FROM students s
JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id
JOIN courses c     ON c.code      = e.course_code;

-- LEFT JOIN keeps every student even if they enrolled in nothing (NULL there)
SELECT s.name, c.title
FROM students s
LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id
LEFT JOIN courses c     ON c.code      = e.course_code;

Two reads of the same data: an INNER JOIN keeps only matching enrollments, while LEFT JOIN keeps every student even when they have no course yet.

What each join type produces, decided by set logic

A join is a filter over the cross product, and every join type is just a rule about which rows survive. That framing makes them derivable rather than memorised. INNER JOIN keeps rows present in both sides — the intersection, and the default when people write a bare JOIN. LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left side and adds matches from the right where they exist — the union-with-nulls, which is what you want when the question is "list everything and its optional related thing". RIGHT JOIN is the mirror and is almost always better written as a LEFT JOIN with the tables swapped, because it reads left to right. FULL OUTER JOIN keeps everything from both, with nulls on both sides — which is what you want when reconciling two lists that may each contain things the other lacks. And CROSS JOIN is the unfiltered product, which is useful for generating combinations and for a COUNT over pairs, and is otherwise a bug. The set logic behind them: inner is intersection, left is "all of A plus matching B", full is union-with-nulls. Once you can state which of those you want, the join type follows and there is nothing to memorise.

Then the null behaviour, which is where left and right joins become genuinely confusing, and the rule to remember is short: NULL means unknown, and comparison with unknown is unknown, so a NULL row satisfies no comparison — including !=. That has three practical consequences. WHERE filters on the joined column destroy the outer join. WHERE b.col IS NOT NULL turns a LEFT JOIN into an inner join, silently, because the where clause is evaluated after the join and discards the null-extended rows. The correct place for that condition is the ON clause of the join, which is evaluated before null-extension. This is the single most common join bug and it produces a result that is subtly too small rather than an error. Aggregate functions ignore nulls. COUNT(b.col) counts only non-null values while COUNT(*) counts rows, so the two differ exactly when there are unmatched rows — which is exactly the case you wrote the outer join to handle. Comparisons need IS NULL, never = NULL. And null-extended rows in a GROUP BY form their own group, which is usually what you want and occasionally not.

/* A join is a filter over the cross product; each type is a survival rule. */
const TYPES = [
  { t: 'INNER JOIN', set: 'intersection - rows present in BOTH sides',
    note: 'the default when people write a bare JOIN' },
  { t: 'LEFT JOIN', set: 'all of A plus matching B',
    use: 'when the question is list everything and its OPTIONAL RELATED THING' },
  { t: 'RIGHT JOIN', is: 'the mirror', betterWrittenAs: 'a LEFT JOIN with the tables swapped',
    why: 'it reads left to right' },
  { t: 'FULL OUTER JOIN', set: 'union with nulls on both sides',
    use: 'reconciling two lists that may each contain things the other lacks' },
  { t: 'CROSS JOIN', set: 'the unfiltered product',
    uses: ['generating combinations', 'a COUNT over pairs'], otherwise: 'a bug' },
];
const NULL_RULE = 'NULL means unknown, and comparison with unknown is unknown, so a NULL row satisfies NO comparison - including !=';
const CONSEQUENCES = [
  { c: 'a WHERE filter on the joined column DESTROYS the outer join',
    detail: 'WHERE b.col IS NOT NULL turns a LEFT JOIN into an inner join, SILENTLY',
    why: 'the WHERE clause is evaluated after the join and discards the null-extended rows',
    correctPlace: 'the ON clause of the join, which is evaluated before null-extension',
    rank: 'the single most common join bug',
    symptom: 'a result that is subtly too small rather than an error' },
  { c: 'aggregate functions IGNORE nulls',
    detail: 'COUNT(b.col) counts only non-null values while COUNT(*) counts rows',
    consequence: 'they differ exactly when there are unmatched rows - exactly the case the outer join was written for' },
  { c: 'comparisons need IS NULL, never = NULL' },
  { c: 'null-extended rows in a GROUP BY form their OWN group',
    usually: 'what you want', occasionally: 'not' },
];

The join traps, and the cost of getting them wrong

Five traps, each of which produces a wrong answer rather than an error, which is what makes them worth knowing. The fan-out. Joining two one-to-many relationships in one query multiplies rows: an order with three lines, each line with two products, produces six rows for two products, and every sum over that table is now three times too large. The fix is to aggregate in a subquery before joining, or to use COUNT(DISTINCT ...) where a count is all you need. Mixing inner and outer joins in one chain silently changes the meaning of every earlier outer join, because the inner join discards the null-extended rows that the outer join was supposed to preserve. Joining on a nullable column never matches when the value is null, so rows with a null foreign key disappear from the result without a word. Joining a derived column in the ON clause — a concatenation, a COALESCE, a function call — means the database cannot use an index on that column, which is the difference between a millisecond and a scan of the table. And assuming the row order of a join's output matches either input, which it does not and which nobody guarantees without an explicit ORDER BY.

Then the practical rules that come out of it, and they are short. Write the join, then write it again as text. Say out loud, in a sentence, what each table contributes to the output row — "this produces one row per order, with the customer's name attached" — because the sentence is what you check against the row count, and a query whose row count you cannot predict is a query you cannot trust. Check the row count. If the join produced far more rows than the left table, you have a fan-out; far fewer, you have an inner join where you wanted an outer. Use ON for join conditions and WHERE for row filters, always, and the exception is a filter you deliberately want to apply after the join. Prefer explicit INNER JOIN to a bare JOIN, because the reader then knows you did not merely forget the word. And when a query joins more than three tables, decompose it — aggregate the leaves in subqueries, then join the aggregates — because a four-table join is unreadable and its fan-out behaviour is impossible to reason about in your head, and the decomposed version is both faster and provably correct.

/* Five traps; each produces a WRONG ANSWER rather than an error. */
const TRAPS = [
  { t: 'the FAN-OUT',
    mechanism: 'joining two one-to-many relationships in one query multiplies rows',
    example: 'an order with three lines, each line with two products, produces six rows for two products',
    symptom: 'every sum over that table is now three times too large',
    fixes: ['aggregate in a subquery before joining', 'use COUNT(DISTINCT ...) where a count is all you need'] },
  { t: 'mixing inner and outer joins in one chain',
    mechanism: 'the inner join discards the null-extended rows the outer join was supposed to preserve',
    consequence: 'silently changes the meaning of every earlier outer join' },
  { t: 'joining on a NULLABLE column',
    symptom: 'never matches when the value is null, so rows with a null foreign key disappear from the result without a word' },
  { t: 'joining on a DERIVED column in the ON clause', instances: ['a concatenation', 'a COALESCE', 'a function call'],
    consequence: 'the database cannot use an index on that column',
    magnitude: 'the difference between a millisecond and a scan of the table' },
  { t: 'assuming the ROW ORDER of a joins output matches either input',
    detail: 'it does not, and nobody guarantees it without an explicit ORDER BY' },
];

/* The practical rules. */
const RULES = [
  { r: 'write the join, then write it again as TEXT',
    how: 'say out loud, in a sentence, what each table contributes to the output row',
    example: 'this produces one row per order, with the customer name attached',
    gain: 'the sentence is what you check against the row count',
    conclusion: 'a query whose row count you cannot predict is a query you cannot trust' },
  { r: 'check the ROW COUNT',
    tooMany: 'far more rows than the left table - you have a fan-out',
    tooFew: 'far fewer - you have an inner join where you wanted an outer' },
  { r: 'use ON for join conditions and WHERE for row filters',
    exception: 'a filter you deliberately want applied after the join' },

    why: 'the reader then knows you did not merely forget the word' },
  { r: 'when a query joins more than THREE tables, decompose it',

Join typeRows kept
INNER JOINOnly rows matching in both tables
LEFT JOINAll left rows + matches from right (NULL if no match)
RIGHT JOINAll right rows + matches from left
FULL OUTER JOINAll rows both sides; NULLs fill the gaps

Only nested loops, hash joins and merge joins exist under the hood — knowing that names the "why is my join slow" question (indexes! Ch. 13).

12.5 Normalization — no redundant truth

Normalization removes duplicated, inconsistent data by organizing tables through the normal forms, most commonly 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF, each eliminating one kind of redundancy such as repeating groups or transitive dependencies. Split tables along their dependencies so each fact lives in exactly one place, then join them back with keys. Real systems deliberately denormalize with indexes, materialized views, or cached columns to win back read speed, treating the normal forms as a starting point.

Normalisation removes duplicated, inconsistent data. The three levels you must know:

  • 1NF: atomic columns, no repeated groups. (No "skills" column holding "Python,SQL" — split it or make a table.)
  • 2NF: no partial dependency — every column depends on the whole primary key (matters for composite keys).
  • 3NF: no transitive dependency — city and country aren’t both stored when country depends on city… store only the key that determines the rest.

The three normal forms, and the anomaly each one prevents

Normalisation is a set of rules for designing tables so that each fact is stored once, and each rule targets a specific kind of wrongness called an update anomaly. The three forms are simpler than they are usually made to sound, and the right way to learn them is as a sequence of increasingly narrow problems. First normal form is about atomicity: every value in a cell is a single value, and there are no repeating groups. So a comma-separated list of phone numbers in one column is a violation, and the fix is a separate table with one row per number. Second normal form is about partial dependency, and it only applies once you are in first normal form: in a table whose primary key is composite, every non-key column must depend on the whole key rather than part of it. The example that makes it click: an order line table keyed by (order_id, product_id) that also stores product_name — the name depends only on the product, so it depends on half the key. Third normal form is about transitive dependency: every non-key column must depend on the key, on nothing but the key. The example is a customer table with a customer_city column where city is determined by the customer's postal code — so the city depends on the key through another column.

Then the reason each form is worth its complexity, because "no anomalies" is too abstract to be useful. Insertion anomaly: you cannot record a fact without recording another fact you do not yet have. Without normalising, you cannot create a customer until they have an order, because the customer's details live in the order row. Update anomaly: one fact is stored in many places and must be updated in all of them. A customer's address in fifty order rows is fifty chances to have one of them wrong, and the queries then have to decide which is correct. Deletion anomaly: deleting one fact destroys another you still need. Deleting the only order for a customer deletes the knowledge that the customer exists. These three are the entire argument, and they are worth more than the formal definitions because they are the reason the rules exist — and because they tell you what you lose if you denormalise, which the next section takes up.

/* Three forms, each targeting a specific update anomaly. */
const FORMS = [
  { f: 'FIRST normal form', about: 'ATOMICITY',
    rule: 'every value in a cell is a single value, and there are no repeating groups',
    violation: 'a comma-separated list of phone numbers in one column',
    fix: 'a separate table with one row per number' },
  { f: 'SECOND normal form', about: 'PARTIAL dependency',
    appliesWhen: 'only once you are in first normal form',
    rule: 'in a table whose primary key is composite, every non-key column must depend on the WHOLE key rather than part of it',
    example: 'an order line table keyed by (order_id, product_id) that also stores product_name',
    whyItViolates: 'the name depends only on the product, so it depends on HALF THE KEY' },
  { f: 'THIRD normal form', about: 'TRANSITIVE dependency',
    rule: 'every non-key column must depend on the key, on nothing but the key',
    example: 'a customer table with a customer_city column where city is determined by the customers postal code',
    whyItViolates: 'the city depends on the key THROUGH ANOTHER COLUMN' },
];

/* The three anomalies - the reason the rules exist. */
const ANOMALIES = [
  { a: 'INSERTION anomaly', is: 'you cannot record a fact without recording another fact you do not yet have',
    example: 'without normalising you cannot create a customer until they have an order, because the customer details live in the order row' },
  { a: 'UPDATE anomaly', is: 'one fact stored in many places and must be updated in all of them',
    example: 'a customer address in fifty order rows is fifty chances to have one of them wrong',
    consequence: 'queries then have to decide which is correct' },
  { a: 'DELETION anomaly', is: 'deleting one fact destroys another you still need',
    example: 'deleting the only order for a customer deletes the knowledge that the customer exists' },
];
const WHY_THESE = 'the three anomalies are more useful than the formal definitions because they are the reason the rules exist, and because they tell you what you lose if you denormalise';

Beyond the third form, and when to stop normalising

Then the higher forms, briefly but correctly, because knowing they exist prevents a mistake and using them is rare. Boyce-Codd normal form addresses a subtler case where a table satisfies third normal form and still has a dependency, when two candidate keys overlap so that one determines another without either being determined by the primary key. Fourth normal form addresses multi-valued dependencies: if a row independently stores two things that are both multi-valued, the representation allows a combination that does not exist — a person with two phone numbers and two email addresses stored in one row permits the cross-product of four, three of which are fiction. The fix is a second junction table. Fifth normal form handles the general case of a join dependency, and its practical rule is: if a table can be losslessly decomposed into three or more tables, decompose it. And then the practical note, which is the honest engineering position: almost nobody designs beyond third normal form on purpose. It is worth being able to recognise a fourth-normal-form violation, and that is where the knowledge is worth having.

Then the other half, and it is the half that distinguishes a schema that ships from a schema that is merely correct: denormalisation is a deliberate, measured choice, not a failure of discipline. The reason to do it is that a join costs something — a normalised design may need a four-table join to answer the common question, and a query that must join four tables to render a page is the query that will be slow. So you duplicate a value, or you precompute one, so that the common read is one table. The cost is precise and should be written down when you do it: a duplicated fact can now be wrong in one place and right in another, and the only thing preventing that is a procedure — a transaction that updates both, a trigger, or a job that reconciles. This is why "denormalised" and "no longer correct under a partial failure" are close to synonyms. And the three rules that keep it honest. Denormalise only against a measurement. The query you are optimising must be one you have profiled, and the answer must be a latency you have observed, because denormalising on a hunch adds a permanent correctness hazard for a benefit you cannot demonstrate. Denormalise the derived, not the source. A count, a total, a denormalised name copied from a foreign table — these can be recomputed and reconciled. Duplicating a fact that is the primary source of truth creates two sources of truth and no way to choose between them. Write down how the duplicate is kept correct, and if the answer is "we will be careful", you have not denormalised, you have introduced a bug with a performance benefit.

/* Higher forms - know they exist, use them rarely. */
const HIGHER = [
  { f: 'Boyce-Codd normal form', addresses: 'a subtler case where a table satisfies third normal form and still has a dependency',
    detail: 'two candidate keys overlap so that one determines another without either being determined by the primary key' },
  { f: 'FOURTH normal form', addresses: 'MULTI-VALUED dependencies',
    problem: 'if a row independently stores two things that are both multi-valued, the representation allows a COMBINATION THAT DOES NOT EXIST',
    example: 'a person with two phone numbers and two email addresses stored in one row permits the cross-product of four, three of which are fiction',
    fix: 'a second junction table' },
  { f: 'FIFTH normal form', rule: 'if a table can be losslessly decomposed into three or more tables, decompose it' },
];
const PRACTICAL_POSITION = 'almost nobody designs beyond third normal form ON PURPOSE - it is worth being able to RECOGNISE a fourth-normal-form violation, and that is where the knowledge pays';

/* The other half. */
const DENORMALISATION = {
  is: 'a deliberate, measured choice, not a failure of discipline',
  reason: 'a join costs something - a normalised design may need a four-table join to answer the common question',
  concreteCost: 'a query that must join four tables to render a page is the query that will be slow',
  theCostInWriting: 'a duplicated fact can now be WRONG IN ONE PLACE AND RIGHT IN ANOTHER',
  onlyPrevention: 'a procedure - a transaction that updates both, a trigger, or a job that reconciles',
  verdict: 'denormalised and no longer correct under a partial failure are close to synonyms',
};
const THREE_RULES = [
  { r: 'denormalise only AGAINST A MEASUREMENT',
    requirements: ['the query you are optimising must be one you have PROFILED',
      'the answer must be a latency you have OBSERVED'],
    ifNot: 'denormalising on a hunch adds a permanent correctness hazard for a benefit you cannot demonstrate' },
  { r: 'denormalise the DERIVED, not the source',
    derivable: ['a count', 'a total', 'a denormalised name copied from a foreign table'],
    whySafe: 'these can be recomputed and reconciled',
    forbidden: 'duplicating a fact that is the primary source of truth creates two sources of truth and no way to choose between them' },
  { r: 'WRITE DOWN how the duplicate is kept correct',
    ifTheAnswerIsCareful: 'you have not denormalised, you have introduced a bug with a performance benefit' },
];

Normalise in the schema; denormalise on purpose. Real systems deliberately denormalise (duplicate data) for read speed — but only when they understand the cost: write duplication and drift. "Third normal form, denormalised where measured" is the professional default.

12.6 Transactions & ACID

ACID is the guarantee that makes database transactions safe. Atomicity rolls back the whole unit if any step fails, consistency keeps every constraint valid, isolation hides half-finished work from concurrent transactions, and durability survives a crash. In practice you bracket statements with BEGIN, COMMIT, and ROLLBACK, pick an isolation level such as Read Committed or Serializable, and understand how locking or row versioning implement each level.

A transaction bundles several operations into one atomic unit: either all happen, or none.

BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1;   -- debit the sender
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT;               -- both took effect. If either fails: ROLLBACK;

A transfer wrapped in BEGIN and COMMIT: both updates apply together, or ROLLBACK undoes them both — the shape of every safe money-moving query.

What each property buys, and why isolation is the one you will fight over

ACID is four guarantees a database gives you about a transaction, and they exist because concurrent and interrupted work otherwise produces damage nobody can repair. Atomicity: the transaction either happens entirely or not at all — no half-applied state, ever. This is what the write-ahead log provides, and it is why a power cut mid-transaction leaves the database consistent rather than with three of five rows written. Consistency: the transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, preserving every constraint — foreign keys, checks, uniqueness. This is a weaker promise than it sounds and worth being precise about: it does not mean the data is correct, it means the declared rules still hold, so a check constraint that says quantity must be positive is enforced while a schema that fails to declare the rule has no protection. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see each other's uncommitted work, and the levels of isolation differ mainly in which anomalies they permit. Durability: once the transaction commits, it survives a crash, which in practice means the log was flushed to disk before the commit was acknowledged. The ordering matters: durability is the most expensive of the four, and a database that returns "committed" before the data is on disk has bought speed with a promise it cannot keep.

Then the isolation levels, and this is where the practical content is. Under read uncommitted, a transaction can see another transaction's uncommitted changes — the dirty read, and the reason the level exists at all is that it is sometimes faster. Under read committed, a transaction sees only committed data, which still permits a non-repeatable read: a row read twice may differ the second time because another transaction committed a change in between. Under repeatable read, reads within the transaction return the same values, which still permits a phantom — a row that did not exist when you started, appearing in a later query — because the guarantee is about rows you have read, not about the row set. And under serializable, the transactions behave as if they ran one at a time in some order, which prevents all of them at the cost of the most concurrency. The three anomalies map onto the levels exactly this way, and knowing the mapping tells you which level fixes which bug — which is the question you actually need answered.

/* The four guarantees. */
const PROPERTIES = [
  { p: 'ATOMICITY', is: 'the transaction either happens entirely or not at all - no half-applied state, ever',
    providedBy: 'the write-ahead log',
    gain: 'a power cut mid-transaction leaves the database consistent rather than with three of five rows written' },
  { p: 'CONSISTENCY', is: 'the transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, preserving every constraint',
    listed: ['foreign keys', 'checks', 'uniqueness'],
    weakerThanItSounds: true,
    preciseMeaning: 'it does not mean the data is CORRECT, it means the DECLARED RULES still hold',
    consequence: 'a schema that fails to declare a rule has no protection' },
  { p: 'ISOLATION', is: 'concurrent transactions do not see each others uncommitted work',
    note: 'the levels differ mainly in which anomalies they permit',
    isTheOneYouWillFightOver: true },
  { p: 'DURABILITY', is: 'once the transaction commits it survives a crash',
    inPractice: 'the log was flushed to disk before the commit was acknowledged',
    orderingMatters: true,
    mostExpensive: true,
    theCheat: 'a database that returns committed before the data is on disk has bought speed with a promise it cannot keep' },
];

/* Isolation levels, in order. */
const LEVELS = [
  { l: 'read uncommitted', permits: 'a transaction can see another transactions uncommitted changes - the dirty read',
    whyItExists: 'it is sometimes faster' },
  { l: 'read committed', guarantees: 'a transaction sees only committed data',
    stillPermits: 'a NON-REPEATABLE READ',
    detail: 'a row read twice may differ the second time because another transaction committed a change in between' },
  { l: 'repeatable read', guarantees: 'reads within the transaction return the same values',
    stillPermits: 'a PHANTOM',
    detail: 'a row that did not exist when you started, appearing in a later query',
    why: 'the guarantee is about rows you HAVE READ, not about the row set' },
  { l: 'serializable', is: 'the transactions behave as if they ran one at a time in some order',
    permits: 'nothing',
    cost: 'the most concurrency' },
];
const MAPPING_NOTE = 'the three anomalies map onto the levels exactly this way, and knowing the mapping tells you which level fixes which bug - which is the question you actually need answered';

Transactions in practice, and the places ACID does not reach

Then transactions as a tool, because the concept is easy and the practice is where the value is. Keep them short. A long transaction holds locks, blocks other writers, and enlarges the window for conflicts — and its benefit is not that more work is atomic, it is that fewer unrelated things are. Never do slow work inside one. A network call inside a transaction holds a database lock for the duration of someone else's latency, which is the most common cause of production lock contention and is entirely avoidable by doing the call first and the write after. Order your updates consistently when touching more than one table — always the same order — because two transactions taking the same two locks in opposite orders is a deadlock that has an exactly matching fix. Handle the failure path deliberately: every transaction needs a rollback path, and the code that opens a transaction without a try around it is the code that will eventually leave a lock held. And understand that a failed commit is a real outcome — a deadlock victim, a constraint violation, a timeout — and each should be handled or retried, not logged and ignored, because "the database refused" is not a reason to continue as though the write succeeded.

Then the places ACID does not reach, and this is the material that connects this chapter to the ones after it. Across databases. A transaction covering two databases is not a transaction; there is no coordinator and no atomicity, and this is the entire reason distributed transactions are the hardest thing in systems design. Outside the database. A transaction cannot include the filesystem or an HTTP call, so "update the database and send the email" has no atomic answer — and the two patterns that handle it, an outbox written in the same transaction and processed separately, and a saga that compensates with a reverse operation, are both out-of-transaction machinery by necessity. Across services. Same problem at a larger scale, and it is why "distributed transactions" and "two-phase commit" have a reputation their difficulty earned. Under replication lag. A read from a replica can be stale, so a read-after-write is not guaranteed unless the read goes to the primary — and applications that assume it will be get an intermittent bug that appears only under load. And against the physical world. You cannot roll back a sent email, a charged card, or a shipped parcel, which is why the compensating-action pattern exists at all. The honest summary: ACID is a promise about one database, inside one process, and every interesting problem is where that promise stops.

/* Transactions as a tool. */
const PRACTICE = [
  { p: 'keep them SHORT', why: ['a long transaction holds locks', 'it blocks other writers',
    'it enlarges the window for conflicts'],
    whatTheBenefitIsNot: 'that more work is atomic',
    whatItIs: 'that fewer unrelated things are' },
  { p: 'never do SLOW work inside one',
    detail: 'a network call inside a transaction holds a database lock for the duration of someone elses latency',
    rank: 'the most common cause of production lock contention, entirely avoidable',
    fix: 'do the call first and the write after' },
  { p: 'order your updates CONSISTENTLY when touching more than one table',
    how: 'always the same order',
    gain: 'two transactions taking the same two locks in opposite orders is a deadlock with an exactly matching fix' },
  { p: 'handle the failure path deliberately',
    rule: 'every transaction needs a rollback path',
    bug: 'code that opens a transaction without a try around it will eventually leave a lock held' },

PropertyPromise
AtomicityAll-or-nothing — no partial transfer
ConsistencyDB moves between valid states only (constraints always hold)
IsolationConcurrent transactions don’t see each other’s half-done work
DurabilityCommitted data survives crashes (write-ahead log)

12.7 SQL that interviewers assume you know

Views, common table expressions (CTEs), and window functions replace repetitive query code with clean building blocks. A view is a saved query reused like a table, a CTE is a named subquery readable within one statement, and window functions such as ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and LAG compute over rows without collapsing them. Control each window with OVER and PARTITION BY, and prefer these tools over tangled self-joins and subqueries.

Beyond CRUD and joins. Three everyday professional tools, each a "if you know this, you’re not a beginner" marker.

-- VIEW: a saved query that behaves like a table (encapsulation for SQL!)
CREATE VIEW active_students AS
SELECT s.id, s.name, COUNT(e.course_code) AS courses
FROM students s
LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id
GROUP BY s.id, s.name;
SELECT * FROM active_students;

A VIEW packages a grouped query as a reusable table-like object, so the app layer SELECTs from active_students instead of repeating the join.

-- CTE (WITH): build the query as readable steps, especially for recursion
WITH enrolled_counts AS (
    SELECT course_code, COUNT(*) AS n
    FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_code
)
SELECT c.title, ec.n
FROM courses c
LEFT JOIN enrolled_counts ec USING (course_code)
WHERE ec.n > 2
ORDER BY ec.n DESC;

A WITH clause builds a query as readable steps: count enrollments first, then join courses and filter on those precomputed counts.

-- WINDOW FUNCTIONS: compute per-group rankings WITHOUT losing rows (JOINs don't do this)
SELECT
    name,
    grade,
    RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY grade DESC)      AS class_rank,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY course_code ORDER BY grade DESC) AS pos_in_course,
    AVG(grade)   OVER (PARTITION BY course_code) AS avg_of_course
FROM enrollments JOIN students ON students.id = enrollments.student_id;

RANK and ROW_NUMBER compute standings per group while keeping every row — the feature that replaces messy self-joins and deduplicating subqueries.

The window-function superpower: "give me each row plus a value computed over its group" — leaderboards, per-store sales vs store average, deduplicating with ROW_NUMBER() = 1. This single feature replaces a pile of messy self-joins and subqueries.

Window functions, subqueries, CTEs, and set operations

Four tools that take SQL past single-table queries, and each one exists for a specific reason. Window functions compute across a set of related rows without collapsing them — which is exactly what GROUP BY cannot do, because grouping produces one row per group and a window keeps one row per row while referencing its neighbours. That makes them the answer to "rank these", "compare each row to the previous one", "what is the running total", "what fraction of the total is this row". The syntax has three parts worth knowing precisely: OVER (PARTITION BY ...) restarts the window at each group, ORDER BY ... sets the ordering the window functions accumulate over, and a ROWS BETWEEN clause sets the frame — ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW for a running total, ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW for a moving average. That frame clause is the part that confuses people and it is where the real power is. CTEs — WITH name AS (...) SELECT ... FROM name — give a name to a subquery, which makes a complex query readable and, more importantly, lets you express recursion. Set operations — UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT — combine result sets with matching column counts, and UNION deduplicates while UNION ALL does not, which is a meaningful performance difference on a large set and a bug when you wanted deduplication.

Then subqueries by name, because knowing which is which removes a real ambiguity. A scalar subquery returns one row and one column, and is used wherever a value goes: WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products). An existential subquery answers yes or no and is written WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ... WHERE ...) — and the SELECT 1 is not a placeholder, it is the idiomatic way of saying "I only care whether a row exists", and it lets the database stop at the first match. A derived table is a subquery in the FROM clause and needs an alias. And a lateral join lets a subquery in the FROM clause reference columns from the table it is being joined to, which is what makes "top three orders per customer" expressible in one query rather than a correlated subquery per row.

/* Window functions. */
const WINDOW = {
  computes: 'across a set of related rows WITHOUT collapsing them',
  whyNotGroupBy: 'grouping produces one row per group; a window keeps one row per row while referencing its neighbours',
  answers: ['rank these', 'compare each row to the previous one', 'what is the running total',
    'what fraction of the total is this row'],
  syntax: [
    { part: 'OVER (PARTITION BY ...)', does: 'restarts the window at each group' },
    { part: 'ORDER BY ...', does: 'sets the ordering the window functions accumulate over' },
    { part: 'ROWS BETWEEN ...', does: 'sets the frame',
      examples: ['ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW for a running total',
        'ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW for a moving average'],
      note: 'the part that confuses people, and where the real power is' },
  ],
};
const CTE = {
  form: 'WITH name AS (...) SELECT ... FROM name',
  gives: 'a name to a subquery',
  gains: ['a complex query becomes readable', 'it lets you express RECURSION'],
};
const SET_OPS = {
  operators: ['UNION', 'INTERSECT', 'EXCEPT'],
  requirement: 'matching column counts',
  keyDifference: 'UNION deduplicates while UNION ALL does not',
  consequences: ['a meaningful performance difference on a large set',
    'a bug when you wanted deduplication and wrote UNION ALL'],
};

/* Subqueries by name. */
const SUBQUERIES = [
  { k: 'SCALAR', returns: 'one row and one column',
    usedWhere: 'a value goes', example: 'WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products)' },
  { k: 'EXISTENTIAL', answers: 'yes or no',
    form: 'WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ... WHERE ...)',
    whySelectOne: 'not a placeholder - the idiomatic way of saying I only care whether a row exists, and it lets the database stop at the first match' },
  { k: 'DERIVED TABLE', is: 'a subquery in the FROM clause', requires: 'an alias' },
  { k: 'LATERAL JOIN', does: 'a subquery in the FROM clause may reference columns from the table it is joined to',
    gain: 'top three orders per customer becomes expressible in one query rather than a correlated subquery per row' },
];

Indexes and query plans, which is where the performance is

Then indexes, which is the highest-leverage topic in the chapter. An index is a second structure built on a column, ordered, that lets the database find rows without reading the table. The cost is real and is the reason this is not a thing to do everywhere: an index makes writes slower, because every insert and update must also update every index on the table, and it consumes storage that is often larger than the table itself. The decision therefore is per-column and depends on how the column is used. Index the columns you filter and join on, especially foreign keys, because a join on an unindexed column forces the database to scan. Composite indexes follow the column order of your query's WHERE clause, and the rule is non-obvious: an index on (a, b) helps a query filtering on a alone, or on a and b, but not a query filtering on b alone — which is why index column order matters and why you sometimes need a second index in the other order. Do not index a low-cardinality column by itself, because a column with three distinct values produces an index that does not narrow anything, and the database will correctly ignore it. Every index slows writes, so a table with fifteen indexes has fifteen structures to maintain on every write.

Then the query plan, which is how you find out what is actually happening. EXPLAIN shows the plan the database chose, and the output is less cryptic than it looks once you know the vocabulary. A sequential scan means the whole table was read — fine for a small table, a problem for a large one. An index scan means the index was used to seek; an index-only scan means the answer was in the index without touching the table, which is the best outcome. A nested loop join means one side was read once and the other looked up per row, which is good when the inner side is indexed and bad when it is not. And the two symptoms worth knowing: rows estimated versus rows actual differing by orders of magnitude means the statistics are stale and the optimiser is choosing badly — the single most common cause of a query that was fast and is now slow with no code change. And a sudden jump in cost after adding rows means the plan changed shape, because the optimiser switches strategy at a threshold — so the query that was fine at ten thousand rows can choose a hash join at ten million and become slower than the plan it replaced. The operational habit: keep the plan. When you write a query against real data, look at the plan, so that a future plan change shows up as a diff rather than as an incident.

/* Indexes - the highest-leverage topic in the chapter. */
const INDEX = {
  is: 'a second structure built on a column, ordered, that lets the database find rows without reading the table',
  cost: ['an index makes writes slower, because every insert and update must also update every index',
    'it consumes storage that is often LARGER THAN THE TABLE ITSELF'],
  therefore: 'a per-column decision that depends on how the column is used',
};
const INDEXING = [
  { rule: 'index the columns you FILTER and JOIN on', especially: 'foreign keys',
    why: 'a join on an unindexed column forces the database to scan' },
  { rule: 'composite indexes follow the column order of your WHERE clause',
    detail: 'an index on (a, b) helps a query filtering on a alone, or on a and b, but NOT one filtering on b alone',
    consequence: 'why index column order matters and why you sometimes need a second index in the other order' },
  { rule: 'do not index a LOW-CARDINALITY column by itself',
    why: 'a column with three distinct values produces an index that does not narrow anything, and the database correctly ignores it' },
  { rule: 'every index slows writes',
    consequence: 'a table with fifteen indexes has fifteen structures to maintain on every write' },
];

/* Reading a plan. */
const PLAN_VOCAB = {
  explain: 'shows the plan the database chose',
  sequentialScan: 'the whole table was read - fine for a small table, a problem for a large one',
  indexScan: 'the index was used to seek',
  indexOnlyScan: 'the answer was in the index without touching the table - the best outcome',
  nestedLoopJoin: 'one side was read once and the other looked up per row',
    good: 'when the inner side is indexed', bad: 'when it is not' },
};
const SYMPTOMS = [
  { s: 'rows ESTIMATED versus rows ACTUAL differing by orders of magnitude',
    means: 'the statistics are stale and the optimiser is choosing badly',
    rank: 'the single most common cause of a query that was fast and is now slow with no code change' },
  { s: 'a sudden JUMP IN COST after adding rows',
    means: 'the plan changed shape, because the optimiser switches strategy at a threshold',
    example: 'a query fine at ten thousand rows can choose a hash join at ten million and become slower than the plan it replaced' },
];
const HABIT = 'KEEP THE PLAN - when you write a query against real data, look at the plan, so that a future plan change shows up as a DIFF rather than as an incident';

CAST and type pitfalls: comparing a literal to a column of different type hurts indexes and surprises everyone. In SQLite use CAST(x AS TEXT) / keep types consistent column-to-column when you join. And remember NULL is not 0, not '' and never equal to anything — always check IS NULL.

12.8 Reading query plans with EXPLAIN

EXPLAIN shows how the database executes a query: which tables are scanned, which indexes are used, and how rows are combined. Run EXPLAIN, or EXPLAIN ANALYZE for real timings, in front of any slow query, reading bottom-up for scan and join nodes and watching for full table scans, missing index lookups, and sorts. Comparing plans before and after adding an index turns debugging from guesswork into investigation.

A query plan is the database’s execution strategy for your SQL: which tables are scanned, which indexes used, how joins are combined, where sorting happens. Reading plans turns "why is this slow?" from guessing into investigation.

-- Ask the database to explain, then read the verbs:
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
  SELECT u.name, o.total
  FROM orders o JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.id
  WHERE o.status = 'paid';

-- 0 | SCAN orders                       <- full table read: BAD for big tables
-- 0 | SEARCH u USING INTEGER PRIMARY KEY<- row lookup by id: GOOD
-- A plan line "SCAN" without an index = the table is read in full.
-- Windows/table scans per row = the join has no index to lean on.

-- Make the scan go away:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status ON orders(status);
-- Now: SEARCH o USING INDEX idx_orders_status (coverage!) ...

EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows the strategy — SCAN reads the whole table while SEARCH uses an index — and a single CREATE INDEX makes the scan disappear.

  • Seq scan vs index scan vs index-only scan: a scan reading the heap is I/O-bound; an index-only scan reads only the index — the fastest.
  • Cost numbers are estimates, not promises — but they rank strategies correctly; compare plans before/after an index and watch the row estimate.
  • When the plan can’t help: low-cardinality filters, "OR" misuse, function-wrapped columns breaking indexes (WHERE YEAR(created) = 2026 defeats created index).
  • Practice daily: run EXPLAIN on any slow query before touching application code.

Exercises 12 (use SQLite, Python’s built-in db)

import sqlite3
conn = sqlite3.connect("uni.db")
c = conn.cursor()
c.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS t (id INT PRIMARY KEY, v TEXT)")  # idempotent: safe to rerun
c.execute("INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 'a')")
conn.commit()
c.execute("SELECT * FROM t")
print(c.fetchall())      # [(1, 'a')]
