13 · Databases II — Indexes, NoSQL & Scaling

Databases II covers the machinery of speed and storage choice: indexes turn O(n) scans into fast lookups, and NoSQL trades relational validation for flexibility and scale. The chapter walks through index internals and query design patterns, then compares document, key-value, wide-column, and graph stores, applies the CAP theorem, and finishes with read replicas, sharding, and partitioning. Its goal is picking the right storage and querying it efficiently.

13.1 Indexes — the speed-up behind every query13.2 Query design patterns that matter13.3 NoSQL — when relational is not the best hammer13.4 CAP theorem & consistency levels13.5 Scaling reads and writes13.6 Partitioning & sharding, in practice

Now we make databases fast and choose the right storage for the job. Two giant topics: how indexes turn O(n) scans into O(log n) lookups, and when to leave relational validation behind for NoSQL flexibility.

13.1 Indexes — the speed-up behind every query

An index is a sorted structure, usually a B-tree, that the database probes instead of scanning the whole table, turning lookups from O(n) into roughly O(log n). Create one with CREATE INDEX on columns you filter, join, or order by, and use composite indexes that match your exact query shape. Each index costs disk and slows writes, so index only what you query and confirm usage with EXPLAIN.

An index is a sorted helper structure (typically a B-tree) on chosen columns, so the engine can jump to the right place instead of scanning the whole table.

-- Before: full scan over 10M rows looking for one email  (slow)
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'ada@uni.edu';

-- Add an index...
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email);

-- ...now the SAME query uses the sorted tree: O(log n)  (fast)

The same query before and after a CREATE INDEX: the engine swaps a full 10M-row scan for an O(log n) B-tree lookup.

  • Cost: indexes speed up reads, slow down writes (every INSERT/UPDATE must maintain the index), and eat disk. Index what you filter/join on.
  • Every PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE constraint already builds an index automatically.
  • A composite index (country, city) helps queries on country, and on country+city — but NOT on city alone (leftmost prefix rule).

Writing WHERE YEAR(birth) = 2000 hides the column inside a function, making the index unusable. Prefer WHERE birth >= '2000-01-01' AND birth < '2001-01-01'.

How an index works, and the three that matter

An index is an ordered structure that maps key values to row locations, so the database can seek to the rows it wants instead of reading them all. Understanding its two defining properties explains everything about when it helps. An index is sorted, which is what makes it useful for range queries — "all orders from January" is a contiguous range of the index and therefore a contiguous range of the file, which is the property that makes it fast and which a hash index does not have. An index is redundant, because it is derived from the table and can always be rebuilt — and every consequence of that follows. It takes storage, often more than the table. It must be updated on every insert, update and delete, so writes get slower in proportion to the number of indexes. And it can be inconsistent with the table if it is not maintained atomically, which is why an index is normally built inside the same transaction as the write.

Then the three kinds and what each is for. A B-tree index is the default and the general-purpose one: sorted, so it serves equality lookups, range scans and sorting, and balanced so its depth grows logarithmically, which is why a million-row index is only about three levels deep and why a lookup is three page reads regardless of table size. A hash index serves equality only — exact key lookups — and is faster than a B-tree for that one case because it computes an address rather than descending, with the limitation that it is unordered and therefore cannot do ranges, ordering or prefix matching. A full-text index tokenises the text into words and stores an inverted index mapping each word to the documents containing it, which turns a search from a scan into a lookup and is what makes search possible at all. And a partial or filtered index — an index over a subset of rows, defined by a predicate — which is the one beginners do not know exists and which is the right answer to "most queries only touch recent rows" or "we only ever query rows where this flag is set".

/* Two defining properties. */
const PROPERTIES = [
  { p: 'an index is SORTED', gain: 'what makes it useful for RANGE queries',
    example: 'all orders from January is a contiguous range of the index and therefore a contiguous range of the file',
    contrast: 'a hash index does not have this' },
  { p: 'an index is REDUNDANT', detail: 'it is derived from the table and can always be rebuilt',
    consequences: ['it takes storage, often more than the table',
      'it must be updated on every insert, update and delete, so writes get slower in proportion to the number of indexes',
      'it can be inconsistent with the table if not maintained atomically'],
    therefore: 'an index is normally built inside the same transaction as the write' },
];

/* Three kinds. */
const KINDS = [
  { k: 'B-TREE index', is: 'the default and the general-purpose one',
    serves: ['equality lookups', 'range scans', 'sorting'],
    whyFast: 'balanced, so its depth grows logarithmically',
    arithmetic: 'a million-row index is about three levels deep, and a lookup is three page reads regardless of table size' },
  { k: 'HASH index', serves: 'EQUALITY only - exact key lookups',
    fasterBecause: 'it computes an address rather than descending',
    limitation: 'unordered, so no ranges, no ordering, no prefix matching' },
  { k: 'FULL-TEXT index', does: 'tokenises the text into words and stores an inverted index mapping each word to the documents containing it',
    gain: 'turns a search from a scan into a lookup',
    significance: 'what makes search possible at all' },
  { k: 'PARTIAL or FILTERED index', is: 'an index over a SUBSET of rows defined by a predicate',
    unknownToBeginners: true,
    rightAnswerTo: ['most queries only touch recent rows', 'we only ever query rows where this flag is set'] },
];

Index design, the rules that follow, and when to remove one

Then index design, and the rules are fewer than people expect. Index columns you filter, join and sort on — and nothing else. Composite indexes follow the query's column order, with the rule from the previous chapter: an index on (a, b) helps a query on a, or on a and b, but not one on b alone. Put the columns in the order the queries use them, and if two queries use different orders, you need two indexes — which is why composite index order is a design decision made by looking at the queries rather than at the columns. Every index must be justified by a query, and the way to justify it is to find it in a query plan: an index the planner does not use is costing you writes and nothing else. And do not index low-cardinality columns alone, because a three-valued column produces an index that narrows nothing and the planner will ignore it.

Then the two operational problems, both of which cause the "it was fast last week" report. Unused indexes. They accumulate — one added for a query that was later deleted, one added optimistically — and each one makes every write slower, silently, because the cost shows up as a general slowdown rather than as a query getting slower. Redundant indexes: an index on (a) and one on (a, b), where the first is a prefix of the second and is therefore never used. And stale statistics, which is the third and the most consequential: the planner chooses a plan based on estimated row counts, so if those estimates are wrong by orders of magnitude it chooses badly, and the query that was fine can become slow with no change to the code and no error. The operational habit that follows, and it is the same reflex as before: when a slow query has no code change behind it, suspect statistics before suspecting the query. And the review question that catches all three at once: for each index, name the query that needs it. An index you cannot name a query for is costing you write throughput, taking storage, and doing nothing.

/* Index design rules - fewer than people expect. */
const RULES = [
  { r: 'index columns you FILTER, JOIN and SORT on - and nothing else' },
  { r: 'composite indexes follow the QUERYS column order',
    rule: 'an index on (a, b) helps a query on a, or on a and b, but not one on b alone' },
  { r: 'put the columns in the order the QUERIES use them',
    consequence: 'if two queries use different orders you need two indexes',
    therefore: 'composite index order is a design decision made by looking at the QUERIES rather than at the columns' },
  { r: 'every index must be JUSTIFIED BY A QUERY',
    how: 'find it in a query plan',
    verdict: 'an index the planner does not use is costing you writes and nothing else' },
  { r: 'do not index low-cardinality columns alone',
    why: 'a three-valued column produces an index that narrows nothing and the planner will ignore it' },
];

/* Two operational problems - both cause it-was-fast-last-week. */
const PROBLEMS = [
  { p: 'UNUSED indexes',
    accumulate: ['one added for a query that was later deleted', 'one added optimistically'],
    symptom: 'each one makes every write slower, SILENTLY, because the cost shows up as a general slowdown rather than as a query getting slower' },
  { p: 'REDUNDANT indexes', example: 'an index on (a) and one on (a, b)',
    why: 'the first is a PREFIX of the second and is therefore never used' },
  { p: 'STALE STATISTICS',
    mostConsequential: true,
    mechanism: 'the planner chooses a plan based on estimated row counts, so estimates wrong by orders of magnitude mean it chooses badly',

Read the query plan. EXPLAIN SELECT … shows whether a query uses an index seek (good) or a full table scan (bad). In SQLite: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM users WHERE email='x';. Make this reflex: any slow query → EXPLAIN.

13.2 Query design patterns that matter

Two query patterns earn their keep daily. Keyset pagination uses a WHERE clause on the last row’s key instead of OFFSET, so deep pages stay fast and stable as data changes, while SELECT FOR UPDATE locks the matching rows in a transaction so a stock decrement never oversells under concurrency. Implement them with indexed columns and short transactions, and avoid combining FOR UPDATE with patterns that yield deadlocks.

-- Pagination: limit + offset (offset gets slow on page 10,000!)
SELECT * FROM posts ORDER BY id LIMIT 20 OFFSET 500;
-- Better for deep pages: keyset pagination (fast, stable)
SELECT * FROM posts WHERE id > 499 ORDER BY id LIMIT 20;

-- Transaction + locking for a safe "decrement stock" (no overselling)
BEGIN;
SELECT stock FROM products WHERE id = 7 FOR UPDATE;   -- locks the row
-- if stock > 0: UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 7;
COMMIT;

Patterns that solve problems you will actually hit

Database design is mostly a small number of recurring problems, and each has a known answer. Row locking for correctness, not for structure. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE takes a lock on the rows it returns, so a read-modify-write cannot interleave with another. It is the answer to "two people buying the last item", because read the stock, check, decrement and write is three steps and two of them can be interleaved. The subtlety worth knowing: FOR UPDATE without a WHERE locks the whole table, which turns a small operation into a global one, and the lock is held until the transaction commits, so a long transaction inside it holds the lock for its whole duration. Keyset pagination instead of OFFSET. LIMIT 50 OFFSET 10000 makes the database produce and discard ten thousand rows to give you fifty, so the cost grows with the page number and deep pagination becomes unusable; the alternative is to remember the last key you saw and filter on it, which is constant cost at every depth. The catch is that keyset pagination requires a stable sort key, so a duplicate or reordered row can be skipped or repeated, and a unique tiebreaker column solves it. And upsert — insert-or-update in one statement — which matters because the "check then insert" pattern has a race in it and the single-statement form does not.

Then the patterns for the harder structural problems. Soft deletes — a deleted flag rather than a row removal — which preserves referential history and makes undo possible, at the cost of every query needing to filter and the flag column existing on every table. Multi-tenant data, and this has three genuinely different answers with different costs: a shared schema with a tenant column is cheapest and leaks most easily, because a forgotten WHERE returns another customer's data and no test catches it unless a test exists for it; a schema per tenant isolates perfectly but makes migrations a loop over every tenant and makes connection pools large; a database per tenant isolates best and costs the most in connections, licensing and per-tenant overhead. Soft-deletion plus a unique constraint is a trap worth naming: a unique constraint on an email column cannot coexist with soft deletes unless the uniqueness includes the deleted flag, at which point two deleted rows with the same address are permitted and re-creating that address twice is possible. And time-series data, where the practical answer is partitioning by time so old data can be dropped by dropping a partition rather than deleting rows.

/* Patterns that solve recurring problems. */
const PATTERNS = [
  { p: 'row locking for correctness, not for structure',
    how: 'SELECT ... FOR UPDATE takes a lock on the rows it returns',
    solves: 'two people buying the last item',
    why: 'read the stock, check, decrement and write is three steps and two of them can be interleaved',
    subtleties: ['without a WHERE clause it locks the WHOLE TABLE, turning a small operation into a global one',
      'the lock is held until the transaction commits, so a long transaction inside it holds the lock for its whole duration'] },
  { p: 'KEYSET pagination instead of OFFSET',
    bad: 'LIMIT 50 OFFSET 10000 makes the database produce and discard ten thousand rows to give you fifty',
    consequence: 'the cost grows with the page number and deep pagination becomes unusable',
    good: 'remember the last key you saw and filter on it',
    goodCost: 'constant at every depth',
    catch: 'keyset pagination requires a stable sort key, so a duplicate or reordered row can be skipped or repeated',
    fix: 'a unique tiebreaker column' },
  { p: 'UPSERT', does: 'insert-or-update in one statement',
    why: 'the check-then-insert pattern has a RACE in it and the single-statement form does not' },
];

/* Structural patterns. */
const STRUCTURAL = [
  { p: 'SOFT DELETES', shape: 'a deleted flag rather than a row removal',
    gains: ['preserves referential history', 'makes undo possible'],
    costs: ['every query needs to filter', 'the flag column exists on every table'] },
  { p: 'MULTI-TENANT data', has: 'three genuinely different answers with different costs',
    options: [
      { a: 'a shared schema with a tenant column', cost: 'cheapest',
        leak: 'leaks MOST easily - a forgotten WHERE returns another customers data',
        whyNoTestCatchesIt: 'unless a test exists for it' },
      { a: 'a schema per tenant', isolation: 'perfect',
        costs: ['migrations become a loop over every tenant', 'large connection pools'] },
      { a: 'a database per tenant', isolation: 'best', cost: 'most in connections, licensing and per-tenant overhead' },
    ] },
  { p: 'SOFT DELETE plus a unique constraint', isA: 'trap worth naming',
    detail: 'a unique constraint on an email column cannot coexist with soft deletes unless the uniqueness includes the deleted flag',
    consequence: 'two deleted rows with the same address are permitted, and re-creating that address twice is possible' },
  { p: 'TIME-SERIES data', answer: 'partitioning by time',
    gain: 'old data can be dropped by DROPPING A PARTITION rather than deleting rows' },
];

Transactions in application code, and the design review

Then the practical discipline, and it is a single rule with several corollaries. One transaction, one use case. A transaction that spans a use case has been given two responsibilities, and it holds locks for the whole of a longer operation, which is the mechanism behind production contention. The corollaries: do the slow work outside the transaction — the HTTP call, the file read, the third-party lookup; do not wrap a whole request handler in one transaction unless you have thought about what it holds; and handle the failure path, because a transaction that is opened and not committed on an exception path is a lock held until the connection times out. And retry on serialisation failure, since that is a normal, expected outcome under concurrency rather than an exceptional one — with the caution that a retry must re-read any state it depends on rather than reusing values it read before the failure.

Then the design review, which is the deliverable of this section and the thing that catches problems before a million rows exist. Six questions. Does every table have a primary key, and is it stable? Does every foreign key have an explicit delete rule? Can you name the query for every index? For every denormalised value, how is it kept correct? What is the slowest query this design will produce, and have you looked at its plan? And the one that catches the most: write out the three most common queries in plain language, and check the design answers them without a five-table join. If it cannot, the schema is wrong for how the data is used — and that is far cheaper to discover now than after the tables are populated and a migration would be required.

/* One rule, with corollaries. */
const RULE = 'ONE TRANSACTION, ONE USE CASE';
const WHY = 'a transaction that spans a use case has been given two responsibilities, and it holds locks for the whole of a longer operation';
const COROLLARIES = [
  { c: 'do the SLOW work outside the transaction', instances: ['the HTTP call', 'the file read', 'the third-party lookup'] },
  { c: 'do not wrap a WHOLE request handler in one transaction unless you have thought about what it holds' },
  { c: 'handle the FAILURE PATH', detail: 'a transaction opened and not committed on an exception path is a lock held until the connection times out' },
  { c: 'retry on SERIALISATION FAILURE', is: 'a normal, expected outcome under concurrency rather than an exceptional one',
    caution: 'a retry must RE-READ any state it depends on rather than reusing values read before the failure' },
];

/* The design review - the deliverable of this section. */
const REVIEW = [
  { q: 'does every table have a primary key, and is it STABLE' },
  { q: 'does every foreign key have an EXPLICIT delete rule' },
  { q: 'can you NAME THE QUERY for every index' },
  { q: 'for every denormalised value, HOW is it kept correct' },
  { q: 'what is the SLOWEST query this design will produce, and have you looked at its plan' },
  { q: 'the one that catches the most',
    how: 'write out the three most common queries in plain language and check the design answers them without a FIVE-TABLE JOIN',
    ifNot: 'the schema is wrong for how the data is used',
    timing: 'far cheaper to discover now than after the tables are populated and a migration would be required' },
];

Deep-page pagination stops using OFFSET in favour of keyset filters, and SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks one row so stock decrements can’t oversell.

13.3 NoSQL — when relational is not the best hammer

NoSQL databases fit data shapes that relational tables force awkwardly: document stores hold self-contained JSON-like records, key-value stores give tiny fast reads, wide-column stores handle massive analytical tables, and graph stores model connected entities. Choose the right one per workload, which is why many stacks run a relational database for core transactional data alongside a NoSQL store for heavy reads or specialized queries. Pick by access pattern, never fashion.

FamilyNamesShape of dataGreat for
DocumentMongoDB, CouchDBJSON-ish documentsFlexible schemas, product data, rapid iteration
Key-valueRedis, Memcachedopaque keys → valuesCaching, sessions, super-low latency
Wide-columnCassandra, BigTablerows with many sparse columnsMassive write throughput, time-series
GraphNeo4j, ArangoDBnodes + edgesFriend-of-friend, recommendation traversals

What actually differs, and why the categories are less clean than the marketing

NoSQL is a marketing term covering several genuinely different designs, and the useful way to learn it is as a set of trade-offs rather than as a list of products. Document stores keep a tree of values per record and are the right answer when an item is read and written whole and its internal shape varies — a product, an event, a user profile. Key-value stores are a hash table that survives restarts, with no query capability beyond "fetch by key", and their entire value is being so fast and so simple that they scale horizontally without thought. Wide-column stores are the closest relative of the relational model and the best fit for time-series or very large sparse datasets. Graph databases store relationships as first-class edges, so "find everyone within three hops" is a traversal rather than a chain of joins. And the honest note about the categories: most systems labelled NoSQL are adding relational features, and most modern systems use several of these at once, because no one data structure answers everything.

Then the trade-offs that genuinely separate them, and the one that decides everything. Consistency versus availability. Under a distributed model with network partitions — and partitions are not an edge case, they are guaranteed — you must choose: either the system stays available and may return stale or contradictory data, or it refuses to answer rather than answer wrongly. This is the CAP theorem, and it is not really a theorem you choose between three ways; it is a statement that in a partition you get either consistency or availability, never both. Then joins. A relational database joins arbitrary tables at query time and the database does the work; a distributed store usually cannot, because the data is on different machines and a network round trip is a thousand times slower than a disk read, so the design pushes the join to write time — you materialise what you would have joined. That is the real meaning of "denormalise for NoSQL": not a style choice but a requirement imposed by the distribution. And schema flexibility, which is genuine and useful — a document store lets a new field exist without a migration — but which is frequently overstated, because a field that is optional for the writer is still something every reader must handle.

/* NoSQL is a marketing term covering several genuinely different designs. */
const FAMILIES = [
  { f: 'document store', keeps: 'a tree of values per record',
    rightWhen: 'an item is read and written WHOLE and its internal shape varies',
    instances: ['a product', 'an event', 'a user profile'] },
  { f: 'key-value store', is: 'a hash table that survives restarts',
    capability: 'no query capability beyond fetch by key',
    value: 'so fast and so simple that they scale horizontally without thought' },
  { f: 'wide-column store', relation: 'the closest relative of the relational model',
    bestFor: 'time-series or very large sparse datasets' },
  { f: 'graph database', keeps: 'relationships as FIRST-CLASS EDGES',
    gain: 'find everyone within three hops is a traversal rather than a chain of joins' },
];
const CATEGORY_HONESTY = 'most systems labelled NoSQL are ADDING RELATIONAL FEATURES, and most modern systems use several of these at once, because no one data structure answers everything';

/* The trade-offs that genuinely separate them. */
const TRADE = [
  { t: 'CONSISTENCY versus AVAILABILITY',
    premise: 'under a distributed model with network partitions - and partitions are not an edge case, they are GUARANTEED',
    choice: 'either stay available and return stale or contradictory data, or refuse to answer rather than answer wrongly',
    cap: 'not a theorem you choose between three ways, but a statement that in a partition you get EITHER consistency OR availability, never both',
    decidesEverything: true },
  { t: 'JOINS',
    relational: 'joins arbitrary tables at query time and the database does the work',
    distributed: 'usually cannot, because the data is on different machines and a network round trip is a THOUSAND TIMES SLOWER than a disk read',
    consequence: 'the design pushes the join to WRITE TIME - you materialise what you would have joined',
    reframe: 'denormalise for NoSQL is not a style choice but a requirement imposed by the distribution' },
  { t: 'schema flexibility',
    genuine: 'a document store lets a new field exist without a migration',
    overstated: 'a field that is optional for the WRITER is still something every READER must handle' },
];

How to choose, and the mistake almost everybody makes

Then the choice, and the rule that prevents most of the mistakes: start with a relational database and shard it when you measure a need, because sharding a relational database is hard but not impossible, and migrating away from one later is far harder than it sounds. The reasoning is worth stating precisely. A relational database gives you joins, transactions and a query planner, which is an enormous amount of functionality you would otherwise rebuild; it gives up horizontal scale, which you can often get another way first — vertical scale, caching, read replicas, better indexes. Those are cheaper and reversible. Sharding is not reversible: once your data is distributed, every query that touched two shards is a distributed query, and every transaction that touched two shards is a distributed transaction, and both are permanently more expensive. The mistake is sharding before you have measured the need, and it is so common because the pressure to appear ready for scale arrives long before the traffic does. A related mistake is choosing a NoSQL store because the application "will need flexible documents eventually", when the flexible documents are a prediction and the transactional guarantees are a requirement.

Then the honest modern architecture, which is not "pick one" but "use each for what it is good at" and is what almost every large system actually looks like. The relational database is the source of truth, because it is the only one giving you transactions, and correctness is not negotiable. A key-value cache in front of it for reads that are expensive and happen often, because this is what removes read load without any change to your data model. A search index derived from the database, for full-text and faceted queries a relational database can do badly. And an analytics store that is a copy optimised for scanning, so the reporting queries do not compete with the transactional workload for the same locks. In every one of those cases the discipline is the same and it is the important part: exactly one system is the truth, and everything else is derived and can be rebuilt. That is the property that makes such a system repairable — because you can throw away the cache and the index and rebuild them from the source, which is not true of a design where two systems each hold a copy of the truth and neither can be reconciled from the other.

/* The rule that prevents most mistakes. */
const RULE = 'start with a relational database and shard it when you MEASURE a need';
const WHY = {
  hardNotImpossible: 'sharding a relational database is hard but not impossible',
  asymmetry: 'migrating away from one later is FAR HARDER than it sounds',
  whatYouGiveUpIfYouStartRelational: ['joins', 'transactions', 'a query planner',
    'an enormous amount of functionality you would otherwise rebuild'],
  whatYouGiveUp: 'horizontal scale',
  cheaperAndReversibleFirst: ['vertical scale', 'caching', 'read replicas', 'better indexes'],
  shardingIsNot: 'sharding is not reversible',
  consequences: ['every query that touched two shards is a distributed query',
    'every transaction that touched two shards is a distributed transaction',
    'both are permanently more expensive'],
  theMistake: 'sharding before you have measured the need',
  whySoCommon: 'the pressure to appear ready for scale arrives LONG BEFORE the traffic does',
  relatedMistake: 'choosing a NoSQL store because the application will need flexible documents eventually',
  asymmetry2: 'the flexible documents are a PREDICTION and the transactional guarantees are a REQUIREMENT',
};

/* The honest modern architecture. */
const MODERN = [
  { component: 'the RELATIONAL DATABASE', role: 'the source of truth',
    why: 'it is the only one giving you transactions, and correctness is not negotiable' },
  { component: 'a KEY-VALUE CACHE in front', role: 'reads that are expensive and happen often',
    gain: 'removes read load without any change to your data model' },
  { component: 'a SEARCH INDEX', role: 'derived from the database',
    for: 'full-text and faceted queries a relational database can do badly' },
  { component: 'an ANALYTICS STORE', role: 'a copy optimised for scanning',
    gain: 'reporting queries do not compete with the transactional workload for the same locks' },
];
const DISCIPLINE = {
  statement: 'EXACTLY ONE system is the truth, and everything else is derived and can be rebuilt',
  whyItMatters: 'that is the property that makes such a system repairable',
  repair: 'you can throw away the cache and the index and rebuild them from the source',
  notTrueWhen: 'two systems each hold a copy of the truth and neither can be reconciled from the other',
};

The truth most courses won’t say: NoSQL gained popularity less because relational is bad and more because sharding a relational DB across machines is hard while some NoSQL systems natively distribute. Modern stacks use both: Postgres for truth, Redis for speed, Elasticsearch for search.

13.4 CAP theorem & consistency levels

The CAP theorem states that when a network partition occurs, a distributed system must choose between consistency, where every node returns the same latest value, and availability, where every request still gets a response. Systems therefore pick one and implement the other partially, which is how eventual consistency, quorum reads and writes, and single-writer primaries arise. In practice you choose per operation instead of per system.

In a distributed database you can’t have all three, so you choose:

The theorem, stated correctly and then corrected

The claim usually taught is "pick two of consistency, availability and partition tolerance". That is wrong in a way that matters, and the correction is short. Network partitions are not a choice. In any distributed system spread over more than one machine, some messages will be delayed or lost — a switch fails, a cable is pulled, a machine is paused by the garbage collector long enough to look dead. This is not an edge case to be traded away; it is guaranteed, and the only question is whether your system handles it or falls over. So the real choice is between consistency and availability, and CAP is telling you that during a partition you cannot have both. Consistency, in the technical sense, means every read sees the most recent write, or the read fails — this is not the everyday meaning of the word and using it loosely is the second way people get this wrong. Availability means every read receives a response, and a stale response counts as a response. The theorem is then: when a partition occurs, the system must choose between returning an answer that might be stale, or refusing to answer.

Then the two corrections that make the theorem usable. CAP is not a three-way menu you choose from at design time. The choice is not between three deployed options; it is a per-operation behaviour, and — crucially — it only applies during a partition. When the network is healthy the system can be both consistent and available, and it should be. So a database advertised as "AP" is not permanently sacrificing consistency; it is sacrificing it during partitions and being perfectly consistent the rest of the time, which is why most systems give you both with slightly different guarantees in different circumstances. And PACELC is the extension that matters in practice: if there is a Partition, choose between Availability and Consistency; Else, choose between Latency and Consistency. The else branch is where nearly all real trade-offs live, because systems are partitioned rarely and are making latency-versus-consistency choices constantly — and this is the version of the idea that actually helps you design something.

/* The claim usually taught. */
const TAUGHT = 'pick two of consistency, availability and partition tolerance';
const WHY_WRONG = 'network partitions are NOT A CHOICE';
const PARTITIONS = {
  fact: 'in any distributed system spread over more than one machine, some messages will be delayed or lost',
  instances: ['a switch fails', 'a cable is pulled', 'a machine is paused by the garbage collector long enough to look dead'],
  status: 'guaranteed, not an edge case',
  onlyQuestion: 'whether your system HANDLES it or falls over',
  therefore: 'the real choice is between CONSISTENCY and AVAILABILITY',
};
const TERMS = {
  consistency: { technicalMeaning: 'every read sees the most recent write, or the read FAILS',
    notThis: 'not the everyday meaning of the word',
    secondMistake: 'using it loosely' },
  availability: 'every read receives a response, and a STALE response counts as a response',
};
const THEOREM = 'when a partition occurs, the system must choose between returning an answer that might be stale, or refusing to answer';

/* Two corrections that make it usable. */
const CORRECTIONS = [
  { c: 'CAP is not a three-way menu you choose from at design time',
    actually: 'the choice is a PER-OPERATION behaviour',
    and: 'it only applies DURING A PARTITION',
    whenHealthy: 'the system can be both consistent and available, and should be',
    explains: 'why a database advertised as AP is not permanently sacrificing consistency - it is sacrificing it during partitions and being perfectly consistent the rest of the time',
    consequence: 'most systems give you both with slightly different guarantees in different circumstances' },
  { c: 'PACELC is the extension that matters in practice',
    branches: ['if there is a PARTITION, choose between Availability and Consistency',
      'ELSE, choose between LATENCY and CONSISTENCY'],
    whyItMatters: 'the else branch is where nearly all real trade-offs live',
    evidence: 'systems are partitioned RARELY and are making latency-versus-consistency choices constantly',
    claim: 'this is the version of the idea that actually helps you design something' },
];

What each side buys in practice, and the design consequences

Then what each choice actually gives you, because the theorem is abstract until you know the price. Choosing consistency — refusing to answer during a partition — is what a bank balance requires: an overdraft that appears when the network recovers is not an acceptable outcome. The cost is that some requests fail, and every caller must handle failure, which is a cost you pay in code everywhere rather than in one place. Choosing availability — answering with possibly-stale data — is what a shopping cart or a likes counter requires: showing yesterday's item count is far better than showing an error. The cost is that the same question can have different answers at different moments, so the code must tolerate inconsistency, which again is a cost paid everywhere. And then the third category, which is not a side of the theorem but the most common real answer: neither, because the conflict can be prevented. If two users cannot edit the same row at the same time, there is no conflict to resolve. Design that partitions the data so that a given operation only ever touches one node eliminates the trade-off rather than choosing within it — and this is why a great deal of effective distributed design is really about avoiding concurrency rather than managing it.

Then the practical consequences, which is where this section should leave you. Every design has an answer and you should write it down: for this system, this operation, during a partition, the answer is stale or it is a refusal — and writing that sentence is what makes the behaviour intentional rather than accidental. Make failure a first-class path, because the availability choice means you must handle a response that is missing, and code that assumes a response will be present is written for the consistency choice and will fail in the partition case. Prefer designs that avoid the conflict: partition by the same key the operation needs, so a write touches one node. Prefer eventual consistency where you can, because it is the option that lets the system keep answering, and then engineer for the delay — show a pending state, allow a refresh, retry on conflict. And know that eventual consistency is not "no consistency": it is a guarantee that all replicas will converge, and the question is only how long that takes and what a read sees in the meantime, which is a design decision with a number attached rather than an absence of a guarantee.

/* What each choice buys, and its price. */
const CHOICES = [
  { c: 'CONSISTENCY', means: 'refusing to answer during a partition',
    requiredWhen: 'a bank balance - an overdraft that appears when the network recovers is not an acceptable outcome',
    cost: 'some requests fail and every caller must handle failure',
    wherePaid: 'in code EVERYWHERE rather than in one place' },
  { c: 'AVAILABILITY', means: 'answering with possibly-stale data',
    requiredWhen: 'a shopping cart or a likes counter - showing yesterdays item count is far better than showing an error',
    cost: 'the same question can have different answers at different moments, so code must tolerate inconsistency',
    wherePaid: 'again, everywhere' },
];

/* The third category: neither, because the conflict can be prevented. */
const AVOIDANCE = {
  idea: 'if two users cannot edit the same row at the same time, there is NO CONFLICT TO RESOLVE',
  design: 'partition the data so that a given operation only ever touches one node',
  effect: 'eliminates the trade-off rather than choosing within it',
  whyItMatters: 'a great deal of effective distributed design is really about AVOIDING concurrency rather than managing it',
};

/* Practical consequences. */
const CONSEQUENCES = [
  { c: 'every design has an answer - WRITE IT DOWN',
    sentence: 'for this system, this operation, during a partition, the answer is stale or it is a refusal',
    gain: 'that is what makes the behaviour intentional rather than accidental' },
  { c: 'make FAILURE a first-class path',
    why: 'the availability choice means you must handle a response that is missing',
    bug: 'code that assumes a response will be present is written for the consistency choice and will fail in the partition case' },
  { c: 'prefer designs that AVOID the conflict',
    how: 'partition by the same key the operation needs, so a write touches one node' },
  { c: 'prefer EVENTUAL consistency where you can',
    why: 'it is the option that lets the system keep answering',
    thenEngineerForTheDelay: ['show a pending state', 'allow a refresh', 'retry on conflict'] },
  { c: 'know that eventual consistency is NOT no consistency',
    is: 'a guarantee that all replicas will CONVERGE',
    theQuestionOnly: 'how long that takes, and what a read sees in the meantime',
    reframe: 'a design decision with a number attached rather than an absence of a guarantee' },

PropertyMeaning
ConsistencyEvery read sees the latest write
AvailabilityEvery request gets a response (even if stale)
Partition toleranceSystem keeps working when network links fail

During a partition, a distributed system must choose C or A. The practical spectrum is eventual consistency: replicas will converge over time, not instantly. Making products tolerate eventual consistency ("your profile edit shows in ≤ 5 s everywhere") is a real engineering discipline.

13.5 Scaling reads and writes

Scaling a database means layering specialized fixes: read replicas absorb SELECT traffic, sharding spreads writes across nodes, and caches serve hot data without touching storage. Each fix brings its own cost, from replica lag and cross-shard joins to cache invalidation and staleness, so measure the bottleneck before adding machinery. Route reads to replicas, partition by a stable key like a user ID, and keep write-heavy, strongly consistent operations on the primary.

  • Read scaling — read replicas: copy data to followers; route reads to them, writes to the leader. Reads scale horizontally.
  • Write scaling — sharding: split rows across machines by a shard key (e.g. user_id). Joins across shards get painful — so you denormalise and accept trade-offs.
  • Caching (write-through/read-through): hot data in Redis; DB is source of truth.

    The three axes, and why they are not independent

    Scaling has three axes and they are usually confused because they are cited together. Vertical scaling makes one machine bigger. It is the cheapest in engineering effort and the most limited in ceiling — there is a largest server, and beyond it you need something else. Its real virtue is that it requires no application change at all, which is why it is always tried first. Horizontal scaling makes many machines, which is unbounded and requires the application to know or not care. The difficulty is not the machines; it is that state is what breaks, because a process that keeps something in memory sees only its own copy. Read scaling — replicas, caching, a CDN — is a special case of horizontal scaling that is worth separating because it is by far the easiest and it covers most of the load. Real traffic is usually read-dominated by a large factor, which is why the first thing that works is a cache and the last thing anyone attempts is sharding.

    Then why the axes are not independent, and this is the part that surprises people. State is the constraint on everything. Stateless processes scale horizontally because a request can go to any machine; stateful processes cannot, so making them stateless is the single highest-leverage scaling work there is — and the techniques are specific. Push state out of the process: sessions into a store, so any machine can serve any request. Push state down into a shared system: a database, so it is consistent and shared. Replicate reads, write one node: so most reads do not touch the write path. And partition the state: so each machine owns a slice, which is sharding and is a different and much harder problem than the first three. The order of that list is the correct order, because the first three are reversible and the fourth is not.

    /* Three axes, cited together and usually confused. */
const AXES = [
  { a: 'VERTICAL', does: 'makes one machine bigger',
    effort: 'cheapest in engineering effort', ceiling: 'most limited - there is a largest server',
    virtue: 'requires NO APPLICATION CHANGE AT ALL, which is why it is always tried first' },
  { a: 'HORIZONTAL', does: 'makes many machines', ceiling: 'unbounded',
    requires: 'the application to know or not care',
    difficulty: 'not the machines - STATE is what breaks, because a process that keeps something in memory sees only its own copy' },
  { a: 'READ scaling', is: 'a special case of horizontal scaling',
    worthSeparating: 'because it is by far the easiest and covers most of the load',
    instances: ['replicas', 'caching', 'a CDN'],
    evidence: 'real traffic is usually READ-DOMINATED by a large factor, which is why a cache is tried first and sharding is attempted last' },
];
const NOT_INDEPENDENT = 'state is the constraint on everything';
const STATEFUL_TO_STATELESS = {
  highestLeverage: 'making processes stateless is the single highest-leverage scaling work there is',
  techniques: [
    { t: 'push state OUT of the process', how: 'sessions into a store', gain: 'any machine can serve any request' },
    { t: 'push state DOWN into a shared system', how: 'a database', gain: 'it is consistent and shared' },
    { t: 'replicate reads, write one node', gain: 'most reads do not touch the write path' },
    { t: 'PARTITION the state', is: 'sharding', difficulty: 'a different and much harder problem than the first three' },
  ],
  theOrderMatters: 'the first three are REVERSIBLE and the fourth is not',
};

    Read scaling, caching, and why invalidation is hard

    Then read scaling, in the order it should actually be attempted. A CDN for static assets, because it moves bytes off your origin entirely and no application change is needed. A cache in front of the database, which is the biggest single win available and the right first database-level intervention. Read replicas, which scales reads and can also serve analytics queries so they stop competing with the transactional workload. And precomputed views — a denormalised summary table maintained on write, for a report that is expensive to compute and read often. Then what a cache is and why invalidation is hard, because this is the topic's reputation and the reputation is deserved. A cache stores a value derived from something else, and it is correct exactly while that something else is unchanged. The difficulty is not the caching; it is that the cache must be told, and there are more ways to change the underlying data than the program has hooks for. A write through your own application code is easy to intercept. A write from a migration, a background job, a manual fix in a database console, another service, or a periodic recomputation is not. Each is a hole through which the cache becomes stale, and the bug appears as a user seeing old data with no error anywhere.

    Then the three invalidation strategies, and the trade is the same one as everywhere. Time-based expiry: a value is valid for a fixed period. Simple, bounded staleness, and it works when staleness is acceptable — which is very often true for a page of product listings and never true for a permission check. Explicit invalidation: the code that writes deletes or updates the cache. Correct when every write goes through code you control, and silently incorrect the moment it does not; this is where the "two hard problems" joke comes from, because the failure is invisible. And versioned keys or generations: instead of deleting anything, bump a generation counter and change the key, so old entries become unreachable and expire on their own. That is correct by construction — nothing can be stale because nothing can be reused — at the cost of old entries occupying memory until they expire, which is the trade that makes it safe. The rule that follows: choose your staleness tolerance first, then pick the strategy that bounds it, and if you cannot state what a stale value would cost, you are not ready to cache.

    /* Read scaling, in the order it should be attempted. */
const READ_SCALING = [
  { t: 'a CDN', for: 'static assets', gain: 'moves bytes off your origin entirely', change: 'no application change is needed' },
  { t: 'a CACHE in front of the database', rank: 'the biggest single win available',
    is: 'the right first database-level intervention' },
  { t: 'READ REPLICAS', gain: ['scales reads', 'serve analytics queries so they stop competing with the transactional workload'] },
  { t: 'PRECOMPUTED VIEWS', shape: 'a denormalised summary table maintained on write',
    rightFor: 'a report that is expensive to compute and read often' },
];
const WHY_INVALIDATION_IS_HARD = {
  what: 'a cache stores a value derived from something else, and is correct exactly while that something else is unchanged',
  notHard: 'the caching itself',
  whatIsHard: 'the cache must be TOLD, and there are more ways to change the underlying data than the program has hooks for',
  easy: 'a write through your own application code is easy to intercept',
  notEasy: ['a migration', 'a background job', 'a manual fix in a database console',
    'another service', 'a periodic recomputation'],
  consequence: 'each is a hole through which the cache becomes stale',
  symptom: 'a user seeing old data with no error anywhere',
};
const INVALIDATION = [
  { s: 'TIME-BASED expiry', does: 'a value is valid for a fixed period',
    good: ['simple', 'bounded staleness'],
    rightWhen: 'staleness is acceptable',
    examples: ['a page of product listings'],
    neverRightWhen: 'a permission check' },
  { s: 'EXPLICIT invalidation', does: 'the code that writes deletes or updates the cache',
    correctWhen: 'every write goes through code you control',
    failure: 'silently incorrect the moment it does not',
    note: 'this is where the two-hard-problems joke comes from, because the failure is INVISIBLE' },
  { s: 'VERSIONED keys or generations',
    does: 'instead of deleting anything, bump a generation counter and change the key, so old entries become unreachable and expire on their own',
    correctByConstruction: true,
    why: 'nothing can be stale because nothing can be reused',
    cost: 'old entries occupying memory until they expire',
    makesItSafe: true },
];
const RULE = 'choose your STALENESS TOLERANCE first, then pick the strategy that bounds it - and if you cannot state what a stale value would cost, you are not ready to cache';
    Cache invalidation is famously "one of the two hard problems in CS" (alongside naming and off-by-one errors).

13.6 Partitioning & sharding, in practice

Partitioning splits a table’s rows across multiple storage units while it stays one logical table, and sharding extends the same idea across separate database servers. Use range or hash partitioning to keep data and indexes manageable, and shard by a stable key so queries hit one node. Both exist because no single machine can hold or serve the volume, and the cost is that cross-partition queries, transactions, and unique constraints get harder.

Partitioning splits a table’s rows across physical storage while staying one logical table; sharding splits across databases/servers entirely. Both exist for one reason: no single node can serve the write/read volume.

# The decision cascade:
#   1 Range partition (by date): perfect for time-series, "this quarter's
#     rows live on one disk", cheap to prune and archive.
#   2 Hash shard (by key): even distribution, BUT all rows with the same
#     key (a user) stay together -> locality preserved.
#   3 Directory/geo shard: city-based; great for relevance, fragile when
#     users move or distribution skews.
# The three costs that never go away:
#   - JOINs across shards are dead: denormalize or go via the app layer
#   - global uniqueness: auto-increment breaks -> UUID/snowflake (Ch.29.5)
#   - hot keys: a celebrity hits one shard -- plan capacity for skew
# And "shard now" prematurely is ALSO an anti-pattern: measure growth,
# grow vertically until you can't, instrument before you split (Ch.21).

A decision cascade for partitioning: range, hash and geo shards each carry costs, and premature sharding is itself an anti-pattern — measure growth first.

Two kinds of split, and only one of them is sharding

Partitioning and sharding are used interchangeably and they are different operations. Vertical partitioning is splitting one table's columns into several tables — putting rarely-read large columns into their own table so that the common query does not read them. It happens inside one machine, it does not distribute anything, and its benefit is measurable immediately and without any distributed-systems work. Horizontal partitioning, or sharding is splitting the rows across several machines, so each machine holds a slice and a query must go to the right slice. That is the distributed one, and everything difficult about sharding follows from a single fact: a query that needs data from more than one slice is now a distributed query. That is the whole problem, stated once, and every difficulty below is an instance of it.

Then the two decisions that define a sharding scheme, and the second one is the one that is usually chosen badly. Where does each row go? The shard key. The good properties are: it is present on every row of the shard so routing is a local decision rather than a lookup; it is high-cardinality so the data spreads rather than concentrating on one node; and its distribution is known in advance — a hash of the key spreads evenly, a range splits predictably but risks a hot shard when keys are sequential. How do we handle a query that spans shards? This is the decision that decides whether the design works. Four answers, in increasing order of difficulty. Fan out to every shard and merge in the application: simple, and linear in shard count, so it does not survive growth. Precompute the cross-shard result and store it duplicated: fast to read and the write path becomes hard. Refuse cross-shard queries and require the application to make several single-shard queries and join them: honest, and moves complexity into the application. Reshape the data so cross-shard queries do not arise — the genuine answer, and it means designing the schema around what is queried rather than around what is normalised.

/* Two kinds of split. */
const SPLITS = [
  { k: 'VERTICAL partitioning', splits: 'one tables COLUMNS into several tables',
    where: 'inside one machine', distributes: false,
    benefit: 'putting rarely-read large columns into their own table so the common query does not read them',
    measure: 'immediately and without any distributed-systems work' },
  { k: 'HORIZONTAL partitioning, or SHARDING', splits: 'the ROWS across several machines',
    shape: 'each machine holds a slice and a query must go to the right slice',
    theWholeProblem: 'a query that needs data from more than one slice is now a DISTRIBUTED QUERY',
    note: 'every difficulty below is an instance of that one fact' },
];

/* Decision 1: the shard key. */
const SHARD_KEY_PROPERTIES = [
  { p: 'PRESENT ON EVERY ROW of the shard', why: 'so routing is a local decision rather than a lookup' },
  { p: 'HIGH-CARDINALITY', why: 'so the data spreads rather than concentrating on one node' },
  { p: 'known distribution IN ADVANCE',
    hash: 'a hash of the key spreads evenly',
    range: 'a range splits predictably but risks a HOT SHARD when keys are sequential' },
];

/* Decision 2: cross-shard queries. */
const CROSS_SHARD = [
  { a: 'FAN OUT to every shard and merge in the application',
    good: 'simple', cost: 'linear in shard count', consequence: 'does not survive growth' },
  { a: 'PRECOMPUTE the cross-shard result and store it duplicated',
    good: 'fast to read', cost: 'the write path becomes hard' },
  { a: 'REFUSE cross-shard queries, requiring the application to make several single-shard queries and join them',
    good: 'honest', cost: 'moves complexity into the application' },
  { a: 'RESHAPE the data so cross-shard queries do not arise',
    is: 'the genuine answer',
    means: 'designing the schema around WHAT IS QUERIED rather than around what is normalised' },
];

The operational costs, and why shard counts are hard to change

Then the costs, which are the reason sharding is a decision made reluctantly. Cross-shard transactions cannot be ACID. This is the direct collision between this chapter and the previous one: a transaction touching two shards is a distributed transaction, which either needs a two-phase commit — with its own blocking and failure modes — or must be abandoned in favour of eventual consistency and compensation. Cross-shard joins lose. A query that sorts or aggregates across shards must either ship all the data to one node or do a partial aggregation per shard and merge, and the second is only correct for sums and counts, not for things like "top ten overall". Uniqueness becomes conditional. A uniqueness constraint can only be enforced within a shard, so a global unique constraint on an email address needs either a separate lookup structure or a sharding scheme that guarantees it. Operational complexity is permanent. Every backup, every failover, every schema migration, every monitoring dashboard now has to work across N machines and to be correct while N−1 are healthy — and each of those is a task that was previously one thing and is now N. And the shard count is nearly immutable. You can add shards, but the hash function means rebalancing requires moving data, and the common approach — a consistent hash with virtual nodes — reduces but does not remove the cost.

Then what to do instead, and this is the practical content worth more than the theory. Do the three cheap things first: add indexes, add a cache, add read replicas. Together these commonly buy a year, and all three are reversible. Partition vertically first if the problem is wide rows, because it is one machine and it is easy to undo. Shard only on a measured need, with a specific number — this query is slow, this table is this large — because a sharding decision without a number is a guess and will be wrong. If you must shard, shard by the key your queries already filter on, so that the common query stays single-shard; if your queries do not share a filter key, that is a signal the schema needs rethinking before the sharding does. And consider whether a different tool solves it: a relational database that scales vertically plus a cache handles far more load than most applications ever reach, and a purpose-built system chosen for one workload beats a general one sharded badly. The honest summary of this section: sharding is the most expensive item on the scaling list and it is nearly always the last one to reach for, because three cheaper options routinely cover the same load.

/* The costs - the reason sharding is decided reluctantly. */
const COSTS = [
  { c: 'cross-shard TRANSACTIONS cannot be ACID',
    collision: 'a direct collision with the previous chapter',
    detail: 'a transaction touching two shards is a distributed transaction',
    options: ['two-phase commit, with its own blocking and failure modes',
      'abandoning it in favour of eventual consistency and compensation'],
    nothingElse: true },
  { c: 'cross-shard JOINS lose',
    options: ['ship all the data to one node', 'do a partial aggregation per shard and merge'],
    limitation: 'the second is correct for sums and counts, NOT for things like top ten overall' },
  { c: 'UNIQUENESS becomes conditional',
    detail: 'a uniqueness constraint can only be enforced within a shard',
    example: 'a global unique constraint on an email address needs either a separate lookup structure or a sharding scheme that guarantees it' },
  { c: 'OPERATIONAL COMPLEXITY IS PERMANENT',
    affected: ['backup', 'failover', 'schema migration', 'monitoring'],

  { c: 'the SHARD COUNT is nearly immutable',
    canAdd: true, cannotEasilyReduce: true,

14 · Computer Networks & The Web

Computer Networks and the Web explains why distributed software behaves differently in production than on a developer laptop. It maps the layered protocol stack, IP addressing, DNS, TCP and UDP, HTTP and HTTPS, sockets, headers and caching, and realtime transports, showing how each layer hands work down to the one beneath. Understanding the model lets you reason about latency, timeouts, proxies, and the failure modes behind it works on my machine.

14.1 The layered model: OSI vs TCP/IP14.2 IP addresses, ports, DNS14.3 TCP vs UDP — reliability vs speed14.4 HTTP — the web’s protocol14.5 HTTPS / TLS — the encrypted wrapper14.6 Sockets — you, talking to the world in code14.7 Headers, caching, cookies and CORS14.8 Realtime: polling, WebSockets, SSE14.9 DNS: the internet’s phone book

When two computers talk, they agree on a stack of protocols. This chapter gives you the mental map of the internet — which is also 99% of debugging "it works on my machine, fails in production".

14.1 The layered model: OSI vs TCP/IP

The OSI and TCP/IP models organize networking into layers so each one only talks to its neighbors, hiding complexity behind stable interfaces. OSI has seven layers from physical to application, while the internet model condenses them to link, network, transport, and application. This separation is why you can swap Wi-Fi for Ethernet, or change an application’s port, without rewriting the rest of the stack.

OSI 7 layers (conceptual)         TCP/IP (real world)
7 Application   HTTP, SMTP, SSH -------- Application
6 Presentation  (mostly folded into 5/7)
5 Session       (TLS, HTTP/2 sits here-ish)
4 Transport     TCP / UDP ------------------ Transport
3 Network       IP --------------------------- Internet
2 Data link     Ethernet / Wi-Fi
1 Physical      cables / radio --------------  Link

Why layering is the design, not a diagram

Layering says each layer offers a service to the layer above using only the service of the layer below, and that single rule is what makes the internet work. Each layer only talks to its neighbours. An HTTP server does not know whether the packet will cross an ocean; a router does not know it is carrying HTTP. This means a router can be replaced without touching any application, and an application can be replaced without touching any router, and that is why the network survived four decades of technology change at every level simultaneously. Each layer adds a header and encapsulates — the layer above's data becomes the layer below's payload — which is the same idea as a Russian doll and is why a packet read at layer seven contains all six lower headers in front of it. And the cost of layering is duplicated work. Each layer adds its own header, so a small payload wrapped in six headers can be mostly headers, and each layer maintains its own state — a connection table here, a routing table there — so the same information is tracked in several places that can disagree.

Then the mapping between the teaching model and the real one, because knowing both is what stops confusion. The OSI model has seven layers — physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, application — and the internet has four or five, and the honest statement is that OSI is a teaching structure and TCP/IP is what actually exists. Physical and data link are real but inside your network card. Network is IP. Transport is TCP or UDP. Session, presentation and application have no separate protocol: the session responsibilities are done by TCP's connection handling and by whatever the application protocol does, and the presentation responsibilities — encoding, encryption, compression — are done by libraries and by TLS, which sits awkwardly across the boundary because it is application data carried over TCP. TCP/IP model: link, internet, transport, application. The mapping is not exact and the mismatch is not a problem in practice; what matters is being able to say which layer a problem lives at, because that determines which tool you reach for.

/* Layering's single rule and what follows. */
const RULE = 'each layer offers a service to the layer above using ONLY the service of the layer below';
const FOLLOWS = [
  { f: 'each layer only talks to its neighbours',
    example: 'an HTTP server does not know whether the packet will cross an ocean; a router does not know it is carrying HTTP',
    gain: 'a router can be replaced without touching any application, and an application without touching any router',
    whyItMattered: 'the network survived four decades of technology change at every level simultaneously' },
  { f: 'each layer adds a header and encapsulates',
    metaphor: 'the same idea as a Russian doll',
    consequence: 'a packet read at layer seven contains all six lower headers in front of it' },
  { f: 'the cost is DUPLICATED WORK',
    details: ['a small payload wrapped in six headers can be mostly headers',
      'each layer maintains its own state - a connection table here, a routing table there - so the same information is tracked in several places that can disagree'] },
];

/* OSI versus TCP/IP. */
const MODELS = {
  osi: ['physical', 'data link', 'network', 'transport', 'session', 'presentation', 'application'],
  tcpip: ['link', 'internet', 'transport', 'application'],
  honestStatement: 'OSI is a teaching structure and TCP/IP is what actually exists',
  mapping: [
    { osi: 'physical and data link', reality: 'real but inside your network card' },
    { osi: 'network', reality: 'IP' },

      session: 'done by TCPs connection handling and by whatever the application protocol does',
      presentation: 'done by libraries and by TLS, which sits awkwardly across the boundary because it is application data carried over TCP' },
  ],
  notAProblem: 'the mapping is not exact and the mismatch is not a problem in practice',
  whatMatters: 'being able to say which layer a problem lives at, because that determines which tool you reach for',
};

Where each layer fails, and the tool that diagnoses it

Then the layer-by-layer failure catalogue, because this is what the rest of this chapter is for. Physical: a cut cable, a failing transceiver, interference, a duplex mismatch. Symptoms are that nothing works at all, or that a link flaps. Data link: MAC address resolution, frame errors, a switch with a wrong VLAN, a duplex mismatch producing late collisions. Symptom is that one machine cannot reach its neighbour while everything else works, which is the signature that localises it here. Network: no route to host, an unreachable subnet, a wrong subnet mask, a routing loop, ICMP filtered. Symptom is that the host resolves and answers a ping on its own subnet but not across the network, which is the signature that localises it here. Transport: a refused connection, a dropped connection after a long idle, a full socket backlog, a firewall dropping SYNs. Symptom is that a connection attempt hangs or is refused, rather than failing fast. Application: a wrong status code, a bad header, a redirect loop, a certificate error, CORS. Symptom is that bytes arrive correctly and the logic is still wrong — which is why the tool here is the browser's network panel rather than a packet capture.

Then the diagnostic habit, and it is the same sequence every time regardless of where the fault is, because a bottom-up walk is faster than a guess. Is the interface up and does it have an address? If there is no address, nothing above can work and no amount of configuration elsewhere will help. Can I reach my own gateway? This isolates the local problem from the remote one. Does DNS resolve? If the name does not resolve, every URL-based tool is useless and you are debugging the wrong layer. Is the port open? A name can resolve and a connection can still be refused, and that distinction is the difference between a DNS problem and a service problem. Does it work from the command line? If a request works with a low-level tool and not with your application, the fault is in your application — and this step alone eliminates half of all network debugging. And look at the actual bytes, at both ends, which is the step people skip and which is the only one that distinguishes "the server received something wrong" from "the server never received anything".

/* Layer-by-layer failure catalogue. */
const FAILURES = [
  { l: 'PHYSICAL', problems: ['a cut cable', 'a failing transceiver', 'interference', 'a duplex mismatch'],
    symptoms: 'nothing works at all, or a link flaps' },
  { l: 'DATA LINK', problems: ['MAC address resolution', 'frame errors', 'a switch with a wrong VLAN', 'a duplex mismatch producing late collisions'],
    signature: 'ONE machine cannot reach its neighbour while everything else works' },
  { l: 'NETWORK', problems: ['no route to host', 'an unreachable subnet', 'a wrong subnet mask', 'a routing loop', 'ICMP filtered'],
    signature: 'the host resolves and answers a ping on its OWN SUBNET but not across the network' },
  { l: 'TRANSPORT', problems: ['a refused connection', 'a dropped connection after a long idle', 'a full socket backlog', 'a firewall dropping SYNs'],
    signature: 'a connection attempt HANGS OR IS REFUSED rather than failing fast' },
  { l: 'APPLICATION', problems: ['a wrong status code', 'a bad header', 'a redirect loop', 'a certificate error', 'CORS'],
    signature: 'bytes arrive correctly and the logic is still wrong',
    toolHere: 'the browsers network panel rather than a packet capture' },
];

/* The diagnostic habit - the same sequence every time. */

    why: 'if there is no address nothing above can work, and no amount of configuration elsewhere will help' },
  { step: 2, q: 'can I reach my own gateway', gain: 'isolates the local problem from the remote one' },
  { step: 3, q: 'does DNS resolve',
    why: 'if the name does not resolve every URL-based tool is useless and you are debugging the wrong layer' },
  { step: 4, q: 'is the port open',
    gain: 'a name can resolve and a connection can still be refused',
    distinguishes: 'the difference between a DNS problem and a service problem' },
