The public-key trick: encrypt with the public key anyone can fetch; only the private key decrypts it. Perfect strangers establish a shared secret without ever exchanging it — the idea behind literally every "s" in "https".

14.6 Sockets — you, talking to the world in code

A socket is the programming interface to a network connection: an endpoint you open, connect, send, receive, and close in code. A basic TCP client in Python or Node creates a socket, connects to an address and port, exchanges bytes, and shuts down cleanly, which is exactly what curl and your browser do under the hood. Master the socket lifecycle and you can build custom protocols or debug strange connection behavior.

# A tiny HTTP "client" with raw sockets (uuid of what curl does)
import socket

s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
s.connect(("example.com", 80))            # HTTP lives on port 80
s.send(b"GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: example.com\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n")

data = b""
while True:
    chunk = s.recv(4096)                  # keep reading until the server closes

    if not chunk:
        break
    data += chunk
s.close()
print(data.decode()[:400])   # the raw HTTP response you've been reading all along

The socket API, and the states a connection goes through

A socket is a file descriptor the operating system routes network traffic through, and the client API is a small set of calls whose order matters. Create: a socket is created with a domain, a type and a protocol — for a normal TCP connection over IPv4, a stream socket. Connect: for a client, this asks the kernel to establish a connection, and it either succeeds or fails, and which one it does is the first place most bugs appear. Bind and listen: for a server, bind claims a local port and listen marks the socket as accepting connections — and a socket bound to a port that another process holds fails, which is the "address already in use" error and which is why a port left in TIME_WAIT after a restart looks like a bug in your program. Accept: the server's call, which takes a connection from the queue and gives back a new connected socket — the subtlety worth knowing is that this is a new descriptor, and state bound to the original socket is shared by all accepted connections, which is a classic source of "why is every request seeing the same user's data". Send and receive: which may return fewer bytes than you asked for, which is not an error and is the single most important fact for anyone writing a protocol.

Then the receive rule, and it is the one that produces every "my data is corrupted" report. A read is not a message. A stream socket guarantees bytes in order and nothing about boundaries, so recv(1024) may return 3 bytes, or 1024, or anything up to the buffer size, and two writes may come back as one read or as two. Consequences: you must frame your own protocol — with a delimiter, a length prefix, or a fixed record size — and the protocol must be unambiguous, because a length prefix needs escaping or framing so a payload containing the delimiter cannot be confused with a boundary. And the correct loop is "read until you have a whole message", not "read once and parse", which is what makes short reads produce malformed input. On the sending side the same rule applies with one extra subtlety: a write can be partial too, and while most high-level libraries handle that for you, writing to a socket in a loop is the correct shape.

/* The API, and the order matters. */
const CALLS = [
  { c: 'create', does: 'a socket is created with a domain, a type and a protocol',
    normal: 'a stream socket for TCP over IPv4' },
  { c: 'connect', who: 'client', does: 'asks the kernel to establish a connection',
    note: 'it either succeeds or fails, and which one it does is the first place most bugs appear' },
  { c: 'bind and listen', who: 'server', does: 'bind claims a local port and listen marks the socket as accepting connections',
    failure: 'a socket bound to a port another process holds fails - the address-already-in-use error',
    whyItLooksLikeABug: 'a port left in TIME_WAIT after a restart' },
  { c: 'accept', who: 'server', does: 'takes a connection from the queue and gives back a NEW connected socket',
    subtlety: 'state bound to the original socket is SHARED BY ALL ACCEPTED CONNECTIONS',
    classicBug: 'why is every request seeing the same users data' },
  { c: 'send and receive', fact: 'may return FEWER BYTES than you asked for',
    notAnError: true,
    importance: 'the single most important fact for anyone writing a protocol' },
];

/* The receive rule. */
const RECEIVE_RULE = {
  statement: 'A READ IS NOT A MESSAGE',
  guaranteed: 'bytes in order, and NOTHING ABOUT BOUNDARIES',
  consequence: 'recv(1024) may return 3 bytes, or 1024, or anything up to the buffer size',
  so: 'two writes may come back as one read or as two',
  therefore: 'you must FRAME YOUR OWN PROTOCOL',
  options: ['a delimiter', 'a length prefix', 'a fixed record size'],
  protocolRequirement: 'it must be UNAMBIGUOUS - a length prefix needs escaping or framing so a payload containing the delimiter cannot be confused with a boundary',
  correctLoop: 'READ UNTIL YOU HAVE A WHOLE MESSAGE, not read once and parse',
  why: 'this is what makes short reads produce malformed input',
  sendingSide: 'a write can be partial too; while most high-level libraries handle that for you, writing to a socket in a loop is the correct shape',
};

Timeouts, ports, and the practical rules

Then the practical rules, each one learned from a specific failure. Always set timeouts. A blocking read on a socket that never receives data holds a thread indefinitely, and a thread held indefinitely is a thread that cannot serve anybody else — so a read timeout, a write timeout, and a connection timeout are all mandatory in production code, and their absence is why services leak threads under partial failure. Handle ECONNRESET as normal. A peer that closes abruptly — which every browser tab does when navigated away, and every load balancer does when it recycles a connection — produces it, so it is not an error condition but an expected event, and a connection pool that treats it as a failure will discard healthy connections and reconnect constantly. Never let one connection hold a lock. If a thread holds a mutex while blocked on a socket, every other thread needing that mutex is blocked on the network. Use SO_REUSEADDR so a restart does not fail on a socket in TIME_WAIT, which is a development convenience that also affects a rolling deployment where the new instance starts before the old one has closed its listener. Be careful with half-closed connections, since one side can close its sending side while still reading, and code that assumes close means "conversation over" truncates responses. And do not write a server unless the exercise requires it — not as an anti-pattern but because the libraries handle connection pooling, timeouts, TLS and protocol framing correctly, and a hand-written server gets one of those wrong, usually timeouts.

Then the mental model worth keeping, because it makes the rest predictable: a socket is a file descriptor, and the kernel delivers bytes to it. It does not deliver messages, it does not deliver boundaries, it does not deliver reliability at this layer, and it does not tell you when a "message" ends. Everything above this line — HTTP, TLS, a database protocol, your own framing — is a protocol you or a library has agreed on, running over a byte pipe that has no opinions. The value of that model is diagnostic: when something goes wrong, it tells you which layer to look at. If bytes are arriving and the parse is failing, the problem is the protocol above. If no bytes are arriving, the problem is the network, the address, or the peer's state. And if bytes arrive out of order or duplicated, the problem is the layer above, because TCP above this point guarantees neither happens.

/* Practical rules, each learned from a specific failure. */
const RULES = [
  { r: 'ALWAYS SET TIMEOUTS', kinds: ['a read timeout', 'a write timeout', 'a connection timeout'],
    why: 'a blocking read on a socket that never receives data holds a thread indefinitely',
    and: 'a thread held indefinitely is a thread that cannot serve anybody else',
    consequence: 'their absence is why services leak threads under partial failure',
    mandatoryIn: 'production code' },
  { r: 'handle ECONNRESET as NORMAL', detail: 'a peer that closes abruptly produces it',
    whoDoes: ['every browser tab navigated away', 'every load balancer recycling a connection'],
    notAnError: 'it is an expected event',
    bug: 'a connection pool that treats it as a failure discards healthy connections and reconnects constantly' },
  { r: 'NEVER let one connection hold a lock', detail: 'if a thread holds a mutex while blocked on a socket, every other thread needing that mutex is blocked on the network' },
  { r: 'use SO_REUSEADDR', why: 'so a restart does not fail on a socket in TIME_WAIT',
    alsoAffects: 'a rolling deployment where the new instance starts before the old one has closed its listener' },
  { r: 'be careful with HALF-CLOSED connections',
    detail: 'one side can close its sending side while still reading',
    bug: 'code that assumes close means conversation over truncates responses' },
  { r: 'do not write a server unless the exercise requires it',
    notAnAntiPattern: true,
    why: 'libraries handle connection pooling, timeouts, TLS and protocol framing correctly',
    likelyWrong: 'one of those, usually TIMEOUTS' },
];

/* The mental model. */
const MODEL = {
  statement: 'a SOCKET IS A FILE DESCRIPTOR, and the kernel delivers BYTES to it',
  doesNot: ['deliver messages', 'deliver boundaries', 'deliver reliability at this layer', 'tell you when a message ends'],
  everythingAbove: 'HTTP, TLS, a database protocol, your own framing - protocols you or a library has agreed on, running over a byte pipe that has no opinions',
  diagnosticValue: 'when something goes wrong it tells you which layer to look at',
  bySymptom: [
    { bytesArriveButParseFails: 'the problem is the protocol ABOVE' },
    { noBytesArrive: 'the problem is the NETWORK, the ADDRESS, or the PEERS STATE' },
    { bytesArriveOutOfOrderOrDuplicated: 'the problem is the layer ABOVE, because TCP above this point guarantees neither happens' },
  ],
};

A raw-socket HTTP client: connect, send one GET line plus the Host header, then read bytes until the server closes — exactly what curl automates.

14.7 Headers, caching, cookies and CORS

HTTP headers carry the web’s invisible decisions: whether caches may store a response, which session a request belongs to, and which security policies such as CSP and HSTS apply. Cookies are small values a server sets and the browser returns with each request, while CORS preflights decide whether another origin may call an API. Reading headers tells you who can call, and what gets served from cache.

HTTP headers carry the invisible decisions of the web: who can read it, is it cached, who’s the user, who is allowed to call.

ConcernHeadersWhat they mean
CachingCache-Control: max-age=3600, ETag, Last-ModifiedClients/proxies reuse copies; ETag gives "304 Not Modified" cheap validation
SessionsSet-Cookie: session=...; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=LaxCookie stored by the browser, sent on next request; HttpOnly = JS can’t read it (XSS shield)
CORSAccess-Control-Allow-OriginServer decides which other origins may call it; required on cross-origin fetch()
SecurityContent-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport-SecurityRules for what scripts can load; force HTTPS

The headers that actually change behaviour

HTTP headers are metadata about a message, and a handful of them change what happens in ways that are not obvious from their names. Host is required on every HTTP/1.1 request and identifies which virtual host you want — without it a server hosting fifty sites cannot know which one you meant. Content-Type tells the receiver how to interpret the body, and omitting it means the client guesses, which for anything but plain text means it guesses wrong. Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding are mutually exclusive ways of saying how the body ends, and a message with both is an attack rather than a mistake — a well-known discrepancy that request-smuggling attacks exploit. Connection controls keep-alive, and its absence is why older HTTP/1.0 opened a new connection per request. Cache-Control is a family of directives rather than one flag, and no-cache means "revalidate" while no-store means "do not keep this at all" — a distinction that produces real bugs when they are confused. Authorization and Cookie carry credentials and are the headers you must never log.

Then CORS, which is the one every developer meets and few understand, and understanding it requires knowing what problem it solves. CORS is a browser-enforced mechanism that lets a page on one origin ask a server on another for permission to read its response. It is not a server-side control at all — the server cannot enforce it, and anything it protects is not protected by it. It exists because of a security model: a logged-in user on their banking site should not be able to have another site's JavaScript read their balance, so the browser refuses to hand a cross-origin response to the requesting page unless the server opts in. The mechanics: the server must send Access-Control-Allow-Origin naming the allowed origin, and for anything beyond a simple request the browser first sends an OPTIONS preflight asking permission for the method and headers. So the failure "my fetch is blocked" is nearly always one of two things: the server did not send the allow-origin header, or the browser cached a preflight and the server's answer changed. And the rule people get wrong: * is invalid with credentials, so a cross-origin request that needs a cookie cannot use a wildcard and must name the origin explicitly.

/* Headers that change behaviour. */
const HEADERS = [
  { h: 'Host', required: 'on every HTTP/1.1 request', identifies: 'which virtual host you want',
    why: 'without it a server hosting fifty sites cannot know which one you meant' },
  { h: 'Content-Type', does: 'tells the receiver how to interpret the body',
    consequence: 'omitting it means the client guesses, which for anything but plain text means it guesses wrong' },
  { h: 'Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding', relation: 'MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE ways of saying how the body ends',
    withBoth: 'an ATTACK rather than a mistake',
    exploitedBy: 'a well-known discrepancy that request-smuggling attacks use' },
  { h: 'Connection', controls: 'keep-alive',
    consequence: 'its absence is why older HTTP/1.0 opened a new connection per request' },
  { h: 'Cache-Control', is: 'a FAMILY of directives rather than one flag',
    trap: 'no-cache means REVALIDATE while no-store means DO NOT KEEP THIS AT ALL',
    consequence: 'a distinction that produces real bugs when they are confused' },
  { h: 'Authorization and Cookie', carry: 'credentials',
    rule: 'these are the headers you must NEVER log' },
];

/* CORS. */
const CORS = {
  is: 'a BROWSER-ENFORCED mechanism letting a page on one origin ask a server on another for permission to read its response',
  notThis: 'a server-side control - the server cannot enforce it, and anything it protects is not protected by it',
  whyItExists: 'a security model',
  theThreat: 'a logged-in user on their banking site should not be able to have another sites JavaScript read their balance',
  soTheBrowser: 'refuses to hand a cross-origin response to the requesting page unless the server opts in',
  mechanics: ['the server must send Access-Control-Allow-Origin naming the allowed origin',
    'for anything beyond a simple request the browser first sends an OPTIONS PREFLIGHT asking permission for the method and headers'],
  debugging: 'my fetch is blocked is nearly always either the server not sending the allow-origin header, or the browser having cached a preflight whose answer changed',
  rulePeopleGetWrong: 'a WILDCARD IS INVALID WITH CREDENTIALS, so a cross-origin request needing a cookie cannot use * and must name the origin explicitly',
};

Caching, cookies, and the stateful parts of HTTP

Then caching, because it is the header set that most changes observed behaviour. Two caches are involved and confusing them is the source of most cache bugs: the shared cache in a proxy or CDN, and the private cache in a browser, which is per-user. A response marked private must never be stored in a shared cache, because that would serve one user's data to another. ETag and Last-Modified enable revalidation: the client sends what it has, the server answers 304 Not Modified if it is still current, and the body is not transferred. That is the mechanism behind a conditional request and it is worth knowing because 304 is not an error — treating it as a failure is a classic bug. And the combination of a cache and authentication is where it gets dangerous: a response that depends on who is asking must either be marked private or vary on the credential, and a cached personalised response served to the wrong user is a data leak rather than a performance bug.

Then cookies and sessions, which is where HTTP becomes stateful and where a great many security properties come from. A cookie is a name-value pair the server asks the browser to store and send back on every request to that domain. Its purpose is to let a stateless protocol act statefully, and the design is nearly fifty years old, which is why the flags below are retrofitted. HttpOnly makes the cookie invisible to JavaScript, which is what makes it not stealable by an XSS attack — and it means client-side code cannot read the session, so any design depending on that is already broken. Secure restricts it to HTTPS. SameSite controls whether it is sent on cross-site requests, and its values are the modern defence against cross-site request forgery: Lax sends it on top-level navigation but not on a cross-origin fetch, which blocks the attack while preserving ordinary link navigation. The session token itself must be unpredictable — this is the whole basis of session hijacking, and a token that is guessable or sequential turns authentication into nothing. And then the operational point: a session store on the server and a session identifier in the cookie, which is the correct pattern, versus putting the session data itself in the cookie, which is signed and therefore tamper-proof but makes the cookie large and puts replayable credentials in storage the user can see.

/* Caching. */
const CACHING = {
  twoCaches: ['the SHARED cache in a proxy or CDN', 'the PRIVATE cache in a browser, per-user'],
  whyItMatters: 'confusing them is the source of most cache bugs',
  rule: 'a response marked PRIVATE must never be stored in a shared cache, because that would serve one users data to another',
  revalidation: { headers: ['ETag', 'Last-Modified'],
    how: 'the client sends what it has; the server answers 304 Not Modified if it is still current, and the body is not transferred',
    gotcha: '304 IS NOT AN ERROR - treating it as a failure is a classic bug' },
  danger: 'a response that depends on who is asking must either be marked private or vary on the credential',
  consequence: 'a cached personalised response served to the wrong user is a DATA LEAK rather than a performance bug',
};

/* Cookies and sessions. */
const COOKIES = {
  is: 'a name-value pair the server asks the browser to store and send back on every request to that domain',
  purpose: 'let a STATELESS protocol act statefully',
  nearlyFiftyYearsOld: true,
  whyFlagsAreRetrofitted: true,
  flags: [
    { f: 'HttpOnly', does: 'makes the cookie invisible to JavaScript',
      gain: 'what makes it not stealable by an XSS attack',
      consequence: 'client-side code cannot read the session, so any design depending on that is ALREADY BROKEN' },
    { f: 'Secure', does: 'restricts it to HTTPS' },
    { f: 'SameSite', does: 'controls whether it is sent on cross-site requests',
      is: 'the modern defence against cross-site request forgery',
      values: 'Lax sends it on top-level navigation but not on a cross-origin fetch, which blocks the attack while preserving ordinary link navigation' },
  ],
  sessionToken: 'must be UNPREDICTABLE - this is the whole basis of session hijacking',
  consequence: 'a token that is guessable or sequential turns authentication into nothing',
  operational: {
    correct: 'a session store on the server and a session identifier in the cookie',
    versus: 'putting the session data itself in the cookie - signed and therefore tamper-proof, but makes the cookie large and puts replayable credentials in storage the user can see',
  },
};

CORS drip you’ll feel. Your frontend at app.example.com fetching api.example.com is a different origin. The browser blocks the response unless the API sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin (and typically preflights via OPTIONS). Fix it on the API, allowlist origins, never * with credentials.

14.8 Realtime: polling, WebSockets, SSE

Realtime features need the server to push data instead of waiting for a client poll. Polling and long-polling reuse plain HTTP but waste requests or hold them open, WebSockets provide a full-duplex persistent connection for chat and games, and Server-Sent Events push one-directional streams such as feeds and notifications with automatic reconnect. Pick the mechanism that matches your latency needs and how much bidirectional traffic you actually have.

HTTP is request/response. When the server must push (chat, notifications, live prices), three idioms exist:

TechniqueMechanismTrade-offs
PollingClient asks every N secondsSimple, wasteful; latency = your interval
Long-pollingServer holds the request until new data existsEliminates empty responses; still HTTP overhead
WebSocketPersistent bidirectional TCP connection (ws://)True realtime; more infra (proxies, reconnects, heartbeats)
SSEServer → client one-way stream over plain HTTPPerfect for feeds/stocks; no client→server channel
# A WebSocket client in 10 lines (pip install websockets)
import asyncio, websockets

async def chat():
    async with websockets.connect("ws://echo.example.com/socket") as ws:
        await ws.send("Hello server")      # client to server
        reply = await ws.recv()            # server to client
        print(reply)

asyncio.run(chat())

Short polling, long polling, SSE, and WebSockets

Server push has four shapes and the choice is a trade between latency, resource cost and simplicity. Short polling means the client asks every second. It is trivial to implement and it does not keep the server holding anything — but you pay one request per client per interval regardless of whether anything changed, which is a cost that scales with your user count and tells you nothing in between. Long polling means the client asks and the server holds the request open until there is something to send, then returns it and the client immediately asks again. Latency is good and it works through any proxy, but the server holds an open connection per waiting client, which is a thread or a suspended request each, and it is the connection the load balancer times out — so this is the technique that most often degrades into short polling under load. Server-sent events means the server holds one connection and pushes formatted events down it, unidirectionally. It is simple, it reconnects automatically, and it works over plain HTTP, but it is one-way — so anything interactive needs a separate channel back. WebSockets means the connection is upgraded to a persistent bidirectional channel after an ordinary HTTP handshake, and both sides can send at any time. It is the right answer for genuinely two-way real-time and it is the most machinery of the four.

Then what each is actually for, and the selection rule. Short polling for data that changes slowly relative to the refresh, for a small number of clients, and whenever the simplest thing is genuinely enough. Long polling for infrequent updates with many clients, when you cannot hold an event-stream connection but must not poll hard. Server-sent events for notifications and one-way updates — progress bars, live dashboards, notifications — because it is a browser primitive requiring no library and it reconnects for you. WebSockets for chat, collaborative editing, trading, gaming state and anything where the client must send as well as receive. And the rule that stops you over-thinking it: if updates are more than a minute apart, poll; if they are seconds apart and one-way, use server-sent events; if they are seconds apart and two-way, use WebSockets. Everything above that boundary is a latency requirement, and the four options differ by factors of tens in cost, not by percentages.

/* Four shapes. */
const SHAPES = [
  { s: 'SHORT POLLING', does: 'the client asks every second',
    good: ['trivial to implement', 'does not keep the server holding anything'],
    cost: 'one request per client per interval REGARDLESS OF WHETHER ANYTHING CHANGED',
    consequence: 'a cost that scales with your user count and tells you nothing in between' },
  { s: 'LONG POLLING', does: 'the client asks and the server holds the request open until there is something to send',
    loop: 'then returns it and the client immediately asks again',
    good: ['good latency', 'works through any proxy'],
    cost: 'the server holds an open connection per waiting client - a thread or a suspended request each',
    failure: 'it is the connection the load balancer TIMES OUT',
    degradesInto: 'short polling under load' },
  { s: 'SERVER-SENT EVENTS', does: 'the server holds one connection and pushes formatted events down it',
    direction: 'UNIDIRECTIONAL',
    good: ['simple', 'reconnects automatically', 'works over plain HTTP'],
    limit: 'one-way, so anything interactive needs a separate channel back' },
  { s: 'WEBSOCKETS', does: 'the connection is upgraded to a persistent bidirectional channel after an ordinary HTTP handshake',
    good: 'the right answer for genuinely two-way real-time',
    cost: 'the most machinery of the four' },
];

/* What each is for, and the rule. */
const USE_FOR = [
  { s: 'short polling', when: ['data changes slowly relative to the refresh', 'a small number of clients',
    'whenever the simplest thing is genuinely enough'] },
  { s: 'long polling', when: 'infrequent updates with many clients, when you cannot hold an event-stream connection but must not poll hard' },
  { s: 'server-sent events', when: 'notifications and one-way updates - progress bars, live dashboards, notifications',
    why: 'it is a browser primitive requiring no library and it reconnects for you' },
  { s: 'WebSockets', when: ['chat', 'collaborative editing', 'trading', 'gaming state',
    'anything where the client must send as well as receive'] },
];
const RULE = 'if updates are more than a minute apart, POLL; if they are seconds apart and ONE-WAY, use server-sent events; if they are seconds apart and TWO-WAY, use WebSockets';
const WHY_SCALE = 'everything above that boundary is a latency requirement, and the four options differ by FACTORS OF TENS in cost, not by percentages';

Making it survive production

Then what breaks real-time systems, and it is a short list with a common theme. Connection limits. Every server, every proxy and every load balancer has a cap on concurrent connections, and WebSockets hold one connection open per client indefinitely, so you exhaust the limit long before you exhaust memory. This is the single most common production failure and it arrives as a service that worked for ten thousand users and does not work for twenty thousand. Reconnection. Networks drop connections, mobile devices sleep, load balancers recycle, and every client must reconnect with backoff and jitter — and the backoff needs jitter or every client retries in lockstep after the outage and knocks the service over again. Ordering and delivery guarantees. A WebSocket guarantees the bytes and their order on one connection, and nothing at all across reconnections, so a message sent while disconnected is lost unless you implement resumption with an identifier. State. A connection is not state; keeping a user's state in the connection's memory loses it on every reconnect and breaks horizontal scaling, so the state belongs in a store and the connection is just a pipe. And backpressure: if a client cannot process messages as fast as they arrive, something must slow down, and either the server buffers without limit — which is a memory leak with a latency cost — or it drops messages, which must be a decision made deliberately rather than by accident.

Then the operational practices, and they are the difference between a demo and a service. Expose a health endpoint that reflects live connections, because the alternative is discovering the limit in production. Measure connection count and message rate as first-class metrics, since both degrade before error rate does. Prefer one connection per client carrying multiplexed messages over several connections, because the per-connection overhead is paid on every heartbeat and every reconnect. Send heartbeats — both because idle connections are killed by proxies and because it is how you detect a peer that has gone without noticing — and keep them cheap. And design for the disconnect as the normal case: if your system only works while connections are up, it will not work, because a network guarantees they are not. That last point is the one worth carrying into the next chapter: every real-time design is really a design for a system that is constantly disconnected and reconnecting, and the transport is the easy part.

/* What breaks, with a common theme. */
const BREAKS = [
  { b: 'CONNECTION LIMITS',
    detail: 'every server, proxy and load balancer has a cap on concurrent connections',
    why: 'WebSockets hold one connection open per client indefinitely',
    rank: 'the single most common production failure',
    arrivesAs: 'a service that worked for ten thousand users and does not work for twenty thousand' },
  { b: 'RECONNECTION', causes: ['networks drop connections', 'mobile devices sleep', 'load balancers recycle'],
    requirement: 'every client must reconnect with backoff AND JITTER',
    whyJitter: 'without it every client retries in LOCKSTEP after the outage and knocks the service over again' },
  { b: 'ORDERING and delivery guarantees',
    guaranteed: 'a WebSocket guarantees the bytes and their order ON ONE CONNECTION',
    notGuaranteed: 'anything at all across reconnections',
    consequence: 'a message sent while disconnected is lost unless you implement resumption with an identifier' },
  { b: 'STATE', detail: 'a connection is NOT state',
    why: 'keeping a users state in the connections memory loses it on every reconnect and breaks horizontal scaling',
    therefore: 'the state belongs in a store and the connection is just a pipe' },
  { b: 'BACKPRESSURE', problem: 'a client cannot process messages as fast as they arrive, so something must slow down',
    options: ['the server buffers without limit - a memory leak with a latency cost',
      'it drops messages'],
    requirement: 'the choice must be made DELIBERATELY rather than by accident' },
];

/* Operational practices. */
const PRACTICE = [
  { p: 'expose a health endpoint that REFLECTS LIVE CONNECTIONS', why: 'the alternative is discovering the limit in production' },
  { p: 'measure CONNECTION COUNT and MESSAGE RATE as first-class metrics',
    why: 'both degrade BEFORE the error rate does' },
  { p: 'prefer ONE CONNECTION PER CLIENT carrying multiplexed messages over several connections',
    why: 'the per-connection overhead is paid on every heartbeat and every reconnect' },
  { p: 'send HEARTBEATS', reasons: ['idle connections are killed by proxies',
    'it is how you detect a peer that has gone without noticing'], note: 'keep them cheap' },
  { p: 'design for the DISCONNECT as the normal case',
    conclusion: 'if your system only works while connections are up it will not work, because a network guarantees they are not',
    carriesForward: 'every real-time design is really a design for a system that is constantly disconnected and reconnecting, and the TRANSPORT is the easy part' },
];

Ten lines of Python open a persistent WebSocket, send one message and await a reply — server-push chat without the HTTP polling loop.

14.9 DNS: the internet’s phone book

DNS is the distributed phone book that translates human-readable domain names into IP addresses. Lookups walk through recursive resolvers, root servers, top-level domain servers, and the authoritative nameserver for the domain, caching every answer with a TTL so repeat lookups stay fast and load stays low. Because of that caching, a nameserver or record change takes time to propagate globally.

You type a name; DNS turns it into the IP address sockets need. It’s a hierarchical, massively cached system — and a surprising amount of real-world networking trouble lives here.

Recursion:
  your app -> resolver (ISP / 8.8.8.8 / 1.1.1.1) -> root servers
    -> .com TLD servers -> authoritative server for example.com
Record types you'll actually meet:
  A      -> IPv4 address
  AAAA   -> IPv6 address
  CNAME  -> alias (www -> example.com)
  MX     -> mail servers
  NM     -> name servers  (the authority for the zone)
  TXT    -> metadata (SPF/DKIM security, verification strings)
Caching: every answer carries a TTL (how long it may be reused).
This is why DNS changes can take "48 hours to propagate" -- and why a
cached STALE answer after you change servers sends users to the old one.

How DNS resolves a name through resolver, root, TLD and authoritative servers, plus the record types and TTL caching behind two-day propagation delays.

  • Tooling: nslookup example.com, dig example.com A, dig +trace to walk the recursion yourself.
  • Security angles (Ch.20 tie-in): DNS rebinding (attacker’s domain points at 127.0.0.1 to reach local services), DNS spoofing, and DNS over HTTPS/TLS which fixes privacy and some poisoning — but corporate/school filtering fights it.
  • When troubleshooting: "site won’t load" → first check DNS (resolver + TTL), then routing, then the server (Ch.14 layer discipline).

How a name becomes an address, and why the resolution is not one lookup

Resolving a name is a distributed lookup over a hierarchy, and the order is what makes it fast. The resolver asks the recursive resolver — usually configured on your machine, run by your provider or in your network. A recursive resolver does the work on your behalf and caches everything it learns. It asks the root servers, which know which server is authoritative for every top-level domain and answer with a referral, not an address. It asks the TLD server — the one for .com — which refers it to the domain's own nameservers. It asks the authoritative nameserver, which holds the actual record and returns the address. Then the caching is what makes this fast, and the caching happens at every level: the root servers are asked millions of times a second and the same answer is returned, the TLD servers likewise, and only the last step changes often. A cold lookup is four round trips; a warm one is none, because the answer is already in a cache.

Then the record types, and each answers a different question. A maps a name to an address — the one everybody means by "the DNS record". AAAA is the IPv6 equivalent. CNAME is an alias, and its rule is the one that catches people: a CNAME cannot coexist with any other record, so a name that is an alias cannot also have a MX or a TXT, and if you need those you must use an A record and alias at the DNS provider instead. MX names mail servers, with a priority number. TXT carries arbitrary text and is now heavily used for domain verification — proving ownership of a domain for a certificate authority or a mail provider. NS delegates a subdomain to other nameservers. And TTL is not a record type but the field on every record, and it is where the behaviour people find surprising comes from: it tells caches how long they may keep the answer, and a change does not take effect until the previous TTL has expired everywhere. So lowering a TTL before a planned change and raising it afterwards is standard practice, and it is also why "I changed DNS an hour ago and it has not taken effect" is a question with a straightforward answer.

/* The order, and why it is fast. */
const ORDER = [
  { step: 1, who: 'the RESOLVER asks the recursive resolver',
    note: 'usually configured on your machine, run by your provider or in your network',
    whatItDoes: 'the work on your behalf and caches everything it learns' },
  { step: 2, who: 'the ROOT SERVERS', answer: 'a REFERRAL, not an address',
    know: 'which server is authoritative for every top-level domain' },
  { step: 3, who: 'the TLD SERVER, such as the one for .com', does: 'refers it to the domains own nameservers' },
  { step: 4, who: 'the AUTHORITATIVE NAMESERVER', holds: 'the actual record', returns: 'the address' },
];
const CACHING_WHY_FAST = {
  where: 'at EVERY level',
  detail: 'the root servers are asked millions of times a second and the same answer is returned; the TLD servers likewise',
  changesOften: 'only the last step',
  arithmetic: 'a cold lookup is four round trips; a warm one is NONE, because the answer is already in a cache',
};

/* Record types. */
const RECORDS = [
  { t: 'A', maps: 'a name to an address', note: 'the one everybody means by the DNS record' },
  { t: 'AAAA', maps: 'the IPv6 equivalent' },
  { t: 'CNAME', is: 'an alias', rule: 'a CNAME CANNOT COEXIST WITH ANY OTHER RECORD',
    consequence: 'a name that is an alias cannot also have an MX or a TXT',
    fix: 'if you need those, use an A record and alias at the DNS provider instead' },
  { t: 'MX', names: 'mail servers', with: 'a priority number' },
  { t: 'TXT', carries: 'arbitrary text',
    heavilyUsedFor: 'domain verification - proving ownership for a certificate authority or a mail provider' },
  { t: 'NS', delegates: 'a subdomain to other nameservers' },
];
const TTL = {
  isNotARecordType: 'it is the field on every record',
  means: 'tells caches how long they may keep the answer',
  surprise: 'a change does not take effect until the previous TTL has expired EVERYWHERE',
  practice: 'lower the TTL before a planned change and raise it afterwards',
  answers: 'I changed DNS an hour ago and it has not taken effect',
};

Common DNS problems and how to diagnose them

Then the failure modes, and each has a signature. Nothing resolves at all, which is almost always the resolver itself rather than your names and is fixed by querying a public resolver directly to distinguish the two. Some records resolve and some do not, which points at a specific missing or malformed record rather than at DNS. The name resolves to the wrong address, which is a stale cache or a missing update rather than a broken zone. It works from one machine and not another, which is a per-machine resolver cache or a hosts-file entry — and the hosts file is the culprit far more often than people expect, because a line somebody added years ago silently overrides DNS forever. Intermittent resolution failures, which are a nameserver capacity or rate-limiting problem and are visible in whether the failures are on the authoritative side or the recursive side. And a stale record in one ISP's resolver, which is the worst kind to debug because it reproduces for some users and not others and the evidence is on a machine you do not control.

Then the diagnostic tools, and the habit of using them in an order. Query a specific nameserver directly to establish the truth about your zone, separately from any cache in between. Query a public resolver to establish whether the problem is your zone or your provider's cache. Check the record from several networks if intermittent, because a resolver cache is per-network and one view tells you nothing about the others. And then the three things to do as prevention, which are cheap. Put a reasonable TTL on everything — long enough to be useful, short enough that a change takes effect. Delegate to at least two nameservers on different networks, because a single nameserver is a single point of failure and a second one on the same network is not a second one at all. And monitor the authoritative nameservers directly, rather than monitoring resolution, because resolution can be healthy through a cache while the authoritative server is not answering — and that is precisely the failure that a monitoring system which only checks resolution will miss until the cache expires.

/* Failure modes, each with a signature. */
const FAILURES = [
  { f: 'NOTHING RESOLVES AT ALL', usually: 'the RESOLVER ITSELF rather than your names',
    fix: 'query a public resolver directly to distinguish the two' },
  { f: 'SOME RECORDS RESOLVE AND SOME DO NOT', pointsAt: 'a specific missing or malformed record rather than at DNS' },
  { f: 'THE NAME RESOLVES TO THE WRONG ADDRESS', cause: 'a stale cache or a missing update rather than a broken zone' },
  { f: 'IT WORKS FROM ONE MACHINE AND NOT ANOTHER', causes: ['a per-machine resolver cache', 'a HOSTS-FILE entry'],
    hostsFileCulprit: 'far more often than people expect, because a line somebody added years ago silently overrides DNS forever' },
  { f: 'INTERMITTENT RESOLUTION FAILURES', cause: 'a nameserver capacity or rate-limiting problem',
    visibleIn: 'whether the failures are on the authoritative side or the recursive side' },
  { f: 'A STALE RECORD IN ONE ISPS RESOLVER', worstKind: true,
    whyHard: 'it reproduces for some users and not others, and the evidence is on a machine you do not control' },
];

/* Diagnostic tools, used in order. */
const DIAGNOSE = [
  { t: 'query a SPECIFIC NAMESERVER directly', establishes: 'the truth about your zone, separately from any cache in between' },
  { t: 'query a PUBLIC RESOLVER', establishes: 'whether the problem is your zone or your providers cache' },
  { t: 'check the record from SEVERAL NETWORKS', when: 'intermittent',
    why: 'a resolver cache is per-network and one view tells you nothing about the others' },
];

/* Prevention. */
const PREVENTION = [
  { p: 'put a REASONABLE TTL on everything', standard: 'long enough to be useful, short enough that a change takes effect' },
  { p: 'delegate to at least TWO NAMESERVERS on DIFFERENT NETWORKS',
    why: 'a single nameserver is a single point of failure, and a second one on the same network is not a second one at all' },
  { p: 'monitor the AUTHORITATIVE NAMESERVERS DIRECTLY rather than monitoring resolution',
    why: 'resolution can be healthy through a cache while the authoritative server is not answering',
    consequence: 'a monitoring system which only checks resolution will MISS IT until the cache expires' },
];
