15 · Software Engineering Processes

15.1 The Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC)15.2 Waterfall vs Agile15.3 Requirements & user stories15.4 Design documents & technical design15.5 Code review — the everyday act of seniority15.6 Engineering metrics and estimation

Software Engineering Processes is the machinery that turns working code into reliable software: requirements, design documentation, code review, and metrics. It covers the SDLC, waterfall versus Agile delivery, user stories, design documents, review practices, and engineering metrics and estimation. Together these habits make outcomes repeatable and let a team ship with confidence rather than hope.

Programming is the easy 20% of software engineering. The rest is: knowing what to build, working with people, designing before coding, and shipping safely. This chapter turns you from "can code" into "can engineer".

15.1 The Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC)

The Software Development Life Cycle is the end-to-end rhythm every delivery approach shares: requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment, and maintenance. Whether a team runs Waterfall, Scrum, Kanban, or continuous deployment, each phase still exists, just with different timing and formality. Knowing which phase you are in tells you what to do next and which artifacts to produce.

The universal rhythm every process variant follows:

  1. Requirements — what must it do? (functional) and how well must it do it? (non-functional: performance, security, usability).
  2. Design — architecture, data model, APIs, tech choices.
  3. Implementation — the coding.
  4. Testing — proving it works (Ch. 16).
  5. Deployment — releasing to users (Ch. 22).
  6. Maintenance — fixes, features, monitoring — where budgets really go.

The stages, and why the order is a discovery process rather than a recipe

The stages are: requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment, maintenance. Each produces something the next one consumes, and the essential point is what each stage is for rather than what it produces. Requirements establish what problem is being solved and for whom, and its failure mode is building the wrong thing efficiently. Design establishes how, and its failure mode is building it in a way that cannot be maintained. Implementation is writing it, and its failure mode is building it wrong. Testing establishes whether it does what was intended, and its failure mode is finding out late. Deployment is making it available, and its failure mode is having written something that cannot be run. Maintenance is where the majority of the lifetime cost lives, and its failure mode is assuming the work is finished. Held together, this is best understood as a funnel for reducing uncertainty: each stage exists to discover something that would otherwise be discovered later at higher cost. Requirements discovery is cheap; discovering a wrong requirement after deployment is not. That framing is why the stages are worth having even when they feel like overhead, and it also explains why the cost of skipping one is not the time saved but the change in where you find out.

Then why the process is a loop and not a line, which is the observation that distinguishes this from the diagram. Each stage's output is input to the next, and the next stage always finds something that changes the previous one. Testing finds that the requirement was ambiguous. Design review finds that the requirement was impossible. Deployment finds that the design assumed a capability the platform does not have. So a stage performed as if the previous one were final is a stage that will produce rework — and rework is not equally expensive at every stage, which is the real reason for the ordering: a requirement changed after design costs a re-design, and the same requirement changed after deployment costs a migration and possibly a breaking API change. The practical consequence is the rule worth having: the purpose of a stage gate is to force the discovery that would otherwise be deferred, and a gate that does not force a decision is theatre.

/* Stages, and what each is FOR rather than what it produces. */
const STAGES = [
  { s: 'requirements', establishes: 'what problem is being solved and for whom',
    failureMode: 'building the wrong thing EFFICIENTLY' },
  { s: 'design', establishes: 'how', failureMode: 'building it in a way that cannot be maintained' },
  { s: 'implementation', is: 'writing it', failureMode: 'building it WRONG' },
  { s: 'testing', establishes: 'whether it does what was intended', failureMode: 'finding out LATE' },
  { s: 'deployment', is: 'making it available', failureMode: 'having written something that cannot be run' },
  { s: 'maintenance', holds: 'the MAJORITY OF THE LIFETIME COST',
    failureMode: 'assuming the work is finished' },
];
const FUNNEL = {
  idea: 'the process is a FUNNEL FOR REDUCING UNCERTAINTY',
  eachStageExists: 'to discover something that would otherwise be discovered later at higher cost',
  example: 'requirements discovery is cheap; discovering a wrong requirement after deployment is not',
  therefore: 'the cost of skipping a stage is not the TIME SAVED but the change in WHERE you find out',
};

/* Why it is a loop, not a line. */
const LOOP = {
  fact: 'each stages output is input to the next, and the next stage ALWAYS FINDS SOMETHING that changes the previous one',
  findings: ['testing finds that the requirement was ambiguous',
    'design review finds that the requirement was impossible',
    'deployment finds that the design assumed a capability the platform does not have'],
  consequence: 'a stage performed as if the previous one were final is a stage that will produce REWORK',
  whyOrderMatters: 'a requirement changed after design costs a re-design; the same requirement changed after deployment costs a migration and possibly a breaking API change',
  theRule: 'the purpose of a stage gate is to FORCE THE DISCOVERY that would otherwise be deferred, and a gate that does not force a decision is THEATRE',
};

Cost, rework, and the numbers that decide

Then the cost model, because "software is cheap to change" is the belief that causes the most damage when it is wrong. The cost of a change is a function of when it is made, and the curve is steep: a change in the requirements is a conversation; the same change after design is a redesign; after implementation it is a rewrite plus retest; after deployment it is a migration, a release, a communication and possibly a breaking change to a published contract. Maintenance is not the after-party. Software decays the moment users touch it — new needs, new browsers, new platforms, newly discovered bugs — and the majority of a system's cost is incurred after the first release, which is worth stating as the reason the first release is not a milestone to be celebrated but the start of the accounting. Technical debt is a loan. Every shortcut taken for speed accrues a future cost, and the useful framing is the same one from the time-space chapter: a debt is only a good decision if you know what you are borrowing against and when you will repay it; a shortcut taken because there was no time and never revisited is not an investment, it is a bug that has not been written down. And the cost of a defect grows with the stage at which it is found, which is the defect that reaches production and is found by a user rather than by a test. Defect cost is not linear in severity. A crash on a rarely used path costs little; the same defect in a payment path costs a lot per occurrence, and the ratio between the two is frequently two orders of magnitude — which is why triage by expected damage beats triage by severity rating.

Then the practical consequence for how you work, which is what this chapter is actually for. Make changes as early as you can. Not "early" as a moral preference but because the curve above is the strongest argument there is. Automate the checks that would otherwise be manual at each gate, because a gate a human forgets is a gate that does not exist. Treat a requirement that cannot be tested as a requirement that is not understood, which is the requirement chapter's point and the reason "make it fast" fails. Keep the stages but shorten them. The stages are useful; a stage that takes three months is producing a document nobody reads, and a week is enough to surface the disagreements that matter. And do not skip a stage; skip the ceremony around it. The distinction is the whole lesson: the value of a stage is the conversation and the discovery inside it, and a meeting that does not change anyone's mind is not a stage, it is a meeting.

/* The cost of a change is a function of WHEN it is made. */
const COST_CURVE = [
  { when: 'in the requirements', cost: 'a conversation' },
  { when: 'after design', cost: 'a redesign' },
  { when: 'after implementation', cost: 'a rewrite plus retest' },
  { when: 'after deployment', cost: 'a migration, a release, a communication and possibly a breaking change to a published contract' },
];
const BELIEF = 'the belief that software is cheap to change causes the most damage when it is wrong';
const MAINTENANCE = {
  notTheAfterParty: true,
  fact: 'software DECAYS the moment users touch it',
  causes: ['new needs', 'new browsers', 'new platforms', 'newly discovered bugs'],
  fact2: 'the MAJORITY of a systems cost is incurred after the first release',
  reframe: 'the first release is not a milestone to be celebrated but the START OF THE ACCOUNTING',
};
const DEBT = {
  is: 'a loan',
  goodDecision: 'a debt is only a good decision if you know WHAT YOU ARE BORROWING AGAINST and WHEN YOU WILL REPAY IT',
  notInvestment: 'a shortcut taken because there was no time and never revisited is not an investment - it is a BUG THAT HAS NOT BEEN WRITTEN DOWN',
};
const DEFECTS = {
  costGrowsWith: 'the stage at which it is found',
  worstCase: 'a defect that reaches production and is found by a USER rather than by a test',
  notLinearInSeverity: true,
  example: 'a crash on a rarely used path costs little; the same defect in a payment path costs a lot per occurrence',
  magnitude: 'the ratio between the two is frequently TWO ORDERS OF MAGNITUDE',
  therefore: 'triage by EXPECTED DAMAGE beats triage by severity rating',
};

/* Practical consequences. */
const WORK = [
  { a: 'make changes AS EARLY AS YOU CAN', why: 'not a moral preference but because the cost curve above is the strongest argument there is' },
  { a: 'automate the checks that would otherwise be MANUAL at each gate', why: 'a gate a human forgets is a gate that does not exist' },
  { a: 'treat a requirement that CANNOT BE TESTED as a requirement that is not understood',
    connectsTo: 'which is why make it fast fails' },
  { a: 'keep the stages but SHORTEN them',
    why: 'the stages are useful, but a stage that takes three months produces a document nobody reads, and a week is enough to surface the disagreements that matter' },
  { a: 'do not skip a stage - skip the CEREMONY around it',
    distinction: 'the value of a stage is the conversation and the discovery inside it',
    test: 'a meeting that does not change anyones mind is not a stage, it is a meeting' },
];

The industry truth: there is NO "done" in software. Software decays the moment users touch it (new bugs, new needs, new browsers). Maintenance is not the after-party; it’s the main event.

15.2 Waterfall vs Agile

Waterfall freezes requirements up front and delivers the whole product in one sequence of phases, which suits regulated, predictable projects. Agile accepts that requirements evolve, shipping small increments in short iterations with constant feedback from the product owner and stakeholders. Most product teams run Agile in a Scrum or Kanban flavor, with Scrum organizing sprints and Kanban limiting work in progress.

What each model optimises for, and why the honest answer is hybrid

Both models are answers to the same question — what to do when you do not know everything up front — and they differ in what they assume about how that knowledge arrives. Waterfall assumes you can know. It front-loads requirements and design, on the reasoning that changes are expensive later, which is correct as far as it goes. Its failure mode is precise: the requirements are a prediction, and a wrong prediction discovered in month eight is very expensive, and the assumption that early work produces stable knowledge is only true where the domain is genuinely knowable. Hardware, construction, aerospace and regulated environments are close, because physical prototyping is expensive and the requirements genuinely are stable. Agile assumes you cannot know. It front-loads discovery of value rather than discovery of solution, delivering in small increments so that real feedback arrives before large commitments. Its failure mode is the mirror: the absence of any plan means the absence of any way to answer "when will this be finished and what will it cost", and a project of thirty sprints with no long-range view has no shape. The honest summary is that both are wrong about the same thing in opposite directions: waterfall over-trusts the front end, agile over-trusts the feedback loop.

Then why the argument did not end, and what actually resolved it. The two are not really competitors because they answer different questions. Whether requirements can be specified up front is an empirical property of the domain, not a matter of preference — it is knowable per project and the answer varies. And the vocabulary hardened and then softened: "agile" began as a manifesto against heavyweight process and became a term for a specific bundle of ceremonies, which is how a method about responsiveness became a method about standups. Then what resolved it in practice: the success criteria differ by failure mode. Agile projects fail by building the wrong thing; waterfall projects fail by building the right thing too slowly or too expensively, and for a product where the wrong thing costs nothing to discover and the right thing takes years, only one of those failures is tolerable. And hybrid is the normal answer, where a project has enough domain knowledge to plan an architecture and enough uncertainty to need weekly feedback — which is nearly every piece of professional software.

/* Both answer the same question: what to do when you do not know everything up front. */
const WATERFALL = {
  assumes: 'you CAN know',
  reasoning: 'changes are expensive later',
  failureMode: 'the requirements are a PREDICTION, and a wrong prediction discovered in month eight is very expensive',
  wrongAssumption: 'that early work produces stable knowledge',
  trueOnlyWhere: 'the domain is genuinely knowable',
  closeExamples: ['hardware', 'construction', 'aerospace', 'regulated environments'],
  why: 'physical prototyping is expensive and the requirements genuinely are stable',
};
const AGILE = {
  assumes: 'you CANNOT know',
  shifts: 'front-loads discovery of VALUE rather than discovery of SOLUTION',
  mechanism: 'delivering in small increments so real feedback arrives before large commitments',
  failureMode: 'the absence of any plan means the absence of any way to answer when will this be finished and what will it cost',
  example: 'thirty sprints with no long-range view has no shape',
};
const HONEST_SUMMARY = 'both are wrong about the same thing in opposite directions - WATERFALL OVER-TRUSTS THE FRONT END, AGILE OVER-TRUSTS THE FEEDBACK LOOP';

/* Why the argument did not end, and what resolved it. */
const RESOLUTION = [
  { p: 'they are not really COMPETITORS because they answer different questions',
    detail: 'whether requirements can be specified up front is an EMPIRICAL property of the domain, not a matter of preference',
    consequence: 'it is knowable per project and the answer varies' },
  { p: 'the vocabulary HARDENED AND THEN SOFTENED',
    detail: 'agile began as a manifesto against heavyweight process and became a term for a specific bundle of ceremonies',
    consequence: 'a method about responsiveness became a method about standups' },
  { p: 'success criteria differ BY FAILURE MODE',
    detail: 'agile projects fail by building the wrong thing; waterfall projects fail by building the right thing too slowly or too expensively',
    whichIsTolerable: 'for a product where the wrong thing costs nothing to discover and the right thing takes years, only one of those failures is tolerable' },
  { p: 'HYBRID is the normal answer',
    shape: 'a project with enough domain knowledge to plan an architecture and enough uncertainty to need weekly feedback',
    scope: 'which is nearly every piece of professional software' },
];

Scrum, Kanban, and how to choose

Then the two frameworks that carry most of the practice, and the honest difference between them is cadence versus flow. Scrum optimises for a fixed cadence. Work is sliced into sprints of a fixed length, and the discipline is that a sprint is time-boxed and its contents are not added to mid-sprint, which is the rule that makes the retrospective data meaningful — if scope can change daily, then velocity measures nothing. Its ceremonies exist to surface the two things a fixed cadence can surface: a plan for what is coming and a retrospective for what went wrong. Kanban optimises for flow. There are no sprints; work moves across columns and the discipline is a work-in-progress limit per column, which forces the team to finish what it started rather than start what it could, and the metric that matters is cycle time — how long an item actually spends in the system — which is the most useful measurement in software delivery because it is what a customer experiences.

Then how to choose, and the failure each is prone to. Choose Scrum when the work benefits from planning in batches — a release, a sprint goal, a fixed date — and when the team benefits from a regular retrospective. Its failure mode is the ceremony becoming the work: the standup lasts an hour, the sprint goal is met by completing tickets rather than by advancing the product, and the process is producing reports rather than decisions. Choose Kanban when work arrives unpredictably — maintenance, support, an interrupt-driven team — because a fixed sprint is meaningless when the items arrive at a random rate, and because the WIP limit is the mechanism that actually limits queue length. Its failure mode is the WIP limit being treated as a suggestion, and a board with eleven items in "in progress" is a board with no limit. And the shared failure, which is the one worth naming: neither framework fixes a team that cannot agree on what "done" means, and every metric in either framework becomes a way of looking busy rather than a way of finishing. If "done" is unclear, the correct fix is a definition of done — tests written, reviewed, deployed, monitored — and it is a prerequisite of both, not an output of them.

/* The honest difference is CADENCE versus FLOW. */
const SCRUM = {
  optimisesFor: 'a FIXED CADENCE',
  mechanism: 'work is sliced into sprints of a fixed length',
  keyDiscipline: 'a sprint is time-boxed and its CONTENTS ARE NOT ADDED MID-SPRINT',
  whyThatRule: 'if scope can change daily then velocity measures nothing',
  ceremoniesExistToSurface: ['a plan for what is coming', 'a retrospective for what went wrong'],
};
const KANBAN = {
  optimisesFor: 'FLOW',
  mechanism: 'no sprints; work moves across columns',
  keyDiscipline: 'a WORK-IN-PROGRESS LIMIT per column',
  whatThatForces: 'the team to finish what it started rather than start what it could',
  metric: 'CYCLE TIME - how long an item actually spends in the system',
  whyThatMetric: 'the most useful measurement in software delivery, because it is what a CUSTOMER EXPERIENCES' },
];

/* How to choose, and the failure each is prone to. */
const CHOOSE = [
  { f: 'SCRUM', when: 'the work benefits from PLANNING IN BATCHES',
    instances: ['a release', 'a sprint goal', 'a fixed date'],
    alsoWhen: 'the team benefits from a regular retrospective',
    failureMode: 'THE CEREMONY BECOMING THE WORK',
    symptoms: ['the standup lasts an hour',
      'the sprint goal is met by completing tickets rather than by advancing the product',
      'the process is producing reports rather than decisions'] },
  { f: 'KANBAN', when: 'work arrives UNPREDICTABLY', instances: ['maintenance', 'support', 'an interrupt-driven team'],
    whyNotScrum: 'a fixed sprint is meaningless when items arrive at a random rate',
    whyItWorks: 'the WIP limit is the mechanism that actually limits queue length',
    failureMode: 'the WIP limit being treated as a SUGGESTION',
    symptom: 'a board with eleven items in in-progress is a board with no limit' },
];
const SHARED_FAILURE = {
  claim: 'neither framework fixes a team that cannot agree on what DONE MEANS',
  consequence: 'every metric in either framework becomes a way of looking busy rather than a way of finishing',
  theFix: 'a DEFINITION OF DONE - tests written, reviewed, deployed, monitored',
  isA: 'PREREQUISITE of both, not an output of them',
};
WaterfallAgile (Scrum / Kanban)
ShapePhases done once, in strict orderSmall increments, continuously delivered
RequirementsFrozen up frontEvolving; welcome change late
FeedbackLate (at delivery)Constant (each sprint / iteration)
RiskBig-bang failure at the endFailure surfaces early, small
When to useRegulated/safety domains, fixed scope (rare these days)Most modern product work

Agile’s core loop (Scrum flavour): a fixed sprint (1–4 weeks) takes items from a backlog into (planning → daily stand-ups → review → retrospective). The retrospective ("what should we improve?") is the part that actually makes teams better.

15.3 Requirements & user stories

Requirements turn a product idea into an explicit agreement about what will be built. User stories capture features from a user’s viewpoint in the format As a role, I want a capability, so that a benefit, and acceptance criteria define the concrete, testable conditions for done. Vague or missing requirements, not hard problems, cause most failed deliveries, so write examples and agree on the details before coding.

Acceptance is written as user stories, and refined into acceptance criteria you can test:

As a shopper, I want to see my cart total instantly,
so that I can decide the items to remove.

Acceptance criteria:
- Total updates within 100 ms of adding/removing an item
- Currency formatting matches regional settings
- Empty cart shows "Your cart is empty"
- Works on mobile and desktop

A requirements sample showing how a user story and its acceptance criteria become measurable, testable constraints.

Requirements versus features, and the three ways a requirement goes wrong

The distinction at the front matters more than any technique in this chapter. A requirement is a property the system must have — a constraint, a behaviour, a quality attribute — stated so that it can be checked. A feature is a capability a user can perform. They are not the same kind of thing, and the confusion between them causes the most expensive class of failure. "Users can reset their password" is a feature; "a password reset is completed within five minutes and the link is single-use and expires after one hour" is a requirement. The first is a button, the second is the specification of what the button must guarantee, and building the first without the second is how a reset link ends up valid forever. Then the three ways a requirement goes wrong, and each is a distinct failure with a distinct fix. It is ambiguous. "Make it fast" has no meaning, and "p95 response under 200 milliseconds with a thousand concurrent users" has meaning — and the transformation from the first to the second is the primary skill in this section. It is not testable. "User-friendly" cannot be checked by any test, so no test will be written for it, so nobody knows whether it was met, which means it was not a requirement but a sentiment. It is unstated and assumed. The requirement everybody agreed on verbally and nobody wrote down, which is the one that surfaces as a defect six months later with no blame attached because everybody remembers agreeing.

Then how to write one that is worth writing, and the structure that does most of the work. State it as a testable property with a number and a condition. The template is: a subject, an action, and an observable outcome with a threshold — "the system returns the result within 200 milliseconds at the 95th percentile, measured over 1,000 concurrent users". Every noun in that sentence is load-bearing: within is the condition, 95th percentile is the choice that makes it meaningful (an average hides the tail, as the scheduling chapter showed), and 1,000 concurrent users is the load that makes the number a requirement rather than an observation. Say what is measured and how. "Fast" measured client-side and server-side are different numbers, and a requirement that does not say which is not a requirement. Write the negative case. For every positive requirement, the behaviour when the condition is not met is a requirement too, and it is the one that gets forgotten and is the one users encounter. And record the reason, because a requirement without a stated reason cannot be traded off against another when they conflict, and a requirement whose only justification is "the stakeholder said so" will be questioned by everyone and defended by nobody.

/* The distinction at the front. */
const DISTINCTION = {
  requirement: 'a property the system must have - a constraint, a behaviour, a quality attribute - stated so that it can be CHECKED',
  feature: 'a capability a user can perform',
  notTheSameKindOfThing: true,
  example: {
    feature: 'users can reset their password',
    requirement: 'a password reset is completed within five minutes, the link is single-use, and it expires after one hour',
    consequence: 'building the first without the second is how a reset link ends up VALID FOREVER',
  },
};
const GOES_WRONG = [
  { f: 'AMBIGUOUS', example: 'make it fast',
    fixedBy: 'p95 response under 200 milliseconds with a thousand concurrent users',
    primarySkill: 'the transformation from the first to the second is the primary skill in this section' },
  { f: 'NOT TESTABLE', example: 'user-friendly',
    chain: 'cannot be checked by any test, so no test will be written, so nobody knows whether it was met',
    reframe: 'it was not a requirement but a SENTIMENT' },
  { f: 'UNSTATED AND ASSUMED', detail: 'the requirement everybody agreed on verbally and nobody wrote down',
    appearsAs: 'a defect six months later with no blame attached, because everybody remembers agreeing' },
];

/* How to write one worth writing. */
const STRUCTURE = {
  template: 'a subject, an action, and an observable outcome with a threshold',
  worked: 'the system returns the result within 200 milliseconds at the 95th percentile, measured over 1000 concurrent users',
  loadBearing: [
    { word: 'within', is: 'the CONDITION' },
    { word: '95th percentile', is: 'the choice that makes it MEANINGFUL - an average hides the tail' },
    { word: '1000 concurrent users', is: 'the load that makes the number a REQUIREMENT rather than an observation' },
  ],
  alsoRequired: [
    { r: 'say what is MEASURED AND HOW', why: 'fast measured client-side and server-side are different numbers, and a requirement that does not say which is not a requirement' },
    { r: 'write the NEGATIVE CASE', why: 'for every positive requirement the behaviour when the condition is not met is a requirement too',
      symptoms: 'it is the one that gets forgotten and the one users encounter' },
    { r: 'record the REASON', why: 'a requirement without a stated reason cannot be traded off against another when they conflict',
      consequence: 'one whose only justification is the stakeholder said so will be questioned by everyone and defended by nobody' },
  ],
};

From wishes to criteria, and the non-functional requirements

Then the technique for the transformation, because it is mechanical once you have the questions. Ask "what would make this acceptable?", because that is a criterion where "nice" is not. Ask "how would you know it failed?", and the answer is a measurement. Ask "compared with what, and for whom?", because "fast" is a relative claim and the baseline and the person are both missing. Ask "what is the worst acceptable version of this?", which finds the actual requirement — often far less demanding than the wish. And write it down in the requirement's language rather than in the implementation's, so that a later implementation can differ from today's without the requirement having failed.

Then the requirements that are not about features, because they are the ones that get skipped and they are what makes a system usable or unusable. Performance — not "fast" but a percentile, a load, and a measurement point. Reliability — an availability target, and what happens when it is missed; the interesting part is not the target but the failure behaviour. Security — who may do what, what must be encrypted, what must be logged, and what happens to the data when it is deleted. Scale — how many users, how much data, how much traffic, at what growth rate, and which of those the design must survive without redesign. Observability — how an operator knows something is wrong, which is a requirement with a number attached, not a nice-to-have. Accessibility — what the product must do for a keyboard-only user, a screen-reader user, a colour-blind user, and a user on a slow connection. And the ones nobody writes: recovery requirements, data retention requirements, and what must happen when a third-party service is unavailable — because those are exactly the requirements whose absence is discovered during an incident, at which point they cannot be met.

/* The transformation - mechanical once you have the questions. */
const QUESTIONS = [
  { q: 'what would make this ACCEPTABLE', why: 'that is a criterion where nice is not' },
  { q: 'how would you know it FAILED', answer: 'a measurement' },
  { q: 'compared with WHAT, and FOR WHOM', why: 'fast is a RELATIVE claim and the baseline and the person are both missing' },
  { q: 'what is the WORST ACCEPTABLE version of this', gain: 'finds the actual requirement - often far less demanding than the wish' },
  { q: 'write it in the REQUIREMENTS language rather than the implementation language',
    why: 'so a later implementation can differ from todays without the requirement having failed' },
];

/* The non-functional requirements. */
const NON_FUNCTIONAL = [
  { r: 'PERFORMANCE', not: 'fast', but: 'a percentile, a load, and a measurement point' },
  { r: 'RELIABILITY', is: 'an availability target, and what happens when it is missed',
    interestingPart: 'not the target but the FAILURE BEHAVIOUR' },
  { r: 'SECURITY', covers: ['who may do what', 'what must be encrypted', 'what must be logged',
    'what happens to the data when it is deleted'] },
  { r: 'SCALE', covers: ['how many users', 'how much data', 'how much traffic', 'at what growth rate'],
    keyQuestion: 'which of those the design must survive WITHOUT REDESIGN' },
  { r: 'OBSERVABILITY', is: 'how an operator knows something is wrong',
    status: 'a requirement with a number attached, not a nice-to-have' },
  { r: 'ACCESSIBILITY', covers: ['a keyboard-only user', 'a screen-reader user', 'a colour-blind user',
    'a user on a slow connection'] },
  { r: 'the ones NOBODY WRITES', instances: ['recovery requirements', 'data retention requirements',
    'what must happen when a third-party service is unavailable'],
    consequence: 'exactly the requirements whose absence is discovered DURING AN INCIDENT, at which point they cannot be met' },
];

Ambiguous requirements are THE source of most failed deliveries. "Make it fast" is not a requirement — "p95 response < 200 ms under 1k concurrent users" is. Practise converting wishes into measurable criteria.

15.4 Design documents & technical design

A design doc forces you to think a change through before writing code: the problem, options considered, the chosen solution, data model, API surface, risks, and rollout plan. It lets the team review and critique that thinking cheaply, when changes are still a few paragraphs instead of thousands of lines. Write it early, keep it short, and update it as decisions evolve.

A design doc answers before a single line is written: what problem (context), options considered, chosen solution (architecture diagram!), data model, API surface, risks, rollout plan. Its real superpower: writing it forces you to think, and it makes the team review your thinking cheaply.

  • Architecture views: context diagram (boxes outside boundaries), component diagram, sequence diagram for key flows.
  • Trade-off honesty: every choice trades something. Write the trade-off explicitly — reviewers respect that more than "Best solution ever!".

What a design document is for, and when it is worth writing

A design document answers one question — what are we building and why this way rather than the obvious alternatives? — and everything about its form follows from that. It is worth writing when there is a genuine decision to record: more than one approach was considered, the choice has consequences that are not obvious from the code, and someone who did not participate will need to understand it in six months. It is not worth writing when the design is obvious, when it is a spike, or when the document will be written once and never updated — because a stale design document is worse than none, since a reader trusts it. The distinction worth holding is between a design document, which records a decision and its reasoning, and a proposal, which asks for a decision before the work starts; the first is written after thinking, the second before, and mixing them is why design documents so often feel like bureaucracy. The parts that earn their place, in order: the problem, stated so a reader who knows nothing can tell whether the design solves it; the constraints, because a design that ignored a constraint is wrong regardless of elegance; the options considered including the obvious one and why it was rejected; the chosen design at a level of detail that explains the consequences rather than restating the code; the consequences, stated as costs as well as benefits; and what would make us change our mind, which is the section that turns a document into a decision someone can revisit.

/* It answers one question. */
const THE_QUESTION = 'what are we building and WHY THIS WAY rather than the obvious alternatives';
const WORTH_WRITING_WHEN = [
  'more than one approach was considered',
  'the choice has CONSEQUENCES that are not obvious from the code',
  'someone who did not participate will need to understand it in six months',
];
const NOT_WORTH_WHEN = [
  'the design is obvious',
  'it is a spike',
  'the document will be written once and never updated',
  whyThird: 'because a STALE DESIGN DOCUMENT IS WORSE THAN NONE, since a reader trusts it',
];
const KINDS = {
  designDocument: { records: 'a decision and its reasoning', written: 'AFTER thinking' },
  proposal: { asks: 'for a decision before the work starts', written: 'before' },
  whyItMatters: 'mixing them is why design documents so often feel like bureaucracy',
};
const SECTIONS_THAT_EARN_THEIR_PLACE = [
  { s: 'the PROBLEM', rule: 'stated so a reader who knows nothing can tell whether the design solves it' },
  { s: 'the CONSTRAINTS', why: 'a design that ignored a constraint is wrong regardless of elegance' },
  { s: 'the OPTIONS CONSIDERED', includes: ['the obvious one', 'why it was rejected'] },
  { s: 'the CHOSEN DESIGN', rule: 'at a level of detail that explains the CONSEQUENCES rather than restating the code' },
  { s: 'the CONSEQUENCES', mustBe: 'stated as COSTS as well as benefits' },
  { s: 'what would make us CHANGE OUR MIND', gain: 'the section that turns a document into a DECISION someone can revisit' },
];

Diagrams, and the discipline that keeps documents alive

Then the three diagrams that earn their place, and why each is one of three. Class diagrams for structure — what holds what, what owns what, what may substitute for what — and their value is the relationships rather than the attributes, as the modelling chapter established. Sequence diagrams for one flow through time, showing the objects involved and the calls between them in order; these are the most valuable of the three for reviewing a design, because a sequence diagram makes an ordering assumption visible, and ordering assumptions are where distributed designs go wrong. State diagrams for the lifecycle of one thing — a ticket's statuses, an order's progress, a connection's states — and their value is that they force the question "what happens from here?" for every state, which is exactly where missing transitions hide. Beyond those three, most of the remaining UML is decoration: a document with seven diagram kinds is a document nobody reads, and the honest position is that a diagram should be made because it answers a question, and if it does not, it is noise.

Then what keeps a document alive, because the failure mode is not that documents are hard to write but that they are hard to keep true. Keep it short. A document longer than a few pages is not read, and an unread document is worse than none because it exists. Version it with the code, in the same commit, so a change that invalidates a diagram is a change that updates the diagram — and the moment they are separate is the moment they diverge. Prefer writing for one reader: the person who will change this in six months, which is usually you, and which is why the parts that matter are the reasoning and the consequences rather than the description. Delete it when the code supersedes it, rather than leaving it as a historical record that new readers will find and trust. And write the failure mode, which is the section most often omitted and the one most useful during an incident: a document that says what this design will do badly is more useful than one that says what it does well.

/* Three diagrams, and why each earns its place. */
const DIAGRAMS = [
  { d: 'CLASS diagrams', for: 'structure - what holds what, what owns what, what may substitute for what',
    value: 'the RELATIONSHIPS rather than the attributes' },
  { d: 'SEQUENCE diagrams', for: 'one flow through time', shows: 'the objects involved and the calls between them in order',
    mostValuable: true,
    why: 'a sequence diagram makes an ORDERING ASSUMPTION visible, and ordering assumptions are where distributed designs go wrong' },
  { d: 'STATE diagrams', for: 'the lifecycle of one thing',
    instances: ['a tickets statuses', 'an orders progress', 'a connections states'],
    value: 'forces the question what happens from here for every state',
    why: 'exactly where MISSING TRANSITIONS hide' },
];
const BEYOND = {
  position: 'most of the remaining UML is decoration',
  symptom: 'a document with seven diagram kinds is a document nobody reads',
  rule: 'a diagram should be made because it ANSWERS A QUESTION, and if it does not, it is noise',
};

/* What keeps a document alive. */
const KEEPING_ALIVE = [
  { p: 'keep it SHORT', why: 'a document longer than a few pages is not read, and an unread document is worse than none because it EXISTS' },
  { p: 'version it WITH THE CODE, in the same commit',
    gain: 'a change that invalidates a diagram is a change that updates the diagram',
    failureMode: 'the moment they are separate is the moment they diverge' },
  { p: 'prefer writing for ONE READER', who: 'the person who will change this in six months, usually you',
    consequence: 'which is why the parts that matter are the reasoning and the consequences rather than the description' },
  { p: 'DELETE it when the code supersedes it',
    notInsteadOf: 'leaving it as a historical record that new readers will find and trust' },
  { p: 'write the FAILURE MODE', mostOftenOmitted: true, mostUseful: true,
    claim: 'a document that says what this design will do BADLY is more useful than one that says what it does well' },
];

UML, kept practical. In industry nobody draws all 14 UML diagram kinds. The ones still used daily: class diagrams (structure), sequence diagrams (one flow through time), state diagrams (a ticket’s statuses). Master those three.

15.5 Code review — the everyday act of seniority

Code review is a structured pass over a change before it merges, checking correctness, readability, maintainability, test coverage, security, and consistency with the codebase. Keep the change small enough to review properly, be honest about trade-offs, and critique the code rather than the author. It is the everyday act that spreads knowledge and hardens quality across a team.

Reviewing someone’s code (and having yours reviewed) is a core engineering activity. What reviewers check, roughly in order:

  1. Correctness & edge cases — empty input, huge input, zero, duplicates.
  2. Readability — names, structure; could this be understood in 6 months?
  3. Tests — do the tests cover the changed behaviour?
  4. Security & performance — injection, PII leaks, obvious O(n²).
  5. Consistency — matches project style, no unrelated changes.

What review is actually for, and the ordering that matters

Code review is usually described as finding defects, and measurement suggests that is a small part of it — most comments in most reviews are about things a test would never catch. The purposes, in roughly descending order of measured value: finding defects before they ship; sharing knowledge of the system, which happens as a side effect and is under-rated; enforcing consistency with existing conventions, which is why a review that ignores style produces a codebase with several styles; improving the design through discussion, which is the highest-leverage and least frequent outcome; and growing the reviewer, which is real and rarely acknowledged. Knowing the order matters because it tells you what to spend time on: a review that spends twenty minutes on naming and five on the design has its priorities inverted.

Then the mechanics that decide whether a review is useful, and the ordering is not arbitrary. Review the design first, then the correctness, then the tests, then the style. Design first because a design problem makes the rest of the review moot — there is no point discussing variable names in a function whose shape is wrong. Correctness second because correctness defects are the expensive kind. Tests third because tests are evidence about the first two. Style last because a formatter should handle most of it and a human should not spend attention on it. Keep the review small. A few hundred lines is the practical ceiling, and beyond it reviewers read less carefully, which is worse than two reviews. Ask questions rather than dictate. "What happens if this list is empty?" produces a discussion; "this is wrong" produces a change and no understanding — and the reviewer's own change is sometimes better than the one they asked for. Explain the comment. "Use a set here" is a directive; "this is O(n) inside a loop over a thousand items, so this is O(n squared) — a set makes it O(n)" is a comment the author will remember in six months when the situation recurs.

/* Finding defects is a small part. */
const PURPOSES = [
  { p: 'finding defects before they ship', frequency: 'common' },
  { p: 'sharing KNOWLEDGE of the system', frequency: 'as a side effect', underRated: true },
  { p: 'enforcing CONSISTENCY with existing conventions',
    why: 'which is why a review that ignores style produces a codebase with several styles' },
  { p: 'improving the DESIGN through discussion', leverage: 'highest', frequency: 'least' },
  { p: 'growing the REVIEWER', real: true, rarelyAcknowledged: true },
];
const WHY_ORDER = 'knowing the order tells you what to spend time on - a review that spends twenty minutes on naming and five on the design has its priorities inverted';

/* The mechanics, in order. */
const MECHANICS = [
  { m: 'review the DESIGN first, then correctness, then tests, then style',
    whyDesignFirst: 'a design problem makes the rest of the review MOOT - there is no point discussing variable names in a function whose shape is wrong',
    whyCorrectnessSecond: 'correctness defects are the EXPENSIVE kind',
    whyTestsThird: 'tests are EVIDENCE about the first two',
    whyStyleLast: 'a formatter should handle most of it and a human should not spend attention on it' },
  { m: 'keep the review SMALL', ceiling: 'a few hundred lines',
    why: 'beyond it reviewers read less carefully, which is worse than two reviews' },
  { m: 'ask QUESTIONS rather than dictate',
    question: 'what happens if this list is empty', produces: 'a discussion',
    directive: 'this is wrong', produces: 'a change and no understanding',
    note: 'the reviewer's own change is sometimes better than the one they asked for' },
  { m: 'EXPLAIN the comment',
    bad: 'use a set here',
    good: 'this is O(n) inside a loop over a thousand items, so this is O(n squared) - a set makes it O(n)',
    why: 'the author will remember it in six months when the situation recurs' },
];

The social dynamics, which are most of it

Then the social half, which is where reviews actually fail. Review the code, not the person. "This function returns none when the list is empty — is that intended?" is answerable and leaves the author able to answer it; "you forgot to handle the empty case" is a claim about competence and produces defensiveness, which produces no information. Distinguish blocking from optional. A comment that must be addressed and a suggestion that may be declined are different kinds of message, and a review that mixes them turns every comment into an argument. The convention of labelling them — "must fix", "should", "nit" — costs nothing and removes most of the friction. Say the good things too. A review where every comment is a fault teaches that reviews are punitive, and people stop reading them carefully. Be fast. A review that arrives two days later gets a mechanical read, and the whole mechanism depends on attention rather than approval. Do not relitigate a decision in the review. If the architecture was argued and decided elsewhere, the review is not the place to reopen it, and a review that does is a sign the earlier decision was not actually made. And approve when it is good enough — the reviewer's job is to improve the code, not to establish that the reviewer could have written it, and perfect is not the standard.

Then the anti-patterns, gathered, because they are common and each is a different mistake. The rubber stamp — approving without reading, which is worse than not reviewing because it consumes the author's trust. The rewrite — a reviewer rewriting the change in comments, which produces a pull request with one commit and a review with two hundred, and which teaches nothing. The style debate in a design review. Reviewing a change you cannot understand because it is too large, and marking it approved anyway. Letting the queue grow, so every review is late and therefore mechanical. And treating a request for changes as a rejection, which is the fastest way to make people stop asking for review at all. The review that catches all of these is the retrospective question: what did this review actually catch, and what did it let through? A team that asks that occasionally improves; a team that reviews only for correctness and never for design produces correct code that nobody can change without breaking something.

/* The social half, where reviews actually fail. */
const SOCIAL = [
  { s: 'review the CODE, not the person',
    good: 'this function returns none when the list is empty - is that intended',
    goodProperty: 'answerable, and leaves the author able to answer it',
    bad: 'you forgot to handle the empty case',
    badProperty: 'a claim about competence that produces defensiveness, which produces no information' },
  { s: 'distinguish BLOCKING from OPTIONAL',
    why: 'a comment that must be addressed and a suggestion that may be declined are different kinds of message',
    consequence: 'a review that mixes them turns every comment into an argument',
    convention: 'labelling them must fix, should, nit costs nothing and removes most of the friction' },
  { s: 'say the GOOD things too',
    why: 'a review where every comment is a fault teaches that reviews are punitive, and people stop reading them carefully' },
  { s: 'BE FAST', consequence: 'a review that arrives two days later gets a MECHANICAL read, and the whole mechanism depends on attention rather than approval' },
  { s: 'do not RELITIGATE a decision in the review',
    why: 'if the architecture was argued and decided elsewhere, the review is not the place to reopen it',
    signal: 'a review that does is a sign the earlier decision was not actually MADE' },
  { s: 'approve when it is GOOD ENOUGH',
    rule: 'the reviewers job is to improve the code, not to establish that the reviewer could have written it',
    standard: 'perfect is not the standard' },
];

/* The anti-patterns. */
const ANTI_PATTERNS = [
  { a: 'the RUBBER STAMP', does: 'approving without reading', why: 'worse than not reviewing, because it consumes the authors trust' },
  { a: 'the REWRITE', does: 'a reviewer rewriting the change in comments',
    produces: 'a pull request with one commit and a review with two hundred',
    consequence: 'which teaches NOTHING' },
  { a: 'the STYLE DEBATE in a design review' },
  { a: 'reviewing a change you cannot understand because it is TOO LARGE', and: 'marking it approved anyway' },
  { a: 'letting the QUEUE grow', consequence: 'every review is late and therefore mechanical' },
  { a: 'treating a request for changes as a REJECTION',
    consequence: 'the fastest way to make people stop asking for review at all' },
];
const CATCHES_ALL = {
  question: 'what did this review ACTUALLY CATCH, and what did it let through',
  effect: 'a team that asks that occasionally improves',
  failure: 'a team that reviews only for correctness and never for design produces correct code that nobody can change without breaking something',
};

Review the code, not the person. "This function returns None when the list is empty — is that intended?" beats "You forgot xyz". Practise asking questions instead of dictating fixes. You’ll be on both sides many thousands of times.

15.6 Engineering metrics and estimation

Engineering metrics reveal how healthy delivery actually is. DORA metrics such as deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, and time to restore measure throughput and stability, while cycle time and flow metrics track how quickly work moves through the system. Story points and velocity make planning possible, and the rule is to measure to improve, never to punish.

  • Cycle time — PR opened → merged. Lead time — idea → production. Small batches keep these small.
  • DORA metrics (industry standard): deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change-failure rate, time to restore.
  • Estimation: teams naturally converge on story points (relative size: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13) rather than hours. Velocity = points delivered per sprint; used for planning, never as a productivity weapon.

Four types of metric, and which of them predict anything

A metric is a number somebody decided to look at, and the useful classification is by what kind of thing the number describes. Velocity — story points or ticket count completed per sprint — is an output metric: it measures what the team produced, not what caused it. Cycle time — how long an item takes from started to done — is a flow metric, and it is the most useful measurement in software delivery because it is what a customer experiences and because it responds to process changes in days rather than sprints. Defect escape rate — defects found in production as a proportion of defects found total — is a quality metric and it is the only one of these that measures something about the future rather than about the present. Change failure rate and time to restore — how often a change causes an incident, and how long recovery takes — are outcome metrics, and they are the two numbers most correlated with the ability to ship often. The distinction that matters: output metrics measure activity and outcome metrics measure consequence, and a team optimising activity while its outcomes get worse has made things worse while all the numbers went up.

Then why metrics are misused, and the four ways. Goodhart's law — when a measure becomes a target it ceases to be a good measure — which is not a warning about metrics in general but a description of what happens to any metric used as a target. The wrong thing becomes easy to measure. Counting tickets completed is easy to count and easy to make small; counting whether the customer can do the thing they came to do is neither. Comparing across contexts. A defect rate for a team maintaining a ten-year-old system and a team building something new are not comparable, and a leader who compares them will destroy the trust that makes measurement honest. And measuring what is easy rather than what matters, which is the most common and the most forgivable, because the things that matter are genuinely harder to measure — user comprehension, maintainability, whether the design will survive the next change — and a team that only reports the easy numbers ends up optimising them. The honest position: a metric is a question you have decided to answer regularly, and it is only worth having if you would act on a bad reading.

/* Four types. */
const TYPES = [
  { m: 'VELOCITY', measures: 'story points or ticket count completed per sprint',
    type: 'OUTPUT', doesNot: 'measure what caused it' },
  { m: 'CYCLE TIME', measures: 'how long an item takes from started to done', type: 'FLOW',
    mostUseful: true,
    why: ['it is what a CUSTOMER EXPERIENCES', 'it responds to process changes in DAYS rather than sprints'] },
  { m: 'DEFECT ESCAPE RATE', measures: 'defects found in production as a proportion of defects found total',
    type: 'QUALITY', unique: 'the only one of these that measures something about the FUTURE rather than the present' },
  { m: 'CHANGE FAILURE RATE and TIME TO RESTORE', measures: ['how often a change causes an incident',
    'how long recovery takes'], type: 'OUTCOME',
    claim: 'the two numbers most correlated with the ability to ship often' },
];
const THE_DISTINCTION = 'OUTPUT metrics measure ACTIVITY and OUTCOME metrics measure CONSEQUENCE - and a team optimising activity while its outcomes get worse has made things worse while all the numbers went up';

/* The four ways metrics are misused. */
const MISUSED = [
  { m: 'GOODHARTS LAW', is: 'when a measure becomes a target it ceases to be a good measure',
    scope: 'not a warning about metrics in general but a description of what happens to ANY metric used as a target' },
  { m: 'the wrong thing becomes EASY TO MEASURE',
    example: 'counting tickets completed is easy to count and easy to make small; counting whether the customer can do the thing they came to do is neither' },
  { m: 'COMPARING ACROSS CONTEXTS',
    example: 'a defect rate for a team maintaining a ten-year-old system and a team building something new are not comparable',
    consequence: 'a leader who compares them will destroy the TRUST THAT MAKES MEASUREMENT HONEST' },
  { m: 'measuring what is EASY rather than what MATTERS', mostCommon: true, mostForgivable: true,
    why: ['the things that matter are genuinely HARDER to measure - user comprehension, maintainability, whether the design will survive the next change',
      'a team that only reports the easy numbers ends up optimising them'] },
];
const HONEST_POSITION = 'a metric is a QUESTION YOU HAVE DECIDED TO ANSWER REGULARLY, and it is only worth having if you would act on a bad reading';

Practical measurement, and the metrics that are worth the trouble

Then what to actually measure, and the surprising answer is that a small set covers nearly everything. Cycle time and its distribution, not its average, because a distribution has a tail and the tail is where the pain is — the same percentile argument as latency. Change failure rate and time to restore, which together say whether the system is safe to change, and which are more actionable than anything about velocity because a team that cannot restore quickly will be told to ship less slowly, which fixes nothing. Deployment frequency, as a proxy for how small the batches are, which is the variable that actually determines risk. Defect escape rate, because it is the only quality number that gives you information about a process you cannot observe directly. And the number of open pull requests, which is a better measure of team health than any survey because it is a direct consequence of how fast people can get work reviewed, and a rising count means the review queue has become the constraint.

Then how to actually use these, because having numbers is not the same as being helped by them. Look for a trend, not a value. A single week's number is noise; the direction over several weeks is information, and a team that reacts to one bad week will make changes that make the next good week worse. Never compare individuals. A metric compared between people becomes a target, and a target becomes Goodhart's law — the effect is that people optimise the measurement and the measurement stops measuring. Hold the line on the two that resist cheating. Defect escape rate and time to restore are nearly impossible to game without actually being better, which is what makes them the ones to lead with. Pair every metric with a number you would act on, which is the test from before, and if you cannot name the action the metric goes. And expect the measurement to change the thing being measured, which is not a problem to solve but a property to plan for: the moment cycle time is measured, teams will find ways to make items smaller, which is usually an improvement and occasionally the opposite.

/* A small set covers nearly everything. */
const MEASURE = [
  { m: 'cycle time AND ITS DISTRIBUTION', notTheAverage: true,
    why: 'a distribution has a tail and the tail is where the pain is - the same percentile argument as latency' },
  { m: 'change failure rate and time to restore', togetherSay: 'whether the system is SAFE TO CHANGE',
    why: 'more actionable than anything about velocity',
    consequence: 'a team that cannot restore quickly will be told to ship less slowly, which fixes nothing' },
  { m: 'deployment frequency', isAProxyFor: 'how SMALL THE BATCHES are',
    why: 'the variable that actually determines risk' },
  { m: 'defect escape rate', why: 'the only quality number that gives you information about a process you cannot observe directly' },
  { m: 'the number of OPEN PULL REQUESTS', betterThanSurvey: true,
    why: 'a direct consequence of how fast people can get work reviewed',
    signal: 'a rising count means the review queue has become THE CONSTRAINT' },
];

/* How to use them. */
const USING = [
  { r: 'look for a TREND, not a value', why: 'a single weeks number is noise; the direction over several weeks is information',
    consequenceOfIgnoring: 'a team that reacts to one bad week will make changes that make the next good week worse' },
  { r: 'NEVER compare individuals',
    chain: ['a metric compared between people becomes a target',
      'a target becomes Goodharts law',
      'the effect is that people optimise the measurement and the measurement STOPS MEASURING'],
  },
  { r: 'hold the line on the TWO THAT RESIST CHEATING', which: ['defect escape rate', 'time to restore'],
    why: 'nearly impossible to game without actually being better',
    consequence: 'which is what makes them the ones to LEAD WITH' },
  { r: 'pair every metric with a NUMBER YOU WOULD ACT ON', isTheTest: true,
    ifNot: 'the metric goes' },
  { r: 'expect the measurement to CHANGE THE THING BEING MEASURED',
    notAProblem: 'a property to plan for',
    example: 'the moment cycle time is measured, teams will find ways to make items smaller, which is usually an improvement and occasionally the opposite' },
];
