16 · Testing & Quality

16.1 The testing pyramid16.2 Writing tests in practice (pytest)16.3 TDD — test-first development16.4 Fakes, mocks, and fixtures16.5 Property-based testing16.6 Continuous integration16.7 Root-cause debugging: testing in reverse

Testing and Quality is how you prove behavior, catch regressions, and ship with confidence instead of hope. The chapter covers the testing pyramid, writing tests with pytest, test-driven development, fakes, mocks, and fixtures, property-based testing, continuous integration, and methodical root-cause debugging. These habits make the suite fast, the failures informative, and the codebase safe to change.

Code untested is code assumed correct by luck. Testing is how you prove behaviour, prevent regressions, and sleep at night after deploying. This is a bachelor’s-course-sized chapter on all of it.

16.1 The testing pyramid

The testing pyramid shapes a healthy suite: many fast, focused unit tests at the base; fewer slower integration tests that verify components working together; and only a handful of end-to-end tests at the apex covering critical user journeys. The ratio matters because speed determines whether tests run on every change. Keep the base broad and the top thin so the suite stays quick enough to run constantly.

        /  E2E  \      few, slow, whole-stack, high confidence
      /  Integration \   some, medium, several units cooperating
     /     Unit        \    many, fast, isolated functions/classes
    ____________________  <-- the big cheap base you rely on most

An ASCII map of the testing pyramid: many fast unit tests at the base, then medium integration tests, and a few slow E2E tests on top.

  • Unit tests — one function/class, fake inputs, check outputs. Run in milliseconds, run on every save.
  • Integration tests — components talking for real (app + database, two services).
  • E2E (end-to-end) — the whole product through its real UI/API. Few, slowest, most brittle — but most faithful.

The three kinds, and why the shape is inverted from what most teams have

Three kinds of test, distinguished by what they replace and how fast they run. Unit tests replace a function call: they exercise one unit in isolation, run in milliseconds, run hundreds of times a day, and are the majority in a healthy suite. Integration tests replace a boundary: they exercise your code together with a real dependency — a real database, a real message queue — so they catch the class of defect that unit tests structurally cannot, which is the mismatch between what your code thinks the dependency does and what it actually does. End-to-end tests replace the whole system with a user: they drive the real interface against a real deployment, and they are the only kind that verifies the wiring. The recommended shape is an inverted triangle — many fast unit tests, a moderate number of integration tests, few end-to-end tests — and almost every team has the opposite, which is why their suites take forty minutes and nobody runs them.

Then why the shape is what it is, in one number each. Unit tests are fast and narrow, so you can have many. Integration tests are slow and flaky, so you have few. End-to-end tests are slowest and most flaky, so you have very few — and the reason for the flakiness is worth stating because it is a property and not a quality: an end-to-end test that depends on timing, on network, or on a third party fails for reasons that have nothing to do with your code, and a flaky test is worse than no test because it trains people to retry rather than to investigate. Then the trap in the middle layer, which is where most teams get it wrong. Integration tests are often called "the slow unit tests" and get resented rather than used properly. Their value is specific and not substitutable: they are the only thing that verifies your assumption about a dependency's behaviour is correct. The classic failure is a team with four hundred fast unit tests all using a fake database and no integration test at all — a suite that proves your code does what you believed the database does, which may be nothing.

/* Three kinds, distinguished by what they replace. */
const KINDS = [
  { k: 'UNIT tests', replace: 'a function call',
    exercise: 'one unit in isolation', speed: 'milliseconds', frequency: 'hundreds of times a day',
    shareInHealthySuite: 'the majority' },
  { k: 'INTEGRATION tests', replace: 'a BOUNDARY',
    exercise: 'your code together with a real dependency - a real database, a real message queue',
    catches: 'the class of defect unit tests STRUCTURALLY CANNOT',
    how: 'the mismatch between what your code thinks the dependency does and what it actually does' },
  { k: 'END-TO-END tests', replace: 'THE WHOLE SYSTEM WITH A USER',
    does: 'drive the real interface against a real deployment',
    unique: 'the only kind that verifies the WIRING' },
];
const SHAPE = 'an inverted triangle - many fast unit tests, a moderate number of integration tests, few end-to-end tests';
const MANY_TEAMS_HAVE = 'almost every team has the OPPOSITE, which is why their suites take forty minutes and nobody runs them';

/* One number each. */
const NUMBERS = [
  { k: 'UNIT', because: 'fast and narrow, so you can have many' },
  { k: 'INTEGRATION', because: 'slow and flaky, so you have few' },
  { k: 'END-TO-END', because: 'slowest and most flaky, so you have very few',
    flakinessIsAProperty: true,
    detail: 'an end-to-end test that depends on timing, on network, or on a third party fails for reasons that have NOTHING TO DO WITH YOUR CODE',
    whyFlakyIsWorse: 'a flaky test trains people to RETRY rather than to INVESTIGATE' },
];

/* The trap in the middle layer. */
const TRAP = {
  name: 'integration tests are often called the slow unit tests and get RESENT rather than used properly',
  value: 'specific and not substitutable',
  whatOnlyTheyVerify: 'that your assumption about a dependencys behaviour is correct',
  classicFailure: 'a team with four hundred fast unit tests all using a fake database and no integration test at all',
  whatThatProves: 'that your code does what YOU BELIEVED the database does, which may be nothing',
};

Building a suite that stays useful

Then the practices, and each addresses a specific reason suites decay. Every test runs on every commit, and the suite is the build's gate. A suite you run sometimes is a suite that has rotted, because nothing detects the rot. Budget the runtime and enforce it. Decide that the suite must complete in some time and make the build fail if it does not, because a suite that grows without limit will eventually cross the point where people stop waiting for it, and that point arrives without warning. Isolate every test from the others — its own database transaction, its own temporary directory, its own fixture — which is the only reliable way to make order-independence true rather than accidental. Never let a test hit a real external service. This is the single largest source of flakiness and the single largest source of slow suites, and the substitution — a fake that returns the shape of the dependency's response — is covered in the next section. Quarantine flaky tests rather than deleting them, and keep a list; deleting silently loses the coverage and leaves the defect that caused the flakiness in place. And test the risky, not the trivial. A test asserting a getter returns a stored field is a line of code that cannot be wrong; a test asserting that a money calculation rounds correctly at a boundary is the one worth writing, and the ratio between them is what separates a suite that helps from a suite that costs.

Then the coverage question, handled properly because it is the one metric people will argue about. Coverage measures execution, not correctness, and 100 per cent is achievable with tests that assert nothing, which is why a high number is not evidence. What it is good for is finding untested code — and that is genuinely useful, because untested code is code where nobody knows what happens, and it is disproportionately the code that has been written recently or is rarely called. So the useful practice is: use coverage to find what has no test, not to prove that what has one is correct. And the target worth holding is 100 per cent of the logic you care about, which is much less than the file, and none of the generated or trivial code. The mistake to avoid is chasing a percentage: a team that brings coverage from 78 to 92 will have written tests for the seventeen lines nobody cared about and left the one branch that would have caused an outage untouched, and the metric moved while nothing improved.

/* Practices, each addressing a specific reason suites decay. */
const PRACTICE = [
  { p: 'every test runs on EVERY COMMIT, and the suite is the builds gate',
    why: 'a suite you run sometimes is a suite that has ROTTED, because nothing detects the rot' },
  { p: 'budget the RUNTIME and ENFORCE it',
    how: 'decide the suite must complete in some time and make the build fail if it does not',
    why: 'a suite that grows without limit will eventually cross the point where people stop waiting for it, and that point arrives WITHOUT WARNING' },
  { p: 'ISOLATE every test from the others', examples: ['its own database transaction', 'its own temporary directory', 'its own fixture'],
    gain: 'the only reliable way to make order-independence TRUE rather than ACCIDENTAL' },
  { p: 'never let a test hit a REAL EXTERNAL SERVICE',
    why: 'the single largest source of flakiness and the single largest source of slow suites' },
  { p: 'QUARANTINE flaky tests rather than deleting them', keepAList: true,
    why: 'deleting silently loses the coverage and LEAVES THE DEFECT THAT CAUSED THE FLAKINESS in place' },
  { p: 'test the RISKY, not the trivial',
    trivial: 'a test asserting a getter returns a stored field is a line of code that cannot be wrong',
    risky: 'a test asserting that a money calculation rounds correctly at a boundary is the one worth writing',
    claim: 'the ratio between them is what separates a suite that helps from a suite that costs' },
];

/* Coverage, handled properly. */
const COVERAGE = {
  measures: 'EXECUTION, not correctness',
  whyAPercentageIsNotEvidence: '100 per cent is achievable with tests that assert nothing',
  whatItIsGoodFor: 'finding UNTESTED CODE',
  whyUseful: 'untested code is code where nobody knows what happens, and it is DISPROPORTIONATELY the code written recently or rarely called',
  practice: 'use coverage to find what has NO TEST, not to prove that what has one is correct',
  targetWorthHolding: '100 per cent of the logic you CARE ABOUT, which is much less than the file, and none of the generated or trivial code',
  theMistake: 'a team that brings coverage from 78 to 92 will have written tests for the seventeen lines nobody cared about and left the one branch that would have caused an OUTAGE untouched',
  consequence: 'the metric moved while nothing improved',
};

Golden rule: most tests, fast tests. If your unit test suite takes 20 minutes, nobody runs it, and it rots. Fast suite = testing becomes a habit instead of a chore.

16.2 Writing tests in practice (pytest)

Unit tests in pytest exercise one function or behavior at a time with controlled inputs, asserting on returned values and observable effects. Name tests with given-when-then clarity, use assert and parametrize to cover edge cases, and test behavior rather than internal calls so refactors do not break the suite. Group tests in classes or modules and use fixtures to keep them independent and deterministic.

# cart.py  -- the code under test
def total_price(items):
    total = sum(i.price * i.qty for i in items)          # add line-item subtotals
    return round(total * (1 - discount_for(items)), 2)

def discount_for(items):
    return 0.10 if sum(i.price * i.qty for i in items) > 100 else 0.0    # 10% over 100

The code under test: sum the line items, then apply a 10% discount once the subtotal passes 100.

# test_cart.py  -- run with:  python -m pytest -q
from cart import total_price, discount_for

class Item:                            # small stand-in for a real line item
    def __init__(self, price, qty):
        self.price, self.qty = price, qty

def test_discount_applied_over_100():  # behaviour tests name the intent
    items = [Item(60, 2)]                    # total 120
    assert total_price(items) == 108.0       # 120 * 0.9

def test_no_discount_under_100():
    items = [Item(30, 3)]                    # total 90
    assert total_price(items) == 90.0

def test_empty_cart_is_0():
    assert total_price([]) == 0.0

# edge cases = the soul of testing
def test_exact_boundary_100():
    assert discount_for([Item(100, 1)]) == 0.1

pytest covers the discount, the no-discount case, an empty cart, and the exact 100 boundary — each naming the behaviour it proves.

What makes a test a unit test, and the parts worth fighting over

The definition is about scope, not size: a unit test exercises one unit of behaviour in isolation, without the network, the filesystem, the clock or a database. It is not about the test being short or the function being small. Four properties are worth arguing for because they determine whether the suite is worth maintaining. Repeatable: the same result every time, which means no dependency on today's date, on a random seed you did not fix, on a third row existing in a table, or on execution order. Independent: it can run alone, in any order, which sounds trivial until you have seen a suite where test B only passes after test A because A cached something. Fast: under a tenth of a second, so you can run hundreds on every save — and this is not a performance nicety, it is what determines whether the tests get run at all, because a twenty-minute suite is a suite nobody runs before pushing. And self-describing: the name states the behaviour and the failure message says what was expected and what happened, because the person reading the failure is frequently not the person who wrote the test and will not read the body.

Then the arrangement that makes them unit tests, and each element has a reason. Arrange: set up exactly the state the test needs, and nothing else — a shared setup containing data some tests do not use is a shared setup that breaks some tests when it changes. Act: call one thing, and the discipline of calling one thing is what makes the failure message meaningful, because a test that asserts on a sequence of calls will fail for a reason unrelated to what it claims to test. Assert: one logical claim, with a message; multiple assertions in one test are acceptable only when they are asserting one outcome, and the usual trap is a test that asserts a return value and then two side effects, where the third assertion failing tells you nothing about which of the three behaviours broke. And the naming: the test name is the specification and it should read as a sentence — "returns zero when the cart is empty" rather than "test cart 3" — because a suite whose names read as sentences can be read as documentation and a suite whose names are identifiers cannot.

/* The definition is about SCOPE, not size. */
const DEFINITION = 'exercises one unit of BEHAVIOUR in isolation, without the network, the filesystem, the clock or a database';
const NOTABOUT = 'not about the test being short or the function being small';
const PROPERTIES = [
  { p: 'REPEATABLE', brokenBy: ['todays date', 'a random seed you did not fix',
    'a third row existing in a table', 'execution order'] },
  { p: 'INDEPENDENT', failure: 'a suite where test B only passes after test A because A cached something' },
  { p: 'FAST', threshold: 'under a tenth of a second, so you can run hundreds on every save',
    notANicety: 'it is what determines whether the tests get RUN AT ALL',
    arithmetic: 'a twenty-minute suite is a suite nobody runs before pushing' },
  { p: 'SELF-DESCRIBING', must: 'the name states the behaviour and the failure message says what was expected and what happened',
    why: 'the person reading the failure is frequently not the person who wrote the test and will not read the body' },
];

/* Arrange, act, assert. */
const AAA = [
  { s: 'ARRANGE', rule: 'set up exactly the state the test needs, and NOTHING ELSE',
    trap: 'a shared setup containing data some tests do not use is a shared setup that breaks some tests when it changes' },
  { s: 'ACT', rule: 'call ONE thing',
    why: 'the discipline of calling one thing is what makes the failure message meaningful',
    consequence: 'a test asserting on a sequence of calls fails for a reason unrelated to what it claims to test' },
  { s: 'ASSERT', rule: 'one logical claim, with a message',
    multipleAllowedWhen: 'they are asserting one outcome',
    trap: 'a test that asserts a return value and then two side effects, where the third assertion failing tells you nothing about which of the three behaviours broke' },
  { s: 'the NAMING', good: 'returns zero when the cart is empty', bad: 'test cart 3',
    why: 'a suite whose names read as sentences can be read as documentation, and a suite whose names are identifiers cannot' },
];

Testing behaviour, and the four mistakes that make suites rot

Then the central discipline: test behaviour, not implementation. Assert what the code does from the outside — what it returns, what it writes, what it sends — and not what it calls internally. The reason is not aesthetic. Implementation tests die on every refactor, and a suite that dies on every refactor produces the behaviour that leads to its own deletion: a developer makes a correct internal change, four tests fail, they cannot tell whether the tests or the code is wrong, and the cheapest resolution is to delete the tests or to stop running them. Behaviour tests survive the same change. And they are also the ones that catch real defects, because a test that asserts "these three methods were called in this order" will pass while the function returns the wrong value, whereas a test that asserts the return value will fail on the actual bug. Then the change the test cannot see is a legitimate boundary: if a function's behaviour is identical whether or not it calls a cache internally, then the cache is not its behaviour and the test should not know.

Then the four ways suites rot, which is worth listing because each has a prevention. Tests coupled to internals — prevented by the discipline above, and the practical measure is whether renaming a private helper requires touching tests. Shared state between tests — a database row left behind, a module-level cache populated by an earlier test; the only reliable fix is each test arranging its own state and the test runner randomising order so the coupling is exposed rather than hidden. Tests that assert the implementation rather than the outcome, including snapshot tests of large structures, which fail on every harmless change and train the team to re-record snapshots without reading them. And coverage as a goal rather than a measure. Coverage tells you which lines executed, not whether the behaviour is correct — a function can be fully covered and assert nothing, and the metric that matters is not the percentage but how many of your failure modes have a test, which is a number you can actually reason about. The other three mistakes share a root cause worth naming: a test that is annoying to maintain gets deleted or ignored, so writing tests that are cheap to maintain is not a style preference but the condition of their survival.

/* The central discipline. */
const RULE = 'test BEHAVIOUR, not implementation';
const WHAT = 'assert what the code does from the outside - what it returns, what it writes, what it sends';
const WHY = {
  notAesthetic: true,
  reason: 'implementation tests DIE ON EVERY REFACTOR',
  consequence: 'a suite that dies on every refactor produces the behaviour that leads to its own deletion',
  theSequence: ['a developer makes a correct internal change', 'four tests fail',
    'they cannot tell whether the tests or the code is wrong',
    'the cheapest resolution is to delete the tests or to stop running them'],
  behaviourTestsSurvive: true,
  alsoCatchRealDefects: 'a test asserting these three methods were called in this order will pass while the function returns the wrong value',
  theBoundary: 'if a functions behaviour is identical whether or not it calls a cache internally, then the cache is NOT ITS BEHAVIOUR and the test should not know',
};

/* Four ways suites rot. */
const ROT = [
  { r: 'tests coupled to INTERNALS',
    prevention: 'the discipline above',
    measure: 'whether renaming a private helper requires touching tests' },
  { r: 'SHARED STATE between tests', examples: ['a database row left behind', 'a module-level cache populated by an earlier test'],
    fix: 'each test arranges its own state',
    plusFix: 'the test runner RANDOMISES ORDER so the coupling is exposed rather than hidden' },
  { r: 'tests that assert the IMPLEMENTATION rather than the outcome',
    instances: ['snapshot tests of large structures'],
    consequence: 'they fail on every harmless change and train the team to RE-RECORD SNAPSHOTS WITHOUT READING THEM' },
  { r: 'COVERAGE as a goal rather than a measure',
    detail: 'coverage tells you which lines executed, not whether the behaviour is correct',
    example: 'a function can be fully covered and assert nothing',
    theMetricThatMatters: 'how many of your FAILURE MODES have a test - a number you can actually reason about' },
];
const ROOT_CAUSE_OF_THREE = 'a test that is ANNOYING TO MAINTAIN gets deleted or ignored, so writing tests that are cheap to maintain is not a style preference but THE CONDITION OF THEIR SURVIVAL';

Test behaviour, not implementation. Assert what happens, don’t assert internal method call logs. The day you refactor internals, behaviour tests still pass — implementation tests die.

16.3 TDD — test-first development

Test-driven development inverts the usual order: write a failing test first, write the smallest code to pass it, then refactor safely. The red-green-refactor cycle forces you to design APIs from the caller’s view and keeps each behavior covered by a regression test. It pays off most when a design is unclear or bugs are costly.

The discipline that makes bugs scarcer: Red → Green → Refactor.

  1. Red: write a failing test for the next behaviour.
  2. Green: write the smallest code that makes it pass.
  3. Refactor: clean it up; tests keep you safe.

The cycle, and why the test comes first

Test-driven development is three steps in a loop: write a failing test, write the least code that passes it, refactor with the test as your safety net. The first step is the one that matters and the one that feels wrong, and the reason it feels wrong is that writing a test requires deciding what the thing should do, which is the design decision — and writing the code first lets you decide what to do and then write a test that agrees with whatever you happened to build. The failing test is the specification, and it is valuable precisely because it is written before the code exists to justify it. The second step's discipline is "the least code that passes", and it is not asceticism: code written to pass a test rather than to be general is fast to produce, easy to see is unnecessary, and often genuinely unnecessary — the test that made it will tell you when it is needed. The third step is where the value is and the one everybody skips under deadline: refactor while you have a test that will tell you whether you broke something. The alternative is refactoring later, when there is no test, which is why codebases carry the same shape for years.

Then what TDD actually buys, because the benefits usually claimed are the wrong ones. Not coverage — coverage is a side effect and you can achieve it by writing tests after. It forces you to think from the caller's point of view, which is why the API you design under TDD matches how it is actually used: you cannot write a failing test until you know how the thing will be called, so the signature is forced to be sensible before any implementation exists to hide behind. It produces small, decoupled units as a consequence rather than a goal, because a unit that is hard to test is a unit doing too much and the difficulty announces itself immediately. It makes the design discussion cheap, because a test is the cheapest possible executable statement of what a thing should do, and twenty minutes of tests can be worth more than a day of arguing. And it makes refactoring safe, which is the benefit that compounds: a codebase where every behaviour has a test is a codebase that can be changed, and one without is a codebase that is afraid of itself.

/* Three steps. */
const CYCLE = ['write a FAILING test', 'write the LEAST CODE THAT PASSES it',
  'refactor with the test as your safety net'];
const WHY_FIRST = {
  step: 'the first step matters and feels wrong',
  why: 'writing a test requires deciding what the thing should do, which IS THE DESIGN DECISION',
  contrast: 'writing the code first lets you decide what to do and then write a test that AGREES WITH WHATEVER YOU HAPPENED TO BUILD',
  value: 'the failing test is the SPECIFICATION, and it is valuable precisely because it is written before the code exists to justify it',
};
const SECOND_STEP = {
  discipline: 'the LEAST CODE THAT PASSES',
  notAsceticism: true,
  why: ['code written to pass a test rather than to be general is fast to produce',
    'easy to see is unnecessary, and often genuinely unnecessary',
    'the test that made it will tell you when it is needed'],
};
const THIRD_STEP = {
  value: 'where the value is, and the one everybody skips under deadline',
  why: 'refactor WHILE YOU HAVE A TEST that will tell you whether you broke something',
  alternative: 'refactoring later, when there is no test, which is why codebases carry the same shape for years',
};

/* What TDD actually buys. */
const BUYS = [
  { b: 'NOT coverage', is: 'a side effect, achievable by writing tests after' },
  { b: 'it forces you to think from the CALLERS POINT OF VIEW',
    why: 'you cannot write a failing test until you know how the thing will be called',
    gain: 'the API you design under TDD matches HOW IT IS ACTUALLY USED, because the signature is forced to be sensible before any implementation exists to hide behind' },
  { b: 'it produces small, decoupled UNITS', as: 'a consequence rather than a goal',
    mechanism: 'a unit that is hard to test is a unit doing too much, and the difficulty announces itself immediately' },
  { b: 'it makes the DESIGN DISCUSSION cheap',
    why: 'a test is the CHEAPEST POSSIBLE EXECUTABLE STATEMENT of what a thing should do',
    magnitude: 'twenty minutes of tests can be worth more than a day of arguing' },
  { b: 'it makes REFACTORING SAFE', compounds: true,
    why: 'a codebase where every behaviour has a test is a codebase THAT CAN BE CHANGED, and one without is a codebase that is afraid of itself' },
];

Where TDD does not fit, and how teams actually adopt it

Then where TDD is the wrong tool, because insisting on it everywhere is how it gets a reputation for being slow. Exploratory work. When you do not know what the thing should do, a test written first is a test written against a guess, and the value of TDD there is zero. The honest answer is to spike — build the ugly version, learn what it is, throw it away — and then build it properly with tests. User interface layout. Screenshot tests of a layout are slow, brittle and produce failures nobody can act on; the exception is component libraries where the visual contract is genuinely the specification. Throwaway prototypes. A spike intended for deletion does not need a test suite; it needs a clear expiry. Performance work. You cannot write a test that asserts a query takes eight milliseconds without a fragile timing assertion that fails on someone else's machine; the honest approach is a benchmark with a generous threshold and a separate measurement tool. And code whose only behaviour is a side effect on an external system, where the test would need to assert about a payment gateway — which is what the next section's doubles are for.

Then how teams actually adopt it, because the failure mode is abandoning it after three weeks. Adopt it on new code only. You cannot write a failing test for existing code with no tests, and retrofitting is slow and produces the worst of both worlds. New code under TDD alongside legacy code without it is normal and works. Start with one class or one module. Not "the whole team from Monday" — one area, where the tests stay fast and the coverage is visible. Write the test at the same time as the fix, which is the minimum viable version: the failing test first is ideal, but the defect reproducing in a test that you watch fail and then pass is most of the value at a fraction of the friction. Never write a test for a bug without first reproducing it in a test, which is the discipline from the debugging chapter and the one practice that reliably converts. And when the suite gets slow, fix the slowness before adding more, because a suite nobody runs is worse than no suite, and the causes are always the same: tests hitting the network or the filesystem, tests sharing state, and tests doing real work where a fake would do.

/* Where TDD is the wrong tool. */
const WRONG_WHEN = [
  { w: 'EXPLORATORY work', detail: 'when you do not know what the thing should do, a test written first is a test written against a GUESS',
    valueOfTddThere: 'zero',
    answer: 'spike - build the ugly version, learn what it is, throw it away - then build it properly with tests' },
  { w: 'USER INTERFACE layout', detail: 'screenshot tests of a layout are slow, brittle, and produce failures nobody can act on',
    exception: 'component libraries where the visual contract is genuinely the specification' },
  { w: 'THROWAWAY PROTOTYPES', detail: 'a spike intended for deletion does not need a test suite; it needs a CLEAR EXPIRY' },
  { w: 'PERFORMANCE work', detail: 'you cannot write a test asserting a query takes eight milliseconds without a FRAGILE TIMING ASSERTION that fails on someone elses machine',
    answer: 'a benchmark with a generous threshold and a separate measurement tool' },
  { w: 'code whose only behaviour is a SIDE EFFECT on an external system',
    detail: 'the test would need to assert about a payment gateway',
    answer: 'which is what doubles are for' },
];

/* How teams actually adopt it. */
const ADOPTION = [
  { a: 'adopt it on NEW CODE ONLY',
    why: ['you cannot write a failing test for existing code with no tests',
      'retrofitting is slow and produces the worst of both worlds'],
    note: 'new code under TDD alongside legacy code without it is normal and works' },
  { a: 'start with ONE CLASS OR ONE MODULE', notWith: 'the whole team from Monday',
    why: 'one area, where the tests stay fast and the coverage is visible' },
  { a: 'write the test AT THE SAME TIME AS THE FIX', isThe: 'minimum viable version',
    detail: 'the failing test first is ideal, but the defect reproducing in a test that you watch FAIL AND THEN PASS is most of the value at a fraction of the friction' },
  { a: 'NEVER write a test for a bug without first reproducing it in a test',
    is: 'the discipline from the debugging chapter',
    effect: 'the one practice that reliably converts' },
  { a: 'when the suite gets SLOW, fix the slowness before adding more',
    why: 'a suite nobody runs is worse than no suite',
    causes: ['tests hitting the network or the filesystem', 'tests sharing state',
      'tests doing real work where a fake would do'],
  },
];

TDD’s real payoff isn’t the ritual — it’s that you’re forced to think from the user’s view, your code is always covered, and the API you design matches how it’s actually used.

16.4 Fakes, mocks, and fixtures

Real databases, networks, clocks, and filesystems are slow, flaky, and hard to control in tests, so tests swap in stand-ins. Fixtures set up and tear down state, fakes are lightweight in-memory replacements with real behavior, and mocks are automated stubs that record calls and return scripted answers. Prefer real code and simple fakes, and use automated mocks only when a dependency is truly uncontrollable or unnecessary.

Real databases, networks and clocks are slow and flaky in tests. Replace them with controllable stand-ins.

# Instead of emailing the real SMTP server in a test, fake it
class FakeMailer:
    def __init__(self):
        self.sent = []                     # record what would have been sent
    def send(self, to, subject, body):
        self.sent.append((to, subject, body))

def notify(event, mailer):
    mailer.send(event.user, "Update", "Your stuff changed")

def test_notify_sends_email():
    mailer = FakeMailer()
    notify(SimpleNamespace(user="ada@x.com"), mailer)
    assert mailer.sent[0][0] == "ada@x.com"  # captured call proves delivery

The four kinds, and which one you actually want

The vocabulary is muddled in common usage and the distinctions matter because they have opposite guidance. A stub returns canned responses, so a test asserts on what your code does with a response you chose. A mock records the calls made to it and lets you assert on them — so a test asserts that your code called the dependency the right way. A fake is a working implementation with a simplified contract: an in-memory database that actually stores and retrieves, a mailer that records messages in a list. A spy wraps the real implementation and records calls while still calling through, so you can assert on behaviour and on interaction. The practical ranking, and it is the useful part of this section: a fake is nearly always better than a mock. A fake preserves behaviour, so tests written against it remain meaningful when the real dependency is substituted; a mock encodes an assumption about the implementation, so a test written against it breaks when the implementation changes correctly.

Then what a fake actually gives you, which is why it is preferable. A fake lets the test exercise real logic rather than asserting a recorded call — so the test verifies the query your code builds, the value it transforms and the retry it performs, rather than verifying that a method was invoked with arguments that a human checked. A fake composes, a mock does not: a fake with twenty methods can be used in twenty tests, and each is free; a mock configured for one interaction is single-use. And the behaviour a fake provides is the behaviour the real thing has, so the test catches drift between your assumption and reality — which is exactly the class of defect the integration layer exists to find, and a fake gets you part of it without the cost. The cost, stated honestly: your fake is a second implementation and it can be wrong. If the fake's where clause does not handle a null the real one does, your tests pass and production fails — so the fake must be built against the real contract, not against your idea of it, and for anything where the contract is complex the integration test is still required.

/* Four kinds, with the distinctions that matter. */
const KINDS = [
  { k: 'STUB', returns: 'canned responses', asserts: 'what your code does with a response you chose' },
  { k: 'MOCK', records: 'the calls made to it', asserts: 'that your code called the dependency the right way' },
  { k: 'FAKE', is: 'a WORKING IMPLEMENTATION with a simplified contract',
    instances: ['an in-memory database that actually stores and retrieves', 'a mailer that records messages in a list'] },
  { k: 'SPY', does: 'wraps the real implementation and records calls WHILE STILL CALLING THROUGH',
    asserts: ['behaviour', 'interaction'] },
];
const RANKING = {
  claim: 'a FAKE IS NEARLY ALWAYS BETTER THAN A MOCK',
  fakeBetter: 'a fake preserves behaviour, so tests written against it remain meaningful when the real dependency is substituted',
  mockProblem: 'a mock encodes an ASSUMPTION ABOUT THE IMPLEMENTATION, so a test written against it breaks when the implementation changes correctly',
};

/* What a fake gives you. */
const WHY_FAKE = [
  { g: 'it lets the test exercise REAL LOGIC rather than asserting a recorded call',
    verifies: ['the query your code builds', 'the value it transforms', 'the retry it performs'],
    contrast: 'rather than verifying that a method was invoked with arguments that a human checked' },
  { g: 'it COMPOSES, a mock does not',
    arithmetic: 'a fake with twenty methods can be used in twenty tests, and each is free; a mock configured for one interaction is single-use' },
  { g: 'the behaviour a fake provides is the behaviour the REAL THING has, so the test catches drift between your assumption and reality',
    catches: 'exactly the class of defect the integration layer exists to find, and a fake gets you part of it without the cost' },
];
const FAKE_COST = {
  honestly: 'your fake is a SECOND IMPLEMENTATION and it can be wrong',
  example: 'if the fakes where clause does not handle a null the real one does, your tests pass and production fails',
  therefore: ['the fake must be built against the REAL CONTRACT, not against your idea of it',
    'for anything where the contract is complex, the integration test is still required'],
};

When mocks are right, and the over-mocking trap

Then when mocking is genuinely the right answer, because it is sometimes correct and pretending otherwise produces unusable tests. When you are testing your code's contract with a dependency — that it retries, that it times out, that it sends the right headers — because a real dependency cannot be made to fail on cue. When the failure mode is one you cannot otherwise provoke: a timeout, a 500, a malformed response, a rate limit. This is the strongest case, because these are the paths that break in production and are the ones a fake must otherwise implement. When the dependency is a collaborator whose behaviour is already tested elsewhere, so your test is about your side of the boundary. When the real thing genuinely cannot run — an external service, an email send, a payment gateway. And the pattern that makes mocking tolerable: mock at your own boundary, not someone else's. Define an interface you own, implement it as a fake in tests and the real client in production, and the mock is a test double for your abstraction rather than an assumption about somebody else's.

Then the over-mocking trap, which is the failure mode of the whole approach. Over-mocked code has no tests left when you change the implementation, because every test asserts an interaction that was a design choice rather than a requirement. The symptoms are recognisable: changing a function's internals breaks twenty tests; a test asserts "the repository's save was called with these exact arguments"; the unit under test does nothing except call other things and check that they were called, which means the test passes and the code does nothing. Such a test has zero defect-detection power, because the defects that matter are wrong values, wrong orderings and missing cases, and none of them is a missing method call. And the deep problem: over-mocking is a symptom of testing structure rather than behaviour, and the way out is to ask what the caller can observe — a returned value, a persisted record, a message sent — and test that, using a fake for the dependency rather than a mock of your own code. The practical rule: if a test would still pass when the function body were replaced with something that does nothing but produce the asserted output, the test is worthless — which is a test you can run in ten seconds and which settles the question without reading the test carefully.

/* When mocking is right. */
const RIGHT_WHEN = [
  { w: 'testing your codes CONTRACT with a dependency',
    does: 'that it retries, that it times out, that it sends the right headers',
    why: 'a real dependency cannot be made to fail on cue' },
  { w: 'the FAILURE MODE is one you cannot otherwise provoke', instances: ['a timeout', 'a 500', 'a malformed response', 'a rate limit'],
    strongestCase: true,
    why: 'these are the paths that break in production and the ones a fake must otherwise implement' },
  { w: 'the dependency is a COLLABORATOR whose behaviour is already tested elsewhere',
    then: 'your test is about your side of the boundary' },
  { w: 'the real thing genuinely CANNOT RUN', instances: ['an external service', 'an email send', 'a payment gateway'] },
];
const TOLERABLE_PATTERN = {
  pattern: 'MOCK AT YOUR OWN BOUNDARY, not someone elses',
  how: 'define an interface you own, implement it as a fake in tests and the real client in production',
  gain: 'the mock is a test double for YOUR abstraction rather than an assumption about somebody elses' },
};

/* The over-mocking trap. */
const OVER_MOCKING = {
  problem: 'over-mocked code has NO TESTS LEFT when you change the implementation',
  why: 'every test asserts an interaction that was a DESIGN CHOICE rather than a requirement',
  symptoms: ['changing a functions internals breaks twenty tests',
    'a test asserts the repositorys save was called with these exact arguments',
    'the unit under test does nothing except call other things and check that they were called, which means the test passes and the code does NOTHING'],
  zeroPower: 'such a test has ZERO DEFECT-DETECTION POWER',
  why: 'the defects that matter are wrong values, wrong orderings and missing cases, and NONE OF THEM IS A MISSING METHOD CALL',
  deepProblem: 'over-mocking is a symptom of testing STRUCTURE rather than BEHAVIOUR',
  wayOut: 'ask what the CALLER CAN OBSERVE - a returned value, a persisted record, a message sent - and test that, using a fake for the dependency rather than a mock of your own code',
};
const QUICK_TEST = {
  question: 'if a test would still pass when the function body were replaced with something that does nothing but produce the asserted output, is the test worthless',
  howLong: 'a test you can run in ten seconds',
  gain: 'settles the question without reading the test carefully',
};

A fake mailer records calls in memory, so the test asserts delivery without ever touching a real SMTP server.

  • Fixture — deterministic setup (a DB with known rows, fixed time, fixed random seed).
  • Mock — automated stand-in that records calls and returns canned values; fine for crossing slow boundaries, but prefer fakes (real, simple in-memory implementations) where possible.
  • Determinism is everything: a test that sometimes passes is worse than one that always fails — you stop trusting the suite.

16.5 Property-based testing

Property-based testing flips the usual approach: instead of hand-written examples, you generate hundreds or thousands of random inputs and assert invariants that must hold for every one. Frameworks such as Hypothesis generate the inputs, and when a case fails they shrink it automatically to the smallest counterexample. It finds edge cases you would never type by hand, especially for parsers, serializers, and numeric logic.

Instead of a few hand-written examples, generate hundreds of random inputs and assert invariants — like "reverse(reverse(x)) == x". When it fails, it shrinks to the smallest failing input. Catches the edge case you’d never think to type.

# pip install hypothesis
from hypothesis import given, strategies as st

@given(st.lists(st.integers()))          # random inputs, not hand-picked ones
def test_sort_is_ordered(xs):
    s = sorted(xs)
    assert all(s[i] <= s[i+1] for i in range(len(s)-1))

@given(st.lists(st.integers()))
def test_sort_preserves_elements(xs):
    assert sorted(xs) == sorted(xs)   # key property: idempotent ordering

Example-based versus property-based, and why the second catches more

An example-based test asserts that specific inputs produce specific outputs. It is precise, readable, and it has a blind spot that is structural rather than accidental: the examples were chosen by a human, and a human chooses the examples they can think of. That misses boundary values, unusual combinations, and anything requiring more inputs than a person would enumerate. A property-based test states a property — a statement that must hold for all inputs in some category — and then a library generates inputs, including the ones you did not think of. The two are complementary rather than alternatives, and the correct position is examples for the cases you care about being documented and property tests for the invariant you cannot afford to get wrong.

Then the properties worth looking for, because the skill is recognising them. Commutativity: does the operation with its arguments swapped give the same answer — addition, set union, sorting by key. Associativity: does grouping a chain of operations differently give the same answer, which is the property that distinguishes a correct implementation of an associative operation from one that happens to work on two operands. Identity: is there an element that leaves everything unchanged — zero for addition, the empty collection for a fold. Idempotence: does applying an operation twice equal applying it once, which is exactly what a database upsert should satisfy and is a very common real defect. Inverse: does undoing an operation restore the original — encode and decode, charge and refund, insert and delete. Round-trip: does serialising and deserialising return the original value, which is the property that catches an entire class of encoding bugs. Invariants: is some condition true after every operation — a balance never negative, a heap's parent always larger than its children, a sorted collection stays sorted after an insert. And no-fewer-solutions: is the number of results within the mathematically possible range.

/* Example-based versus property-based. */
const EXAMPLES = {
  asserts: 'that specific inputs produce specific outputs',
  good: ['precise', 'readable'],
  blindSpot: 'the examples were chosen by a human, and a human chooses the examples they CAN THINK OF',
  misses: ['boundary values', 'unusual combinations', 'anything requiring more inputs than a person would enumerate'],
};
const PROPERTIES_BASED = {
  states: 'a PROPERTY - a statement that must hold for all inputs in some category',
  does: 'a library generates inputs, including the ones you did not think of',
  relationship: 'complementary rather than alternatives',
  position: 'examples for the cases you care about being documented; property tests for the invariant you cannot afford to get wrong',
};

/* The properties worth looking for. */
const PROPERTIES = [
  { p: 'COMMUTATIVITY', q: 'does the operation with its arguments swapped give the same answer',
    instances: ['addition', 'set union', 'sorting by key'] },
  { p: 'ASSOCIATIVITY', q: 'does grouping a chain of operations differently give the same answer',
    distinguishes: 'a correct implementation of an associative operation from one that happens to work on two operands' },
  { p: 'IDENTITY', q: 'is there an element that leaves everything unchanged',
    instances: ['zero for addition', 'the empty collection for a fold'] },
  { p: 'IDEMPOTENCE', q: 'does applying an operation twice equal applying it once',
    instance: 'exactly what a database upsert should satisfy', commonRealDefect: true },
  { p: 'INVERSE', q: 'does undoing an operation restore the original',
    instances: ['encode and decode', 'charge and refund', 'insert and delete'] },
  { p: 'ROUND-TRIP', q: 'does serialising and deserialising return the original value',
    catches: 'an ENTIRE CLASS of encoding bugs' },
  { p: 'INVARIANTS', q: 'is some condition true after every operation',
    instances: ['a balance never negative', 'a heaps parent always larger than its children',
      'a sorted collection stays sorted after an insert'] },
  { p: 'NO-FEWER-SOLUTIONS', q: 'is the number of results within the mathematically possible range' },
];

Shrinking, and the traps that make property tests fail on purpose

Then shrinking, which is the feature that makes property-based testing usable rather than merely clever. When a generated input fails, the library minimises it — it repeatedly tries smaller and simpler inputs looking for one that still fails, and reports the smallest. Without this you get a failure reported on a generated list of two thousand integers and spend an hour reading it; with it you get a failure on a three-element list and see the bug in a minute. The smallest failing case is usually the informative one, because it is the one where your assumption and the implementation diverge with the least in the way. And it is worth understanding what shrinking is doing: it is not finding a different bug, it is finding the simplest witness to the one you have, and that witness is usually the one whose behaviour you can reason about directly.

Then the four ways property tests fail for reasons that are not defects, and each is worth recognising because it produces an afternoon of confusion. The property is wrong. You have asserted something that is not actually true — round-tripping a function that normalises timestamps does not return the original, and the test is telling you something real about the API even though you called it a failure. The generator makes invalid input. It generates a list of integers when the function requires a sorted list, a non-negative number, or a string with a length; the fix is to constrain the generator rather than to change the function, because a function that crashes on a negative number when negative is excluded by contract is correct. Flakiness from non-determinism. The property is nondeterministic — depends on time, on a random seed, on iteration order of a set — and the fix is to fix the seed and to sort before asserting. And the test is slow. Property testing generates many inputs, so a property over a large structure with a thousand generated cases can be slower than the whole rest of the suite; the fixes are fewer cases during normal runs and more when a failure occurs, which most libraries support as a setting. The discipline that keeps this productive: write properties you can state in one sentence, because a property you cannot state simply is usually a property you have not understood, and shrinking will then find a case you cannot interpret.

/* Shrinking. */
const SHRINKING = {
  does: 'when a generated input fails, the library MINIMISES it',
  how: 'repeatedly tries smaller and simpler inputs looking for one that still fails, and reports the smallest',
  withoutIt: 'a failure reported on a generated list of two thousand integers, and an hour reading it',
  withIt: 'a failure on a three-element list, and the bug visible in a minute',
  whySmallestIsInformative: 'it is the one where your assumption and the implementation diverge with the LEAST in the way',
  notFindingADifferentBug: 'it is finding the SIMPLEST WITNESS to the one you have',
  thatWitness: 'usually the one whose behaviour you can reason about directly' },
];

/* Four ways property tests fail for reasons that are not defects. */
const NOT_DEFECTS = [
  { f: 'the PROPERTY IS WRONG', detail: 'you have asserted something that is not actually true',
    example: 'round-tripping a function that normalises timestamps does not return the original',
    note: 'the test is telling you something REAL about the API even though you called it a failure' },
  { f: 'the GENERATOR MAKES INVALID INPUT', examples: ['a list of integers when the function requires a sorted list',
    'a non-negative number', 'a string with a length'],
    fix: 'constrain the GENERATOR rather than change the function',
    why: 'a function that crashes on a negative number when negative is EXCLUDED BY CONTRACT is correct' },
  { f: 'FLAKINESS from non-determinism', causes: ['time', 'a random seed', 'iteration order of a set'],
    fix: 'fix the seed and sort before asserting' },
  { f: 'the TEST IS SLOW', why: 'property testing generates many inputs',
    magnitude: 'a property over a large structure with a thousand generated cases can be slower than the whole rest of the suite',
    fix: 'fewer cases during normal runs and more when a failure occurs, which most libraries support as a setting' },
];
const DISCIPLINE = 'write properties you can STATE IN ONE SENTENCE, because a property you cannot state simply is usually a property you have not understood - and shrinking will then find a case you cannot interpret';

Hypothesis feeds random integer lists to the sort properties and shrinks any failure to its smallest reproducing input.

16.6 Continuous integration

Continuous integration runs the full quality gate, lint, typecheck, tests, and build, on a shared server for every push so failures surface minutes after they are written. A red pipeline blocks merging until the change is fixed, making it a hard backstop rather than a suggestion. Cheap to start with tools like GitHub Actions, it saves whole weeks of integration pain later.

Automate the checks on every push: lint + typecheck + unit tests + build run on a server; a red pipeline blocks the merge. Do this early; it costs little at the start and saves entire weeks later.

# .github/workflows/ci.yml  (GitHub Actions)
name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]                # run the pipeline on every push or PR
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with: { python-version: '3.12' }
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: python -m pytest -q          # a red test blocks the merge
      - run: pip install ruff && ruff check .

What CI actually is, and the distinction from a build server

Continuous integration is a discipline before it is a tool: everyone commits to a shared mainline frequently, and every commit is verified by an automated build. Both halves matter and both are routinely dropped. Committing daily means the integration conflict window is a day rather than a quarter, so conflicts are small and mechanical. Verifying every commit means the state of mainline is always known to be good, which is what makes the daily deployment possible that chapter fifteen argued for. A CI system without the frequent-committing half is a slow build server — it verifies whatever arrives, whenever — and that configuration produces the worst of both: builds that are slow because they are huge, and conflicts that are big because they have accumulated. And the pipeline is the part everyone thinks CI means: the sequence of steps that takes a commit and produces a verified, deployable artifact. The critical property of the pipeline is that it is a gate. A check that reports a failure and does not block the merge is a report, not a gate, and a report is ignored exactly as often as it is read.

Then what belongs in the pipeline and in what order, and the ordering is not arbitrary because each stage's value depends on the previous one being fast. Fast checks first. Formatting and linting take seconds and catch the most common problems, and putting them after the tests means every developer waits a minute to be told about a missing semicolon. Unit tests next — the bulk of the value, in a few minutes. Integration tests next, because they need a database or a container and are slower. Build the artifact — and the discipline worth stating is that this produces the thing you deploy, not something similar, because "we build in CI and build again for release" is how a release ships a different binary from the one that was tested. End-to-end and smoke tests last, in a deployed environment, and they are few because they are slow and flaky. And security checks — dependency scanning, secret detection, static analysis — placed after the fast checks and before the build, because a finding is most useful when the developer is still present to read it.

/* A discipline before it is a tool. */
const CI = {
  is: ['everyone commits to a shared mainline FREQUENTLY', 'every commit is verified by an automated build'],
  bothHalves: true,
  routinelyDropped: true,
  frequentCommitting: { why: 'the integration conflict window is a DAY rather than a quarter',
    gain: 'conflicts are small and MECHANICAL' },
  verifyingEveryCommit: { why: 'the state of mainline is always known to be GOOD',
    gain: 'what makes the daily deployment possible that chapter fifteen argued for' },
  withoutFrequentCommitting: 'a CI system without it is a SLOW BUILD SERVER - it verifies whatever arrives, whenever',
  worstOfBoth: 'builds that are slow because they are huge, and conflicts that are big because they have accumulated',
};
const GATE = {
  criticalProperty: 'the pipeline IS A GATE',
  notAGate: 'a check that reports a failure and does not block the merge is a REPORT',
  consequence: 'a report is ignored exactly as often as it is read',
};

/* What belongs in the pipeline, in order. */
const STAGES = [
  { s: 'FAST CHECKS first', what: ['formatting', 'linting'],
    cost: 'seconds', catches: 'the most common problems',
    why: 'putting them after the tests means every developer waits a minute to be told about a missing semicolon' },
  { s: 'UNIT TESTS next', why: 'the bulk of the value, in a few minutes' },
  { s: 'INTEGRATION TESTS next', needs: ['a database', 'a container'], note: 'slower' },
  { s: 'BUILD THE ARTIFACT', discipline: 'this produces the thing you DEPLOY, not something similar',
    why: 'we build in CI and build again for release is how a release ships a DIFFERENT BINARY from the one that was tested' },
  { s: 'END-TO-END and smoke tests last', where: 'in a deployed environment',
    few: 'because they are slow and flaky' },
  { s: 'SECURITY CHECKS', what: ['dependency scanning', 'secret detection', 'static analysis'],
    placed: 'after the fast checks and before the build',
    why: 'a finding is most useful when the developer is STILL PRESENT to read it' },
];

Making it fast, and the traps that make it not

Then the traps, and every one of them is common enough that a new pipeline has most of them by the end of the first week. The suite that takes forty minutes. The cause is nearly always a test hitting a real service or a real database where a fake would do, and the fix is the same as the test-speed chapter's: the pipeline should run in minutes because anything slower does not get run on every commit and the discipline collapses. Flaky tests, which are worse than slow tests because they get retried rather than fixed, and the correct response is to quarantine, fix, and treat a rising quarantine list as a defect. No caching of dependencies, where every run re-downloads and rebuilds everything. Sequential jobs where parallel is safe — the single largest easy win, and it is usually a configuration change rather than a code change. Secrets and environment differences, where a test passes locally and fails in CI because a variable was set locally and not in CI, which is a class of bug that the pipeline exists to find and is found much earlier if the environment is deliberately as close to local as possible. Running everything on every change — the obvious optimisation is to run the fast checks on every push and the full suite on the merge request, which trades a little safety for a great deal of speed.

Then what makes it actually work in a team, which is more about policy than configuration. Fix the pipeline before enforcing it. Enforcing a gate on a suite that is slow and flaky means the team learns to bypass the gate, and once they have learned to bypass it, making it faster does not bring them back. Never let a broken mainline stay broken — it is acceptable to be red while fixing and unacceptable to merge into red, because a permanently failing build teaches that the build's opinion is optional. Make the failure message good, because the pipeline's output is read by a person in a hurry and a message that says "tests failed" will be ignored while a message naming the test and the difference will be acted on. Time-box a red build. The rule "mainline is broken for at most an hour" is a forcing function that produces smaller changes and a culture that fixes things. And measure the pipeline as a product, because its users are your colleagues: how long it takes, how often it fails for reasons nobody can explain, and how often people bypass it are the three numbers that tell you whether the discipline is real.

/* The traps. */
const TRAPS = [
  { t: 'the suite that takes FORTY MINUTES',
    cause: 'nearly always a test hitting a real service or a real database where a fake would do',
    consequence: 'anything slower does not get run on every commit and the discipline COLLAPSES' },
  { t: 'FLAKY tests', worseThanSlow: true,
    because: 'they get RETRIED rather than FIXED',
    response: ['quarantine', 'fix', 'treat a rising quarantine list as a DEFECT'] },
  { t: 'NO CACHING of dependencies', symptom: 'every run re-downloads and rebuilds everything' },
  { t: 'SEQUENTIAL jobs where parallel is safe', impact: 'the single largest easy win',
    note: 'usually a configuration change rather than a code change' },
  { t: 'SECRETS and environment differences',
    symptom: 'a test passes locally and fails in CI because a variable was set locally and not in CI',
    note: 'a class of bug the pipeline exists to find, found much earlier if the environment is deliberately as close to local as possible' },
  { t: 'running EVERYTHING on every change',
    optimisation: 'fast checks on every push, full suite on the merge request',
    trade: 'a little safety for a great deal of speed' },
];

/* What makes it work in a team - policy, not configuration. */
const POLICY = [
  { p: 'fix the PIPELINE before enforcing it',
    why: 'enforcing a gate on a suite that is slow and flaky means the team learns to BYPASS the gate',
    consequence: 'once they have learned to bypass it, making it faster does not bring them back' },
  { p: 'never let a BROKEN MAINLINE stay broken',
    acceptable: 'being red while fixing', unacceptable: 'merging into red',
    why: 'a permanently failing build teaches that the builds opinion is OPTIONAL' },
  { p: 'make the FAILURE MESSAGE good',
    why: 'the pipelines output is read by a person in a hurry',
    evidence: 'a message saying tests failed will be ignored, while a message naming the test and the difference will be acted on' },
  { p: 'TIME-BOX a red build', rule: 'mainline is broken for at most an hour',
    effect: 'a forcing function that produces SMALLER CHANGES and a culture that fixes things' },
  { p: 'measure the PIPELINE AS A PRODUCT', users: 'your colleagues',
    numbers: ['how long it takes', 'how often it fails for reasons nobody can explain',
      'how often people bypass it'],
    gain: 'these three tell you whether the discipline is REAL' },
];

A GitHub Actions workflow that installs dependencies, runs pytest, and lints on every push or pull request, blocking merges when red.

16.7 Root-cause debugging: testing in reverse

Root-cause debugging treats a bug as a test you have not written yet. The disciplined loop is reproduce it reliably, isolate the smallest failing input, simplify the code path, fix the root cause rather than the symptom, and prove the fix with a regression test. This methodical routine cracks the works-on-my-machine mysteries that random edits and print statements never solve.

A test asserts the correct behavior; a bug is a test you haven’t written yet that fails. Debugging is the disciplined reverse: reproduce → isolate → simplify → fix → prove. Every "it only happens on Tuesdays" mystery yields to this loop.

# The 5-step loop
#  1 REPRODUCE: find the minimal input that triggers it. If you can't
#    reproduce, you're guessing -- instrument logs that capture the state.
#  2 ISOLATE: binary search your suspicions (the data? the caller? the
#    cache?). git bisect finds the committing change (Ch.6.7).
#  3 SIMPLIFY: strip everything irrelevant; a failing 5-observation vs
#    a failing 50,000-row case is the SAME bug wearing a costume.
#  4 FIX at the root, not the symptom: "we added a null check" without
#    knowing why null appeared = tomorrow's bug with a different name.
#  5 PROVE: write a regression test that fails on the old code and
#    passes on the fixed code. No test = the bug is still 'asleep'.

# Root-cause trap taxonomy:
#   blaming the last change (symptom, not cause)
#   fixing the error message instead of the state that produced it
#   "works on my machine" (environment is a variable -- dockerize)
#   the fix that hides the error with a better null-check

The five-step debugging loop and the classic root-cause traps: reproduce, isolate, simplify, fix at the root, and prove with a regression test.

Rubber-duck debugging works because explaining forces you to make assumptions explicit. Same function as writing a failing test: you either find the bug or write the test that will find it.

Why most investigations fail, and the four whys that keep stopping early

Root cause analysis fails in one specific way: people stop at the first cause that explains the symptom, and the first cause is usually proximate. The proximate cause is "the deployment replaced the connection pool" and it explains the symptom completely, which is what makes it satisfying and what makes it wrong — nothing is wrong with the pool, and deploying something else would have caused the same failure. The root cause is one or two levels further back, and "why" is the tool for getting there, with the discipline that you must answer each why with a because, not with another why, and you stop when the answer is something you can change. So: the pool was replaced because the new version needed more connections, which is true, and the new version needed more connections because a new feature tripled the query rate, which is the beginning of a real answer, and the feature tripled the query rate because nothing on the page was cached, which is actionable. Stopping at the first why would have produced a fix that reapplied the old pool, and the same incident would have returned a month later. The test of a genuine root cause is that fixing it prevents recurrence — and a cause that cannot be changed is not a root cause, it is a context.

Then why this is hard in practice, and the four biases that produce the wrong answer. Stopping early, at the first sufficient explanation. The proximity bias — the nearest cause is the most psychologically available and the one most likely to be accepted by the people involved, because it usually names somebody. Confirmation bias — once a team has a theory, evidence is read as supporting it, and the counterfactual "what if this were unrelated" is never seriously entertained. And blame, which is not an analysis error so much as a social one: a team that expects the analysis to name a person will produce an analysis that names a person, and a person is not a cause you can change, so the output is not actionable by construction. Then the tool that makes this rigorous rather than conversational: write the timeline first. Not the analysis — the facts, in order, with timestamps, and distinguishing what the system did from what a person assumed. The value is disproportionate because most disagreements in a root cause investigation are not about the analysis at all but about a disputed fact, and a timeline resolves those disputes before anyone argues about causes.

/* Why investigations fail. */
const FAILURE = 'people stop at the FIRST CAUSE THAT EXPLAINS THE SYMPTOM, and the first cause is usually proximate';
const WORKED = {
  proximate: 'the deployment replaced the connection pool',
    whyWrong: 'nothing is wrong with the pool, and deploying something else would have caused the same failure',
  chain: [
    { because: 'the new version needed more connections', true: true },
    { because: 'a new feature tripled the query rate', true: true, note: 'the beginning of a real answer' },
    { because: 'nothing on the page was cached', actionable: true },
  ],
  stoppingEarlyWouldHave: 'produced a fix that reapplied the old pool, and the same incident would have returned a month later',
};
const RULES = {
  discipline: 'you must answer each WHY with a BECAUSE, not with another why',
  stopWhen: 'the answer is something you can change',
  test: 'a genuine root cause is one where FIXING IT PREVENTS RECURRENCE',
  notARootCause: 'a cause that cannot be changed is a CONTEXT',
};

/* Four biases that produce the wrong answer. */
const BIASES = [
  { b: 'STOPPING EARLY', at: 'the first sufficient explanation' },
  { b: 'the PROXIMITY BIAS', detail: 'the nearest cause is the most psychologically available',
    and: 'the one most likely to be accepted by the people involved',
    why: 'because it usually NAMES SOMEBODY' },
  { b: 'CONFIRMATION BIAS', detail: 'once a team has a theory, evidence is read as supporting it',
    counterfactual: 'what if this were unrelated is never seriously entertained' },
  { b: 'BLAME', isNot: 'an analysis error so much as a social one',
    mechanism: 'a team that expects the analysis to name a person will produce an analysis that names a person',
    consequence: 'a person is not a cause you can change, so the output is NOT ACTIONABLE BY CONSTRUCTION' },
];
const TOOL = {
  do: 'write the TIMELINE FIRST',
  notTheAnalysis: 'the FACTS, in order, with timestamps',
  distinguish: 'what the system did from what a person ASSUMED',
  whyDisproportionate: 'most disagreements in a root cause investigation are not about the analysis at all but about a DISPUTED FACT',
  gain: 'a timeline resolves those disputes BEFORE anyone argues about causes',
};

Writing it up so it changes something

Then the write-up, and this is where most of the value is lost. Start with impact — who was affected, for how long, in what way, and what the business cost was. Not because it is the most interesting part but because a document that opens with the impact is read by people who can act on it, and a document that opens with the timeline is read by people who cannot. Give the timeline with timestamps, and distinguish observed from inferred — a reader needs to know which facts are measurements and which are reconstructions, because a reconstruction presented as a measurement is how a wrong conclusion survives review. State the contributing factors separately from the root cause. Several things usually contributed, and the discipline of separating them prevents the single-cause framing that makes action impossible; a contributing factor is a condition that made the incident more likely or worse, and treating several of them as causes produces several cheap fixes rather than one good one. Then actions, each with an owner and a date, because an action without an owner is a wish. Distinguish actions that prevent recurrence from actions that reduce impact — a fix that makes the incident less bad is genuinely valuable and is not a substitute for the fix that makes it impossible, and conflating the two is how an incident produces a dashboard instead of a repair. And write the blameless version first, which is not a soft exercise: it is the version that can be read aloud to a team, and a document that can only be shared privately is a document that will not change anything.

Then the habits that make this reliable rather than occasional. Do it for every incident, including the small ones, because the practice is what matters and a culture that analyses only the big ones teaches that the small ones do not matter. Keep the timeline template, because reconstructing an event from memory eight days later is not possible and the template forces the facts to be captured while they exist. Ask what made this possible, not only what made it happen — the questions have different answers, and the first is the one about design and the second is the one about circumstance. Look for the near-miss, because the version that nearly failed has the same cause and no impact, so it is free to analyse and the lesson is available. And track whether the actions were completed, because a root cause analysis whose actions were never done is not an analysis, it is a document, and the tracking is the only thing that tells the two apart.

/* The write-up, where most of the value is lost. */
const WRITE_UP = [
  { s: 'start with IMPACT', covers: ['who was affected', 'for how long', 'in what way', 'what the business cost was'],
    notBecause: 'it is the most interesting part',
    why: 'a document that opens with impact is read by people who can ACT on it; one that opens with the timeline is read by people who cannot' },
  { s: 'give the TIMELINE with timestamps', distinguish: 'OBSERVED from INFERRED',
    why: 'a reader needs to know which facts are measurements and which are reconstructions',
    consequence: 'a reconstruction presented as a measurement is how a wrong conclusion SURVIVES REVIEW' },
  { s: 'state CONTRIBUTING FACTORS separately from the root cause',
    detail: 'several things usually contributed',
    gain: 'the discipline of separating them prevents the single-cause framing that makes action impossible',
    definition: 'a contributing factor is a CONDITION that made the incident more likely or worse',
    result: 'treating several as causes produces SEVERAL CHEAP FIXES rather than one good one' },
  { s: 'then ACTIONS, each with an OWNER and a DATE', why: 'an action without an owner is a wish' },
  { s: 'distinguish actions that PREVENT RECURRENCE from actions that REDUCE IMPACT',
    bothValuable: true,
    reframe: 'a fix that makes the incident less bad is not a substitute for the fix that makes it IMPOSSIBLE',
    consequence: 'conflating the two is how an incident produces a DASHBOARD instead of a repair' },
  { s: 'write the BLAMELESS version FIRST',
    notASoftExercise: true,
    why: 'it is the version that can be READ ALOUD TO A TEAM',
    consequence: 'a document that can only be shared privately is a document that will not change anything' },
];

const HABITS = [
  { h: 'do it for EVERY incident, including the small ones',
    why: 'the practice is what matters, and a culture that analyses only the big ones teaches that the small ones DO NOT MATTER' },
  { h: 'keep the TIMELINE TEMPLATE', why: 'reconstructing an event from memory eight days later is not possible',
    gain: 'the template forces the facts to be captured WHILE THEY EXIST' },
