17 · Web Frontend — HTML, CSS, JavaScript

17.1 Semantic HTML — structure with meaning17.2 CSS — layout systems that actually work17.3 JavaScript — the browser’s language17.4 The problem frameworks solve17.5 Tooling: package managers & build steps17.6 Responsive design17.7 Client-side storage and single-page apps

Web Frontend covers the three languages the browser runs natively: semantic HTML for structure, CSS for layout and style, and JavaScript for behavior. The chapter also covers frameworks and the virtual DOM, package managers and build tooling such as npm and Vite, responsive design, and client-side storage. Together these skills let you build interfaces that are accessible, fast, and maintainable on every screen size.

The browser is the most deployed runtime in history. Frontend engineering is not "just styling": it’s semantic structure, layout systems, and event-driven UI state — plus a lots of product thinking.

17.1 Semantic HTML — structure with meaning

Semantic HTML uses elements for their meaning rather than their appearance, so links use an anchor tag, buttons use a button tag, navigation lives in a nav tag, and headings form an outline. That hands you accessibility, SEO, and self-documenting structure for free, and assistive technology such as screen readers depends on it. Use the semantic tag by default and reach for a div only when no meaningful element exists.

Use elements for what they mean, not what they look like. Semantics give you accessibility (screen readers), SEO, and sane structure for free.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <title>My Blog</title>
</head>
<body>
  <header><h1>My Blog</h1><nav>...</nav></header>
  <main>
    <article>
      <h2>A Post</h2>
      <time datetime="2026-09-13">Sep 13 2026</time>
      <p>The body of the post.</p>
    </article>
  </main>
  <aside>sidebar stuff</aside>
  <footer>&copy; 2026 Me</footer>
</body>
</html>

A minimal semantic HTML page using header, nav, main, article, aside, and footer — structure that carries meaning for screen readers and search engines.

Semantics, and what they actually buy you

An element is semantic when it describes what its content is rather than how it looks. <nav> says this is navigation, <button> says this performs an action, <h2> says this is a heading at a level. And the value is not aesthetic, it is four concrete things. Accessibility, which is the largest. A screen reader navigates by landmark and by heading level: a user can jump between <h1> and <h2> as links, and a button is announced as a button and appears in the button list of every assistive technology. A <div> with a click handler is announced as nothing. Default behaviour you get free: a <button> is focusable, activates on Enter and Space, is in the tab order, and shows a focus ring — all of which you must reimplement on a <div> and will get at least partly wrong. Behaviour that browsers optimise for: a real link can be opened in a new tab, copied, bookmarked and prefetched; a <div> cannot. And correctness independent of styling — a page with no stylesheet is still a document with a table in it, and one built from <div>s is a wall of text. The practical rule: reach for the element whose name matches what the thing is, before reaching for the element whose name matches what it looks like. A <div class="button"> is a lie in the document; it is a button that has forgotten what it is.

Then the elements that carry more weight than their size suggests, and each has a specific failure it prevents. <label for> binds a label to an input, and the consequences are large: clicking the label focuses the input, the input announces the label, and — because the association is by id — a screen reader links them. A placeholder is not a label: it disappears when the user types, it is not reliably announced, and it fails any contrast requirement reliably. Heading levels must not skip. A document's structure is its outline, and a level three heading under a level one heading tells a screen-reader user the document is malformed. Headings are chosen for structure, not for size, and the size is set with CSS — which is why a page that looks fine and is read badly is almost always a page whose heading levels were chosen to match its fonts. <form> is required, not a wrapper: it makes Enter submit, it gives assistive technology a grouping, and it enables browser autofill, which is a conversion feature as much as an accessibility one. <table> for tabular data only, because a screen reader announces a real table's rows and cells and their relationships, and announces a layout table as an unordered jumble — which is why a table used for layout is worse than a <div> used for the same purpose.

/* Semantic means it describes what the content IS, not how it looks. */
const SEMANTIC = {
  is: 'describes what its content is rather than how it looks',
  examples: ['nav says this is navigation', 'button says this performs an action',
    'h2 says this is a heading at a level'],
  valueIsNot: 'aesthetic',
  theFourThings: [
    { v: 'ACCESSIBILITY', isTheLargest: true,
      detail: ['a screen reader navigates by landmark and by heading level',
        'a user can jump between h1 and h2 as LINKS',
        'a button is announced as a button and appears in the button list of every assistive technology',
        'a div with a click handler is announced as NOTHING'] },
    { v: 'DEFAULT BEHAVIOUR YOU GET FREE', what: 'a button is focusable, activates on Enter and Space, is in the tab order, shows a focus ring',
      contrast: 'all of which you must reimplement on a div and will get at least partly wrong' },
    { v: 'BEHAVIOUR BROWSERS OPTIMISE FOR', what: 'a real link can be opened in a new tab, copied, bookmarked and prefetched',
      contrast: 'a div cannot' },
    { v: 'CORRECTNESS INDEPENDENT OF STYLING',
      detail: 'a page with no stylesheet is still a document with a table in it',
      contrast: 'one built from divs is a wall of text' },
  ],
  rule: 'reach for the element whose NAME MATCHES WHAT THE THING IS, before the one whose name matches what it looks like',
  theLie: 'a div with class button is a lie in the document - it is a button that has forgotten what it is',
};

Documents, images, and the rules that are not obvious

Then the document structure and the rules that are not obvious, which is where most real-world markup is wrong. One <h1> per page, and it is the page's subject; everything else is a level below. Not for accessibility compliance — for the outline, because a document with two <h1>s has no single subject and every user who navigates by heading has to guess which one they are in. Skip-level rule: do not go from <h2> to <h4>, because the skipped level reads as missing content. And the correction that matters most: a heading is not a label. A heading introduces a section; a label names a field. Using a heading for a field name produces a document outline full of form fields. Then the image rules, and the third one is the one people argue about. alt describes the image's purpose, not its appearance. "A red bicycle" describes appearance; "Bicycle leaning against a wall" describes what a reader needs. Decorative images take alt="", which is not an omission — an empty alt tells assistive technology to skip it, and that is the only correct markup for an image that carries no information. A meaningful image inside a link needs alt text on the image, not on the link, and the most common failure is a link with no text at all containing only an icon, which is completely inaccessible. An image inside a link that already has text takes alt="", so the link's text is read once rather than twice. And an image that conveys data needs its number in text nearby, because an alt attribute is not selectable and not findable.

Then the rest of the document-level details that are cheap to do right. Language on the <html> element, because it drives screen-reader pronunciation and browser translation and its absence makes the page unintelligible to half its users. Character encoding declared, because the default the browser guesses is not reliable. Title on every page, which is the document's name in the tab, in bookmarks, in history and in search results — and a site whose title is the domain name on every page has told the user nothing. type and width/height on <script> and <img> — the script one because the default behaviour changed and a defer is now usually what you want; the image one because a browser cannot reserve space for an image whose dimensions it does not know, so the page reflows as images load, which is the largest single contributor to perceived slowness. And the document validates, which is worth doing not because the validator is right but because a validator catches the unclosed tag and the mis-nested element that you will not see.

/* Document structure rules that are not obvious. */
const STRUCTURE = [
  { r: 'ONE h1 per page', isThe: 'pages subject', everythingElse: 'a level below',
    notFor: 'accessibility compliance',
    why: 'a document with two h1s has no single subject, and every user who navigates by heading has to guess which one they are in' },
  { r: 'the SKIP-LEVEL rule', doNot: 'go from h2 to h4', why: 'the skipped level reads as MISSING CONTENT' },
  { r: 'a HEADING IS NOT A LABEL',
    distinction: ['a heading introduces a SECTION', 'a label names a FIELD'],
    consequence: 'using a heading for a field name produces a document outline full of form fields' },
];
const IMAGES = [
  { r: 'alt describes the images PURPOSE, not its appearance',
    appearance: 'a red bicycle', purpose: 'bicycle leaning against a wall',
    why: 'describes what a READER NEEDS' },
  { r: 'decorative images take alt=""', notAnOmission: true,
    whatItDoes: 'tells assistive technology to SKIP it',
    claim: 'the only correct markup for an image that carries no information' },
  { r: 'a meaningful image inside a LINK needs alt text on the IMAGE, not on the link',
    mostCommonFailure: 'a link with no text at all containing only an icon, which is COMPLETELY INACCESSIBLE' },
  { r: 'an image inside a link that already has text takes alt=""', why: 'so the links text is read ONCE rather than twice' },
  { r: 'an image that CONVEYS DATA needs its number in text nearby',
    why: 'an alt attribute is NOT SELECTABLE and NOT FINDABLE' },
];

/* The rest of the document-level details. */
const DOCUMENT = [
  { r: 'LANGUAGE on the html element',
    drives: ['screen-reader pronunciation', 'browser translation'],
    consequence: 'its absence makes the page unintelligible to half its users' },
  { r: 'CHARACTER ENCODING declared', why: 'the default the browser guesses is NOT reliable' },
  { r: 'TITLE on every page', is: 'the documents name in the tab, in bookmarks, in history and in search results',
    symptom: 'a site whose title is the domain name on every page has told the user nothing' },
  { r: 'type and width/height on script and img',
    script: 'because the default behaviour CHANGED and a defer is now usually what you want',
    image: 'because a browser cannot reserve space for an image whose dimensions it does not know, so the page reflows as images load',
    significance: 'the largest single contributor to PERCEIVED SLOWNESS' },
  { r: 'the document VALIDATES', why: 'not because the validator is right',
    gain: 'a validator catches the unclosed tag and the mis-nested element that YOU WILL NOT SEE' },
];

A11y = accessibility. Never use a <div> where a <button> belongs; always have <label for> on inputs; provide alt text on images. Accessibility features are invisible to sighted devs but the whole web to millions of users — and it’s usually also better semantics.

17.2 CSS — layout systems that actually work

CSS layout runs on two modern systems: Flexbox aligns items along a single axis and handles spacing and wrapping, while Grid lays out content in explicit rows and columns for two-dimensional regions. Together they replace the older float and table hacks, and combine with units, the box model, and media queries. Use flexbox for one-directional lists and toolbars, and grid for full-page layout.

Two layout engines do 95% of modern layout: Flexbox (one dimension, distribution) and Grid (two dimensions, regions).

<style>
  /* Flexbox: the navbar trick */
  .nav { display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; }

  /* Grid: a responsive card wall */
  .cards {
    display: grid;
    gap: 16px;
    grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr));
  }
  .card { border: 1px solid #ddd; border-radius: 8px; padding: 16px; }

  /* Theme switch with one line */
  :root { --bg: white; --text: #111; }
  @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
    :root { --bg: #0d1117; --text: #e6edf3; }
  }
  body { background: var(--bg); color: var(--text); }
</style>

Flexbox builds the navbar, CSS Grid with auto-fit builds a responsive card wall, and custom properties flip the whole theme with one line.

The cascade, and why specificity is a trap rather than a system

CSS decides which declaration wins through three filters, in order. Importance: a declaration marked !important beats everything that is not. Origin: author styles beat user-agent styles, and user styles — a user's own accessibility preferences — beat author styles, which is why a site that sets everything in !important can defeat a user's high-contrast setting. Specificity: among declarations of equal importance and origin, the more specific selector wins. And that is the whole algorithm. Specificity is a tuple of four numbers — inline styles, then class and attribute and pseudo-class selectors, then element and pseudo-element selectors, then the element itself — compared left to right. #header .nav a beats .nav a beats a, because each has one more component in an earlier position.

Then the source order, which is the fourth tie-breaker: among declarations of identical specificity, the later one wins. And that is where the whole thing becomes unusable as a system, because a specificity tie is resolved by accident — by which rule somebody happened to write further down the file. So the practical consequence, which is the thing worth internalising: specificity is not a priority system; it is a consequence of selector shape, and the only reliable way to win a cascade fight is to have fewer selectors, not more specific ones. A single class selector beats almost anything you can construct out of element selectors, and a single class selector is also far more readable. Which gives the practical ladder, in order: one class selector, then two, then a descendant selector, and only as a last resort an id. And then the rules that keep it maintainable. Never use !important except to override someone else's !important — it exists for user styles and for utility frameworks, and every use is a local fix for a global problem. Never use an id in a selector for styling: ids are unique, so the rule cannot be reused, and its specificity is so high that nothing can override it without !important. Keep the cascade shallow: a rule should not need to know what other rules exist. And when two rules fight, delete one rather than adding specificity — because the fight is a symptom of a rule that is either too broad or in the wrong place.

/* Three filters, in order. */
const FILTERS = [
  { f: 'IMPORTANCE', does: 'a declaration marked important beats everything that is not' },
  { f: 'ORIGIN', order: ['author styles beat user-agent styles', 'USER styles - a users own accessibility preferences - beat author styles'],
    consequence: 'a site that sets everything in important can DEFEAT A USERS HIGH-CONTRAST SETTING' },
  { f: 'SPECIFICITY', applies: 'among declarations of equal importance and origin, the more specific selector wins' },
];
const SPECIFICITY = {
  is: 'a tuple of FOUR numbers',
  order: ['inline styles', 'class, attribute and pseudo-class selectors', 'element and pseudo-element selectors', 'the element itself'],
  compared: 'left to right',
  worked: '#header .nav a beats .nav a beats a, because each has one more component in an EARLIER POSITION',
};
const SOURCE_ORDER = {
  is: 'the fourth tie-breaker',
  rule: 'among declarations of identical specificity, the LATER one wins',
  whyThatIsAProblem: 'a specificity tie is resolved by ACCIDENT - by which rule somebody happened to write further down the file',
  thePoint: 'specificity is NOT A PRIORITY SYSTEM; it is a CONSEQUENCE OF SELECTOR SHAPE',
  howToWinReliably: 'have FEWER SELECTORS, not more specific ones',
  evidence: 'a single class selector beats almost anything constructed out of element selectors, and is also far more readable',
};
const LADDER = ['one class selector', 'two', 'a descendant selector', 'only as a last resort, an id'];
const RULES = [
  { r: 'never use important except to OVERRIDE SOMEONE ELSES important',
    existsFor: ['user styles', 'utility frameworks'],
    cost: 'every use is a LOCAL FIX for a GLOBAL PROBLEM' },
  { r: 'never use an ID in a selector for styling',
    problems: ['ids are unique, so the rule cannot be reused',
      'its specificity is so high that NOTHING CAN OVERRIDE IT without important'] },
  { r: 'keep the cascade SHALLOW', rule: 'a rule should not need to know what other rules exist' },
  { r: 'when two rules fight, DELETE ONE rather than adding specificity',
    why: 'the fight is a symptom of a rule that is either too broad or in the wrong place' },
];

Layout, the modern model, and the properties worth reaching for

Then the layout model, because this is where most of the confusion is and it is largely historical. Every element is a box, and it is one of four kinds: block, which takes full width and stacks vertically; inline, which flows within text; inline-block, which flows inline but is a block internally; and flex item or grid item once its parent is a container. Then the box model in four numbers: content, padding, border, margin — and the property that trips everybody is box-sizing. With the default content-box, a declared width sets the content width and the padding and border are added, so a width: 100% element with padding overflows its container. With border-box, the declared width includes padding and border, which is what everyone intends. Set box-sizing: border-box globally, in a reset, because the alternative is a design that is correct only when nothing has padding. Then flow versus positioned versus flex versus grid, and choosing between the last two is worth stating: flex is for one dimension — a row or a column of items that share a space, a toolbar, a sidebar-and-content pair, a list of cards — and it excels at distributing space and alignment. Grid is for two dimensions — an actual page layout, a form, anything where you are placing things in rows and columns and want to control both axes at once. And grid-template-areas is the clearest description of a page layout anyone has invented, because the CSS is a diagram of the layout and can be read by a person who does not write CSS.

/* Every element is a box, of four kinds. */
const BOXES = [
  { k: 'block', trait: 'takes full width and stacks vertically' },
  { k: 'inline', trait: 'flows within text' },
  { k: 'inline-block', trait: 'flows inline but is a block internally' },
  { k: 'flex item or grid item', when: 'once its parent is a container' },
];
const BOX_MODEL = {
  four: ['content', 'padding', 'border', 'margin'],
  thePropertyThatTripsEverybody: 'box-sizing',
  contentBox: { isTheDefault: true,
    means: 'a declared width sets the CONTENT width and padding and border are ADDED',
    consequence: 'a width of 100 per cent element with padding OVERFLOWS its container' },
  borderBox: means: 'the declared width INCLUDES padding and border, which is what everyone intends' },
  recommendation: 'SET box-sizing border-box GLOBALLY, in a reset',
  why: 'the alternative is a design that is correct only when nothing has padding',
};

/* Choosing between flex and grid. */
const FLEX_VS_GRID = {
  flex: { for: 'ONE dimension',
    detail: 'a row or a column of items that share a space',
    instances: ['a toolbar', 'a sidebar-and-content pair', 'a list of cards'],
    excelsAt: 'distributing space and alignment' },
  grid: { for: 'TWO dimensions',
    detail: 'an actual page layout, a form, anything where you place things in rows AND columns',
    control: 'both axes at once' },
  areas: 'grid-template-areas is the CLEAREST DESCRIPTION OF A PAGE LAYOUT anyone has invented',
    why: 'the CSS is a DIAGRAM of the layout and can be read by a person who does not write CSS',
};

Positioning, and the properties that replaced it

Then positioning, which is the remaining area of confusion and where the modern replacements matter. Static is the default and means "in the flow, positioned by nothing". Relative offsets the element from where it would have been, without removing it from the flow — which is exactly why it does not break siblings, and it is what you use for a badge positioned over an image. Absolute removes the element from the flow and positions it relative to its nearest positioned ancestor, which is the property to be careful with: the containing block is whatever ancestor has position set, and if you have not set one the element is positioned relative to the page, which is the classic bug where an absolutely-positioned element jumps to the corner of the document. Fixed is relative to the viewport and does not scroll — which is what a sticky header needs, and also what makes a fixed element a content problem on mobile. Sticky is the good version: it stays in flow and only sticks within a scrolling ancestor. And the direction of travel is worth stating as a rule: almost everything you would position absolutely should instead be a grid or flex container. The reason is that position removes the element from the flow and therefore from being able to size itself or be pushed by its siblings; the properties that replaced this pattern are gap instead of margin hacks, place-items and place-content shorthands, aspect-ratio instead of the padding-top percentage hack, clamp for fluid type, min(), max() and minmax() for fluid sizing, custom properties for values used in several places, and container queries so a component responds to the size of its container rather than the viewport — which is the change that finally makes components reusable.

/* Positioning, and the containing-block trap. */
const POSITIONING = [
  { p: 'STATIC', isTheDefault: true, means: 'in the flow, positioned by nothing' },
  { p: 'RELATIVE', offsets: 'the element from where it would have been, WITHOUT removing it from the flow',
    whyUseful: 'exactly why it does not break siblings',
    use: 'a badge positioned over an image' },
  { p: 'ABSOLUTE', removes: 'the element from the flow', positionsRelativeTo: 'its NEAREST POSITIONED ANCESTOR',
    trap: 'if you have not set one, the element is positioned relative to THE PAGE',
    classicBug: 'an absolutely-positioned element jumps to the corner of the document' },
  { p: 'FIXED', relativeTo: 'the viewport', scrolls: false,
    use: 'a sticky header needs it', alsoAProblemOn: 'mobile - a fixed element is a content problem' },
  { p: 'STICKY', isTheGoodVersion: true,
    detail: 'stays in flow and only sticks WITHIN a scrolling ancestor' },
];

/* The direction of travel. */
const DIRECTION = {
  rule: 'almost everything you would POSITION ABSOLUTELY should instead be a GRID OR FLEX CONTAINER',
  why: 'position removes the element from the flow and therefore from being able to SIZE ITSELF or be pushed by its siblings',
  replacements: [
    { p: 'gap', insteadOf: 'margin hacks' },
    { p: 'place-items and place-content shorthands' },
    { p: 'aspect-ratio', insteadOf: 'the padding-top percentage hack' },
    { p: 'clamp', for: 'fluid type' },
    { p: 'min(), max() and minmax()', for: 'fluid sizing' },
    { p: 'custom properties', for: 'values used in several places' },
    { p: 'CONTAINER QUERIES', effect: 'a component responds to the size of its CONTAINER rather than the viewport',
      significance: 'the change that finally makes components REUSABLE' },
  ],
};

Never center via floats or table hacks. display:flex; align-items:center; justify-content:center; or grid is the 2026 answers. Old tutorials will try to sell you dead techniques.

17.3 JavaScript — the browser’s language

JavaScript is the browser’s dynamic, event-driven language: code reacts to clicks, form submissions, and network responses rather than running top to bottom. Master the modern core, const and let, arrow functions, array methods such as map and filter, destructuring, and async and await for promises, always aware that this event-driven nature shapes how your code orders itself. The developer tools are the standard way to inspect runtime behavior.

JS is dynamic and event-driven: your code reacts to clicks, keystrokes, network arrivals.

<button id="go">Say hi</button>
<p id="out"></p>

<script>
  // select an element, listen for events, manipulate the DOM
  const btn = document.getElementById('go');
  const out = document.getElementById('out');

  btn.addEventListener('click', () => {
    out.textContent = 'Hello from JavaScript!';
    btn.disabled = true;                 // state lives in the DOM or in JS
  });
</script>

Event-driven JavaScript: find an element, listen for a click, update the DOM, and disable the button once used.

Key modern-JS ideas you must internalise: const/let (never var), arrow functions, template literals (`Hi ${name}`), arrays with .map/.filter/.reduce, destructuring, and the DOM as a tree you change imperatively (until Ch. 17.5 gives you a framework).

const numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
const doubled  = numbers.map(n => n * 2);        // [2,4,6,8,10]
const evens    = numbers.filter(n => n % 2 === 0); // [2,4]
const total    = numbers.reduce((acc, n) => acc + n, 0); // 15

async function loadUsers() {
  const res  = await fetch('/api/users');         // async network call
  const data = await res.json();
  console.log(data.length);
}

Functional array methods (map, filter, reduce) plus an async fetch with await — bread-and-butter modern JavaScript.

The type system you actually have, and the two conversions that surprise

JavaScript has seven types plus objects, and the ones that matter for understanding the language are fewer. undefined means a variable has no value — declared and never assigned, or assigned nothing. null means deliberately no value, the "intentionally empty" marker. The distinction matters because they behave differently: typeof undefined is "undefined" while typeof null is "object", which is a bug from 1995 preserved for compatibility and will be with us forever. object covers arrays, functions, dates and plain objects, which is why typeof [] is "object" and why Array.isArray exists. symbol is a unique identifier, and its purpose is avoiding collisions — a Symbol key on an object is invisible to Object.keys and to JSON, which is how libraries attach internal state without colliding with yours. And then the truthiness rules, which produce most of the bugs: the falsey values are exactly six — false, 0, "", null, undefined and NaN — and everything else is truthy, including [], {} and "0". An empty array is truthy, which is almost never what you meant.

Then the two conversions that surprise people, and understanding them removes a whole class of bug. Equality: == versus ===. The strict operator compares type and value; the loose operator converts first, which produces the rules nobody can recall — 0 == "", null == undefined, "" == " " (whitespace is trimmed during the numeric conversion), and "0" == false. Those are not bugs in the operator, they are consequences of converting to a number, and the whole reason they are confusing is that the coercion happens before the comparison. Use === always, with one exception people accept: == null is true for exactly null and undefined and nothing else, which is occasionally convenient. And the second conversion: + is overloaded — numeric addition when both sides look numeric, string concatenation otherwise — so 1 + 2 is 3 and 1 + "2" is "12", and the expression that catches everybody is "5" - 2 being 3 because there is no sensible string meaning for - so both sides convert to numbers. The consequence is the rule: do not mix types in arithmetic, and convert explicitly at the boundary where data enters from outside — a form field, a query parameter, a JSON body — because every one of those is a string until you say otherwise, and the --behaves-differently accident is exactly what happens.

/* The types that matter. */
const TYPES = [
  { t: 'undefined', means: 'a variable has no value - declared and never assigned, or assigned nothing' },
  { t: 'null', means: 'DELIBERATELY no value - the intentionally-empty marker' },
];
const UNDEF_VS_NULL = {
  differBecause: 'they BEHAVE differently',
  detail: 'typeof undefined is undefined while typeof null is object',
  why: 'a bug from 1995 preserved for compatibility, and will be with us forever',
};
const MORE_TYPES = [
  { t: 'object', covers: ['arrays', 'functions', 'dates', 'plain objects'],
    consequence: 'why Array.isArray exists' },
  { t: 'symbol', is: 'a unique identifier', purpose: 'avoiding collisions',
    how: 'a Symbol key is invisible to Object.keys and to JSON',
    usedBy: 'how libraries attach internal state without colliding with yours' },
];
const TRUTHY = {
  falseyExactly: ['false', '0', 'an empty string', 'null', 'undefined', 'NaN'],
  everythingElseIsTruthy: ['including an empty array', 'an empty object', 'the string zero'],
  surprise: 'AN EMPTY ARRAY IS TRUTHY, which is almost never what you meant',
};

/* Equality. */
const EQUALITY = {
  strict: 'compares type AND value',
  loose: 'converts first',
  rulesNobodyCanRecall: ['0 equals an empty string', 'null equals undefined',
    'an empty string equals a string of spaces - whitespace is trimmed during the numeric conversion',
    'the string zero equals false'],
  notBugs: 'consequences of converting to a number',
  whyConfusing: 'the coercion happens BEFORE the comparison',
  rule: 'use the strict operator ALWAYS',
  acceptedException: '== null is true for exactly null and undefined and nothing else, which is occasionally convenient',
};

/* The overloaded plus. */
const PLUS = {
  behaviour: 'numeric addition when both sides look numeric, string concatenation otherwise',
  worked: ['1 + 2 is 3', '1 + "2" is the string "12"'],
  catchesEverybody: '"5" - 2 is 3, because there is no sensible string meaning for the minus sign, so both sides convert to numbers',
  theRule: 'do NOT MIX TYPES IN ARITHMETIC, and convert EXPLICITLY AT THE BOUNDARY',
  boundary: ['a form field', 'a query parameter', 'a JSON body'],
  why: 'every one of those is a string until you say otherwise, and the minus-behaves-differently accident is exactly what happens',

Scope, closures, and async/await

Then scope and closures, which is where the language's real power is and where the surprises live. Three scopes: global, function, and block. var is function-scoped, so a variable declared inside an if or a loop is visible after it, and the classic consequence is a loop that shares one variable across iterations, which is why for (let i = ...) exists — let creates a new binding per iteration, so closures created inside a loop capture the value they saw rather than the final value. let versus const: const prevents reassignment but not mutation, so a const array can be pushed to; the rule that pays off is default to const and use let only for a variable that genuinely changes. Hoisting means declarations are processed before execution — var and function declarations become available at the top of their scope, while let and const are in the temporal dead zone and using one before its declaration throws, which is a better failure than the silent undefined that var gives. A closure is a function that remembers the variables from where it was defined, and that one sentence explains why callbacks work, why a counter in a loop prints the wrong value, why memory is retained, and why a function returned from another function keeps its private state. The practical consequence to know: a closure keeps its captured variables alive as long as the closure exists, which is why a closure over a large array in a long-lived handler is a memory leak.

Then asynchronous code, and the model. JavaScript runs on one thread. Anything blocking blocks everything, including the interface — which is why a tight synchronous loop freezes the page. A promise represents a future value. It is pending, then fulfilled or rejected, and a promise cannot change state after settling, which is what makes it safe to attach handlers at any time. Three states and the chain: then for success, catch for failure, finally for cleanup that runs either way, and the crucial consequence: you catch errors by chaining, not by wrapping in try/catch, because a try block around a promise does nothing — the promise is not settled synchronously, so the catch never fires. async/await is syntax over promises: await pauses that function and lets the event loop run, which does not block the page, and the one rule that matters is that await only works inside an async function. Then the bugs. Forgetting to await, which yields [object Promise] — the number-one beginner bug — and the fix is to await it or handle it. Not handling rejection, which surfaces as an unhandled rejection warning and, in some environments, a crash. A promise returned from a callback nobody awaits, so the error disappears. A loop with sequential awaits where the operations were independent, which is a thousand times slower than starting them all and awaiting the group. And a race where two operations race and the loser writes last — the reason an operation must be cancelled or ignored when its request has been superseded.

/* Scope. */
const SCOPES = ['global', 'function', 'block'];
const SCOPE_NOTES = [
  { s: 'var', is: 'function-scoped', consequence: 'a variable declared inside an if or a loop is visible AFTER it',
    classicConsequence: 'a loop that SHARES ONE VARIABLE across iterations',
    whyLetExists: 'for with let creates a NEW BINDING PER ITERATION, so closures created inside a loop capture the value they saw rather than the final value' },
  { s: 'let vs const', detail: 'const prevents REASSIGNMENT but not MUTATION, so a const array can be pushed to',
    rule: 'default to const and use let only for a variable that genuinely changes' },
  { s: 'HOISTING', means: 'declarations are processed before execution',
    whatHoists: ['var', 'function declarations'],
    doesNotHoist: ['let', 'const'],
    temporalDeadZone: 'using a let or const before its declaration THROWS',
    betterThan: 'a better failure than the silent undefined that var gives' },
];
const CLOSURE = {
  is: 'a function that REMEMBERS THE VARIABLES FROM WHERE IT WAS DEFINED',
  explains: ['why callbacks work', 'why a counter in a loop prints the wrong value',
    'why memory is retained', 'why a function returned from another function keeps its private state'],
  consequence: 'a closure keeps its captured variables ALIVE as long as the closure exists',
  leak: 'a closure over a large array in a long-lived handler is a memory leak',
};

  why: 'which is why a tight synchronous loop FREEZES THE PAGE',

  states: ['pending', 'fulfilled', 'rejected'],
  keyProperty: 'a promise CANNOT change state after settling',

  { b: 'a PROMISE RETURNED FROM A CALLBACK NOBODY AWAITS', consequence: 'the error disappears' },

Async basics: fetch() returns a Promise; await pauses until it resolves; the UI never blocks. If you see [object Promise] printed somewhere, it means you logged the promise instead of awaiting it — the #1 JS beginner bug.

17.4 The problem frameworks solve

Hand-editing the DOM directly makes state and UI drift apart as applications grow, because every update must be manually mirrored into the page. Frameworks solve this by declaring the UI as a function of state and letting a diffing engine such as React’s virtual DOM apply only the changes the state requires. Build components declaratively, change state through a controlled update path, and let the framework reconcile the rest.

Hand-editing the DOM ("out.textContent = ...", then "add this class") gets unmaintainable as UI grows — the DOM and state drift out of sync. The solution: declare the UI as a function of state, and let a framework find the DOM changes. This mental model is React’s big idea.

// React (declarative): "describe the UI for this state"
function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = React.useState(0);

  return (
    <div>
      <p>You clicked {count} times</p>
      <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>+1</button>
    </div>
  );
}
// State changes -> React re-renders (recomputes) the component -> diffs the DOM
// You never touch the DOM yourself. That's the whole magic.

Why a virtual DOM exists, and what the diff is for

A virtual DOM is a JavaScript representation of a DOM tree, and the reason it exists is a specific performance bet rather than a stylistic preference. Reading from the real DOM is slow; writing to it is slower. The bottleneck is not the JavaScript — it is the interface between JavaScript and the browser's rendering engine, and every read forces the engine to reconcile what the page actually looks like with what the document object model claims. So the strategy is: render to JavaScript objects, compute the difference, and apply only the difference to the real DOM. The bet is that comparing two JavaScript trees is far cheaper than touching the DOM, and that bet holds. Then the diff algorithm, and its shape is the interesting part. It is not a general tree diff, because a general diff is slow and the tree is not general — it comes from a component whose input is a small set of values. So it works on sibling lists keyed by identity, and it makes three decisions: is this the same element (same type and same key), what changed in its attributes, and what is different about its children. That produces the algorithm: walk both trees in step, skip matched subtrees entirely, apply attribute changes to the matched elements, and for children either patch by position when unkeyed or patch by key when keyed.

Then why keys matter so much, because it is the single most consequential detail in the whole topic. A key is a stable identity, not a position. Without keys the diff compares children by position, so if the first item is removed from a list, the diff believes every subsequent item changed and rewrites them all — which costs performance and, worse, breaks state: any state attached to a component instance moves to the wrong item, so an input's value or a component's internal state jumps from one row to another. With keys, the diff matches by identity, so removing the first item only removes one node and everything else keeps its own state. The rule: always use a stable, unique identifier from the data — the database id — and never an array index when the list can be reordered, filtered or have items inserted. An index is stable only while nothing before it moves, which in a user-facing list is almost never.

/* A performance bet, not a preference. */
const WHY = {
  slow: 'reading FROM the real DOM is slow; WRITING to it is slower',
  bottleneck: 'not the JavaScript - the INTERFACE between JavaScript and the browsers rendering engine',
  mechanism: 'every READ forces the engine to reconcile what the page actually looks like with what the DOM claims',
  strategy: ['render to JavaScript objects', 'compute the difference', 'apply ONLY the difference to the real DOM'],
  theBet: 'comparing two JavaScript trees is far cheaper than touching the DOM',
  holds: true,
};

/* The diff algorithm's shape. */
const DIFF_SHAPE = {
  isNot: 'a general tree diff',
  whyNot: 'a general diff is slow, and the tree is not general - it comes from a component whose input is a small set of values',
  worksOn: 'SIBLING LISTS KEYED BY IDENTITY',
  makes: 'a small set of values',
  threeDecisions: ['is this the same element - same type and same key',
    'what changed in its attributes', 'what is different about its children'],
  algorithm: ['walk both trees in step', 'skip matched subtrees entirely',
    'apply attribute changes to the matched elements',
    'for children, patch BY POSITION when unkeyed or BY KEY when keyed'],
};
const KEYS = {
  is: 'a STABLE IDENTITY, not a position',
  withoutKeys: 'the diff compares children BY POSITION, so removing the first item makes it believe every subsequent item changed',
  costs: ['performance - it rewrites them all', 'STATE - state attached to a component instance moves to the wrong item, so an inputs value or internal state jumps from one row to another'],
  withKeys: 'the diff matches by identity, so removing the first item only removes one node and everything else keeps its own state',
  rule: 'always use a STABLE, UNIQUE IDENTIFIER from the data - the database id',
  never: 'an array index when the list can be reordered, filtered or have items inserted',
  why: 'an index is stable only while nothing before it moves, which in a user-facing list is almost never',
};

State, reconciliation, and where frameworks differ

Then state, and the model underneath every framework. State is data that changes over time and causes the interface to change. The central rule is one-way data flow: changing state triggers a re-render, the render produces a new tree, the diff is computed, and only the differences are applied to the DOM. Nothing else updates the interface. That single direction is why frameworks are predictable: there is one place where change enters the system and one path it takes to the screen. Then the derivation rule, which is the one people get wrong: derived data is computed during render, not stored in state. A filtered list, a total, a formatted date should be computed from the source every time it renders, because storing it creates a second source of truth that can disagree with the first — and the bug where a total is wrong after adding an item is almost always a stored derived value that was not updated. The related rule: state must be minimal. Everything else is derived, and every piece of state you add is a thing that can be stale.

Then where the frameworks actually differ, and knowing this tells you which problem you have. How updates are scoped. A coarse library re-renders the whole tree on any state change and relies on the diff to keep the cost low, which is simple and correct and pays a cost proportional to tree size. A fine-grained library tracks which parts of the interface depend on which piece of state and updates only those, which is more machinery and much cheaper on a large interface. When rendering happens. A virtual-DOM framework re-renders when state changes; a compile-time framework transforms your components once and updates only what the dependency analysis says changes. Whether rendering can be interrupted. A render that can be interrupted and restarted costs less when the user is typing, because the framework can discard work that is already stale; a render that cannot must be finished even if its result is no longer needed. And what reactivity is primitive. Some systems model the whole interface as a function of state; others let you write a calculation that re-runs when its inputs change, which is smaller and faster and requires understanding which inputs a calculation depends on.

Then the practical rules that apply whichever framework you use, and they are framework-independent on purpose. Do not mutate state; replace it. The diff compares identity, so mutating an object in place produces a tree that looks unchanged and nothing updates — the single most common framework bug. Keep state as close to where it is used as possible, because lifting it further than necessary widens the set of things that re-render when it changes. Make state updates immutable, which for a nested structure means copying the path from the root to the changed part rather than the whole tree, and which the framework's update functions exist to make ergonomic. Never derive state during render by setting it, because that produces an update during a render and a render during an update. And do not put a value in state that you could look up, — a duplicate of something you already have is a second source of truth, and the framework will not tell you when they diverge.

/* The model underneath every framework. */
const STATE = {
  is: 'data that changes over time and causes the interface to change',
  centralRule: 'ONE-WAY DATA FLOW',
  theFlow: ['changing state triggers a RE-RENDER', 'the render produces a NEW TREE',
    'the diff is computed', 'only the differences are applied to the DOM'],
  nothingElseUpdates: 'nothing else updates the interface',
  whyPredictable: 'there is ONE PLACE where change enters the system and ONE PATH it takes to the screen',
};

/* The derivation rule. */
const DERIVATION = {
  rule: 'DERIVED DATA IS COMPUTED DURING RENDER, not stored in state',
  instances: ['a filtered list', 'a total', 'a formatted date'],
  why: 'storing it creates a SECOND SOURCE OF TRUTH that can disagree with the first',
  classicBug: 'a total that is wrong after adding an item is almost always a stored derived value that was not updated',
  corollary: 'state must be MINIMAL - everything else is derived, and every piece of state you add is a thing that can be stale',
};

const RULES = [
  { r: 'do NOT MUTATE STATE; REPLACE IT', why: 'the diff compares identity, so mutating an object in place produces a tree that LOOKS UNCHANGED and nothing updates', rank: 'the single most common framework bug' },
  { r: 'keep state AS CLOSE TO WHERE IT IS USED as possible',
    why: 'lifting it further than necessary WIDENS the set of things that re-render when it changes' },
  { r: 'make state updates IMMUTABLE',
    how: 'for a nested structure, copy the PATH FROM THE ROOT to the changed part rather than the whole tree',
    ergonomics: 'the frameworks update functions exist to make this pleasant' },
  { r: 'never derive state during render by SETTING IT', why: 'that produces an update during a render and a render during an update' },
  { r: 'do NOT put a value in state that you could LOOK UP',
    why: 'a duplicate of something you already have is a second source of truth, and the framework will not tell you when they diverge' },
];

A declarative Counter component: state drives render and the framework diffs the DOM, so you never touch the DOM yourself.

Concepts that transfer to Vue/Svelte/Angular: state → render → event → state. Mastering one framework teaches you all of them.

17.5 Tooling: package managers & build steps

Modern frontend work is built, not served as loose files. npm manages packages and scripts, while a bundler such as Vite serves the source during development and compiles, minifies, and splits it into optimized bundles for production. The pipeline also handles transpiling, asset hashing, and tree shaking, with the whole setup configured through package.json and build commands.

  • npm — the package manager (npm create vite@latest my-app boots a modern project in seconds).
  • Vite — dev server + bundler; the default choice of new React/Vue projects.
  • The "build" transforms: TS → JS, minify, asset-hash, tree-shake.

What a build actually does, and why the bundle is not one file

A build step transforms source into an artefact, and the transformations are fewer than people assume. Bundling follows the import graph from an entry point and produces files containing the code needed, which is why a bundle is not one file by default: static imports are followed into the graph, while dynamic imports — a call that is only reached at runtime — become separate chunks, and that is the mechanism by which a large application ships its initial view small and loads the rest when the user reaches it. Transpiling rewrites code from one version of the language to another, most usefully to run modern syntax on older browsers, and it can also remove types if they were only annotations. Minifying removes whitespace, shortens identifiers and rewrites the syntax to be smaller, which is where most of the byte reduction comes from — and it also removes anything a stack trace would have referred to, which is the reason to keep a readable, unminified build for debugging. Processing assets converts images and fonts, generates hashed filenames. And tree shaking removes exports nobody imports, which depends on the module system being statically analysable — which is why a module that does something surprising when imported for its side effects will defeat it, and why the "side effects" declaration in a package manifest exists.

Then the three things that make a build slow, and the reason each is slow. Transpiling many small modules. A module system with thousands of tiny files is slow to process, and the remedies are bundling into fewer files and reducing how much you transform. Type checking. This is genuinely expensive and grows with the size of the project, and the honest response is that it should be run in the pipeline rather than on every keystroke — a fast feedback loop uses a lighter check and the full check happens on commit. And source maps, which can be the largest cost of all, because generating them for a large bundle means the build holds a mapping for every generated character, and the fix is to generate them only for error reporting rather than always. Then the outputs worth knowing, and which you ship when. The production build — minified, hashed filenames, no source maps — and the hashing is what makes caching work: a changed file has a changed name, so a returning visitor's browser fetches only what changed. The development build — unminified, with source maps, watching for changes and rebuilding. Source maps, which let a browser's debugger show your original source and line numbers, and which should be uploaded to an error-reporting service rather than served publicly, both because they are large and because they reveal your source.

/* Fewer transformations than people assume. */
const TRANSFORMATIONS = [
  { t: 'BUNDLING', does: 'follows the import graph from an entry point and produces files containing the code needed',
    whyNotOneFile: 'static imports are followed into the graph, while DYNAMIC IMPORTS - a call only reached at runtime - become SEPARATE CHUNKS',
    gain: 'the mechanism by which a large application ships its INITIAL VIEW SMALL and loads the rest when the user reaches it' },
  { t: 'TRANSPILING', does: 'rewrites code from one version of the language to another',
    mostUseful: 'running modern syntax on older browsers',
    also: 'it can remove types if they were only annotations' },
  { t: 'MINIFYING', does: ['removes whitespace', 'shortens identifiers', 'rewrites the syntax to be smaller'],
    whereBytesComeFrom: 'most of the byte reduction',
    cost: 'it removes anything a stack trace would have referred to',
    therefore: 'keep a readable, unminified build for debugging' },
  { t: 'PROCESSING ASSETS', does: ['converts images and fonts', 'generates hashed filenames'] },
  { t: 'TREE SHAKING', does: 'removes exports nobody imports',
    dependsOn: 'the module system being statically analysable',

];

Dependencies, deployment, and the parts that are easy to get wrong

Then dependencies, which is where the cost is. A lockfile pins the exact versions of everything, and committing it is what makes two machines install the same tree — without it, two developers have different code because a dependency published a new version, which is the "it works on my machine" problem in its most literal form. Dependencies are transitive and they are your responsibility, which is why an application that has six direct dependencies may have six hundred in its tree, and why a vulnerability in something four levels down is a real vulnerability in your application. Audit and update deliberately, with a tool, because the alternative is finding out from an announcement. And prefer a dependency only when writing it yourself would take longer than maintaining it — which is a smaller threshold than people assume, because a dependency carries its own bugs, its own update cadence, its own licence, and its own behaviour changes that arrive without a changelog entry in your project.

Then deployment, and the four things that are easy to get wrong. The environment is not your machine. Configuration differs, the file system is read-only in many platforms, the clock and locale differ, and a program that reads /etc/hosts or writes a temporary file will fail in a way it never did locally. Build and the runtime are different environments, so anything in the development dependencies that the application actually needs at run time must be in the production dependencies, and this is the most common deployment failure there is. Configuration comes from the environment, not from a file committed to the repository, so a secret is not in version control and the same artefact runs in staging and production. Health checks and graceful shutdown, which are the difference between a rolling deployment and an outage: a process must report readiness before traffic arrives and must finish in-flight work before exiting, and a service that is killed mid-request produces errors for users during every deployment — which is the concrete cost of not having them. And then the habit that ties the chapter together: make the build reproduce the artefact that was tested. Build once, test that artefact, deploy that same artefact — because "build again for production" is how a release ships something that was never verified.

/* Dependencies, where the cost is. */
const DEPENDENCIES = [
  { p: 'a LOCKFILE pins the exact versions of everything',
    commitIt: true,
    gain: 'two machines install the same tree',
    without: 'two developers have different code because a dependency published a new version',
    name: 'the works-on-my-machine problem in its most literal form' },
  { p: 'dependencies are TRANSITIVE and they are YOUR responsibility',
    arithmetic: 'an application with six direct dependencies may have SIX HUNDRED in its tree',
    consequence: 'a vulnerability in something four levels down is a REAL VULNERABILITY in your application' },
  { p: 'AUDIT and update deliberately, with a tool', why: 'the alternative is finding out from an announcement' },
  { p: 'prefer a dependency only when WRITING IT YOURSELF WOULD TAKE LONGER THAN MAINTAINING IT',
    thresholdSmallerThanAssumed: true,
    why: ['a dependency carries its own bugs', 'its own update cadence', 'its own licence',
      'its own behaviour changes that arrive WITHOUT A CHANGELOG ENTRY in your project'],
  },
];

/* Deployment - four things easy to get wrong. */
const DEPLOYMENT = [
  { m: 'the ENVIRONMENT IS NOT YOUR MACHINE',
    differences: ['configuration differs', 'the file system is read-only in many platforms',
      'the clock and locale differ'],

  { m: 'BUILD and the RUNTIME are different environments',

    rank: 'the most common deployment failure there is' },
  { m: 'CONFIGURATION comes from the ENVIRONMENT, not from a file committed to the repository',

Web ≠ files. Production sites are built: source files compiled to a handful of optimised bundles. If a tutorial tells you to just script src="file.js", it’s a 2015 tutorial.

17.6 Responsive design

Responsive design makes a layout adapt to any screen size, from phones to desktops. Practically this means fluid units like rem and percentage instead of fixed pixels, flexbox and grid layouts that reflow naturally, and media queries that switch rules at defined breakpoints, usually designed mobile-first. Keep images and fonts efficient and lazy-load below-the-fold content so the page stays fast on weak connections.

  • Fluid units (rem, %, vw/vh) instead of fixed pixels for layout.
  • Media queries: @media (max-width: 700px) { ... } adapt at breakpoints.
  • Mobile-first: write the phone layout first, then enhance up — forces you to keep the essential minimal.
  • Performance: fewer/smaller requests, loading="lazy" on images, system font stacks,

    The three mechanisms, and what each one is actually for

    Responsive design is three mechanisms and choosing between them is most of the skill. Fluid units — percentages, viewport units, and above all clamp — size things relative to their container or the viewport, so they need no breakpoints at all for simple cases. Media queries change rules at a width, and the honest modern position is that they are needed far less often than they were because fluid units cover most of it; where they are needed is when the layout should change, not merely the sizes. Container queries change rules based on the size of the component's container rather than the viewport, and this is the one that solves the problem every component library has: a card that is wide on a two-column page and narrow in a sidebar must be told about its container, and only a container query knows. Then the two design decisions that actually determine whether a layout works. Where does width go? A fixed-width page cannot be viewed usefully on a phone, and the answer is a content-driven maximum width with fluid sizing inside it — the column gets wider until it stops being comfortable to read and then stops growing. What reflows? Reflow means the content changes position rather than scrolling off screen, and it is the mechanism that makes a page usable at a different size; a layout where only the text reflows while the navigation does not becomes unusable long before it becomes ugly.

    Then the breakpoints, and the more useful question of where they should come from. Breakpoints should be where the design breaks, not where a device is. Add width until the layout stops working, then add a query there — and the reason this is better is that it makes the breakpoints self-maintaining: a design change moves the breakpoint automatically because the number is derived from the content, whereas "at 768 pixels because that is a tablet" stays at 768 while the design around it changes. Then the practical scale, and the reason the mobile-first order matters. Start with the smallest screen and add breakpoints upward. The reason is that the constraints are strongest there — a narrow screen forces a single column, small type and few controls, which is the layout everything else must also work as. Building upward means the design degrades gracefully rather than needing separate maintenance per device. And the rule that follows from it: design the narrow layout to be complete, not merely functional. A mobile layout that is a stripped-down version of the desktop one is a worse product and often more work, because "stripped down" still has to be designed, tested and maintained.

    /* Three mechanisms. */
const MECHANISMS = [
  { m: 'FLUID UNITS', units: ['percentages', 'viewport units', 'above all clamp'],
    sizes: 'relative to their container or the viewport',
    means: 'they need no breakpoints AT ALL for simple cases' },
  { m: 'MEDIA QUERIES', change: 'rules at a width',
    modernPosition: 'needed far less often than they were, because fluid units cover most of it',
    neededWhen: 'the LAYOUT should change, not merely the sizes' },
  { m: 'CONTAINER QUERIES', change: 'rules based on the size of the COMPONENTS CONTAINER rather than the viewport',
    solves: 'the problem every component library has - a card that is wide on a two-column page and narrow in a sidebar must be told about its container, and only a container query knows' },
];

/* Two design decisions. */
const DECISIONS = [
  { q: 'WHERE DOES WIDTH GO', problem: 'a fixed-width page cannot be viewed usefully on a phone',
    answer: 'a CONTENT-DRIVEN MAXIMUM WIDTH with fluid sizing inside it',
    mechanism: 'the column gets wider until it stops being comfortable to read and then stops growing' },
  { q: 'WHAT REFLOWS', is: 'the content CHANGES POSITION rather than scrolling off screen',
    why: 'it is the mechanism that makes a page usable at a different size',
    consequence: 'a layout where only the text reflows while the navigation does not becomes UNUSABLE long before it becomes ugly' },
];

/* Where breakpoints come from. */
const BREAKPOINTS = {
  rule: 'breakpoints should be where the DESIGN BREAKS, not where a DEVICE IS',
  how: 'add width until the layout stops working, then add a query there',
  whyBetter: 'it makes the breakpoints SELF-MAINTAINING - a design change moves the breakpoint automatically because the number is derived from the content',
  contrast: 'at 768 pixels because that is a tablet stays at 768 while the design around it changes' },
];
const MOBILE_FIRST = {
  rule: 'start with the SMALLEST SCREEN and add breakpoints upward',
  why: 'the constraints are STRONGEST there - a narrow screen forces a single column, small type and few controls, which is the layout everything else must also work as',
  gain: 'building upward means the design DEGRADES GRACEFULLY rather than needing separate maintenance per device',
  corollary: 'design the narrow layout to be COMPLETE, not merely functional',
  why: 'a mobile layout that is a stripped-down version of the desktop one is a worse product and often MORE WORK, because stripped down still has to be designed, tested and maintained',
};

    Images, performance, and the accessibility that overlaps

    Then images, which are usually the largest thing on the page and the easiest to improve. Always set explicit dimensions, because without them the browser cannot reserve space and the page reflows as images load — and that reflow is the largest single contributor to perceived slowness, more than the image's bytes. Use the right format. A modern format with a widely available fallback, which the <picture> element and its source sets provide, typically cuts image weight substantially at the same visual quality. Serve the size that is displayed, including for high-density screens, using the source set rather than one enormous file for everybody. Lazy-load below the fold, because an image the user must scroll to does not need to have downloaded, and lazy-loading above the fold makes it slower for no benefit. Preload the one image that is definitely needed first, which buys several hundred milliseconds on the largest contentful element. And compress everything, which is free.

    Then the performance items that are not images, and the accessibility items that are the same items — which is why they belong in one section. content-visibility on long-page sections skips rendering work for content below the fold, which is a large win on a long document. A system font stack renders in the system's font with no download at all, and the performance difference is enormous. Defer and lazy-load scripts, because a script blocks parsing and a script below the fold blocks rendering. Cache and version assets so a returning visitor gets nothing new. And then the accessibility overlap, which is the interesting part: respect the reduced-motion preference, because a large fraction of users have it and animation causes actual symptoms for some of them. Ensure contrast, which is a measurable requirement and not a matter of taste. Make focus visible — removing the focus ring without replacing it makes a page unusable by keyboard. Ensure targets are large enough to hit, which is a touch requirement and an accessibility one simultaneously. And do not disable zoom, which is a real and still-common mistake that makes the page unusable for anyone who needs to magnify it.

    /* Images - usually the largest thing on the page. */

  { p: 'always set EXPLICIT DIMENSIONS', why: 'without them the browser cannot reserve space and the page reflows as images load',
    significance: 'that reflow is the LARGEST SINGLE CONTRIBUTOR TO PERCEIVED SLOWNESS, more than the images bytes' },
  { p: 'use the RIGHT FORMAT', how: 'a modern format with a widely available fallback via picture and source sets',
    gain: 'typically cuts image weight SUBSTANTIALLY at the same visual quality' },
  { p: 'serve the SIZE THAT IS DISPLAYED', including: 'high-density screens', how: 'the source set rather than one enormous file for everybody' },
  { p: 'LAZY-LOAD below the fold', why: 'an image the user must scroll to does not need to have downloaded',
    caveat: 'lazy-loading ABOVE THE FOLD makes it slower for no benefit' },
  { p: 'PRELOAD the one image that is definitely needed first', gain: 'several hundred milliseconds on the largest contentful element' },

17.7 Client-side storage and single-page apps

Client-side storage gives web pages a place to keep data between visits. localStorage and sessionStorage hold key-value strings, cookies are values sent with each request, and IndexedDB is a client-side database for larger structured data, which together enable single-page apps, caching, and offline support. Never put secrets in localStorage, any XSS can read it; tokens belong in HttpOnly cookies.

The browser has four built-in places to keep data. Which one goes with which job?

StorageSize/capLives untilUse for
localStorage~5 MBForever (per site)User prefs, draft content, cached settings
sessionStorage~5 MBTab closesOne-session state (a wizard’s steps)
Cookies~4 KBPer expirySession identifiers — sent to server on every request
IndexedDBHundreds of MB+Until clearedReal offline data (messages, media)
// SPA pattern: an app that boots from local storage state
const saved = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("theme") || '"light"');
document.documentElement.dataset.theme = saved;   // apply saved theme on load

function saveTheme(t) {
  localStorage.setItem("theme", JSON.stringify(t));
}

A tiny SPA boots from a saved theme and persists each change — and the warning below explains why secrets must never live here.

Never put secrets or session tokens in localStorage. Any XSS can read it. Tokens belong in HttpOnly cookies (Ch. 14.7), which JavaScript can’t touch.

SPA vs MPA: a Single-Page App loads one HTML shell and swaps content via fetch + re-render (React-style); a Multi-Page App serves new HTML per navigation. SPAs feel app-like but must handle routing, state, and SEO more carefully — the industry runs both, and "wrong choice" debates are endless. For your first big frontend: an SPA with a framework is the modern default.

Cookies, local storage, and session storage compared

Three client-side stores, and they differ in ways that matter. Cookies are sent to the server with every matching request, are limited to about four kilobytes, and can be marked HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite — which is why they are the right store for a session identifier and the wrong store for anything else. Local storage persists until explicitly cleared, holds roughly five to ten megabytes, is synchronous, and is shared with the server in the sense that it is not — it is not sent anywhere, so a value there is invisible to your backend unless you send it. Session storage is identical except that it is cleared when the tab closes, and that single difference is what makes it correct for a wizard's intermediate state and wrong for anything you want to survive.

Then the properties that cause real bugs, and they are the same for all three. It is a string store. Everything is serialised to text, so a number comes back a string, an object must be serialised and parsed explicitly, and a Date must be converted because it becomes a string and there is no automatic revival. It is synchronous. Every read and write blocks the thread, which is why putting a large object in there is a performance problem and why a store is not the place for anything big. It is origin-scoped, so localhost and your deployed domain are different stores entirely — which is the single most common "why did my value disappear" report during development. And quota is a real error: exceeding it does not throw a useful exception, it silently refuses the write in some browsers, so a value that was there before is now absent and nothing says why.

/* Three stores, differing in ways that matter. */
const STORES = [
  { s: 'COOKIES', sentToServer: 'every matching request', size: 'about four kilobytes',
    flags: ['HttpOnly', 'Secure', 'SameSite'],
    rightFor: 'a session identifier', wrongFor: 'anything else' },
  { s: 'LOCAL STORAGE', persists: 'until explicitly cleared', size: 'roughly five to ten megabytes',
    synchronous: true, sentToServer: false,
    note: 'not sent anywhere, so a value there is INVISIBLE TO YOUR BACKEND unless you send it' },
  { s: 'SESSION STORAGE', sameExcept: 'it is cleared when the tab closes',
    singleDifferenceWhyItMatters: true,
    rightFor: 'a wizards intermediate state', wrongFor: 'anything you want to survive' },
];

/* Properties that cause real bugs. */
const PROPERTIES = [
  { p: 'it is a STRING STORE', detail: 'everything is serialised to text',
    consequences: ['a number comes back a string', 'an object must be serialised and parsed explicitly',
      'a Date must be converted because it becomes a string and there is no automatic revival'] },
  { p: 'it is SYNCHRONOUS', detail: 'every read and write BLOCKS THE THREAD',
    consequence: 'putting a large object in there is a performance problem, and a store is not the place for anything big' },
  { p: 'it is ORIGIN-SCOPED', detail: 'localhost and your deployed domain are DIFFERENT STORES entirely',
    classicBug: 'the single most common why did my value disappear report DURING DEVELOPMENT' },
  { p: 'QUOTA IS A REAL ERROR', detail: 'exceeding it does not throw a useful exception - it SILENTLY REFUSES THE WRITE in some browsers',
    symptom: 'a value that was there before is now absent and NOTHING SAYS WHY' },
];

Cookies as storage, and the security rules that follow

Then cookies as a storage mechanism specifically, because it is still done and it is worse than people expect. A cookie is sent with every request to its domain, so a large cookie adds bytes to every single request including every image request, and a session cookie holding meaningful data is a performance problem before it is a security one. Cookies are tamper-evident only when signed, and an unsigned cookie is a value the client can edit — so anything in a cookie that matters must be signed or, better, not be in a cookie at all. The SameSite attribute is the defence against cross-site request forgery and it is not on by default everywhere it should be, so setting it explicitly is the difference between being protected and not. And the fundamental limit: a cookie has a four-kilobyte ceiling and is transmitted on every request, which makes it the wrong tool for caching anything substantial and the right tool for one small identifier.

Then the security rules, which apply to everything stored client-side. Never store a secret in client storage. Anything in local storage, session storage or a readable cookie is readable by any script on the page, which includes any script that got injected, and there is no mechanism that makes it safe — the same-origin policy stops other origins reading it, not the page's own script. A token in local storage is available to any script that runs on your origin, so a single third-party script with a vulnerability, or one injected via a dependency, can read it; a cookie marked HttpOnly cannot be read by script at all, which is the entire reason that flag exists. Nothing in client storage is an authorisation decision. Hiding a feature in the interface is not access control, because anyone can call the endpoint directly, and every check must be made on the server where the data is. And then the practice that covers most of it: if you must store something sensitive client-side, keep it as short-lived and as opaque as possible — an identifier that means nothing on its own, with the actual session state held server-side, which is the correct pattern for the same reason a cookie holding a session identifier is the correct pattern.

/* Cookies as storage - worse than people expect. */
const COOKIE_STORAGE = [
  { c: 'sent with EVERY request to its domain', consequence: 'a large cookie adds bytes to every single request INCLUDING EVERY IMAGE REQUEST',
    order: 'a performance problem before it is a security one' },
  { c: 'TAMPER-EVIDENT ONLY WHEN SIGNED', detail: 'an unsigned cookie is a value the CLIENT CAN EDIT',
    therefore: 'anything in a cookie that matters must be signed or, better, NOT BE IN A COOKIE AT ALL' },
  { c: 'SameSite is the defence against CROSS-SITE REQUEST FORGERY', notDefault: 'everywhere it should be',
    consequence: 'setting it explicitly is the difference between being protected and not' },
  { c: 'the FUNDAMENTAL LIMIT', ceiling: 'a four-kilobyte ceiling, and it is transmitted on every request',
    therefore: 'the wrong tool for caching anything substantial, and the RIGHT TOOL FOR ONE SMALL IDENTIFIER' },
];

/* The security rules. */
const SECURITY = [
  { r: 'NEVER STORE A SECRET in client storage', why: 'anything in local storage, session storage or a readable cookie is READABLE BY ANY SCRIPT ON THE PAGE',
    who: 'including any script that got injected',
    whyThereIsNoSafeVersion: 'the same-origin policy stops OTHER ORIGINS reading it, not the pages own script' },
  { r: 'a TOKEN IN LOCAL STORAGE is available to any script that runs on your origin',
    examples: ['a single third-party script with a vulnerability', 'one injected via a dependency'],
    contrast: 'a cookie marked HttpOnly CANNOT BE READ BY SCRIPT AT ALL',
    note: 'which is the ENTIRE REASON that flag exists' },
  { r: 'nothing in client storage is an AUTHORISATION DECISION', detail: 'hiding a feature in the interface is not access control',
    why: 'anyone can call the endpoint directly, so every check must be made on the SERVER where the data is' },
  { r: 'if you must store something SENSITIVE, keep it SHORT-LIVED and OPAQUE',
    means: 'an identifier that means nothing on its own, with the actual session state held server-side',

];

18 · Backend & APIs

18.1 Client–server in one mental picture18.2 REST — resources spoken over HTTP18.3 A real API in Node/Express18.4 Error design & versioning18.5 Authentication & authorization18.6 From one app to a system18.7 Hardening a production API18.8 Rate limiting, retries & graceful degradation

Backend and APIs covers the server side that holds the truth of a product: application servers, databases, authentication, and the API contracts every client shares. It builds the mental model from a single client-server request through REST design, Express practice, error and versioning conventions, auth, and hardening production systems with rate limits and retries. Everything hangs off one picture: requests in, queries run, JSON out.

The frontend renders; the backend holds truth, enforces rules, and speaks to every other system. Backend work is servers, databases, authentication, and — above all — defining clean API contracts the whole product shares.

18.1 Client–server in one mental picture

The entire backend world hangs off one picture: a browser sends an HTTP request, a server runs queries and business logic, and structured JSON flows back as a response. That round trip explains latency, scaling, authentication, and error handling, since everything on one side has a contract with the other. Keep the request small, the server stateless, and the response shape predictable.

Browser                     Server                     Database
   |-- HTTP request --------> |                           |
   |   GET /api/users         |--- SQL query ------------>|
   |                          |<-- rows ----------------|
   |   <-- HTTP response -----|  {users:[...]}             |
   | JSON -------------------> JS renders                 |

One request, end to end

Following a single request through the stack teaches more than any diagram, because each hop adds a responsibility and a way to fail. The client builds a request: method, path, headers, body. It opens a connection — or reuses one, which is the keep-alive point from the networking chapter. A name becomes an address through DNS, which is a round trip to a resolver that may be cached and may not. The address becomes a connection through a TCP handshake, three round trips of pure overhead before a byte of data moves, unless the connection is reused. The request crosses the network to whatever machine the load balancer chose, and this is where TLS negotiation happened or happens, adding another round trip on a new connection. At the server, the request arrives at a process that may be anything — several servers behind a balancer, so what you are reasoning about is one of many identical processes. Middleware runs in order, and the order is a design decision with real consequences: authentication must happen before anything that touches the request's data, and rate limiting must happen before the expensive work. The handler does the work, and for anything non-trivial that work includes another round trip to a database — over a local network, so fast that people forget it is a network call, and it is why a query inside a loop is a network call inside a loop. The response goes back through the same middleware in reverse, serialised, and the connection is closed or kept alive depending on headers.

Then the two hops people forget, and both are network calls that behave like local operations. The database, and the rule that follows from it: every query is a network call, so the number of queries per request matters more than how fast each one is, which is why the N-plus-one query is the classic performance defect in an API — a loop doing one query per item, which is a hundred queries for a hundred items, and the fix is a single query with a join or an IN clause. The cache, and the rule that follows: a cache lookup is a network call too, so a cache that saves one expensive query but adds four cheap ones has made things worse, and the reason to measure a cache is precisely that the assumption is not reliable.

/* Each hop adds a responsibility and a way to fail. */
const HOPS = [

  { h: 'the ADDRESS BECOMES A CONNECTION', via: 'a TCP handshake',

  { h: 'the REQUEST CROSSES THE NETWORK', to: 'whatever machine the load balancer chose',
