Statelessness, and the trade it makes

Then statelessness, which is the chapter's central architectural claim, and it is worth being precise about what it costs. Stateless means the server keeps nothing between requests. Everything needed to serve a request arrives in it. That gives three things, and each is significant. Any server can serve any request, so adding capacity is starting processes behind a balancer, and a process can be killed at any moment without an effect a user can observe. Horizontal scaling becomes trivial, because there is nothing to keep in sync between processes. Retries are safe, because there is no in-progress state on the server that a retry would duplicate. And the costs, which are real and which is why the claim "stateless is better" is incomplete. Every request repeats work the previous one did — authentication is re-verified, configuration is re-read, lookups that could have been cached are repeated. Each request carries more bytes, because the session state travels in every request rather than living on the server. A multi-request operation has no built-in way to resume: a checkout that spans four requests has state that must live somewhere, and if the server keeps none of it, it lives in the client. And the "stateless" claim is often false in practice — a process holding a connection pool, a cache in memory, or a rate-limit counter is stateful, and pretending otherwise is how a system acquires a dependency on a process's identity it cannot scale past.

Then where the state should actually go, which is the practical answer. In the client, for state that is genuinely the client's — a wizard's progress, an unsaved draft, a filter the user chose — and the constraint is that it must be tamper-evident, which is the same argument as the signed cookie. In a shared store, for state that must be authoritative — sessions, cart contents, rate-limit counters — and the requirement is that the store is a real dependency with its own availability and latency, which is the cost of statelessness paid honestly. In the request itself, for anything small and infrequent — a signed assertion, which is what a token is. And never in a process's memory, unless losing it is acceptable, because a process that loses its memory on restart has turned a cache into a correctness problem. The resulting architecture, and it is the one most mature systems converge on, is: processes hold caches with a short life and no authority; all authoritative state lives in a store the client or another service reads directly. That is stateless in the sense that matters, and it is the difference between a claim and a design.

/* Three gains. */
const GAINS = [
  { g: 'any server can serve ANY request', gains: ['starting processes behind a balancer',
    'a process can be killed at any moment without an effect a user can observe'] },
  { g: 'HORIZONTAL SCALING becomes trivial', why: 'there is nothing to keep in sync between processes' },
  { g: 'RETRIES are SAFE', why: 'there is no in-progress state on the server that a retry would duplicate' },
];
/* Three costs. */
const COSTS = [
  { c: 'every request REPEATS WORK the previous one did',
    instances: ['authentication is re-verified', 'configuration is re-read', 'lookups that could have been cached are repeated'] },
  { c: 'each request carries MORE BYTES', why: 'the session state travels in every request rather than living on the server' },
  { c: 'a MULTI-REQUEST OPERATION has no built-in way to resume',
    detail: 'a checkout that spans four requests has state that must live somewhere',
    and: 'if the server keeps none of it, it lives in the CLIENT' },
  { c: 'the stateless claim is OFTEN FALSE IN PRACTICE',
    examples: ['a process holding a connection pool', 'a cache in memory', 'a rate-limit counter'],
    consequence: 'pretending otherwise is how a system acquires a DEPENDENCE ON A PROCESSES IDENTITY it cannot scale past' },
];
const INCOMPLETE_CLAIM = 'stateless is better is incomplete, because the costs are real';
/* Where state should go. */
const WHERE_STATE = [
  { place: 'IN THE CLIENT', for: 'state that is genuinely the clients',
    instances: ['a wizards progress', 'an unsaved draft', 'a filter the user chose'],

};

An ASCII walkthrough of one request: browser to server to database and back again, handing the results to JavaScript as JSON.

18.2 REST — resources spoken over HTTP

REST designs APIs around resources addressed by URLs and manipulated with HTTP verbs: GET reads, POST creates, PUT or PATCH updates, DELETE removes, with status codes and headers doing the bookkeeping. Resources are named as plural nouns, collections sit under one path, and a single resource under its ID. A well-designed REST API reads like a table of contents of your product and is commonly documented with OpenAPI.

REST treats data as resources addressed by URLs, manipulated with the four HTTP verbs. A well-designed REST API reads like a table of contents of your product.

The constraints, and why the name means something specific

Representational State Transfer is a set of constraints, not a style guide, and most things called REST do not satisfy all of them — which is worth knowing so you can use the vocabulary honestly. Client-server: the two are separate and the client initiates. Stateless: every request carries everything needed to understand it, and this is the constraint that does the most work, because it is what makes a server interchangeable and therefore scalable. Cacheable: a response declares whether it may be stored, and the constraint is meaningful because of the stateless rule — a cached response is useless if the server must have state. Uniform interface: resources have identifiers, representations carry media types, and methods have defined meanings. Layered system: a component does not know what it is talking to. And code on demand, optional, which is the least used. The reason the name is worth enforcing is that the constraints buy something: intermediaries. Because the client does not know the server's implementation, a proxy, a load balancer, a cache or a gateway can sit between them and do their work without either end cooperating. That is not a feature REST invented for its own sake; it is why the web has grown a layer of infrastructure that applications do not have to know about.

Then resources, and the naming discipline that makes an API readable. A resource is a thing, not an action — /orders, not /createOrder. The action belongs in the method, which is what methods are for. URLs name resources; the request carries the action. Resources are nouns and collections are plural: /orders and /orders/42, and the collection and the item are different resources with different operations. Nesting reflects containment, and nesting stops. /orders/42/items/7 reads well; /customers/9/orders/42/items/7/reviews/3 does not, and the reason is that it makes the parent identity implicit in every operation. Two levels of nesting is a good ceiling. And the two distinctions that cause the most confusion and deserve stating separately: the collection versus the instance. A collection accepts creation and listing; an instance accepts retrieval, replacement and deletion. And the resource versus the representation: /orders/42 is the resource; the JSON you get back is one representation of it, and the same resource can be represented as XML, as CSV, or as a PDF, which is what the media type is for.

/* Constraints, not a style guide. */
const CONSTRAINTS = [
  { c: 'CLIENT-SERVER', means: 'the two are separate and the client initiates' },
  { c: 'STATELESS', means: 'every request carries everything needed to understand it',
    doesMostWork: true,
    gain: 'it is what makes a server INTERCHANGEABLE and therefore scalable' },
  { c: 'CACHEABLE', means: 'a response declares whether it may be stored',
    meaningfulBecause: 'of the stateless rule - a cached response is useless if the server must have state' },
  { c: 'UNIFORM INTERFACE', parts: ['resources have identifiers', 'representations carry media types',
    'methods have defined meanings'] },
  { c: 'LAYERED SYSTEM', means: 'a component does not know what it is talking to' },
  { c: 'code on demand', optional: true, leastUsed: true },
];
const WHY_ENFORCE = {
  constraintsBuy: 'INTERMEDIARIES',
  how: 'because the client does not know the servers implementation, a proxy, a load balancer, a cache or a gateway can sit between them',
  withoutCooperation: 'and do their work without either end cooperating',
  reframe: 'not a feature REST invented for its own sake - it is why the web has grown a layer of infrastructure applications do not have to know about',
};

/* Resource naming. */
const NAMING = [
  { r: 'a RESOURCE IS A THING, not an action', good: '/orders', bad: '/createOrder',
    rule: 'the action belongs in the METHOD, which is what methods are for' },
  { r: 'URLs name RESOURCES; the request carries the ACTION' },
  { r: 'resources are NOUNS and collections are PLURAL', good: '/orders and /orders/42',
    distinction: 'the collection and the item are DIFFERENT RESOURCES with different operations' },
  { r: 'NESTING REFLECTS CONTAINMENT, and nesting stops', good: '/orders/42/items/7', bad: '/customers/9/orders/42/items/7/reviews/3',
    ceiling: 'TWO LEVELS', why: 'deeper nesting makes the parent identity implicit in every operation' },
];
const TWO_DISTINCTIONS = [
  { d: 'the COLLECTION versus the INSTANCE',
    collection: 'accepts creation and listing', instance: 'accepts retrieval, replacement and deletion' },
  { d: 'the RESOURCE versus the REPRESENTATION',
    resource: '/orders/42', representation: 'the JSON you get back',
    point: 'the same resource can be represented as XML, as CSV, or as a PDF - which is what the media type is for' },
];

Methods, status codes, and errors

Then methods, and the semantics are the networking chapter's, applied. The three rules that keep an API honest. The method must match the operation's semantics, because intermediaries act on the difference — a crawler follows GET links, a proxy caches them, a retry layer repeats them. Use the method that matches the safety property: retrieval is GET because it is safe and idempotent; creation is POST because it is neither; a full replacement is PUT because it is idempotent; a partial change is PATCH; removal is DELETE, which is idempotent in effect even though the second call returns a different status. And do not put verbs in URLs, which is covered above and is the most common violation. Then status codes, and the discipline that makes an API usable by a program: the code carries the class, the body carries the detail. 2xx for success — and 200, 201, 204 are not interchangeable, because a client that cannot distinguish "created" from "ok, no content" will misbehave. 3xx for redirection. 4xx for the client's problem and 5xx for the server's, and the distinction matters operationally because the two produce different alerts: a spike in 4xx is usually a broken client, a spike in 5xx is usually you. 401 versus 403: 401 means you have not proved who you are and should carry a challenge; 403 means you are identified and not allowed and should not.

Then errors, and this is where most APIs are unusable because the shape is inconsistent. An error body needs a machine-readable code and a human-readable message, and the two are not the same thing: "Not found" is a message, and a client that must parse English to decide what to do is a client that breaks when someone improves the wording. The correct shape is a stable identifier — ORDER_NOT_FOUND — plus a message for a person, plus optionally a field pointing at the specific part of the request that was wrong. The status code is not enough detail, because 400 does not say which field, and a client that has to guess cannot present a useful error. And three rules that follow. Never leak internals: a stack trace in an error response is a map of your system for anyone who can trigger it, and it must go to your logs, not to the caller. Be consistent across the whole API, because the value of a convention is that a client can handle every failure with one piece of code. Make errors actionable, which means a validation error names the field and says what was expected, because an error the client cannot act on will be retried and will then look like a server fault.

/* Three rules that keep an API honest. */
const METHOD_RULES = [
  { r: 'the METHOD must match the operations SEMANTICS',
    why: 'intermediaries act on the difference - a crawler follows GET links, a proxy caches them, a retry layer repeats them' },
  { r: 'use the method that matches the SAFETY PROPERTY',
    retrieval: 'GET - safe and idempotent',
    creation: 'POST - neither',
    replacement: 'PUT - idempotent',
    partial: 'PATCH', removal: 'DELETE - idempotent in effect even though the second call returns a different status' },
  { r: 'do NOT PUT VERBS IN URLS', note: 'the most common violation' },
];

/* Status codes. */
const STATUS = {
  discipline: 'the code carries the CLASS, the body carries the DETAIL',
  classes: {
    '2xx': 'success - and 200, 201, 204 are NOT interchangeable, because a client that cannot distinguish created from ok-no-content will misbehave',
    '3xx': 'redirection',
    '4xx': 'the CLIENTS problem',
    '5xx': 'the SERVERS problem',
    operational: 'the distinction matters because a spike in 4xx is usually a broken CLIENT and a spike in 5xx is usually YOU',
  },
  '401 vs 403': '401 means you have not proved who you are and should carry a challenge; 403 means you are identified and not allowed and should not',
};

/* Errors. */
const ERRORS = {
  needs: 'a MACHINE-READABLE CODE and a HUMAN-READABLE MESSAGE, and the two are not the same thing',
  example: 'Not found is a message, and a client that must parse English to decide what to do is a client that breaks when someone improves the wording',
  correctShape: ['a stable identifier such as ORDER_NOT_FOUND', 'a message for a person',
    'optionally a field pointing at the specific part of the request that was wrong'],
  statusNotEnough: '400 does not say WHICH FIELD, and a client that has to guess cannot present a useful error',
  threeRules: [
    { r: 'never leak internals', detail: 'a stack trace in an error response is a MAP OF YOUR SYSTEM for anyone who can trigger it', destination: 'your logs, not the caller' },
    { r: 'be CONSISTENT across the whole API', why: 'the value of a convention is that a client can handle every failure with ONE PIECE OF CODE' },
    { r: 'make errors ACTIONABLE', means: 'a validation error names the field and says what was expected',
      consequence: 'an error the client cannot act on will be RETRIED and will then look like a server fault' },
  ],
};

18.3 A real API in Node/Express

Express turns a small Node script into a working API. In practice you parse incoming JSON with express.json(), define route handlers with app.get and app.post, read parameters from req.params and req.query, validate the request body at the boundary, and return proper status codes such as 201 for creation and 404 for missing resources. Mount middleware, group routes, and keep handlers thin so logic stays testable.

// app.js  --  npm init -y && npm i express
const express = require("express");
const app = express();
app.use(express.json());                    // parse JSON bodies

let nextId = 3;
let users = [ {id:1,name:"Ada"}, {id:2,name:"Grace"} ];

app.get("/api/users", (req, res) => res.json(users));

app.get("/api/users/:id", (req, res) => {
  const u = users.find(x => x.id === Number(req.params.id));
  u ? res.json(u) : res.status(404).json({ error: "not found" });   // missing id → 404
});

app.post("/api/users", (req, res) => {
  const u = { id: nextId++, name: req.body.name };
  users.push(u);
  res.status(201).json(u);
});

app.listen(3000, () => console.log("API on :3000"));
// test:  curl http://localhost:3000/api/users

A minimal Express API with list, read-one, and create routes, proper status codes, and an in-memory users array.

Middleware, and why the order is an architectural decision

Express is built on one idea: a request passes through a chain of functions, each of which can act on the request, the response, or call the next function. Everything else follows. Middleware runs in registration order on the way in and in reverse on the way out, and the order is not a style choice — it is the program's architecture. The chain that makes sense, and the reasoning for each position. Request identification first, so every later log line and error can be tied to a request. Body parsing next, because nothing downstream can read a body that has not been parsed. Then security headers, and then the cross-origin policy, because both are response properties that apply to everything. Then rate limiting, before authentication, because limiting by cost rather than by identity is the only thing that protects you against an unauthenticated flood. Then authentication, so that authorisation has an identity to work with. Then authorisation, which is a separate step and where most access-control bugs live. Then validation, so no handler ever sees unvalidated input. Then the handler. And the error handler last, because it must be the last thing in the chain to catch errors thrown by everything before it — which is also why it takes four arguments and why a framework treats a handler with the right arity as an error handler rather than as middleware.

Then what makes a handler well written, because the framework's defaults encourage the opposite. One thing per handler. A handler that validates, calls three services and formats a response is a handler nobody can test and nobody can change. Do not touch the database from a handler if it can live in a model — not for purity but because the handler is the layer that changes most and the layer that should know least. Return, do not next(), on success. Calling next() after sending a response is a bug waiting for a second handler to try to send headers that have already gone, and the error it produces — "headers already sent" — points at the wrong line entirely. Let errors propagate. Call next(err) with the error and let the error handler decide what the client sees, because a handler that catches its own error and sends a response has now decided the error shape, and it will do it differently from every other handler. And keep handlers free of configuration — a handler that reads a feature flag from the database on every request is a handler whose behaviour you cannot determine from its code.

/* One idea; everything else follows. */
const THE_IDEA = 'a request passes through a chain of functions, each of which can act on the request, the response, or call the next function';
const ORDER_NOTE = {
  runs: 'in REGISTRATION ORDER on the way in and in REVERSE on the way out',
  isNot: 'a style choice',
  is: 'the programs ARCHITECTURE',
};
const CHAIN = [
  { step: 1, what: 'request identification', why: 'every later log line and error can be tied to a request' },
  { step: 2, what: 'body parsing', why: 'nothing downstream can read a body that has not been parsed' },
  { step: 3, what: 'security headers, then the cross-origin policy', why: 'both are response properties that apply to everything' },
  { step: 4, what: 'RATE LIMITING', before: 'authentication',
    why: 'limiting BY COST rather than by identity is the ONLY thing that protects you against an UNAUTHENTICATED FLOOD' },
  { step: 5, what: 'authentication', why: 'so that authorisation has an identity to work with' },
  { step: 6, what: 'AUTHORISATION', isSeparate: true, note: 'where most access-control bugs live' },
  { step: 7, what: 'VALIDATION', why: 'so no handler ever sees unvalidated input' },
  { step: 8, what: 'the handler' },
  { step: 9, what: 'the ERROR HANDLER, LAST',
    why: 'it must be the last thing in the chain to catch errors thrown by everything before it',
    also: 'which is why it takes FOUR ARGUMENTS and why a framework treats a handler with the right arity as an error handler rather than as middleware' },
];

/* What makes a handler well written. */
const HANDLER = [
  { r: 'ONE THING per handler', why: 'a handler that validates, calls three services and formats a response is a handler NOBODY CAN TEST and nobody can change' },
  { r: 'do not touch the database from a handler if it can live in a model', notForPurity: true,
    why: 'the handler is the layer that CHANGES MOST and the layer that should know LEAST' },
  { r: 'RETURN, do not next, on success',
    bug: 'calling next after sending a response is a bug waiting for a second handler to try to send headers that have already gone',
    errorIsMisleading: 'headers already sent points at the WRONG LINE entirely' },
  { r: 'let ERRORS PROPAGATE', how: 'call next with the error and let the error handler decide what the client sees',
    why: 'a handler that catches its own error and sends a response has DECIDED THE ERROR SHAPE, and will do it differently from every other handler' },
  { r: 'keep handlers free of CONFIGURATION', example: 'a handler that reads a feature flag from the database on every request',
    consequence: 'a handler whose BEHAVIOUR YOU CANNOT DETERMINE FROM ITS CODE' },
];

Validation, the router, and the deployment shape

Then validation, which the chapter's warning is really about. Never trust req.body. Everything in it came from outside your process and is attacker-controlled, which means every field is a possible type error, an oversized string, a value outside its range, or a string that will be rendered somewhere else. Validate at the boundary, in middleware, before any handler runs — because a validation rule enforced in one handler and forgotten in nine is nine vulnerabilities, and the boundary is the only place where the rule can be applied to all of them. Validate shape, type, range, length and format separately, because each catches a different mistake and a type check does not stop a million-character string. Reject the unknown fields rather than ignoring them, which is the strictest and safest choice and which surfaces client bugs immediately instead of silently. And never use the input for anything that is not data — never as a column name, a file path, a shell command or part of a query string, because a value that is meant to be data and is used as code is the injection class in the next chapter.

Then the router and the deployment shape, which are the two things a beginner copies without understanding. The router maps paths and methods to handlers, and the things that go wrong are: route order, because /orders/:id registered before /orders/summary captures the second path as an order with the id "summary" — so the specific routes must come first, and this is the single most common Express routing bug. Parameter validation, because a route parameter is just as untrusted as a body field and is usually not validated. Fat routers, where the routing layer contains business logic and the handlers do nothing, which inverts the structure and makes the logic untestable. And hand-written repetition, where a route has five handlers that are the same five lines. Then deployment shape: a process per instance behind a balancer, a reverse proxy in front for TLS termination and static files, because doing TLS in the application means every request pays the handshake cost and every instance needs a certificate. Health checks on a separate path that check dependencies rather than returning 200 unconditionally. And graceful shutdown, which is the difference between a deploy and an outage: on a termination signal, stop accepting new connections, finish in-flight requests, then exit — and the reason this matters is that without it, every deploy kills requests that are mid-flight and produces a burst of user-visible errors.

/* Validation. */
const VALIDATION = {
  rule: 'never trust the request body',
  why: 'everything in it came from OUTSIDE YOUR PROCESS and is attacker-controlled',
  means: ['a possible TYPE ERROR', 'an OVERSIZED STRING', 'a value OUTSIDE ITS RANGE',
    'a STRING THAT WILL BE RENDERED SOMEWHERE ELSE'],
  where: 'AT THE BOUNDARY, in middleware, before any handler runs',
  whyThere: 'a validation rule enforced in one handler and forgotten in nine is NINE VULNERABILITIES',
  gain: 'the boundary is the only place where the rule can be applied to ALL of them',
  checksSeparately: ['shape', 'type', 'range', 'length', 'format'],
  whySeparate: 'each catches a different mistake, and a TYPE CHECK DOES NOT STOP A MILLION-CHARACTER STRING',
  unknownFields: 'REJECT rather than ignore', status: 'the strictest and safest choice',
  whyReject: 'it surfaces client bugs IMMEDIATELY instead of silently',
  neverUseInputFor: ['a column name', 'a file path', 'a shell command', 'part of a query string'],
  reframe: 'a value that is meant to be DATA and is used as CODE is the injection class in the next chapter',
};

/* The router. */
const ROUTER = [
  { b: 'ROUTE ORDER', example: 'a parameterised route registered before a specific one',
    symptom: 'the specific path is captured as an item with the id of the specific segments name',
    fix: 'the SPECIFIC routes must come first', rank: 'the single most common Express routing bug' },
  { b: 'PARAMETER VALIDATION', detail: 'a route parameter is JUST AS UNTRUSTED as a body field and is usually not validated' },
  { b: 'FAT ROUTERS', detail: 'the routing layer contains business logic and the handlers do nothing',
    consequence: 'inverts the structure and makes the logic UNTESTABLE' },
  { b: 'HAND-WRITTEN REPETITION', detail: 'a route has five handlers that are the same five lines' },
];

/* Deployment shape. */
const DEPLOYMENT = [
  { s: 'a PROCESS PER INSTANCE behind a balancer' },
  { s: 'a REVERSE PROXY in front', for: ['TLS termination', 'static files'],
    why: 'doing TLS in the application means every request pays the handshake cost and every instance needs a certificate' },
  { s: 'HEALTH CHECKS on a separate path', detail: 'that CHECK DEPENDENCIES rather than returning 200 unconditionally' },
  { s: 'GRACEFUL SHUTDOWN', isThe: 'difference between a deploy and an outage',
    how: ['on a termination signal, stop accepting new connections', 'finish in-flight requests', 'then exit'],
    why: 'without it, EVERY DEPLOY KILLS REQUESTS THAT ARE MID-FLIGHT and produces a burst of user-visible errors' },
];

Never trust req.body — validate it. A "name" longer than 1,000,000 chars, or containing HTML you store and render later, is a real attack (Ch. 20). Validation at the boundary is not optional ceremony.

18.4 Error design & versioning

Error design and API versioning decide how resilient and evolvable your API stays. Errors should share one predictable envelope, typically JSON with a machine-readable code and a human message, and must never leak stack traces to clients. Version the API once someone consumes it, usually as a path prefix such as api/v1, and keep an OpenAPI spec so docs and clients stay honest.

// Consistent error shape helps every client
{
  "error": { "code": "USER_NOT_FOUND", "message": "No user with id 42" }
}
// codes = machine-readable, message = human, details = debugging hints

The response shape, and why one shape is worth enforcing

An API's error responses are its interface, and the reason most clients are fragile is not that the codes are wrong but that the shape varies. A client that has to check whether the body has error, or message, or detail, or whether the error is a string or an object, needs a branch for every endpoint it consumes. So: one shape, everywhere, always. The components worth having are: a machine-readable code that is a stable identifier and part of your contract — VALIDATION_FAILED, ORDER_NOT_FOUND, RATE_LIMITED, CONFLICT — and it must be stable, because clients branch on it and renaming it is a breaking change. A human-readable message for a developer looking at a log, and it is allowed to change at any time. An optional details object for structured specifics, such as which fields failed and why. And optionally a correlation identifier, which is the single highest-value field for debugging: when a user reports a failure, that identifier is the thread connecting their report to your logs, and without it the investigation is a search through a log aggregator hoping to find the right request by timestamp.

Then mapping failures onto codes, and the decisions involved. A validation failure is 422 in most modern APIs and 400 in older ones, and the distinction from a 400 is that a 400 means the request was malformed — unparseable, missing a required field entirely — while a 422 means it was well-formed but the content was unacceptable. A missing resource is 404. A conflict is 409, and it is the code most misused: it should mean the request cannot be applied to the current state, such as deleting an order that has shipped, or a unique constraint that already exists. An authentication failure is 401 and an authorization failure is 403, as covered. Rate limiting is 429 and it should include a header saying when to retry, so a client can back off correctly rather than guessing. And then the failures that are yours, not the caller's: a dependency that timed out is a 502 or a 504, not a 500, because the distinction tells the caller whether retrying is sensible; an unexpected exception is a 500 with a correlation identifier and nothing else in the body.

/* One shape, everywhere, always. */
const COMPONENTS = [
  { c: 'a MACHINE-READABLE CODE', is: 'a stable identifier and part of your contract',
    examples: ['VALIDATION_FAILED', 'ORDER_NOT_FOUND', 'RATE_LIMITED', 'CONFLICT'],
    mustBeStable: true,
    why: 'clients BRANCH ON IT, and renaming it is a BREAKING CHANGE' },
  { c: 'a HUMAN-READABLE MESSAGE', for: 'a developer looking at a log', mayChange: 'at any time' },
  { c: 'an optional DETAILS object', for: 'structured specifics such as which fields failed and why' },
  { c: 'a CORRELATION IDENTIFIER', optional: true, highestValue: true,
    for: 'when a user reports a failure, that identifier is the THREAD connecting their report to your logs',
    withoutIt: 'the investigation is a search through a log aggregator hoping to find the right request by timestamp' },
];
const WHY_ONE_SHAPE = 'a client that has to check whether the body has error, or message, or detail, or whether the error is a string or an object, needs A BRANCH FOR EVERY ENDPOINT it consumes';

/* Mapping failures onto codes. */
const MAPPING = [
  { f: 'a VALIDATION FAILURE', is: '422 in most modern APIs and 400 in older ones',
    distinction: 'a 400 means the request was MALFORMED - unparseable, missing a required field entirely',
    '422': 'well-formed but the CONTENT was unacceptable' },
  { f: 'a MISSING RESOURCE', code: '404' },
  { f: 'a CONFLICT', code: '409', mostMisused: true,
    means: 'the request cannot be applied to the CURRENT STATE',
    instances: ['deleting an order that has shipped', 'a unique constraint that already exists'] },
  { f: 'an AUTHENTICATION failure', code: '401' },
  { f: 'an AUTHORIZATION failure', code: '403' },
  { f: 'RATE LIMITING', code: '429', mustInclude: 'a header saying when to retry',
    why: 'so a client can back off correctly rather than GUESSING' },
  { f: 'a DEPENDENCY that timed out', code: '502 or 504, NOT 500',
    why: 'the distinction tells the caller whether RETRYING IS SENSIBLE' },
  { f: 'an UNEXPECTED EXCEPTION', code: '500', body: 'a correlation identifier and NOTHING ELSE' },
];

Design rules that keep clients working

Then the design rules that come out of this, and each one prevents a class of client breakage. Never change the meaning of an existing code or field. Add fields; do not repurpose them. A client that was written against a documented contract is a client you have broken silently every time you changed something. Version the API deliberately, either in the path or in a header, and the discipline is to keep serving the old version for as long as any client uses it — which means versioning is a maintenance commitment, not a change you can make in an afternoon. Make pagination consistent and documented, with one mechanism across every list endpoint, because pagination that differs per endpoint is pagination every client implements three times. Return the created resource from a creation, rather than a bare success, so the client does not need a second request to learn what was created — and if the identifier is server-generated, this is the only way the client learns it. Support filtering and sorting with the same query-parameter convention everywhere, and document the allowed values rather than accepting anything and failing. And include enough information in the response to let the client avoid a second request — that is not a performance trick, it is what makes an API pleasant to consume, and the corollary is that a client library that exists to work around your API is your API's fault.

/* Rules that prevent a class of client breakage. */
const DESIGN_RULES = [
  { r: 'never change the MEANING of an existing code or field', doInstead: 'add fields; do not REPURPOSE them',
    consequence: 'a client written against a documented contract is a client YOU HAVE BROKEN SILENTLY every time you changed something' },
  { r: 'version the API DELIBERATELY', where: ['in the path', 'in a header'],
    discipline: 'keep serving the old version for as long as any client uses it',
    reframe: 'versioning is a MAINTENANCE COMMITMENT, not a change you can make in an afternoon' },
  { r: 'make PAGINATION CONSISTENT and documented', how: 'one mechanism across every list endpoint',
    why: 'pagination that differs per endpoint is pagination EVERY CLIENT IMPLEMENTS THREE TIMES' },
  { r: 'return the CREATED RESOURCE from a creation', notInstead: 'a bare success',
    gain: 'the client does not need a second request to learn what was created',
    when: 'and if the identifier is server-generated, this is the ONLY WAY the client learns it' },
  { r: 'support FILTERING and SORTING with the same query-parameter convention everywhere',
    document: 'the ALLOWED VALUES rather than accepting anything and failing' },
  { r: 'include enough information in the response to let the client AVOID A SECOND REQUEST',
    notAPerformanceTrick: 'it is what makes an API PLEASANT TO CONSUME',
    corollary: 'a client library that exists to work around your API is YOUR APIs FAULT' },
];

A consistent JSON error shape: machine-readable codes plus human messages, so every client parses failures the same way.

  • Never return raw stack traces. Log them server-side; keep API responses clean.
  • Version your API (/v1/api/... or header) the moment anything might consume it — you will need to change it, and breaking every mobile client is a crisis.
  • Docs that stay true: OpenAPI (Swagger) specs let you generate docs and client SDKs from one source.

18.5 Authentication & authorization

Authentication is proving who you are; authorization is deciding what you are allowed to do. Sessions keep server-side state keyed by a cookie and revoke instantly, JWTs carry signed claims that scale across services but need care around expiry and revocation, and OAuth delegates identity to a third-party provider. Pick the trade-off that matches your need for statelessness versus the ability to kick someone out.

Two different questions: authN = "who are you?", authZ = "are you allowed to do this?".

TechniqueHowTrade-offs
Session + cookieServer stores session; browser sends cookie automaticallyTried, true; needs sticky or shared session store
JWTServer signs a token with claims; client sends it in AuthorizationStateless (great for scale); hard to revoke, keep expiry short
OAuth2 / OIDCDelegate to a provider ("Sign in with Google")Modern standard; complexity shifts but your risk drops
// A minimal password wash (NEVER store plaintext!):
const crypto = require("crypto");
function makeHash(password, salt = crypto.randomBytes(16).toString("hex")) {
  // 100k iterations: deliberately slow, to blunt brute-force attacks
  const hash = crypto.pbkdf2Sync(password, salt, 100000, 64, "sha256").toString("hex");
  return { salt, hash };
}
// Recompute with the stored salt and compare hashes. Constant-time compare!

Passwords are salted and hashed with pbkdf2 — deliberately slow to blunt brute force — and never stored as plaintext.

Authentication versus authorization, and sessions versus tokens

Two different questions, and conflating them is why access-control bugs exist. Authentication is who you are. Authorization is what you may do. A system can be perfectly authenticated and completely unauthorized — a logged-in user with no permission to delete — and the second is where every serious breach lives. Then the two ways to carry identity, and the trade is precise. Session cookies: the server holds the session state and the client holds an opaque identifier. Every request carries it automatically, which is what makes a browser experience easy; the cost is that the client must be stateful for the browser to send it, which brings back the exact thing REST said not to do, and which is why a token exists at all. Tokens: the client holds a signed assertion and the server verifies it without looking anything up. That makes the server stateless, and it makes revocation hard — a stateless token cannot be revoked before it expires, because there is nothing on the server that says "this one is cancelled". And the two failure modes to know: a stolen token is a valid credential until it expires, which is why token lifetime should be short, and tokens must be stored where scripts cannot read them, which is the storage chapter's argument repeated.

Then how to build this properly, and the specific rules. Hash passwords slowly and with a salt. This is the single most important rule in the section, and the reason is that a fast hash is a gift to an attacker: a database of password hashes is worth attacking precisely because passwords are low-entropy and reused, so a fast hash can be tested against a large wordlist at billions of attempts per second. A deliberately slow function with a per-password salt makes each attempt cost milliseconds, and the salt means one precomputed table does not work across accounts. Never a general-purpose hash — not MD5, not SHA-1, not even plain SHA-256, all of which are designed to be fast and therefore useless here. Never store a password, ever. Not encrypted, not reversibly; a hash is not encryption and cannot be decrypted. Compare with a constant-time comparison, because a byte-by-byte comparison returns early on the first difference and leaks how much of the guess was right through timing — a subtle attack but a real one. And rate-limit the login attempt, and return the same response whether the user exists or the password was wrong, because a different message for "no such user" enumerates your users for anybody who can send requests.

/* Two questions. */
const TWO = {
  authentication: 'WHO YOU ARE',
  authorization: 'WHAT YOU MAY DO',
  whyItMatters: 'a system can be perfectly authenticated and COMPLETELY UNAUTHORIZED - a logged-in user with no permission to delete',
  and: 'the second is where every serious breach lives',
};

/* Two ways to carry identity. */
const MECHANISMS = [
  { m: 'SESSION COOKIES', serverHolds: 'the session state', clientHolds: 'an opaque identifier',
    everyRequestCarriesIt: true, gain: 'which is what makes a browser experience easy',
    cost: 'the client must be STATEFUL for the browser to send it, which brings back the exact thing REST said not to do',
    whyThat: 'which is why a token exists at all' },
  { m: 'TOKENS', clientHolds: 'a signed assertion', serverDoes: 'verifies it WITHOUT LOOKING ANYTHING UP',
    gain: 'the server is stateless',
    cost: 'revocation is hard - a stateless token CANNOT BE REVOKED BEFORE IT EXPIRES, because there is nothing on the server saying this one is cancelled',
    twoFailureModes: ['a STOLEN TOKEN is a valid credential until it expires, which is why token lifetime should be short',
      'tokens must be stored where SCRIPTS CANNOT READ THEM'],
  },
];

/* How to build it properly. */
const RULES = [
  { r: 'hash passwords SLOWLY and with a SALT',
    mostImportant: true,
    whySlow: ['a fast hash is a GIFT TO AN ATTACKER',
      'a database of password hashes is worth attacking precisely because passwords are LOW-ENTROPY and REUSED',
      'so a fast hash can be tested against a large wordlist at BILLIONS OF ATTEMPTS PER SECOND'],
    gain: ['a deliberately slow function makes each attempt cost MILLISECONDS',
      'the salt means ONE PRECOMPUTED TABLE DOES NOT WORK across accounts'] },
  { r: 'never use a general-purpose hash', never: ['MD5', 'SHA-1', 'even plain SHA-256'],
    why: 'they are designed to be FAST and therefore useless here' },
  { r: 'NEVER STORE A PASSWORD, EVER', notEven: ['encrypted', 'reversibly'],
    clarification: 'a hash is not encryption and CANNOT BE DECRYPTED' },
  { r: 'compare with a CONSTANT-TIME comparison',
    why: 'a byte-by-byte comparison RETURNS EARLY on the first difference and leaks how much of the guess was right through timing',
    subtlety: 'a subtle attack but a real one' },
  { r: 'RATE-LIMIT the login attempt', and: 'return the SAME RESPONSE whether the user exists or the password was wrong',
    why: 'a different message for no such user ENUMERATES YOUR USERS for anybody who can send requests' },
];

Tokens, scopes, and the operational rules

Then tokens specifically, and the properties that decide the design. Signed means verifiable, not secret. The payload is readable by anyone holding it; what the signature guarantees is that it was not altered. So a token carrying a role and an expiry is fine and a token carrying a password is a leak. Short-lived, with a longer-lived refresh token. An access token lives for minutes and is verified on every request; a refresh token lives longer, is used only to obtain new access tokens, and — because it is long-lived — must be stored more carefully and revocable. That split is what makes short lifetimes workable. Scope: what the token can do. A token issued for reading should not be able to delete, and a token issued to one service should not be accepted by another. Then stateless versus server-side state, and the honest note: almost every production system keeps server-side state anyway — a revocation list, a token version, a session record — because statelessness was the goal and revocation turned out to be a requirement, and the resolution is stateless verification with a cheap check against a small amount of state. Then three operational rules. Never put anything sensitive in the payload. Revoke on password change and on logout, which requires the server-side state and is the reason it exists. And accept that a token is a credential with an expiry and treat it like one — which means never in a URL, because URLs are logged, because never in a local storage where a script can read it, and because a token in a URL ends up in a browser history and in a referrer header.

/* Token properties that decide the design. */
const PROPERTIES = [
  { p: 'SIGNED means VERIFIABLE, not secret',
    detail: 'the payload is READABLE by anyone holding it; the signature guarantees only that it was not ALTERED',
    fine: 'a token carrying a role and an expiry',
    wrong: 'a token carrying a PASSWORD is a leak' },
  { p: 'SHORT-LIVED, with a longer-lived refresh token',
    access: 'lives for MINUTES, verified on every request',
    refresh: 'lives longer, used ONLY to obtain new access tokens',
    refreshMustBe: ['stored more carefully', 'revocable'],
    gain: 'that split is what makes SHORT LIFETIMES WORKABLE' },
  { p: 'SCOPE: what the token can do',
    rules: ['a token issued for reading should not be able to DELETE',
      'a token issued to one service should not be accepted by ANOTHER'],
  },
];
const STATELESS_REALITY = {
  ideal: 'stateless verification',
  reality: 'almost every production system KEEPS SERVER-SIDE STATE ANYWAY',
  why: ['a revocation list', 'a token version', 'a session record'],
  whyTheIdealLost: 'statelessness was the goal and REVOCATION turned out to be a requirement',
  resolution: 'stateless verification with a CHEAP CHECK against a SMALL AMOUNT OF STATE',
};

/* Operational rules. */
const OPERATIONAL = [
  { r: 'never put anything SENSITIVE in the payload' },
  { r: 'REVOKE on password change and on logout',
    requires: 'the server-side state',
    note: 'which is the reason it exists' },
  { r: 'accept that a token is a CREDENTIAL WITH AN EXPIRY and treat it like one',
    never: ['in a URL - URLs are LOGGED',
      'in a local storage where a script can read it',
      'in a URL at all, because a token in a URL ends up in BROWSER HISTORY and in a REFERRER HEADER'],
  },
];

60% of data breaches start with leaked credentials. Use a proper slow-key-derivation function (bcrypt/argon2/pbkdf2), never MD5/SHA1 of the password. Rate-limit login (429) to blunt brute-force.

18.6 From one app to a system

Where the boundaries go, and what decides them

The chapter's job is to explain why a system is split the way it is, and the honest answer is that boundaries are decided by what changes together and what must be independently reliable — not by an architectural diagram drawn in advance. Two things should live together because they change for the same reasons and are hard to separate safely: a piece of data and the rule that governs it, and two pieces of logic that must be consistent with each other in order to be correct at all. Two things should be separated because their failure modes differ or because they scale differently: a cache and the thing it caches, a web tier and a worker, a synchronous request path and an asynchronous one. The common error is separating things that must stay consistent — putting validation in one service and the invariant it protects in another — because then no single transaction can enforce the rule and the invariant is enforced by convention. Then the two boundaries that matter most in a typical application, and what belongs on each side. What belongs in the web tier: authentication, authorisation, validation, request shaping, response shaping, and rate limiting. Everything there is about the request and must complete synchronously, because the client is waiting. What belongs behind it: business rules, data access, and anything slow. And the rule for deciding: if it can be retried later, it does not belong in the request path, because a request path that includes slow work has a latency the client experiences and a failure mode that takes the request down with it.

Then the three shapes most systems take, and each is right for a reason. Monolith with a modular interior: one deployable, internally layered, with the layers treated as boundaries because the code enforces them. This is the right answer more often than the industry admits, because it eliminates every distributed-systems problem while you are still learning the domain, and a monolith whose modules are well separated can be split later — whereas a distributed system built prematurely has distributed all the difficulty and none of the benefits. Services with a clear split: each deployable owns its data and is responsible for its availability. The benefit is independent deployment and independent scaling; the costs are every call is now a network call, cross-service transactions no longer exist, and a single service's outage becomes the whole system's outage unless you degrade gracefully. Event-driven: producers publish facts and consumers react, which decouples them in time as well as in deployment. The benefit is that a slow consumer does not block the producer; the costs are that the data becomes eventually consistent, that debugging a chain of events across five services is genuinely difficult, and that you now need to reason about ordering and duplicates.

/* Boundaries are decided by two questions. */
const DECIDED_BY = {
  whatChangesTogether: 'a piece of data and the rule that governs it; two pieces of logic that must be CONSISTENT to be correct at all',
  whatMustBeIndependent: 'a cache and the thing it caches; a web tier and a worker; a synchronous request path and an asynchronous one',
  notThis: 'not by an architectural diagram drawn in advance',
};
const COMMON_ERROR = {
  error: 'separating things that MUST STAY CONSISTENT',
  example: 'putting validation in one service and the invariant it protects in another',
  consequence: 'NO SINGLE TRANSACTION can enforce the rule, and the invariant is enforced by CONVENTION',
};
/* What belongs on each side. */
const WEB_TIER = {
  belongs: ['authentication', 'authorisation', 'validation', 'request shaping', 'response shaping', 'rate limiting'],
  why: 'everything there is about the REQUEST and must complete SYNCHRONOUSLY, because the client is waiting',
};
const BEHIND_IT = {
  belongs: ['business rules', 'data access', 'anything slow'],
  theRule: 'if it can be retried LATER, it does not belong in the request path',
  why: 'a request path that includes slow work has a LATENCY THE CLIENT EXPERIENCES and a failure mode that takes the request down with it',
};

/* Three shapes. */
const SHAPES = [
  { shape: 'MONOLITH with a modular interior', is: 'one deployable, internally layered, with the layers treated as boundaries because the code enforces them',
    rightAnswerMoreOftenThanAdmitted: true,
    why: ['it ELIMINATES every distributed-systems problem while you are still learning the domain',
      'a monolith whose modules are well separated CAN BE SPLIT LATER',
      'whereas a distributed system built prematurely has distributed all the DIFFICULTY and none of the BENEFITS'] },
  { shape: 'SERVICES with a clear split', each: 'owns its data and is responsible for its availability',
    benefits: ['independent deployment', 'independent scaling'],
    costs: ['every call is now a NETWORK CALL', 'cross-service TRANSACTIONS NO LONGER EXIST',
      'a single services outage becomes the whole systems outage unless you DEGRADE GRACEFULLY'] },
  { shape: 'EVENT-DRIVEN', does: 'producers publish facts and consumers react',
    benefit: 'decouples them IN TIME as well as in deployment, so a SLOW CONSUMER DOES NOT BLOCK THE PRODUCER',
    costs: ['the data becomes EVENTUALLY CONSISTENT', 'debugging a chain of events across five services is GENUINELY DIFFICULT',
      'you now need to reason about ORDERING AND DUPLICATES'],
  },
];

Synchronous versus asynchronous, and the failure modes to design for

Then the synchronous-versus-asynchronous boundary, because it is the most consequential architectural line in a typical system and it is usually drawn in the wrong place. Synchronous work is on the request path: the client is waiting, so its latency is your latency and its failure is the user's failure. Asynchronous work is off it: the client gets an acknowledgement and the work happens later. The rule that decides is worth stating precisely: if the user must see the result, it is synchronous; if they only need to know it started, it is asynchronous. And then the operational consequence, which is where this bites: the request path must contain nothing slow — no email, no report, no image processing, no call to a third party whose latency you do not control. Each of those turns your latency into a function of someone else's uptime, and the arithmetic is unforgiving: ten dependencies at 200 milliseconds each, even in parallel, is a request that is slow enough that users will notice and that a small drop in any one dependency pushes past what a browser will wait for. Then what asynchronous work requires that people forget: a queue, a worker, and a way to know what happened. The queue is where the work waits; the worker is what consumes it and must handle the work being consumed twice, because a worker that crashes after doing the work but before marking it done will process it again — so every job needs to be idempotent, which is the same requirement as the retry section and for the same reason. And observability: a job queue turns a synchronous failure into an asynchronous one, which means the failure now appears in a log nobody is watching. The queue needs a depth metric, an age metric for the oldest pending job, and a failure count, and a job that has been stuck for an hour must be visible as an alert rather than as a surprise.

/* The most consequential line in a typical system. */
const SYNC_VS_ASYNC = {
  synchronous: 'on the request path - the client is waiting, so its latency is YOUR latency and its failure is the USERS failure',
  asynchronous: 'off it - the client gets an acknowledgement and the work happens later',
  theRule: 'if the user MUST SEE THE RESULT it is synchronous; if they only need to know it STARTED it is asynchronous',
};
const SLOW_IN_REQUEST_PATH = {
  rule: 'the request path must contain NOTHING SLOW',
  instances: ['email', 'a report', 'image processing', 'a call to a third party whose latency you do not control'],
  why: 'each turns YOUR LATENCY into a function of SOMEONE ELSES UPTIME',
  arithmetic: 'ten dependencies at 200 milliseconds each, even in parallel, is a request that is SLOW ENOUGH that users will notice',
  and: 'a small drop in any one dependency pushes past what a BROWSER WILL WAIT FOR',
};

/* What asynchronous work requires. */
const ASYNC_REQUIRES = {
  three: ['a QUEUE - where the work waits', 'a WORKER - what consumes it',
    'a way to know WHAT HAPPENED'],
  idempotence: {
    requirement: 'a worker that CRASHES AFTER DOING THE WORK but before marking it done will process it AGAIN',
    therefore: 'every job needs to be IDEMPOTENT',
    connectsTo: 'the retry section, and for the same reason',
  },
  observability: {
    problem: 'a job queue turns a SYNCHRONOUS FAILURE into an ASYNCHRONOUS one, which means the failure now appears in a LOG NOBODY IS WATCHING',
    needs: ['a depth metric', 'an AGE METRIC for the oldest pending job', 'a failure count'],
    alertOn: 'a job that has been STUCK FOR AN HOUR must be visible as an alert rather than as a surprise',
  },
};

Growing from one app to a system means dividing responsibilities so the codebase stays testable and scalable. MVC separates models, views, and controller logic; a service layer isolates business logic from HTTP so it can be tested without the web server; and job queues move slow work such as emails and image processing out of the request path. Each layer communicates through stable interfaces and stays replaceable.

  • MVC (Model-View-Controller) — separate data (model), rendering (view), and logic (controller). The first architecture you’ll see in every framework.
  • Service layer — business logic between API and data; easy to test without HTTP.
  • Background work: emails, image processing, reports → a job queue (Redis/queue), not the request path. Requests stay fast; work happens in workers (Ch. 21).

18.7 Hardening a production API

The gap between works on my machine and survives real traffic is a list of engineering disciplines: paginate every list endpoint, make mutating operations idempotent so retries are safe, rate-limit abusive clients, set timeouts and circuit breakers so one slow dependency cannot stall everything, and expose health checks that monitors, load balancers, and orchestrators can probe. Apply them as a checklist to every service you deploy.

The gap between "works on my machine" and "survives real traffic" is a list of disciplines. Apply each one, in roughly this order of pain:

// Middleware order that sane APIs use:
// 1. Request logging  ->  attach request ID (correlates logs across services)
// 2. Rate limiting    ->  429 when a client exceeds a per-window budget
// 3. AuthN/AuthZ      ->  reject unknown callers before any work
// 4. Input validation ->  assert shape/types/ranges at the border
// 5. Route + handler  ->  the actual logic
// 6. Error handler    ->  map exceptions to clean HTTP responses + log

Configuration, secrets, and the boundaries that leak

Hardening is a set of defaults that cost nothing and prevent whole categories of incident. Configuration comes from the environment, never from a file in the repository, for two separate reasons: a secret in the repository is in the history forever, and the same built artefact must run in several environments. A configuration value is validated at startup, and the process refuses to start if it is missing or malformed — which is the single highest-value line of defence in this section, because a process that starts with a default and silently misbehaves is a process that fails on the customer's server rather than yours. Fail fast, fail loudly, and never fail open on a security control. Then secrets, and the rules that have become standard because their absence is catastrophic. Never in the repository, including in a file that is later deleted. Never in the container image, because the image is a layer and every copy of it contains the layer — an environment variable at run time is what separates one deployment from another. Never logged, including indirectly: a library that logs a configuration object on startup will log your secret, so either redact the value or do not log the object. And rotate them, and know that rotation is only real if every consumer reads from the new place — a rotation that does not restart every process leaves half your fleet using the old secret, which is a worse state than never rotating.

Then the input and output boundaries, which are where most of the concrete attacks live. Validate every input, at the boundary, with an allow-list rather than a deny-list. The distinction matters more than anything else here: a deny-list enumerates the bad values, and the person attacking you did not read your list, so a deny-list always misses something; an allow-list says what is acceptable, and anything not named is rejected by default. Parameterise every query — and this is not a style preference, it is the difference between a value and code, as the next chapter is entirely about. Escape on output, for the context you are writing into. Escaping for HTML is not escaping for an attribute, not escaping for JavaScript and not escaping for a URL, and a value placed in the wrong context is a vulnerability even if it was escaped for the right one. Set the security headers, and each has a specific attack it prevents: a content-type policy stops content being interpreted as a script; a frame policy stops your page being embedded; a content-security-policy stops injected scripts from running at all, which is the single most effective header and also the hardest to deploy; a referrer policy stops URLs with tokens in them leaking to third parties; and HttpOnly on cookies is what makes a stolen cookie less useful.

/* Configuration. */
const CONFIG = {
  from: 'the ENVIRONMENT, never from a file in the repository',
  twoReasons: ['a secret in the repository is IN THE HISTORY FOREVER',
    'the same built artefact must run in SEVERAL ENVIRONMENTS'],
  validatedAtStartup: true,
  onInvalid: 'the process REFUSES TO START',
  rank: 'the single highest-value line of defence in this section',
  why: 'a process that starts with a default and silently misbehaves is a process that FAILS ON THE CUSTOMERS SERVER rather than yours',
  rule: 'fail FAST, fail LOUDLY, and never FAIL OPEN on a security control',
};

/* Secrets. */
const SECRETS = [
  { r: 'never IN THE REPOSITORY', including: 'a file that is later deleted' },
  { r: 'never IN THE CONTAINER IMAGE', why: 'the image is a LAYER and every copy of it contains the layer',
    instead: 'an environment variable at run time is what separates one deployment from another' },
  { r: 'never LOGGED', including: 'INDIRECTLY',
    detail: 'a library that logs a configuration object on startup will log your secret',
    fix: ['redact the value', 'do not log the object'] },
  { r: 'ROTATE them', and: 'know that rotation is only real if EVERY CONSUMER READS FROM THE NEW PLACE',
    consequence: 'a rotation that does not restart every process leaves HALF YOUR FLEET on the old secret',
    worseThanNeverRotating: true },
];

/* Input and output boundaries. */
const BOUNDARIES = [
  { r: 'validate every input, at the boundary',
    with: 'an ALLOW-LIST rather than a deny-list',
    why: ['a deny-list ENUMERATES the bad values, and the person attacking you did not read your list',
      'so a deny-list ALWAYS MISSES something',
      'an allow-list says what is acceptable, and anything not named is REJECTED BY DEFAULT'] },
  { r: 'PARAMETERISE every query', notAStylePreference: true,
    why: 'it is the difference between a VALUE and CODE, as the next chapter is entirely about' },
  { r: 'escape ON OUTPUT, for the CONTEXT you are writing into',
    detail: ['escaping for HTML is not escaping for an attribute', 'not escaping for JavaScript',
      'not escaping for a URL'],
    consequence: 'a value placed in the WRONG CONTEXT is a vulnerability even if it was escaped for the right one' },
