const SECURITY_HEADERS = [
  { h: 'content-type policy', prevents: 'content being interpreted as a SCRIPT' },
  { h: 'frame policy', prevents: 'your page being EMBEDDED' },
  { h: 'content-security-policy', prevents: 'INJECTED SCRIPTS FROM RUNNING AT ALL',
    rank: 'the single most effective header and also the HARDEST TO DEPLOY' },
  { h: 'referrer policy', prevents: 'URLS WITH TOKENS in them leaking to third parties' },
  { h: 'HttpOnly on cookies', effect: 'what makes a STOLEN COOKIE LESS USEFUL' },
];

Timeouts, retries, and the dependencies you do not control

Then timeouts, which is the hardening item most often missing and the one that converts a dependency outage into an outage of your own. Every network call needs a timeout, without exception, and the reason is structural: a call with no timeout does not fail, it waits forever, and a handler that waits forever holds a connection, holds a thread, and eventually exhausts whatever bounds it — so a slow dependency becomes resource exhaustion in your service and the failure spreads from one place to everywhere. The timeout must be shorter than the caller's own timeout, and shorter than any request deadline upstream, because otherwise your caller's deadline expires first and the work is wasted. Set a deadline rather than a duration where you can, so that a chain of calls shares one budget rather than each taking its own maximum — this is the difference between a total operation bounded by one timeout and one bounded by the sum of six. And connect and read timeouts are different: a connect timeout guards against a host that is unreachable, and a read timeout guards against a host that accepted the connection and is then silent, and only setting the connect one leaves the second case uncovered.

Then retries, and this is where hardening goes wrong if you are not careful, because retrying is not always safe and an unbounded retry is worse than no retry. Retry only idempotent operations, or operations with an idempotency key — a retried payment that is not idempotent is a double charge, and this is the single most expensive consequence of an indiscriminate retry policy. Use exponential backoff with jitter, because a fixed delay synchronises every client and produces a repeating thundering herd that never subsides, and jitter is what breaks the synchronisation. Bound the number of attempts, and make the final failure propagate rather than being swallowed — a retry wrapper that returns a plausible-looking empty result on final failure converts a clear error into silent data loss, which is far worse and much harder to diagnose. And never retry inside a loop you do not control, because the effective retry count becomes the product of two loops and nobody knows what it is. The summary that covers all of it: retries are for transient failures, which means you must distinguish transient from permanent — a connection refused will not fix itself, a 400 will never fix itself, a 503 or a dropped connection probably will, and a policy that retries everything turns a permanent failure into a sustained load on a dependency that is already struggling.

/* Timeouts - most often missing, and it spreads the failure. */
const TIMEOUTS = {
  rule: 'EVERY NETWORK CALL NEEDS A TIMEOUT, without exception',
  whyStructural: ['a call with no timeout does not FAIL, it WAITS FOREVER',
    'a handler that waits forever holds a connection and holds a thread',
    'and eventually exhausts whatever bounds it',
    'so a SLOW DEPENDENCY BECOMES RESOURCE EXHAUSTION in your service',
    'and the failure spreads from one place to EVERYWHERE'],
  shorterThan: ['the callers own timeout', 'any request deadline upstream'],
  whyShorter: 'otherwise your callers deadline EXPIRES FIRST and the work is wasted',
  deadlineNotDuration: {
    prefer: 'a deadline where you can',
    gain: 'a chain of calls SHARES ONE BUDGET rather than each taking its own maximum',
    difference: 'a total operation bounded by ONE timeout versus one bounded by THE SUM OF SIX',
  },
  twoKinds: ['CONNECT timeout - guards against a host that is UNREACHABLE',
    'READ timeout - guards against a host that ACCEPTED THE CONNECTION and is then SILENT',
    note: 'setting only the connect one leaves the second case uncovered'],
};

/* Retries. */
const RETRIES = {
  warning: 'retrying is not always safe, and an UNBOUNDED RETRY IS WORSE THAN NO RETRY',
  rules: [
    { r: 'retry only IDEMPOTENT operations, or operations with an idempotency key',
      consequence: 'a retried payment that is not idempotent is a DOUBLE CHARGE',
      rank: 'the single most expensive consequence of an indiscriminate retry policy' },
    { r: 'exponential backoff WITH JITTER',
      whyJitter: 'a fixed delay SYNCHRONISES EVERY CLIENT and produces a repeating thundering herd that never subsides',
      detail: 'jitter is what breaks the synchronisation' },
    { r: 'BOUND the number of attempts, and make the final failure PROPAGATE rather than being swallowed',
      bug: 'a retry wrapper that returns a plausible-looking EMPTY RESULT on final failure converts a clear error into SILENT DATA LOSS',
      worse: 'which is far worse and much harder to diagnose' },
    { r: 'never retry INSIDE A LOOP YOU DO NOT CONTROL', why: 'the effective retry count becomes the PRODUCT OF TWO LOOPS and nobody knows what it is' },
  ],
  summary: 'retries are for TRANSIENT failures, which means you must DISTINGUISH TRANSIENT FROM PERMANENT',
  classified: ['a connection refused will not fix itself', 'a 400 will never fix itself',
    'a 503 or a dropped connection probably will'],
  danger: 'a policy that retries everything turns a PERMANENT FAILURE into a SUSTAINED LOAD on a dependency that is already struggling',
};
The ordered middleware chain a sane API applies: logging with request IDs, rate limiting, auth, validation, handler, and a central error handler.

  • Pagination on every list endpoint — ?limit=&cursor= (keyset, Ch. 13.2) or limit/offset; cap the limit.
  • Idempotency keys for mutations: client sends Idempotency-Key; your server deduplicates retries. Without it, a network hiccup after a payment can double-charge.
  • Rate limits with clear Retry-After, per-user and per-IP, plus exponential backoff on the client side.
  • Timeout everywhere outbound — a backend that waits forever on a dead dependency queues up and melts.
  • Health & readiness endpoints (/healthz) that load balancers probe.
# A tiny retry-with-backoff you'll re-write constantly
def call_with_retry(fn, attempts=3, base_delay=0.1):
    for attempt in range(attempts):
        try:
            return fn()
        except Exception:
            if attempt == attempts - 1:
                raise                              # last attempt: surface the error
            time.sleep(base_delay * (2 ** attempt))   # 0.1s, 0.2s, 0.4s

A tiny retry wrapper with exponential backoff that re-raises after the final attempt instead of hiding the failure.

18.8 Rate limiting, retries & graceful degradation

APIs are damaged by floods, both accidental and deliberate, so production systems shape their own load. Token buckets or sliding windows cap requests per client, retries use exponential backoff with jitter, and graceful degradation sheds non-critical work first, with loud error signals, while the essential path stays up. Combined, they keep the service alive for everyone else even under attack.

APIs die from floods, not malice: one buggy client, one viral link, one misconfigured webhook. Rate limiting is the guardrail that keeps the service alive for everyone else.

# Token bucket -- the classic, simple, burst-friendly:
class TokenBucket:
    def __init__(self, capacity, refill_per_sec):
        self.cap = capacity; self.refill = refill_per_sec
        self.tokens = capacity; self.ts = time.time()
    def allow(self):
        now = time.time()
        self.tokens = min(self.cap, self.tokens + (now - self.ts) * self.refill)
        self.ts = now
        if self.tokens >= 1:  self.tokens -= 1; return True
        return False
# Deploy as a separate layer (nginx/Redis) so the app code stays simple.
# Reply 429 + Retry-After header -- and NEVER silently drop: tell the client.

# Retries are a band-aid with physics: exponential backoff + JITTER
# (3 tries, 1s/2s/4s + random 0-1s) so a herd doesn't all retry at once
# (that deliberate stampede is called "thundering herd").

# Graceful degradation: when a dependency is down, degrade loudly but
# keep the product up (stale cache + "last updated 3m ago"), rather than
# erroring the whole page. Same idea as circuit breakers in Ch.29.6.

A token-bucket rate limiter to run as its own layer: reply 429 with Retry-After, back off with jitter, and degrade loudly rather than die.

Why rate limiting is a security control, not a courtesy

A rate limit is the only control that protects against the attacks no amount of input validation will stop, because those attacks use valid input, correctly formed, sent many times. Brute-force authentication succeeds not because the password was weak but because thousands of guesses were tried. Credential stuffing succeeds because a list of known-breached passwords was tried against thousands of accounts. Resource exhaustion succeeds because a cheap request was made a hundred thousand times. In all three the payload is legitimate and only the volume is the attack — so validation sees nothing wrong, and only a limit sees it. That is the framing that makes rate limiting a security control: it defends the property that matters, which is that a resource is consumed at a rate a human can produce.

Then the three dimensions you can limit, and which each one protects. By client identity — by API key, or by user after authentication. This is the useful one for abuse and the one that fails against a botnet, because a botnet has thousands of identities. By source address, which stops one attacker and is what every basic limit does. Its weakness is worth stating precisely because it produces a genuine trade-off: it punishes shared addresses. A corporate network behind one address, a university, a mobile carrier's network-to-network gateway, and a household behind carrier-grade NAT all present one address for hundreds or thousands of real users, so an address-based limit set conservatively will block legitimate users, and the usual resolution is to limit by address and to let authenticated clients carry a much higher allowance, which is a real design decision rather than a compromise. And by cost, — an expensive endpoint has a lower allowance than a cheap one, and this is the most honest of the three because it does not depend on knowing who the caller is.

Then the algorithms, and the difference that matters. Fixed window: count requests in each clock interval and reset. One line of code, and it has two exploitable flaws. Token bucket: a bucket holds tokens, a request consumes one, tokens are added at a steady rate, and the bucket has a capacity — so a client may burst up to the capacity and then proceeds at the refill rate. Sliding window: count requests over the trailing interval rather than a fixed one. The flaws of the fixed window are worth naming because they are real: a client can send double the intended rate by spending the whole allowance at the end of one window and the whole allowance at the start of the next, and the limit is therefore not the limit the operator intended; and a fixed boundary produces a thundering herd, where every client that was blocked retries at the same instant the window resets. Token bucket handles both — the burst is bounded by capacity and the refill is continuous — which is why it is the algorithm most libraries implement and the right default.

/* Defends against attacks validation will never stop. */
const WHY_SECURITY = {
  attacks: ['brute-force authentication succeeds not because the password was weak but because THOUSANDS OF GUESSES WERE TRIED',
    'credential stuffing succeeds because a list of known-breached passwords was tried against thousands of accounts',
    'resource exhaustion succeeds because a CHEAP REQUEST was made a hundred thousand times'],
  commonFeature: 'the payload is LEGITIMATE and only the VOLUME is the attack',
  therefore: 'validation sees nothing wrong, and only a limit sees it',
  theProperty: 'a resource is consumed at a rate A HUMAN CAN PRODUCE',
  reframe: 'this is what makes rate limiting a SECURITY CONTROL',
};

/* Three dimensions. */
const DIMENSIONS = [
  { d: 'by CLIENT IDENTITY', by: ['an API key', 'a user after authentication'],
    useFor: 'abuse', failsAgainst: 'a botnet, because a botnet has THOUSANDS OF IDENTITIES' },
  { d: 'by SOURCE ADDRESS', stops: 'one attacker', note: 'this is what every basic limit does',
    theWeakness: 'it PUNISHES SHARED ADDRESSES',
    whoIsShared: ['a corporate network behind one address', 'a university',
      'a mobile carriers network-to-network gateway', 'a household behind carrier-grade NAT'],
    magnitude: 'one address for HUNDREDS or THOUSANDS of real users',
    consequence: 'a conservative limit blocks legitimate users',
    resolution: 'limit by address AND give authenticated clients a much higher allowance',
    isA: 'REAL DESIGN DECISION rather than a compromise' },
  { d: 'by COST', detail: 'an expensive endpoint has a lower allowance than a cheap one',
    mostHonest: true, why: 'it does not depend on knowing WHO THE CALLER IS' },
];

/* Algorithms. */
const ALGORITHMS = [
  { a: 'FIXED WINDOW', does: 'count requests in each clock interval and reset',
    lines: 'one line of code', exploitable: true,
    flaws: ['a client can send DOUBLE THE INTENDED RATE by spending the whole allowance at the end of one window and the whole allowance at the start of the next',
      'the limit is therefore NOT THE LIMIT THE OPERATOR INTENDED',
      'a fixed boundary produces a THUNDERING HERD, where every client that was blocked retries at the same instant the window resets'] },
  { a: 'TOKEN BUCKET', does: 'a bucket holds tokens, a request consumes one, tokens are added at a steady rate, and the bucket has a CAPACITY',
    permits: 'a client may BURST up to the capacity and then proceeds at the refill rate',
    handlesBothFlaws: ['the burst is bounded by capacity', 'the refill is continuous'],
    status: 'the algorithm most libraries implement, and THE RIGHT DEFAULT' },
  { a: 'SLIDING WINDOW', does: 'count requests over the TRAILING interval rather than a fixed one',
    trade: 'more accurate and more memory',
    comparedToFixed: 'removes the double-rate burst at the cost of needing per-client state over the interval' },
];

Responding, storing state, and the headers that help

Then how to respond, and this is part of the mechanism rather than a detail. Return 429 when limiting and set a Retry-After header saying how long to wait — without that header a client cannot back off correctly and will retry immediately, which makes the situation worse rather than better and can produce a self-sustaining overload. Then where the count is stored, and the choice is a real architectural decision. In the process's memory is the simplest and is wrong in a scaled system, because each process counts separately and the effective limit is the per-process limit multiplied by the number of processes — so a limit of ten per minute across ten processes permits a hundred, which is exactly the class of mistake that makes limits unreliable in the systems where they matter. In a shared store — Redis is the usual choice — is correct and adds a network call to every request, which is why the store must be in the request path only if the limit must be global; an alternative is to limit per instance with a deliberately conservative per-instance number so the cluster total is the intended figure. And the store's own availability becomes part of your availability, which is the argument for failing open rather than closed: if the limiter is down and you fail closed, a limiter outage becomes a total outage.

Then the client-facing headers that let a well-behaved client cooperate, and the ones worth knowing by name. Retry-After, saying when to retry, in either seconds or a date. X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining and X-RateLimit-Reset, which let a client pace itself without being rejected — this is the difference between a client that throttles gracefully and one that discovers the limit by being blocked. And RateLimit and RateLimit-Policy, the newer standardised version of those headers, which are worth preferring for new APIs because they describe the policy rather than one measurement. And then the discipline that makes this work rather than being set and forgotten: set different limits per endpoint by cost, set a separate and much stricter limit on authentication, and monitor how many times the limit is actually hit — because a limit that is never hit is either wrong or unnecessary, and a limit that is constantly hit is either correct or the reason your users are unhappy, and you cannot tell which without looking.

/* Responding is part of the mechanism. */
const RESPOND = {
  code: 429, header: 'Retry-After saying how long to wait',
  withoutTheHeader: 'a client cannot back off correctly and will RETRY IMMEDIATELY',
  consequence: 'which makes the situation WORSE rather than better and can produce a SELF-SUSTAINING OVERLOAD',
};

/* Where the count is stored. */
const STORAGE = [
  { where: 'in the PROCESSES MEMORY', simple: true, wrongInScaledSystems: true,
    why: 'each process counts separately and the effective limit is the PER-PROCESS LIMIT MULTIPLIED BY THE NUMBER OF PROCESSES',
    arithmetic: 'a limit of ten per minute across ten processes permits a HUNDRED',
    consequence: 'exactly the class of mistake that makes limits UNRELIABLE in the systems where they matter' },
  { where: 'in a SHARED STORE', note: 'Redis is the usual choice',
    correct: true, cost: 'a network call on every request',
    whenRequired: 'only if the limit must be GLOBAL',
    alternative: 'limit per instance with a DELIBERATELY CONSERVATIVE per-instance number so the cluster total is the intended figure' },
  { where: 'the STORES OWN AVAILABILITY BECOMES PART OF YOUR AVAILABILITY',
    therefore: 'fail OPEN rather than closed',
    why: 'if the limiter is down and you fail closed, a limiter outage becomes a TOTAL OUTAGE' },
];

/* Client-facing headers. */
const HEADERS = [
  { h: 'Retry-After', says: 'when to retry', in: 'either seconds or a date' },
  { h: 'X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining and X-RateLimit-Reset',
    gain: 'let a client PACE ITSELF without being rejected',
    difference: 'the difference between a client that throttles gracefully and one that DISCOVERS THE LIMIT BY BEING BLOCKED' },
  { h: 'RateLimit and RateLimit-Policy', isThe: 'newer standardised version',
    prefer: 'for new APIs because they describe the POLICY rather than one measurement' },
];
const DISCIPLINE = [
  'set DIFFERENT LIMITS PER ENDPOINT BY COST',
  'set a separate and MUCH STRICTER limit on authentication',
  'monitor how many times the limit is ACTUALLY HIT',
  because: ['a limit that is never hit is either WRONG OR UNNECESSARY',
    'a limit that is constantly hit is either correct or the reason your users are unhappy',
    'and you cannot tell which without looking'],
};

  2. Write a minimal integration test that boots the app, POSTs, then GETs (superagent or fetch) and asserts status codes.

19 · Clean Code, SOLID & Design Patterns

19.1 The art of readable code19.2 SOLID — five rules of changeable design19.3 The patterns that pay rent19.4 The other paradigm: functional thinking

Clean Code, SOLID and Design Patterns is about writing code that can change without breaking. The chapter covers the SOLID principles that reveal when a design resists change, the reusable shapes known as design patterns, functional thinking, and the discipline of readable names and small functions. These habits compound into a codebase that welcomes the next feature instead of fighting it.

Senior software is not "more clever" code; it’s code structured so it can change without breaking. This chapter teaches the principles (SOLID), the reusable shapes (patterns), and the discipline to keep code clean as it grows.

19.1 The art of readable code

Readable code is a set of habits, not a gift: names that say what a thing means, short functions that do one job, comments that explain why rather than what, and small reviewable commits and pull requests. Aim for code that reads like prose, with the happy path visible and surprises minimized. These habits deliver most of the maintainability a codebase will ever have.

  • Names are 80% of readability. price_before_tax, send_invoice(user) explain intent; x, doStuff() force the reader to reverse-engineer.
  • Short functions, one job each. If a function needs a "what this part does" comment, extract that part into a named function.
  • Comment the why, not the what. # keep outer join: NULL stocks historically valid is gold; # add 1 is noise.
  • Small PRs. A 50-line change gets reviewed properly; a 2000-line one gets skimmed and leaks bugs.
# Hard to read
def f(d):
    return sum(i * (1 - 0.1) for i in d if i > 100)

# Reads like prose
def discounted_total(prices):
    DISCOUNT_RATE = 0.10                    # name explains the magic number
    eligible = [p for p in prices if p > 100]
    return sum(eligible) * (1 - DISCOUNT_RATE)

Naming, which is where most of the readability lives

A program is read far more often than it is written, and the first thing a reader encounters is names. The rules are short and the effects are large. Name things after what they mean, not what they are. user_list not l; retry_count not n; a boolean named is_valid rather than check, because the second tells the reader nothing about what true means. Make the units and the scope visible in the name. timeout_ms and timeout_seconds are different values and the bug is prevented by the name. Do not encode the type in the name when the language has types — age_string in a typed language is noise, while age_years in an untyped one is essential. Names should be sentences at the call site. The test is whether reading the call aloud tells you what happens: if user.is_eligible_for_discount(): is a sentence; if check(u): is not. Boolean names should read as conditions, with a prefix that makes them unambiguous — is_, has_, can_, should_ — because enabled in a list of five settings is unreadable while is_dark_mode_enabled is not. And avoid the same word for two different things, which is the most damaging naming mistake there is, because a reader who sees user in one place will reasonably assume it means the same thing everywhere.

Then the four smells, and each has a mechanical fix rather than a matter of taste. Duplicated code: the same logic in two places is two places to change and one place somebody will not. The fix is not always a function — sometimes the duplication is the lesser evil, and three similar lines that are each obvious beat one abstraction that must be read carefully — but the rule of three is a useful heuristic: after the third occurrence, the duplication is likely to be a missing concept. Long functions: a function that does five things is five functions, and the test is not the line count but whether you can name its steps; if naming them requires reading the body, the names do not exist yet. Long parameter lists: five parameters usually means the function does five things, or that the parameters belong together in an object — and the signal is that callers must remember an ordering. Feature envy: a method that reaches into another object's data more than its own has the logic in the wrong place, and the fix is to move it, not to add a getter. And the comment that explains what rather than why, which is the classic: a comment restating the code is noise that goes stale, while a comment explaining why an unusual decision was made is the only comment that earns its place, and the test is whether deleting it would leave a reader puzzled.

/* Naming - where most of the readability lives. */
const NAMING = [
  { r: 'name things after WHAT THEY MEAN, not what they are',
    examples: ['user_list not l', 'retry_count not n', 'is_valid rather than check'],
    why: 'the second tells the reader NOTHING about what true means' },
  { r: 'make the UNITS AND THE SCOPE visible', examples: ['timeout_ms', 'timeout_seconds'],
    gain: 'they are different values and the bug is PREVENTED BY THE NAME' },
  { r: 'do NOT encode the type in the name when the language has types',
    noise: 'age_string in a typed language',
    essential: 'age_years in an untyped one' },
  { r: 'names should be SENTENCES at the call site',
    test: 'reading the call aloud tells you what happens',
    good: 'if user.is_eligible_for_discount()', bad: 'if check(u)' },
  { r: 'BOOLEAN names should read as conditions', prefixes: ['is_', 'has_', 'can_', 'should_'],
    why: 'enabled in a list of five settings is UNREADABLE while is_dark_mode_enabled is not' },
  { r: 'avoid the SAME WORD for two different things', rank: 'the most damaging naming mistake there is',
    why: 'a reader who sees user in one place will reasonably assume it means the same thing everywhere' },
];
/* The four smells, each with a mechanical fix. */
const SMELLS = [
  { s: 'DUPLICATED CODE', cost: 'two places to change and one place SOMEBODY WILL NOT',
    fixIsNotAlways: 'a function',
    whenDuplicationIsBetter: 'three similar lines that are each obvious beat one abstraction that must be read carefully',
    heuristic: 'the RULE OF THREE - after the third occurrence the duplication is likely to be a MISSING CONCEPT' },
  { s: 'LONG FUNCTIONS', testIsNot: 'the line count',
    testIs: 'whether you can NAME ITS STEPS',
    ifNamingRequiresReading: 'the names DO NOT EXIST YET' },
  { s: 'LONG PARAMETER LISTS', fiveMeans: 'the function does five things, or the parameters belong together in an object',
    signal: 'callers must remember an ORDERING' },
  { s: 'FEATURE ENVY', detail: 'a method that reaches into another objects data more than its own has the logic in the wrong place',
    fix: 'MOVE IT, not add a getter' },
  { s: 'the COMMENT that explains WHAT rather than WHY',
    noise: 'a comment restating the code is noise that goes stale',
    earnsItsPlace: 'a comment explaining WHY an unusual decision was made',
    test: 'whether deleting it would leave a reader PUZZLED' },
];

Functions, comments, and reviewing your own code

Then function-level practice, which is where the naming rules meet the structure. One reason to exist per function, and if it needs a comment saying what it also does, it is two functions. Early returns over nested blocks, because a function with four if-return pairs at one indentation level can be read top to bottom while the same logic nested reaches four levels by the last branch. Keep the parameter list short and pass one object when there are several, and the trigger is not the count but whether callers must remember an ordering. Do not mutate an argument you were given, which is covered in the C chapter and is the same rule here: a function that sorts a list in place changes the caller's data invisibly. And make the failure path as considered as the success path, because the majority of real code is error handling and a function written to assume success ends with a catch-all that hides everything, converting a small bug into an unexplained outage.

Then the practice that most improves other people's code and is most skipped: review your own diff before opening the pull request. The value is specific and it is not about catching typos. You have the original intent and nobody else does, so the question "does this do what I meant" is one you can answer and one no reviewer can. Read the diff as a stranger would, and the things that jump out are almost always real: a name that only makes sense if you remember the implementation, a test that asserts the implementation rather than the behaviour, an error message that names a variable that no longer exists. Check the boundary cases you did not test, and this is where the self-review earns its keep — empty input, one item, the maximum, the value just past the maximum, the concurrent access. And ask whether the change is one thing, because a diff that changes behaviour and reformats a file cannot be reviewed by anybody, including you, and the discipline of splitting it is the same discipline that makes the pull request reviewable. Then the two smaller habits: delete commented-out code, because version control has it and the comment only tells a reader that something was once true, and fix the formatting at commit time so that a diff shows only logic.

/* Function-level practice. */
const FUNCTIONS = [
  { r: 'ONE REASON TO EXIST', test: 'if it needs a comment saying what it ALSO DOES, it is two functions' },
  { r: 'EARLY RETURNS over nested blocks',
    good: 'a function with four if-return pairs at one indentation level can be read top to bottom',
    bad: 'the same logic nested reaches FOUR LEVELS by the last branch' },
  { r: 'keep the PARAMETER LIST short', passOneObjectWhen: 'there are several',
    trigger: 'not the count but whether CALLERS MUST REMEMBER AN ORDERING' },
  { r: 'do NOT MUTATE AN ARGUMENT you were given', detail: 'a function that sorts a list in place changes the callers data INVISIBLY' },
  { r: 'make the FAILURE PATH as considered as the success path',
    fact: 'the majority of real code is ERROR HANDLING',
    consequence: 'a function written to assume success ends with a CATCH-ALL that hides everything, converting a small bug into an UNEXPLAINED OUTAGE',
  },
];

/* Review your own diff. */
const SELF_REVIEW = {
  notAbout: 'catching typos',
  values: [
    { v: 'you have the ORIGINAL INTENT and nobody else does',
      gain: 'the question does this do what I meant is one you can answer and one NO REVIEWER CAN' },
    { v: 'read the diff AS A STRANGER WOULD',
      whatJumpsOut: ['a name that only makes sense if you remember the implementation',
        'a test that asserts the IMPLEMENTATION rather than the behaviour',
        'an error message that names a VARIABLE THAT NO LONGER EXISTS'],
      claim: 'the things that jump out are almost always real' },
    { v: 'check the BOUNDARY CASES you did not test', whereSelfReviewPays: 'here',
      list: ['empty input', 'one item', 'the maximum', 'the value just past the maximum',
        'the concurrent access'] },
    { v: 'ask whether the change is ONE THING',
      why: 'a diff that changes behaviour and reformats a file CANNOT BE REVIEWED BY ANYBODY, including you',
      discipline: 'splitting it is the same discipline that makes the pull request reviewable' },
  ],
  twoHabits: [
    { h: 'delete COMMENTED-OUT CODE', why: 'version control has it, and the comment only tells a reader that something was ONCE TRUE' },
    { h: 'fix the FORMATTING AT COMMIT TIME', gain: 'a diff shows only logic' },
  ],
};

The same logic twice: cryptic and prose-like. Names and a named constant are what make the second version readable.

19.2 SOLID — five rules of changeable design

SOLID is five rules for spotting designs that resist change. Single Responsibility gives each class one reason to change, Open-Closed allows extension without modification, Liskov keeps subclasses usable where their base type is expected, Interface Segregation avoids fat interfaces, and Dependency Inversion makes high-level modules depend on abstractions. Treat them as warning signals: a violation is a smell to fix, not a law to obey.

LetterPrincipleIn one sentence
SSingle ResponsibilityOne class, one reason to change
OOpen/ClosedExtend behaviour without modifying existing code
LLiskov SubstitutionSubclasses must be usable wherever the parent is promised
IInterface SegregationDon’t force clients to depend on methods they don’t use
DDependency InversionDepend on abstractions, not concrete implementations
# S: this class does TWO jobs (bad)
class Report:
    def __init__(self, rows): self.rows = rows
    def render_html(self): ...
    def send_email(self, to): ...          # <-- second responsibility

# Fix: separate
class HtmlRenderer: ...
class EmailSender: ...

The S of SOLID: a class doing two jobs is split into separate classes, each with one reason to change.

# D + O: depend on an abstraction (the Strategy pattern in one shot)
class PaymentMethod:                       # the abstraction
    def charge(self, amount): raise NotImplementedError

class Card(PaymentMethod):
    def charge(self, amount):
        print(f"Card charging {amount}")

class PayPal(PaymentMethod):
    def charge(self, amount):
        print(f"PayPal charging {amount}")

def checkout(order, method: PaymentMethod):
    method.charge(order.total)             # checkout doesn't care WHICH method

checkout(order, Card())                    # adding a new method later:
checkout(order, PayPal())                  # new class + this call = DONE

Dependency inversion plus Strategy: checkout depends on a PaymentMethod abstraction, so a new payment type slots in without touching existing code.

The five principles, each as a specific smell

The five principles are best understood as five answers to five distinct questions, and each has a smell that tells you it is being violated. Single responsibility: does this have one reason to change? The test is not "is this small" but "can you describe why this might change without naming a second reason". A class that validates input and formats an error response and knows the database schema has three reasons to change, and every one of them is a change somebody makes for an unrelated reason, which is why such a class is constantly being edited by people who are working on something else entirely. Open/closed: will this require modification when a new variant appears? The good case is a switch on a type where a new variant is a new case — that is genuinely closed. The bad case is a chain of if type == "a" ... else if type == "b" in five places, where a sixth variant means finding them all, and one of them will be missed. Liskov: can this be used anywhere its parent is expected? This is the hardest to state and the easiest to violate by accident. Interface segregation: can a client depend on the smallest interface that gives it what it needs? A repository interface with forty methods that a read-only caller must implement has failed, and it has failed in the way that matters — every implementation now carries code it will never call. Dependency inversion: do the high-level policies depend on abstractions rather than on low-level details? A test that cannot run without a database is not a unit test; a caller that must import a specific HTTP client is coupled to it.

Then Liskov in detail, because the others are comparatively straightforward and this one causes the most damage. The rule: a subclass must be usable everywhere its parent is, and must not strengthen preconditions or weaken postconditions. If the parent's method promises it accepts a positive width, the subclass must not reject it. If the parent promises the height is unchanged by setting the width, the subclass must not change it. The classic violation: a Square inheriting from a Rectangle must make the two dimensions equal, so overriding the width setter to change the height violates the parent's promise that setting the width leaves the height alone — and code that was correct against a rectangle now behaves differently, silently. The fix is not a comment; it is that a Square is not a Rectangle in the type sense, because it has an invariant the rectangle does not have, and modelling it as a subclass is asking the type system to guarantee something it cannot. Either model both as a shape with two dimensions and no constraint, or model them separately. And the general rule for spotting it: if you have to document that a subclass behaves differently, or add an override that contradicts the parent, you have a subclass that is not substitutable — and the cost will be paid by a caller that trusted the parent's contract.

/* Five questions, five smells. */
const PRINCIPLES = [
  { p: 'SINGLE RESPONSIBILITY', q: 'does this have ONE REASON TO CHANGE',
    testIsNot: 'is this small',
    testIs: 'can you describe why this might change WITHOUT NAMING A SECOND REASON',
    bad: 'a class that validates input, formats an error response, and knows the database schema has THREE reasons to change',
    consequence: 'every one is a change somebody makes for an UNRELATED REASON, which is why such a class is constantly edited by people working on something else' },
  { p: 'OPEN/CLOSED', q: 'will this require modification when a NEW VARIANT appears',
    goodCase: 'a switch on a type where a new variant is a new case - that is genuinely closed',
    badCase: 'a chain of if-else on type in five places, where a sixth variant means FINDING THEM ALL',
    consequence: 'and one of them will be MISSED' },
  { p: 'LISKOV', q: 'can this be used ANYWHERE ITS PARENT IS EXPECTED',
    hardest: true, easiestToViolate: 'by accident' },
  { p: 'INTERFACE SEGREGATION', q: 'can a client depend on the SMALLEST INTERFACE that gives it what it needs',
    failure: 'a repository interface with forty methods that a read-only caller must implement',
    howItFailed: 'every implementation now carries code it will NEVER CALL' },
  { p: 'DEPENDENCY INVERSION', q: 'do the HIGH-LEVEL POLICIES depend on abstractions rather than on low-level details',
    symptoms: ['a test that cannot run without a database is not a unit test',
      'a caller that must import a specific HTTP client is COUPLED to it'],
  },
];

/* Liskov in detail. */
const LISKOV = {
  rule: 'a subclass must be usable EVERYWHERE ITS PARENT IS, and must not STRENGTHEN PRECONDITIONS or WEAKEN POSTCONDITIONS',
  preconditions: 'if the parents method promises it accepts a positive width, the subclass must not REJECT it',
  postconditions: 'if the parent promises the height is unchanged by setting the width, the subclass must NOT CHANGE IT',
  classic: {
    case: 'a Square inheriting from a Rectangle must make the two dimensions equal',
    howItViolates: 'overriding the width setter to change the height violates the parents promise that setting the width LEAVES THE HEIGHT ALONE',
    consequence: 'code that was CORRECT against a rectangle now behaves differently, SILENTLY',
    theFixIsNotAComment: true,
    theRealFix: 'a Square is NOT A Rectangle in the type sense, because it has an INVARIANT the rectangle does not have',
    reframe: 'modelling it as a subclass is asking the type system to guarantee something IT CANNOT',
    options: ['model both as a shape with two dimensions and no constraint', 'model them separately'],
  },
  spottingIt: 'if you have to DOCUMENT THAT A SUBCLASS BEHAVES DIFFERENTLY, or add an override that contradicts the parent, you have a subclass that is not substitutable',
  whoPays: 'a caller that trusted the parents contract',
};

Applying the principles, and when not to

Then how to use them, because the failure mode is applying them by reflex. These are heuristics, not a target architecture. A five-method class with three reasons to change is a problem; a class with one reason to change and four hundred lines is a much smaller problem, and splitting it because a principle suggests it can produce five classes with four reasons to change each and no clearer design. The signal to act on is a change that keeps touching the same code for unrelated reasons. That is the empirical test of single responsibility and it is better than any structural heuristic: if three unrelated changes over a year all edited the same file, the responsibility is genuinely mixed, and no amount of counting methods would have told you. Apply the principles at the boundary, not everywhere. A domain object with validation is a good use of them; a value object wrapping an integer is a waste of a file. And the strongest argument for them is not elegance, it is substitution — a system that obeys them can have a fake implementation of anything, so a test can run without a database and a feature can be swapped without touching its callers, and both of those are concrete benefits that show up as speed and as testability rather than as beauty.

/* These are heuristics, not a target architecture. */
const NOT_A_TARGET = {
  problemExample: 'a five-method class with three reasons to change',
  smallerProblem: 'a class with ONE reason to change and four hundred lines',
  overApplying: 'splitting it because a principle suggests it can produce FIVE CLASSES WITH FOUR REASONS TO CHANGE EACH and no clearer design',
};
/* The empirical test. */
const EMPIRICAL_TEST = {
  signal: 'a CHANGE THAT KEEPS TOUCHING THE SAME CODE for unrelated reasons',
  isTheRealTestOf: 'single responsibility',
  betterThan: 'any structural heuristic',
  evidence: 'if three unrelated changes over a year all edited the same file, the responsibility is genuinely MIXED',
  and: 'no amount of counting methods would have told you',
};
/* Where and how far to apply them. */
const APPLY = [
  { where: 'at the BOUNDARY, not everywhere', good: 'a domain object with validation',
    waste: 'a value object wrapping an integer is a WASTE OF A FILE' },
  { strongestArgument: 'it is not ELEGANCE, it is SUBSTITUTION',
    gains: ['a system that obeys them can have a FAKE IMPLEMENTATION of anything',
      'a test can run without a database',
      'a feature can be swapped without touching its callers'],
    benefitShowsUpAs: ['speed', 'testability'],
    ratherThan: 'beauty',
  },
];

Liskov in one trap: if a Square subclass of Rectangle overrides set_width to also change height, code that promised a rectangle now silently behaves differently → bugs nobody sees coming. Favour composition, and never make a subclass that violates the parent’s contract.

19.3 The patterns that pay rent

Design patterns are the shared vocabulary for shapes that recur across codebases. Strategy swaps algorithms at runtime, Observer notifies listeners of changes, Factory centralizes object creation, Repository abstracts data access, Decorator layers behavior on an object, and Adapter lets incompatible interfaces talk. Learn them as language, not commandments, and reach for the simplest variant that solves today’s problem.

PatternProblem it solvesOne-line shape
StrategyMultiple interchangeable behavioursPass in the algorithm (above)
ObserverMany things must react to one eventSubject keeps a list of listeners; notify() calls them all (DOM events!)
FactoryCreating objects of varying typesA function that returns the right subclass
RepositoryHide the database from the domain codeClass with get(id)/save(x) wrapping SQL
DecoratorAdd behaviour without changing the classWrap an object in another that adds a step before/after
AdapterTwo incompatible interfacesA wrapper converting one API into the other
Singleton"Exactly one shared instance"…but prefer dependency injection; use sparingly, it hides global state
# Repository: the data layer stays swappable
class UserRepository:
    def __init__(self, db): self.db = db
    def get(self, user_id):
        return self.db.fetch_one("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?", user_id)
    def save(self, user):
        self.db.exec("INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES (?)", user.name)
# Business code calls repository methods - never SQL scattered everywhere

# Decorator (Python has native syntax)
def logged(fn):
    def wrapper(*a, **k):
        print(f"calling {fn.__name__}")
        return fn(*a, **k)
    return wrapper

@logged
def greet(name): return f"Hi {name}"
print(greet("Ada"))     # calling greet  /  Hi Ada

What patterns actually are, and why the criticism is partly right

A design pattern is a named, reusable solution to a recurring problem, and the description in that sentence contains both its value and its cost. Value: the solution is already designed, which means you do not have to discover it, and it is described in a vocabulary other people already know, so this is a strategy pattern tells a reader more in four words than an hour of reading the code would. And crucially, the name carries the trade-offs with it — a reader who knows the name knows what the pattern is good at and where it hurts, and that is information you cannot get from reading the code. Cost: a pattern adds indirection, and indirection has a real cost in a small problem — five lines become a class, an interface and two implementations to express something a conditional would say directly. And the classic misuse is coding to the pattern rather than to the problem: looking for a pattern to apply rather than recognising a problem a pattern solves. The honest test is the one that appears throughout this chapter: would this be simpler without it? If a three-line function with a conditional is more readable than an abstract factory with four participants, it is more readable, and the pattern's only remaining benefit is that it might be reused someday, which is speculative.

Then the small set worth knowing, and the value of knowing them is mostly that you can recognise problems rather than invent solutions. Strategy — swap an algorithm at run time; the fix for the conditional chain that grows a new branch every time a variant appears. Factory — centralise the decision about which concrete thing to create, so callers do not know the classes. Repository — put an interface in front of persistence so business logic does not know it is talking to a database, which is what makes that logic testable without one. Observer — when something must react to a change without being wired to the thing that changed; the mechanism behind events, callbacks and most of the reactive plumbing in a modern application. Adapter — make an interface you do not control look like one you do, which is the pattern for every third-party integration and for the code that makes a legacy component usable. Decorator — add behaviour by wrapping, without changing the original; the mechanism behind middleware and it is why middleware chains compose. Singleton — one instance with global access, and the one pattern that is more often a mistake than a solution: it makes state global, it makes testing painful, and it hides dependencies rather than declaring them.

/* A named, reusable solution to a recurring problem. */
const PATTERN = {
  is: 'a named, reusable solution to a recurring problem',
  value: [
    { v: 'the solution is ALREADY DESIGNED', gain: 'you do not have to discover it' },
    { v: 'it is described in a VOCABULARY other people already know',
      example: 'this is a strategy pattern tells a reader more in four words than an HOUR OF READING THE CODE' },
    { v: 'the name CARRIES THE TRADE-OFFS WITH IT',
      why: 'a reader who knows the name knows what the pattern is good at and where it HURTS',
      note: 'that is information you CANNOT GET from reading the code',
  ],
  cost: {
    indirection: 'a pattern adds indirection, and indirection has a REAL COST in a small problem',
    example: 'five lines become a class, an interface and two implementations to express something a CONDITIONAL WOULD SAY DIRECTLY',
    misuse: 'CODING TO THE PATTERN rather than to the problem - looking for a pattern to apply rather than recognising a problem a pattern solves',
    theTest: 'would this be SIMPLER WITHOUT IT',
    worked: 'if a three-line function with a conditional is more readable than an abstract factory with four participants, it is more readable',
    remainingBenefit: 'that it might be reused someday, which is SPECULATIVE',
  },
};

/* The set worth knowing. */
const WORTH_KNOWING = [
  { p: 'STRATEGY', does: 'swap an ALGORITHM at run time',
    fixes: 'the conditional chain that grows a new branch every time a variant appears' },
  { p: 'FACTORY', does: 'CENTRALISE THE DECISION about which concrete thing to create',
    gain: 'so callers do not know the classes' },
  { p: 'REPOSITORY', does: 'puts an INTERFACE IN FRONT OF PERSISTENCE',
    gain: 'business logic does not know it is talking to a database, which is what makes that logic TESTABLE WITHOUT ONE' },
  { p: 'OBSERVER', does: 'something reacts to a change WITHOUT BEING WIRED to the thing that changed',
    behind: ['events', 'callbacks', 'most of the reactive plumbing in a modern application'] },
  { p: 'ADAPTER', does: 'make an interface YOU DO NOT CONTROL look like one you do',
    usedFor: ['every third-party integration', 'the code that makes a LEGACY COMPONENT USABLE'] },
  { p: 'DECORATOR', does: 'add behaviour by WRAPPING, without changing the original',
    behind: 'middleware', gain: 'which is why middleware chains COMPOSE' },
  { p: 'SINGLETON', isOneInstanceWithGlobalAccess: true,
    moreOftenAMistakeThanASolution: true,
    problems: ['it makes state GLOBAL', 'it makes TESTING PAINFUL', 'it HIDES DEPENDENCIES rather than declaring them'],
  },
];

Middleware, and deciding whether you need anything

Then the two that are worth arguing about properly, because they are the ones most projects use. Middleware as a decorator chain: a request passes through a list of handlers, each of which can act, call the next, or stop the chain. The value is that cross-cutting concerns — logging, authentication, rate limiting, error handling — live in one place and apply to every route without every route remembering them, and the ordering becomes the architecture, as the previous chapter showed. The costs are real: the chain is invisible at the call site, so a reader looking at a handler does not know what runs around it, and the chain is ordered, so inserting one in the wrong place breaks a route that worked. Repository as a data access abstraction: business logic talks to a collection-like interface rather than to a database, and the benefit is concrete — the logic is testable with an in-memory implementation, and the query is expressed once rather than scattered. The costs: the abstraction leaks when the query is complex, because an interface shaped as a collection cannot express every query, and at that point you either widen the interface until it is the database or you bypass it, and both are worse than admitting that some code needs SQL.

Then how to decide, and the checklist that prevents both over- and under-engineering. Do you have a problem this pattern solves? Name it. If the answer is "this would be tidier", that is not a problem. How many variants are there? Strategy and factory earn their place when there are several; with one, a conditional is correct. Is the indirection justified by a test you can now write? This is the strongest argument, because it is measurable: if the pattern lets you test business logic without a database or a network, that is worth real indirection; if it does not, it is cost. Will the next person understand it? A pattern in a codebase where nobody knows patterns is a puzzle, and the answer is to name it in the code, comment it once with why, and keep it to the one place that needs it. And prefer the language's own mechanism where one exists: a generator is a strategy, a context manager is a decorator, a module is a namespace, and an if is a strategy with one variant.

/* The two worth arguing about. */
const MIDDLEWARE = {
  does: 'a request passes through a list of handlers, each of which can act, call the next, or stop the chain',
  value: ['cross-cutting concerns - logging, authentication, rate limiting, error handling - live in ONE PLACE',
    'they apply to EVERY ROUTE without every route remembering them',
    'the ordering BECOMES THE ARCHITECTURE'],
  costs: ['the chain is INVISIBLE AT THE CALL SITE, so a reader looking at a handler does not know what runs around it',
    'the chain is ORDERED, so inserting one in the wrong place breaks a route that worked'],
};
const REPOSITORY = {
  does: 'business logic talks to a COLLECTION-LIKE INTERFACE rather than to a database',
  benefit: 'the logic is TESTABLE with an in-memory implementation, and the query is expressed ONCE rather than scattered',
  cost: 'the abstraction LEAKS WHEN THE QUERY IS COMPLEX',
  why: 'an interface shaped as a collection cannot express every query',
  thenYouEither: ['WIDEN the interface until it IS the database', 'BYPASS it'],
  verdict: 'both are worse than admitting that some code needs SQL',
};

/* The checklist. */
const CHECKLIST = [
  { q: 'do you have a PROBLEM this pattern solves', how: 'name it',
    ifNot: 'this would be tidier is NOT a problem' },
  { q: 'how many VARIANTS are there', rule: 'strategy and factory earn their place when there are SEVERAL',
    withOne: 'a conditional is CORRECT' },
  { q: 'is the INDIRECTION JUSTIFIED BY A TEST YOU CAN NOW WRITE', strongestArgument: true,
    why: 'it is MEASURABLE',
    yes: 'if the pattern lets you test business logic without a database or a network, that is worth REAL indirection',
    no: 'if it does not, it is COST' },
  { q: 'will the NEXT PERSON UNDERSTAND IT',
    inACodebaseWhereNobodyKnowsPatterns: 'a puzzle',
    answer: ['name it in the code', 'comment it ONCE with why', 'keep it to the ONE PLACE that needs it'] },
  { q: 'PREFER THE LANGUAGES OWN MECHANISM where one exists',
    examples: ['a generator is a strategy', 'a context manager is a decorator',
      'a module is a namespace', 'an if is a strategy with ONE VARIANT'],
  },
];

A Repository wraps SQL so business code never touches the database, and a native-Python decorator adds logging around any function.

19.4 The other paradigm: functional thinking

Functional thinking favors immutability, pure functions, and higher-order functions, which make concurrency dramatically safer because no shared state mutates underfoot. Real teams apply it as a style inside larger programs, using objects and layers for boundaries and functional patterns such as map, reduce, and composed functions in the inner logic. Separate pure logic from effectful edges to get the best of both paradigms.

The second giant paradigm. Core ideas — and they make concurrency dramatically safer:

  • Immutable data — once created, never mutated.
  • Pure functions — same input, same output, no side effects; trivially testable.
  • Higher-order functions — map/filter/reduce, passing functions as values.
# Pure & immutable-friendly version of the earlier logic
def apply_discount(price, rate):
    return price * (1 - rate)    # pure: same input, same output, no side effects

prices = [120, 50, 300, 25]
result = sum(map(lambda p: apply_discount(p, 0.1),
                 filter(lambda p: p > 100, prices)))
# 120*0.9 + 300*0.9 = 378   -- no mutations, no surprises, easy to test each bit

A pure, immutable-style pipeline built from map and filter over higher-order functions — no mutations, no surprises, easy to test.

Real teams mix styles. Use OOP to draw boundaries (interface, encapsulation) and functional style inside for logic (purity, immutability). Dogma to either side is a smell.

Pure functions, immutability, and why they make concurrency disappear

Three ideas, and each solves a specific class of problem. A pure function returns the same output for the same inputs and does nothing else — no mutation of anything it was given, no reading of anything outside its arguments, no network, no clock, no random. The second half is the one people skip: a function that reads the current time is not pure even though it is perfectly deterministic-looking. Immutability is the discipline of never changing what exists, and creating a new value instead — which in most languages is a discipline you enforce by convention and in a few the language enforces for you. Referential transparency is the consequence: an expression using only pure functions can be replaced by its value without changing the meaning of the program. And the reason this matters more than elegance is that immutability removes an entire category of bug. If nothing changes after creation, two things cannot interfere, so there is no race, no stale read, no ordering problem, no "who was supposed to update this". That is not a small simplification — it is why functional-style code runs concurrently without locks, and why the hardest problems in this chapter's concurrency section simply do not appear.

Then the cost, stated honestly, because a section that does not mention it is not useful. Data copying. Every change creates a new value, and copying a large structure is expensive — which is why persistent data structures exist, where "changing" something produces a structure that shares almost all of its memory with the original and differs only in the path to the change. Allocation pressure. More objects are created, and in a language with a garbage collector that is more collection work; in a language without one it is a cost you pay explicitly. Some problems genuinely need mutation — an in-place sort of a very large array, a buffer being filled, a data structure whose whole purpose is efficient incremental modification — and pretending otherwise produces an algorithm that is correct and quadratic. And the composition of small functions has a runtime cost in a language without aggressive optimisation, because each call is a call. Then the practical middle, which is where most code should sit. Push immutability to the boundaries and keep the hot path mutable. Configuration, state held in the application, and anything passed between modules are immutable, so reasoning about them is easy; a local buffer inside a tight loop is mutable, because nothing can see it and copying it would dominate the runtime. Make the core functions pure and let impure ones be visible. A pure core with a thin impure shell — the pure functions do the work, the shell does the I/O — is a design that is testable without mocking anything and is worth doing even in a codebase that has no functional programming in it at all.

/* Three ideas, each solving a class of problem. */
const PURE = {
  is: 'returns the SAME OUTPUT for the same inputs and DOES NOTHING ELSE',
  alsoMustNot: ['mutate anything it was given', 'read anything OUTSIDE ITS ARGUMENTS',
    'use the network', 'use the clock', 'use random'],
  skippedByPeople: 'the second half - a function that reads the current time is not pure even though it is PERFECTLY DETERMINISTIC-LOOKING',
};
const IMMUTABLE = {
  is: 'never changing what exists, and CREATING A NEW VALUE instead',
  enforcedBy: 'convention in most languages', inAFew: 'the language enforces it for you',
};
const TRANSPARENCY = { is: 'an expression using only pure functions can be REPLACED BY ITS VALUE without changing the meaning of the program' };
const WHY_IT_MATTERS = {
  not: 'elegance',
  is: 'IMMUTABILITY REMOVES AN ENTIRE CATEGORY OF BUG',
  argument: 'if nothing changes after creation, TWO THINGS CANNOT INTERFERE',
  therefore: ['no race', 'no stale read', 'no ordering problem', 'no who was supposed to update this'],
  significance: 'not a small simplification - it is why functional-style code runs concurrently WITHOUT LOCKS, and why the hardest problems in the concurrency section SIMPLY DO NOT APPEAR',
};

/* The cost. */
const COST = [
  { c: 'DATA COPYING', does: 'every change creates a new value, and copying a large structure is expensive',
    answer: 'persistent data structures, where changing produces a structure that SHARES ALMOST ALL of its memory and differs only in the PATH TO THE CHANGE' },
  { c: 'ALLOCATION PRESSURE', detail: 'more objects are created',
    withGc: 'more COLLECTION WORK', withoutOne: 'a cost you pay EXPLICITLY' },
  { c: 'some problems GENUINELY NEED MUTATION',
    instances: ['an in-place sort of a very large array', 'a buffer being filled',
      'a data structure whose whole purpose is efficient incremental modification'],
    consequence: 'pretending otherwise produces an ALGORITHM THAT IS CORRECT AND QUADRATIC' },
  { c: 'COMPOSITION of small functions has a RUNTIME COST',
    when: 'in a language without aggressive optimisation',
    why: 'each call is a call' },
];
/* The practical middle. */
const MIDDLE = [
  { p: 'push IMMUTABILITY TO THE BOUNDARIES and keep the hot path MUTABLE',
    immutable: ['configuration', 'state held in the application', 'anything passed between modules'],
    mutable: 'a local buffer inside a tight loop',
    why: 'nothing can see it and COPYING IT WOULD DOMINATE THE RUNTIME' },
  { p: 'make the CORE FUNCTIONS PURE and let the impure ones be VISIBLE',
    shape: 'a PURE CORE with a THIN IMPURE SHELL - the pure functions do the work, the shell does the I/O',
    gain: 'TESTABLE WITHOUT MOCKING ANYTHING',
    note: 'worth doing even in a codebase that has no functional programming in it at all',
  },
];

Composition, side effects, and the practical adoption

Then composition versus inheritance, and the argument is short. Composition: has-a. Inheritance: is-a. Everything else follows: composition has no coupling between the parts, so changing one does not constrain the other; inheritance couples the child to the parent's implementation, which is the fragile-base-class problem; composition is testable because the part can be replaced with a fake, while a subclass cannot be replaced by its parent; and composition is what the Liskov discussion concluded you should reach for. Then side effects and the discipline around them, because this is where pure functions pay. A side effect is anything outside the function's own computation that the rest of the program can observe — writing a variable, mutating an argument, printing, logging, hitting a network, writing a file, and notably reading the clock or a random source. The discipline is not "never have side effects" but keep them at the edges and name them honestly: a function called send_email tells the reader a side effect is happening, while one called notify does not. And keep side effects out of expressions, because a side effect inside an expression makes the evaluation order observable, and any refactoring that changes the order changes the behaviour.

Then how to adopt this without rewriting a codebase, which is the practical question. Start with the pure parts. Most code is arithmetic on data, and making those functions pure — taking inputs, returning outputs, mutating nothing — is a mechanical change with no architectural consequences. Return new values rather than mutating, in the layers where data flows. That single change removes a large fraction of the bugs in a codebase, because a large fraction of bugs are somebody's mutation arriving at the wrong time. Push I/O to the edges. A function that reads a configuration value is untestable; a function that takes the configuration as an argument and reads it once at the top of the call stack is. Keep the impure shell thin and resist the temptation to move logic into it, because logic in a shell cannot be tested without the thing the shell exists to abstract. And then the honest final note, which is the one that decides whether any of this is worth doing for your project: none of this requires a functional language. Pure functions and immutable data are available in every language, they cost nothing to adopt incrementally, and the benefit — code that can be reasoned about, tested without setup, and run concurrently — is the same benefit the language provides. The language is not the thing that makes code reliable; the discipline is, and the discipline is optional in a language that enforces it and available in one that does not.

/* Composition versus inheritance. */
const VS = {
  composition: 'HAS-A', inheritance: 'IS-A',
  follows: ['composition has NO COUPLING between the parts, so changing one does not constrain the other',
    'inheritance COUPLES THE CHILD TO THE PARENTS IMPLEMENTATION - the fragile-base-class problem',
    'composition is TESTABLE because the part can be replaced with a fake, while a subclass CANNOT BE REPLACED BY ITS PARENT',
    'composition is what the Liskov discussion concluded you should reach for'],
};

/* Side effects. */
const SIDE_EFFECTS = {
  is: 'anything OUTSIDE THE FUNCTIONS OWN COMPUTATION that the rest of the program can observe',
  instances: ['writing a variable', 'mutating an argument', 'printing', 'logging',
    'hitting a network', 'writing a file', 'reading the clock', 'a random source'],
  disciplineIsNot: 'never have side effects',
  disciplineIs: 'keep them at the EDGES and NAME THEM HONESTLY',
  naming: 'send_email tells the reader a side effect is happening, while notify DOES NOT',
  keepThemOutOfExpressions: true,
  why: 'a side effect inside an expression makes the EVALUATION ORDER OBSERVABLE',
  consequence: 'any refactoring that changes the order CHANGES THE BEHAVIOUR',
};

/* How to adopt this. */
const ADOPT = [
  { s: 'start with the PURE PARTS', detail: 'most code is ARITHMETIC ON DATA',
    change: 'making those functions pure - taking inputs, returning outputs, mutating nothing - is a MECHANICAL change with no architectural consequences' },
  { s: 'return NEW VALUES rather than mutating, in the layers where data flows',
    removes: 'a large fraction of the bugs in a codebase, because a large fraction of bugs are SOMEBODYS MUTATION ARRIVING AT THE WRONG TIME' },
  { s: 'push I/O to the EDGES',
    untestable: 'a function that reads a configuration value',
    testable: 'a function that TAKES the configuration as an argument and reads it once at the top of the call stack' },
  { s: 'keep the IMPURE SHELL THIN', resist: 'the temptation to move logic into it',
    why: 'logic in a shell CANNOT BE TESTED WITHOUT the thing the shell exists to abstract' },
];
const FINAL_NOTE = {
  point: 'NONE OF THIS REQUIRES A FUNCTIONAL LANGUAGE',
  because: ['pure functions and immutable data are available in EVERY language',
    'they cost NOTHING to adopt incrementally',
    'the benefit - code that can be reasoned about, tested without setup, and run concurrently - is the SAME benefit the language provides'],
  reframe: 'the LANGUAGE is not the thing that makes code reliable; the DISCIPLINE is',
  nuance: 'the discipline is OPTIONAL in a language that enforces it and AVAILABLE in one that does not',
};
