20 · Security Engineering

Security fails at the seams, not in theory, so Security Engineering is about a threat-model-first mindset and concrete defenses. The chapter covers thinking like an attacker with CIA and STRIDE, injection and the never-concatenate rule, the OWASP Top 10, the cryptography you pick rather than design, a hardening checklist, and walkthroughs of five famous attack classes. These habits stop most real-world breaches before they start.

20.1 Thinking like an attacker: CIA + STRIDE20.2 Injection & the #1 rule: never concatenate20.3 OWASP Top 10 (the ones that matter for you now)20.4 Cryptography you must actually know20.5 Practical hardening checklist20.6 A walk through five famous attack classes

Security is a property of the whole system, not a feature you bolt on. This chapter gives you the threat model, the OWASP Top 10, and the concrete habits that stop the most common breaches.

20.1 Thinking like an attacker: CIA + STRIDE

Before defending anything you must know what you protect and how an attacker would come at it. The CIA triad names the goals, confidentiality, integrity, and availability, while STRIDE is a checklist for finding holes: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, and privilege elevation. Use it to build a threat model for every feature, naming the assets and the attacks that matter.

CIAMeaningExample
ConfidentialityOnly who should can read itUser passwords, PII
IntegrityData isn’t altered without permissionBank balance, signed software
AvailabilitySystem stays up under attackAnti-DDoS, rate limits

Threat modelling = for your system, list who can attack through which surface, and what they gain. "Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, DoS, Elevation of privilege" (STRIDE) is the classic checklist.

CIA, and what each one actually needs

Three properties, and each has a distinct failure mode that requires different mechanisms. Confidentiality means only the intended parties can read it. The mechanisms are access control — because most data breaches are an authorisation failure, not a cryptographic one — plus encryption at rest and in transit, plus the discipline of not putting secrets where they need no protection. Integrity means nobody can change it undetected. The mechanism is not encryption; encryption without authentication provides confidentiality and no integrity at all, which is why an unauthenticated message can be modified by anyone holding the key. Integrity needs either an authenticated mode — which combines confidentiality and integrity in one construction — or a signature, which provides integrity without confidentiality and also provides authenticity, meaning you know who sent it. Availability means it is there when needed, and it is the property developers most consistently under-think because it is not a data property at all: it is about redundancy, about capacity, and about the design decisions — a synchronous dependency, a hard failure, a single point of failure — that determine whether a dependency's bad afternoon becomes your bad afternoon.

Then the fourth property that is not in the triad and matters as much as any of them: authenticity — knowing that a message came from who it claims to. And the reason it is separate is instructive: confidentiality protects a message from being read; authentication protects it from being faked, and the two are independent. A message can be confidential and unauthenticated — encrypted with a shared key anybody possesses — which means everybody with the key can produce it. It can also be authenticated and not confidential — a signed message is verifiable but readable by anyone. This is the reason a signature exists and the reason "encrypt it" is not a complete answer to "is this genuine". Then the two properties that are usually conflated with the triad: non-repudiation, which means a party cannot plausibly deny having sent something, achieved by a signature with the private key under their sole control, and which is a property of signatures and not of shared-key encryption because with a shared key either party could have produced it.

/* Three properties, distinct failure modes, distinct mechanisms. */
const CIA = [
  { p: 'CONFIDENTIALITY', means: 'only the intended parties can read it',
    mechanisms: ['access control', 'encryption at rest', 'encryption in transit',
      'not putting secrets where they need no protection'],
    observation: 'most data breaches are an AUTHORISATION FAILURE, not a cryptographic one' },
  { p: 'INTEGRITY', means: 'nobody can change it undetected',
    mechanismIsNot: 'encryption',
    why: 'encryption WITHOUT AUTHENTICATION provides confidentiality and NO INTEGRITY AT ALL',
    consequence: 'which is why an unauthenticated message can be MODIFIED BY ANYONE HOLDING THE KEY',
    needs: ['an authenticated mode, which combines confidentiality and integrity in one construction',
      'a signature, which provides integrity WITHOUT confidentiality and also provides authenticity'],
  },
  { p: 'AVAILABILITY', means: 'it is there when needed',
    isNotADataProperty: true,
    isAbout: ['redundancy', 'capacity',
      'design decisions - a synchronous dependency, a hard failure, a single point of failure'],
    consequence: 'whether a dependencys bad afternoon becomes YOUR bad afternoon',
    underThought: 'because developers most consistently under-think it',
  },
];

/* The fourth property, and the two usually conflated. */
const FOURTH = {
  p: 'AUTHENTICITY', means: 'knowing that a message came from WHO IT CLAIMS',
  isSeparateBecause: 'confidentiality protects a message from being READ; authentication protects it from being FAKED',
  independent: [
    { case: 'confidential AND unauthenticated', example: 'encrypted with a shared key ANYBODY POSSESSES',
      consequence: 'everybody with the key can PRODUCE it' },
    { case: 'authenticated AND not confidential', detail: 'a signed message is verifiable but READABLE BY ANYONE' },
  ],
  whySignatureExists: 'which is the reason a signature exists and the reason encrypt it is not a complete answer to is this genuine',
};
const OTHERS = [
  { p: 'NON-REPUDIATION', means: 'a party cannot plausibly deny having sent something',
    achievedBy: 'a signature with the private key under their SOLE CONTROL',
    whyNotSharedKey: 'with a shared key EITHER PARTY COULD HAVE PRODUCED it' },
];

Threats, vulnerabilities, and risk

Then the vocabulary that makes a security discussion precise rather than anxious. A threat is a potential cause of harm — an attacker, an accident, a bug, a flood. A vulnerability is a weakness you have that a threat could exploit. An exploit is working code or a technique that uses a vulnerability. A risk is the probability of harm multiplied by its impact, and this definition is doing real work, because it says that a catastrophic vulnerability with no plausible attacker and a trivial vulnerability on a system nobody can reach may both be low risk, while a moderate vulnerability holding the thing everybody wants is high. Then defence in depth, which is the most important structural idea in the chapter. Any single layer can fail; the stack survives if there is more than one. The layers in a well-defended system are independent — input validation, parameterised queries, a least-privilege database user, encryption, monitoring — and independence is the point: two controls that both fail together are one control. A validation layer that depends on the same library as the query layer is not depth. And the layer you cannot skip is the one that assumes the others have failed, which is usually authorisation, because it is the only layer whose job is to say no, and it is the one most often left implicit.

Then the reasoning that makes risk analysis useful rather than a formality, because the instinct to protect everything protects nothing. Not all data is equal. Sort it: what would be catastrophic, what would be embarrassing, what would merely be inconvenient — and the controls follow the classification, not the fear. Not all threats are equal. A determined attacker with a script will try every endpoint you have; an unsophisticated one will try the login form. Knowing which you face tells you where to spend the effort, and the honest answer for most systems is that bulk automated attacks are far more common than targeted ones, which means credential strength, rate limiting and patching beat most of what appears in threat models. Reduce surface first. Every endpoint, port, library and feature is something that can be attacked, and removing things is free while protecting them is not. And accept some risk deliberately, with the reasoning written down — because a risk nobody has decided to accept is a risk nobody is watching, and a documented decision is one you can revisit when the circumstances change.

/* Precise rather than anxious. */
const VOCABULARY = {
  threat: 'a potential CAUSE OF HARM', instances: ['an attacker', 'an accident', 'a bug', 'a flood'],
  vulnerability: 'a WEAKNESS YOU HAVE that a threat could exploit',
  exploit: 'working code or a technique that USES a vulnerability',
  risk: 'the PROBABILITY OF HARM MULTIPLIED BY ITS IMPACT',
  whyRiskMatters: ['a catastrophic vulnerability with no plausible attacker may be low risk',
    'a trivial vulnerability on a system nobody can reach may be low risk',
    'a MODERATE vulnerability holding the thing everybody wants is HIGH risk'],
};

/* Defence in depth. */
const DEPTH = {
  is: 'any single layer can fail; the stack survives if there is more than one',
  layers: ['input validation', 'parameterised queries', 'a least-privilege database user',
    'encryption', 'monitoring'],
  independenceIsThePoint: true,
  notDepth: 'two controls that BOTH FAIL TOGETHER are ONE CONTROL',
  example: 'a validation layer that depends on the same library as the query layer is not depth',
  theLayerYouCannotSkip: 'the one that ASSUMES THE OTHERS HAVE FAILED',
  usuallyThatIs: 'AUTHORISATION',
  why: 'it is the only layer whose job is to say NO, and it is the one most often left IMPLICIT',
};

/* Reasoning that makes risk analysis useful. */
const REASONING = [
  { p: 'not all DATA IS EQUAL', sortIt: ['what would be CATASTROPHIC', 'what would be EMBARRASSING',
    'what would merely be INCONVENIENT'],
    follow: 'the controls follow the CLASSIFICATION, not the fear' },
  { p: 'not all THREATS ARE EQUAL',
    examples: ['a determined attacker with a script will try EVERY ENDPOINT you have',
      'an unsophisticated one will try the LOGIN FORM'],
    payoff: 'knowing which you face tells you where to spend the effort',
    honestForMostSystems: 'BULK AUTOMATED ATTACKS are far more common than targeted ones',
    therefore: 'credential strength, rate limiting and patching beat most of what appears in threat models' },
  { p: 'reduce SURFACE first',
    detail: 'every endpoint, port, library and feature is something that can be attacked',
    economics: 'REMOVING THINGS IS FREE while protecting them is not' },
  { p: 'accept SOME RISK DELIBERATELY, with the reasoning written down',
    why: 'a risk NOBODY HAS DECIDED TO ACCEPT is a risk nobody is watching',
    gain: 'a documented decision is one you can REVISIT when the circumstances change' },
];

Defense in depth: layers of independent protections. Input validation and parameterised SQL and least-privilege DB user and encryption and monitoring. Any single layer can fail; the stack survives.

20.2 Injection & the #1 rule: never concatenate

Injection is the most common way code gets broken: attacker-supplied text is treated as executable code. The fix is one rule, never concatenate untrusted input into a command, query, or output. Use parameterized queries or prepared statements for SQL, escape or encode for HTML, shell, and URLs, and validate input against an allowlist at the boundary.

# DANGEROUS: string-concatenated SQL (SQL injection)
user = "' OR '1'='1'; --"            # attacker input
q = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + user + "'"
# Result: WHERE name = '' OR '1'='1'; --'  -> returns EVERY user. Disaster.

# SAFE: parameterised queries separate code from data
q = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?"   # '?' placeholder; value passed separately
cur.execute(q, (user,))              # values can NEVER become SQL

Why injection works, and it is one idea not several

Injection is not a family of unrelated bugs. SQL injection, command injection, and script injection are the same defect: data is concatenated into a piece of code that a component will parse and execute. The component cannot tell which part was meant to be code, because there is nothing marking it. Every defence in this section is the same idea applied: keep data and code separate so the parser cannot be confused. And the reason this has been the most exploited class of vulnerability for over two decades is not that programmers are careless — it is that the vulnerable form is the natural way to write the code, because it looks like every other string operation and it produces exactly the right result for every input the author thought of. Then SQL injection specifically, and the mechanics worth knowing. The application builds a query as a string and sends it to the database, which parses it. If a value is concatenated in, the value's contents become part of the syntax. A value of '; DROP TABLE users; -- is not a value any more; it is a statement terminator, a new statement, and a comment that hides the rest. The reason a parameterised query fixes it is precise: the parameter is not part of the query text at all. The query and the values travel separately, the database parses the query before it sees any value, and there is therefore no string a caller can send that changes what the query does. It is not escaping, and the difference matters: escaping has to be correct for the context and can be got wrong; parameterisation is structural and cannot be.

Then the other three, and the same shape in each. Command injection, where a user-supplied string becomes part of a shell command — and the fix is to pass the arguments as a list rather than as a command line, so the operating system does the parsing and a value containing a space or a semicolon is a space or a semicolon rather than a syntax change. Script injection in a page, where user data is written into a page and the browser parses it, and which has two variants worth separating: stored, where the malicious value is saved and executed for every visitor who views the page, and reflected, where it arrives in a link and executes for the one person who clicked it — and stored is much worse, because it affects everybody and can be triggered without any user action at all. Header injection, where a value containing a newline is written into a response header, letting an attacker inject an entirely new header or a second response. Template injection, where a template is compiled from a string that contained user input, giving the attacker the template language itself. And path traversal, where a filename containing ../ reads outside the intended directory — which is injection into a path, and the fix is the same: resolve the path and check it is still inside the directory you meant.

/* Not a family of unrelated bugs. */
const ONE_IDEA = {
  is: 'SQL injection, command injection and script injection are the SAME DEFECT',
  defect: 'DATA IS CONCATENATED INTO A PIECE OF CODE that a component will parse and execute',
  whyTheComponentCannotTell: 'there is NOTHING MARKING WHICH PART was meant to be code',
  everyDefence: 'the same idea applied - KEEP DATA AND CODE SEPARATE so the parser cannot be confused',
  whyItPersistsForTwoDecades: 'the vulnerable form is the NATURAL WAY to write the code',
  because: ['it looks like every other string operation',
    'and it produces EXACTLY THE RIGHT RESULT for every input the author thought of'],
};

/* SQL injection mechanics. */
const SQL = {
  mechanism: 'the application builds a query as a STRING and the database PARSES IT',
  whatHappens: 'if a value is concatenated in, the values contents BECOME PART OF THE SYNTAX',
  example: "a value of a semicolon, drop table users, and a comment is not a VALUE any more",
  itIs: 'a statement terminator, a NEW STATEMENT, and a COMMENT that hides the rest',
  whyParameterisationFixesIt: 'the parameter is NOT PART OF THE QUERY TEXT AT ALL',
  how: 'the query and the values TRAVEL SEPARATELY, and the database PARSES THE QUERY BEFORE IT SEES ANY VALUE',
  therefore: 'there is NO STRING a caller can send that changes what the query does',
  isNotEscaping: true,
  whyThatMatters: ['escaping has to be CORRECT FOR THE CONTEXT and can be got wrong',
    'PARAMETERISATION IS STRUCTURAL and cannot be'],
};

/* The other four. */
const OTHERS = [
  { v: 'COMMAND INJECTION', detail: 'a user-supplied string becomes part of a SHELL COMMAND',
    fix: 'pass the arguments as a LIST rather than as a command line',
    why: 'the operating system does the parsing, and a value containing a space or a semicolon is A SPACE OR A SEMICOLON rather than a syntax change' },
  { v: 'SCRIPT INJECTION in a page', detail: 'user data is written into a page and the BROWSER PARSES IT',
    variants: [
      { n: 'STORED', detail: 'the malicious value is SAVED and executed for every visitor who views the page',
        worse: 'affects EVERYBODY and can be triggered WITHOUT ANY USER ACTION at all' },
      { n: 'REFLECTED', detail: 'arrives in a link and executes for the ONE PERSON who clicked it' },
    ] },
  { v: 'HEADER INJECTION', detail: 'a value containing a NEWLINE is written into a response header',
    gain: 'letting an attacker inject an ENTIRELY NEW HEADER or a SECOND RESPONSE' },
  { v: 'TEMPLATE INJECTION', detail: 'a template is COMPILED FROM A STRING that contained user input',
    gain: 'giving the attacker THE TEMPLATE LANGUAGE ITSELF' },
  { v: 'PATH TRAVERSAL', detail: 'a filename containing parent-directory segments reads outside the intended directory',
    isA: 'injection into a path', fix: 'the same idea - RESOLVE THE PATH and check it is still inside the directory you meant' },
];

Preventing it, and the escaping mistakes

Then how to prevent each, and the ordering by strength is the same for all of them. First: eliminate the possibility. Can the operation be done without concatenation at all — a parameterised query, a prepared statement, an argument list, an escaping function from a vetted library? This is the strongest answer because it removes the class rather than an instance. Second: use an allow-list. If the value must be one of a known set, validate that it is, and reject everything else — and this is much stronger than trying to detect the bad values, because the person attacking you did not read your list of bad values. Third: escape, and escape for the specific context. And this is where mistakes happen: escaping for HTML is not escaping for an attribute, not escaping for JavaScript, and not escaping for a URL. A value correctly escaped for a text node and placed in an attribute is still a vulnerability, and this is why hand-written escaping is a bad idea even when the escaping itself is correct. Fourth: reduce privileges. A database user that cannot drop tables cannot have its tables dropped; a process that cannot write outside one directory cannot write outside it. Privilege is the layer that survives every other layer's failure, which is why defence in depth is a structure and not a slogan. And then the two practices that prevent the bug from being written at all. Static analysis and linters catch concatenation into a query or a command, reliably enough to be worth running in continuous integration, because they do not require understanding the application's semantics. And code review with a specific question — where does this value come from, and does it reach anything that parses it — catches the cases a linter misses, and it catches them because the question is one a reviewer can always answer.

/* Ordering by strength, the same for all of them. */
const PREVENT = [
  { r: 1, r2: 'ELIMINATE THE POSSIBILITY',
    can: 'the operation be done WITHOUT CONCATENATION',
    instances: ['a parameterised query', 'a prepared statement', 'an argument list',
      'an escaping function from a vetted library'],
    whyStrongest: 'it removes the CLASS rather than an instance' },
  { r: 2, r2: 'use an ALLOW-LIST',
    condition: 'the value must be one of a KNOWN SET',
    strongerThan: 'trying to detect the bad values',
    why: 'the person attacking you DID NOT READ your list of bad values' },
  { r: 3, r2: 'escape, and escape for the SPECIFIC CONTEXT',
    mistake: ['escaping for HTML is not escaping for an ATTRIBUTE',
      'not escaping for JAVASCRIPT', 'not escaping for a URL'],
    consequence: 'a value correctly escaped for a text node and placed in an attribute is STILL A VULNERABILITY',
    whyHandWrittenEscapingIsBad: 'even when the escaping itself is correct' },
  { r: 4, r2: 'reduce PRIVILEGES',
    instances: ['a database user that CANNOT DROP TABLES cannot have its tables dropped',
      'a process that cannot write outside one directory cannot write outside it'],
    whyItMatters: 'PRIVILEGE IS THE LAYER THAT SURVIVES every other layers failure',
    therefore: 'defence in depth is a STRUCTURE and not a slogan' },
];
/* Practices that prevent the bug being written at all. */
const LINTERS_AND_REVIEW = [
  { p: 'STATIC ANALYSIS and linters catch CONCATENATION INTO A QUERY OR A COMMAND',
    where: 'in continuous integration',
    reliability: 'reliably enough to be worth running',
    why: 'they do NOT REQUIRE UNDERSTANDING the applications semantics' },
  { p: 'code review with a SPECIFIC QUESTION',
    questions: ['where does this value COME FROM', 'does it reach ANYTHING THAT PARSES IT'],
    gain: 'catches the cases a linter misses',
    why: 'it catches them because the question is one a reviewer can ALWAYS ANSWER' },
];

Shows why string-concatenated SQL lets attacker input rewrite the query, and how parameterised queries keep code and data separate so input can never become SQL.

Same story in web land: never build HTML from user input without escaping it (XSS), never trust a header for logic, never eval() user data. The mantra: treat all input as hostile until proven otherwise.

20.3 OWASP Top 10 (the ones that matter for you now)

The OWASP Top 10 is the shared vocabulary of the most critical web application security risks, published and updated by the Open Worldwide Application Security Project. Current entries center on broken access control, injection flaws, authentication failures, and insecure configurations, among others. Each risk is a failure you can name and a defense you can apply today, making it the standard checklist for building and reviewing web apps.

The list, and what it is actually for

The OWASP Top Ten is a list of the categories that account for the large majority of application compromises, and two things about it are worth knowing before reading it. It is a list of categories, not of exploits — "broken access control" covers several hundred distinct bugs — and so it tells you what to look for rather than what to patch. And it changes over time, and that is the point: injection has been on every list since the beginning and remains the most-exploited in practice, while items are added as attacks become common enough to be worth naming. So use it as a checklist for review rather than as a statement of current risk, and note that a category being absent does not mean your application is safe from it. Now the categories, with what each one actually is and what stops it.

Then each one, because the value is in the mechanism. Broken access control, and it is first because it is consistently the most damaging: a user changing an identifier in a request and receiving somebody else's data. The mechanism is almost always the same — the server checks that the user is authenticated but not that the thing belongs to them — and the fix is to check authorisation on every single request, not on the screen. Cryptographic failures, which in practice means sensitive data sent without encryption, passwords stored without a slow salted hash, or validation performed by comparing against a weak secret. Injection, which the previous section covered. Insecure design, which is the absence of a control that no code bug would reveal: a business rule that lets a discount be applied repeatedly, a password reset that never expires, a limit that exists in the interface and not in the backend. Security misconfiguration, which is the largest category in practice because it includes default credentials, directory listing, verbose errors, a database reachable from anywhere and a framework running with its development mode on. Vulnerable and outdated components, which is usually found by knowing what you depend on rather than by discovering it. Authentication failures, which overlap with the credentials chapter. Software and data integrity failures — an unverified update, a deserialiser that will construct objects of arbitrary type. And logging and monitoring failures, which are the reason breaches take longer to notice than to cause.

/* Two things about the list. */
const ABOUT = [
  { f: 'it is a list of CATEGORIES, not of exploits',

    therefore: 'it tells you WHAT TO LOOK FOR rather than what to patch' },

    use: 'as a CHECKLIST FOR REVIEW rather than as a statement of current risk',
    caveat: 'a category being ABSENT does not mean your application is safe from it',
};

Reviewing against it, and what the list does not cover

Then how to use the list rather than memorise it, and the process is what makes it useful. For each category, ask the specific question rather than "have we considered this". For access control: list every endpoint, and for each one state which check applies to which object — a table with one row per endpoint and a column per authorisation rule, with any empty cell being a finding. That table is worth more than any checklist because it forces enumeration, and unenumerated endpoints are where the bugs are. For injection: find every place a value is concatenated into a query, a command, a template, a header or a path. For cryptography: list every secret, where it lives, how it is protected, and when it is rotated. Review the boundary of each, and the boundary is where the mistake is — the parse function, the shell call, the query builder, the escaping function — because the middle of a well-written function is rarely where a security defect lives. And do it as someone else would: a colleague who has not written the code, because the author's reasoning is exactly what will mislead them.

Then what the list does not cover, and this is the part that matters most in practice. Business logic flaws. Nothing in the list says "the user can apply a discount to the same order forty times", because that is not a category — it is a rule nobody wrote down, and it is usually found by asking what the user could do that would be wrong but would not look wrong. Availability and denial of service. A resource-exhaustion attack is a real compromise and is not on the list, because it does not fit the framing of confidentiality and integrity. Supply chain and third-party risk. A dependency you have never read and cannot audit is a risk you have accepted, whether or not it is on a list. Your own operational security — who has access to production, how they get it, whether that access is logged, and whether the logging is reviewable. And the insider threat, which is the one every list under-weights and the one no control set prevents entirely. The honest summary: the list is a floor, not a ceiling, and it is a floor for the categories it names. A system that has addressed every item on it can still have a business rule that lets one customer read another's data, and the reason is that the list was written by people looking at common technical failures rather than at your specific system, which is why the review has to be about your system and not about the list.

/* How to use the list rather than memorise it. */
const PROCESS = [
  { ask: 'for each category, ask the SPECIFIC QUESTION rather than have we considered this',

20.4 Cryptography you must actually know

You rarely need to design ciphers; you need to pick the right ones. Hash passwords with slow, salted algorithms such as bcrypt or Argon2, encrypt data with authenticated modes like AES-GCM, detect tampering with HMAC, and treat integrity hashing as different from encryption for confidentiality. Never use homemade cryptography; use established libraries and their defaults.

ToolPurposeNever useUse instead
HashFingerprint (checksums, passwords)MD5, SHA1, plain SHA256-of-passwordargon2/bcrypt (password), SHA-256 fine for checksums
Symmetric encryptionEncrypt data (both sides share key)DES, ECB mode, homemadeAES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305
AsymmetricKey exchange & signatures (TLS, GPG)RSA with tiny keysRSA 2048+/ECDSA (use libraries!)
MAC / signaturesDetect tamperingHash alone for payment payloadsHMAC or digital signature

Symmetric and asymmetric, and what each is actually for

Two families of cipher and the confusion between them is worth resolving precisely. Symmetric: one shared key. Fast, and the same key encrypts and decrypts, which means both parties need it and therefore either you have to deliver it over a channel that is already secure — chicken and egg — or you wrap it with something else. Asymmetric: a key pair. What is public can be given to anyone; what is private must never be. What is asymmetric gives you is authentication: a message signed with a private key can be verified by anyone holding the corresponding public key, and nobody else can have produced it. The performance difference is two orders of magnitude, which is why nobody encrypts data with asymmetric cryptography: real systems use asymmetric crypto once, at the start, to agree a symmetric key — which is exactly what the TLS section described — and then use symmetric crypto for everything. So the two are not competing; they solve different problems, and the composite construction is what you almost always want.

Then the four properties that distinguish a correct cipher from a broken one, and every real-world failure is one of these being violated. Confidentiality: without the key, the ciphertext reveals nothing. Integrity: without the key, nobody can modify the ciphertext and have the modification go undetected. Authentication: the message really came from the claimed sender. And forward secrecy: if the long-term key is later compromised, previously recorded traffic cannot be decrypted. That last one exists because of an attack nobody anticipated: an attacker who records encrypted traffic for years and later steals the server's private key could decrypt all of it, and forward secrecy — which requires a fresh ephemeral key per session, so compromising the long-term key reveals nothing about past sessions — is the defence. Then authenticated encryption, and this is the single most important practical rule in the section: use an authenticated mode, not encryption plus a separate integrity check. Encrypt-then-MAC, encrypt-and-MAC and MAC-then-encrypt are three constructions with subtly different failure modes, and choosing the wrong one has produced real vulnerabilities in real software; a modern mode such as an AEAD construction gives you confidentiality and integrity in one construction with the composition already correct, and it is what you should reach for.

/* Two families. */
const FAMILIES = [

    problem: 'both parties need it, so either you deliver it over a channel that is ALREADY SECURE - chicken and egg - or you WRAP IT with something else' },
  { f: 'ASYMMETRIC', key: 'a KEY PAIR',
    gives: 'AUTHENTICATION - a message signed with a private key can be verified by anyone holding the corresponding public key, and NOBODY ELSE CAN HAVE PRODUCED IT',
    performance: 'two orders of magnitude slower',
    consequence: 'NOBODY ENCRYPTS DATA with asymmetric cryptography',
    whatRealSystemsDo: 'asymmetric crypto ONCE, at the start, to agree a symmetric key, then symmetric crypto for everything',
    reframe: 'the two are not competing; they solve DIFFERENT PROBLEMS',
  },
];
/* Four properties, and every real-world failure is one being violated. */
const PROPERTIES = [
  { p: 'CONFIDENTIALITY', is: 'without the key, the ciphertext reveals NOTHING' },
  { p: 'INTEGRITY', is: 'without the key, NOBODY CAN MODIFY the ciphertext and have the modification go undetected' },

const AEAD = {

  rank: 'the single most important practical rule in this section',

Hashing, keys, and what to use

Then hashing, which is not encryption and the distinction matters more than anywhere else in the chapter. A hash has no key. The same input always produces the same output, anyone can compute it, and nobody can reverse it to recover the input. A cipher has a key and is reversible with it. So hashing is for verifying integrity and storing passwords; encryption is for confidentiality, and using a cipher where you needed a hash — encrypting a password because you want to be able to check it — is wrong because it means the value is recoverable and therefore that a key compromise recovers every password. Then the three hash properties that matter. Deterministic: the same input, the same output, every time, which is what lets you look something up. Avalanche effect: a one-bit change in the input changes about half the output bits, so an attacker cannot iteratively refine a guess. Preimage resistance: finding an input for a given output is computationally infeasible. And the fourth, which is what makes a hash useful as a commitment: collision resistance — finding two inputs with the same output. And then the rule that catches people: never use a general-purpose hash for a password, and never use it for integrity. For passwords you need a deliberately slow, salted function, which the authentication section covered. For integrity you need either a MAC — which has a key and therefore cannot be forged — or an authenticated mode, because an unkeyed hash of some data next to the data can simply be replaced along with the data.

Then keys, and the operational rules that decide whether any of it works. Key length matters and length alone is not enough — a longer key beats every cleverer algorithm, and an algorithm nobody has attacked beats a slightly longer key with an obsolete cipher. Keys must be generated from a cryptographically secure random source, never from a language's ordinary random function, which is designed for simulation and is predictable. Keys must be stored separately from the data they protect, so that compromising the data store does not compromise the keys. Keys must be rotated, and rotation is the only defence against the fact that every key will eventually be exposed. And encrypt the right things: everything at rest on disk, everything in transit, and the secrets themselves; and do not bother encrypting a field whose disclosure reveals nothing, because encryption has a cost in queryability, in debugging and in key management, and it is a cost paid for every row you encrypted on no benefit.

/* Hashing is not encryption. */
const HASH_VS_CIPHER = {
  hash: { hasKey: false, deterministic: true, anyoneCanCompute: true, reversible: false },
  cipher: { hasKey: true, reversible: 'with the key' },
  therefore: ['hashing is for VERIFYING INTEGRITY and STORING PASSWORDS',
    'encryption is for CONFIDENTIALITY'],
  wrong: 'encrypting a password because you want to be able to check it',
  why: 'it means the value is RECOVERABLE, and therefore a key compromise recovers EVERY PASSWORD',
};

/* Three properties that matter, and the fourth. */
const HASH_PROPERTIES = [
  { p: 'DETERMINISTIC', is: 'the same input, the same output, every time', why: 'what lets you LOOK SOMETHING UP' },
  { p: 'AVALANCHE EFFECT', is: 'a one-bit change in the input changes about HALF the output bits',
    gain: 'an attacker cannot ITERATIVELY REFINE a guess' },
  { p: 'PREIMAGE RESISTANCE', is: 'finding an input for a given output is COMPUTATIONALLY INFEASIBLE' },
  { p: 'COLLISION RESISTANCE', is: 'finding TWO inputs with the same output', role: 'what makes a hash useful as a COMMITMENT' },
];
const HASH_RULES = {
  never: ['a general-purpose hash for a PASSWORD', 'it for INTEGRITY'],
  forPasswords: 'a DELIBERATELY SLOW, SALTED function',
  forIntegrity: 'either a MAC - which HAS A KEY and therefore cannot be forged - or an AUTHENTICATED MODE',
  whyNotBareHash: 'an unkeyed hash NEXT TO THE DATA can simply be replaced ALONG WITH THE DATA',
};

/* Keys. */
const KEYS = [
  { r: 'LENGTH MATTERS and length alone is not enough',
    better: 'a longer key beats EVERY CLEVERER algorithm',
    also: 'an algorithm NOBODY HAS ATTACKED beats a slightly longer key with an obsolete cipher' },
  { r: 'generate from a CRYPTOGRAPHICALLY SECURE RANDOM SOURCE',
    never: 'a languages ORDINARY random function', why: 'it is designed for SIMULATION and is PREDICTABLE' },

    note: 'a cost paid FOR EVERY ROW you encrypted on no benefit' },
];

Never roll your own crypto. The library you didn’t write has had a hundred researchers with decades trying to break it; yours has had you. Use vetted libraries (cryptography, OpenSSL, libsodium) — the algorithm choice is a spec review, not a creative coding exercise.

20.5 Practical hardening checklist

The checklist, and how to actually run it

A list of security practices is worthless without a way to know whether they are in place, so the useful shape is one that pairs each item with the evidence that would show it. Six items, and the evidence is what makes them auditable rather than aspirational. Secrets are not in the repository. Evidence: a secret-scanning tool in continuous integration that fails the build, plus a check that the history is clean — because a secret deleted today is still in the history, and the evidence for that item is a scan of the history, not of the working tree. Dependencies are current and inventoried. Evidence: automated scanning with a policy about what severity blocks a build, plus a list of what you depend on that is generated rather than remembered. Input is validated at every boundary. Evidence: validation in middleware rather than in handlers, and a parameterised query builder with no string concatenation anywhere near it. Authentication and authorisation are separate and both enforced. Evidence: an authorisation check on every endpoint, and a test that demonstrates a user cannot read another user's object — because a check that is not tested is a check that can be removed. Security headers and TLS are configured. Evidence: a test that fetches the deployed site and asserts on the headers, because a header that is only set in a development environment is not set anywhere else. And errors do not leak. Evidence: a production configuration that returns a generic message and a log entry that returns the detail, with the stack trace never reaching the caller.

Then the practices that are cheap, unglamorous, and prevent more incidents than any of the above. Least privilege everywhere: the application runs as a user with only the permissions it needs; the database account it uses cannot create tables, let alone drop them; each service has its own credential rather than sharing one, because a shared credential means you cannot tell who did what and you cannot revoke one without revoking all. Patch on a schedule, not on an incident. A weekly window is uninteresting and effective; patching in response to an announcement is a race you will sometimes lose. Automated dependency updates, because the version you installed eight months ago has had eight months of security fixes and the version you installed yesterday has had none. Multi-factor authentication everywhere it is possible, and especially on anything that reaches production, because it removes the most common path rather than making it harder. Keep an inventory — of what you run, on what, with which versions — because you cannot patch, monitor or decommission what you do not know exists, and an unknown host on your network is an asset nobody is defending.

/* Useless without EVIDENCE that would show each item is in place. */
const CHECKLIST = [
  { item: 'secrets are NOT IN THE REPOSITORY',

    whyHistory: 'a secret deleted today is still in the HISTORY',
    theEvidenceIs: 'a scan of the history, not of the working tree' },
  { item: 'dependencies are CURRENT and INVENTORIED',
    evidence: ['automated scanning with a policy about what severity BLOCKS A BUILD',

  { item: 'input is validated at EVERY BOUNDARY',
    evidence: ['validation in MIDDLEWARE rather than in handlers',

Responding, and the habits that compound

Then response, because the list is about prevention and prevention is not sufficient. Have a written plan before you need it, and its content matters more than its existence: who decides to declare an incident, who talks to customers, who talks to the press, who talks to a regulator, and who is authorised to take the service down. The decisions are the plan, and making them during an incident is making them slowly. Assume you will be compromised and design for that rather than hoping otherwise, which means the specific practical measures: credentials stored where a compromised host cannot read them, logs sent somewhere the compromised host cannot delete them, and administrative access that does not come from the same machine as the production application. Have a revocation list ready — the ability to rotate every credential quickly, because the first thing an investigation establishes is which credentials were on the machine and the second is that they must all be replaced. And rehearse it, because the plan's failure mode is the assumption that everyone knows what to do, and the only way to remove that assumption is to have done it once.

Then the habits, and the honest observation that most of them are boring. Review security when you change something, not on a schedule. A new endpoint needs an authorisation check; a new dependency needs to be on the inventory; a new place data is stored needs an encryption decision — and a quarterly review misses all three because they are all changes. Write the security decision down when you make it. Why this endpoint has no authorisation check, why this field is not encrypted, why this dependency is acceptable — because in a year nobody will remember and the answer will be a guess. Treat a security finding as a defect with a severity, not as a special category of work; the reason findings rot is that they sit in a different queue from ordinary bugs and get a different kind of attention. And keep dependencies few. Every dependency is code you did not write, have not read, do not control the update cadence for, and will be responsible for — and the single most effective security change available to most teams is deleting three dependencies, which is a change nobody puts on a roadmap and everybody benefits from.

/* Prevention is not sufficient. */
const RESPOND = [

      'who talks to a regulator', 'who is authorised to TAKE THE SERVICE DOWN'],
    key: 'THE DECISIONS ARE THE PLAN', consequence: 'making them during an incident is MAKING THEM SLOWLY' },

The practical hardening checklist is a short, concrete list of moves with immediate payoff: keep dependencies patched, enforce least privilege on every account and role, lock down headers with CSP and HSTS, use HTTPS everywhere, guard secrets in a vault rather than the repo, and enable logging and alerting on suspicious behavior. Run it against every service you deploy, treating each item as a checkbox rather than a debate.

  1. HTTPS everywhere, HSTS header — even in development thinking.
  2. Parametrise everything (SQL, LDAP, shell).
  3. Secrets never in code: env vars / secret store (.env gitignored, Ch. 6).
  4. Least privilege: DB user can only do what it must; containers run as non-root.
  5. Input validation at the boundary (types, ranges, lengths, allow-lists).
  6. Security headers: CSP, X-Frame-Options, referrer policy.
  7. Log + alert on login failures, privilege changes, admin actions.
  8. Keep dependencies patched with automated scans in CI.

20.6 A walk through five famous attack classes

Five famous attack classes, seen from the attacker’s chair once so you recognize them in your own code forever: cross-site scripting, SQL injection, cross-site request forgery, broken authentication or session handling, and path traversal. For each one you trace the mechanics, who is harmed, and the defense that stops it, from encoding output to validating every path and input. Recognition is the first line of a strong defense.

See them from the attacker’s chair once, and you’ll recognise them in your own code forever.

AttackWhat happensYou defend by
Stored XSSAttacker posts <script>stealCookies()</script>; every viewer’s browser runs itEscape output (never innerHTML with user data), CSP header, HttpOnly cookies
CSRFYou’re logged into bank.com; evil site submits a forged POST /transfer and your cookie goes along for freeSameSite=Strict cookies, CSRF tokens in forms, check Origin header
SSRFAttacker makes your server fetch an internal URL like http://169.254.169.254/ (cloud metadata!)Validate/denylist outbound URLs, block link-local ranges on internal proxies
Open redirect/login?next=//evil.com ships the victim to a phishing siteAllowlist where redirects may point
RCE via deserializationAttacker crafts a pickle/object blob that runs code when the server unpacks itNever deserialize untrusted data; prefer signed, typed formats (JSON)
// The output-encoding triad, in one glance:
// 1. NEVER:   el.innerHTML = userInput
// 2. Instead: el.textContent = userInput        (safe: no parsing)
// 3. If HTML is a hard requirement: escape < > & " ' before insertion
function escapeHtml(s) {   // turn special chars into safe entities
  return s.replace(/[&<>"']/g, ch => ({
    '&': '&', '<': '<', '>': '>', '"': '"', "'": '''
  }[ch]));
}

The output-encoding triad for defeating XSS: never innerHTML, prefer textContent, and if HTML is required, escape every special character before insertion.

Reflex: anywhere user input meets SQL, shell, HTML, or URL building, your first thought should be your nearest injection. A good code review reads every execute() call and every innerHTML and how the data got there.

The attack surface, and how an attacker chooses a target

The useful mental model is that the internet is a machine that will attempt to log into every host it can reach, continuously, and your server is one of them. Exposure is the first thing that matters, because an attack requires reachability, and everything about how you are exposed changes the probability enormously. Automated scanning is universal. Port scans, banner grabs and known-vulnerability probes run against the whole internet continuously; a host with a public address and an unpatched service will be found within minutes to hours, and that is not a prediction, it is an observation. Unpatched is the finding that recurs, and the reason is structural: new vulnerabilities are published continuously, a scan for them is trivially automated, and a host that was safe last week is not necessarily safe today. Then the specific things that attract attention, and knowing them is worth more than knowing exploit techniques. Default credentials — an exposed database, a management panel or a device shipped with a known username and password, which is not a rare occurrence but the single most common way a host is taken over. Credentials in a repository, which is now common enough to be automated: secret-scanning services watch public repositories for keys and report them to the provider within minutes of being pushed. Exposed services that were never meant to be public — a database port, a management interface, an internal API reachable because a firewall rule was wrong. And deliberately advertised value, which is the unusual case but the one worth naming: a system that is interesting enough to attract a person rather than a script.

Then the classes of attack that matter and how they differ, because the distinction determines what you can do about each. Unauthenticated remote — no credentials needed, aimed at parsing bugs in network-facing services; this is the class where a patch is the fix. Authenticated — valid credentials but insufficient privileges, aimed at authorisation checks, and this is the class where privilege boundaries are the fix. Privilege escalation — a foothold at low privilege seeking a higher one; this is the class where least privilege is the fix and where the vast majority of real intrusions consist of this step rather than the initial one. Social — convincing a person rather than attacking software, and the reason two-factor authentication works is not that it is unguessable but that it removes the target from the path. And supply chain — a legitimate dependency or update that is compromised; this is the class where the answer is patching plus knowing your inventory, because you cannot audit code you did not know you had.

/* The model. */
const MODEL = 'the internet is a MACHINE THAT WILL ATTEMPT TO LOG INTO EVERY HOST IT CAN REACH, continuously, and your server is one of them';
const EXPOSURE = {
  mattersFirst: 'because an attack requires REACHABILITY',
  changes: 'everything about how you are exposed changes the PROBABILITY enormously',

  notAPrediction: 'this is not a prediction, it is an OBSERVATION',

};

The compromise chain, and what actually stops it

Then what an actual compromise looks like, because real attacks are sequences and the value of understanding the sequence is that each stage has a different control. Initial access: a valid credential, an unpatched service, or a phished person. Execution: the payload runs. Persistence: they install something that survives a restart — an account, a scheduled job, a modified startup script, a key. Privilege escalation: they move from whatever they got to what they want. Discovery: they map the network and find the systems that matter. Lateral movement: they move between them. Exfiltration: they take the data out, often through a channel that looks ordinary. Then the observation that changes how you should prioritise: detection is most likely in the middle, not at either end. Initial access is designed to be silent. Exfiltration is often hidden in ordinary traffic. But persistence, privilege escalation, discovery and lateral movement all generate unusual behaviour — a process from an unexpected parent, an account used from a new location, a service account reaching systems it has never reached — and that is where monitoring earns its keep. So the practical consequence: assume initial access and focus detection and controls on what happens next.

Then what actually stops each stage, in order. Reduce what there is to attack — fewer services, fewer dependencies, less exposed surface. Make each credential unique and strong, because most initial access is a reused password. Remove the passwords entirely where possible — key-based access, hardware tokens — because that removes the most common path rather than strengthening it. Patch quickly, and measure the gap between publication and application, because the exploitable window is that gap and it is usually the only number that matters. Run as least privilege, so the initial foothold is small and the escalation has nowhere to go. Log the things that matter and keep the logs somewhere the compromised host cannot alter them, because a log the attacker can delete is not evidence. And alert on behaviour, not on events — a login is an event and there are billions of them; a service account connecting to forty hosts it has never touched is a behaviour and there are none.

/* Real attacks are SEQUENCES, and each stage has a different control. */
const CHAIN = [
  { s: 'INITIAL ACCESS', means: ['a valid credential', 'an unpatched service', 'a phished person'] },
  { s: 'EXECUTION', does: 'the payload runs' },
  { s: 'PERSISTENCE', does: 'installs something that SURVIVES A RESTART',
    instances: ['an account', 'a scheduled job', 'a modified startup script', 'a key'] },
  { s: 'PRIVILEGE ESCALATION', does: 'moves from whatever they got to WHAT THEY WANT' },
  { s: 'DISCOVERY', does: 'map the network and find the systems that MATTER' },
  { s: 'LATERAL MOVEMENT', does: 'move between them' },
  { s: 'EXFILTRATION', does: 'take the data out, often through a channel that LOOKS ORDINARY' },
];

21 · System Design & Scalability

System Design and Scalability is the discipline of adding simple, separable building blocks as traffic grows. It covers the scaling toolbox, load balancers, caches, CDNs, queues, replicas and sharding, vertical versus horizontal scaling, stateless request flows, per-feature consistency choices, a URL shortener case study, and observability with logs, metrics, and traces. Learn each block and why it exists so bottleneck diagnosis becomes pattern matching.

21.1 The scaling toolbox21.2 Vertical vs horizontal scaling21.3 The stateless request flow (draw this from memory)21.4 Consistency & the CAP triangle applied21.5 Case study: design a URL shortener21.6 Observability: logs, metrics, traces

This is where a bachelor’s engineers become architects: designing systems for 1 user and for 100 million users. The interview "Design X" question is also a distilled version of real architecture work. You’ll finish this knowing the building blocks that make anything scale.

21.1 The scaling toolbox

Load balancers, caches, CDNs, queues, replicas, and shards are the standard scaling toolkit. Load balancers spread traffic across servers, caches and CDNs answer hot requests without hitting origin, queues decouple producers from consumers, replicas absorb reads, and shards split writes. Learn what each does and when it applies so diagnosing a slow system becomes matching symptoms to the right block.

The axis that actually matters, which is not scale

Serverless is not a scale story, and treating it as one leads to every wrong conclusion about it. The thing that changed is the unit of deployment. In a traditional application you deploy a program that runs continuously, holds resources while it is idle, and is billed for its existence. In a serverless model you deploy a function, the platform runs it when an event arrives, it exists for the duration, and it is billed for the work it did. Everything else — scaling to a million concurrent invocations, no servers to patch — follows from that one change rather than from any property of the underlying technology. Then the three consequences that are architectural rather than marketing. Your compute has no memory between invocations. So state must live somewhere else, which is the same statelessness argument as the previous chapter arriving by a different route — and it is why serverless and a stateless application are the same idea. Your execution has a bounded lifetime and a bounded environment. A function may have a maximum duration and a maximum memory, it cannot rely on a local filesystem persisting, and it cannot install a dependency at run time. And your cold start is a real cost. An instance must be created, your code loaded, and your dependencies initialised before the first request is served; a warm instance starts in milliseconds and a cold one in hundreds of milliseconds or a second, which is why serverless is a poor fit for latency-sensitive interactive work and a good fit for irregular, bursty, event-driven work.

Then what it is genuinely good at, and the reasoning connects to the shape of the traffic rather than the volume. Bursty and unpredictable load, because capacity is available on demand and idle capacity costs nothing, so the case is strongest where a conventional deployment would have to provision for the peak and pay for it continuously. Event-driven work — a message on a queue, an object created, a scheduled tick — because the model is a function reacting to an event and that is exactly what these are. Short, infrequent, and independently scalable, where a whole deployed service would be disproportionate. Spiky internal tools, where the load is a team rather than a customer base. And glue — the small functions that transform data between two systems, where the work is a few milliseconds and the alternative is a service with its own deployment pipeline. And what it is poor at, for the same reasons in reverse. Latency-sensitive interactive paths, because of cold starts and because the network hop to the platform is real. Long-running work, because of the duration limit. Anything with persistent connections or heavy state, because there is nothing between invocations to hold it. Work with a predictable, steady baseline, where a normal deployment is cheaper because you are paying for capacity whether you use it or not.

/* Not a scale story. */
const WHAT_CHANGED = {
  is: 'the UNIT OF DEPLOYMENT',
  before: ['you deploy a PROGRAM that runs continuously',
    'holds resources while it is idle', 'is billed for its EXISTENCE'],
  after: ['you deploy a FUNCTION', 'the platform runs it when an event arrives',
    'it exists for the duration', 'it is billed for the WORK IT DID'],
  follows: 'everything else - scaling to a million concurrent invocations, no servers to patch - follows from that ONE CHANGE rather than from any property of the underlying technology',
};

The cost model, and the trap in the pricing

Then the cost model, because this is where serverless decisions are actually made. You pay for invocations and for the duration of each. A function that takes 200 milliseconds and does little is charged for 200 milliseconds of a machine that is doing almost nothing — and the lever is often the runtime configuration rather than the code. Memory is priced per megabyte, and memory is often the biggest lever, because more memory means a faster CPU on most platforms, so a function that is slow because it is on a small configuration can be faster and cheaper on a larger one. That single interaction catches everybody. Concurrency limits and throttles are real, so a burst that would be handled by a queue of servers instead queues inside the platform, and the error you see is a throttling error rather than a capacity failure. And then the trap, which is worth stating because it is the reason a serverless bill can be surprising: a function that is invoked in a loop, or that retries, or that is wired to two events, multiplies its invocations. A design where one user action produces five invocations is five times the cost, and this is not obvious from reading the code because the invocations happen in configuration rather than in the function. The disciplined response is the same as everywhere else: put a budget alert on the account, so the surprise arrives as an email rather than as an invoice, and know which function is the expensive one by measuring rather than by guessing.

/* The cost model. */
const PRICING = [
  { p: 'you pay for INVOCATIONS and for the DURATION OF EACH',

    lever: 'often the RUNTIME CONFIGURATION rather than the code' },

    therefore: 'a function that is slow because it is on a SMALL configuration can be FASTER AND CHEAPER on a larger one',
    note: 'this single interaction catches EVERYBODY' },
  { p: 'CONCURRENCY LIMITS and THROTTLES ARE REAL',
    consequence: 'a burst that would be handled by a queue of servers instead QUEUES INSIDE THE PLATFORM',
    symptom: 'the error you see is a THROTTLING ERROR rather than a capacity failure' },
];
const THE_TRAP = {

  whyNotObvious: 'because the invocations happen in CONFIGURATION rather than in the function',
  discipline: 'put a BUDGET ALERT on the account',

ToolWhat it doesWhen you need it
Load balancerSpreads requests across serversWhen one server overflows
CacheKeeps hot data near the user/fastRead-heavy apis, hot objects
CDNServes static assets from edge nodes worldwideGlobal users, images, JS bundles

21.2 Vertical vs horizontal scaling

Vertical scaling adds more CPU, memory, and disk to one machine, which is simple but finite and increasingly expensive. Horizontal scaling adds more machines, which is unbounded but forces you to solve state, since a request may land on any node. When servers become disposable, shared state must live elsewhere, in databases, caches, or object stores, so the app tier stays stateless and replaceable.

  • Vertical: buy a bigger machine (more CPU/RAM). Easy, but has a ceiling and a single point of failure.
  • Horizontal: add more modest machines behind a load balancer. Scales almost without limit — but now your state becomes the problem. Sessions, caches and databases must survive "an app server just died".

The four modes, and the arithmetic that chooses between them

There are four things you can do to a system, and confusing them is what produces bad scaling decisions. Vertical scaling — a bigger machine. Cheap in engineering, limited in ceiling, and the right first move because it requires no code change. Horizontal scaling — more machines. Unbounded, requires the application to not care which machine, and the reason it is harder is the statelessness requirement. Caching — answer from somewhere cheaper. This is almost always the highest-value change because it removes load rather than adding capacity, and it is the one most neglected. Sharding — split the data across machines. Unbounded, and by far the most expensive, and the one that should be last. Then the order, and it is not a preference. Measure first, because the bottleneck determines the answer and the bottleneck is frequently not where it is assumed. Fix the algorithm and the query, because an N-plus-one query wastes the entire machine's capacity on round trips and no amount of capacity fixes it. Add indexes, where a missing index turns a linear scan into a seek and costs nothing. Cache, which converts the most frequent requests into no work. Read replicas, because most systems are read-dominated by a large factor. Add caches and increase connection limits, which are capacity changes rather than architecture changes. Vertical scale, which buys time cheaply. Break up the monolith into services with clear boundaries. And shard, last, because it is the only one that makes your data model, your queries and your operations permanently harder, and you should be certain there is no alternative before you do it.

Then the numbers that make the decision, and the estimation is the part people skip and the part that matters. Requests per second, and the peak rather than the average — the peak is typically several times the average and the peak is what the capacity must survive. Requests per day and per year, because storage grows linearly and three years of growth is a different machine than one year. Bytes per request, which is what determines bandwidth rather than request count. Working set size, because a working set larger than memory is the cliff from the operating-systems chapter and no amount of capacity fixes it. Read-to-write ratio, because it decides whether replicas help enormously or not at all. Then the derived quantities, and the derivation is arithmetic rather than intuition. A million daily active users with each taking twenty actions a day is twenty million requests a day; at a peak-to-average ratio of four that is roughly a thousand requests a second at peak. At one kilobyte per response, that is about a megabyte a second at peak, or roughly three and a half terabytes a day of egress — and that last number is usually the one that surprises people, because egress is billed and bandwidth is a resource you have to provision separately from CPU.

/* Four things you can do, often confused. */
const MODES = [
  { m: 'VERTICAL', does: 'a bigger machine',
    effort: 'cheap in engineering', ceiling: 'limited',
    firstMove: true, why: 'it requires NO CODE CHANGE' },
  { m: 'HORIZONTAL', does: 'more machines', ceiling: 'unbounded',
    requires: 'the application to NOT CARE which machine',
    whyHarder: 'the STATELESSNESS requirement' },
  { m: 'CACHING', does: 'answer from somewhere CHEAPER',
    highestValue: true, neglectedMost: true,
    why: 'it REMOVES LOAD rather than adding capacity' },
  { m: 'SHARDING', does: 'split the DATA across machines', ceiling: 'unbounded',

];
