Reading the symptoms, and the failure modes to plan for

Then reading the symptoms, because in practice the diagnosis is the skill and the pattern is always the same four questions. Is one request slow or all of them? One slow request is a slow query, a large response, or a cold cache; all of them slow is saturation, and the two have completely different fixes. Is CPU or memory or I/O? A high-utilisation process is CPU-bound and adding instances may not help if the contention is a lock; high memory is a working-set problem; high I/O wait is storage, and it is the one that scaling the application tier does not fix at all. Does latency rise with load or sit flat? Rising latency is queueing, and it is the signature of approaching saturation — and the useful fact is that it rises steeply near the limit, which means a system at eighty per cent utilisation has far less headroom than it appears. Is it one tenant or all of them? A single noisy neighbour on a shared resource is a partition or quota problem and not a capacity one, and it is diagnosed by comparing per-tenant rather than per-system numbers. Then the failure modes to plan for, because a scaling plan that does not include them is not a plan. Cascade failure, where one dependency slows down and the resource it holds backs up through every caller until the whole system is down — and the defence is a timeout on every call and a bulkhead so the failure cannot propagate. Retry storms, where a recovering dependency is overwhelmed by every client retrying at once, and the defence is backoff with jitter. Thundering herd at a cache expiry, where every key expires simultaneously and the database receives the full load at once, and the defence is a little randomness in the expiry. And the scaling cliff itself, where one dimension of capacity runs out and adding more of the others changes nothing.

/* Four diagnostic questions. */
const DIAGNOSE = [
  { q: 'is ONE REQUEST slow or ALL of them',
    one: 'a slow query, a large response, or a cold cache',
    all: 'SATURATION',
    why: 'the two have COMPLETELY DIFFERENT FIXES' },
  { q: 'is CPU or MEMORY or I/O',
    cpu: 'CPU-bound, and adding instances may not help if the contention is a LOCK',
    memory: 'a WORKING-SET PROBLEM',
    io: 'storage - and it is the one that scaling the application tier DOES NOT FIX AT ALL' },
  { q: 'does latency RISE WITH LOAD or sit flat',
    rising: 'queueing, and the signature of approaching saturation',
    fact: 'it rises STEEPLY near the limit, which means a system at eighty per cent utilisation has FAR LESS HEADROOM than it appears' },
  { q: 'is it ONE TENANT or all of them',
    one: 'a noisy neighbour on a shared resource - a PARTITION or QUOTA problem, not a capacity one',
    diagnoseBy: 'comparing PER-TENANT rather than PER-SYSTEM numbers' },
];

/* Failure modes a plan must include. */
const FAILURES = [
  { f: 'CASCADE FAILURE', does: 'one dependency slows down and the RESOURCE IT HOLDS backs up through every caller',
    consequence: 'the whole system is down',
    defence: ['a TIMEOUT on every call', 'a BULKHEAD so the failure cannot propagate'] },
  { f: 'RETRY STORM', does: 'a recovering dependency is OVERWHELMED by every client retrying at once',
    defence: 'backoff WITH JITTER' },
  { f: 'THUNDERING HERD at a cache expiry', does: 'every key EXPIRES SIMULTANEOUSLY and the database receives the full load at once',
    defence: 'a little RANDOMNESS in the expiry' },
  { f: 'the SCALING CLIFF itself', does: 'one DIMENSION of capacity runs out and adding more of the others changes nothing' },
];

The classic scaling failure isn’t the load balancer — it’s statelessness betrayal. A server that keeps user sessions in its local memory breaks the moment two requests for the same user hit two different servers. Rule: app servers stateless; state lives in shared stores (DB, Redis, object storage).

21.3 The stateless request flow (draw this from memory)

If any request can land on any server in a fleet and still get the correct answer, you can scale freely. The rule is that state moves out of application servers and into shared stores: a relational database for truth, a distributed cache for hot session data, and object storage for files, so the app tier stays dumb and replaceable. Draw this flow once from memory and it becomes the skeleton of every scale design.

Users
  |
  v
[CDN] -------- static assets
  |
  v
[Load Balancer]
  |        |        |
 App1    App2     App3        (stateless, identical, autoscaled)
  \        |        /
   v       v       v
   [Service / API    ]  -->  [Cache: Redis]
   [Auth service     ]  -->  [Queue] --> [Workers]
            |                       \--> [Object storage]
   [Primary DB] <- [Read replicas]

What stateless actually requires, and why it is harder than it sounds

The architecture in the figure is a load balancer in front of several identical application servers, with all the shared state — the database, the cache, the queue, object storage — behind them rather than inside them. Statelessness is a property of the application tier only, and the requirement is precise: any request may be served by any instance, and the response must not depend on anything that instance remembers from a previous request. That is a stronger requirement than "the server does not write to disk", because it also excludes a module-level cache, a connection to a specific peer chosen at startup, and — the one everybody misses — a counter or a rate-limit table held in the process's memory. Then what that buys, and the four gains are each worth a specific operational capability. Adding an instance requires no coordination, which means scaling is starting a process and changing the balancer's pool — seconds, not the coordination a stateful system needs. Losing an instance is invisible to users, because no instance holds anything that would have been lost, so a crash is a capacity event rather than a data-loss event. Deploys become rolling, because a mixed fleet of old and new versions is fine when neither holds state that the other will look for. And horizontal scaling of the application tier is automatic and requires no sharding of the data, which is the difference between scaling the tier and scaling the whole system.

Then what it costs and why people get it wrong, and the failure is specific enough to name. State must go somewhere, and everywhere you put it is a network call. A session that was a memory read is now a cache lookup; a configuration value that was a module constant is now a query at startup; a rate-limit counter that was an integer increment is now an atomic operation in a shared store. Each of those is correct and each is slower, and the aggregate is the cost of statelessness — you have traded memory locality for a network hop, and the honest measurement is whether the thing you gained is worth it, not whether statelessness is philosophically better. Then the internal state that sneaks back in, which is the thing to watch for in a codebase that was stateless and stopped being: a memoised value with no expiry; a connection pool sized from the process's own observed load; a circuit breaker whose state is per-process, so three instances have three different opinions about whether a dependency is down; an in-process cache of a configuration value with a five-minute expiry, which is a stale value whose lifetime nobody chose. None of these are wrong — they are the right design for a cache and the wrong design for correctness — and the discipline is to make the distinction explicit: if losing it changes behaviour, it is state and it must be shared; if it only changes speed, it is a cache and it may be local.

/* A property of the APPLICATION TIER ONLY. */
const REQUIREMENT = {
  is: 'any request may be served by any instance',
  full: 'and the response must not depend on anything THAT INSTANCE REMEMBERS from a previous request',
  strongerThan: 'the server does not write to disk',
  alsoExcludes: ['a MODULE-LEVEL CACHE', 'a connection to a SPECIFIC PEER chosen at startup',
    'and the one everybody misses: a COUNTER or a RATE-LIMIT TABLE held in the processs memory'],
};

/* Four gains, each worth a capability. */
const GAINS = [
  { g: 'adding an instance requires NO COORDINATION',
    gain: 'scaling is starting a process and changing the balancers pool - SECONDS, not the coordination a stateful system needs' },
  { g: 'losing an instance is INVISIBLE TO USERS',
    why: 'no instance holds anything that WOULD HAVE BEEN LOST',
    consequence: 'a crash is a CAPACITY EVENT rather than a DATA-LOSS EVENT' },
  { g: 'DEPLOYS BECOME ROLLING', why: 'a mixed fleet of old and new versions is fine when NEITHER HOLDS STATE that the other will look for' },
  { g: 'HORIZONTAL SCALING of the application tier is AUTOMATIC and requires NO SHARDING of the data',
    significance: 'the difference between scaling the tier and scaling the WHOLE SYSTEM',
  },
];

/* The cost. */
const COST = {
  fact: 'state must go SOMEWHERE, and everywhere you put it is a NETWORK CALL',
  examples: ['a session that was a MEMORY READ is now a CACHE LOOKUP',
    'a configuration value that was a MODULE CONSTANT is now a QUERY AT STARTUP',
    'a rate-limit counter that was an INTEGER INCREMENT is now an ATOMIC OPERATION in a shared store'],
  eachIs: ['correct', 'slower'],
  theAggregate: 'the cost of statelessness',
  theTrade: 'you have traded MEMORY LOCALITY for a NETWORK HOP',
  honestMeasurement: 'whether the thing you GAINED is worth it, not whether statelessness is philosophically better',
};

/* Internal state that sneaks back in. */
const SNEAKS_BACK = [
  { x: 'a MEMOISED VALUE with no expiry' },
  { x: 'a CONNECTION POOL SIZED from the processs own observed load' },
  { x: 'a CIRCUIT BREAKER whose state is PER-PROCESS',
    consequence: 'three instances have THREE DIFFERENT OPINIONS about whether a dependency is down' },
  { x: 'an IN-PROCESS CACHE of a configuration value with a five-minute expiry',
    isA: 'a STALE VALUE whose LIFETIME NOBODY CHOSE' },
];
const NOT_WRONG = 'none of these are WRONG - they are the right design for a cache and the wrong design for correctness';
const THE_DISCIPLINE = {
  test: 'if LOSING IT CHANGES BEHAVIOUR, it is state and it MUST BE SHARED; if it only changes SPEED, it is a cache and it MAY BE LOCAL',
};

Where state should live, and the practices that keep it out

Then where the state goes, and the taxonomy is the whole design. Authoritative state — the thing that is true — belongs in a database with transactions, because only that store can enforce the invariants when two requests arrive simultaneously. Derived state that is expensive to compute belongs in a cache with a stated lifetime, because it can always be rebuilt and the only question is how stale it may be. Transient state — the per-request working set — belongs in the process, and dies with the request; this is the free case, and the discipline is to make sure it really is per-request and nothing escapes. Long-lived but per-user state — a shopping cart, a draft, a wizard's progress — belongs in a store with an explicit lifetime, because a cart in process memory is a cart that disappears when the process is replaced. And state you do not have — anything derivable — should be derived on read rather than stored, because a stored derived value is a second source of truth that will eventually disagree with the first.

/* The taxonomy IS the design. */
const TAXONOMY = [
  { k: 'AUTHORITATIVE state', example: 'the thing that is TRUE',
    where: 'a DATABASE WITH TRANSACTIONS',
    why: 'only that store can ENFORCE THE INVARIANTS when two requests arrive simultaneously' },
  { k: 'DERIVED state that is expensive to compute', where: 'a CACHE with a STATED LIFETIME',
    why: 'it can always be REBUILT and the only question is HOW STALE IT MAY BE' },
  { k: 'TRANSIENT state', example: 'the per-request working set', where: 'THE PROCESS',
    lifetime: 'dies with the request', isTheFreeCase: true,
    discipline: 'make sure it REALLY IS per-request and nothing escapes' },
  { k: 'LONG-LIVED but per-user state', instances: ['a shopping cart', 'a draft', 'a wizards progress'],
    where: 'a store with an EXPLICIT LIFETIME',
    why: 'a cart in process memory is a cart that DISAPPEARS when the process is replaced' },
  { k: 'state you DO NOT HAVE', meaning: 'anything derivable', action: 'derive it ON READ rather than store it',
    why: 'a stored derived value is a SECOND SOURCE OF TRUTH that will eventually DISAGREE with the first' },
];

An ASCII architecture of a horizontally scalable service: stateless app servers behind a load balancer, with caches, queues and replicas holding all shared state.

21.4 Consistency & the CAP triangle applied

What consistency models actually promise

A consistency model is a promise about what a reader will observe, and the useful thing about them is that they are ordered by strength rather than by adjective. Strong consistency — also called linearizability — means the system behaves as if there were one copy of the data. Every read sees the most recent write, and operations appear to take effect in a single order. It is the model people assume when they say "the database is consistent", and it is achievable, at a cost. Sequential consistency means all operations appear in some single order, and each process's operations appear in its own program order — but the order need not be real time. It is slightly weaker than linearizability, because two operations that did not overlap may be ordered either way, which is a distinction that matters only under concurrency. Causal consistency means operations that happened after each other are seen in that order, and concurrent operations may be seen in any order — which is the model human reasoning about causality actually expects, and it is the point where most products stop. Read-your-writes is the guarantee a specific user cares about: after you save, you see your save. Monotonic reads is the weaker guarantee that a reader never sees the value go backwards. And eventual consistency means no promise beyond convergence: every replica will reach the same value if writes stop, and the time it takes is the convergence delay.

Then why the strong models cost something, and the mechanism rather than the slogan. Contradiction between availability and latency. If a write happened on one node and a read arrives at another, the only way to return the newest value is to wait for the first node to tell the second, and waiting is exactly the latency you were trying to avoid. So a strong model is a statement about how long a read may take as much as about correctness, and that is the honest way to think about it. Coordination is not free. Even on the same machine, making two participants agree costs an exchange, and a majority-quorum protocol costs a round trip for the second and third participants. Availability is reduced, because a node that cannot reach a quorum must refuse — and refusing is the correct behaviour under a strong model, which is why such a system degrades by returning errors rather than by returning stale data. And the engineering burden, which is rarely mentioned and is the real cost: a strongly consistent distributed data store is a considerably harder thing to build and to operate than one that converges, and its failure modes are stranger.

/* Ordered by STRENGTH rather than by adjective. */
const MODELS = [
  { m: 'STRONG CONSISTENCY', also: 'linearizability',
    promise: 'the system behaves as if there were ONE COPY of the data',
    guarantees: ['every read sees the MOST RECENT write', 'operations appear to take effect in a SINGLE ORDER'],
    isTheDefaultAssumption: true, achievable: true, atACost: true },
  { m: 'SEQUENTIAL CONSISTENCY', promise: 'all operations appear in SOME SINGLE ORDER and each processs operations appear in its own program order',
    weakerThan: 'linearizability', because: 'the order need not be REAL TIME',
    differenceMattersOnly: 'under concurrency - two operations that did not overlap may be ordered either way' },
  { m: 'CAUSAL CONSISTENCY', promise: 'operations that happened AFTER EACH OTHER are seen in that order; concurrent operations may be seen in any order',
    isTheModel: 'human reasoning about causality ACTUALLY EXPECTS',
    stopPoint: 'this is where most products stop' },
  { m: 'READ-YOUR-WRITES', promise: 'after you save, you see your save',
    is: 'the guarantee a SPECIFIC USER cares about' },
  { m: 'MONOTONIC READS', promise: 'a reader never sees the value GO BACKWARDS' },
  { m: 'EVENTUAL CONSISTENCY', promise: 'no promise beyond CONVERGENCE',
    detail: 'every replica will reach the same value if writes STOP, and the time it takes is the CONVERGENCE DELAY' },
];

/* Why the strong models cost something. */
const COSTS = [
  { c: 'CONTRADICTION between availability and latency',
    detail: 'if a write happened on one node and a read arrives at another, the only way to return the NEWEST value is to WAIT for the first node to tell the second',
    reframe: 'a strong model is a statement about HOW LONG A READ MAY TAKE as much as about correctness',
    and: 'that is the honest way to think about it' },
  { c: 'COORDINATION IS NOT FREE',
    detail: 'even on the same machine, making two participants AGREE costs an exchange',
    magnitude: 'a majority-quorum protocol costs A ROUND TRIP for the second and third participants' },
  { c: 'AVAILABILITY IS REDUCED', mechanism: 'a node that cannot reach a quorum MUST REFUSE',
    correct: 'and refusing is the CORRECT BEHAVIOUR under a strong model',
    therefore: 'such a system DEGRADES BY RETURNING ERRORS rather than by returning stale data' },
  { c: 'the ENGINEERING BURDEN', rarelyMentioned: true, isTheRealCost: true,
    detail: 'a strongly consistent distributed data store is a CONSIDERABLY HARDER thing to build and to operate than one that converges',
    and: 'its failure modes are STRANGER' },
];

Choosing, and what to do while waiting

Then how to choose, and the rule is simpler than the theory suggests. Ask what a user would consider a bug. If a user would be confused or harmed by seeing stale data, that path needs something stronger than eventual consistency — and the ones that always qualify are a payment, a balance, an inventory count, a permission check, and a one-time token. If a user would merely find it odd, eventual consistency is fine and you should add a small affordance — a "just now" label, a spinner, a refresh — rather than a stronger model. Then use the strongest model at the smallest scope that needs it. A global strong model to protect one balance is enormously more expensive than a strong check on that one value, and the strong version is usually a conditional write — a compare-and-set, a unique constraint, a transaction — rather than a distributed consensus protocol. Then pick consistency per operation, not per system. A real system is a mixture: the account balance is strict, the product description is eventual, the follower count is eventual with a read-your-writes guarantee for the person who pressed the button. Then what to do about the delay, and the three techniques that matter. Read-your-writes, achieved by writing to the same node you will read from, or by pinning the user to a replica until they see their own write. Monotonic reads, achieved by pinning a client to one replica for the duration of a session, which is simple and removes a whole class of confusing behaviour. And make the delay visible, because a spinner that resolves to the right answer in half a second and one that resolves in three seconds are different experiences, and the design that shows the user something meaningful during the wait is the one that gets tolerated.

/* The rule is simpler than the theory suggests. */
const CHOOSE = [
  { q: 'ask what a USER WOULD CONSIDER A BUG',
    ifHarmed: 'that path needs something STRONGER than eventual consistency',
    alwaysQualify: ['a payment', 'a balance', 'an inventory count', 'a permission check', 'a one-time token'],
    ifOnlyOdd: 'eventual consistency is fine',
    then: 'add a SMALL AFFORDANCE - a just now label, a spinner, a refresh - rather than a STRONGER MODEL' },
  { q: 'use the STRONGEST MODEL AT THE SMALLEST SCOPE THAT NEEDS IT',
    example: 'a global strong model to protect one balance is ENORMOUSLY MORE EXPENSIVE than a strong check on that one value',
    howTheStrongVersionUsuallyWorks: 'a CONDITIONAL WRITE - a compare-and-set, a unique constraint, a transaction',
    rather: 'a distributed consensus protocol' },
  { q: 'pick consistency PER OPERATION, not per system', isA: 'real system is a MIXTURE',
    examples: ['the account balance is STRICT', 'the product description is EVENTUAL',
      'the follower count is EVENTUAL WITH A READ-YOUR-WRITES guarantee for the person who pressed the button'],
  },
];
/* What to do about the delay. */
const DELAY = [
  { t: 'READ-YOUR-WRITES', achievedBy: ['writing to the SAME NODE you will read from',
    'pinning the user to a replica until they see their own write'] },
  { t: 'MONOTONIC READS', achievedBy: 'pinning a client to ONE REPLICA for the duration of a session',
    gain: 'SIMPLE, and removes a WHOLE CLASS of confusing behaviour' },
  { t: 'MAKE THE DELAY VISIBLE', why: 'a spinner that resolves to the right answer in half a second and one that resolves in three seconds are DIFFERENT EXPERIENCES',
    and: 'the design that shows the user something MEANINGFUL during the wait is the one that gets TOLERATED' },
];

CAP is not an exam question; it is a per-feature decision. When a network partition happens you choose consistency, where every node returns the same latest value, or availability, where every request is answered, or a partial trade in between that is usually eventual consistency. Applied deliberately, strong consistency protects money movements while eventual consistency accepts small delays for likes and feeds, so make the choice per operation rather than by accident.

Revisit Ch. 13.4 CAP and make it concrete: a "likes counter" that must be globally consistent forces synchronous replication (slower, higher p99). A "last-seen timestamp" tolerates eventual consistency (fast, cheaper). Decide consistency per feature, not per database.

  • Strong consistency: orders, balances, inventory.
  • Eventual: likes, feeds, presence, search indexes.

21.5 Case study: design a URL shortener

Designing a URL shortener is a complete tour of the scaling toolbox in one small system. You choose how to generate short keys, how to store the mapping so lookups stay index-fast, and how to handle redirects, expiration, and abuse, then add caching and analytics as traffic grows. Work through it once and you have seen load balancers, indexing, caching, and observability in miniature.

The canonical interview problem — and a complete tour of the toolbox.

  • Requirements: create short links, redirect to target, analytics, never link to a dead short code.
  • Data: table links(code PK, target, created_at), plus counter table. ~7 chars base62 = 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 trillion codes — enough.
  • Redirect: GET /:code → lookup → 302 to target. 302 (temporary) lets you change targets; 301 (permanent) is cached by browsers — this matters.
  • Hot path: every redirect is a very hotspot read → cache code→target in Redis (TTL). Cache miss → DB → aside semantics.
  • Scale numbers: 500 B requests/year ≈ 1,600 rps. One tiny DB with caching + replicas handles it; further scale → shard on first character of code.
  • Failure modes: DB down → region cutover; analytics are eventually consistent; rate-limit creation to stop spam.

Working the design, and the order that makes it work

A design conversation has a shape, and the shape is what separates a considered answer from a list of technologies. Start by clarifying the requirements and the constraints, and write them down in numbers. Not "it should scale" but: how many users, how many requests per user, what latency, what availability, what consistency, how much data and growing how fast. The reason numbers matter is that they make the rest of the conversation checkable — without them, every design decision is a matter of taste, and with them most decisions have an obviously right answer. Then estimate. Do the arithmetic out loud: requests per day, peak requests per second, storage per year, bandwidth, and the growth in two years. This is not busywork; it is the step that eliminates whole classes of bad design, because the arithmetic frequently shows that the thing you were about to build is unnecessary — a thousand requests a second is not a scale problem, and a petabyte a year is. Then sketch the read and write paths separately, because they have different characteristics and one is usually simpler: a read path is cache-lookup then database; a write path is validate then write then notify, and the write path is where every complication appears. Then choose the technology for the bottleneck, not for the diagram you had in mind.

Then the four things every design must answer, and a design that cannot answer them is not finished. What happens when a dependency is down? Not "we would retry" but: does the request fail, does it degrade, does it queue, and what does the user see? What happens when it is slow? Because slow is worse than down — a dependency that fails fast can be handled, and one that hangs holds your resources until it times out. How do we know it is working? Which metric, which dashboard, which alert. And what happens when we need to change the schema? Which is the question nobody asks and everybody discovers at the worst time, because adding a non-nullable column to a table with ten million rows means a rewrite or a migration strategy. Then the three mistakes that fail most design conversations, and each is a conversation failure rather than a technical one. Starting with the technology. "We will use Kafka" before anyone has established that the requirement involves ordering, throughput or decoupling — and then the design bending to fit the tool. Not estimating. Which means no basis for any decision, and therefore the argument becomes about preference. Ignoring the boring parts — the schema change, the migration, the data cleanup, the operator who has to run this — which is where real projects are made or broken, and which takes no more than ten minutes to discuss.

/* The shape of the conversation. */
const SHAPE = [
  { step: 1, do: 'clarify REQUIREMENTS and CONSTRAINTS, and write them down IN NUMBERS',
    notThis: 'it should scale',
    instead: ['how many users', 'how many requests per user', 'what latency', 'what availability',
      'what consistency', 'how much data and GROWING HOW FAST'],
    whyNumbers: 'they make the rest of the conversation CHECKABLE',
    withoutThem: 'every design decision is a MATTER OF TASTE, and with them most decisions have an OBVIOUSLY RIGHT ANSWER' },
  { step: 2, do: 'ESTIMATE', compute: ['requests per day', 'peak requests per second',
    'storage per year', 'bandwidth', 'the growth in two years'],
    notBusywork: 'it is the step that ELIMINATES whole classes of bad design',
    because: 'the arithmetic frequently shows that the thing you were about to build is UNNECESSARY',
    examples: ['a thousand requests a second is NOT a scale problem', 'a petabyte a year IS'],
  },
  { step: 3, do: 'sketch the READ and WRITE paths SEPARATELY',
    why: 'they have different characteristics and ONE IS USUALLY SIMPLER',
    readPath: 'cache lookup then database',
    writePath: 'validate then write then notify',
    and: 'the WRITE PATH is where every complication appears',
  },
  { step: 4, do: 'choose the technology for the BOTTLENECK, not for the diagram you had in mind' },
];

/* Four things every design must answer. */

  { q: 'what happens when a DEPENDENCY IS DOWN',
    not: 'we would retry',

  { q: 'what happens when it is SLOW',
    worse: 'SLOW IS WORSE THAN DOWN',
    why: ['a dependency that FAILS FAST can be handled',

  { q: 'what happens when we need to CHANGE THE SCHEMA',

    whyAsked: 'it is the question NOBODY ASKS and EVERYBODY DISCOVERS at the worst time',
  },

/* Three mistakes. */
const MISTAKES = [
  { m: 'STARTING WITH THE TECHNOLOGY', example: 'we will use Kafka before anyone has established that the requirement involves ordering, throughput or decoupling',
    consequence: 'and then the design BENDING TO FIT THE TOOL' },
  { m: 'NOT ESTIMATING', consequence: 'no basis for any decision, and therefore the argument becomes ABOUT PREFERENCE' },
  { m: 'IGNORING THE BORING PARTS', instances: ['the schema change', 'the migration', 'the data cleanup',
    'the operator who has to RUN THIS'],
    where: 'real projects are MADE OR BROKEN',
    fix: 'and it takes NO MORE THAN TEN MINUTES to discuss' },
];

Worked example: estimating a design before choosing it

The recipe only reads as useful once it is run on something, so here is the estimate for an ordinary product — a social feed with an API behind it — done the way the section says. Requirements, in numbers. Two hundred thousand registered users; ten per cent active daily, so twenty thousand daily actives; each opening the app eight times a day; each fetch returning roughly twenty kilobytes of feed. Derived. Twenty thousand daily actives times eight is one hundred and sixty thousand feed requests a day. At a peak-to-average ratio of five, peak is around nine hundred requests a second. At twenty kilobytes each that is eighteen megabytes a second of egress — roughly a terabyte and a half a day — which at a month's egress pricing is the largest line item in the bill and the first thing a careful design would attack. Storage: each user has some content and some metadata, call it a kilobyte each, so two hundred megabytes of user data plus content; with feed precomputed, a few tens of gigabytes a year. What the arithmetic eliminates. Nine hundred requests a second is not a scale problem. A single well-indexed database handles an order of magnitude more than that. The design therefore does not need sharding, does not need a distributed cache cluster, and does not need a message broker, and every hour spent designing those is an hour spent on something that will not be the bottleneck for two years.

Then the design that follows from the numbers rather than from preference, and the point is that almost all of it is boring. One application service, stateless, behind a load balancer, because it needs to be stateless so it can be replaced during a deploy and so it can scale without coordination. One relational database with proper indexes, because the queries are joins over user relationships and a relational store does that better than anything else; the index work is the design. A cache in front of the feed, keyed by user, with a short lifetime — and the arithmetic says why: the eighteen megabytes a second of egress is the cost, and a large fraction of feed requests are for content that has not changed, so a cache with a minute of staleness removes most of the egress. Static assets on a content-delivery network, because they are the same bytes for every user and they should never touch your servers at all. No message queue yet, because nothing in the requirements is asynchronous — a notification can be written to a table and sent by a periodic job until that job becomes slow, at which point there is a measured reason to introduce a queue. And then the failure answers, which are the part most designs skip: if the cache is down, requests go to the database and the site is slower but works; if the database is down, the site returns an error and nothing is lost because nothing was accepted; if the CDN is down, assets are served from the origin and the site is slower but works. Every one of those is a degradation rather than an outage, and that property is a consequence of the design decisions above rather than a separate effort.

/* Requirements, in numbers. */
const REQUIREMENTS = {
  registeredUsers: 200000,
  dailyActiveRate: '10 per cent', dailyActives: 20000,
  fetchesPerActivePerDay: 8, responseSize: 'roughly 20 KB of feed',
};

/* Derived. */
const DERIVED = [
  { calc: '20000 daily actives x 8', is: '160,000 FEED REQUESTS A DAY' },
  { calc: 'peak-to-average ratio of FIVE', is: 'around 900 REQUESTS A SECOND at peak' },
  { calc: '900 x 20 KB', is: '18 MB A SECOND of egress - roughly 1.5 TB A DAY',
    isTheLargestLineItem: true,
    firstTarget: 'and the FIRST THING a careful design would attack' },
  { calc: 'user data plus precomputed feed content', is: 'a few TENS OF GIGABYTES A YEAR' },
];

/* What the arithmetic eliminates. */
const ELIMINATES = {
  fact: '900 requests a second is NOT A SCALE PROBLEM',
  because: 'a single well-indexed database handles an ORDER OF MAGNITUDE more than that',
  thereforeDoesNotNeed: ['sharding', 'a distributed cache cluster', 'a message broker'],
  cost: 'every hour spent designing those is an hour spent on something that WILL NOT BE THE BOTTLENECK for two years',
};

/* The design that follows. */
const DESIGN = [
  { c: 'ONE APPLICATION SERVICE, stateless, behind a load balancer',
    why: ['so it can be REPLACED DURING A DEPLOY', 'so it can scale without coordination'] },
  { c: 'ONE RELATIONAL DATABASE with proper indexes',
    why: 'the queries are JOINS OVER USER RELATIONSHIPS and a relational store does that better than anything else',
    and: 'the INDEX WORK is the design' },
  { c: 'A CACHE in front of the feed, keyed by user, with a SHORT LIFETIME',
    arithmeticSays: 'the 18 MB a second of egress is the cost',
    why: 'a LARGE FRACTION of feed requests are for content that HAS NOT CHANGED',
    gain: 'a cache with a minute of staleness removes MOST OF THE EGRESS' },
  { c: 'STATIC ASSETS on a content-delivery network',
    why: 'they are THE SAME BYTES FOR EVERY USER and should never touch your servers at all' },

    instead: 'a notification can be written to a table and sent by a PERIODIC JOB',

];
/* The failure answers - the part most designs skip. */
const FAILURES = [
  { if: 'the CACHE is down', then: 'requests go to the database and the site is SLOWER BUT WORKS' },
  { if: 'the DATABASE is down', then: 'the site returns an error and NOTHING IS LOST because nothing was accepted' },
  { if: 'the CDN is down', then: 'assets are served from the origin and the site is SLOWER BUT WORKS' },
];
const PROPERTY = 'every one is a DEGRADATION rather than an OUTAGE, and that property is a CONSEQUENCE OF THE DESIGN DECISIONS above rather than a separate effort';

System design recipe (interview or real): (1) clarify requirements & constraints and estimate numbers (rps, storage per year); (2) sketch the read/write paths; (3) pick the scaling tools for the bottleneck; (4) discuss failures & trade-offs out loud. Confident articulation beats memorised diagrams.

21.6 Observability: logs, metrics, traces

At scale you cannot log into the one server that is failing, so you instrument everything. Logs say what happened in detail, metrics such as request rate, error rate, and latency say what is happening across the fleet, and traces stitch a single request through every service it touches. Centralize all three, add dashboards and alerting, and debugging becomes fast and collaborative.

At scale you can’t "look at the server". The three pillars:

  • Logs — what happened (searchable text).
  • Metrics — numbers over time (latency p50/p95/p99, error rate, saturation).
  • Traces — one request’s journey across services.

Learn the alerting math soon: p50 tells you the typical user, p99 tells you the unlucky user — and it’s p99 that customers actually feel. Add "SLIs/SLOs" (service-level indicators/objectives) when the course gets serious.

Logs, metrics, traces, and why the three are not interchangeable

Three signals, and each answers a different question, which is why having one is not having two. Logs answer "what happened at this moment" and are the highest-fidelity signal, containing the specific facts of one event — but they are expensive to store, hard to query in aggregate, and useless at a scale where the interesting question is "how often". Metrics answer "how often and how much" as numbers over time: counters, gauges, histograms. They are cheap to store, cheap to query, and aggregable across everything, which makes them the right signal for an alert and a dashboard — but a metric cannot tell you which request, so a metric tells you the rate is up and nothing about why. Traces answer "where did the time go" for one request, following it across every service it touched, and they are the only signal that reveals a problem spanning services — which is most production problems, because a request that takes four seconds has almost always spent them in two other services. The failure mode of each is worth knowing: logs are lost because nobody decided to keep them, metrics are unlabelled and therefore useless, traces are not sampled consistently and therefore show you the fast requests instead of the slow ones. And the relationship: a trace gives you the identifiers that let you find the logs, and the metrics tell you which trace to look at — so they are a pipeline, and instrumenting them together is what makes a system diagnosable.

Then metrics specifically, and the four types because using the wrong one is a real mistake. A counter only goes up and is reset by the process restarting — requests served, errors returned, bytes sent. A gauge can go up or down and represents an instantaneous value — connections open, queue depth, memory in use. A histogram buckets observations and, critically, lets you compute percentiles over them, which is the metric that actually matters for a latency requirement. A summary is similar but keeps quantile estimates rather than buckets and cannot be aggregated across time. And the trap worth naming: a histogram lets you compute a percentile, and an average does not. The average latency is a number almost nobody cares about; the ninety-fifth and ninety-ninth are what users experience, and the schema chapter's requirement for a latency figure was for exactly this reason. The second trap: labels are expensive and unbounded. A metric labelled with a user identifier creates one time series per user, which is millions of time series, which the storage system cannot hold — so label with what you will aggregate by and nothing more.

/* Three signals, three questions. */
const SIGNALS = [
  { s: 'LOGS', answer: 'what happened at THIS MOMENT',
    good: ['highest-fidelity', 'contains the specific facts of one event'],
    bad: ['expensive to store', 'hard to query in aggregate',
      'USELESS at a scale where the interesting question is how often'],
    failureMode: 'LOST, because nobody decided to keep them' },
  { s: 'METRICS', answer: 'how OFTEN and HOW MUCH',
    types: ['counters', 'gauges', 'histograms'],
    good: ['cheap to store', 'cheap to query', 'aggregable across EVERYTHING'],
    rightFor: ['an alert', 'a dashboard'],
    cannotTellYou: 'WHICH REQUEST', consequence: 'a metric tells you the rate is up and NOTHING ABOUT WHY',
    failureMode: 'UNLABELLED and therefore useless' },
  { s: 'TRACES', answer: 'WHERE DID THE TIME GO for one request',
    does: 'follows it across every service it touched',
    unique: 'the only signal that reveals a problem SPANNING SERVICES',
    whyThatMatters: 'most production problems span services, because a request that takes four seconds has almost always spent them in TWO OTHER SERVICES',
    failureMode: 'not sampled CONSISTENTLY, so they show you the FAST requests instead of the SLOW ones' },
];
const PIPELINE = 'a trace gives you the IDENTIFIERS that let you find the logs, and the METRICS tell you which trace to look at - they are a PIPELINE, and instrumenting them together is what makes a system diagnosable';

/* Four metric types. */
const TYPES = [
  { t: 'COUNTER', direction: 'only goes UP', resetBy: 'the process restarting',
    examples: ['requests served', 'errors returned', 'bytes sent'] },
  { t: 'GAUGE', direction: 'up OR down', is: 'an INSTANTANEOUS value',
    examples: ['connections open', 'queue depth', 'memory in use'] },
  { t: 'HISTOGRAM', does: 'buckets observations',
    unique: 'lets you compute PERCENTILES over them', why: 'the metric that actually MATTERS for a latency requirement' },
  { t: 'SUMMARY', does: 'keeps quantile estimates rather than buckets', cannot: 'be aggregated across TIME' },
];
const TRAPS = [
  { t: 'a HISTOGRAM lets you compute a PERCENTILE, and an AVERAGE does not',
    fact: 'the average latency is a number ALMOST NOBODY CARES ABOUT; the ninety-fifth and ninety-ninth are what USERS EXPERIENCE',
    connectsTo: 'the schema chapters requirement for a latency figure was for exactly this reason' },
  { t: 'LABELS ARE EXPENSIVE and UNBOUNDED',
    example: 'a metric labelled with a USER IDENTIFIER creates one time series per user',
    magnitude: 'which is MILLIONS OF TIME SERIES that the storage system cannot hold',
    rule: 'label with WHAT YOU WILL AGGREGATE BY and nothing more' },
];

Structured logging, and alerts that wake people up

Then logging practice, and the structured argument is the one worth having properly. A log line should be a structured record, not a sentence. A sentence requires a person or a brittle parser to extract the parts; a structured record — a timestamp, a level, a message, and fields — can be queried, aggregated and alerted on, and it is the difference between "error in payment" and "payment failed with a card decline for user 4213 at 14:02". The practical rules: always include a request identifier, because it is the thread that connects a user's report to your logs and it must be generated at the edge and propagated through every call. Include the identifiers you will need later — the user, the order, the upstream service — because a log line without them is a log line you cannot use when you most need it. Never log a secret, which is the requirement with the worst track record because libraries log configuration objects and people log whole request bodies. And log at the right level: errors for things that need attention, warnings for things that are unusual but handled, and nothing at error level for an expected condition, because a log full of errors at error level is a log nobody reads.

Then alerting, and the rule that distinguishes a useful alert from noise. Alert on symptoms, not causes. Page a human when users are affected — error rate, latency, availability — and record the cause as a metric or a dashboard, because a page caused by a specific internal condition is a page that fires at three in the morning for something nobody could act on. Every alert must be actionable. The test: if this fired at three in the morning, would a human know what to do, and would doing it help? If not, it is not an alert; it is a report, and it belongs in a dashboard nobody is woken for. Alert on a rate over a window, not an absolute value, because an absolute threshold is either so low it always fires or so high it fires too late. And prefer fewer alerts that matter, because a page that is not actionable is worse than no page: it trains people to ignore alerts, and the one that mattered is then ignored too. The complementary practice is a post-incident review that asks what was missing rather than who did it — including, specifically, which alert would have told us sooner, because that question is what improves the monitoring rather than the behaviour.

/* Structured records, not sentences. */
const STRUCTURED = {
  is: 'a TIMESTAMP, a LEVEL, a MESSAGE, and FIELDS',
  argument: ['a sentence requires a person or a brittle parser to extract the parts',
    'a structured record can be QUERIED, AGGREGATED and ALERTED ON'],
  gain: 'the difference between error in payment and payment failed with a card decline for user 4213 at 14:02',
  rules: [
    { r: 'ALWAYS INCLUDE A REQUEST IDENTIFIER', why: 'it is the THREAD connecting a users report to your logs',
      must: 'be GENERATED AT THE EDGE and PROPAGATED THROUGH EVERY CALL' },
    { r: 'include the IDENTIFIERS YOU WILL NEED LATER', instances: ['the user', 'the order', 'the upstream service'],
      why: 'a log line without them is A LOG LINE YOU CANNOT USE when you most need it' },
    { r: 'never log a SECRET', worstTrackRecord: true, because: 'LIBRARIES LOG CONFIGURATION OBJECTS and people log WHOLE REQUEST BODIES' },
    { r: 'log at the RIGHT LEVEL', levels: ['errors for things that NEED ATTENTION',
        'warnings for things that are UNUSUAL BUT HANDLED', 'nothing at error level for an EXPECTED CONDITION'],
      why: 'a log full of errors at error level is a LOG NOBODY READS' },
  ],
};

/* Alerting. */
const ALERTS = [
  { r: 'alert on SYMPTOMS, not causes',
    pageOn: ['error rate', 'latency', 'availability'],
    recordInstead: 'the cause, as a metric or a dashboard',
    why: 'a page caused by a specific internal condition is a page that FIRES AT THREE IN THE MORNING for something NOBODY COULD ACT ON' },
  { r: 'every alert must be ACTIONABLE',
    test: 'if this fired at three in the morning, would a human know WHAT TO DO, and would doing it HELP',
    ifNot: 'it is not an alert; it is a REPORT, and it belongs in a dashboard nobody is woken for' },
  { r: 'alert on a RATE OVER A WINDOW, not an absolute value',
    why: ['an absolute threshold is EITHER so low it always fires OR so high it fires too late'],
  },
  { r: 'prefer FEWER ALERTS THAT MATTER', why: 'a page that is not actionable is WORSE THAN NO PAGE',
    consequence: 'it TRAINS PEOPLE TO IGNORE ALERTS, and the one that mattered is then ignored too' },
];
const POST_INCIDENT = {
  asks: 'what was MISSING rather than who did it',
  specifically: 'WHICH ALERT WOULD HAVE TOLD US SOONER',
  why: 'that question is what improves the MONITORING rather than the behaviour',
};

22 · Cloud, Containers & DevOps

Cloud, Containers, and DevOps is about shipping software reliably rather than installing it. The chapter covers containers versus virtual machines, Docker packaging, Kubernetes orchestration, CI/CD pipelines with deployment strategies, cloud service models from IaaS to SaaS, infrastructure as code, and production operations with observability and incident response. Together they form the release pipeline that takes a commit to a running, monitored service.

22.1 Virtual machines vs containers22.2 Docker in one flow22.3 Orchestrating at scale: Kubernetes22.4 CI/CD — the delivery pipeline22.5 Cloud foundations22.6 Infrastructure as Code22.7 Production ops: observability and incidents

Modern software is shipped, not sold on an installer. This chapter is the modern release pipeline: containers for packaging, CI/CD for automating, clouds for hosting, and the disciplines that make releases boring.

22.1 Virtual machines vs containers

Virtual machines isolate a full guest operating system with its own kernel on a hypervisor, while containers share the host kernel and package only the application and its dependencies. That makes containers smaller and far faster to start but weaker in isolation and tied to the host kernel. Choose VMs when you need strict security boundaries or a different operating system, and containers when you want density and speed.

What a container actually is, mechanically

A virtual machine is an emulated computer: a hypervisor presents what looks like hardware, and a guest operating system with its own kernel, drivers and processes runs inside it. That design buys strong isolation — the guest cannot see the host's memory or kernel at all — and it costs a boot time measured in tens of seconds and a gigabyte or more of memory for an operating system nobody is using. A container is not that. A container is a process on the host, with two things added. Namespaces give it its own view of system resources: its own process tree, so it sees only its own processes; its own mount table, so its filesystem is separate; its own network stack, so it has its own interfaces and ports; its own identifiers, so it can have its own user and group numbers. Control groups limit and account for the resources it uses: CPU, memory, disk I/O, process count. And optionally a union filesystem that assembles layers so an image is a description of what to add rather than a copy of everything. So the accurate statement is: a container is a restricted process that believes it is alone. It shares the host kernel, so it starts in tens of milliseconds and costs a few megabytes of overhead, and the price is that isolation depends on kernel features rather than on a hypervisor.

Then the isolation difference, which is the one that decides everything else. Virtual machines have a hardware boundary; a container has a kernel-configuration boundary. A kernel vulnerability that lets a process escape its namespace is a container escape, and there have been several. This is why multi-tenant hosting on containers requires additional containment — a stronger sandbox, a separate virtual machine for untrusted code, or a hardened kernel. And the guest kernel is the other difference: a virtual machine runs whatever kernel its image contains, so you can run Linux containers, Windows containers and different kernel versions side by side on one host, while containers on a Linux host share that host's kernel and therefore its version and its configuration. Then the practical comparison, and the decision criterion is workload shape rather than preference. Containers start in tens of milliseconds and a virtual machine in tens of seconds, which matters enormously for scaling and for restart-on-failure. Containers have megabytes of overhead and a virtual machine has gigabytes, which determines how many fit on a machine. Containers share the kernel, so a virtual machine gives you a stronger isolation boundary, which matters when the code is untrusted or when two tenants must not be able to affect each other at all. And a virtual machine carries a whole operating system, so it can run anything — a kernel module, a system service, a different operating system — while a container can run a process and expects a specific runtime.

/* What a virtual machine is. */
const VM = {
  is: 'an EMULATED COMPUTER',
  how: 'a hypervisor presents what looks like hardware, and a GUEST OPERATING SYSTEM with its own kernel, drivers and processes runs inside it',
  buys: 'strong isolation - the guest CANNOT SEE the hosts memory or kernel at all',
  costs: ['a boot time measured in TENS OF SECONDS',
    'a GIGABYTE OR MORE of memory for an operating system nobody is using'],
};

/* What a container actually is. */
const CONTAINER = {
  isNot: 'a mini-virtual-machine with SSH',
  is: 'A PROCESS ON THE HOST, with two things added',
  adds: [
    { t: 'NAMESPACES', gives: ['its own process tree, so it sees only its OWN PROCESSES',
      'its own mount table, so its FILESYSTEM IS SEPARATE', 'its own network stack, so its own interfaces and ports',
      'its own identifiers, so it can have its own USER AND GROUP numbers'] },
    { t: 'CONTROL GROUPS', limits: ['CPU', 'memory', 'disk I/O', 'process count'],
    also: 'and ACCOUNT for what it uses' },
    { t: 'a UNION FILESYSTEM', optional: true,
    makes: 'an image a DESCRIPTION OF WHAT TO ADD rather than a copy of everything' },
  ],

  price: 'isolation depends on KERNEL FEATURES rather than on a hypervisor',
};

/* The isolation difference - decides everything else. */
const ISOLATION = {

  container: 'a KERNEL-CONFIGURATION BOUNDARY',
  consequence: 'a kernel vulnerability that lets a process escape its namespace is a CONTAINER ESCAPE, and there have been several',

Choosing, and the places containers surprise people

Then how to choose, and the criterion is the workload's isolation requirement rather than which is newer. Containers when the code is yours and the isolation requirement is ordinary. That is most web services, and the reasons are startup speed, density and packaging. Virtual machines when the code is untrusted or the isolation must be strong, and the canonical cases are running code uploaded by strangers, multi-tenant hosting where a bug in one tenant must not affect another, and anything requiring a different kernel or a real system service. Virtual machines when you need the whole operating system — a database server that must be managed by its own tooling, a legacy application expecting a system environment. And both together, which is the modern answer and is not a compromise: containers inside virtual machines, so the hardware isolation boundary comes from the virtual machine and the density and packaging come from the container. Many managed container platforms do exactly this, and it is worth knowing that the "container" you are running may well be in a virtual machine for reasons of the first point above.

Then the places containers surprise people, and each has a specific cause. State inside a container disappears when it does. The filesystem of a container is disposable by design, so anything written there is lost on restart — which means a database inside a container without a volume loses its data, and the correct arrangement is a volume outside the container's lifecycle. One process per container is not a style rule — it is a consequence of how a container is a process: a process tree with a supervisor inside is possible but it makes signals, exit codes and log streaming behave ambiguously, and an orchestrator's model of "restart this thing" assumes the thing is one thing. Images are not small because of compression — they are small because of layering, with each instruction creating a layer and the final image being the union, which is why a build order that installs dependencies before copying source produces an image that is re-sent whenever the source changes. Resource limits bite in unexpected ways, because a limit enforced by control groups does not fail gracefully: a memory limit is an out-of-memory kill rather than a slower run, so a limit set too low produces a container that dies with no diagnostic. And the host kernel is shared, so a kernel upgrade on the host restarts every container on it, which is a fact about the architecture rather than a bug.

/* The criterion is the isolation REQUIREMENT, not which is newer. */
const CHOOSE = [
  { when: 'CONTAINERS', conditions: ['the code is YOURS', 'the isolation requirement is ORDINARY'],
    covers: 'most web services', why: ['STARTUP SPEED', 'DENSITY', 'PACKAGING'] },
  { when: 'VIRTUAL MACHINES', conditions: ['the code is UNTRUSTED or the isolation must be STRONG',
    'you need a whole operating system - a database server managed by its own tooling, a legacy application expecting a system environment'],
    instances: ['running code uploaded by STRANGERS', 'multi-tenant hosting where a bug in one tenant must not affect another',
      'anything requiring a DIFFERENT KERNEL or a real system service'] },
  { when: 'BOTH TOGETHER', notACompromise: true,
    shape: 'containers INSIDE virtual machines',
    how: 'the hardware isolation boundary comes from the virtual machine and the DENSITY AND PACKAGING come from the container',
    reality: 'the container you are running may well BE IN A VIRTUAL MACHINE for reasons of the first point above',
  },
];

  { s: 'ONE PROCESS PER CONTAINER is not a style rule',

22.2 Docker in one flow

Docker packages an application and its runtime so it runs identically anywhere a container engine exists. A Dockerfile records the setup: a base image, working directory, dependency installation, port exposure, and the start command, then docker build creates the image and docker run starts a container. Build once, run anywhere becomes literally true, and the same image moves from laptop to CI to production unchanged.

# Dockerfile -- the "recipe" that packages your app immutably
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .    # copy deps first so the layer caches
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
CMD ["python", "app.py"]  # start command for the container

A minimal Dockerfile: pinned base image, dependencies installed from a list, source copied last, and the start command declared for when the container runs.

docker build -t myapp .  # build image tagged myapp
docker run -p 8000:8000 myapp  # map host port 8000 to container
docker compose up            # run several services (web, db, redis) together

The three everyday Docker commands: build an image, run it with a port mapping, and bring up a whole multi-service stack with compose.

What an image is, and the vocabulary that follows from it

An image is an immutable, layered description of a filesystem plus the metadata needed to run it: the command to run, environment variables, and who to run it as. Immutable is the load-bearing word. An image does not change; a container is a running instance of one. And layered is the other load-bearing word: each instruction in a build produces a layer, the image is the union of the layers, and each layer records only what changed. That is why an image is a few hundred megabytes rather than a few gigabytes — shared base layers are stored once and referenced — and it is also why a build order matters: putting the dependency install before the source copy means the expensive layer is cached and only a tiny layer changes when the source does. The rest of the vocabulary, and each term is a specific thing. A container is a running instance of an image. A tag is a movable name for an image version, and the property that causes real incidents is that latest is a tag that moves, so a deployment described by latest is not reproducible: the same command deployed twice can run different code. A registry is where images are stored and the one you pull from in production is part of your system's definition. A Dockerfile is the build recipe, and its instructions are what determine the layer structure, so its order is a performance design and not a formatting preference. A volume is storage that outlives the container, and a bind mount is a host directory made visible inside one, which is how you get code into a development container without copying it. And a multi-stage build compiles in one stage and copies only the artefact into the final image, which is how a compiled binary ends up in a final image that contains no compiler — the mechanism by which a runtime image is a fraction of the size of a build image.

/* An image. */
const IMAGE = {
  is: 'an IMMUTABLE, LAYERED description of a filesystem plus the metadata needed to run it',
  metadata: ['the command to run', 'environment variables', 'who to run it as'],
  immutableIsLoadBearing: true,
  layers: 'each instruction in a build produces a layer; the image is the UNION of the layers, and each layer records only what CHANGED',
  whySmall: 'shared base layers are STORED ONCE AND REFERENCED',
  whyOrderMatters: 'putting the dependency install BEFORE THE SOURCE COPY means the expensive layer is cached and only a TINY LAYER CHANGES when the source does',
};

/* The vocabulary. */
const TERMS = [
  { t: 'a CONTAINER', is: 'a RUNNING INSTANCE of an image' },
  { t: 'a TAG', is: 'a MOVABLE NAME for an image version',
    incident: 'the property that causes REAL INCIDENTS',
    latest: 'latest is a tag that MOVES, so a deployment described by latest is NOT REPRODUCIBLE - the same command deployed twice can run DIFFERENT CODE' },
  { t: 'a REGISTRY', is: 'where images are STORED',
    note: 'the one you pull from in production is PART OF YOUR SYSTEMS DEFINITION' },
  { t: 'a DOCKERFILE', is: 'the build recipe',
    note: 'its instructions DETERMINE THE LAYER STRUCTURE, so its order is a PERFORMANCE DESIGN and not a formatting preference' },
  { t: 'a VOLUME', is: 'storage that OUTLIVES the container' },
  { t: 'a BIND MOUNT', is: 'a host directory made visible inside a container',
    use: 'how you get code into a DEVELOPMENT CONTAINER without copying it' },
  { t: 'a MULTI-STAGE BUILD', does: 'compiles in one stage and copies ONLY THE ARTEFACT into the final image',
    gain: 'a compiled binary ends up in a final image that CONTAINS NO COMPILER',
    significance: 'how a runtime image ends up a FRACTION of the size of a build image' },
];

Writing a Dockerfile, and running things well

Then how to write one, and the seven rules that matter, each with its reason. Order from least-frequent change to most — base image, then dependencies, then application code — so that a source change invalidates one cheap layer rather than everything above it. Copy the dependency manifest before the source, because that is what makes the layer cache work; copy everything, run install, then copy the source, in that order. Combine commands in one layer, because each layer is a diff and a chain of commands in one layer leaves no deleted file behind in an earlier layer — which is the common cause of an image that is mysteriously large despite a cleanup command. Run as a non-root user, always, because a container that runs as root has no meaningful containment from the host's perspective and because it means a compromise of the process is a compromise of the host's files. Use a minimal base image, because every package in it is a package with vulnerabilities you have to track. Do not put secrets in a build argument or an environment variable in a Dockerfile, because the build argument is visible in the image's history and the environment variable is visible to anything that can inspect the container. Add a health check and a signal handler, so the orchestrator can tell whether the thing is working and so a stop signal reaches the process that can act on it.

Then running things well, and the operational rules that are separate from the build. One process per container, covered above. Make the container stateless — the same argument as the scaling chapter, and it is why a container is a good unit of deployment: it can be replaced without consequence. Put configuration in the environment, so the same image runs in staging and production. Never patch inside a running container: a change made inside a container exists only in that container, so the next deployment silently reverts it, and the fix is to rebuild and redeploy. Set resource limits, because without them one process can consume the host's memory and take everything with it. And log to standard output, not to a file, because a container's logs are collected from its output streams and a file inside the container is lost with it.

/* Seven rules for a Dockerfile. */
const DOCKERFILE = [
  { r: 1, do: 'ORDER FROM LEAST-FREQUENT CHANGE TO MOST', example: ['base image', 'dependencies', 'application code'],
    gain: 'a source change invalidates ONE CHEAP LAYER rather than everything above it' },
  { r: 2, do: 'copy the DEPENDENCY MANIFEST before the source',
    why: 'that is what makes the LAYER CACHE WORK', order: ['copy everything', 'run install', 'then copy the source'] },
  { r: 3, do: 'COMBINE COMMANDS IN ONE LAYER',
    why: 'each layer is a DIFF and a chain of commands in one layer leaves NO DELETED FILE in an earlier layer',
    consequence: 'which is the common cause of an image that is MYSTERIOUSLY LARGE despite a cleanup command' },
  { r: 4, do: 'RUN AS A NON-ROOT USER, ALWAYS',
    reasons: ['a container that runs as root has NO MEANINGFUL CONTAINMENT from the hosts perspective',
      'and a compromise of the process is a compromise of the HOSTS FILES'] },
  { r: 5, do: 'use a MINIMAL BASE IMAGE', why: 'every package in it is a package with VULNERABILITIES YOU HAVE TO TRACK' },
  { r: 6, do: 'NEVER put secrets in a BUILD ARGUMENT or an ENVIRONMENT VARIABLE in a Dockerfile',
    why: 'the build argument is VISIBLE IN THE IMAGES HISTORY and the environment variable is VISIBLE to anything that can inspect the container' },
  { r: 7, do: 'add a HEALTH CHECK and a SIGNAL HANDLER',
    why: ['so the orchestrator can tell WHETHER THE THING IS WORKING',
      'so a stop signal reaches THE PROCESS THAT CAN ACT ON IT'] },
];

/* Running well. */
const RUNNING = [
  { r: 'ONE PROCESS per container', covered: 'above' },
  { r: 'make the container STATELESS',
    sameArgumentAs: 'the scaling chapter',
    gain: 'a container is a GOOD UNIT OF DEPLOYMENT - it can be REPLACED WITHOUT CONSEQUENCE' },
  { r: 'put CONFIGURATION in the ENVIRONMENT', gain: 'the same image runs in staging AND production' },
  { r: 'NEVER PATCH INSIDE A RUNNING CONTAINER',
    why: 'a change made inside a container EXISTS ONLY IN THAT CONTAINER, so the next deployment SILENTLY REVERTS IT',
    fix: 'REBUILD AND REDEPLOY' },
  { r: 'set RESOURCE LIMITS', why: 'without them ONE PROCESS can consume the hosts memory and TAKE EVERYTHING WITH IT' },
  { r: 'log to STANDARD OUTPUT, not to a file',
    why: 'a containers logs are collected from its OUTPUT STREAMS and a file inside the container is LOST WITH IT' },
];

Containers are not mini-VMs with SSH. Best practice: one process per container, no state inside the container (volumes for data), run as non-root, and treat the image as immutable (never patch inside a running container — rebuild and redeploy).

22.3 Orchestrating at scale: Kubernetes

Kubernetes orchestrates containers at scale, taking a declared desired state, such as three replicas of a service with a CPU limit, and continuously reconciling the cluster to match it. It handles scheduling, load balancing, scaling, rolling updates, and auto-healing when a pod dies. Start with the vocabulary, pods, deployments, services, and namespaces, and use a local tool such as Docker Compose or Minikube for class projects before standing up a real cluster.

Kubernetes ("k8s") runs many container replicas, auto-scales, restarts failures, and load-balances them. Vocabulary you should be able to walk someone through:

  • Pod — smallest unit (usually one container).
  • Deployment — declares "run 3 replicas of X" and reconciles reality to it.
  • Service — stable name/IP in front of a set of pods.
  • Ingress — outside → inside routing with TLS.
  • ConfigMap / Secret — config and secrets as first-class objects.
  • Probes: readiness (traffic-worthy?) and liveness (restart? unstick me?).

Desired state and controllers, which is the whole idea

Every orchestration system is the same idea with different syntax: you describe the desired state, and a controller makes the world match it. You do not say "start three containers"; you say "there should be three instances of this image, always", and a control loop observes that there are one and starts two more. That single shift is worth understanding carefully because everything else follows from it. It makes the system self-healing, because the controller's loop is continuously checking reality against the declaration, so a process that dies is a discrepancy and the discrepancy is corrected — the mechanism is a health check and a restart, and the insight is that healing is not a feature you added but a consequence of the model. It makes scaling a declaration rather than a command, because "six instances" is a statement and the controller does whatever is needed. It makes deploys a change of declaration, which means a roll-out is gradual and observable rather than instantaneous and frightening. And it makes the system declarative in a way that means the current state can always be recomputed from the declaration, which is what makes drift detectable and what makes a new environment reproducible.

Then the pieces, and each answers a question that arises the moment you have more than one machine. A workload specification — the image, the resources, the ports, the environment — which is a declaration, not a script. A replica count, which is the scaling knob and the thing the controller reconciles. A service — a stable address and a load-balancing policy in front of a changing set of instances, which is what lets a client not know or care which instance serves it. Ingress — the routing from an external address to services, including the certificate handling and the host-based routing that is usually what a person means by "ingress". Configuration and secrets, delivered separately from the image so that the same image runs in several environments. A health check, which is the mechanism by which the controller knows whether an instance is serving, and its subtlety is worth knowing: liveness asks whether to restart the process and readiness asks whether to send it traffic, and they are different questions whose failure modes are different — a service whose readiness check is too strict will never receive traffic, and one whose liveness check is too strict will restart forever.

/* Every orchestration system is the same idea. */
const THE_IDEA = {
  is: 'you describe the DESIRED STATE, and a CONTROLLER makes the world match it',
  notThis: 'you do not say start three containers',
  instead: 'you say there should be THREE INSTANCES of this image, ALWAYS',
  whatTheControllerDoes: 'a CONTROL LOOP observes that there are one and starts two more',
  whyWorthUnderstanding: 'everything else FOLLOWS from that single shift',
  follows: [
    { f: 'it makes the system SELF-HEALING',
      mechanism: ['the controllers loop is continuously checking reality against the declaration',
        'so a process that dies is a DISCREPANCY and the discrepancy is CORRECTED'],
      detail: 'the mechanism is a health check and a restart',
      insight: 'healing is NOT A FEATURE YOU ADDED but a CONSEQUENCE OF THE MODEL' },
    { f: 'it makes SCALING A DECLARATION rather than a command', because: 'six instances is a STATEMENT and the controller does whatever is needed' },
    { f: 'it makes DEPLOYS A CHANGE OF DECLARATION',
      gain: 'a roll-out is GRADUAL AND OBSERVABLE rather than instantaneous and frightening' },
    { f: 'it makes the system DECLARATIVE in a way that means the current state can always be RECOMPUTED from the declaration',
      gain: ['what makes DRIFT DETECTABLE', 'what makes a NEW ENVIRONMENT REPRODUCIBLE'],
    },
  ],
};

/* The pieces. */
const PIECES = [
  { p: 'a WORKLOAD SPECIFICATION', is: ['the image', 'the resources', 'the ports', 'the environment'], isA: 'DECLARATION, not a script' },
  { p: 'a REPLICA COUNT', is: 'the scaling knob and the thing the controller RECONCILES' },
  { p: 'a SERVICE', is: 'a STABLE ADDRESS and a load-balancing policy in front of a changing set of instances',
    gain: 'what lets a client NOT KNOW OR CARE which instance serves it' },
  { p: 'INGRESS', does: ['routing from an external address to services', 'certificate handling', 'host-based routing'],
    note: 'usually what a person means by ingress' },
  { p: 'CONFIGURATION and SECRETS', deliveredSeparatelyFrom: 'the image',
    why: 'so the SAME IMAGE runs in several environments' },
  { p: 'a HEALTH CHECK', is: 'the MECHANISM BY WHICH THE CONTROLLER KNOWS whether an instance is serving',
    subtlety: ['liveness asks WHETHER TO RESTART THE PROCESS',
      'readiness asks WHETHER TO SEND IT TRAFFIC'],
    whyDifferent: 'they are DIFFERENT QUESTIONS whose failure modes are different',
    failures: ['a service whose readiness check is too STRICT will never receive traffic',
      'one whose liveness check is too strict will RESTART FOREVER'],
  },
];

Rolling updates, the cost, and when you need it

Then rolling updates, which is the capability that justifies the complexity. A rolling update replaces instances gradually — bring up a new one, wait for it to pass its readiness check, send it a share of the traffic, repeat, and remove the old ones — and each of those steps exists for a reason. Waiting for readiness is what stops traffic reaching an instance that is not serving yet, which is the single most common cause of a deploy causing errors even though the new version is correct. Gradual traffic is what lets you watch, so a bad version affects a small fraction of requests and is caught before everyone is affected. Having a mix of versions means the two must be compatible in both directions — a database change must not break the old code, and the old code must not break the new schema — which is the requirement that makes schema migration a genuine engineering problem and not a deployment detail. And the rollback must be fast, which it is only if the previous image is still available and the configuration change was also reversible.

Then the cost, because orchestration is not free and the honest accounting is what decides whether you need it. It is a distributed system with a control plane, so it has the failure modes of one: the control plane is a dependency, its state is authoritative, and its own upgrade is a project. YAML and abstractions hide complexity rather than removing it, so a simple deployment that would be one file on three machines becomes a template with a dozen parameters, and the question "what is this actually running" requires a tool. Debugging is indirect, because the thing you want to look at is the difference between a declaration and reality, and getting that difference means asking the system rather than reading a file. The API surface is large and it changes, so a cluster is something you can be on an older version of, which is a real operational burden. And cost is not trivial, both in what you pay for the control plane and in the engineer-hours a cluster consumes that would otherwise be spent on the product. So when is it worth it? When you have more than one machine and need them coordinated — rolling deploys, automatic restart, scaling on load. When availability matters more than simplicity. When you have many services and the deployment coordination is real work. And usually not otherwise — for a project with one machine and a handful of processes, the coordination is a script, and a control plane is a great deal of machinery to operate in order to do what the script does. The discipline that follows, and it is the one in the chapter's tip: use the simplest thing that gives you the properties you need, because every layer of orchestration you add is a layer you must operate, monitor, upgrade and eventually explain to whoever inherits it.

/* Rolling updates - each step exists for a reason. */
const ROLLING = {
  does: 'brings up a new instance, waits for it to pass its readiness check, sends it a share of the traffic, repeats, and removes the old ones',
  steps: [
    { s: 'waiting for READINESS', why: 'what stops traffic reaching an instance that is NOT SERVING YET',
      rank: 'the single most common cause of a DEPLOY CAUSING ERRORS even though the new version is correct' },
    { s: 'GRADUAL traffic', why: 'lets you WATCH',
      gain: 'a bad version affects A SMALL FRACTION of requests and is caught before everyone is affected' },
    { s: 'a MIX OF VERSIONS', requires: 'the two must be COMPATIBLE IN BOTH DIRECTIONS',
      detail: ['a database change must not break the OLD CODE', 'the old code must not break the NEW SCHEMA'],
      consequence: 'which is what makes schema migration A GENUINE ENGINEERING PROBLEM and not a deployment detail' },
    { s: 'a FAST ROLLBACK', possibleOnlyIf: ['the previous image is still available',
      'the configuration change was also REVERSIBLE'],
    },
  ],
};

/* The cost. */
const COST = [
  { c: 'it is a DISTRIBUTED SYSTEM WITH A CONTROL PLANE', so: 'it has the failure modes of one',
    detail: ['the control plane is a DEPENDENCY', 'its state is AUTHORITATIVE',

  { c: 'YAML AND ABSTRACTIONS HIDE COMPLEXITY rather than removing it',
    example: 'a simple deployment that would be ONE FILE on three machines becomes a TEMPLATE WITH A DOZEN PARAMETERS',
    consequence: 'the question what is this actually running requires A TOOL' },
  { c: 'DEBUGGING IS INDIRECT',
    detail: 'the thing you want to look at is THE DIFFERENCE between a declaration and reality',
    how: 'getting that difference means ASKING THE SYSTEM rather than reading a file' },
  { c: 'the API SURFACE IS LARGE and it CHANGES', consequence: 'a cluster is something you can be ON AN OLDER VERSION OF',

/* When it is worth it. */
const WORTH_IT = [
  { w: 'you have MORE THAN ONE MACHINE and need them COORDINATED',
