For a class project, do NOT run your own k8s cluster — use Docker Compose. Learn orchestration concepts when a team needs rolling deploys and auto-healing; the biggest lesson is declarative desired-state: "I describe the target; the controller makes the world match."

22.4 CI/CD — the delivery pipeline

CI/CD is the pipeline that catches what you broke and ships it safely. Continuous integration runs quality gates on every push, then continuous delivery or deployment promotes the artifact through staging to production. Blue-green, canary, and rolling deployments switch traffic gradually, and feature flags turn a change off instantly, converting a bad release from a fire into measured pain.

Extend Ch. 16.6 CI to delivery:

Commit --> CI (lint, typecheck, unit+integration tests, build image) --> CD:
  canary / staging deploy --> smoke tests --> promote to prod
Behind the scenes: feature flags, blue-green, rolling, canary.

The pipeline, and why each gate is where it is

The pipeline is a sequence of checks on the way from a commit to production, and the ordering is not arbitrary — it is arranged so that the cheapest check that can catch a class of problem runs first, and so that a failure surfaces while the person who wrote the code is still present. On every push: the fast checks. Linting, formatting, and the unit tests. Seconds to a couple of minutes, catches the majority of problems, and the whole point is that it is fast enough to run on every change. On every pull request: the integration tests and a build. Minutes, needs more environment, and is the gate that says "this can be merged" rather than "this is syntactically valid". On merge to main: deploy to an environment that is like production, and immediately run the smoke and end-to-end tests against it — which is what catches the class of problem where the code is correct and the configuration is not, and that class is not small. On main: promote the same artefact. And this is the detail that matters most: the artefact promoted to production must be the one that was built and tested, not a rebuild. Build once, promote that. A pipeline that rebuilds for each environment is testing one artefact and shipping another, which means the tests are decorative.

Then the deployment strategies, in increasing order of risk to the user and decreasing order of confidence to the deployer. Recreate: stop everything, start the new version. Simple, brief downtime, and every version change is a total outage for a period. Rolling: replace instances gradually, which the orchestration chapter covered, and which is the default for most services. Blue-green: run two full environments and switch traffic between them, which gives a rollback that is a DNS change or a load-balancer target change and is therefore fast and certain — at the cost of double the capacity while it is in effect, and of a schema change that both versions must tolerate. Canary: send a small fraction of real traffic to the new version and watch. The best risk-to-information ratio of the four, because a real problem in a small fraction is a small incident rather than a full one, and the cost is the complexity of routing by percentage and of being able to compare the two versions' behaviour. And then feature flags, which are orthogonal to all of these and worth separating out because they change the deploy question. A flag means the code is deployed but the behaviour is not yet enabled, so deploying and enabling become separate decisions — which means you can deploy on a Friday and enable on a Tuesday, and roll back a behaviour change without a deploy at all. The cost is that the codebase now contains branches that will be exercised once and then removed, and the discipline that makes that safe is a rule: a flag is temporary and has an owner and an expiry date, because a permanent flag is an untested code path that nobody remembers.

/* Ordering: cheapest first, and failure surfaces while the author is present. */
const PIPELINE = [
  { stage: 'on every PUSH', what: ['linting', 'formatting', 'unit tests'],
    cost: 'seconds to a couple of minutes', catches: 'the MAJORITY of problems',
    point: 'it is fast enough to run ON EVERY CHANGE' },
  { stage: 'on every PULL REQUEST', what: ['integration tests', 'a build'], cost: 'minutes', needs: 'more environment',
    gate: 'says this CAN BE MERGED rather than this is syntactically valid' },
  { stage: 'on MERGE to main', what: ['deploy to an environment that is LIKE PRODUCTION',
    'immediately run smoke and end-to-end tests against it'],
    catches: 'the class where the CODE IS CORRECT and the CONFIGURATION IS NOT',
    whyItMatters: 'that class is NOT SMALL' },
  { stage: 'on main', what: 'promote the SAME ARTEFACT' },
];
const THE_DETAIL = {
  rule: 'the artefact promoted to production MUST BE THE ONE THAT WAS BUILT AND TESTED, NOT A REBUILD',
  process: ['build once', 'promote that'],
  why: 'a pipeline that REBUILDS for each environment is TESTING ONE ARTEFACT AND SHIPPING ANOTHER',
  consequence: 'which means the TESTS ARE DECORATIVE',
};

/* Strategies, in increasing risk to the user. */
const STRATEGIES = [
  { s: 'RECREATE', does: 'stop everything, start the new version',
    good: ['simple', 'a brief downtime'],
    cost: 'every version change is A TOTAL OUTAGE for a period' },
  { s: 'ROLLING', does: 'replace instances GRADUALLY', status: 'the DEFAULT for most services' },
  { s: 'BLUE-GREEN', does: 'run two full environments and SWITCH TRAFFIC between them',
    rollback: 'a DNS change or a load-balancer target change', therefore: 'FAST AND CERTAIN',
    costs: ['double the capacity while it is in effect',
      'a schema change that BOTH VERSIONS must tolerate'] },
  { s: 'CANARY', does: 'send a SMALL FRACTION of real traffic to the new version and watch',
    ratio: 'the BEST RISK-TO-INFORMATION RATIO of the four',
    why: 'a real problem in a small fraction is A SMALL INCIDENT rather than a full one',
    costs: ['complexity of ROUTING BY PERCENTAGE', 'being able to COMPARE the two versions behaviour'] },
];

/* Feature flags are orthogonal. */
const FLAGS = {
  is: 'the code is DEPLOYED but the BEHAVIOUR IS NOT YET ENABLED',
  therefore: ['deploying and ENABLING BECOME SEPARATE DECISIONS',
    'you can DEPLOY ON A FRIDAY and ENABLE ON A TUESDAY',
    'and ROLL BACK a behaviour change WITHOUT A DEPLOY at all'],
  cost: 'the codebase now contains BRANCHES that will be exercised once and then removed',
  discipline: 'a flag is TEMPORARY and HAS AN OWNER AND AN EXPIRY DATE',
  why: 'because a PERMANENT FLAG is an UNTESTED CODE PATH that nobody remembers',
};

The delivery pipeline in one glimpse: every commit is checked and tested, then staged and promoted to production, with feature flags and phased deploys behind the scenes.

  • Blue-green: new version fully deployed alongside old; flip traffic at once. Instant rollback = flip back.
  • Canary: send 5% of traffic to new version, watch errors, increase gradually.
  • Rolling: replace instances few at a time — most common for stateless pods.
  • Feature flags: ship code to production hidden behind a flag; turn features on per-user. Decouples deploy from release — the modern way.

22.5 Cloud foundations

Cloud computing rents somebody else’s computers in graduated slices of control. IaaS gives raw virtual machines, PaaS gives a managed runtime for your code, FaaS runs individual functions on demand, and SaaS delivers finished applications. Pick the slice that matches your workload’s shape, spiky and event-driven favors FaaS, long-running and predictable favors IaaS or PaaS, trading control for convenience at every step.

The service models, and what each is buying you

Cloud computing is three service models and the differences are about who manages what, not about quality. Infrastructure as a service gives you virtual machines, networks and storage, and you manage the operating system, the runtime and the application. Platform as a service gives you an environment your application deploys into, and you manage the application and the data only. Software as a service is someone else's finished application, and you manage nothing but your data and your access. The decision between them is a trade of control against effort, and the useful framing is that each one moves work from your team onto somebody else's, which is exactly what you are paying for and exactly what you give up. Then the specific properties that change when your compute is not a machine you own. Failure is a normal event rather than an exception. A physical machine in a rack has a life measured in years; a virtual instance is a resource that can be reclaimed, restarted, moved or terminated, and a design that assumes its compute is permanent will fail in ways it never did before. Everything is an API, which is convenient and also means every part of your infrastructure has credentials, rate limits, and a version to consider. Identity is the network boundary, rather than the network itself, so access control is a policy document and a misconfigured policy is a public resource. Storage and compute are separate and elastic, so the pairing that a physical machine forced — the disk with the box — is now something you chose and must keep choosing. And billing follows the resource, not the outcome, which means an idle machine costs exactly as much as a busy one and a runaway loop costs nothing until it costs a great deal.

Then the trade-offs, stated honestly, because the marketing is one-sided. You trade control for elasticity and for the absence of capital cost, and the control you lose is real: you cannot patch the hypervisor, you cannot inspect the hardware, and a provider's outage is an outage you cannot fix. You trade a predictable bill for a variable one, and the variable bill arrives at the worst possible time for most teams, which is why budgets and alerts exist. You trade a known environment for a shared one, so noisy neighbours and region-wide outages are possible in ways a dedicated machine is not. You acquire a dependency on a company's product decisions — a price change, a feature retired, a product folded into another — and some of those are merely inconvenient and some are migrations you did not choose. And you sometimes pay more than you would have, because a small workload is cheaper on ordinary hardware and the cloud's advantage begins somewhere above a size, which is worth stating because "we moved to the cloud to save money" is frequently false for small systems. Then the workloads where cloud genuinely wins, and they share a shape. Spiky or unpredictable demand, because capacity is available and idle capacity costs nothing. Short-lived environments — a test environment for an afternoon, a build machine for a week. Global reach, where putting a service near users is a configuration change rather than a purchase. Unpredictable growth, where the alternative is provisioning ahead of demand you cannot forecast. And the case for not, which is worth hearing: steady load, tight cost control, unusual hardware requirements, or a regulatory environment where leaving your own infrastructure is not an option.

/* Three service models - the difference is about who manages what, not quality. */
const MODELS = [
  { m: 'INFRASTRUCTURE AS A SERVICE', gives: ['virtual machines', 'networks', 'storage'],
    youManage: ['the operating system', 'the runtime', 'the application'] },
  { m: 'PLATFORM AS A SERVICE', gives: 'an environment your application deploys into',
    youManage: ['the application', 'the data'] },
  { m: 'SOFTWARE AS A SERVICE', is: 'someone elses FINISHED APPLICATION',
    youManage: ['your data', 'your access'] },
];
const THE_TRADE = 'each one moves WORK FROM YOUR TEAM ONTO SOMEBODY ELSES, which is exactly what you are paying for and exactly what you give up';

  { t: 'you SOMETIMES PAY MORE THAN YOU WOULD HAVE',
    because: 'a small workload is CHEAPER on ordinary hardware and the clouds advantage begins somewhere ABOVE A SIZE',
    namedFalsehood: 'we moved to the cloud to save money is FREQUENTLY FALSE for small systems' },
];

/* Where cloud genuinely wins - they share a shape. */
const WINS = [
  { w: 'SPIKY or UNPREDICTABLE DEMAND', why: 'capacity is available and IDLE CAPACITY COSTS NOTHING' },
  { w: 'SHORT-LIVED ENVIRONMENTS', instances: ['a test environment for an afternoon', 'a build machine for a week'] },
  { w: 'GLOBAL REACH', gain: 'putting a service near users is a CONFIGURATION CHANGE rather than a purchase' },
  { w: 'UNPREDICTABLE GROWTH', why: 'the alternative is provisioning AHEAD OF DEMAND YOU CANNOT FORECAST' },
];
const NOT = {
  conditions: ['steady load', 'tight cost control', 'unusual hardware requirements',
    'a regulatory environment where LEAVING YOUR OWN INFRASTRUCTURE is not an option'],
};
OfferingMeaningExamples
IaaSYou rent raw compute/storageAWS EC2, GCP Compute Engine
PaaSManaged runtime — just push codeHeroku, Vercel, AWS Elastic Beanstalk
FaaSFunctions that run on demand (serverless)AWS Lambda, Cloud Functions
SaaSFinished product you consumeGmail, Notion

The serverless myth, and the cost model that decides it

"Serverless" is a bad name for a specific and accurate idea, and the name is worth arguing with because it is the source of most of the confusion. There is a server. It exists, it runs your code, and somebody operates it. What you do not have is a machine you manage — you do not choose the processor, you do not patch the kernel, you do not see the operating system, and you do not know how many machines there are. What you have is the ability to describe code and have it run when an event occurs, for as long as the event takes. And the accounting that follows from that is the second half of the correction: serverless is priced per execution and virtual machines are priced per hour. That single difference produces the entire cost behaviour, and it is worth doing the arithmetic explicitly because it is the decision. A function invoked once an hour, taking a hundred milliseconds, costs a hundredth of a percent of a machine-hour; the same function invoked a hundred thousand times a second, taking a second each, costs more than any fixed number of machines you would buy. And there is a middle band where the two are comparable, and which side of it you are on depends on the traffic pattern rather than on the workload's nature — a batch job that runs for eight hours a day is cheaper on a virtual machine that you switch on for those eight hours, and cheaper still on a scheduled one if your provider has them.

Then the shapes that follow from the pricing, because they are genuinely different and the differences are useful. Short, frequent invocations are the best case: a hundred requests a day at a hundred milliseconds is nothing, and a monthly bill of pennies. Bursty workloads are the second best case, because the burst is what would have forced you to provision for the peak permanently, and here you pay for the burst and nothing else. Long-running work is the bad case: a function that runs for fifteen minutes is billed for fifteen minutes, it hits the duration limit, and the same work on a machine costs nothing extra because the machine is on anyway. Steady, predictable load is the case where serverless loses on cost, and it loses without ambiguity, because you are paying per invocation for something a machine does continuously at a flat rate. Latency-sensitive interactive paths is the case where it loses on experience, because a cold start adds hundreds of milliseconds to a request that should take twenty. And the practical note that decides most cases: the interesting question is not "is this workload serverless-shaped" but "what does this cost at my traffic, and what does it cost at ten times my traffic" — because the two curves have different shapes, and a system that is cheaper today and catastrophically more expensive after a successful launch is a system that will be rewritten under pressure rather than before it.

/* A bad name for a specific and accurate idea. */
const MYTH = {
  claim: 'serverless',
  truth: 'THERE IS A SERVER - it exists, it runs your code, and somebody operates it',
  whatYouDoNotHave: ['a machine you manage', 'a choice of processor', 'the kernel to patch',
    'the operating system to see', 'knowledge of HOW MANY MACHINES there are'],
  whatYouDoHave: 'the ability to DESCRIBE CODE and have it run when an event occurs, for as long as the event takes',
  theAccounting: 'SERVERLESS IS PRICED PER EXECUTION and VIRTUAL MACHINES ARE PRICED PER HOUR',
  whyItMatters: 'that single difference produces the ENTIRE COST BEHAVIOUR, and it is the decision',
  arithmetic: [
    { case: 'invoked ONCE AN HOUR for 100 milliseconds', cost: 'a HUNDREDTH OF A PERCENT of a machine-hour' },
    { case: 'invoked A HUNDRED THOUSAND TIMES A SECOND for a second each', cost: 'MORE THAN ANY FIXED NUMBER of machines you would buy' },
    { case: 'a BATCH JOB running eight hours a day', cost: 'cheaper on a virtual machine YOU SWITCH ON for those eight hours',
      and: 'cheaper still on a SCHEDULED ONE if your provider has them' },
  ],
  theBand: 'there is a MIDDLE BAND where the two are comparable, and which side of it you are on depends on the TRAFFIC PATTERN rather than on the workloads nature',
};

/* Shapes that follow from the pricing. */
const SHAPES = [
  { shape: 'SHORT, FREQUENT invocations', best: true,
    example: 'a hundred requests a day at a hundred milliseconds', cost: 'NOTHING - a monthly bill of pennies' },
  { shape: 'BURSTY workloads', secondBest: true,
    why: 'the burst is what would have forced you to PROVISION FOR THE PEAK PERMANENTLY',
    gain: 'here you pay for the BURST and nothing else' },
  { shape: 'LONG-RUNNING work', bad: true, detail: ['a function that runs fifteen minutes is BILLED FOR FIFTEEN MINUTES',
    'it HITS THE DURATION LIMIT'],
    contrast: 'the same work on a machine costs nothing extra because THE MACHINE IS ON ANYWAY' },
  { shape: 'STEADY, PREDICTABLE load', losesOn: 'COST', how: 'without ambiguity',
    why: 'you are paying PER INVOCATION for something a machine does continuously at a FLAT RATE' },
  { shape: 'LATENCY-SENSITIVE interactive paths', losesOn: 'EXPERIENCE',
    detail: 'a COLD START adds hundreds of milliseconds to a request that should take twenty' },
];
const THE_QUESTION = 'not is this workload serverless-shaped but WHAT DOES THIS COST AT MY TRAFFIC, and what does it cost at TEN TIMES MY TRAFFIC';
const WHY_THE_QUESTION = 'the two curves have DIFFERENT SHAPES, and a system that is cheaper today and CATASTROPHICALLY MORE EXPENSIVE after a successful launch is a system that will be REWRITTEN UNDER PRESSURE rather than before it';

Serverless myth-crushing: there IS a server — you just don’t see or maintain it. Serverless shines for spiky, event-driven workloads and terrible for long-running, steady CPU. Cost modelling: serverless = pay per execution; VMs = pay per hour.

22.6 Infrastructure as Code

Infrastructure as Code writes your infrastructure in declarative files, so servers, networks, and databases get review, version history, and reproducibility just like application code. Tools such as Terraform compare the declared state against reality, plan the exact difference, and apply it, while configuration management tools handle setup inside machines. Destroy and recreate whole environments from the same files instead of clicking through consoles.

Provision servers, networks, and pipelines from files that go through code review, just like application code. Two schools you’ll meet: Terraform (declarative, plan/apply, the default) and Ansible (imperative configuration). The wins: reproducibility, reviewability, and that infra is versioned history too.

# Terraform: declaring a cloud resource as code
resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  ami           = "ami-0c55b159cbfafe1f0"  # the machine image to launch
  instance_type = "t3.micro"  # small instance; fine for a demo
  tags          = { Name = "web-1" }
}
# terraform plan   --> shows the diff
# terraform apply  --> makes reality match the code

What infrastructure as code actually gives you

The value is not that it is faster to provision, and it usually is not — describing infrastructure in a file and applying it is slower than clicking, and pretending otherwise is the first thing that makes people distrust it. The value is that infrastructure becomes a versioned, reviewable, reproducible artefact. Four consequences, and each is a real operational capability rather than a convenience. You can review it. A change to production configuration goes through the same diff, the same review and the same history as a change to code, which means the question "what changed and why" has an answer instead of a guess. You can reproduce it. Building a new environment is running the same file that built the old one, so a staging environment that genuinely matches production is achievable rather than aspirational. You can see the drift. Because the desired state is in a file, a tool can compare it to what is actually running and report the difference — and drift is the single largest cause of "the new engineer could not reproduce the incident", because the environment was changed by hand in a console six months ago and nobody wrote it down. And you can destroy and rebuild safely, which is a capability that changes what you are willing to try, because an environment that can be recreated from code can also be thrown away and recreated when it goes wrong.

Then the shape of every infrastructure tool, which is the same three ideas regardless of the vendor. Declarative: you describe what should exist, not the sequence of commands that creates it — which is what makes the difference between a plan and an apply, and what makes the state comparable. Plan before apply: the tool computes what changes and shows you, without changing anything. This is the feature that makes the whole approach safe, and it is the one to insist on: a change that has not been planned has not been reviewed. State is external: the tool reads the real infrastructure and compares. That is what makes drift detectable, and it is also why the plan is honest — it is derived from the actual state rather than from what the file says, so a file that has drifted produces a plan that includes the drift. And then the three practices that separate a working setup from a demo. Store the configuration in version control, in the same repository as the application if possible, because a change that spans both is one review rather than two. Never edit in the console. Not once, not "just to fix this", not "just to test something" — because that is exactly how drift begins and it is invisible until the environment is rebuilt from a file that no longer matches. Apply changes through the pipeline, so the plan is reviewed and the apply is automatic, and a manual apply from a laptop is where a typo becomes an outage. And destroy and recreate for a new environment, because the alternative — hand-building a new environment from memory — is how the second environment quietly becomes different from the first.

/* Not that it is faster to provision - it usually is not. */
const THE_VALUE = {

  is: 'infrastructure becomes a VERSIONED, REVIEWABLE, REPRODUCIBLE ARTEFACT',
  consequences: [
    { c: 'you can REVIEW IT', detail: 'a change to production configuration goes through the SAME DIFF, the same review and the same history as a change to code',
      gain: 'the question what changed and why HAS AN ANSWER instead of a guess' },
    { c: 'you can REPRODUCE IT', gain: 'a staging environment that GENUINELY MATCHES production is achievable rather than aspirational' },
    { c: 'you can see the DRIFT',

Declares an AWS instance as plain code; plan previews the exact diff and apply makes the real world match, which is the whole point of infrastructure as code.

22.7 Production ops: observability and incidents

Deploying is not the finish line; running the service well is. Production operations monitor the golden signals, latency, traffic, errors, and saturation, alert on user impact rather than noise, and run blameless post-mortems after incidents so fixes focus on systems rather than people. Turn every incident into a permanent change in code, runbooks, or tests.

Deploying is not the end of a feature — running it well is the feature. The operational playbook every engineer internalises:

  • Golden signals for every service: latency (p50/p95/p99), traffic (requests/s), errors (rate + 5xx), saturation (CPU/memory/queue depth).
  • Alert on user impact, not on internals: "p99 > 800 ms for 5 min" fires because users are unhappy, not because a gauge twitched.
  • Dashboards answer questions, alerting answers "what to do now". Separate them mentally.
  • Incident response recipe: mitigate first (rollback, feature flag off, scale up), then find root cause, write a blameless post-mortem (the system failed, not the person), and turn it into automated checks so it can’t recur silently.
# The outline every post-mortem follows
Title: incident summary (time window, severity, duration)
Timeline: when things started changing, when we noticed, when we fixed
Impact: how many users / requests / dollars, measured
Root cause: the one chain that led here
Why not caught: which check/monitor was missing
Action items: each tagged [alert][test][docs][code] with owners and dates

The standard structure of a blameless post-mortem: timeline, measured impact, root cause, the missing check, and owner-tagged action items that prevent recurrence.

Feature flags are the seatbelt. The seniorest-releasers use "canary: 1% → 10% → 100%" plus automatic rollback, so a bad deploy is measured pain, not a fire. And every rollback practice you rehearse now is the one that works at 3 a.m.

What operations actually is, and the four kinds of work

Operations is the work of keeping a system running, and the useful mental model divides it into four kinds, each with a different time horizon and a different measure of success. Running the thing — deploying it, monitoring it, keeping it up. The measure is availability and time to restore. Changing the thing — releases, configuration, infrastructure. The measure is how safe and how reversible a change is. Understanding the thing — knowing what is running, what changed, what broke and why. The measure is time to diagnose. And Improving the thing — making the next change cheaper and the next failure less likely. The measure is whether the same problem takes less time next time. Most teams invest heavily in the first, adequately in the second, poorly in the third, and not at all in the fourth — and the fourth is the one that compounds, because it is the only one that makes the other three easier. Then the practices that constitute good operations, and each is unglamorous. Automate the runbook. If a procedure is documented in a wiki and executed by a person under pressure at three in the morning, it will be executed differently every time and will eventually be executed wrongly; a script is faster, identical every time, and reviewable. Make the deployment boring. The frequency of deployments is the best measure of how safe the process is, because a process you are afraid of is a process you batch changes into, and batching is what makes a change large and therefore risky. Have a rollback that is fast and rehearsed, rather than one that is documented. Monitor what users experience, not what the machine reports — error rate, latency percentiles, and the business number — because a machine at low utilisation serving a slow application is a healthy-looking system that is failing. And write the incident down while it is happening, because the timeline during the incident is the only point at which the facts are available and nobody is reconstructing them from memory afterwards.

/* Four kinds of work, each with a different time horizon and measure. */
const FOUR_KINDS = [
  { k: 'RUNNING THE THING', does: ['deploying it', 'monitoring it', 'keeping it up'],
    measure: ['availability', 'time to restore'] },
  { k: 'CHANGING THE THING', does: ['releases', 'configuration', 'infrastructure'],
    measure: 'how SAFE and how REVERSIBLE a change is' },
  { k: 'UNDERSTANDING THE THING', does: ['knowing what is running', 'what changed', 'what broke and why'],
    measure: 'time to DIAGNOSE' },
  { k: 'IMPROVING THE THING', does: 'making the NEXT CHANGE CHEAPER and the next failure less likely',
    measure: 'whether the same problem takes LESS TIME next time' },
];
const WHERE_TEAMS_INVEST = {
  first: 'heavily', second: 'adequately', third: 'poorly', fourth: 'NOT AT ALL',
  and: 'the fourth is the one that COMPOUNDS, because it is the only one that MAKES THE OTHER THREE EASIER',
};

/* Practices. */

  { p: 'AUTOMATE THE RUNBOOK',
    problem: 'a procedure documented in a wiki and executed by a person under pressure at three in the morning',
    consequence: ['it will be EXECUTED DIFFERENTLY EVERY TIME', 'and will eventually be EXECUTED WRONGLY'],
    gain: ['a script is FASTER', 'IDENTICAL every time', 'REVIEWABLE'] },
  { p: 'make the DEPLOYMENT BORING',
    measure: 'the FREQUENCY of deployments is the best measure of how safe the process is',
    why: ['a process you are AFRAID OF is a process you BATCH CHANGES INTO',
      'and batching is what makes a change LARGE and therefore RISKY'] },
  { p: 'have a ROLLBACK that is fast and REHEARSED, rather than one that is documented' },
  { p: 'MONITOR WHAT USERS EXPERIENCE, not what the machine reports',

23 · Concurrency & Performance

Concurrency and Performance is about turning fast single things into reliable many things. The chapter covers why concurrency is hard, locks and deadlock, Python’s threads versus asyncio, performance engineering with profiling, the lock-free ideal of actors and message passing, and async and event loops in depth. The recurring enemy is shared mutable state, and each tool is a different way of managing or removing it.

23.1 Why concurrency is hard23.2 Locks, deadlock, and the survivors23.3 Python, threads vs asyncio — which lever when23.4 Performance engineering: measure first, always23.5 The lock-free ideal: actors and message passing23.6 Async/await & event loops, in depth

The final technical deep-dive: making systems handle many things at once without corrupting each other, and making them fast. Concurrency is where "it’s my screw-up" meets "it’s physics".

23.1 Why concurrency is hard

Concurrency is hard because memory operations are not atomic, so two threads can interleave while reading and writing shared data and corrupt it mid-flight. Data races, visibility problems, and lost updates all spring from that one fact. The entire discipline of concurrency is managing shared mutable state: locking it, making it immutable, or isolating it so only one owner touches it.

Modern CPUs have multiple cores; modern apps serve thousands of users. But memory operations are not atomic — a read-modify-write from two threads can interleave mid-way and corrupt state (you saw exactly this in Ch. 11.6). The discipline is managing shared mutable state.

# The three strategies, in order of preference:
# 1. No shared mutable state (message passing, immutable data)
# 2. Confined state (each thread owns its data; never hand it out)
# 3. Synchronise (locks/atomics) when 1 and 2 can't apply

import threading, collections

# Actor-ish pattern in threads: each worker owns a queue; no shared globals
boxes = [collections.deque() for _ in range(4)]

def worker(i):
    while True:
        item = boxes[i].popleft()   # each worker reads ONLY its own box
        item()                      # so: zero locks needed

# If you must share: protect with a lock, keep critical section tiny
lock = threading.Lock()
total = 0
with lock:
    total += item.value            # <-- atomic region, short & simple

The three strategies and what each costs

Three ways to get more work done at once, and each trades a different thing. Threads give concurrency by sharing an address space, so communication is free and the cost is that every piece of shared state is a potential race. Processes give parallelism by running separate address spaces, so communication must be explicit — through a pipe, a socket, shared memory — and the cost is that data must be copied or serialised, and that the operating system has to create and destroy address spaces. Coroutines or tasks, which the async section covers, give concurrency on one thread by suspending at an await point and letting another task run, so communication is explicit and cheap — no copying — and the cost is that a task that does CPU work without yielding blocks every other task, which is the trap that catches everybody. Then the shape of the decision, and it is a question about what your work spends its time doing rather than about how much of it there is. I/O-bound work spends most of its time waiting, and a thread or a task that is waiting costs the system almost nothing — so a thousand threads waiting on a thousand sockets is fine, because the operating system multiplexes them and only the ready ones get a core. CPU-bound work needs more than one core, and in a language with a global lock, threads cannot provide it and processes must be used instead, which is the interpreter chapter's subject and the reason for a constraint that is unique to one language. And mixed work needs both, with the split at the boundary: the orchestration is I/O, the computation is CPU, and the code that dispatches between them is where the language's limitation bites.

Then why the third option — not needing concurrency — should be tried first, because it is the one nobody considers and it is often the right answer. Batch the work. A thousand individual round trips is a thousand network calls; one call with a thousand items is one. Do less of it. A cache, a smarter algorithm, a batched write, or simply not computing something nobody asked for removes the need for parallelism entirely. Make the work cheaper. The fastest concurrent version of an inefficient algorithm is still an inefficient algorithm. Use the runtime's parallelism, which for numeric work and for file-system operations is usually available and invisible. And push work out of the request, into a job queue, where it happens without occupying the resources you are trying to protect. None of these is a compromise and none is a workaround — each is a genuine improvement that removes the problem rather than managing it, and the discipline is to spend a few minutes asking whether the concurrency is necessary before spending a day getting it correct.

/* Three strategies, each trading a different thing. */
const STRATEGIES = [
  { s: 'THREADS', give: 'concurrency by SHARING AN ADDRESS SPACE',
    good: 'communication is FREE', cost: 'every piece of SHARED STATE is a potential RACE' },
  { s: 'PROCESSES', give: 'parallelism by running SEPARATE ADDRESS SPACES',
    good: 'communication must be EXPLICIT - through a pipe, a socket, shared memory',
    cost: ['data must be COPIED OR SERIALISED', 'the operating system has to CREATE AND DESTROY address spaces'] },
  { s: 'COROUTINES or TASKS', give: 'concurrency on ONE THREAD by suspending at an await point',
    good: 'communication is EXPLICIT AND CHEAP - no copying',
    cost: 'a task that does CPU WORK WITHOUT YIELDING blocks every other task',
    trap: 'which is the trap that catches EVERYBODY' },
];

/* The decision is a question about what the work SPENDS ITS TIME doing. */
const DECISION = [
  { w: 'I/O-BOUND work', detail: 'spends most of its time WAITING',
    result: 'a thread or task that is waiting costs the system ALMOST NOTHING',
    therefore: 'a THOUSAND THREADS ON A THOUSAND SOCKETS is fine, because the operating system MULTIPLEXES them and only the ready ones get a core' },
  { w: 'CPU-BOUND work', needs: 'MORE THAN ONE CORE',
    inPython: 'threads CANNOT provide it and processes must be used instead',
    note: 'which is the interpreter chapters subject' },
  { w: 'MIXED work', needs: 'both',
    splitAt: 'the boundary - the orchestration is I/O, the computation is CPU',
    whereBites: 'the code that DISPATCHES between them is where the language limitation bites' },
];

/* The option nobody considers. */
const NOT_NEEDING = [
  { a: 'BATCH THE WORK', example: 'a thousand individual round trips is a THOUSAND NETWORK CALLS; one call with a thousand items is ONE' },
  { a: 'DO LESS OF IT', instances: ['a cache', 'a smarter algorithm', 'a batched write',
    'not computing something NOBODY ASKED FOR'],
    gain: 'removes the need for parallelism ENTIRELY' },
  { a: 'MAKE THE WORK CHEAPER', reframe: 'the FASTEST CONCURRENT VERSION of an inefficient algorithm is still an INEFFICIENT ALGORITHM' },
  { a: "use the RUNTIME'S PARALLELISM", for: ['numeric work', 'file-system operations'],
    trait: 'usually AVAILABLE AND INVISIBLE' },
  { a: 'PUSH WORK OUT OF THE REQUEST', into: 'a job queue',
    gain: 'it happens WITHOUT OCCUPYING THE RESOURCES you are trying to protect' },
];
const THE_DISCIPLINE = 'NONE OF THESE IS A COMPROMISE and none is a workaround - each is a genuine improvement that REMOVES THE PROBLEM rather than managing it, so spend a few minutes asking WHETHER THE CONCURRENCY IS NECESSARY before spending a day getting it correct';

Ranks the three concurrency strategies from best to worst, shows lock-free per-worker queues, and keeps the one true shared update under a tiny locked section.

23.2 Locks, deadlock, and the survivors

Mutexes, semaphores, and condition variables are the classic toolkit for coordinating threads. A mutex guarantees one thread inside a critical section at a time, a semaphore limits how many, and a condition variable lets threads wait until a predicate becomes true. Deadlock is the classic failure, when threads hold locks and wait on each other in a cycle, so learn the warning signs and practice consistent ordering, timeouts, and lock hierarchies.

  • Mutex — mutual exclusion; the classic lock.
  • Semaphore — a counter gate ("at most N threads in here") — great for connection pools.
  • Condvar / condition variable — wait until a predicate holds, then notify (worker pool wake-ups).
  • Deadlock — circular wait. Prevention: enforce a global lock order; timeout your lock acquisitions; or prefer lock-free structures.
  • Atomics / CAS (compare-and-swap) — hardware-supported tiny operations that are queue-free — base of lock-free queues and counters.

Locks, and what they are actually for

A mutex does one thing: it guarantees that at most one thread is inside a region at a time. That is all, and almost every difficulty with locking comes from expecting more of it. It does not make the code inside it correct. If the critical section has a logic error, the lock serialises the error rather than removing it. It does not make an operation atomic. Reading a variable, deciding what to write, and writing it is three operations, and a lock held across all three makes them indivisible — but if the lock is held only across the read and not the write, the guarantee is nothing, and that is the most common misuse in practice. It does not prevent a deadlock, and holding two of them is how deadlocks happen. And it does not help across processes, because a thread's mutex is invisible to another process, which is why the answer for cross-process is a different primitive entirely. Then the two questions that decide whether a lock is the right tool. How long is the critical section? Short — the work inside the lock should be arithmetic on a few variables, not anything that touches the network or the disk. How contended is it? If fifty threads want the same lock, they serialise and the concurrency is theatre, and the right response is usually to reduce the shared state rather than to make the lock faster.

Then the two rules that keep it correct, and the deadlock question deserves the detail because it is the failure people fear. Always acquire multiple locks in the same global order. Two threads taking A then B and B then A will deadlock, and imposing a total order on the locks makes that impossible — every thread takes the lower-numbered lock first, so no cycle can form. It requires that the order be global rather than per-code-path, and it is worth the small awkwardness. Then never hold a lock while doing something slow: not a network call, not a disk write, not a computation that can block, because a thread holding a lock through a slow operation converts one slow operation into every thread queueing behind it — and that is the mechanism behind most production contention. The rule is mechanical: do the slow thing outside the lock, take the lock, check or compute the short thing, release, then do the slow thing. And prefer not needing one, which is the functional-style argument from the previous chapter: if the shared state is immutable, there is nothing to lock, and the answer is not a better lock but no lock.

/* A mutex does one thing. */
const MUTEX = {
  does: 'guarantees that AT MOST ONE THREAD is inside a region at a time',
  doesNot: [
    'make the CODE INSIDE IT correct - a logic error is SERIALISED rather than removed',
    'make an OPERATION atomic',
    'prevent a DEADLOCK - holding two of them is how deadlocks happen',
    'help ACROSS PROCESSES - a threads mutex is INVISIBLE to another process',
  ],
};
/* The most common misuse. */
const ATOMICITY = {
  detail: 'reading a variable, deciding what to write, and writing it is THREE OPERATIONS',
  rule: 'a lock held across all three makes them INDIVISIBLE',
  misuse: 'if the lock is held only across the READ and not the WRITE, the guarantee is NOTHING',
  frequency: 'the MOST COMMON MISUSE in practice',
};
const TWO_QUESTIONS = [
  { q: 'HOW LONG is the critical section',
    answer: 'SHORT - the work inside the lock should be ARITHMETIC ON A FEW VARIABLES, not anything touching the network or the disk' },
  { q: 'HOW CONTENDED is it',
    problem: 'if fifty threads want the same lock they SERIALISE and the concurrency is THEATRE',
    response: 'usually to REDUCE THE SHARED STATE rather than to make the lock faster' },
];

/* Two rules. */
const RULES = [
  { r: 'always ACQUIRE MULTIPLE LOCKS IN THE SAME GLOBAL ORDER',
    deadlock: 'two threads taking A then B and B then A WILL DEADLOCK',
    defence: 'imposing a TOTAL ORDER on the locks makes that impossible - every thread takes the LOWER-NUMBERED LOCK FIRST, so NO CYCLE CAN FORM',
    requires: 'that the order be GLOBAL rather than per-code-path', worthIt: 'the small awkwardness' },
  { r: 'NEVER HOLD A LOCK WHILE DOING SOMETHING SLOW',
    not: ['a network call', 'a disk write', 'a computation that can block'],
    mechanism: 'a thread holding a lock through a slow operation converts ONE SLOW OPERATION into every thread queueing behind it',
    and: 'that is the mechanism behind MOST PRODUCTION CONTENTION',
    mechanicalFix: ['do the slow thing OUTSIDE the lock', 'take the lock', 'check or compute the short thing',
      'release', 'then do the slow thing'] },
  { r: 'PREFER NOT NEEDING ONE', because: 'if the shared state is IMMUTABLE there is nothing to lock',
    answer: 'the answer is not a BETTER LOCK but NO LOCK' },
];

Condition variables, semaphores, and barriers

The other two primitives, because each answers a question a mutex cannot. A condition variable is for waiting until something becomes true — not for mutual exclusion, but for the fact that a thread has to wait for a condition another thread will make true. The critical discipline is the one the chapter's warning names: wait in a loop, and re-check the condition inside it. A condition variable can wake spuriously, and more importantly it can wake for a different condition than the one you are waiting for — several predicates sharing one variable, or a signal delivered while you were not yet waiting. A bare wait(condition) therefore returns and finds the condition still false and the code proceeds anyway. The loop is not defensive style; it is the correctness requirement, and a wait without one is a bug that appears under load rather than in testing. And notify is not a signal to a particular waiter, it is a broadcast to whoever is waiting, so a thread that is notified must still check whether the state is actually what it wanted, which is the same loop from the other side.

Then a semaphore is a counter, and it answers the question a mutex cannot: how many of these may proceed at once. A semaphore of five permits five concurrent holders; each acquire takes a permit, each release returns one. That makes it the right primitive for a connection pool, a rate limiter, or bounding how many concurrent requests touch a resource that has a real limit. And a barrier is a rendezvous point: several threads wait until a specified number have arrived, and then all proceed. It is the correct primitive for the phases of a parallel algorithm — all workers compute their share, everyone waits at the barrier, then everyone merges — and using a counter and a condition variable instead of a barrier produces exactly the sort of code where one worker is still computing when another starts merging, which produces results that are wrong on some inputs and right on others. Then the practical selection, which is short enough to hold in your head. Mutex: protecting a piece of shared state so only one thread is in there. Condition variable: waiting for a condition, always with a mutex and always in a loop. Semaphore: limiting how many threads may be in a region. Bread: limiting how many threads may be in a region. Bread: the count is waiting for the Nth. And then the three ways primitives are misused, which together account for most of the bugs in concurrent code: holding a lock while blocking, so every other thread needing it is blocked on a condition that may take minutes; nesting locks across functions, so nobody can know the acquisition order and deadlocks become likely rather than possible; and using the wrong primitive — a mutex where a semaphore is right, which silently restricts to one when you meant five, and is correct under light load and wrong under heavy load.

/* A condition variable is for WAITING until something becomes true. */
const CONDITION_VARIABLE = {
  isNot: 'for mutual exclusion',
  isFor: 'the fact that a thread has to WAIT FOR A CONDITION another thread will make true',
  theDiscipline: 'wait in a LOOP, and re-check the condition inside it',
  whyNotDefensive: ['a condition variable can WAKE SPURIOUSLY',
    'and more importantly it can wake for a DIFFERENT CONDITION than the one you are waiting for',
    'several predicates sharing one variable', 'a signal delivered while you were NOT YET WAITING'],
  bareWait: 'therefore returns, finds the condition still FALSE, and the code proceeds anyway',
  verdict: 'the loop is not defensive style - it is the CORRECTNESS REQUIREMENT',
  aWaitWithoutOne: 'is a bug that appears UNDER LOAD rather than in testing',
  notifyIsNot: 'a signal to a particular waiter - it is a BROADCAST to whoever is waiting',
  consequence: 'a thread that is notified must STILL CHECK whether the state is what it wanted',
  sameLoop: 'which is the same loop from the OTHER SIDE',
};

/* The other primitives. */
const SEMAPHORE = {
  is: 'a COUNTER',
  answers: 'the question a mutex CANNOT - how many of these may PROCEED AT ONCE',
  permits: 'a semaphore of five permits FIVE CONCURRENT HOLDERS',

  rightFor: ['a connection pool', 'a rate limiter', 'bounding how many concurrent requests touch a resource that has a REAL LIMIT'],
};
const BARRIER = {
  is: 'a RENDEZVOUS POINT',
  does: 'several threads wait until a specified number have ARRIVED, and then all proceed',
  rightFor: 'the PHASES of a parallel algorithm - all workers compute their share, everyone waits, then everyone merges',
  doingItWrong: 'using a COUNTER AND A CONDITION VARIABLE instead of a barrier produces exactly the sort of code where one worker is STILL COMPUTING when another starts merging',
  consequence: 'which produces results that are WRONG ON SOME INPUTS and right on others',
};

/* Selection. */
const SELECT = [
  { p: 'MUTEX', for: 'protecting a piece of shared state so ONLY ONE THREAD is in there' },
  { p: 'CONDITION VARIABLE', for: 'waiting for a condition',
    always: ['with a mutex', 'in a loop'] },
  { p: 'SEMAPHORE', for: 'limiting how many threads may be in a region' },

];
/* Three ways primitives are misused. */
const MISUSE = [

  { m: 'NESTING LOCKS ACROSS FUNCTIONS', consequence: 'nobody can know the ACQUISITION ORDER and deadlocks become LIKELY rather than possible' },
  { m: 'USING THE WRONG PRIMITIVE', example: 'a MUTEX where a SEMAPHORE is right, which silently restricts to one when you meant five',
    symptom: 'correct under LIGHT LOAD and wrong under HEAVY LOAD' },
];

Two warning signs: a lock held while doing slow I/O (everyone queues behind a little sleep) — release before I/O; and locks inside nested functions (nobody can remember the order) — acquire in one clear place.

23.3 Python, threads vs asyncio — which lever when

Python threads, asyncio, and processes each fit a different bottleneck. Under the Global Interpreter Lock, plain Python threads cannot parallelize CPU work, so use asyncio for I/O-bound tasks like network calls, processes for true multi-core work, and threads mainly when a library does blocking I/O. Match the tool to the actual bottleneck.

Threadsasyncio (async/await)Processes / multiprocessing
Good forI/O-bound tasks with blocking callsMany concurrent I/O on ONE threadCPU-bound heavy compute (uses all cores)
Shared memoryYes — risk of races (GIL serialises Python bytecode but not your read-modify-write)Single thread, cooperative — no preemption racesNo — separate memory; share via queues/pipes
GotchaGIL means threads don’t parallelise CPU workBlocking calls inside async code freeze everythingPickling data + heavier spawn cost
import asyncio

async def fetch(url, delay_ms):
    await asyncio.sleep(delay_ms / 1000)      # pretend network I/O
    return url

async def main():
    results = await asyncio.gather(  # run all three concurrently
        fetch("A", 200), fetch("B", 50), fetch("C", 100),
    )
    print(results)     # all three done in ~200ms total, not 350ms

asyncio.run(main())

Three async fetches that run concurrently finish in roughly the slowest one’s time, showing how a single thread can juggle many I/O-bound tasks.

What the lock actually restricts, and the workaround people find

The global interpreter lock exists because of how CPython manages memory: objects are reference-counted, and freeing an object decrements a count, so two threads freeing objects simultaneously could race on that count and free something still in use. A single lock around object allocation and deallocation makes that safe. The consequence is well known and worth stating precisely: only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time. The lock is taken and released between bytecode instructions, so threads do interleave — but the pure-Python work is serialised, and a thread running a tight loop in Python code gets essentially the whole core to itself while the others wait. And the important qualifier, because this is where most blog posts are wrong: I/O releases the lock. A thread blocked on a socket, on a file read or on a sleep has released the interpreter lock, which is exactly why a threaded server handling many waiting connections works well under CPython. The lock hurts compute and does not hurt waiting. Then the consequences, and the second one surprises people. One thread doing pure computation is a waste of the other cores, which is why a single-threaded benchmark looks fine while a threaded one does not scale. The lock is taken frequently, so a highly concurrent pure-compute workload is not merely serialised but slower than serial execution, because the contention cost is paid and nothing is gained. And I/O-bound libraries may release the lock internally, which means a "threaded" program is only parallel where those libraries release it — a distinction that matters when reading whether a given operation parallelises.

Then what to do, in the order to try it. Use processes for CPU-bound work. This is the direct answer and it costs you a serialisation boundary: each process has its own memory, so data must be copied or shared deliberately, and the overhead of starting a process is much higher than starting a thread. Use threads or tasks for I/O-bound work, because the lock is released while waiting and the concurrency is real. Push the computation to something that releases the lock or runs elsewhere — a compiled extension, a vectorised numeric library, a subprocess, a native library — because the computation itself is then performed without the interpreter lock in the way. And use a language or implementation that does not have the constraint, which is the honest long answer if the workload is genuinely CPU-parallel and the code is going to exist for years. Then the pragmatic rules that come out of it. Measure before concluding the lock is your problem, because the same symptom — low CPU utilisation on a many-core machine — has several causes and the lock is one of them. Never make an architectural decision about concurrency based on a micro-benchmark, because a micro-benchmark measures the lock and not your workload. And keep the shared work small and the shared state few, so that the serialised portion of your program is small enough that it does not matter — which is a design principle that holds regardless of the lock.

/* Why it exists. */
const WHY_EXISTS = 'objects are REFERENCE-COUNTED, and freeing an object decrements a count, so two threads freeing objects simultaneously could RACE on that count and free something still in use';
const CONSEQUENCE = {
  is: 'only ONE THREAD EXECUTES PYTHON BYTECODE AT A TIME',

  importantQualifier: 'I/O RELEASES THE LOCK',
  example: 'a thread blocked on a socket, a file read or a sleep HAS RELEASED THE INTERPRETER LOCK',
  whyThatMatters: 'which is exactly why a THREADED SERVER handling many waiting connections works well under CPython',
  summary: 'the lock HURTS COMPUTE and does NOT HURT WAITING',

/* What to do, in order. */

  { r: 'never make an ARCHITECTURAL DECISION about concurrency based on a MICRO-BENCHMARK',
    why: 'a micro-benchmark MEASURES THE LOCK and not your workload' },
  { r: 'keep the SHARED WORK small and the SHARED STATE few',

Golden rule: I/O-bound concurrency → asyncio (or threads); CPU-bound parallelism → processes (or a different language). And try always to not need locks: functional style, immutable data, queues.

23.4 Performance engineering: measure first, always

Performance engineering is measured and evidence-driven: profile first, find the one real bottleneck, fix it, and re-measure, or you will optimize the wrong layer. Keep a benchmark in CI so regressions surface the moment they land, and let profilers and traces rather than intuition choose what to optimize. Small, verified wins compound into large speedups.

The #1 performance rule: profile before optimising. You will guess wrong every time. The workflow:

  1. Measure — time it, count database queries, read p99s.
  2. Find the bottleneck — the one slow step (usually I/O, a query, or an N² loop).
  3. Optimise that — better algorithm, cache, index, batching, connection pooling.
  4. Re-measure — is it actually faster? Keep a benchmark test.
# The N+1 problem: one query per row — the #1 API slowness
# BAD:  for every order -> SELECT ... per order   (N+1 queries)
orders = db.query("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = ?", uid)
total = sum(len(db.query("SELECT * FROM items WHERE order_id = ?", o["id"]))
            for o in orders)
# GOOD: 1 query to fetch all related rows (+ group in Python) or SQL JOIN
# Rule: batch your I/O. N+1 makes a 1-request API into a 100-request one.

Where the time goes, and why intuition is wrong

Concurrency problems are almost always found by measurement, and the reason is that intuition about which operation is expensive is systematically unreliable. The reliable statements are these. A network round trip is roughly a thousand times slower than a memory read and roughly fifty to a hundred times slower than a function call, which is why the number of round trips dominates and their individual cost barely matters. A disk read is roughly a thousand times slower than a memory read, which is why an index that turns a sequential scan into a seek is worth more than any amount of micro-optimisation. A context switch costs microseconds, which is small and which is why thread-based concurrency works at all — but it is not free, and a system doing millions of them per second is spending real time in the scheduler. Lock contention can exceed the cost of the work it protects, because the wait is not proportional to the critical section and a thread can be blocked far longer than the work is long. And the profiling result frequently contradicts the guess, which is the entire argument for measuring. Then the two measurement techniques, and which catches which problem. A sampling profiler periodically captures where execution is and aggregates — cheap, low overhead, and it catches the thing that is eating the time, whether that is a function, a lock, or a wait. A tracing profiler records every call and every wait, which produces far more data and shows you the call graph, and it is what you want when the time is going somewhere you cannot see — inside a lock, inside I/O, inside a library you are not instrumenting. The honest workflow: sample to find where the time is, then trace to find why.

Then the specific performance defects worth recognising on sight, and each is a shape rather than a value. The N-plus-one query — a loop that fetches a list and then fetches related rows one at a time, which is one round trip for the list and one per item, and which is the single most common cause of a slow endpoint. The fix is a join, an IN clause, or one aggregated subquery, and the shape to recognise is "a call inside a loop". Unbatched writes — a thousand individual inserts in a transaction that could have been one statement, which is a thousand round trips where one would do, and which is a loop again. Chatty interfaces — an object that makes several network calls per method rather than one, which is a design problem rather than a performance bug and which becomes visible only at scale. Work done per request that could be done once — a configuration read, a schema parse, a feature-flag evaluation, on every single request rather than at startup. Lock held across I/O, covered in the primitives section and worth repeating because it presents as throughput rather than as contention. And queue depth growing, which is not a defect but the symptom, and which is the one measurement that tells you the real problem is elsewhere.

Contrasts the N+1 query pattern, one round trip per row, with fetching related rows in a single batch. It is the single most common source of slow APIs.

  • I/O batching and connection pooling routinely produce 10–100× wins before you touch a single algorithm.
  • Fish-slab old advice still applies: an O(n²) hidden inside a loop is your enemy far more often than a slow-but-clean O(n).
  • Baselines & benchmarks in CI prevent silent regressions: pytest-benchmark on hot paths.

23.5 The lock-free ideal: actors and message passing

Message passing and actors replace locks with structure: each actor owns its own state, never shared, and communicates only by sending messages through queues. Because there is no shared mutable state, there is nothing to lock and therefore nothing to deadlock. This is how Erlang builds telecom-grade reliability and how Kubernetes spreads work without lock contention.

Every lock you write is a place a deadlock can hide. The structural alternative that entire systems (Erlang/Elixir, Akka, Kubernetes controllers, most async runtimes) use: no two things ever touch the same memory. Each unit owns its data and communicates only by messages.

# The actor shape, simplified: an object + its own queue + a loop
import threading, queue

class Counter:
    def __init__(self):
        self._q = queue.Queue()          # this actor's inbox
        self.value = 0
        threading.Thread(target=self._run, daemon=True).start()

    def _run(self):
        while True:
            msg = self._q.get()          # block until a message arrives
            if msg == "inc":
                self.value += 1          # ONLY this thread touches .value
            elif msg == "stop":
                break

counter = Counter()
for _ in range(1000):
    counter._q.put("inc")                # send messages, never shared vars
print(counter.value)                     # 1000 -- no locks, no races

A minimal actor: its own thread, its own inbox queue, and exactly one owner mutating its state, so no locks are ever needed and no races can occur.

Why it scales: each actor has a single owner thread, so its state needs no lock; the only coordination is the queue, which is safe by construction. Message passing is how Erlang runs millions of actors, how the web "event loop" stays single-threaded (Ch. 23.3), and how microservices avoid sharing databases (Ch. 29).

Messaging, and what it buys over a shared lock

Message passing replaces shared state with communication: one component owns a piece of state and others send it messages to read or change that state. The gain is not performance, which is usually worse, but isolation. The owner's state is not visible to anybody, so it cannot be modified by accident, it does not need a lock because nobody else can reach it, and the reasoning about it is local rather than global. The costs are the mirror: messages are slow relative to a function call, because they involve serialisation and often a network hop; senders must know what a message means, which is a coupling that a direct function call does not have — the receiver's interface becomes a contract others depend on; and the ordering and delivery guarantees are weaker, so a design built on messages must reason about what happens when a message is lost, duplicated, or arrives out of order, and that reasoning is a substantial part of the work.

Then when messaging is the right choice, and the criteria are about the workload rather than the preference. Many small workers processing the same stream, where adding a worker is adding a reader of the same queue and no coordination is needed. Retries and timeouts matter, because a message that fails can be redelivered and a caller that is a queue is not holding a connection while it does. Partial failure must be survivable, because a consumer that dies mid-message loses the in-flight message rather than the whole system. You need to scale producers and consumers independently, because they may be on different trajectories. And you are already asynchronous, where adding a lock-based synchronous call is more disruptive than adding a queue. And when shared state is the right choice, which is the honest other half. A small, short critical section, where a mutex is the simplest thing that works and a queue would be several hundred lines and a new deployment. State that is genuinely one thing, — a counter, a cache index, a connection pool — where the ownership argument for messaging is weak because there is one reader and one writer who are both right there. And low latency matters more than throughput, because a message round trip is slower than a lock-protected read and if you need the answer in a microsecond a queue cannot give it to you.

/* Messaging replaces shared state with communication. */
const MESSAGING = {
  model: 'ONE COMPONENT OWNS a piece of state and others SEND IT MESSAGES to read or change that state',
  gain: 'ISOLATION, not performance',
  because: ['the owners state is NOT VISIBLE TO ANYBODY, so it cannot be modified by accident',
    'it does not NEED A LOCK because nobody else can reach it',
    'the reasoning about it is LOCAL rather than global'],

    'the ORDERING AND DELIVERY GUARANTEES ARE WEAKER, so a design must reason about loss, duplication and out-of-order arrival'],
  andThatReasoning: 'is a SUBSTANTIAL PART OF THE WORK',
};

  { c: 'MANY SMALL WORKERS processing the same stream',

/* When shared state is right - the honest other half. */
const SHARED_WHEN = [
  { c: 'a SMALL, SHORT critical section', why: 'a mutex is THE SIMPLEST THING THAT WORKS',
    contrast: 'a queue would be SEVERAL HUNDRED LINES and a NEW DEPLOYMENT' },
  { c: 'state that is GENUINELY ONE THING', instances: ['a counter', 'a cache index', 'a connection pool'],
    why: 'the ownership argument for messaging is WEAK because there is one reader and one writer WHO ARE BOTH RIGHT THERE' },
  { c: 'LOW LATENCY matters more than throughput', why: 'a message round trip is SLOWER than a lock-protected read, and if you need the answer in a MICROSECOND a queue cannot give it to you' },
];

When to choose messaging over locks: many small workers, retries and timeouts matter, you want to survive partial crashes, or you’re already async. When to keep shared state: a small, short critical section where a mutex is the simplest thing that works. Simplicity wins.

23.6 Async/await & event loops, in depth

An event loop gives one thread the throughput of thousands of concurrent I/O operations by waiting on many connections at once and resuming each when its data arrives. Async and await make that code readable by suspending a function at an await point without blocking the thread. Async wins for I/O-bound workloads, and any blocking call inside the loop ruins it for everyone else.

Threads are one concurrency tool; asynchronous I/O is the other — one thread, many in-flight operations, no waiting. Event-loop programming is the heart of Node, modern Python (asyncio), and every network server.

import asyncio

async def fetch(url):
    print(f"GET {url}")
    await asyncio.sleep(0.5)          # awaited work = non-blocking
    return f"<{url} ok>"

async def main():
    results = await asyncio.gather(   # run MANY at once on one thread
        fetch("https://a.example"),
        fetch("https://b.example"),
        fetch("https://c.example"),
    )
    print(results)                    # ~0.5s total, not 1.5s

asyncio.run(main())

# Why it's fast: while one op awaits I/O, the event loop runs another.
# The ONE rule that breaks it: blocking calls (time.sleep, sync DB, CPU
# loops) block the WHOLE loop -- with threads you'd only lock one worker.
# So: asyncio for I/O-bound fan-out; threads/processes for CPU/blocking.

Gather runs many async calls on a single thread, and the closing comments warn exactly which blocking calls will freeze the whole event loop.

  • The GIL (Ch.23.3) doesn’t kill asyncio — async spends almost zero CPU waiting, so a single-threaded loop scales to huge concurrency on I/O.
  • Debugging: never mix blocking sleep with await asyncio.sleep; detect violations with asyncio debug or timeout wrappers.
  • Interview frame: "threads = multiple workers, async = one worker juggling many tasks" — know when each wins.

What asynchronous means, and what it does not

Asynchronous is a way of structuring a program, not a way of making it faster, and the confusion about this causes a great deal of wasted effort. An asynchronous function returns as soon as it reaches something it cannot complete immediately, handing the caller a promise or a task, and resumes later when the result is available. The program continues meanwhile. That means the concurrency is achieved by interleaving — many operations in flight, one thread — rather than by parallelism — many operations at the same instant on many cores. And in a language whose execution is single-threaded, it cannot make CPU-bound work faster at all, because nothing runs in parallel. What it does is enormous for I/O-bound work: a thousand requests, each waiting a tenth of a second, take a tenth of a second in total rather than a hundred, because the waiting is interleaved instead of serialised. That is the entire case for it and the limit of it. Then the cost, which is the reason it is not simply better. Code becomes non-linear to read. A function containing an await splits into before and after, and understanding what happens between them requires understanding what else ran in the meantime — which is a real cost paid by every reader. Errors change shape, because an exception thrown inside an asynchronous function does not propagate to the caller the way it does synchronously; it becomes a rejected promise, and if nobody handles it, it surfaces as an unhandled rejection rather than at the line that caused it. Stack traces are less useful, because the frames between the two halves are gone. And you cannot await inside a synchronous function, which forces every function that touches an asynchronous operation to be asynchronous, and that propagation reaches further than you expect — a small helper somewhere in the middle of a call chain becomes a promise-returning function and every one of its callers must change.

Then the mistakes, and each is the same mistake in a different form. Blocking inside asynchronous code. A synchronous sleep or a synchronous file read or a synchronous CPU-heavy computation inside a task blocks the entire loop, so nothing else runs, and the symptom is that the whole program freezes rather than one operation being slow — and the fix is to move the blocking work to a thread or a process pool. Awaiting in a loop where the work is independent, which serialises operations that could have run together, and the correct shape is to start them all and await the group, because the whole point of the model is that waiting is free. Forgetting to await, which yields a promise rather than a value and is the object-promise bug the front-end chapter described. Forgetting to handle a failure, where one failed operation leaves the others running and the caller believes everything succeeded. And unstructured concurrency, where a task started and not awaited keeps running after the code that started it has moved on — which is a leak rather than a bug, and the reason the discipline of scoping tasks to the operation that created them is worth having even when the language does not require it.

/* A way of structuring a program, not a way of making it faster. */

  handsBack: 'a promise or a task', and: 'resumes later when the result is available',

  concurrencyIs: 'INTERLEAVING - many operations in flight, one thread',
  parallelismIs: 'MANY OPERATIONS AT THE SAME INSTANT on many cores',

24 · Capstone Project & Career Launch

Capstone Project and Career Launch is how everything you learned becomes evidence for employers. The capstone ties every layer together into one deep project you can present, and portfolio standards such as READMEs, CI health, and honest history signal quality to reviewers. Then the interview playbook turns your experience into DSA screeners, STAR stories, and system design answers, followed by habits for growing forever.

24.1 The capstone that proves everything24.2 Portfolio standards that open doors24.3 The interview playbook24.4 Keep growing forever

Everything you’ve learned is proven to the world — and to yourself — by building, and by your portfolio. This chapter is the plan for the capstone that becomes your resume’s centrepiece, plus the real-world rules of getting hired without prior experience.

24.1 The capstone that proves everything

The capstone should be one project that touches every layer, database, API, frontend, deployment, and tests, built deeply rather than a set of half-finished screens. Plan it in weekly slices with a tested vertical slice each week, finish one core flow brilliantly, and deploy it live so you can show real screens with real data. One complete flow done well outweighs many partially built features.

Pick a project that touches every layer: a web app with authentication, a relational DB, REST API, async background jobs, tests, Docker, CI, and a live deployment. One classic that does: "Project tracker (Trello-like)". But follow the recipe, not the topic:

  1. Scope ruthlessly. One core flow done brilliantly > five half-broken screens. Start with "user + auth + boards + lists + cards".
  2. Design first: ERD, API routes table, wireframes — even rough sketches count (Ch. 15 docs habit).
  3. Sprint in 1-week slices. Each week ends with something running (Ch. 15.2).
  4. Tests on the tierpyramid: unit for logic, integration for the API+DB (Ch. 16).
  5. Ship the whole thing in Docker + CI + a free PaaS URL (Ch. 22).
  6. Write the README like a product one: demo GIF/screenshot, architecture diagram, how to run, tests, and what you’d do with 10× more users (Ch. 21 thinking).

Choosing what to build, and the scope that makes it finishable

The capstone fails on scope far more often than on ability, and the failure has a shape: the person picks something whose difficult part is the part they cannot yet do. Pick a problem you actually have. Not a hypothetical one — a real annoyance, something that currently costs you thirty minutes a week, because a real problem gives you a user, which tells you what matters and which is the single strongest predictor of whether the finished thing is good. Choose the scope so the first version is embarrassingly small. One feature, one screen, one data source, no polish. The reason is not that small is better; it is that a first version you finish teaches you four things that a large version you abandon teaches you none: what it is to debug your own unfinished thing, what it feels like to be three days into a problem, how to read documentation for an unfamiliar library, and what you should have built differently — and only the fourth is available at the end, so it must be reachable. Then write down what version one is before writing any code, in a list short enough to finish, because the list is what stops the second week from becoming a redesign. And decide the boring questions on day one: where the data lives, how it is deployed, who will run it, and what happens when the free tier you are using changes its terms — because these are not the interesting part and they are what actually determines whether the project exists in six months.

Then what building it teaches, and this is the content of the chapter stated as a list of skills the project will demand whether or not you plan them. Requirements, by having to write down what it does — you will discover you cannot describe a feature until you try, and the second draft is always shorter. Data modelling, by having to store something — the first schema is always wrong in a way you could not have predicted. Interfaces, by having something other than yourself use it. Error handling, by having a thing fail that you did not expect — and this is the skill most projects never reach, which is why most demos fail in front of a user and never in front of a test. Deployment, by having it exist somewhere other than your laptop. Reading code you did not write, by adding a dependency — and this is the one most projects skip and the one that takes the longest. Writing tests, once you have something worth protecting. And getting feedback, by showing it to one person and watching them use it — which will tell you in ten minutes what a month of your own testing could not, because you cannot see a problem you have been inside for a month. Then the review questions, which turn a finished project into evidence. What broke and what did you not notice? What did you cut, and would you have been wrong to? If you had a week, what would you change first? And what does it do when the dependency you rely on disappears?

What to build with, and the shape of a defensible scope

What makes a capstone work is that the interesting part is not the hard part of the domain. If you build a collaborative editor you will spend the project on conflict resolution and race conditions and never reach deployment, which is the thing that teaches you the most. Pick a domain that is boring at its core and interesting at its edges. A bookmarking tool has trivial core logic and interesting edges: authentication, list management, sharing, offline behaviour. A recipe manager has none of the distributed-systems difficulty and all of the data-modelling difficulty, which is what most people actually need. A tool that processes a folder of files has one interesting question — what happens when it fails halfway — and that question is the one worth answering. Then pick a data shape that is not uniform, because a uniform table teaches nothing and every real system has one table that is a little awkward. Make one part of the system have a rule that is not obvious, — a scoring formula, a permission model, a scheduling constraint — because that is where you find out whether you can work out what you meant. And make it have at least one user who is not you, because the difference between what you built and what somebody needed is the difference between a project and a product, and you can only learn it by watching. Then the defensible scope, which is a short list you can finish and a longer list you will not. The version-one list should contain: one real use, one user who is not you, one deployment, one external dependency, one thing that can fail, one thing that takes time, and a test suite for the part with the rules. Everything else is version two. And the discipline that makes the scope hold: write the version-two list before you start, because the features you will think of at 11pm in week three are exactly the ones you did not plan and will not finish, and a written list makes them a decision rather than a temptation.

Then the four things to do during the build, and they are the things that separate a project you can talk about from one you cannot. Keep a work log, dated, and it should be three lines a day: what you did, what went wrong, and what you are doing next. This is the single highest-value artefact in the project and it costs five minutes a day, because it is the raw material for every interview story and reconstructing it three months later is impossible. Record the bugs properly — the symptom, what you assumed, what was actually true, and how you found out — because the story of a good bug hunt is worth more than the story of a feature, and because writing it down while it is happening is the only time the details are accurate. Commit at the end of each working session with a message describing what works, because that produces the history that demonstrates you worked steadily rather than in threepanic bursts at the end. And write the readme as you go, not at the end, because the readme is where you discover what the project does not yet do, and writing it at the end means writing what you wish it did. Then what the capstone is worth at the end, which is larger than the application. You will have a working thing, which is worth more than three abandoned ones. You will have a story about a real bug, which is what every interview asks for. You will have a data model, which you can defend. You will have deployed and maintained something, which is the thing most portfolios cannot demonstrate. And you will know whether you like this, which is worth more than any amount of deciding.
