24.2 Portfolio standards that open doors

Portfolio quality signals open doors: three deeply done projects beat a dozen shallow ones. Senior reviewers look at honest READMEs that explain what each project does, its architecture, screenshots, and how to run it, at green CI on the repository, and at a commit history that reads like real engineering rather than one giant dump. Curate a few projects where you can defend every decision.

  • Three projects, deeply done — one you’re proud of reading, one showing algorithms/DSA, one showing full-stack + ops. Depth beats breadth.
  • Quality signals: READMEs with architecture diagrams, CI green badges, tests visible, sensible commit history (Ch. 6), dependencies current.
  • Clean code review: re-read your own repo six months later — every logging/comment/name decision reveals itself. Refactor it; then it’s genuinely yours.

    • What a portfolio is actually for

    A portfolio exists to answer one question before it is asked, and everything about it should follow from that question: can this person build something that works? Not what they know — what they have finished. The consequence is that a portfolio is not a gallery of half-projects and it is not a list of technologies; it is evidence, and evidence has to be checkable. Then what one project needs, and the list is short because what matters is a small number of things done properly rather than a large number done partially. It runs. Somebody, not you, can start it and see it work, from the instructions in the readme, without asking you anything. That is the entire bar and most projects fail it. The readme is the product. A stranger decides whether this is real work based on whether they understand what it is, why it exists, and how to run it — in the first thirty seconds — and a project whose readme is a paragraph and a screenshot is a project whose quality is in doubt. The history is the evidence. Commit messages, dates, branches and pull requests are the only record of how you worked rather than only what you produced, and a repository with one enormous initial commit answers a question about you that an interviewer did not intend to ask. It has tests, because a project without them announces that verification was not part of the work. It has no secrets and no credentials, and this is not only a security point: a repository whose history contains a key tells a reader that you have shipped something you should not have. And it explains what it does not do, because a project that names its own limitations reads as considered rather than unfinished.

    Then the mistakes, which are consistent and worth naming together. Too many projects, none finished. Fourteen repositories with no releases says you start things; two with releases says you finish them, and two is a better portfolio. Tutorials copied as projects. A tutorial project is recognisable — it has the tutorial's structure, the tutorial's naming, and the tutorial's bugs — and one of them does more harm than having none. Only technology, no problem. "Built with React and PostgreSQL" is a list of nouns; "a tool that lets a restaurant manager stop taking phone bookings by hand" is a description of something that had a user. No readme. No licence. A commit history that is one commit, which removes the only continuous record of your work. And dead projects left running. A deployment from three years ago with a vulnerability in it is a liability you published, and a portfolio is a public thing. Then the two practices that make a portfolio accumulate rather than rot. Build in public as you go, which is a mild social obligation and creates a record that does not have to be reconstructed at the end. And go back and improve an old project every few months, because a commit dated today on a project from two years ago demonstrates that you still read your own code and that you have learned something since — which is the specific thing a portfolio cannot otherwise show.

  notThese: ['what they KNOW', 'a gallery of half-projects', 'a list of technologies'],
  is: 'EVIDENCE, and evidence has to be CHECKABLE',
};

    worseThanNone: 'one of them does MORE HARM than having none' },
  { m: 'only TECHNOLOGY, no PROBLEM',
    list: 'built with React and PostgreSQL is a LIST OF NOUNS',
    better: 'a tool that lets a restaurant manager stop taking phone bookings by hand is a DESCRIPTION OF SOMETHING THAT HAD A USER' },
  { m: 'no README' },
  { m: 'no LICENCE' },
  { m: 'a COMMIT HISTORY that is one commit', removes: 'the only CONTINUOUS RECORD of your work' },
  { m: 'DEAD PROJECTS left running',
    detail: 'a deployment from three years ago with a vulnerability in it is a LIABILITY YOU PUBLISHED',
    and: 'a portfolio is a PUBLIC THING' },
];

/* Practices that make it ACCUMULATE rather than rot. */
const PRACTICES = [
  { p: 'BUILD IN PUBLIC AS YOU GO', isA: 'mild social obligation',
    gain: 'creates a record that does not have to be RECONSTRUCTED at the end' },
  { p: 'GO BACK AND IMPROVE AN OLD PROJECT every few months',
    demonstrates: ['that you still READ YOUR OWN CODE', 'that you have LEARNED SOMETHING SINCE'],
    isThe: 'specific thing a portfolio CANNOT OTHERWISE SHOW' },
];

    Choosing, and the mechanics of the one that carries the interview

    Which project you put first matters more than how many you have, and the criterion is not quality — it is whether it demonstrates something the interviewer is trying to find out. A project that shows you can ship, read code, handle failure and think about users answers more questions than two that show you can implement an algorithm. So the practical procedure is: list the capabilities you want demonstrated, one per line — read code you did not write, handle a real failure, ship something other people use, design a data model, measure something, write tests. Then choose the project that demonstrates the most of them, and be honest about whether any project does. If you have not deployed anything, that is the gap to close, and it is a bigger gap than not having built anything difficult. And make the first project one you can talk about for five minutes without notes, because a project whose story you cannot recall is not usable in an interview, however good it is. Then what a five-minute story contains, because "I built an app" is not a story and the structure is worth having. What problem it solved and whose it was — two sentences, and "whose it was" is the sentence that demonstrates you thought about a user. What was hard about it, specifically, and the best answers name something real: a race condition, a data model that turned out wrong, an N-plus-one query found under load, a dependency that changed its API. What you did not know and how you found out, which demonstrates the debugging loop. What you would do differently, which demonstrates judgement rather than pride, and which is the sentence experienced interviewers listen for hardest. And what you would do next if you had a week, which demonstrates that you still think about it.

    Then the presentation, and the details that make a repository readable to a stranger in thirty seconds. Put the screenshot and the one-line description at the top of the readme, because that is what gets read. Include a screenshot or two — not because it looks good but because a reader who has never seen the project cannot picture what it does from a description alone. Say how to run it in copyable steps, including the prerequisite versions, because "npm install then npm start" is not sufficient and the versions are the part people get stuck on. Link to something live, because a live deployment is the single strongest signal available and it also proves the thing works. Keep the readme short enough to read, — a thousand words is too long, and the sections that earn their space are what it is, how to run it, and one screenshot. And include a licence, which signals that you understand the legal side of publishing code and takes one line. Finally, the maintenance question, and it is the one that decides whether the portfolio is an asset or a liability. Everything public is a permanent commitment. A repository with a vulnerability in it, a demo with expired credentials, a dependency that no longer installs — these are published surface, and they are found, not merely visited. So the maintenance rule is short: keep at most three projects actively maintained, and archive the rest honestly — an archived repository with a note saying "no longer maintained, here is what it did" reads as considered, while a dead repository that silently stopped working in 2021 reads as abandonment.

    /* Which project goes first. */
const FIRST = {
  criterion: 'not QUALITY - it is whether it DEMONSTRATES something the interviewer is trying to find out',
  demonstrates: ['that you can SHIP', 'read code you did not write', 'handle a REAL FAILURE', 'think about users'],
  and: 'answers more questions than two that show you can implement an algorithm',
  procedure: [
    { s: 'LIST THE CAPABILITIES you want demonstrated, one per line',
      instances: ['read code you did not write', 'handle a real failure', 'ship something other people use',
        'design a data model', 'measure something', 'write tests'],

    { s: 'choose the project that demonstrates the MOST OF THEM',
      honestQuestion: 'whether ANY PROJECT DOES',
      and: 'if you have not DEPLOYED ANYTHING, that is the GAP TO CLOSE',
      biggerThan: 'not having built anything difficult',
    },
    { s: 'make the first project one you can talk about for FIVE MINUTES WITHOUT NOTES',
      why: 'a project whose story you CANNOT RECALL is not usable in an interview, however good it is',

  ],
};

/* What a five-minute story contains. */
const STORY = [

24.3 The interview playbook

Interviews are a rehearsed skill, not a personality test. Practice data structure and algorithm screeners with a repeatable method, state the problem, test edge cases, discuss complexity, code, then test, prepare STAR stories for behavioral questions, and practice system design with the scaling toolbox. A defined process makes interviews less random and your preparation more effective.

  • DSA screeners (big tech style): 2–4 problems at Ch. 8–9 level. The proven recipe: restate the problem → ask edge cases → brute-force → optimise while narrating → code clean → test by hand. Practise timed, and keep a file of the problems you missed to repeat.
  • Behavioural / STAR: Situation → Task → Action → Result. Prepare 5 stories: a bug hunt, a conflict, a failure, a leadership moment, an estimate that was wrong. Tell the result with numbers ("p95 dropped from 3 s to 200 ms").
  • System design (advanced roles): Ch. 21 recipe with the numbers shown out loud.
  • Your projects ARE senior-level evidence when you can talk hours about design trade-offs, not just features.

    • What an algorithm interview actually measures

    An algorithm interview is not primarily a test of algorithm knowledge, and preparing for it as though it were is the single most common mistake. It measures how you think when you do not know the answer. The interviewer has seen a hundred correct solutions to the same problem; what they are evaluating is whether you can get from a blank page to a working solution while narrating your reasoning — because that is a proxy for how you will handle a problem in six months that nobody has prepared you for. The consequence is that the process matters more than the answer: restate the problem, ask about the constraints, produce a brute-force solution, then improve it. That sequence is not a warm-up, it is the actual demonstration. The restatement shows you read the question. The constraints — how large, how fast, what shape — determine the answer, and a candidate who asks for them before writing anything is a candidate who will produce something appropriate. The brute force shows you can solve it at all, which is the thing most important to establish because a candidate who cannot get a working solution and then optimises will produce a fast wrong answer. And the improvement step is where the interview actually lives.

    Then what to prepare, which is narrower than the internet suggests. The core set is small: two-sum with a hash map, binary search on a sorted array, merge sort or quicksort, a linked-list reversal, a stack-valid-brackets check, two pointers on a sorted array, sliding window for an array or a string, a breadth-first and a depth-first search over a tree or a graph, and dynamic programming on one or two classic recurrences. That is enough to cover most interviews, because the questions are variations on those shapes rather than new problems. Know the complexity of each and be able to say it without thinking, because the ability to state why a solution is linear rather than quadratic is what demonstrates understanding, and the ability to state it is what the interviewer is checking. Be able to write working code, because "explaining" your approach is not the same as being asked to produce it, and a candidate who narrates an algorithm fluently and cannot write it has demonstrated that the fluency was memorised. Be able to trace your own code by hand, because the interviewer will ask you to walk through it and because a bug in your own logic found while tracing is a good thing that happened in the interview rather than after it.

    Then the practical process, and the advice that matters most is about the failure mode rather than the technique. Think aloud the whole time, because a silent ten minutes followed by a correct answer reads as luck, and a narrated ten minutes followed by a wrong answer reads as a person who can be followed and helped — and the second is what they are looking for. When stuck, say what you are stuck on and ask a specific question; "I am not sure" is acceptable and silence is not. Do not apologise for thinking slowly. If you get it wrong, diagnose it out loud, which is a separate skill and a common failure: a candidate who realises their approach is wrong and silently starts again has learned nothing, and one who says "this will fail on the empty case because..." has demonstrated exactly the thinking the interview is for. And ask questions about the problem when they are genuinely unclear, because a real engineer does, and because an interview is partly an assessment of whether you will interrupt a colleague. Then the thing worth saying last: the interview is a sample. It is one conversation about one problem on one day, and treating it as a verdict produces more anxiety than it is worth and does not improve your ability to build — which is the thing the sample was supposed to predict.

    /* What it actually measures. */
const MEASURES = {
  isNot: 'primarily a test of ALGORITHM KNOWLEDGE',
  is: 'how you THINK WHEN YOU DO NOT KNOW THE ANSWER',
  why: ['the interviewer has seen a HUNDRED CORRECT SOLUTIONS to the same problem',
    'what they are evaluating is whether you can get from a BLANK PAGE to a WORKING SOLUTION while NARRATING YOUR REASONING',
    'because that is a PROXY for how you will handle a problem in six months that nobody has prepared you for'],
  consequence: 'the PROCESS matters more than the answer',

};

/* The failure mode that matters most. */
const PROCESS = [
  { p: 'THINK ALOUD THE WHOLE TIME',
    silentThenCorrect: 'reads as LUCK', narratedThenWrong: 'reads as a person WHO CAN BE FOLLOWED AND HELPED',
    and: 'the second is what they are looking for' },
  { p: 'when stuck, SAY WHAT YOU ARE STUCK ON and ask a SPECIFIC QUESTION',
    note: 'I am not sure is ACCEPTABLE and silence is not' },
  { p: 'do NOT APOLOGISE for thinking slowly' },
  { p: 'if you get it wrong, DIAGNOSE IT OUT LOUD', isASeparateSkill: true,
    commonFailure: 'a candidate who realises their approach is wrong and SILENTLY STARTS AGAIN has learned nothing',

  { p: 'ask questions when they are GENUINELY UNCLEAR',
    because: 'a real engineer does, and because an interview is partly an assessment of whether you WILL INTERRUPT A COLLEAGUE' },

const THE_LAST_THING = 'the interview is a SAMPLE - one conversation about one problem on one day - and treating it as a VERDICT produces more anxiety than it is worth and DOES NOT IMPROVE your ability to build, which is the thing the sample was supposed to predict';

    A worked example, and what the interviewer was watching

    Two-sum, because it is the cleanest illustration of the whole sequence. The problem: given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of the two that add up to it. Restate and ask: does a solution exist or may the answer be empty? Are there negative numbers? Are the indices guaranteed distinct? Each answer changes the code, and asking is what tells the interviewer you know they matter. Brute force: a nested loop over every pair, comparing the sum — correct, obviously, O(n²). Say its complexity out loud. Improve: notice that for each element you are asking "have I already seen its complement?". That is a lookup, and a hash table is a constant-time lookup. So: keep a map from value to index, walk the array once, and for each element look up target - value; if it is present, return the pair; otherwise record the current value and index and continue. O(n) time, O(n) space — and the space cost is worth naming, because the trade is time for memory and the interviewer will notice whether you noticed. Now what the interviewer was actually watching, and this is the part the exercise does not say. Did the constraints change the answer? A candidate who wrote the hash version immediately and never asked whether duplicates or negatives were possible has demonstrated a solution and not a process. Did they produce something that worked before improving it? A candidate who describes the clever version without ever stating the brute force has skipped the part where they demonstrate they can solve the problem at all. Did they trace it? Running the hash version by hand on [2, 7, 11, 15] with target 9 — recording the map after each step — takes forty seconds and is where a bug in the logic would show, and it shows the interviewer that the candidate can debug their own reasoning, which is the transfer. And did they name the complexity without being asked? Not because it is required but because it distinguishes someone who understands the solution from someone who found it.

    /* The example. */
const TWO_SUM = {
  problem: 'given an array of integers and a target, return the INDICES of the two that add up to it',

  approach: ['keep a map from value to index', 'walk the array once',

    'otherwise record the current value and index'],

  andWorthNaming: 'the trade is TIME FOR MEMORY and the interviewer will notice whether you noticed',

/* What the interviewer was watching. */
const WATCHING = [
  { w: 'did the CONSTRAINTS CHANGE THE ANSWER',
    failure: 'a candidate who wrote the hash version IMMEDIATELY and never asked about duplicates or negatives has demonstrated A SOLUTION and not A PROCESS' },
  { w: 'did they produce something that WORKED before improving it',
    failure: 'a candidate who describes the clever version without ever stating the brute force has SKIPPED THE PART where they demonstrate they can solve the problem at all' },
  { w: 'did they TRACE IT',

    cost: 'forty seconds',

24.4 Keep growing forever

Software engineering is a compounding skill, so the degree or course is a start, not a finish. Read other people’s code, write what you learn down, specialize deliberately in one direction, and teach what you know to cement it. Publish small things, track what you build, and let curiosity set the roadmap.

  • Read other people’s code: any open-source project you use. Fork, read one file, fix a typo PR, then a real bug. Unbeatable education.
  • Write — blog posts and docs force clear thinking (Ch. 19.1 applies to prose too).
  • Specialise deliberately: after the degree, choose two depth areas, e.g. distributed systems + Go, or ML + Python, or security + cloud.
  • Teach and mentee: tutoring a learner 6 chapters behind you is the highest-yield way to solidify chapters 1–9.

Learning as a system, and the two loops that matter

The thing that separates people who are getting better from people who are not is not hours and it is not courses. It is the loop between doing and finding out what you did not know. Programming is unusual in how little you can tell about your own understanding from having written working code — a person can copy an answer, produce a program that runs, and learn almost nothing, and there is no test for that. The practical substitute is a practice, and the best-known one is explaining something to somebody else — because the places where your explanation becomes vague are exactly the places where your understanding is vague, and you cannot be vague when someone is asking. Second is being deliberately wrong: predicting what a piece of code does before running it, and being wrong often enough that you start paying attention. A programmer who never predicts is a programmer who is watching the computer rather than reading the code, and watching is how you develop the illusion of understanding without the substance. Then what to learn and in what order, and the order matters more than the list. The language before the framework, because a framework hides what it is doing and you cannot debug what you cannot see. The fundamentals before the tooling, because tooling is a productivity multiplier and multiplying zero gives zero. One deep project before many shallow ones, because a project that runs is the only thing that teaches the parts that tutorials omit: what it feels like to be stuck for an afternoon, how to find something you did not know was missing, and how to read documentation under pressure. And writing code that nobody asked for, because the things you choose to build are the things you understand.

Then what to do when stuck, because this is the skill the course is actually for and it has a procedure. Read the error, all of it, and read the line number. Most wasted debugging time is not spent not looking — it is spent looking at the wrong line, because a traceback points at the line where the failure surfaced and the defect is frequently earlier. Reduce it. A failing case you cannot reproduce is not debuggable, and the smallest input that fails is worth more than an hour of reading. Read the code rather than the assumptions, because the code is the only thing you actually know; every statement about what the code does is a hypothesis until you have read it. Explain what you expect, in writing, before you run it, because the difference between your prediction and the result is the bug, and writing it down means you cannot quietly revise your prediction. And then the escalation, which is a habit rather than a technique: when you have been stuck for twenty minutes, do something else, and come back — because the actual mechanism is that you stop holding the wrong model in your head long enough for the right one to surface, and twenty minutes of reading the same function is the opposite of what is needed.

The learning loop, and how to build one that survives contact with a job

Everything about learning well reduces to one loop, and the loop has a failure mode that most people discover only when it is too late. Read, then do, then explain. Reading a chapter produces the feeling of understanding and almost none of the substance, because reading is passive and recognition is not retrieval — you can recognise a correct answer and be entirely unable to produce one. Doing produces the substance and reveals precisely which parts you did not understand, because the point where your code does not do what you expected is the point where your model was wrong. And explaining converts that realisation into something you can use, because you cannot give a muddled explanation of something you actually understand. The loop's failure mode is doing without explaining, which feels productive and produces a person who can write code they do not understand — which is a perfectly good way to be employed and a terrible way to progress, and it is the state most people are in after a few years of work without consciously addressing it. Then what to learn is a function of where you are, and the four categories are worth separating because they are learned differently. Concepts you can look up — a function's signature, a protocol's fields, a language's syntax — do not need study, they need retrieval, and looking them up costs thirty seconds. Concepts you can only learn by doing — what a race condition is, why a cache goes stale, how to structure a migration — need repetition with feedback, and no amount of reading produces them. Judgement you cannot acquire from a book — when to cache, when to denormalise, when a function is too long, whether a design will survive its next change — can only come from seeing many examples and from being corrected, and the correction is the mechanism. And the meta-skill of learning how to learn, which is knowing what kind of thing you are trying to learn and therefore what to do about it.

Then how to keep learning while employed, because the environment actively works against it and the counter-measures are specific. Work deliberately rather than conveniently: when a task arrives that you cannot do, that is the most valuable thing available to you, and taking it is a deliberate choice that is easy to decline accidentally. Read code you did not write, on purpose, because it is the only source of how things are actually done and it is the only material that is not written to teach. Write things down as you learn them, because a note written this week is worth more than a note written in a year from memory, and the writing is what forces the precision. Pick up something outside your current stack deliberately — a language you would never use in work, a tool from a domain you do not work in — because the transferable ideas come from outside the domain, and the specific knowledge does not transfer at all. Have a project that is yours, where nobody is paying you and therefore nobody is telling you what to do, and where the only constraint is your own interest — because interest is the only renewable fuel and it is not supplied by a project plan. And take the review seriously as a learning opportunity, because a review is a person telling you precisely where your mental model diverges from the code, which is the most valuable feedback available and is routinely received as an insult.

/* The loop and its failure mode. */
const LOOP = {
  steps: ['READ', 'DO', 'EXPLAIN'],
  whyReadingFails: 'reading is PASSIVE and RECOGNITION IS NOT RETRIEVAL - you can recognise a correct answer and be entirely unable to produce one',
  whyDoingFails: 'doing produces the substance and REVEALS PRECISELY WHICH PARTS you did not understand',
  whyExplainingWorks: 'you cannot give a MUDDLED EXPLANATION of something you actually understand',
  failureMode: 'DOING WITHOUT EXPLAINING',
  whatThatProduces: 'a person who can write code they DO NOT UNDERSTAND',
  andThatIs: 'a perfectly good way to be employed and a TERRIBLE WAY TO PROGRESS',
  stateAfterAYears: 'most people are in it without consciously addressing it',
};

25 · Theory of Computation & Formal Languages

Computability theory studies the boundaries of what algorithms can do: which problems are decidable, how efficiently they can be solved, and under which formal model. It explains the limits of regular expressions, why compilers need a richer formalism, and why the halting problem makes certain questions provably unanswerable. Practically, it guides tool choice, since matching a problem’s needed expressive power to the right grammar class or automaton tells you whether a regex, a context-free parser, or full Turing power is required.

25.1 Why abstract machines25.2 Finite automata and regular expressions — the same thing25.3 Turing machines and the halting problem25.4 Complexity classes: P, NP, and why the P≠NP question matters

The question this field answers is the deepest in all of computer science: what can computers fundamentally compute, how fast, and what can they never do at all? A bachelor’s CS degree teaches it as a full course; it also quietly explains why regex works, why compilers exist, and why your "solve everything" hack can’t exist.

25.1 Why abstract machines

Abstract machines such as finite automata, pushdown automata, and Turing machines reduce computation to its essential moving parts so that precise proofs become possible. The Chomsky hierarchy orders their grammars from regular to recursively enumerable, showing step by step what each level can and cannot compute. Real software maps onto this hierarchy, for example a lexer reads a regular language and a parser reads a context-free one, which defines which algorithms will succeed on your input.

We study simplified machines (automata) because their simplicity makes proofs possible. Each machine defines a language — the set of strings it accepts. The hierarchy between machines is the Chomsky hierarchy, and real software releases one lifetime inside it:

Why the question exists, and what a proof is

Computability asks which problems can be solved by a program at all, and the question became answerable only once "program" was defined precisely enough to argue about. That was Turing's contribution: a formal model of computation simple enough to reason about and general enough to represent any actual machine. The model is a tape read left to right with a finite set of states and a lookup table, and the power comes from the model's simplicity — you can simulate the rules on paper, so you can prove things about what they can and cannot do. And then the question, asked in 1936 and unanswered since: is there a program that decides, for any program and input, whether that program will ever finish? The answer is no, and the proof is short, and the argument is worth understanding because it is the template for a whole family of results. Suppose such a program exists. Call it H. Now build a program G that does this: run H on its own source code; if H says "halts", loop forever; if H says "does not halt", stop. Now run G on G. If H says G halts, then G loops, so it did not halt — contradiction. If H says it does not halt, then G stops, so it did halt — contradiction. Either answer is wrong, so H cannot exist. That is the whole proof, and its structure is the mechanism: a supposed decider is turned into a program that feeds itself to the decider and does the opposite of what it is told.

Then what follows, and this is the part that changes how you think. Some problems are provably impossible, and this is not a limitation of the particular machine or the particular language — it is a property of computation itself, and moving to a faster computer or a different language does not help, because those are all programs. Undecidability is not the same as difficulty. There is a difference between a problem no program can ever solve and a problem no program can solve quickly, and the second is the only one that practical work involves — but knowing the first exists tells you that some improvements are impossible in principle, which is a genuine constraint on what a design can achieve. Reducibility is the working tool. To show a problem is hard you show that solving it would solve a known-hard problem; to show a problem is easy you show it reduces to a known-easy one. And the decidable-but-slow class is where every practical question lives — halting is not decidable, sorting a list certainly is, and the entire field of complexity is about which decidable problems are also fast.

Classifying a problem, and what each classification is good for

Before any theory helps, a problem has to be classified, and the classification tells you what to expect. Decidable versus undecidable: is there an algorithm at all? If not, stop — no amount of effort helps and this is the one classification that ends a project. Decidable problems then split by cost: how does the runtime grow with input size? Constant, logarithmic, linear, polynomial of some degree, exponential, factorial. The split matters because these behave completely differently: a polynomial is viable and an exponential is not, whatever the constant factor, and the boundary between them is the most consequential line in all of computing. Within polynomial, is the worst case acceptable? A quadratic algorithm on a thousand items is four hundred thousand operations and fine; on ten million items it is fifty trillion and it is not. So the question is never "is this polynomial" but "is this polynomial for the size of the input we actually have". And within the impractical, is it decidable but hard, or undecidable? A problem can be decidable and completely intractable — the travelling salesman on a large graph, an exact scheduling optimum — and these are the cases where approximation is the right answer and exactness is a waste of effort nobody asked for.

Then what each classification licenses you to do, because this is the practical content. Undecidable: you are looking for something that does not exist. The productive moves are to change the problem — restrict it so a solution is findable — or to accept an approximation, and both are legitimate engineering rather than defeat, because the question is rarely "compute the exact answer" and is almost always "compute an answer good enough for a decision". Exponential: same, more firmly, plus the mechanical wins — a better algorithm, a better data structure, a smaller input, a bounded search. Polynomial but slow: the best situation, because this is a constant-factor problem and constant factors are what optimisation is for — a better data structure, a cache, parallelism, vectorisation. Polynomial and fast: you are done thinking about complexity and should be thinking about correctness. Then the three questions to ask about any problem before designing a solution, and they are the ones that save the most time. What is the actual input size? Not the theoretical one — the one that will exist in production, and it is usually larger than the example and smaller than the worst case. How many times will this run? A quadratic algorithm that runs once is a better plan than a linear algorithm that runs a hundred thousand times, and this is the question that most often inverts the answer. And what does "correct" require? An exact answer, an answer within a tolerance, or an answer that is probably right — because an approximate algorithm is the correct answer to a different question and the honest thing is to decide which question you have.

25.2 Finite automata and regular expressions — the same thing

A deterministic finite automaton recognizes exactly the same set of strings as a regular expression, so the two are interchangeable representations of the regular languages. Practically, you can convert between them, and tools such as grep, lex, and most validating regex engines operate precisely at this expressive level. Recognizing the equivalence tells you when regex is the right tool and when it never can be, because matching balanced parentheses or nested structures requires a stronger model.

A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) walks an input string left to right, holding one of a finite set of states, changing state per character; it accepts if it ends in an accepting state. This IS regex: the pattern a(b|c)* is exactly a state machine that accepts "a", "ab", "abc", "accb", …

# Model a DFA in code: states, transitions, accept states
transitions = {
    "S0": {"a": "S1"},
    "S1": {"b": "S1", "c": "S1"},     # loop on b and c
}
accept = {"S1"}                        # accept S1

def accepts(transitions, start, accept, word):
    state = start
    for ch in word:
        if ch not in transitions[state]:
            return False               # no transition -> reject
        state = transitions[state][ch]
    return state in accept

print(accepts(transitions, "S0", accept, "abccb"))   # True  (matches a(b|c)*)
print(accepts(transitions, "S0", accept, "ba"))      # False

This Python model of a DFA walks a word state-by-state and accepts only if it ends in an accepting state, which is exactly what the regular expression a(b|c)* describes.

The distinction, and the mechanical test that separates them

A regular expression describes a language with no memory, and the consequence is a precise limitation that is worth stating as a rule you can apply. A regular expression cannot count without bounds, and cannot match anything requiring nesting. Balanced parentheses, balanced brackets, well-formed XML, valid nested JSON — all require remembering how many openings are outstanding, which requires unbounded memory, and a finite automaton has none. The mechanical test is: can you decide the answer by looking at each character once, in order, without remembering anything about earlier characters? If yes, a regular expression is probably the right tool. If the answer requires knowing what is outstanding — how deep we are, whether the thing we are inside has been closed, whether an opening has been matched — then it requires a stack and a regular expression is the wrong tool entirely. That test covers a surprising number of cases: ^d{3}-d{4}$ for a phone number is regular, while "is this HTML well-formed" is not, and the difference is not size or difficulty but the memory requirement.

Then the hierarchy, which gives you the right tool rather than merely ruling out the wrong one. Regular expressions and finite automata match strings with no internal structure: a pattern, an identifier, a date, a log level, a URL of fixed shape. Pushdown automata and context-free grammars add a stack, which is exactly enough for nesting: balanced brackets, arithmetic with parentheses, nested XML, a programming language's expressions, JSON. Turing machines add unbounded memory in both directions, which is what makes them general. And the practical translation, which is the part worth memorising: a regex handles a pattern, a stack handles a nesting, and a real parser handles a language. The second is exactly what a JSON or HTML parser does — it reads characters, pushes opening delimiters, pops on closing ones, and errors if the stack is wrong at the end — and it is why those parsers are stack-based and why a regex cannot replace them. Then the practical guidance, and the trap is the one the chapter's warning names. Do not use a regular expression to validate nested markup. A regex that attempts it will appear to work on your sample, fail on the third real document, and be expensive to fix, because matching backtracking over nested structures is pathological — the catastrophic backtracking the networking chapter described, at a scale determined by the input. And do not use a regex to parse a programming language, however small: the language has nesting, the regex will appear to work on the examples you tried, and the failure will be on valid input you did not try.

/* The rule, stated so it can be APPLIED. */

The regex-pumping lesson: regular languages can’t do nesting ("balanced parentheses") — the regex can’t "remember how many". Regular expressions in programming languages are regex-plus-extras; true balanced parsers need a stack, which is what your JSON/HTML parser actually uses. Reaching for regex on nested markup is the legendary wrong tool.

25.3 Turing machines and the halting problem

A Turing machine formalizes computing by rules: a finite control, an infinite tape, and a transition table that any real computer can simulate. It defines what it means for a problem to be computable at all. The halting problem then proves that no program can decide, for every program and input, whether it halts, which settles that some questions are undecidable regardless of hardware or cleverness.

A Turing machine = infinite tape + read/write head + state table. It’s humanity’s formal definition of "doing computation by following rules". Two outcomes shake the field:

  • Universal Turing machine: one machine can simulate any other (read the description on tape). That’s us: programs are data (Ch. 10.1) — "an interpreter" is a universal machine.
  • Halting problem (Turing, 1936): no program H(x) can decide whether program x halts for every input. Proof by contradiction: suppose H exists, build G that runs H on itself and loops iff H says it halts — paradox. Consequence: some things are provably impossible, and "will this ever finish?" is undecidable in general.

    • The Church-Turing thesis, and why it is the right model

    The thesis is that a sufficiently powerful model of computation can express every computation that any other model can express — equivalently, that there is a single notion of "computable" that does not depend on the machine. It does not say all models are equally powerful, and the difference is instructive: a stack automaton cannot match balanced parentheses, a finite automaton cannot count to unbounded length, and only machines with enough memory to hold arbitrarily much state reach the general case. What the thesis says is that once you have that memory, the details stop mattering — which is why a modern machine with a hardware multiplier is not more computable than Turing's tape machine, and why the decades of architectural progress have produced no new computable problems. Then the consequences, and each is a statement about programming practice rather than about mathematics. Anything computable is computable slowly. A Turing-complete language can do anything any language can, so "our language cannot do that" is almost never a fact about the language — it is a fact about a missing library, a missing extension, or a missing interface. Any algorithm can be simulated on any machine, so a problem that is slow on your language is slow because of constants and memory model, not because the algorithm is unavailable. And there is no general way to prove a program correct, which follows from halting undecidability and is the reason code review, testing and types exist — they are the practical substitutes for a proof that cannot be had.

    Then what the theory tells a practitioner, and the honest answer is less than people hope. It does not tell you which problems are hard. Computability is about possibility and complexity is about cost, and a problem can be trivially computable and hopelessly expensive — the travelling salesman is the canonical example, and it is computable by brute force on a small enough input. It does not give you an algorithm. Turing's contribution is a negative result: a proof that something cannot be done, which is valuable precisely because it is rare. It does not tell you how to divide a problem. That is design, and design is done by people noticing structure that the theory does not describe. And the useful practical reframe: theory tells you which walls exist, and engineering is about what you build given that. The practical consequences are four and they are concrete. Look for a library before an algorithm, because a proven implementation is worth more than your cleverness. Reduce to a known problem rather than solving from scratch, because the known problem is studied. Assume the answer is "yes, but slowly", and find out how slowly, because that number decides the design. And recognise impossibility when you see it — general program synthesis, deciding whether two programs are equivalent,

    What this means in practice

    Four practical consequences, and they are more useful than the theorem because each one tells you what to do differently. A missing capability is a missing library, not a missing language. Almost every time someone says a language "can't do that", the thing the language genuinely cannot do is spawning a process, calling a system call, or touching hardware — and all three are things the language can do through its standard library or a foreign-function interface. The honest list of things a high-level language cannot do directly is short: allocate arbitrary raw memory, execute an arbitrary instruction, and control the hardware — and all three have mechanisms, which is what a compiler and an operating system exist to provide. Different languages optimise for different constants. When a language is ten times slower, it is usually ten times slower at one thing and the same or faster at another, and the productive question is which. A primitive exists whenever the specification demands it. Every significant capability someone asks for eventually appears in some language, because the demand is real and there is a commercial reason to meet it. And memory is the resource that bounds everything. Unbounded memory is what makes the model general, so a real machine's finite memory is what makes the theory inconvenient — and every practical limit, from the recursion depth error to the out-of-memory failure to the stack overflow, is a memory limit expressed in a way you did not expect.

    Then how to think about the theory as a working tool, and the honest answer is that it is a tool for stopping rather than for building. It tells you which problems are worth attempting. If a problem requires unbounded search over an unbounded space with no structure to prune it, that is a signal to look for an approximation or a different formulation, and recognising it early saves weeks. It tells you which speedups are available. There are only two ways to make a program faster — do less work, or do the same work in less time — and everything in the rest of this course is a technique for one of those two, which is a genuinely clarifying way to think about performance. It tells you what lower bounds exist. Sorting cannot be faster than n log n comparisons, which means once you are there you should stop looking for something asymptotically better and start reducing constants, and knowing the bound is what tells you when to stop. And it tells you what is worth proving versus worth measuring. Whether an implementation is correct is a question for types, tests and review, not for theory; whether it is fast is a question for measurement. Then the discipline worth forming, which is the one that keeps theory useful rather than decorative: use theory to decide what to attempt, and measurement to decide what to keep. The failure mode on both sides is real — theory without measurement produces elegant programs nobody can run, and measurement without theory produces fast implementations of the wrong algorithm — and the combination is the whole discipline.

25.4 Complexity classes: P, NP, and why the P≠NP question matters

P contains problems solvable in polynomial time, while NP contains those whose solutions can be verified in polynomial time, and the P versus NP question asks whether the two classes are equal. Recognizing that a problem is NP-hard, such as by a polynomial-time reduction from a known NP-complete problem, tells you not to chase an exact efficient algorithm. In practice you then use heuristics, approximations, or parameterized algorithms instead.

  • P: solvable in polynomial time (sorting, shortest path, matching) — "fast", practical.
  • NP: solutions checkable in polynomial time (Sudoku, knapsack, TSP, SAT, 3-colouring). Whether P = NP is the open problem of mathematics (US$1M Millennium Prize).
  • NP-complete: the hardest problems in NP — every NP problem reduces to them. Find one hard instance, and thousands of other problems become easy too.

Why it’s not academic: your encryption’s entire security assumes factoring is hard (not in P). Every "find the best schedule / best route / best cut" for real businesses is NP-hard, so engineers ship approximations and heuristics (greedy, 2-approximations, simulated annealing) and prove error bounds. Recognising "this is NP-hard" saves months of chasing an exact solver.

The problem, and what the notation actually says

P versus NP is the question of whether every problem whose solution can be verified quickly can also be found quickly. P is the class of problems solvable in polynomial time — the ones where the runtime grows as a power of the input size, so doubling the input at most doubles the work by a constant factor, and there is a fixed practical ceiling. NP is the class whose solutions can be verified in polynomial time — checking a proposed certificate is fast, but finding one may not be. The notation is misleading in a way worth correcting once: NP does not mean non-polynomial; it means non-deterministic polynomial, a model of computation that guesses the answer and then verifies in polynomial time, and the honest restatement is that NP is the class of problems where a correct answer is easy to check. NP-hard means at least as hard as every problem in NP — not that it is itself in NP, and a problem can be NP-hard and not be in NP at all. And NP-complete means NP-hard and in NP: if you find a fast algorithm for one NP-complete problem, you have one for all of them, which is why the class is defined by a handful of specific problems rather than a general theory.

Then why the question matters and what the current position is. The practical position: NP-completeness is a practical warning. You do not need to know whether P equals NP to act — an NP-complete problem found in a real system means the formulation is wrong, or the constraint is missing, or an approximation is required, and finding that out is worth doing immediately. The interesting problems are almost all NP-hard. Scheduling, routing, packing, partitioning, constraint satisfaction, most of combinatorial optimisation — and real systems solve them with heuristics, approximations, and small inputs, not exact algorithms. Exact algorithms are exponential and only viable on small inputs, which is why a brute-force search that is fine for ten items is hopeless for ten thousand, and why the exponential-factor improvements everyone is excited about are worth exactly what the name says: they take the practical range from ten to twelve. And the honest note on whether it will be solved: most researchers expect not, and the argument is not that it is hard but that a proof of P equals NP would be a proof of a very specific kind of structure, and a proof of P not equal to NP would require a technique nobody has conceived. Both are believed to be beyond what we can currently do, which is why the question is a statement about the limits of a field rather than an open exercise.

/* What the notation says. */
const NOTATION = {

How the theory is used, and the four moves for a hard problem

Nobody solves NP-complete problems in general, and the entire practical content of the theory is a set of moves for when you have found one. Look for structure the problem does not require you to exploit. NP-hardness is about the general problem; real instances usually have structure — a geographic layout, a time constraint, a partial ordering, an input that is mostly tree-shaped — and a problem that is NP-hard in general can be easy on structured inputs, and finding the structure is most of the work. Reduce the search space with a good bound. Branch and bound with a sensible objective bound prunes most of the tree and turns an intractable instance into a tractable one, and the quality of the bound is what matters — a trivial bound prunes nothing. Accept an approximation and quantify it. Almost every application can use an answer within a percentage, and a guarantee of "within ten per cent of optimal, in polynomial time" is often more useful than no answer at all. Greedy set-cover gives a factor-of-logarithmic approximation; nearest-neighbour routing gives a factor of about two. Bound the input. Exact algorithms that are exponential in the number of items can be entirely fine on the twenty-item instances that actually occur, so an explicit statement of what the real maximum is turns "intractable" into "viable". Then the two things worth doing alongside, which are less theoretical and more often decisive. Change the problem. Almost no real requirement is "compute the exact optimum". Requirements are "schedule these classes so nobody is unhappy", "route these deliveries so nobody waits more than twenty minutes", "pack these items so nothing is wasted more than five per cent" — and every one of those is a relaxation, and each relaxation has a formulation that is tractable. Precompute. A problem that is intractable per query may be trivial once, offline, over a smaller space — which is what a cache, a lookup table and a precomputed route planner all are, and it converts a computational problem into a data problem.

Then the failures, and they are worth naming because each produces a project that does not finish. Assuming NP-hardness means impossible. It means exact-and-fast in general, and real systems are full of NP-hard problems running fine because their inputs are structured, bounded, or approximate. Using a heuristic without a bound and calling it correct. A greedy solution with no guarantee is a guess, and the distinction matters the day the input turns out to be one of the cases where the guess is wrong. Waiting for a better algorithm. Every few years there is a genuine improvement, and a system designed to improve when the algorithm improves is a system that has been idle for a decade. Proving the problem is easy when it is not, which is usually a proof that assumes something the input does not guarantee. And proving it hard and stopping. Proving a problem NP-hard is the beginning of an engineering conversation, not the end of one: it establishes that you need a heuristic or an approximation, and then the work is choosing one that is good enough and quantifying how good. Then the honest summary, and it is the thing to remember from this chapter: complexity theory tells you which problems to think about differently, and every one of them still ships. Real systems route deliveries, schedule timetables, pack containers and allocate resources using approximations, heuristics and brute force over bounded inputs, and they work — not because the theory is wrong but because the theory was telling them what to expect, and they had made their peace with it deliberately.

26 · Compilers, Parsers & How Languages Work

The compiler pipeline is the machinery that turns human-readable source text into a runnable program, passing through lexical analysis, parsing, semantic analysis, optimization, and code generation. Understanding it explains why languages differ in startup time, when they catch errors, and how fast their code runs. When you pick a language you are really choosing where along its pipeline the implementation stops, trading compile-time checking against interpreted flexibility.

26.1 The compiler pipeline26.2 Lexing: from characters to tokens26.3 Parsing: from tokens to a tree26.4 Write a whole interpreter in 40 lines26.5 Types: static vs dynamic, strong vs weak26.6 The performance machinery: JIT and garbage collection

You’ve spent this whole course in languages. Now see the machine that your languages ride: the pipeline that turns a text file into something a CPU or VM can run. Learning this makes "why is Python slow", "what’s a linter doing", and "how does a framework load this weird syntax" — answered forever.

26.1 The compiler pipeline

Every language implementation runs the same journey: source text becomes tokens, tokens become a syntax tree, and the tree is then analyzed, optimized, and turned into machine code or bytecode. An interpreter stops early and executes the tree directly, while a compiler goes further and emits native instructions. Understanding each stage tells you where errors surface and why compiled languages catch problems early and start fast while interpreted ones are simpler but slower.

source text
   |  1. LEXER (scanner)   -> tokens:  KEYWORD(if) IDENT(x) OP(+) NUM(2)
   |  2. PARSER            -> AST:     a tree saying "this is an if-statement"
   |  3. Semantic analysis  -> types, scopes, name resolution (the compiler's
   |      (checking)          "logical" stage; catches x undeclared, 1+"a")
   |  4. (optional) ONR/CANONICALISATION / optimisation passes
   |  5. Code generation    -> machine code / bytecode / JS / something else
   v
runnable program

What each stage is for, and what is actually optimisable

A compiler is a pipeline and each stage exists to remove a specific kind of information the next stage does not need. Lexing and parsing turn characters into a tree; nothing to optimise yet. Semantic analysis — name resolution, type checking, scope checking — turns the tree into a tree that is guaranteed to make sense, and this is the stage where most "correctness" errors are found, and the reason a compiler that does it properly never emits a program that does not compile. Optimisation removes work the program does not need to do, and it works on the tree or on a lower-level representation. Code generation produces the target. Then the optimisation levels, and the distinction worth internalising is that they differ in what information they are allowed to assume. Local optimisation works within a basic block and does constant folding, dead code elimination, common subexpression elimination and copy propagation; it needs no global information and cannot do much. Global optimisation uses data-flow analysis — computing, for each program point, which variables are definitely assigned, which are definitely live, and what values they may hold — and it can then delete unreachable code, hoist a loop-invariant computation out of a loop, and delete a store to a variable that is never read afterwards. Interprocedural goes across function boundaries and can inline a small function and specialise a call for one caller. And the one optimisation that matters more than all the others: inlining a function is worth more than every other optimisation combined, because it removes a call, which removes the register spills around it, which lets the surrounding code keep more values in registers, which enables constant propagation into the callee — so inlining is not one optimisation but a change that enables a dozen.

Then what a modern optimiser actually does, and this is where the mental model from the previous chapters has to be revised. Most of the work is deciding which values are live and which are dead, which is a graph problem on the control-flow graph and is done with liveness analysis. Register allocation is a graph-colouring problem, and it is the step that makes the whole thing worthwhile: a register is a limited resource, values compete for it, and the allocation decides how much memory traffic your program has, which is why it is the optimisation that maps most directly to speed. Instruction selection and scheduling choose what instruction and in what order, matching the processor's available operations and avoiding stalls. Vectorisation identifies loops whose iterations are independent and replaces them with a wider operation, and it is the one that produces the largest speedups — sometimes an order of magnitude — and the one that most often fails silently, because a loop the compiler believes is independent may not be, and the mistake produces a program that is faster and wrong. Then the practical reality. Optimisation changes code size, sometimes dramatically, inlining being the main cause, which is why the debug build is unoptimised. Optimisation makes debugging harder, because the variable you set a breakpoint on may not exist. Optimisation does not change semantics in principle and does occasionally in practice, where the source had undefined behaviour and the optimiser was entitled to assume it could not happen. And the optimiser is right more often than you are when you think it has made your program slower, which is the last thing in this chapter worth believing.

/* Each stage removes a specific kind of information the next stage does not need. */

];

This diagram shows the compiler pipeline from lexer and parser through semantic analysis, optimization, and code generation, ending in a runnable program.

Languages differ in where they stop: C runs 1–5 to machine code at build time. Java compiles to portable bytecode, interpreted by a JVM at runtime (and JIT-optimised there). Python compiles fast to bytecode on first use, then interpreted — which is why it starts up slower but catches fewer type errors. JavaScript engines interpret, then JIT-compile hot functions to machine code while running.

26.2 Lexing: from characters to tokens

The lexer scans a stream of characters and groups them into tokens, each carrying a type such as identifier, keyword, number, or operator plus its position in the source. It is produced by hand or with a generator such as lex or Flex, driven by regular expressions that define each token pattern. Whitespace and comments are usually skipped here, and their handling, plus rules for the longest match and reserved words, make this stage subtler than it first appears.

import re

TOKEN_SPEC = [
    ("NUM",   r"\d+"),
    ("OP",    r"[+\-*/]"),
    ("LPAREN", r"\("),
    ("RPAREN", r"\)"),
    ("WS",    r"\s+"),          # skip whitespace
]

def lex(code):
    tokens = []
    pos = 0
    while pos < len(code):
        for kind, pattern in TOKEN_SPEC:   # try each rule at the current spot
            m = re.match(pattern, code[pos:])
            if m:
                text = m.group(0)
                if kind != "WS":
                    tokens.append((kind, text))
                pos += len(text)
                break
        else:
            raise SyntaxError(f"bad char at {code[pos:pos+10]!r}")   # no rule matched
    return tokens

print(lex("1 + 2 * (3 + 4)"))
# [('NUM','1'),('OP','+'),('NUM','2'),('OP','*'),('LPAREN','('),('NUM','3'),('OP','+'),('NUM','4'),('RPAREN',')')]

What a token is, and why splitting is not trivial

The lexer's job is to turn a stream of characters into a stream of tokens, and the reason it is a separate stage is that the character stream is not the same shape as the language. The problem is maximal munch: given ==, is that two equals operators or one assignment? Given a+b, is that three identifiers and an operator or something else? The rule that resolves it is that the lexer takes the longest sequence of characters that forms a valid token — so == is one token — and the entire difficulty of lexing is recognising where one token ends and the next begins. Three problems make that genuinely hard. Overlapping patterns: if and ifelse both start with if, and a rule set ordered carelessly matches the prefix. Context: in x++ the plus is an operator, in x += 1 it is part of a compound assignment, and whether + is an operator depends on what follows it — which is why some languages require maximal munch and others explicitly do not allow it. And nesting: strings and comments contain characters that would otherwise be tokens, so the lexer needs a mode, and the mode is why a lexer is a small state machine rather than a list of regular expressions.

Then how it is built, and the two approaches worth knowing. Regular expressions per token type. Write one pattern per kind of token, run them in order, and take the first that matches at the current position — simple, and its correctness depends entirely on the ordering. A hand-written state machine. Consume characters, transition between states, and emit a token when you reach an accepting state. More code, and the reason the major languages all do it this way is that it is faster, it handles the nesting cases without difficulty, and the error messages can say what was expected where. And the two details that produce most lexer bugs. Whitespace and comments are consumed silently — they produce no tokens at all, and forgetting to skip them is the most common way a hand-written lexer fails on its first test. The position must be tracked for error messages, because "unexpected character at position 214" is useful and "syntax error" is not, and a lexer that does not track position cannot produce the first. Then the output, and why it is a stream rather than a list. A lexer usually yields tokens lazily, one at a time, so that a parser can stop after the first few and never lex a program it does not need — which is a real saving on a large file and is also why a syntax error at the end of a file is reported late, because everything before it had to be lexed to get there.

/* Tokens, and the shape mismatch. */
const THE_JOB = 'turn a stream of CHARACTERS into a stream of TOKENS';
const WHY_SEPARATE = 'the character stream is NOT THE SAME SHAPE as the language';
/* Maximal munch. */
const MAXIMAL_MUNCH = {
  problem: 'given two equals, is that two equals OPERATORS or one ASSIGNMENT',
  rule: 'the lexer takes the LONGEST SEQUENCE OF CHARACTERS THAT FORMS A VALID TOKEN',
  and: 'the entire difficulty of lexing is RECOGNISING WHERE ONE TOKEN ENDS AND THE NEXT BEGINS',
};

const HARD = [

];

/* Lazy output. */
const OUTPUT = {

};

This lexer scans code left to right, splitting characters into token types while silently dropping whitespace, and raises SyntaxError whenever no pattern matches at the current position.

The lexer’s job is trivial-looking and fussy all at once: deal with whitespace, comments, string literals, and be unambiguous. Modern tools (flex, ANTLR lexer) generate lexers from specs like this.

26.3 Parsing: from tokens to a tree

The parser takes the token stream and imposes grammar, respecting operator precedence, associativity, and nesting to build an abstract syntax tree. Recursive descent, writing one function per grammar rule, is the classic handwritten way to build one and is easy to debug. Alternatively, parser generators such as Yacc or ANTLR construct the parser from a formal grammar, while hand-written descent stays common because error messages and tooling can be controlled directly.

The parser imposes grammar: operator precedence (2+3×4 = 14, not 20), nesting, statements. The classic handwritten technique is recursive descent — one function per grammar rule, calling each other recursively:

# A tiny recursive-descent parser for arithmetic:  expr ::= term (('+'|'-') term)*
class Parser:
    def __init__(self, tokens):
        self.tokens = tokens; self.i = 0
    def peek(self):  return self.tokens[self.i][1] if self.i < len(self.tokens) else None
    def pop(self):
        t = self.tokens[self.i]; self.i += 1; return t

    def expr(self):
        val = self.term()
        while self.peek() in ("+", "-"):    # same precedence, left to right
            op = self.pop()[1]; right = self.term()
            val = val + right if op == "+" else val - right
        return val

    def term(self):
        return float(self.pop()[1])    # (numbers only, for brevity)

def calc(code):
    return Parser(lex(code)).expr()

print(calc("2 + 3 + 1"))   # 6.0   -- precedence is structurally correct

Why a grammar, and what the two kinds buy you

A grammar is a formal description of the valid shapes of a program, and using one rather than hand-written parsing code buys you something specific: the parser becomes a direct translation of the rules, so the code and the specification cannot disagree. The rules are written in a notation — a context-free grammar — where each rule says what a construct is made of. An expression might be a number, or a name, or a binary operation with a left and a right expression, or a parenthesised expression. Each of those is a rule; a program is valid if a sequence of rules derives it. Then the two parser kinds, and the difference is where the difficulty lives. Recursive descent means one function per grammar rule, calling itself for sub-rules. It is the easiest to write, it is what most hand-written parsers use, and it gives excellent error messages because you know exactly which rule you were in. Its two limitations are precise: left recursion breaks it, because expr → expr + term makes the function call itself before it has consumed anything and it never terminates, so every real recursive-descent grammar is rewritten to be right-recursive; and precedence must be encoded in the structure — typically one function per precedence level, so addition is parsed in a function that calls multiplication and not the reverse, which is why precedence in a hand-written parser is a matter of function nesting rather than of a table. A table-driven parser — LR or LALR — is generated from the grammar rather than written by hand, and it handles any context-free grammar including left recursion and ambiguity, and it is what most languages actually use. The cost is that its code is machine-generated and unreadable, and its error messages are poor.

Then what happens between a grammar and a tree, and the step that is easier to overlook than it should be. The grammar defines structure; the parser builds a tree of nodes. Each node carries what the grammar rule says it carries — an operator node knows which operator, an identifier node knows its name — and the node type is what makes the next stage possible. The tree is the interface between parsing and everything after it, and its shape is a design decision that is usually made once and lived with for years: does an addition node have two children, or is it a list node with a list of children, which is what lets you support a variable number of operands; is there a distinct node for a parenthesised expression, which matters for whether the tree records the parentheses or only their effect; is a literal a node with a value or a field on a generic node. Each of those choices is small and each propagates, and the advice worth giving is that the tree is worth designing deliberately because every later stage — evaluation, optimisation, code generation — reads it and nothing else, so a tree that is awkward to evaluate makes three later stages awkward, while a tree that is awkward to parse is a problem confined to the parser.

/* Why a grammar. */
const GRAMMAR = {
  is: 'a formal DESCRIPTION OF THE VALID SHAPES of a program',
  buys: 'the parser becomes a DIRECT TRANSLATION of the rules, so the CODE AND THE SPECIFICATION CANNOT DISAGREE',
  rules: 'each rule says what a CONSTRUCT IS MADE OF',
  example: 'an expression might be a number, or a name, or a binary operation with a left and a right expression, or a parenthesised expression',
  valid: 'a program is valid if a SEQUENCE OF RULES DERIVES IT',
};

/* Two kinds. */
const KINDS = [
  { k: 'RECURSIVE DESCENT', means: 'ONE FUNCTION PER GRAMMAR RULE, calling itself for sub-rules',
    good: ['easiest to write', 'what most hand-written parsers use',
      'EXCELLENT ERROR MESSAGES because you know exactly which rule you were in'],
    limitation1: { l: 'LEFT RECURSION BREAKS IT',

    },
  },
  { k: 'TABLE-DRIVEN, LR or LALR', means: 'GENERATED FROM THE GRAMMAR rather than written by hand',
    good: ['handles ANY CONTEXT-FREE GRAMMAR including left recursion and ambiguity',

    cost: ['its code is MACHINE-GENERATED and UNREADABLE', 'its ERROR MESSAGES are poor'],

/* Grammar to tree. */
const TREE = {
  what: 'the grammar defines STRUCTURE; the parser builds a TREE OF NODES',
  node: 'carries WHAT THE GRAMMAR RULE SAYS IT CARRIES - an operator node knows which operator, an identifier node knows its name',
  nodeTypeIsWhat: 'makes the NEXT STAGE possible',
  isThe: 'INTERFACE BETWEEN PARSING AND EVERYTHING AFTER IT',
  choices: ['does an addition node have TWO CHILDREN, or is it a list node with a list of children, which is what lets you support a VARIABLE NUMBER OF operands',

    'is a LITERAL a node with a value or a field on a generic node'],
  eachChoiceIs: 'small, and each PROPAGATES',
  advice: 'the tree is worth designing DELIBERATELY because every later stage - evaluation, optimisation, code generation - READS IT AND NOTHING ELSE',
  consequence: 'a tree that is awkward to evaluate makes THREE LATER STAGES awkward, while a tree that is awkward to PARSE is a problem CONFINED TO THE PARSER',
