This recursive-descent parser reads operator tokens and builds left-associative sums, so that operator precedence is enforced structurally by the grammar rules themselves.

Everything you type in code languages, JSON, YAML, SQL — some parser reads those tokens into a tree. That tree (the AST) is what linters, formatters, sandbox analysers, IDEs and compilers all walk.

26.4 Write a whole interpreter in 40 lines

An interpreter is fundamentally a function that walks an abstract syntax tree and evaluates it: literals, variable lookups, arithmetic, if statements, and function calls each map to a small piece of code. For arithmetic expressions a tree-walking evaluator can fit in dozens of lines, making it the fastest way to see every stage of the pipeline in action. Building your own toy language this way teaches lexing, parsing, evaluation, and environments for good.

# eval on the AST: the "meaning" of the program
import operator

OPS = {"+": operator.add, "-": operator.sub, "*": operator.mul, "/": operator.truediv}

def eval_ast(node, env):
    kind = node[0]
    if kind == "num":
        return node[1]
    if kind == "var":
        return env[node[1]]
    if kind == "binop":                 # apply operator to both children
        return OPS[node[1]](eval_ast(node[2], env), eval_ast(node[3], env))
    raise ValueError(kind)

# tree for:  x = 3;  x * 2 + 1
code_tree = ("binop", "+", ("binop", "*", ("var", "x"), ("num", 2)), ("num", 1))
print(eval_ast(code_tree, {"x": 3}))   # 7

Tree-walking, and why it is the right first design

The simplest interpreter walks the syntax tree once and evaluates each node as it visits it, and it is worth understanding why this is a good design rather than a shortcut. The tree already contains the answer to "what does this node mean". A binary operation node's meaning is "evaluate the left, evaluate the right, apply the operator" — so an evaluator is a function per node type, and it is short, and it has no intermediate representation to get wrong. It is where you find out whether your grammar was right, because a grammar that produces a tree you cannot evaluate is a grammar that was missing something, and the tree-walking evaluator is what tells you. And the performance problem is understood rather than mysterious: it re-evaluates a subtree if the same tree is evaluated twice, it has no way to reuse work, and its constant factor is a chain of function calls per node. Those are all addressable and none of them makes the design wrong. Then what tree-walking does badly, and the fixes are worth knowing because they are the progression every real interpreter follows. Repeated evaluation: an expression that appears in a loop body is re-walked every iteration. The fix is closure compilation — evaluate the tree once into a tree of closures, so the loop body's work is done once and the loop only re-enters a closure. Function call overhead: a call in the source becomes a chain of evaluator calls through every node on the way to the callee, and the fix is to compile a call into something that does not walk. No compilation at all for the host's own code: the interpreter is running on top of another language's virtual machine, so every node costs a dispatch in that virtual machine too, and the fix is eventually to emit that language's code rather than walk your tree. The order is the progression: tree-walking, then closures, then bytecode, then native, and each step removes one layer of indirection that the previous step could not.

Then environment, which is the part that makes an interpreter capable rather than merely demonstrative. A variable's name is a string and its value is anything, so the environment is a mapping, and the whole design question is how that mapping is represented. A flat dictionary is simplest and O(n) per lookup by scope name, and is fine for a toy language with hundreds of names. Nested dictionaries per scope, with lookup walking outward, gives lexical scoping naturally and costs a chain walk. A compile-time-resolved chain of indices — where each variable reference becomes a level number and a slot, resolved once by walking scopes at compile time — is what real interpreters do, and it turns a lookup into an array index, which is the difference between usable and not. And closures capture their defining environment by reference, not by value, which is the detail that makes closures work and the one that surprises people: a closure over a variable that changes sees the change, and a closure that captures a loop variable by reference sees the final value, which is why copying the variable into a new scope before the closure is the standard workaround.

/* Why tree-walking is a good design. */
const WHY = [
  { r: 'the tree already contains the ANSWER TO WHAT DOES THIS NODE MEAN',
    detail: 'a binary operation nodes meaning is evaluate the left, evaluate the right, apply the operator',
    consequence: 'an evaluator is a FUNCTION PER NODE TYPE, it is SHORT, and it has no INTERMEDIATE REPRESENTATION to get wrong',
  },
  { r: 'it is where you find out WHETHER YOUR GRAMMAR WAS RIGHT',
    detail: 'a grammar that produces a tree you cannot EVALUATE is a grammar that was MISSING SOMETHING',
    and: 'the tree-walking evaluator is what tells you',
  },
  { r: 'the performance problem is UNDERSTOOD rather than MYSTERIOUS',
    known: ['it re-evaluates a subtree if the same tree is evaluated twice', 'it has no way to REUSE WORK',
      'its constant factor is a CHAIN OF FUNCTION CALLS per node'],
    and: 'those are all ADDRESSABLE and none of them makes the design WRONG',
  },
];

/* What it does badly, and the fixes. */
const IMPROVEMENTS = [
  { p: 'REPEATED EVALUATION', detail: 'an expression that appears in a loop body is RE-WALKED EVERY ITERATION',
    fix: 'CLOSURE COMPILATION - evaluate the tree once into a tree of CLOSURES, so the loop bodys work is done once and the loop only RE-ENTERS A CLOSURE' },
  { p: 'FUNCTION CALL OVERHEAD', detail: 'a call in the source becomes a CHAIN OF EVALUATOR CALLS through every node on the way to the callee',
    fix: 'compile a call into something that does not WALK' },
  { p: 'NO COMPILATION for the hosts own code', detail: 'the interpreter runs on top of ANOTHER LANGUAGEs VIRTUAL MACHINE, so every node costs a DISPATCH there too',
    fix: 'eventually to EMIT THAT LANGUAGES CODE rather than walk your tree' },
];
const PROGRESSION = ['tree-walking', 'closures', 'bytecode', 'native'];
const WHY_PROGRESSION = 'each step removes ONE LAYER OF INDIRECTION that the previous step could not';

/* Environment. */
const ENVIRONMENT = {
  what: 'a variables NAME is a string and its VALUE is anything',
  so: 'the environment is a MAPPING', and: 'the whole design question is HOW THAT MAPPING IS REPRESENTED',
  representations: [
    { r: 'a FLAT DICTIONARY', lookup: 'O(n) per lookup by scope name', fineWhen: 'a toy language with hundreds of names' },
    { r: 'NESTED DICTIONARIES PER SCOPE', lookup: 'walks OUTWARD',
      gain: 'gives LEXICAL SCOPING NATURALLY', cost: 'a chain walk' },
    { r: 'A COMPILE-TIME-RESOLVED CHAIN OF INDICES',
      does: 'each variable reference becomes a LEVEL NUMBER AND A SLOT, resolved once by walking scopes at compile time',
      whatRealInterpretersDo: true,
      gain: 'turns a lookup into an ARRAY INDEX, which is the difference between USABLE and not',
    },
  ],
  closures: {
    capture: 'their DEFINING ENVIRONMENT BY REFERENCE, not by value',
    detail: 'the detail that makes closures WORK and the one that surprises people',
    consequences: ['a closure over a variable that CHANGES sees the change',
      'a closure capturing a LOOP VARIABLE BY REFERENCE sees the FINAL VALUE',
      'which is why COPYING THE VARIABLE into a new scope before the closure is the STANDARD WORKAROUND'],
  },
};

This tiny evaluator walks an AST and computes its meaning, showing that a language is just a lexer, a parser, and a function that assigns values to nodes.

That’s it — the soul of every interpreter. Real ones add scopes, functions, objects, and error handling, but a language is "just" a lexer, a parser, and a meaning function. Building your own toy language is one of the best resume projects in existence.

26.5 Types: static vs dynamic, strong vs weak

Static typing checks types before the program runs, catching whole classes of mistakes at compile time, while dynamic typing defers checks to runtime, letting you write and change code faster. Strong typing rejects implicit conversions between unrelated types, whereas weak typing permits them and quietly coerces values. The right mix is a team-scale decision balancing early safety, expressiveness, and iteration speed, so the pragmatic answer picks the policy that fits the codebase and failure tolerances.

AxisMeaningExamplesTrade-off
Static typingTypes checked at compile timeJava, C#, TS, Go, RustCatches classes of bugs early; more annotations upfront
Dynamic typingTypes checked when values flowPython, JS, RubyFast to write; surprises at runtime
Strong typingFew implicit conversions; types resistedPython, Java, RustFewer silent surprises
Weak typingValues coerced implicitlyJS ("5"*2 → 10)Convenient but "sneaky" bugs

The four decisions a type system makes

A static type system is four decisions made in advance, and knowing which four turns the terminology into something you can reason about. Where are the types attached? Statically means before the program runs; dynamically means at run time, from the value. This decision alone determines when errors are found, which is the largest practical difference between the two. How strong is the type system? A strong system forbids many operations that are technically expressible and semantically meaningless — adding a number to a string — while a weak one permits them and defines what happens. Are types inferred or declared? Inferred means the compiler derives them; declared means you write them. Is it sound? A sound type system never permits an operation that could be unsafe; an unsound one does, which is a deliberate trade and always a real one.

Then the trade between static and dynamic, stated in the terms that actually matter rather than in adjectives. Static catches errors before the program runs, and the errors it catches are the ones that are expensive — a type error found in development is minutes; the same mistake found in production is an incident. Dynamic catches errors at the point of failure, which means the error message is exactly where the mistake is, and the code that could not have existed under a static system can be written and is often clearer. Static's cost is friction: you must satisfy the checker, which means annotating, working around cases the checker cannot see, and occasionally fighting it — and the friction is real enough that it is the reason many teams pick dynamic typing for prototypes and static for production. Dynamic's cost is discovery: a type error is found when that line runs, which may be when a user's data takes a shape you did not anticipate, and which no amount of testing finds if you did not think of the case. Static enables tooling that dynamic cannot support at all — precise refactoring, autocomplete that knows what a function returns, and the ability to change a signature and find every caller — and this is an argument about the whole development experience rather than about the code. And dynamic wins on programs whose shape is genuinely not known at build time, which is real: a JSON document of unknown structure, a plugin system, a script run against a third party's data.

Then the honest modern position, and it is that this is no longer an either/or. Gradual typing is the resolution, and the insight is that a type can be checked when the programmer supplies information and skipped when it does not — so a codebase can be typed incrementally, module by module, with a boundary where checked code meets unchecked. The pragmatic recommendation follows the career arc in the chapter's tip: dynamic typing while you are learning and the program is small and the shapes are changing, because the friction of static typing while you are still finding out what the program should be is paid for nothing. Static typing when the codebase is shared, when it must survive, or when the people reading it did not write it — which is almost all professional code. And start by typing the boundaries, not the interior, because the boundaries are where the mistakes that hurt live: input validation, function signatures that are part of an API, data crossing a module. That gets most of the benefit for a fraction of the cost. Then the four practices that make static typing pay rather than annoy, and each addresses a specific source of friction. Let inference do the work and annotate only what inference cannot derive. Use the strictest setting you can tolerate, gradually, because a system with no strictness is worse than none — it catches nothing and costs the same. Make the common path easy and the impossible path impossible, so that the type system's help is felt as flow rather than as administration. And keep types close to the data they describe, rather than duplicating a declaration of the same shape in a place that can drift from the thing it describes — which is the same argument the database chapter made about a second source of truth.

/* Four decisions. */
const DECISIONS = [
  { d: 'WHERE ARE THE TYPES ATTACHED', static: 'before the program runs', dynamic: 'at run time, FROM THE VALUE',
    determines: 'WHEN ERRORS ARE FOUND', largestDifference: true },

Structural typing, nominal typing, and the costs of each

Where the types come from decides what the type system can express, and this is a genuinely different axis from static versus dynamic. Nominal typing: two types are compatible only if they are the same declared type or a declared subtype, and the name is what matters. A Dog is not a Animal unless it says so, and a structurally identical type that was never declared related is still incompatible. This is the model in Java, C#, TypeScript's declaration form and Rust, and its strength is that the compiler can tell you what a value actually is: if a function accepts a Dog, it can rely on the dog's behaviour without inspecting it, and a class can have a private field, a final method, an invariant that only it can maintain. Its cost is the ceremony: two types that have the same shape but no declared relationship do not fit together, and you write an interface or a conversion to bridge them, which is friction paid for a guarantee. Structural typing: two types are compatible if they have the same shape, and the shape is the whole story. A value with the right members is accepted regardless of what it was declared as, and this is the model in Python's duck typing promoted to the type level, in TypeScript's inference, in Go's structural interfaces and in most of the functional languages. Its strength is that you do not have to declare relationships you do not care about — any object with the right members works, so a function can accept a very small interface without knowing about any particular class, and this is the mechanism behind the dependency-inversion argument from the design chapter. Its cost is that the type system cannot reason about intent: because compatibility is by shape, two types with the same members but different meanings are interchangeable, and a method named close that means "close the connection" is interchangeable with one that means "close the window".

Then the practical consequences of structural typing, and they are mostly good with one sharp edge. It makes interfaces cheap and therefore small, which is the single best thing about it: an interface with one method is trivial to satisfy and does not drag in a class hierarchy, so you can declare exactly what a function needs and nothing more. It makes generics and containers work naturally, because a list of things satisfying a small interface needs no common ancestor. It makes external types usable, because anything with the right methods fits whether or not its authors ever heard of your interface. And the sharp edge: the compiler will not tell you when a type gains a method and every implementation silently changes meaning, because in a structurally typed system adding a member to a declared type can make unrelated types compatible or incompatible, and the diff looks harmless. In a nominally typed system, adding a member to an interface produces a compile error at every implementation, which is either helpful or annoying depending on whether you wanted the change.

/* Nominal: the NAME is what matters. */

The career arc cup: start dynamically typed (you did, Python) to think about ideas; add static types (TypeScript, mypy, later Rust) when the codebase and teammates grow — type strength is a team-scale decision, not a religion.

26.6 The performance machinery: JIT and garbage collection

Just-in-time compilers identify hot paths at runtime and compile them to native machine code, which is why managed and dynamic languages approach native speed where it matters. Garbage collectors reclaim unreachable memory automatically, freeing developers from manual allocation in return for pauses and overhead. Together JITs and GCs explain most real differences in language startup and throughput and shape tuning choices such as heap size and compiler flags.

  • JIT (Just-In-Time): the engine observes a hot loop and compiles it to optimised machine code while it runs (V8 does this). That’s how JS/Java approach C speed for hot paths.
  • Garbage collection reclaims memory you stopped using. Three families: refcounting (Python — immediate but pays per object), tracing mark-and-sweep (Java, Go — pause when collecting), generational (most modern: young objects die fast, collect them often and cheaply).
  • Why Python is "slow": interpreted bytecode + runtime dispatch on every operation + GIL limiting one-thread parallelism (Ch. 23.3). Then libraries like NumPy hand the heavy loops to compiled C — which is why data/ML work in Python is actually fast.

Interpreting versus compiling, and why the boundary keeps moving

The two approaches differ in one thing: when the work happens. An interpreter executes as it reads, so there is no separate output; a compiler produces an artefact that runs later, so the analysis and translation happen once and the running is cheap. Everything else follows. Interpretation starts instantly and runs slowly; compilation takes time up front and runs fast. Interpretation is easy to write and hard to make fast, because every execution pays for the tree-walking and there is no place to put the result of the analysis you have already done. Compilation is harder to write and pays for itself on the second run, — which is why an interpreted language is perfectly reasonable for a script that runs once and absurd for one that runs ten thousand times. And the boundary between them is not a category but a slider that both sides keep moving, because hybrid designs work. A byte-code interpreter with a just-in-time compiler is both: it does not compile to machine code up front, and it is not tree-walking either, because it has an intermediate representation that is compiled once per method and then executed repeatedly.

Then what decides the choice in practice, and the four questions. How often does it run? Once — interpret. A hundred thousand times — compile, because the compilation cost is amortised and the arithmetic is not close. How long does the program run once? A short script with a startup cost — interpret, because compilation overhead is a fixed tax on a short run and can exceed the entire program. A long-running program — compile, because you pay once and run for hours. Does it need the host's ecosystem? This is the question that decides most real choices, and it is not a performance question at all: an interpreted language with a rich library ecosystem for your problem domain will be chosen regardless of its speed, because the alternative is implementing that library yourself. And how much dynamic behaviour is there? Runtime evaluation, dynamic loading, monkey-patching, and code generated from data are all natural in an interpreter and each is awkward in a compiler, which is why languages with those features tend to have compilers rather than interpreters despite their dynamism. Then the four costs that are structural rather than incidental. Interpreted code cannot be handed to a machine that does not have the interpreter, so the interpreter must be installed everywhere — which is a deployment cost, a version-skew cost, and the reason people wrap things to make them self-contained. Compiled code is specific to an architecture and an operating system, so shipping it everywhere means shipping several builds. Compilation is a build step, and a build step is a thing that can be stale, run on the wrong machine, or be skipped, and every one of those has happened in production. And interpretation makes the stack traces much better, because the interpreter knows which line of your source it was executing, which is why a stack trace from interpreted code points at your code and a stack trace from compiled code points at something you cannot see unless you kept debug information.

Just-in-time compilation, and how a hybrid gets the best of both

The interesting answer to "interpreted or compiled" is a system that does neither purely, and understanding how it works resolves most of the confusion in performance discussions. The pipeline has three stages: the source is parsed once into a tree; the tree is compiled into an intermediate representation — bytecode, or a register-machine instruction set — which is the form actually executed; and a just-in-time compiler translates the intermediate representation into native code while the program is running, when it can see the actual types and the actual call targets. The third stage is the whole trick, and it is worth being precise about what it can do that an ahead-of-time compiler cannot. It knows the concrete types. A variable declared as "a number or a string" costs a runtime tag check on every operation in an ahead-of-time compiled program, while a just-in-time compiler that has watched which branch actually ran can compile that site as arithmetic with no check at all. It knows which call targets are hot. When a call site has resolved to the same function two hundred times, that call can be compiled as a direct jump, and a megamorphic site that dispatches to a dozen targets is left as an indirect call. It can speculatively inline and deoptimise — compile a call as if the type were one thing, put a check at the point where that assumption fails, and if it fails, throw away the compiled code and go back to the interpreter for that path, which is fast in the common case and correct in all of them.

Then what that buys and what it costs, because the cost is where the mysterious performance behaviour comes from. It buys the optimisations that need runtime knowledge — profile-guided branch layout, speculative inlining, on-stack replacement for objects that do not escape — none of which are possible when you must produce a binary before the program has run. It costs startup time, because the code must be compiled before it can run, which is why the first invocation of a function is slower than the second and why a short script has the worst of both worlds. It costs unpredictability, because a program whose performance depends on which paths the compiler happened to observe can be fast in testing and slow in production, since production input distribution is not the distribution you tested with. And it costs code size, because several compiled versions of the same function may exist for different type profiles. Then why it won, which is the real answer and it is not performance alone. Portability: the intermediate representation is a bytecode you control, so the same artefact runs on every platform — which is the entire reason Java and Python are portable and which a compiler emitting machine code cannot be. Safety: the runtime can do things a static binary cannot, such as never executing an invalid pointer, and can deoptimise rather than trust a speculative assumption. Compatibility: the language can gain features that are expensive for a static compiler to implement, because the cost lands on the runtime rather than on every compile. And startup is a solved problem well enough, with tiered compilation — start at the interpreter, promote the hot code, and stop optimising a method once the benefit stops justifying the cost — which is the design that made this hybrid the default answer rather than a compromise.

/* Three stages. */
const PIPELINE = [
  { s: 1, does: 'the source is PARSED ONCE into a tree' },

    gain: 'because at that moment it can see the ACTUAL TYPES and the ACTUAL CALL TARGETS',
    isTheTrick: true },
];

27 · Math for Computing: Linear Algebra & Calculus

Linear algebra manipulates arrays of numbers, vectors, and matrices to represent transformations and data, while calculus studies change through derivatives and integrals. Together they are the math under machine learning, computer graphics, game physics, optimization, and scientific simulation. Learning to think of data as vectors, model transforms as matrix products, and tune systems by slopes gives you a shared mathematical vocabulary across all of computing.

27.1 Vectors and matrices — the grid under everything27.2 Matrix multiplication: transformations in action27.3 Eigenvalues: find the direction that doesn’t change27.4 Calculus for optimisers: derivatives and gradient descent27.5 Expected value, variance and distributions

A second maths course appears in every software degree: linear algebra (the maths of tables of numbers) and calculus (the maths of change). They are the engine room of machine learning, 3D graphics, game physics, optimisation, and modern data analysis.

27.1 Vectors and matrices — the grid under everything

Vectors are ordered lists of numbers and matrices are grids of them, and nearly every structure in modern computing, from coordinates in a 3D scene to the weights of a neural network, is represented as one of the two. The dot product measures how much two vectors align and is the atomic operation in attention and neural network computation. Master vector addition, scaling, the norm, and matrix indexing and you can read most machine learning and graphics code.

A vector is an ordered list of numbers (coordinates; a row of a spreadsheet is a vector). A matrix is a grid of numbers — a whole dataset, a rotation, the network of a page, the weights of a model. Everything "big" in computing is a matrix with a name.

# Represent data as a matrix: each ROW is an item, each COLUMN a feature
#   [area, bedrooms, age_years]         -- a tiny house dataset
houses = [
    [120, 3, 8],
    [85,  2, 25],
    [200, 4, 1],
]
feature_names = ["area", "bedrooms", "age"]

# Vector dot product sums element-wise products -- the atom of neural nets
def dot(a, b):
    return sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))

weights = [2000, 500000, -8000]          # some "price model" per feature
print(dot(houses[0], weights))           # 120*2000 + 3*500000 + 8*(-8000) = 1,676,000
# Linear algebra is 90% these three verbs: add, scale, dot/multiply.

This block shows raw data as a matrix of rows and columns and implements the dot product by hand, the atomic operation behind neural networks.

The operations, and why they are not the same as in a maths course

A vector in machine learning is a column of numbers, and almost everything about it follows from one decision: the shape is a choice you make and defend. A batch of images arrives as something like a hundred and twenty-eight by a hundred and twenty-eight by three; flattening it to a single column of forty-nine thousand entries gives you something a matrix multiply can consume, and the flatten is the moment the spatial structure of the image is thrown away. That is why convolutional networks do not flatten, and it is the first thing to understand about vectors: the ordering of the entries carries meaning and a different ordering is a different object. Then the operations, and each has a shape rule you can check in your head. Adding: element-wise, and the shapes must match exactly — which is why broadcasting is the operation that catches people, because NumPy will add a thousand-by-one to a thousand-by-thousand by treating the first as a row it copies a thousand times, and that is a semantic decision disguised as convenience. Dot product: two vectors of equal length become a scalar, and it is the single most important operation in machine learning because a linear layer is a stack of dot products and every parameter in a network is learned to make some dot product large or small. Outer product: two vectors become a matrix, and it is how one vector influences another. Matrix multiply: the shape rule is that the inner dimensions must agree — an m by k times a k by n gives an m by n — and it is the operation that makes a network layer possible, because it computes every output from every input in one call rather than in a loop.

Then the two properties that decide whether the maths is useful or merely valid. Orthogonal vectors have a dot product of zero, which means they carry no shared information, and a set of mutually orthogonal vectors is a basis: any vector can be written as a combination of them. This is why dimensionality reduction picks orthogonal directions — they are independent, so keeping the first few loses the least information — and why an orthogonal basis is what a transform to a new coordinate system produces. Unit vectors have length one, and they matter because a dot product with a unit vector is exactly a projection: it answers "how much of this vector points in that direction". Two orthogonal unit vectors form the axes of a coordinate system, which is the whole point of rotating a space — you have not changed any lengths, you have changed which directions you are measuring against. Then the two operations that break the intuition carried over from geometry. Normalisation: a vector is normalised by dividing by its length, producing length one, and it is what makes distance comparisons meaningful when features are on different scales. Projection: taking the component of one vector along another is the dot product with a unit vector, and it discards the perpendicular part — which is the operation behind dimensionality reduction, because projecting onto the leading basis vectors keeps the components that vary most. And the failure worth knowing, because it produces a silent bug rather than an error: a vector of zeros has no direction, and normalising it divides by zero.

};

Install numpy for real work (pip install numpy): matrices as np.array, with GPU-speed operations and million-row dot products. Everything you write by hand here is already in numpy — but writing it by hand once teaches what numpy actually does.

27.2 Matrix multiplication: transformations in action

Multiplying a vector by a matrix applies a linear transformation such as rotation, scaling, or projection, and composing matrices by multiplying them composes their transformations in one combined step. A fully connected neural network layer computes exactly W times x plus b, weights times activations plus bias, followed by a nonlinearity. Because matrix multiplication is so central, fast libraries such as BLAS and GPU tensor cores make it nearly free.

Multiplying a matrix by a vector produces a new vector: rotate it, scale it, mix its features (a single dense layer of a neural net is exactly W·x + b). Multiplying matrices composes two transformations into one.

def matmul(A, B):
    """A of shape (m,n) times B of shape (n,p) -> (m,p)."""
    m, n = len(A), len(A[0])
    p = len(B[0])
    out = [[0] * p for _ in range(m)]
    for i in range(m):
        for j in range(p):
            out[i][j] = sum(A[i][k] * B[k][j] for k in range(n))   # row i dot column j
    return out

# 90-degree rotation in 2D
ROT = [[0, -1], [1, 0]]
v = [1, 0]                    # point (1,0)
print(matmul(ROT, [[x] for x in v]))   # [[0],[1]] -> (0,1): rotated

Why multiply instead of add, and what that buys

Both operations combine input features, and the difference is what a layer can express. Adding, with no non-linearity between layers, collapses to a single linear map. Compose two linear maps and you get one linear map — the composition of affine transformations is affine — so a network of twenty purely additive layers computes exactly one affine function, which means a stack of them has no more expressive power than one of them. That is the reason non-linearities exist, and the reason they appear between every pair of weight layers and never after the last one. Multiplying weights gives a second degree of freedom that addition does not. Each output becomes a learned, input-dependent weighted combination of the inputs rather than a fixed sum, so the network can construct features that are products of pairs of inputs — which is exactly what an exclusive-or requires and what no fixed combination of the inputs can express. The nonlinearity is what buys depth. Without it, extra layers are free to add; with it, each layer can carve the input space differently, and the composition of many such carvings is a highly non-linear decision boundary.

Then the rest of the structure, and each choice has a reason. The bias term is what makes a layer able to shift. A neuron that computes a weighted sum without a bias can only produce hyperplanes through the origin, so it cannot represent a function whose correct answer is "yes if this is above five" — it can represent "yes if this is above zero" and nothing else; the bias moves the threshold to where it needs to be, and a layer without biases has a strictly smaller expressive power. Width is capacity and depth is composition. A wider layer computes more features at each step; a deeper network composes more steps, and empirically depth buys more expressive power than width at equal parameter count, which is the empirical observation behind the deep architectures everyone uses. Activation functions are what make it non-linear, and the choice among them changes what the network can carve: a rectified linear activation clips at zero and produces piecewise-linear behaviour, which is what makes deep rectified networks tractable to optimise and is also their known weakness — a unit whose input has been negative for every training example has zero gradient and cannot recover. A smooth activation avoids that but is more expensive. And the last layer is usually linear, because a regression output is a number and a classification output is a set of scores that are turned into probabilities afterwards — putting a non-linearity on the output would restrict what values the model can produce for no benefit.

/* Adding alone collapses depth. */
const WHY_MULTIPLY = [
  { r: 'ADDING with no non-linearity between layers COLLAPSES TO A SINGLE LINEAR MAP',
    detail: 'compose two linear maps and you get one linear map - the composition of AFFINE TRANSFORMATIONS IS AFFINE',
    consequence: 'a stack of twenty purely additive layers computes EXACTLY ONE AFFINE FUNCTION, which means a stack of them has NO MORE EXPRESSIVE POWER than one of them',
    therefore: 'why non-linearities exist',
    and: 'why they appear BETWEEN EVERY PAIR of weight layers and NEVER after the last one',
  },
  { r: 'MULTIPLYING WEIGHTS gives a SECOND DEGREE OF FREEDOM that addition does not',
    detail: 'each output becomes a LEARNED, INPUT-DEPENDENT WEIGHTED COMBINATION of the inputs rather than a fixed sum',
    gain: 'the network can construct FEATURES THAT ARE PRODUCTS OF PAIRS OF INPUTS',
    whyThat: 'which is exactly what an EXCLUSIVE-OR requires and what NO FIXED COMBINATION of the inputs can express',
  },
  { r: 'the NONLINEARITY is what BUYS DEPTH',
    detail: 'without it, extra layers are FREE TO ADD; with it, each layer can CARVE THE INPUT SPACE differently',
    and: 'the composition of many such carvings is a HIGHLY NON-LINEAR DECISION BOUNDARY',
  },
];

/* The rest of the structure. */
const STRUCTURE = [
  { s: 'the BIAS TERM', isWhat: 'makes a layer able to SHIFT',
    withoutIt: 'a neuron computing a weighted sum without a bias can only produce HYPERPLANES THROUGH THE ORIGIN',
    consequence: 'it cannot represent a function whose correct answer is yes if this is above five - it can represent yes if this is above zero and NOTHING ELSE',
    gain: 'the bias moves the THRESHOLD to where it needs to be',

  },
  { s: 'WIDTH is CAPACITY and DEPTH is COMPOSITION',
    detail: 'a wider layer computes MORE FEATURES at each step; a deeper network composes MORE STEPS',
    empirically: 'DEPTH BUYS MORE EXPRESSIVE POWER THAN WIDTH at equal parameter count',
    is: 'the empirical observation behind the deep architectures everyone uses',

This hand-written matrix multiplication loops over rows and columns performing dot products, and the rotation example shows the same machinery that neural network layers use.

Also learn to read matrix shapes: (m×n)·(n×p) is legal, costs O(m·n·p), and the result is (m×p). Interview "matrix rotation / spiral / transpose" problems are just these rules plus index care.

27.3 Eigenvalues: find the direction that doesn’t change

An eigenvector is a nonzero vector that a square matrix only scales, leaving its direction unchanged, and the eigenvalue is that scale factor for the direction. Eigen-decomposition reveals the matrix’s action in its most natural coordinates and anchors PageRank, where the dominant eigenvector is the ranking, and PCA, which finds directions of greatest variance for dimensionality reduction.

For many matrices there are special vectors where M·v = λ·v — the matrix only scales that direction, by λ. These eigenvectors/eigenvalues are the "axes that matter" of any system:

  • Google’s PageRank: the eigenvector of the link matrix — pages with the biggest entry are the most important.
  • PCA (principal component analysis): eigenvalues rank which directions carry the most data variance; you keep the top-k and the rest is "noise".
  • Stabililtiy/systems: eigenvalues of a system matrix tell whether it converges or blows up (control theory, physics engines).

What eigenvectors and eigenvalues are for

Decomposition in a vector space is the same idea as factorisation in arithmetic: you take something that is hard to work with and write it as a product of things that are not. A matrix is hard because it mixes every direction — apply it to a vector and every component depends on every input component. Eigen-decomposition finds the directions the matrix does not mix. An eigenvector is a non-zero vector that the matrix acts on by scaling and nothing else: applying the matrix to it gives the same vector multiplied by a scalar. That scalar is the eigenvalue. So for those directions the matrix is just a multiplication, which is why they are the directions worth understanding about any matrix. The eigenvalue is the factor by which that direction is stretched. Greater than one means growth in that direction, less than one means decay, and negative means the direction is reversed as well as scaled — which is why a negative eigenvalue makes iteration oscillate rather than converge. Real matrices can have complex eigenvalues, and the complex ones encode rotation: a purely imaginary pair multiplies a vector by a rotation of a certain angle, so a matrix whose eigenvalues have a nonzero imaginary part turns the space rather than stretching it, and repeated application traces a spiral.

Then why this matters, because the applications are what make it worth the machinery. It is the analysis of what a matrix does. Diagonalising a matrix turns applying it into a sequence of independent scalings, and everything you know about a linear map becomes a property of a list of numbers. Iteration converges or diverges depending on the dominant eigenvalue: this is the entire theory behind power iteration, used to find the leading eigenvector and behind the principal component that appears in the previous section, and the practical statement is that convergence rate is set by the ratio of the largest eigenvalue to the next largest, so two nearly equal eigenvalues mean slow convergence. Principal component analysis is eigenvalue decomposition of the covariance matrix, which is why it finds the direction of greatest variance and why the result is a rotation plus a rescaling. Markov chains are diagonalised to get their stationary distribution, and the eigenvalue one corresponds to a distribution that does not change. And then the two honest limitations, which decide when not to bother. Not every matrix has a complete set of eigenvectors — a non-symmetric matrix may have fewer eigenvectors than dimensions, or repeated eigenvalues with not enough independent eigenvectors, so the decomposition is not always possible and the technique is not always applicable. And computing eigenvalues is numerically delicate in a way that surprises people: the algorithm is stable, but the problem is ill-conditioned near a repeated eigenvalue, which means a matrix that is mathematically diagonalisable may produce results that are accurate but not accurate enough, and the symptom is an answer that changes when you perturb the input slightly.

/* The idea. */
const IDEA = {
  analogy: 'decomposition in a vector space is the same as FACTORISATION in arithmetic',
  theProblem: 'a matrix is hard because it MIXES EVERY DIRECTION - apply it to a vector and every component depends on every input component',
  theAnswer: 'EIGEN-DECOMPOSITION FINDS THE DIRECTIONS THE MATRIX DOES NOT MIX',
  eigenVector: 'a NON-ZERO VECTOR that the matrix acts on by SCALING AND NOTHING ELSE - applying the matrix to it gives the same vector MULTIPLIED BY A SCALAR',
  eigenValue: 'that SCALAR',
  consequence: 'for those directions the matrix is JUST A MULTIPLICATION',
  whyThatIsThePoint: 'which is why they are the DIRECTIONS WORTH UNDERSTANDING about any matrix',
};

/* What the eigenvalue tells you. */
const READS_AS = [
  { v: 'GREATER THAN ONE', meaning: 'GROWTH in that direction' },
  { v: 'LESS THAN ONE', meaning: 'DECAY in that direction' },
  { v: 'NEGATIVE', meaning: 'the direction is REVERSED as well as scaled',
    consequence: 'which is why a negative eigenvalue makes ITERATION OSCILLATE rather than converge' },

    and: 'repeated application TRACES A SPIRAL',
  },
];

/* The applications. */
const APPLICATIONS = [
  { a: 'it is the ANALYSIS OF WHAT A MATRIX DOES',
    gain: 'DIAGONALISING a matrix turns applying it into a SEQUENCE OF INDEPENDENT SCALINGS',

  { a: 'PRINCIPAL COMPONENT ANALYSIS is EIGENVALUE DECOMPOSITION of the covariance matrix',

/* The two honest limitations. */
const LIMITATIONS = [
  { l: 'NOT EVERY MATRIX HAS A COMPLETE SET OF EIGENVECTORS',
    detail: 'a NON-SYMMETRIC matrix may have FEWER EIGENVECTORS than dimensions',
    or: 'repeated eigenvalues with NOT ENOUGH INDEPENDENT eigenvectors',
    consequence: 'so the DECOMPOSITION IS NOT ALWAYS POSSIBLE and the technique is NOT ALWAYS APPLICABLE',
  },
  { l: 'COMPUTING EIGENVALUES is NUMERICALLY DELICATE in a way that surprises people',
    split: ['the ALGORITHM is stable', 'but the PROBLEM is ILL-CONDITIONED near a repeated eigenvalue'],
    symptom: 'a matrix that is MATHEMATICALLY DIAGONALISABLE may produce results that are accurate but NOT ACCURATE ENOUGH',
    and: 'the symptom is an answer that CHANGES WHEN YOU PERTURB THE INPUT SLIGHTLY',

You’ll compute them with np.linalg.eig(m) in practice; the degree course proves why they work

Decomposition, singular values, and the decision table

Singular value decomposition is the general version of the eigen-decomposition, and the difference is what makes it the tool you reach for by default. Every matrix can be decomposed this way. Any rectangular matrix, any non-symmetric matrix, including one with repeated singular values — the decomposition exists for all of them, where an eigen-decomposition may not exist at all. It is three objects rather than one pair: two orthogonal matrices that rotate the space, and a diagonal matrix in between holding the singular values, which are always non-negative and always ordered largest first. The reading of it is direct: the left rotation aligns the space to its principal directions, the diagonal matrix scales each direction, and the right rotation brings it back. Singular values are the stretching of a matrix, and that is a more useful statement than eigenvalues because it needs no assumptions — the largest singular value is how much the matrix can stretch, the smallest is how much it can crush, and a singular matrix is one whose smallest singular value is zero, which is the computational definition of "this matrix loses information". Then why it is the tool of choice, and there are three concrete reasons. It is numerically well behaved, because it degrades gracefully where eigen-decomposition does not. It gives the best low-rank approximation by construction — truncate the diagonal matrix after the largest few singular values and you have, among all matrices of that lower rank, the one closest to the original, which is the theorem behind every recommendation system built on truncated SVD. And it makes least squares solvable for any matrix, including the rank-deficient ones where the normal equations have no solution.

Then a decision table, because the honest answer to "which one" is a table rather than a preference. Symmetric positive-definite matrix? Eigen-decomposition is simpler, faster, and the eigenvectors are guaranteed orthonormal. Any other square matrix? Use singular value decomposition, or an eigen-decomposition of the transpose times the matrix if you only need the singular values and want them cheaply. Rectangular matrix? Singular value decomposition is the only one of the two that applies. Large or sparse matrix? Neither explicitly — factorise, and do not form the matrix, which is why a recommendation system on ten million users does not compute a ten-million-by-ten-million matrix. Just want the top component? Power iteration, which converges to the dominant eigenpair without any of the decomposition and is what you use when you need one direction rather than all of them. And then the failure that catches people, which is worth stating because it is not a numerical detail but a modelling error: the matrix you decompose may be badly scaled — columns on wildly different ranges — in which case the decomposition is dominated by the largest column and the result tells you about your units rather than about your data, and the fix is to standardise the columns before you factorise, which is the same normalisation the previous section described and it is a step people skip because nothing fails.

/* SVD versus eigen-decomposition. */
const SVD = {
  general: 'EVERY MATRIX CAN BE DECOMPOSED THIS WAY',
  covers: ['any RECTANGULAR matrix', 'any NON-SYMMETRIC matrix', 'including one with REPEATED singular values'],
  contrast: 'where an EIGEN-DECOMPOSITION MAY NOT EXIST AT ALL',
  threeObjects: ['two ORTHOGONAL MATRICES that rotate the space',
    'a DIAGONAL MATRIX in between holding the SINGULAR VALUES, always NON-NEGATIVE and always ORDERED LARGEST FIRST'],
  reading: ['the LEFT ROTATION aligns the space to its PRINCIPAL DIRECTIONS',
    'the DIAGONAL MATRIX scales each direction', 'the RIGHT ROTATION brings it back'],
  whatSingularValuesAre: 'the STRETCHING OF A MATRIX',
  whyBetterThanEigenvalues: 'because it needs NO ASSUMPTIONS',
  largest: 'how much the matrix can STRETCH', smallest: 'how much it can CRUSH',
  singularMatrix: 'one whose SMALLEST SINGULAR VALUE is zero, which is the computational definition of THIS MATRIX LOSES INFORMATION',
};

/* Why it is the tool of choice. */
const WHY = [
  { r: 'it is NUMERICALLY WELL BEHAVED', gain: 'it DEGRADES GRACEFULLY where eigen-decomposition does not' },
  { r: 'it gives the BEST LOW-RANK APPROXIMATION BY CONSTRUCTION',
    how: 'truncate the diagonal matrix after the largest few singular values',
    theorem: 'among all matrices of that lower rank, it is the ONE CLOSEST TO THE ORIGINAL',
    isBehind: 'every RECOMMENDATION SYSTEM built on truncated SVD' },
  { r: 'it makes LEAST SQUARES SOLVABLE for any matrix',
    including: 'the RANK-DEFICIENT ones where the normal equations have NO SOLUTION' },
];

/* The decision table. */
const DECIDE = [
  { if: 'the matrix is SYMMETRIC POSITIVE-DEFINITE', then: 'EIGEN-DECOMPOSITION',
    why: ['it is SIMPLER and FASTER', 'the eigenvectors are GUARANTEED ORTHONORMAL'] },
  { if: 'any OTHER SQUARE matrix', then: 'SINGULAR VALUE DECOMPOSITION',
    or: 'an eigen-decomposition of the TRANSPOSE TIMES THE MATRIX if you only need the singular values and want them CHEAPLY' },
  { if: 'a RECTANGULAR matrix', then: 'SINGULAR VALUE DECOMPOSITION', is: 'the ONLY ONE of the two that applies' },
  { if: 'a LARGE or SPARSE matrix', then: 'NEITHER EXPLICITLY', doInstead: 'FACTORISE, and DO NOT FORM THE MATRIX',
    example: 'which is why a RECOMMENDATION SYSTEM on ten million users does not compute a ten-million-by-ten-million matrix' },
  { if: 'you just want the TOP COMPONENT', then: 'POWER ITERATION',
    why: ['it converges to the DOMINANT EIGENPAIR without any of the decomposition',
      'it is what you use when you need ONE DIRECTION rather than all of them'] },
];

/* The failure. */
const SCALING_TRAP = {
  problem: 'the matrix you decompose may be BADLY SCALED - columns on WILDLY DIFFERENT RANGES',
  consequence: 'the decomposition is DOMINATED BY THE LARGEST COLUMN, so the result tells you about YOUR UNITS rather than about YOUR DATA',
  isA: 'a MODELLING ERROR, not a numerical detail',
  fix: 'STANDARDISE THE COLUMNS BEFORE YOU FACTORISE',
  sameAs: 'the same NORMALISATION the previous section described',
  whySkipped: 'because NOTHING FAILS',
};
and when they exist.

27.4 Calculus for optimisers: derivatives and gradient descent

A derivative measures the instantaneous slope of a function at a point, telling you which way the function rises and how steeply. Gradient descent follows the negative gradient downhill, updating parameters by a learning rate times the slope, and repeating until the minimum. This single loop is how neural networks learn, with backpropagation efficiently computing the gradient through every layer of the network.

A derivative measures how fast a function changes at a point — the slope. Optimisers earn their living on this one idea: follow the slope downhill to the minimum.

# Gradient descent of f(x) = x^2 + 1  (minimum at x=0, f=1)
def f(x):        return x * x + 1
def f_prime(x):  return 2 * x          # its slope, known by calculus

x, lr, steps = 3.0, 0.1, 50            # lr = how big a step to take
for _ in range(steps):
    x = x - lr * f_prime(x)            # step DOWN the slope
print(round(x, 4), round(f(x), 4))     # ~0.0 1.0 -- converged to min

# The SAME loop, with the slope estimated numerically diff(f, x):
def num_prime(h=1e-6):  return (f(x + h) - f(x)) / h
# This is literally how neural networks "learn": walk down the loss slope.

This loop steps repeatedly down the slope of a function until it converges on the minimum, and the numerical derivative shows the same learning mechanism neural networks use.

# And if f has many inputs (a cost function over model weights):
# the vector of all slopes is the GRADIENT; "gradient descent" = this:
#   weights = weights - learning_rate * gradient(weights)
# In ML the gradient comes from backpropagation (Ch. 28.5).

This pure-comment block reminds you that for functions of many inputs

Why the chain rule becomes backpropagation

Every quantity in a network is a function of the inputs, and the question that makes learning possible is: given how wrong the output is, which parameter should change, and by how much? The chain rule answers it exactly. Differentiate the output with respect to each parameter, going backwards through the operations. At each step the derivative of a composition is the derivative of the outer function times the derivative of the inner one, evaluated at that point — which is precisely what makes it possible to compute one derivative per parameter with a single backward pass instead of a separate forward pass per parameter, and that efficiency is the whole reason the technique has that name and that shape. The three pieces you need to hold onto. The chain rule gives you a product, not a sum, so the sensitivity of an early parameter to the error passes through every intermediate operation and shrinks by the factor each one contributes — which is the intuition behind the vanishing gradient, and behind why a network that is very deep has difficulty learning from the earliest layers. The derivative is evaluated at the current parameter values, which is why gradients describe a local slope and are only a good approximation of the direction of steepest descent near where you are. And the gradient points uphill, so you subtract it: moving in the direction of minus the gradient decreases the error fastest, locally.

Then what this means for training, and the constraints that follow. The gradient is local: it is a slope, not a distance. A large gradient does not mean the parameter is far from correct, only that moving it changes the loss quickly; and a large step with a large gradient is how a training run diverges. You take small steps, and the step size is the learning rate — the one hyperparameter that matters more than any other, and the one that makes training fail in both directions: too large and the loss oscillates or diverges, too small and training takes so long that it looks broken. A batch is an approximation, and its variance is a real cost. A gradient computed from a thousand examples is an average of a thousand different slopes, which is a much better estimate of the true slope than any one of them, and averaging costs nothing except waiting — but averaging over correlated examples (five copies of the same photograph) produces an estimate that is confidently wrong. And the loss surface is not smooth in the way the picture suggests: it has valleys, ridges and saddles, and the practical reason momentum exists is that plain gradient descent oscillates across a narrow valley instead of descending along it, and momentum — carrying an average of past gradients — damps the oscillation and accelerates the descent along the valley floor.

/* The question that makes learning possible. */
const QUESTION = 'given HOW WRONG the output is, WHICH PARAMETER SHOULD CHANGE, and by how much';
const THE_ANSWER = 'differentiate the output WITH RESPECT TO EACH PARAMETER, going BACKWARDS through the operations';

/* Three pieces to hold onto. */
const PIECES = [
  { p: 'the chain rule gives you a PRODUCT, not a sum',
    detail: 'the sensitivity of an EARLY PARAMETER to the error PASSES THROUGH EVERY INTERMEDIATE operation and SHRINKS by the factor each one contributes',
    explains: 'the intuition behind the VANISHING GRADIENT',
    and: 'why a network that is VERY DEEP has difficulty learning from the EARLIEST LAYERS',
  },
  { p: 'the derivative is EVALUATED AT THE CURRENT PARAMETER VALUES',
    consequence: 'gradients describe a LOCAL SLOPE',
    and: 'are only a good approximation of the direction of steepest descent NEAR WHERE YOU ARE',
  },
  { p: 'the gradient POINTS UPHILL, so you SUBTRACT it',
    detail: 'moving in the direction of MINUS the gradient decreases the error FASTEST, LOCALLY',
  },
];
const WHY_IT_IS_CALLED_BACKPROPAGATION = 'the chain rule lets you compute ONE DERIVATIVE PER PARAMETER with a SINGLE BACKWARD PASS instead of a SEPARATE FORWARD PASS per parameter - and that efficiency is the WHOLE REASON for the shape';
the vector of all slopes is the gradient, which machine learning updates by descending.

Two extra pieces the course will formalise: the chain rule (backpropagation’s entire machinery — "local slopes multiply along a path") and partial derivatives + Jacobians (slope of a multi-input function in each direction).

27.5 Expected value, variance and distributions

Expected value summarizes where a random quantity centers on average, variance measures how far it spreads, and distributions such as normal, Bernoulli, and Poisson describe the full shape of randomness. Fluency with these summaries is most of applied machine learning, because models are really statements about data distributions. Confidence intervals and error bounds, for example, all reduce to reasoning about mean, spread, and the distribution family at hand.

Machine learning is probability dressed in vectors. The two numbers that summarise any random quantity:

  • Expected value E[X] — the average you’d get sampling forever: Σ x·P(x).
  • Variance/σ² — how spread out values are; standard deviation σ is its square root. "P99 latency" (Ch. 21) is a distribution statement.
# Simulate vs formula: expected value of a fair die
rolls = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
ev = sum(x * (1 / 6) for x in rolls)        # 3.5
print(ev)

# Empirical estimate from a sample (and it converges -- law of large numbers)
import random, statistics
sample = [random.randint(1, 6) for _ in range(100_000)]
print(round(statistics.mean(sample), 3))    # ~3.5
print(round(statistics.stdev(sample), 3))   # ~1.7 (sd of uniform die)

This simulates the expected value of a fair die by formula and then estimates it from a huge random sample, demonstrating the law of large numbers.

Distributions you’ll meet on sight: uniform, binomial (counts of successes), normal/Gaussian (errors everywhere, central limit theorem), exponential (time between requests — the Poisson process that models web traffic).

What a distribution is, and the vocabulary that follows

A distribution is a function from outcomes to probabilities, and everything in this chapter follows from two requirements: the probabilities are non-negative, and they sum to one. That is all. The support is where the distribution is non-zero, and it is the first thing to identify because a distribution with a different support has completely different behaviour. The mean is the probability-weighted average, which is the centre of mass and also a statement about the long run: the average of a very large number of independent samples converges to it. The variance is the average squared distance from the mean, and it is the measure of spread that the mean alone cannot capture; because it squares the deviations it is in different units from the data, which is why the standard deviation is the square root of the variance and is the number you usually see. And the median, which matters because it is not distorted by a few extreme values in a way the mean is. Then the shapes, and each is a statement about a different kind of world. Normal: symmetric, bell-shaped, tail behaviour that makes extreme events less likely than intuition suggests. Bernoulli and binomial: a single trial and a count of successes in a fixed number of trials. Poisson: a count of events in a fixed interval, and the distribution of things that happen independently at a constant average rate — arrivals at a queue, errors per hour, typos per page. Exponential: the waiting time between Poisson events, and the distribution of things that decay — and it has the memoryless property, which is a mathematical statement about why a queue that behaves exponentially keeps behaving exponentially no matter how long it has been running. Uniform: everything equally likely, and the one that is genuinely rare in practice and most often assumed by mistake.

Then the two things that matter most for modelling, and they are the ones that turn a list of shapes into a method. Which distribution, and which of its parameters. The choice is made by asking what the data can be and what produces it: a count in a fixed interval is Poisson; a continuous positive measurement with a peak and a tail is usually log-normal; a proportion is bounded and is usually modelled with something other than a normal because a normal can produce a value above one. Central limit theorem: the sum of many independent draws, whatever their individual distributions, approaches a normal as the number of draws grows. This is why the normal is the workhorse of statistics and it is worth understanding the reason rather than the slogan: it is not that the data is normal, it is that averages become approximately normal regardless of what is being averaged. And then the two traps that a beginner meets immediately and that a professional meets in disguised form forever. A distribution is a model, and a model is wrong somewhere. Every fitted distribution is wrong in the tails, and the tails are exactly where the expensive decisions live — a risk model that is right about typical cases and wrong about the tail produces a company that fails during the one event that mattered. Real data is a mixture. A distribution fitted to all your users describes an average of several populations, and a mixture that is unimodal overall can be composed of several distinct groups, so the fit is excellent and the segments are wrong.

/* A distribution, and the two requirements. */
const REQUIREMENTS = ['the probabilities are NON-NEGATIVE', 'they SUM TO ONE'];
const VOCABULARY = [
  { t: 'SUPPORT', is: 'where the distribution is NON-ZERO',
    whyFirst: 'a distribution with a DIFFERENT SUPPORT has completely different behaviour' },
  { t: 'MEAN', is: 'the PROBABILITY-WEIGHTED AVERAGE',
    also: 'the centre of mass',
    and: 'a statement about the LONG RUN - the average of a very large number of INDEPENDENT SAMPLES converges to it' },
  { t: 'VARIANCE', is: 'the AVERAGE SQUARED DISTANCE from the mean',
    is: 'the measure of SPREAD that the mean alone CANNOT CAPTURE',
    awkward: 'it SQUARES THE DEVIATIONS so it is in DIFFERENT UNITS from the data',
    therefore: 'the STANDARD DEVIATION is the square root of the variance, and that is the number you usually SEE' },
  { t: 'MEDIAN', matters: 'it is NOT DISTORTED by a few EXTREME VALUES in a way the mean is' },
];

/* The shapes, each a statement about a different kind of world. */
const SHAPES = [
  { s: 'NORMAL', trait: 'symmetric, bell-shaped, with TAIL BEHAVIOUR that makes EXTREME EVENTS LESS LIKELY than intuition suggests' },
  { s: 'BERNoulli and BINOMIAL', trait: 'a SINGLE TRIAL, and a COUNT OF SUCCESSES in a fixed number of trials' },
  { s: 'POISSON', trait: 'a COUNT OF EVENTS in a fixed interval',
    is: 'the distribution of things that HAPPEN INDEPENDENTLY AT A CONSTANT AVERAGE RATE',
    instances: ['arrivals at a queue', 'errors per hour', 'typos per page'] },
  { s: 'EXPONENTIAL', trait: 'the WAITING TIME between Poisson events, and the distribution of things that DECAY',
    property: 'the MEMORYLESS property',
    means: 'a mathematical statement about why a queue that behaves exponentially KEEPS BEHAVING EXPONENTIALLY no matter how long it has been running' },
  { s: 'UNIFORM', trait: 'everything EQUALLY LIKELY',

28 · AI & Machine Learning Fundamentals

Machine learning flips ordinary programming around: instead of writing rules, you present labeled examples and the system infers the rule, from fitting a line to training a large model. The core loop is data, a model family, a loss function, and optimization by gradient updates. The chapter explains the real mechanisms behind supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, and generative methods so you can judge claims about modern AI by how they fit that loop.

28.1 What machine learning actually is28.2 Supervised learning by hand — linear regression28.3 The eternal trap: overfitting28.4 Neural networks — intuition without the mystery28.5 Large language models in 2026 — and how to stay honest28.6 Evaluating and any responsibility bar28.7 Transformers, attention & fine-tuning — the mechanics

A bachelor’s AI course introduces concepts you’ll then saw everywhere in industry: from autocomplete to fraud detection to the LLMs of 2026. This chapter gives you the actual mechanism — not vibes — and the honesty skills to evaluate it.

28.1 What machine learning actually is

Supervised learning maps inputs to labeled outputs from example pairs, unsupervised learning finds structure such as clusters in unlabeled data, reinforcement learning maximizes reward through trial and error, and generative learning models how to produce new data. Each answers a different question and needs different data, loss functions, and evaluation. A single framework of objective, model, and optimizer covers nearly all modern AI, including deep learning.

Classic programming: you write rules, data flows through, outputs come out. Machine learning flips it: you provide data + expected answers, and the system learns the rules. Why now? More data, cheaper compute, and better architectures (deep neural networks).

The framing that makes it a real skill

Machine learning is a specific kind of program, and the reason it needs its own vocabulary is that it is the kind of program where the behaviour is not specified — it is learned from examples. A conventional program is written by stating the rules; a learned program is written by stating an architecture and then supplying data and letting optimisation find the parameters that minimise a measured error. Everything that follows from that one sentence is what distinguishes the field from ordinary programming. You do not write the logic, you write the search. The program's behaviour is the result of an optimisation process over a parameter space, which means the output is a function of the data as much as of the code. You cannot know whether it works until you have measured it on data it has not seen, and the reason is not caution — it is that a system evaluated on its own training data is reporting its memory rather than its capability. There is no test for "correct"; there is only a measured error. And the failure mode is not a wrong answer but a confidently wrong answer on data unlike the training data, which is why the whole apparatus of splits and held-out data exists.

Then the three kinds of learning, and the distinction that actually matters is where the supervision comes from and what happens to the model. Supervised learning has labelled data: each example comes with the right answer, and the model learns a mapping from input to output. Classification predicts a category; regression predicts a number. It is the best-understood kind and the one where the evaluation machinery is mature. Unsupervised learning has no labels: the model is given data and asked to find structure, which means every objective is a modelling choice you made rather than a truth you were given — clustering assumes that points near each other belong together, which is an assumption and is false for data where similarity does not mean membership. Reinforcement learning has no labels at all: the model acts, receives rewards or penalties, and learns a policy maximising expected return. It is the hardest of the three because there is no fixed answer to compare against — the credit for an outcome has to be assigned to the actions that caused it, across possibly thousands of steps, which is the assignment problem the section on the algorithm addresses. And then the three axes along which any task is specified, which is the framework that makes the vocabulary useful. What is the input, and what are the features — because the representation determines everything downstream and

How the field got here, and what each advance actually changed

Six ideas account for almost all of the progress, and each solved a specific obstruction rather than being an increment on the previous one. The perceptron, 1958. A single neuron that learns a linear threshold, with a training rule derived from the loss. It worked on simple problems and was proved in 1969 to be incapable of learning anything requiring nonlinearity — the XOR problem — which stopped the field for roughly a decade. Backpropagation, rediscovered 1986. Efficient gradient computation through many layers, which is the piece that made depth possible, though the idea was found in a 1970 paper on a different model and the connection was made later. Convolutional networks, 1998 and later. Weight sharing and local receptive fields, giving translation invariance with far fewer parameters than a fully connected layer, and they solved image recognition by making the architecture match the structure of the data. Long short-term memory, 1997. A recurrent architecture with a gated memory cell that survives long intervals without the gradients dying, which made sequence learning practical. Transformers, 2017. Attention without recurrence, which removed the sequential dependency, made training parallelisable across the sequence, and produced the scaling behaviour the previous section described — attention was not better on every task, but it was better at scale, and scale turned out to matter. Large language models, from 2020. The observation that performance improves predictably with parameter count, data and compute, and that the improvement is not only in benchmark scores but in the emergence of capabilities that were not designed for — following instructions, writing code, reasoning about problems.

Then why it worked when it worked, because the honest answer is not the architecture. Three things had to be available together: enough labelled data from the internet, enough computation to train on it, and an algorithm that could use both. Any one of the three alone is not enough — data without compute is inaccessible, compute without an efficient algorithm is unaffordable, and an algorithm without data has nothing to learn from. The scaling observation is the empirical foundation, and it is worth stating as it was discovered: performance on a benchmark improves smoothly and predictably as a power law of the resources applied, over several orders of magnitude, which is unusual and which is what turned model building from an art into an engineering discipline with a budget. And the trend line has a shape that matters. Returns diminish as you scale further, so the cost of reaching a given capability falls while the cost of reaching the next one rises, and this is the honest answer to "will this continue" — the curve is not exponential and the useful capabilities cluster. Then the thing that is genuinely new and genuinely hard to reason about: capabilities that nobody trained for. A model trained to predict text is not trained to follow instructions, to write a function, or to solve a problem, and it does all of these. The honest position is that these behaviours are present in the data and become reachable at a scale that makes them expressible, and the consequences of that are the ones the ethics section has to address — a system whose capabilities you did not specify has properties you did not choose.

28.2 Supervised learning by hand — linear regression

Linear regression is supervised learning in its smallest complete form: pick a line of best fit by minimizing the squared distance from each labeled point to the prediction. You compute the prediction as weights times features, define a mean squared error loss, and solve or descend to the minimum. Deep learning keeps that exact loop, loss plus gradient updates, and only makes the learned function vastly more expressive.

# A model is just f(x) = w*x + b; "training" finds the best w,b.
# Least squares closed form: w = cov(x,y)/var(x)
import random, statistics

random.seed(7)
xs = [i for i in range(1, 21)]
ys = [3 * x + 2 + random.uniform(-3, 3) for x in xs]   # hidden truth: y=3x+2+noise

mean_x, mean_y = statistics.mean(xs), statistics.mean(ys)
w = sum((x - mean_x) * (y - mean_y) for x, y in zip(xs, ys)) / \
    sum((x - mean_x) ** 2 for x in xs)
b = mean_y - w * mean_x
print(f"learned: y = {w:.2f}x + {b:.2f}")   # should recover ~3 and ~2

predict = lambda x: w * x + b
print(predict(21))    # ~65: extrapolate to a brand-new input

Overfitting, underfitting, and the trade that governs everything

Every supervised model is balancing two errors, and the balance is the whole subject. Underfitting is a model too simple to represent the structure — a straight line through data that is clearly curved. Its error is high on both the training set and the test set, and the diagnosis is immediate: the model lacks capacity. Overfitting is a model so flexible it has memorised the training data, including its noise. Its error is low on the training set and high on the test set, and the diagnosis is the opposite: the model has more capacity than the data supports. The gap between the two errors is the diagnostic, and it is more informative than either number alone — a small gap with high error is underfitting, a small gap with low error is fine, and a large gap is overfitting regardless of how good the training error looks. And the mechanism behind overfitting is worth understanding precisely: the model has enough parameters to describe any function of the input, including a function that passes through every training point exactly, so the unlabelled degree of freedom is filled with noise. Then the three ways to control it, and each has a different character. More data — the only one that cannot fail and the slowest to arrive, because the noise has to be diluted rather than the capacity removed. Regularisation — penalising large weights, which is a statement that among functions that fit the data, you prefer the one that is smallest, and the penalty coefficient is how much you are willing to give up fit for simplicity. Reduce capacity — fewer layers, fewer units, stronger pruning, a smaller model, which is the honest answer when you have little data because the model you are using is too big for the amount of data you have.

Then the evaluation machinery, because a model without honest evaluation is a model with a guess attached. Split before you preprocess. Fit the scaler, the imputer, the encoder and every other learned transformation on the training portion only, then apply it to the test portion — fitting on the whole set leaks information about the test data into the training process, and it is the most common serious mistake in the field. Understand what your score means. For an imbalanced problem — a rare event where 99.5 per cent of cases are negative — accuracy is a trap, because a model that always says "no" scores 99.5 per cent and does nothing; the right measures are precision, recall, and the trade between them, plus the area under the precision-recall curve. Prefer a baseline before a model. Always fit the trivial predictor and report its number, because a complex model that does not beat it is a complex model that should be deleted, and no review will catch that for you. Cross-validate when data is small, rotating the held-out portion so every example has served as test data, because a single split on a thousand examples has enough variance to reverse a conclusion. And evaluate on the data the problem will actually meet, which is the failure that has produced retired models: a model evaluated on data from one hospital, one country or one period, and deployed into a population that differs in exactly the ways the evaluation could not see.

/* Two errors, and the trade. */
const UNDER = {
  is: 'a model TOO SIMPLE to represent the structure',
  example: 'a straight line through data that is clearly curved',
  error: 'HIGH ON BOTH the training set and the test set',
  diagnosis: 'the model LACKS CAPACITY',
};
const OVER = {
  is: 'a model SO FLEXIBLE it has MEMORISED the training data, including its noise',
  error: 'LOW on the training set and HIGH on the test set',
  diagnosis: 'the model has MORE CAPACITY THAN THE DATA SUPPORTS',
};

  use: 'the GAP BETWEEN THE TWO ERRORS, and it is MORE INFORMATIVE THAN EITHER NUMBER ALONE',

    'a LARGE GAP is OVERFITTING regardless of how good the training error LOOKS'],

  so: 'the UNLABELLED DEGREE OF FREEDOM is filled with NOISE',
};

/* Three ways to control it. */

  { m: 'REGULARISATION', does: 'penalising LARGE WEIGHTS',

  { r: 'SPLIT BEFORE YOU PREPROCESS',

  },
  { r: 'PREFER A BASELINE BEFORE A MODEL',

  { r: 'EVALUATE ON THE DATA THE PROBLEM WILL ACTUALLY MEET',
