This fits a line to noisy labeled data using the closed-form least-squares solution, recovering the hidden slope and intercept, then extrapolates to a brand-new input.

That’s the entire soul of supervised learning: minimise a loss function (here, squared error) over the data. Deep learning keeps this loop and makes f vastly more expressive (millions of learnable weights).

28.3 The eternal trap: overfitting

Overfitting means the model memorizes the training set instead of learning general rules, so training accuracy stays high while performance on new data collapses. You defend against it by holding out an untouched test set, controlling model capacity, using regularization such as weight decay or dropout, and checking a validation split during training. Cross-validation, early stopping, and a strict policy of never tuning on the test set keep evaluations honest.

A model that memorises the training data scores 100% on it and fails on new data — that’s overfitting. The machinery that keeps it honest:

  • Train/validation/test split (e.g. 70/15/15): tune on train, check on validation, final honest score on the untouched test set.
  • Bias vs variance: high bias = too simple (underfits); high variance = too flexible (overfits). Balance is the art.
  • Regularisation: penalty terms (L1/L2, dropout) that nudge weights small/simple.
  • Cross-validation: train several folds so the validation isn’t one lucky slice.
# The cardinal sin, in one glance:
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
train_score = model.score(X_train, y_train)     # 0.99 -- do not celebrate this
test_score  = model.score(X_test,  y_test)      # 0.61 -- THIS is the real number
# Only the test-set number means anything for the future.

This shows the cardinal sin at a glance: an excellent training score on the training set, while the test-set number is the only one that means anything for the future.

Leakage, drift, and the training-serving skew

Three failure modes that are worse than overfitting because none of them shows up as a bad score. Data leakage is information that should not be available at prediction time being available during training, and the mechanism is always the same shape: a transformation fitted on the full dataset before the split. Fitting a scaler on everything, filling missing values with a mean computed over everything, selecting features by looking at their relationship with the label across everything, or shuffling rows before splitting so that near-duplicates land on both sides — each of these puts test-set information into the training process, and each produces a model whose measured performance is a fiction. The rule is mechanical: the split is the first operation, and everything that learns anything is fitted after it on the training side only. And the subtle variant that survives a correct split: a feature computed from future information — a field describing what happened later, a total that includes a refund, a customer's lifetime value computed from their whole history when predicting whether they will churn next month. The score is excellent and the model is worthless, because at prediction time that number does not exist. Concept drift is the world changing after training, and it is a different problem because the model was correct when it was built. It is handled by monitoring — comparing the distribution of the input on live traffic against the distribution in training, and watching the performance metric itself — and by retraining, which is a permanent operational commitment rather than an event. Training-serving skew is the same computation performed differently in the two places, and it is the most expensive of the three because the model file is identical and the bug is in the code around it. It appears when the training pipeline joins two tables and the serving path calls an endpoint, when training uses a feature computed at midnight for the whole day and serving computes it on the fly, or when a feature was renamed and one code path was updated.

Then what to do about it, and the practices in order. Build the split into the pipeline as a non-optional step, so that leaking is not something you remember to avoid but something the code makes impossible. Have a feature store with one definition per feature, used by training and serving alike, which is the only structural fix for training-serving skew and the reason that component exists as a category. Write down for every feature where it comes from and when it is available, — the "available at" timestamp — because a feature you cannot place in time is a feature you have leaked. Monitor input distributions in production, not just outputs, and alert on a shift rather than on an absolute value, because no single distribution has a natural alarm threshold. Keep a shadow deployment running the current model on live inputs without affecting decisions, so that when you do retrain you can compare the candidate against the incumbent on real data before switching. And treat every score as provisional until it survives contact with data from a different period — the honest test is whether the number holds up on last month's traffic, and a number that only worked on the data it was selected on was never a measurement.

/* Leakage. */
const LEAKAGE = {
  is: 'INFORMATION THAT SHOULD NOT BE AVAILABLE at prediction time being available DURING TRAINING',
  mechanism: 'always the same shape - a TRANSFORMATION FITTED ON THE FULL DATASET before the split',
  instances: ['fitting a SCALER on everything',
    'filling MISSING VALUES with a mean computed over everything',
    'SELECTING FEATURES by looking at their relationship with the label across everything',
    'SHUFFLING ROWS before splitting so that near-duplicates land on both sides'],
  consequence: 'each of these puts TEST-SET INFORMATION into the training process, and each produces a model whose MEASURED PERFORMANCE IS A FICTION',
  rule: 'the SPLIT IS THE FIRST OPERATION, and everything that learns anything is FITTED AFTER IT on the training side only',
  survivesACorrectSplit: 'a FEATURE COMPUTED FROM FUTURE INFORMATION',
  examples: ['a field DESCRIBING WHAT HAPPENED LATER', 'a TOTAL that includes a refund',
    'a CUSTOMERS LIFETIME VALUE computed from their whole history when predicting whether they will CHURN NEXT MONTH'],
  symptom: 'the score is EXCELLENT and the model is WORTHLESS, because at prediction time that number DOES NOT EXIST',

/* Drift. */
const DRIFT = {
  is: 'the WORLD CHANGING after training',
  difference: 'a DIFFERENT PROBLEM, because the model was CORRECT when it was built',
  handledBy: ['monitoring - comparing the DISTRIBUTION OF THE INPUT on live traffic against the distribution in training',

  and: 'retraining, which is a PERMANENT OPERATIONAL COMMITMENT rather than an event',
};

Leakage horror stories: scaling the test data with train statistics, sorting before the split, including the label as a feature ("airport near the crash" model). Data scientists' job interviews revolve around these traps. Split before any preprocessing.

28.4 Neural networks — intuition without the mystery

A neural network is a stack of matrix multiplications and nonlinear activation functions that turns raw input into features and then into predictions. Training uses backpropagation to compute the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight, and gradient descent updates those weights to reduce the loss. The same mechanism powers image classifiers, speech systems, and large language models, differing only in data, size, and architecture choices.

A neural network is a stack of matrix multiplications with nonlinear twists (W₁·x+b₁, squashed by relu, then W₂·…). Training loops:

  1. Forward pass: compute predictions (a whole bunch of matmuls).
  2. Loss: how wrong are they?
  3. Backpropagation: chain rule backwards through the matmuls — gives each weight the slope of the loss (Ch. 27.4's derivative).
  4. Gradient descent step: nudge every weight down its slope.
  5. Repeat a few hundred thousand times on GPU-shaped batches.
# Mini perceptron: one neuron, the basic building block
import math
def perceptron(x, w, b):
    z = sum(wi * xi for wi, xi in zip(w, x)) + b
    return 1 if z > 0 else 0            # activation: fire or not

# AND gate: w=[1,1], b=-1.5
w, b = [1.0, 1.0], -1.5
print(perceptron([0, 0], w, b), perceptron([0, 1], w, b),
      perceptron([1, 0], w, b), perceptron([1, 1], w, b))   # 0 0 0 1
# Stack many of these with nonlinearities and you get a "deep" net.

The neuron, and why depth is what makes it work

A neuron is three steps: take a weighted sum of the inputs, add a bias, and pass the result through a non-linearity. That is the entire unit, and the whole of a neural network is a wiring of these. The weighted sum is the unit's memory of what matters. Each input has a weight saying how much it should count, and a weight learned to be large means that input strongly influences this unit's output. The non-linearity is what makes stacking work, and the previous chapter's argument is the reason it exists: without it, a layer is an affine map, and composing affine maps gives an affine map, so depth buys nothing. Training adjusts the weights. The gradient tells you how much each weight contributed to the error, and the optimiser moves each one against that gradient — and note what this means: training is not choosing among candidate programs, it is moving a few thousand numbers in a direction that reduces a measured error. Then why depth changes what a network can represent, and the honest mechanism. Each layer builds features out of the previous layer's features. The first layer can detect edges; the second can detect corners and curves made of edges; the third can detect shapes made of curves; the fourth can detect parts of objects made of shapes. Each layer widens the class of functions the network can express, and the intuition that a wide layer computes many features at each step while a deep layer composes more steps is why depth empirically buys more expressive power than width at equal parameter count. And the last layer is a plain linear map because the output is a number or a set of scores — putting a non-linearity there restricts the outputs for no benefit, since a probability is produced afterwards.

Then why it works at all, and the two arguments that explain the phenomenon without over-claiming. The universal approximation theorem says a network with one hidden layer of sufficient width can approximate any continuous function on a compact domain. That is a statement about capacity, not about learning, and the distinction is the one that trips people up: it says the function is representable, not that optimisation will find it, and a one-layer net that can in principle represent a perfect classifier is in practice a worse classifier than a deep one because optimisation has not succeeded in finding it. Deep networks are unusually good at the functions that matter — images, text, audio — and the honest reason is partly empirical: natural data has hierarchical structure, and a hierarchy of features maps onto a hierarchy of layers. The other reason is that composition is a good inductive bias, which is a statement about what happens when you use a generic architecture on data with the right structure. And then the three things that limit it, which are worth knowing because they are what a chapter on applications has to work around. Data hunger: a network has far more parameters than a hand-written rule, and parameters you cannot determine need data. Opacity: there is generally no way to state why it produced an answer, which is a real problem in the regulated domains and the reason the ethics section exists. And optimisation difficulty: non-convex landscapes, gradients that vanish or explode with depth, and the sensitivity of the result to initialisation and to the learning rate — which is why training is finicky in a way ordinary software is not.

/* Three steps. */

This is a single neuron that fires above a threshold, correctly computing an AND gate, and stacking many such neurons with nonlinearities yields a deep network.

28.5 Large language models in 2026 — and how to stay honest

In 2026 large language models are massively scaled next-token predictors now used as grounded engineering components with tool calling, retrieval, and structured outputs. Treat them as unreliable pieces of a pipeline to verify with tests and evals rather than as oracles. Best practice is to pin versions, give them narrow scopes, validate their outputs programmatically, and keep a fallback path for when the model is unavailable.

  • Mechanically: a huge transformer predicts the next token given context, trained on internet-scale text. All the "reasoning" you experience is next-token prediction at massive scale plus alignment training.
  • Usable today: they’re tools — code completion, drafting, summarising. The skills that keep compounding are: prompt engineering, retrieval (RAG) to ground answers, eval harnesses, and — above all — verifying output (tests on generated code, human review on generated prose).
  • Risks are engineering problems: hallucination, prompt injection ("ignore your instructions"), bias, privacy, model collapse. Journalists hype them; engineers build guardrails.

    • From a model to a product, and what changes

    A language model is a next-token predictor; a product built on one is an interface to a system that is confident, fast, and wrong in a specific way, and the gap between those two things is where the engineering is. Prompting is a programming surface with no types, and the properties that follow explain most of what practitioners complain about. The same prompt produces different output. That is not a bug being worked around — it is inherent, because the model samples, and the sampling parameters — temperature, top-p, presence penalty — are controls on the distribution rather than on the output. Order matters and nobody knows how much. Instructions placed before long context are followed more reliably than instructions placed after it, because the attention mechanism weights recency, and this is a property of the architecture rather than a tuning issue. Small wording changes cause large behaviour changes, and there is no reliable way to predict which ones. Long context degrades in the middle, — information at the beginning and end of a long context is used better than in the middle, which is why the practical pattern is to put the important material at both ends and to retrieve rather than include everything. And the model has no way to tell you what it does not know, which is not fixable by prompting and is the reason retrieval exists.

    Then the four components that turn a model into something you can put in front of users, and each solves a different failure. Retrieval: fetch relevant documents, put them in the context, and instruct the model to answer from them. This addresses the knowledge-cutoff problem and is the single most valuable addition to almost any product — because it moves the facts out of the weights and into a document you control, which also means you can delete and update them. Tool use: let the model call functions — search, a database query, an HTTP request — so it can act rather than only describe. This addresses the "it cannot know today's data" problem properly, and the engineering is mostly about making each tool's contract unambiguous and about the failure mode that comes with it, which is that a tool call can be confidently wrong. Structured output: constrain the output to a schema and parse it. This is not cosmetic: a system that must write to a database or call an API needs a parseable answer, and free-form prose has to be parsed by a second model, which is where most of the unreliability comes from. Guardrails: validate input and output, enforce rate limits, and check that the response complies with policy before it reaches a user. And then the four things that decide whether any of it works, and none of them is the model. Evaluate before you ship and keep evaluating after. A set of real prompts with known-good answers, run on every change, is the only thing that distinguishes an improvement from a rearrangement. Watch cost and latency as first-class metrics, because output length is a lever you can control and cost per request is often dominated by it. Keep the model away from decisions it should not make, — the outputs are suggestions until something deterministic has checked them. And know what you cannot fix:

    Retrieval, and why it is not an optimisation

    Retrieval-augmented generation is the most valuable single addition to almost any language-model product, and the reason is not accuracy — it is that it moves knowledge out of the weights and into documents you own. That has three consequences that nothing else in the stack provides. You can delete and update it. A fact in the weights cannot be removed without retraining, cannot be corrected without a new training run, and cannot be verified against a source; a fact in a document can be edited, version-controlled and audited. Answers become attributable. A system that cites a specific document can be checked by a person, and a system that cannot be checked is a system whose errors have to be discovered by users. And the knowledge stops being the bottleneck. A model's weights represent a compressed, undated, all-purpose summary of text; your documents are precise, current and scoped to what you actually need to know. Then the pipeline, and each stage has a specific failure. Chunking decides what can be found at all. A chunk too small loses the context that makes it interpretable; a chunk too large dilutes the embedding with unrelated text and retrieves worse; and a chunk that splits a table or a definition across a boundary retrieves a fragment. Embedding decides what matches. A dense embedding captures semantic similarity and is strong on paraphrases; a keyword index captures exact terms, product codes and names, which is exactly what dense retrieval is worst at. Most production systems use both and combine the scores, and the reason is that a user searching for an error code needs the exact string. Reranking decides what reaches the context, and it matters more than people expect because a model's context is small: retrieving twenty candidates and reranking to the best three is far better than putting twenty in the context, where the weakest passages dilute attention and can cause the model to answer from the wrong one. And then the failure modes that this fixes and the ones it does not. Retrieval fixes being wrong about facts you have documents about. It does not fix reasoning errors, arithmetic, or the model's tendency to blend two sources into a claim that appears in neither. And it introduces new ones: retrieval failure is silent — a system given no relevant passage will answer from its weights without saying so, so a relevance threshold and a refusal behaviour are not optional, and documents become attack surface, because text in a retrieved document is text the model reads, which is the mechanism behind prompt injection through retrieved content and the reason retrieved documents must be treated as untrusted input.

28.6 Evaluating and any responsibility bar

On skewed data raw accuracy misleads, so evaluation must use precision, recall, and ROC-AUC, which separately report how much the model catches and how much it mistakes. High-stakes applications add fairness metrics across groups, explainability such as feature attribution, and an audit trail of the data and decisions. Choosing the right metric is a responsibility decision: it decides who pays when the model is wrong.

  • Metrics: accuracy lies at skewed classes (99.9% spam-free: a "predict all spam" model scores 99.9%!). Use precision/recall/F1 and ROC-AUC, and choose the right one per cost (missed fraud vs false-flagged fraud).
  • Fairness: biased training data → biased model. If the data you train on discriminates, the model will too. "Blind" features don’t fix it (zip code proxies race).
  • Explainability & audit: for hiring, loans, medicine — "the model said no" is not a defence. Log decisions, monitor drift, keep humans in the loop.

    • The four obligations, and what each requires of a system

    Machine learning raises ethical questions that are not new — fairness, privacy, accountability and transparency are old concerns — but it changes their shape, because a decision that used to be traceable to a person is now traceable to a function of data, and a person cannot be the answer. Fairness is the obligation that a system's outcomes should not be systematically worse for a group, and the difficulty is technical rather than rhetorical: the criteria are mutually incompatible. You cannot simultaneously have equal error rates across groups, equal calibration across groups, and equal selection rates across groups — this is a mathematical result about what the word "fair" means when made precise, not a political claim. So a team must choose a definition, state it, measure it, and accept that they have made a trade-off; a team that has not chosen has chosen by accident, and the choice was made by whoever wrote the training data. Privacy is the obligation that a person's data is not used beyond what they agreed to, and the specific hazards are technical. Training data memorises. A sufficiently large model can be induced to reproduce individual training examples verbatim, and with a name, an address and a rare medical condition in the training set, that output is a disclosure regardless of intent. Inference is a disclosure too: a model that can answer "does this person have diabetes" from their features has already inferred it, whether or not it was trained on that specific record. And a model is a permanent disclosure surface, because it cannot be deleted from — the way a row can be deleted from a database.

    Then accountability and transparency, and the reason they are the hardest. Accountability means a named person or organisation is answerable for an outcome, and the difficulty is that a model produces an answer no one intended. Explainability means being able to state why, and there are three levels of honest claim. Post-hoc explanation — a separate method that produces a plausible story about a decision after the fact — is the weakest and by far the most commonly offered, and the problem is that the explanation is of the explainer's behaviour, not the model's, and a plausible story is what you get. Intrinsic interpretability — a model whose structure is legible, a decision tree, a small linear model, a rule list — gives a real answer at the cost of predictive power. Mechanistic interpretability — tracing what the network's internal representations actually correspond to — is genuine progress and is still early. And then the practices that make these obligations real rather than aspirational. Log every decision with its inputs, its output and the model version, because an unlogged decision is one nobody can investigate. Monitor for drift on both the inputs and the outcomes, and know that the outcome monitor is the only one that detects a fairness violation. Keep a human in the loop for consequential decisions — and be honest that "in the loop" is often decorative, which is true when the human does not have the information or the time to disagree. Have a way to contest a decision, which means the person affected can see it, understand roughly why, and have it reviewed; a system that cannot be contested is one that has removed the accountability. And write down what the system will not be used for, before it is built, because

    The law, and the practical obligations it creates

    Regulation has arrived in stages and the direction is consistent, which is itself informative: the obligations are about process and documentation, not about the model. The European Union's AI Act is the broadest, and its shape is a risk-tiered structure — prohibited uses (social scoring, certain biometric categorisation, untargeted facial-image scraping), high-risk uses with substantial obligations, transparency obligations for systems that interact with people or generate synthetic content, and minimal obligations for everything else. The GDPR's relevant mechanisms are narrower and have been in force long enough to apply: purpose limitation — collect and use data only for stated purposes; data minimisation — do not collect what you do not need; the right to an explanation of automated decisions, which is the one with real technical teeth and which most systems cannot satisfy; profiling transparency, so a person knows they are being profiled; and the general principle that a data subject's rights survive the processing, which includes deletion and which is in direct tension with a trained model. That tension is worth spelling out because it is the clearest example of the law and the technology being in genuine conflict: deleting a row from a database is a bounded operation; deleting a person's influence from a trained model is not, and the industry answers are either retrain without the data — expensive — or accept that the deletion was incomplete and document it. Then the three practical obligations that follow for anyone deploying a model, and each is engineering rather than policy. Document what the system does. A model card: what it was trained on, what it is intended for, what it is not intended for, measured performance including subgroup performance, and known limitations. The value is that writing it forces the gaps to be noticed, and the second-order value is that it is what you hand to a regulator, a customer or a journalist. Assess impact before deployment, and the useful version is a list of affected groups, plausible harms, and the mitigations for each — which again is valuable mostly because the gaps are visible when you write them down. And keep human oversight that can actually override, which means the reviewer needs access to the case, authority to change the outcome, and time to think — and if the model's output is already the only information in front of them, the oversight is notional.

  isInformative: true,
};

28.7 Transformers, attention & fine-tuning — the mechanics

Attention lets every token in a sequence compute a weighted contribution from every other token, removing the distance bottleneck of older models and enabling parallel training, which is why it revolutionized natural language processing. Pretraining fits a base model to predict text at huge scale; fine-tuning adapts that model to a task; and alignment such as RLHF shapes its behavior into a helpful assistant. Retrieval and tool use then ground its answers in real data.

Every 2026-era LLM runs the same core: a transformer. Its magic is attention: each token looks at every other token and decides how much weight to give it. That one idea — sequence-wide interaction instead of left-to-right RNN memory — is the entire revolution.

# Attention in one picture: sentence, each word asks others
# "how relevant am I to you?" and mixes weighted reprequences.
   ["The", "bank", "eroded", "the", "river", "bank"]
# query[bank] × key[river] high  -> "bank" pays attention to "river"

# The pipeline you'll build on:
#  PRETRAIN  (huge text, next-token prediction, weeks of GPUs)
#    -> base model: predicts text, follows no instructions well
#  FINE-TUNE  (curated instruction answer pairs) -> behaves like an assistant
#  ALIGNMENT (RLHF / preference) -> helpful, honest, safe-ish, refusal-y
# That's why "just ask ChatGPT" ≠ "build a product": the base + tuning
# pipeline, the eval harness, and the serving infra are the actual work.

# Engineering terms to know cold:
#  tokens (≈4 chars English) -> context window (max tokens at once)
#  temperature / top-p (sampling creativity), system prompts
#  embeddings + vector search / RAG (Ch.35) for grounding with your data
#  fine-tune vs prompt-engineer: fine-tune changes behavior durably;
#  prompting is cheap and reversible -- try prompts first

This comment block sketches attention with a concrete sentence, the pretrain-fine-tune-alignment pipeline, and the engineering vocabulary that surrounds real LLM products.

An LLM has no fact-checker — it outputs patterns. Products that ship raw model output ship confabulated citations (Ch.26-style trust work applies to engineers too). Ground, verify, evaluate, and never let "the model said so" bypass a test.

Attention, and why it displaced everything else

Attention is a mechanism for deciding what to look at, and the reason it displaced recurrent networks is a single property. Attention computes, for each position, a weighted average of every position, where the weights come from the data. Recurrent networks process tokens one at a time, so relating two tokens far apart requires carrying information through many steps, and information degrades and gradients vanish over distance. Attention relates any two positions directly, in one step, so the path length between any two tokens is constant — which is the whole architectural advantage, and it is why a transformer handles a long document where a recurrent network handles a sentence. Then the mechanism, in four parts, because each part answers a question. Query, key and value: each position produces three vectors from its own representation. The query is what this position is looking for; the key is what this position offers; the value is what it would contribute if wanted. Scores: the dot product of a query with every key, scaled by the square root of the dimension, which keeps the values in a range where the following softmax does not saturate. Weights: those scores through a softmax, giving a probability distribution over positions — this is the attention map, and it is the one thing about a transformer you can actually look at and interpret. Output: the weighted sum of the values. And then the two design decisions that made it work at scale. Multi-head attention runs several of these in parallel with different projections, so different heads can attend to different relationships — one head for the previous token, one for the syntactic dependency, one for a coreference far away — and this is why the number of heads is a parameter rather than a detail. And positional information has to be added explicitly, because attention is permutation-invariant: without a position encoding, "the dog bit the man" and "the man bit the dog" produce identical attention weights, since attention only knows about which positions relate, not what order they were in.

Then the rest of the architecture, and each part is there for a reason. Residual connections around every sublayer so that gradients have a path straight through, which is the structural answer to vanishing gradients in a deep stack. Layer normalisation applied to each sublayer's output, which stabilises training and is one of the details that had to be right for depth beyond about a dozen layers to train at all. Feed-forward sublayers between attention blocks, the same dense transformation at every position, and their presence is what gives the network its capacity — attention moves information between positions, and the feed-forward sublayer is what processes the information at each position. Decoder-only versus encoder-decoder: the encoder half reads the input bidirectionally and the decoder half generates one token at a time while attending to the encoder's output; a decoder-only model attends to what it has generated so far and nothing else, and that asymmetry is why it is both simpler and better at generation. And then the costs, honestly, because they are what a deployment has to plan for. Attention is quadratic in sequence length, since every position attends to every other, so doubling the context quadruples the work and the memory — which is the entire motivation for the sparse and efficient variants that approximate it. Attention is constant in depth rather than linear in sequence, so it scales better with sequence length but worse with depth, and depth is expensive in memory. And the model does not know what it does not know, which is the practical consequence of a loss computed over the next token: it optimises for plausibility, and a confident, fluent, wrong answer is exactly what an optimised next-token predictor produces.

/* The mechanism. */
const ATTENTION = {
  does: 'for each position, a WEIGHTED AVERAGE OF EVERY POSITION, where the weights come from the DATA',
  whyItWon: 'a RECURRENT NETWORK processes tokens ONE AT A TIME, so relating two tokens far apart requires CARRYING INFORMATION THROUGH MANY STEPS',
  and: 'information DEGRADES and GRADIENTS VANISH over distance',
  transformerAdvantage: 'attention relates ANY TWO POSITIONS DIRECTLY, in ONE STEP, so THE PATH LENGTH BETWEEN ANY TWO TOKENS IS CONSTANT',
  consequence: 'which is why a transformer handles a LONG DOCUMENT where a recurrent network handles a SENTENCE',
};

/* Four parts. */

  { p: 'QUERY, KEY and VALUE',

29 · Distributed Systems, Advanced

Distributed systems is what happens when software spans many machines: partial failure, coordination, and consistency become the dominant problems, plus the family of patterns that contain them. This material anchors most senior and staff interview rounds because it turns systems intuition into a checklist. Key ideas include consensus, replication, distributed transactions, time and clocks, and resilience patterns, each with named techniques you can reach for.

29.1 When to go distributed (and when not to)29.2 Replication and the consistency menu29.3 Consensus: how machines agree (Raft, simplified)29.4 Distributed transactions: 2PC vs the saga29.5 IDs, clocks and time in a distributed world29.6 The resilience pattern shelf

Beyond one server: what breaks when software is spread across machines, and the established patterns for making it still work. This is the final frontier of most software engineering careers — and the core of "senior" interview rounds.

29.1 When to go distributed (and when not to)

Distribution is a cost you accept only when you buy something concrete: scale past one machine’s limits, independence for separate teams to ship, or resilience against whole-region failure. For most applications, including the large majority of web backends, a single well-run database and a monolith remain the correct, cheaper answer. The mature move is to start simple and let a measured requirement, not fashion, push you onto a distributed architecture.

Distributed systems add cost: harder debugging, new failure modes, latency, teams. The triggers that justify it:

  • One machine cannot hold or serve all the data.
  • Independent teams must deploy independently.
  • You need availability across a whole region failing.

What actually gets harder when you split a service

The honest accounting starts with what a network call costs you relative to a function call, because every difficulty below follows from that number. A network call is roughly a thousand times slower than a memory read and fifty to a hundred times slower than a function call — and it can fail, it can be slow, and it can succeed after you have given up. So the split replaces a local call that cannot fail with a remote one that can, and every design decision that follows is about handling that. Transactions stop working across the boundary. A database transaction cannot span two databases, which means either a distributed transaction with its own blocking and failure modes, or the compensation pattern the previous sections describe — and this is the single most damaging consequence of a split, because it converts "do these three writes atomically" into "do these three writes and write code that undoes them". Debugging gets harder in a specific, describable way. You cannot attach a debugger across the boundary; a request that crosses four services produces a trace rather than a stack; and the failure moves from an exception you can catch to a partial state you have to infer. Network calls inside a loop become the dominant cost — the same N-plus-one defect from the API chapter, but now the loop is over the network, so a hundred iterations is a hundred connections. Deploying becomes coordinated, because a change spanning two services is a change that cannot be deployed atomically, so you are back to the compatibility problem the rolling-update section described. Local development gets worse — five services means five terminals or a compose file with a dozen parameters. There is more code and it is mostly not yours, because every boundary needs serialisation, a client with retries and timeouts, error translation, and monitoring that somebody has to own.

Then the decision, and the discipline worth having is that you should not be able to state the problem a split solves. That is the test in the chapter's warning and it is a good one, because a split made for a reason you cannot name is a split made for the appearance of the reason. The three legitimate reasons, and they are genuinely different. Independent scaling requirements: one part of the system needs ten times the capacity of the rest, and paying for the whole system at that ratio is the reason to separate them — this is the strongest reason and the one that is measurable today. Independent release cadence and team ownership: parts change at different rates or belong to different teams, and coordinating their releases is the cost being removed. Different resource profiles: one part needs a database and long-lived connections and the rest needs to scale to zero between requests, and running both on the same infrastructure forces the worst of both on the rest. And then the three answers that are usually better than a split. Modularise the monolith first — put clear internal boundaries and a rule that a module may only reach another through its interface; then the split is a deployment change rather than a rewrite, and a module that is already well separated is a service that can be extracted. Keep it in one process and scale it horizontally — a stateless service scaled to six instances behind a balancer solves the capacity problem with none of the costs, and if the component is genuinely stateless this is strictly better. Use a queue or a shared store to decouple rather than a boundary — most of the coupling people split to remove is temporal, and a queue removes temporal coupling without a network hop in the request path. And the discipline that follows: measure the problem first, and let the split be the last response rather than the first.

};

What a split looks like in practice, and what it replaces

Before splitting anything it is worth being concrete about the two shapes, because the choice between them is where most of the difficulty lives. Modular monolith: one deployable unit containing several modules, with the boundaries enforced by language or build tooling — a private visibility modifier, an interface-only export, a package boundary. The property you get is that a module cannot reach another without going through its interface, and the cost is that everything ships together and scales together. Services: several deployables, each with its own process, data store and release cycle, communicating over the network. What you get is independent scaling and independent deployment, and what you pay is the entire list above. And the middle option, which is usually right: modular monolith now, services later, where the modules are designed so that the future split is a deployment change — each module owns its data access, talks to others only through its interface, and has no shared tables with anything else. That is a real design constraint, not a slogan: the discipline is a table has exactly one owner module, and a module that needs another's data goes through that module's interface. Systems that follow it are extractable in a week; systems that do not are rewritten.

/* Two shapes. */
const SHAPES = [
  { s: 'MODULAR MONOLITH', contains: 'several MODULES in ONE DEPLOYABLE',
    boundaries: 'ENFORCED BY LANGUAGE OR BUILD TOOLING - a private visibility modifier, an interface-only export, a package boundary',
    propertyYouGet: 'a module CANNOT REACH another without going through its interface',
    cost: 'everything SHIPS TOGETHER and SCALES TOGETHER' },
  { s: 'SERVICES', contains: 'several DEPLOYABLES, each with its OWN PROCESS, data store and release cycle',
    communicates: 'OVER THE NETWORK',
    gains: ['INDEPENDENT SCALING', 'INDEPENDENT DEPLOYMENT'],
    pays: 'the entire cost list above' },
];

/* The middle option, which is usually right. */
const MIDDLE = {
  shape: 'MODULAR MONOLITH NOW, SERVICES LATER',
  condition: 'the modules are DESIGNED SO THAT the future split IS A DEPLOYMENT CHANGE',
  how: ['each module OWNS ITS DATA ACCESS',
    'talks to others ONLY THROUGH ITS interface',
    'has NO SHARED TABLES with anything else'],
  isA: 'a REAL DESIGN CONSTRAINT, not a slogan',
  theDiscipline: 'A TABLE HAS EXACTLY ONE OWNER MODULE, and a module that needs anothers data GOES THROUGH THAT MODULES INTERFACE',
  payoff: 'systems that follow it are EXTRACTABLE IN A WEEK; systems that do not are REWRITTEN',
};

The old monolith is still the right answer for 95% of Web apps. Microservices as a fashion statement creates the "distributed monolith" — network calls that behave like function calls but can’t be debugged. Ask "what problem does splitting solve?" before splitting.

29.2 Replication and the consistency menu

Replication copies data to multiple nodes for durability and read scalability, and it forces a consistency choice per feature, from linearizable at the strong end to eventual at the weak end, with guarantees such as read-your-writes in between. The classic recipe is leader-follower: the leader takes writes, followers serve reads, and routing reads through the writer gives read-your-writes. Quorum-based operations let you dial the freshness and durability trade per request.

What each model guarantees, and how to choose

Consistency models are promises about what a reader will observe, and the useful thing about them is that they are ordered by strength rather than by adjective — so you can read down the list and stop at the weakest one that satisfies your requirement. Linearizable: the operation appears to take effect instantaneously at some point between invocation and response, so every read sees the most recent completed write. It is the strongest and the most expensive, and it requires a quorum per operation. Sequential: all operations appear in one order consistent with each client's own program order, but that order need not match real time — so two non-overlapping operations may be ordered either way, which is a distinction that only matters under concurrency. Causal: operations that happened after each other are seen in that order; concurrent operations may be seen in any order. This is the model human reasoning about causality actually expects, and it is where most products stop. Read-your-writes: after your write, you see your write. Monotonic reads: a reader never sees a value go backwards. Eventually consistent: no promise beyond convergence — every replica reaches the same value if writes stop, and the time it takes is the convergence delay. And then why the strong ones cost something, which is a statement about latency rather than about correctness. A read that must be certain has to wait for a write to be certain, and waiting is the latency you were trying to avoid — so a strong model is as much a statement about how long a read may take as about correctness. Coordination is not free: even on one machine, two participants agreeing costs an exchange, and a majority protocol costs a round trip for the participants beyond the first. Availability is reduced: a node that cannot reach a quorum must refuse, and refusing is the correct behaviour under a strong model, which means such a system degrades by returning errors rather than by returning stale data. And the engineering burden, which is rarely mentioned and is the real cost — a strongly consistent distributed store is considerably harder to build and to operate than one that converges, and its failure modes are stranger.

Then how to choose, and the discipline is shorter than the theory. Ask what a user would consider a bug. If a user would be confused or harmed by seeing stale data, that path needs more than eventual consistency — and the ones that always qualify are a payment, a balance, an inventory count, a permission check and a one-time token. If a user would merely find it odd, eventual consistency is fine and you should add a small affordance: a "just now" label, a spinner, a refresh. Use the strongest model at the smallest scope that needs it. A global strong model to protect one balance is enormously more expensive than a strong check on that one value, and the strong version is usually a conditional write — a compare-and-set, a unique constraint, a local transaction — rather than a distributed consensus protocol. Pick consistency per operation, not per system. A real system is a mixture: the account balance is strict, the product description is eventual, the follower count is eventual with read-your-writes for the person who pressed the button. And then what to do about the delay, because it is not acceptable on its own. Read-your-writes, achieved by writing to the node you will read from, or by pinning the user to a replica until they see their own write. Monotonic reads, achieved by pinning a client to one replica for a session, which is simple and removes a whole class of confusing behaviour. And make the delay visible, because a spinner that resolves in half a second and one that resolves in three seconds are different experiences, and the design that shows the user something meaningful during the wait is the one that gets tolerated.

/* Ordered by STRENGTH rather than by adjective. */

Quorums, and the arithmetic behind every availability number

Almost every availability and latency figure in a distributed system is a consequence of quorum arithmetic, and the whole calculation is three lines. For n replicas, the write quorum is w and the read quorum is r, and the condition for consistency is r + w > n. The reason is that the read quorum and the write quorum must overlap in at least one replica, and with n replicas they overlap only if their sum exceeds n. Everything else follows. For a five-node cluster, n = 5 and w = 3, so a read quorum of 3 also gives consistency — this is the configuration that gives you both consistency and four of five replicas available, and it is the default because 3 + 3 = 6 > 5 leaves one replica of slack in each direction. Raising the write quorum makes reads cheaper and writes more expensive; lowering it does the reverse. And a 3 + 2 configuration is also consistent, because 3 + 2 = 5 is not greater than 5 — it is not, and this example is worth doing because it shows what the strict inequality is for: with n = 5, w = 3, r = 2, a write could be applied to three replicas and a read could be served by the two that did not receive it, so a stale value is possible, which is exactly the bug the quorum inequality exists to prevent. Then the three things quorums give you that people are surprised by. A quorum can be reached from any combination of replicas, so a read may be served by any node that has a sufficiently up-to-date value — which is what allows reads to be served locally rather than only by the leader. The overlap replica is what makes the value "committed", so the number of replicas that must be durable is a quorum, not one, and this is why a write is acknowledged only after a quorum has persisted it. And the availability number is derived, not configured: with a five-node cluster and a three-node quorum, the system tolerates two failures — and with a three-node cluster and a two-node quorum, it tolerates one, which is the arithmetic behind the odd-number rule the previous section named. Then where the model and the quorum interact, which is the part people get wrong. A read served by a lagging replica violates the consistency you assumed, even though the quorum arithmetic was satisfied — the quorum guarantees the write is durable somewhere, not that every replica has it. Read repair is the mechanism for catching a lagging replica up: when a read is served by a node whose value is older than the version the read quorum confirms, that node is updated as a side effect of serving the read. And the consistency model you choose is a statement about which operations use which quorums — a system can be strongly consistent for its ledger and eventually consistent for its catalogue in the same deployment, and the architecture is the decision about which operations get the expensive quorum and which do not.

/* The calculation. */
const QUORUM = {
  inputs: 'for n replicas, the WRITE QUORUM is w and the READ QUORUM is r',
  conditionForConsistency: 'r + w GREATER THAN n',
  why: 'the read quorum and the write quorum MUST OVERLAP in at least one replica, and with n replicas they overlap ONLY IF their sum EXCEEDS n',
  everythingElseFollows: true,
};

/* Worked: five nodes. */
const FIVE = {

  gives: ['CONSISTENCY', 'FOUR OF FIVE replicas available'],
  isTheDefault: true,
};

The canonical pattern is leader-follower replication: all writes hit the leader; followers copy and serve reads. If the leader dies, follow a failover plan (promote a follower) — but "who is leader now" must be agreed, which is where consensus arrives.

29.3 Consensus: how machines agree (Raft, simplified)

Raft makes a group of machines agree on an ordered log despite crashes: it elects a single leader, replicates entries to a quorum, and commits once a majority has stored them. You adopt it rather than implement it, through etcd or ZooKeeper, which provide the consensus primitive for leader election, distributed locks, and shared configuration. The price is a quorum round trip per decision and multiple nodes, typically three or five, to tolerate failures.

Machines "agreeing" is harder than it looks — messages drop, machines stall, and "majority of what?" matters. Raft (2014, now the standard taught in classes) solves it with elections + logs:

  1. Nodes are follower / candidate / leader; they elect a leader by majority vote.
  2. The leader appends commands to a replicated log, and a command is committed once a majority quorum (not all) has it.
  3. Minority failures are survivable: a 3-node cluster survives 1 failure; a 5-node survives 2.

How Raft actually works, and why you should adopt it rather than build it

Three mechanisms, and each solves a specific problem that a previous section's attempt created. Terms and the leader. Time is divided into numbered terms. Each term has at most one leader, and the leader is elected by a majority. A server's state carries the term it last saw, and any message from an older term is rejected — a single monotonic counter that resolves every stale-message problem at once, which is the design decision that makes the rest tractable. Election safety. Within a term there is at most one leader, which follows from the majority requirement: two leaders would each need a majority, and two majorities intersect. Log replication. The leader maintains a log of commands. Append entries carry the previous log index and term; a follower rejects an entry whose previous entry does not match its own, and that consistency check is what guarantees the logs stay identical in the overlap region. Commit by majority. An entry is committed once it is stored on a majority, and the rule that matters is that a leader may only commit entries from its own term directly; entries from earlier terms become committed implicitly. Without that restriction a leader could overwrite a committed entry — the exact bug the previous versions of the protocol had. The state machine safety rule — if a log entry has been applied, no other entry with the same index can ever be applied — then follows from the replication and election rules, and it is the property that makes the whole thing a database.

Then what a client actually experiences, because this is where the abstract becomes a set of engineering obligations. Reads are the surprising part. A read on a follower may return stale data, because the leader may have committed a write the follower does not yet have. There are three correct options and each is a different cost: read from the leader, which is simple and puts every read on the leader; use the read-index protocol, where the follower asks the leader for its current commit index and confirms it has that entry before reading, which is correct and cheap and costs a round trip; or lease-based reads, which are fast but require assuming bounded clock drift and are the source of some very bad bugs. Writes must go through the leader, and a client that needs to be certain its write is durable waits for the leader's commit — and the read-your-writes guarantee for a client means pinning its reads to the leader or carrying the term. A client that cannot reach the leader fails rather than reading stale data, which is the availability consequence the consistency section established and which is correct but which applications are always surprised by. Membership changes need care, because adding a server changes every quorum calculation, and the standard approach is a joint configuration where decisions require majorities of both the old and the new set. And then the operational reality, which is why the recommendation is to adopt. Consensus code is the code you should never write. Its correctness argument spans pages, its failure modes are exotic, and the bugs that do exist appear under partition and reordering that your test suite will not produce. The systems to adopt are etcd, ZooKeeper and Consul, and they differ in more than API. Then what the chapter is really for: understand the quorum arithmetic because every operational decision depends on it — how many nodes to run, what happens when you lose one, when you can safely replace it. Understand that consensus has a real latency price, because every write syncs to a majority before it is acknowledged, and that price is why a five-node cluster in one data centre and a three-node cluster per region are both common and neither is a mistake. Do not put anything in it that does not need to be consistent — consensus state is the most expensive place a byte can live, and configuration, coordination and leader election belong there while everything else belongs in a database. And remember it is a coordination tool, not a store: reading a large range of keys from it is possible and is a mistake.

Failure, recovery, and how to reason about whether the cluster is healthy

Every consensus system fails in the same small set of ways, and being able to name them is most of what you need to operate one. Network partition. The cluster splits, or a minority does. The majority side continues; the minority side stops accepting writes because it cannot reach a quorum, and it is correct to refuse — so a symptom of a partitioned minority is that a service's reads start failing even though its database is fine, and the diagnosis is quorum arithmetic rather than an application bug. Leader loss. The leader dies or is slow, a new one is elected, and every client that was talking to the old one must reconnect. This is a brief unavailability and it is why client-side retry with backoff is not optional. A slow node that has not failed. This is the nastier one: a node that is reachable and slow rather than down, which means it may have received a write and not responded, which means the client retried, which means the leader may have received the same write twice — so the slow-node case is the practical source of the duplicate-write problem, and the idempotency key is what makes it harmless. Slow clock or paused process. A node that was paused long enough for its leases to expire can come back believing it still holds a lease it has lost, which is the exact scenario the fencing tokens in the lock structure exist to defeat. And then what recovery looks like, and why it is boring. State is recovered by replaying the log. A node restarting replays its log to reconstruct its state machine, which is why a large log means a slow restart. A snapshot is a checkpoint of the log, so that recovery does not have to replay everything from the beginning; the discipline that makes snapshots safe is that the snapshot is only taken at an index the leader has committed, and entries after it are retained, so a snapshot never discards something that was not durably decided. Membership changes use a joint configuration and take effect at a term boundary, because changing the quorum while the old configuration is still in force is the operation that has broken more than one implementation. Then the health checks, which are the three questions worth having. Is there a leader, and is its term advancing? A cluster with a leader whose term is not moving is partitioned or stuck, and nothing is writable. Can every node see the same commit index? A node lagging by a large amount means the cluster is making slow progress, which is a capacity problem and not a correctness one. And is there always a majority available? — because if the answer is no, then the availability of the entire system is zero regardless of how healthy the application looks, and that is the single number worth having on a dashboard.

/* The failure set. */

    correct: 'it is CORRECT TO REFUSE',
    symptom: 'a service whose READS START FAILING even though its DATABASE is fine',
    diagnosis: 'QUORUM ARITHMETIC rather than an application bug' },

You never hand-roll Raft — you adopt etcd/ZooKeeper/Consul, which provide it. What you must internalise: quorum arithmetic, and that consensus has a real latency price (every write syncs to a majority).

29.4 Distributed transactions: 2PC vs the saga

Two-phase commit gives distributed transactions atomicity across services, but it blocks on prepare, holds resources, and becomes fragile when a coordinator fails mid-flight. Sagas instead break a transaction into local steps and run compensating actions, guided by orchestration or choreography, for any step that fails, with idempotent operations making retries safe. Real products usually ship sagas plus an outbox pattern for exactly-once effect, accepting eventual consistency in exchange for availability.

Two-phase commit (2PC), the "classic" way:
   coordinator  ->  "prepare?" to every participant   (voting round)
   participants ->  "yes" (lock everything, promise), or "no"
   coordinator  ->  "commit" ONLY if ALL said yes; else roll back all
   Cost: slow, blocks on lock-holding, and the coordinator is a SPOF.
   Used inside databases; miserable across services.

The Saga alternative (microservice-friendly):
   a purchase: [create order] -> [reserve stock] -> [charge card] -> [ship]
   each step committed NORMALLY; if any fails, run compensating steps:
   [refund card] -> [unreserve stock]
   Trade-off: no global atomicity (brief inconsistencies window) that you
   handle with compensating actions + idempotent steps (Ch. 18.7).

What a distributed transaction has to give up, and why

Two-phase commit coordinates participants through a coordinator, and its structure explains why it is used less than the textbooks suggest. The first phase is prepare: every participant is asked whether it can commit, and each one does all the work it can — writes flushed, locks held, constraints checked — and then votes. Crucially, a participant that votes yes is now unable to abort, because it has promised. The second phase is commit: the coordinator tells everyone to commit, and each one finishes. The properties that matter are the good ones and the bad ones. It is atomic: all participants commit or all abort. It is durable: a participant that has voted yes must commit even if the coordinator dies immediately afterwards, which is what the write-ahead log gives it. And then the three costs. It blocks. If a participant votes yes and the coordinator then dies before telling it what to do, the participant holds its locks and cannot proceed — indefinitely — because it is not permitted to abort. It has to wait for a new coordinator to run recovery, which means the availability cost is not a small latency but an indefinite stall of every transaction touching that resource. The coordinator is a single point of failure. It must be highly available and it must be durable, which means a replicated coordinator, which is a consensus system, which means the coordinator is itself built on consensus — so the complexity does not disappear, it moves somewhere else and you now maintain two of it. And the participant must be online to hear the second phase. It has durably recorded its vote, so it can recover, but it needs someone to tell it, which adds a network round trip to every transaction and a recovery process for every restart.

Then the alternative and why it is the more common answer, because the comparison is the substance of the section. A saga splits the transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each of which commits normally, and defines a compensating transaction for each step. The difference in kind: two-phase commit gives you isolation by holding locks and waiting; a saga gives you isolation by ensuring intermediate states are not observable to others — a reservation that expires rather than a booking that persists. Each step commits locally and immediately, so nothing is held and nothing blocks, and a failure requires no rollback at all — only the compensating actions for the steps that already succeeded. And the compensating action need not restore the original state exactly; it must produce a state acceptable to the business, which is a more honest requirement than exact restoration and often the correct one. The three properties that follow and the failure that follows them. No isolation between steps, so a concurrent reader can see a half-finished saga, which is why every saga needs a way to make intermediate states invisible — a status field checked by every reader, or a reservation with an expiry. Eventual consistency across participants, which is the availability price. Compensations can fail, so a saga needs its own compensation of the compensation, and this recursion is why sagas are more code and more thought than a transaction rather than less. And the failure mode that catches people: a compensating action that is not idempotent, run twice by a retry, produces a different result than intended. So every step and every compensation needs an idempotency key, which is the same requirement from the API chapter arriving again — the recurring theme being that every technique that gives up atomicity buys it back with idempotency, and that is the real price of distribution.

This plain-text block contrasts two-phase commit, which blocks and has a single point of failure, with sagas that commit each step normally and call compensating steps to undo failures.

Industry verdict: sagas + idempotency + outbox patterns are how real distributed products behave acceptably; 2PC survives mostly inside single databases.

29.5 IDs, clocks and time in a distributed world

Distributed systems cannot trust auto-increment counters or wall clocks, because separate nodes can generate the same sequence and clocks skew, so they use UUIDs, snowflake identifiers, or logical clocks that stay unique and orderable without coordination. Wall clock time is unreliable for causality, so logical and vector clocks track order instead. Message delivery is commonly at-least-once, which is why consumers deduplicate by idempotent keys rather than assuming exactly-once delivery.

  • IDs: auto-increment breaks when many writers exist. Use UUIDv4 (random, unguessable, zero coordination) or snowflake-style (timestamp + machine id + counter — sortable at scale).
  • Clocks lie. NTP sync makes wall-clocks drift anyway; never order events by timestamps across machines. Instead: Lamport clocks or vector clocks give causal order, and hybrid clocks sort within one process.
  • At-least-once vs exactly-once: networks make "exactly once" nearly impossible; systems provide at-least-once + dedup (idempotency keys again) and call it good enough.

    • Identity, and the three properties a distributed system cannot have

    Two nodes cannot simultaneously guarantee three things, and the reason is worth deriving rather than accepting. Every message can be delayed, duplicated, reordered or lost. Not because the network is broken but because of ordinary behaviour: a sender does not know whether its message arrived, so it re-sends; a retransmission arrives after the original; two nodes processing concurrently cannot see each other's writes until they synchronise. Given that, suppose you want consistency — every node sees the same value in the same order. And availability — every request gets a response. And partition tolerance — the system continues to operate despite any message being lost or delayed. You cannot have all three: during a partition, the nodes on one side cannot know what the nodes on the other side decided, so either they answer — risking two nodes deciding differently — or they refuse — sacrificing availability. That is the same argument as the CAP chapter's, and its practical form is the CAP theorem: in a partitioned system you choose between returning a possibly-stale answer and refusing to answer. Two consequences that shape everything else. A majority is the only thing that resolves it, because two nodes cannot both claim to have the deciding value, so a decision requires agreement from a majority of the cluster, which is why every consensus algorithm has a quorum size of n/2 + 1 and why an odd number of nodes is preferred. And every consensus operation costs at least one round trip to a majority, which is the latency price that the last section of this chapter names.

    Then the two families and the difference, because choosing between them is the actual decision. Paxos and its derivative Raft solve the same problem with a different emphasis. Paxos is the original and the proof is famously hard to read; the protocol has multiple phases whose names do not communicate anything, and a single leader per log segment, and it is implemented by Zookeeper and, in its Multi-Paxos form, by etcd. Raft was designed to be understandable: the log is divided into terms, each term has a leader, and a server either agrees to append what the leader proposes or it does not, with three sub-problems — leader election, log replication, and safety — each of which fits on a page. The differences that matter in practice. Raft is what people implement, because an implementable protocol is one you can get right, and a protocol nobody can implement correctly provides no availability. Both require a majority for every write, so a five-node cluster tolerates two failures and a three-node cluster tolerates one — and the failure tolerance is n/2 − 1, which is why adding a third node to a two-node cluster takes it from zero tolerated failures to one, which is a larger improvement than adding a fifth, which is why odd sizes are the standard. Neither is fast on a wide area network, and the honest number is that a leader round trip is a few milliseconds in one data centre and tens to a hundred milliseconds across continents, which is why a global deployment partitions into regional clusters rather than running one consensus group worldwide. And neither gives you more than one consistent operation at a time per group, because a leader serialises writes — which is why systems that need high write throughput shard the key space and run an independent consensus group per shard.

    What you actually store in a coordination service

    The abstraction that makes these systems usable is that they are not databases — they are ordered logs plus ephemeral keys, and knowing which is which prevents almost every mistake people make with them. A key that is set, read and overwritten is the unit of coordination: a leader lease, a configuration value, a lock, a watch. A value that is only ever appended is the unit of durable history: an entry in a replicated log, from which state is derived by replaying it. The distinction matters because the two have very different cost and very different semantics. Appending is expensive and linearisable — it requires a quorum — while reading and writing a key is cheap and serialisable per key. This is why the correct pattern is few large appends rather than many small ones: updating a key a thousand times in a second is a thousand operations each paying the coordination cost, where appending one entry describing the desired state and having each node watch and apply it is one. And the four structures almost every system is built from, each worth naming because they are recognisable in any codebase that coordinates. A lock — exclusive, with a lease rather than a permanent hold, because a node that holds a lock and dies must not hold it forever; every correct lock implementation is a lease with a duration and an owner token, and the token exists so a process that paused long enough for its lease to expire cannot come back and release a lock someone else now holds. A leader election — a lease on a well-known key, where every contender competes to create the same key and only one succeeds; the consensus algorithm is generally doing this for you. A queue — an ordered log plus a cursor per consumer, which is why queue semantics on these systems are at-least-once: a consumer reads an index, processes, then advances the index, and a crash in between causes a redelivery, which is why every consumer must be idempotent. A watch or a broadcast — a way to be told when something changed rather than polling for it, which is what makes configuration change propagate in milliseconds instead of on a timer.

    /* The abstraction. */

29.6 The resilience pattern shelf

Each resilience pattern targets a specific failure class: timeouts and retries with jitter handle transient errors, circuit breakers stop calls to failing services, bulkheads isolate one bad component into its own pool, and backpressure pushes load to the producer instead of the overwhelmed consumer. Combined with idempotency and graceful degradation they form the standard robustness toolkit. Chaos engineering, deliberately killing components in production-like environments, then proves the runbooks actually work.

PatternResponds toRecipe
Retries + backoff + jitterTransient failuresRetry 3× with growing delay + random jitter
Circuit breakerA dependency that’s down-hardAfter N failures, "open": fail fast without calling; half-open to test recovery
Timeout + deadlineHung dependenciesPropagate a deadline so slow calls don’t pile up
BulkheadingOne service hogs resourcesPer-service connection pools so a rogue client can’t exhaust everything
Queue backpressureLoad spikesMessage queue between producer/consumer; overflow → shed, don’t crash

Chaos engineering is the grown-up version: deliberately kill a node/zone in staging (and sometimes prod) and prove the runbooks work. Netflix’s Chaos Monkey started it; every serious platform runs failure drills.

The patterns, and the pressure each one absorbs

Each pattern exists because a particular pressure has a known shape, and knowing the pressure is more useful than knowing the name. Command: encapsulate a request as an object so it can be stored, queued, logged and retried. The pressure is asynchrony — work that cannot happen inline. What it buys is that a queue needs to serialise something, and a serialised command is a durable record of intent; what it costs is indirection through an object you now have to read to understand a code path. Event: publish a fact that something happened, with no knowledge of who reacts. The pressure is decoupling in time. What it buys is that a producer cannot be broken by a consumer being unavailable; what it costs is that the coupling has moved from the type system into the shape of the message, and a badly shaped event is a hidden interface that everything depends on. Retry with backoff: the pressure is transient failure, which is what the hardening chapter's retry section established — a call with no retry fails permanently on a one-second blip. Idempotency key: the pressure is at-least-once delivery, which is what every queue provides, so a retry can duplicate a write and the key is how the receiver recognises the duplicate. Circuit breaker: the pressure is a dependency that is down. What it buys is that a failing dependency stops consuming your threads, connections and time, because after a threshold of failures the breaker opens and calls fail immediately without attempting the request. Bulkhead: the pressure is cascading failure, and the mechanism is partitioning your resources so that one exhausted pool cannot consume all of them. Outbox: the pressure is the atomicity gap from the consistency chapter — writing to the database and publishing a message cannot both be atomic, so you write both to the same transaction and a separate process publishes what is there. Saga: the pressure is a workflow spanning services, covered above. Sidecar: the pressure is shared infrastructure per service — a proxy for mutual TLS, tracing, retries — so each service does not implement it, at the cost of one more process per service and one more thing to debug. And then the distinction between the two most confused pairs, because getting these the wrong way round produces the wrong architecture. Command versus event: a command names a recipient and says do this; an event names nobody and says this happened. A command may have exactly one handler and its failure is the caller's problem; an event has zero or many handlers and its failure belongs to nobody, which is precisely why events require monitoring that commands do not. Concurrency versus parallelism: concurrency is making progress on several things by interleaving, which works on one core and applies to anything that waits; parallelism is doing several things at the same instant on several cores, which needs more hardware and applies to anything that computes.

/* Pressure first, name second. */

Anti-patterns, and how to recognise one in a codebase you did not write

Six, and each is recognisable from a symptom rather than from a name. The distributed monolith. Several services that must be deployed together because they call each other synchronously, which means you have paid for the network, the partial failure and the debugging cost and gained none of the independence — and it is worse than a monolith because now a single failure can take all of them down. The symptom is a change that requires coordinating several deployments. Chatty microservices. A logical operation becomes dozens of network round trips, so a page render that needs three data sources makes forty calls, and the latency budget is spent before the work begins. The symptom is a trace showing hundreds of spans for one user action. Shared database across services. Two services reading and writing the same tables, which means neither owns its data, neither can migrate independently, and every schema change is a cross-team coordination problem. The symptom is a service that breaks when a table it does not know about gains a column. The resilience theatre. Retries with no backoff, retries with no bound, circuit breakers that open on a single failure and never reset, timeouts longer than the caller's own timeout — all of which make an outage worse rather than better, and the retry section's argument in concrete form. The symptom is a dependency outage that takes down its callers. Consensus used as a database. Reading a large key range out of a coordination service, or storing application data in it because it is the one thing that is reliably consistent. The symptom is a coordination service whose memory usage grows with your data volume. Retrying non-idempotent operations. Covered several times in this chapter and the most expensive of the six: a retried payment that is not idempotent is a double charge, and the retry policy that caused it usually looked reasonable in review.

    symptom: 'a coordination service whose MEMORY USAGE GROWS with your data volume' },
  { a: 'RETRYING NON-IDEMPOTENT OPERATIONS', covered: 'several times in this chapter',
    mostExpensive: 'a retried payment that is NOT IDEMPOTENT is a DOUBLE CHARGE',
    and: 'the retry policy that caused it USUALLY LOOKED REASONABLE IN REVIEW' },
];
