30 · Data Engineering & Big Data

When one database can no longer cheaply answer analytical questions, a data platform grows around it: raw data is ingested, transformed, stored in a warehouse or lake, and served to analysts and models. This chapter covers how data is moved, shaped, and trusted at warehouse scale, including OLTP versus OLAP engines, pipelines, batch and streaming, and data quality. The goal is knowing which engine and pattern fits each workload.

30.1 Two worlds: OLTP vs OLAP30.2 The moving-data pipeline: ETL vs ELT30.3 Batch vs streaming30.4 Data quality, governance and the "data mesh" argument

When an organisation’s data outgrows one database’s cheap querying, a whole engineering practice appears: moving, shaping and serving data at warehouse scale. This is the "behind the dashboards" layer of every analytics, recommendation and ML pipeline.

30.1 Two worlds: OLTP vs OLAP

OLTP databases serve large numbers of small, transactional operations such as orders and account updates, and are tuned for low-latency row access with strong consistency. OLAP warehouses scan enormous column-oriented datasets to answer aggregate business questions and prioritize throughput. Knowing which world a workload lives in tells you which engine to reach for, and analytics should normally run against a warehouse copy rather than the production transaction database.

The two workloads, and why one database cannot serve both

Online transaction processing and analytical processing have opposite shapes, and the tension between them is the entire history of data engineering. A transaction is a small read or write of a few rows, arriving one at a time, from thousands of users at once, and each must be correct. It wants an index on every column it filters by, so the cost of a write is several index updates. It wants row storage, so a query that needs three unrelated columns touches three separate places on disk. It wants serialisable isolation, which means locking and retrying. And it wants durability, which means a synchronous write to a log before acknowledging — a deliberate, expensive choice made per transaction. An analytical query is a scan of millions of rows, usually by one user, usually occasionally, and it needs many columns. It wants no indexes, because a full scan of sequential storage is faster than a random walk through an index for a query touching most of the table. It wants column storage, so the four columns it needs are four contiguous reads. It wants to read a snapshot without blocking anybody. And it can tolerate being a few seconds stale. Every one of those is the opposite of the other, which is why trying to make one system do both means compromising on all of them: an analytical query on a transactional database does index lookups it does not need while holding a structure that makes them expensive, and a transaction on an analytical database pays for columnar scans on every write.

Then the two ways of solving it, and the trade-offs are sharper than they first look. One database, two models — a modern system with both a row store for transactions and a column store for analytics, automatically choosing per workload. This is genuinely good and the reason the answer is no longer "you must have two databases". Its costs: two engines means two things to tune, two failure modes and two sets of optimisation decisions, and the row and column copies can disagree unless the system guarantees when they are reconciled — which is usually on a schedule or on a threshold, and which means the analytical numbers can be stale in a way the transactional numbers never are. Two databases, with replication between them — a write goes to the transactional store and is also published to an analytical store. This gives full control over both shapes and a clean design, at the cost of the pipeline from the previous section: the copy is asynchronous, so the analytical store is always behind, and every consumer of the analytical numbers must accept that. And the subtle failure is worth naming: a schema change on the transactional store can break the analytical pipeline silently, because the pipeline fails, nobody reads that log, and the numbers quietly stop updating — which is why freshness of the analytical store is a thing to monitor rather than assume. Then the decision rule, and it is short enough to remember. If your analytical queries are occasional and touch the whole dataset, use one system and accept the query being slow. If they are frequent or your transactional workload is heavy, separate them. If your data is small enough to fit comfortably in memory, the whole question is usually moot — and a surprising number of production systems never leave that state, which is worth knowing because it means the architectural sophistication on offer is often solving a problem that has not arrived.

/* Two workloads, opposite in every respect. */
const OLTP = {

};

const DECIDE = [

  { if: 'your data is small enough to fit COMFORTABLY IN MEMORY', then: 'the whole question is USUALLY MOOT',
    note: 'and a SURPRISING NUMBER of production systems never leave that state',

Transactions, isolation, and what happens under contention

The transactional model exists because concurrency produces wrong answers that are not obviously wrong, and each isolation level is a specific promise about which wrong answers are permitted. A transaction is a group of operations that appear to others as a single unit. Lost update: two transactions read the same value, both compute, both write, and one write vanishes — the classic read-modify-write race, and the reason every framework's optimistic-concurrency mechanism exists. Dirty read: one transaction reads another's uncommitted write, and if that transaction rolls back, the reader has acted on data that never existed — which is why this is the failure that makes intermediate results useless for anything but a scratchpad. Non-repeatable read: a transaction reads the same row twice and gets different values because another transaction committed in between, which breaks the assumption that your own reads are consistent. Phantom read: a transaction runs a query twice and the second returns more rows, because a row was inserted between them and there was no lock on the gap. And the four levels, in increasing strength and increasing cost. Read uncommitted: no promises, and the only reason it exists is that it is marginally faster. Read committed: you never see uncommitted data, so dirty reads are impossible; non-repeatable reads are still possible. This is the default in most databases and in Postgres. Repeatable read: within your transaction you see the same snapshot, so non-repeatable reads are impossible; phantoms are still possible depending on the engine. Serializable: transactions appear to run one at a time, so none of the above can happen, at the cost of the most concurrency and a meaningful retry rate. Then the practical mechanisms, which is what you actually need. Pessimistic locking: take a row lock before reading it, so nobody else can touch it; correct and it holds the lock for the duration of the transaction, which under load is the mechanism behind most database contention. Optimistic concurrency: attach a version number to each row, include it in the update, and treat a zero-rows-affected result as a conflict — which is cheap because it takes no locks and fails only on actual conflicts. Advisory locks: application-level mutual exclusion where the database stores no state, which is what you use for "only one worker per tenant" style problems that are not row-shaped. And the two things that catch people: the deadlock, which the transaction chapter's ordering rule prevents, and lost updates in code that reads, decides and writes without a guard — which no isolation level prevents, because the whole point is that no other transaction has touched the row yet at the moment you read it. A guard is the only answer: a version column, or a conditional update.

/* Anomalies. */
const ANOMALIES = [
  { a: 'LOST UPDATE', detail: 'two transactions READ the same value, both COMPUTE, both WRITE, and one write VANISHES',
    note: 'the classic READ-MODIFY-WRITE RACE', and: 'the reason every frameworks OPTIMISTIC-CONCURRENCY mechanism exists' },
  { a: 'DIRTY READ', detail: 'one transaction reads ANOTHERS UNCOMMITTED write, and if that transaction ROLLS BACK the reader has acted on data that NEVER EXISTED',
    consequence: 'which is why this makes INTERMEDIATE RESULTS USELESS for anything but a SCRATCHPAD' },
  { a: 'NON-REPEATABLE READ', detail: 'a transaction reads the same row TWICE and gets DIFFERENT VALUES because another transaction committed in between',
    breaks: 'the assumption that YOUR OWN READS ARE CONSISTENT' },
  { a: 'PHANTOM READ', detail: 'a transaction runs a query TWICE and the second returns MORE ROWS',
    why: 'a row was INSERTED between them and there was NO LOCK ON THE GAP' },
];

/* Four levels. */
const LEVELS = [
  { l: 'READ UNCOMMITTED', promises: 'none', existsOnlyBecause: 'it is MARGINALLY FASTER' },

Why columnar wins in OLAP: a row store must read every byte of every row; a column store reads only the 2 columns you need, and compresses them brilliantly (same values repeat). 100× differences are normal. This is the same lesson as Ch. 10.4 — data lives in the layer you ask for.

30.2 The moving-data pipeline: ETL vs ELT

ETL transforms data before loading it into the warehouse, while ELT loads raw extracts first and performs the transformation inside the warehouse using SQL or engine-native transforms. The shift to ELT simplified pipelines, since loading is cheap and raw data stays permanently reusable, and modern warehouses made it fast. Tooling such as dbt plus a cloud warehouse like Snowflake or BigQuery is the common modern stack.

ETL: Extract -> Transform -> Load        (transform in a staging cluster)   # transform first
ELT: Extract -> Load -> Transform        (dump raw into the warehouse,   # load raw first
                                           transform there with its compute)

The ELT shift: warehouses got so fast/cheap that "store everything raw,
transform on demand (dbt)" beats pre-transforming. The payoffs:
 - raw data is never destroyed (re-analysis later is possible)
 - fewer brittle pipelines; the repo of logic (dbt/SQL) is versioned   # logic in git

Why extract-load-transform lost, and what replaced it

Extract-transform-load was the default for fifteen years, and the reason it lost is a single observation: the transformation logic was the part that changed, and it lived outside the data. The extract step copied data faithfully, the load step wrote it faithfully, and everything that encoded a business rule about what the data means sat in a script somewhere — untested, unversioned, and impossible to reproduce from the data alone. The consequence is the failure everyone lived with: you could not rebuild a report, because rebuilding it required re-running transformation code that had since changed. Load-first reverses the order. Extract and load the raw data unchanged, into a store with no opinions, and then transform it, in place, in that store, using transformations that live in the database, are tested, and are version-controlled alongside the code that reads the result. Three properties follow. The raw data is immutable and complete, so any question can be asked of it later, including questions nobody had when the data first arrived — which is the single most valuable property and the reason the approach is called a data lake rather than a warehouse. Every transformation is re-runnable, because it reads from raw and writes a derived table, so a bug in a transformation is fixed by changing it and re-running, not by migrating data. And the cost is storage, plus the operational burden of a store that holds everything in its least-processed form — which is why the modern version of this usually adds a small curated layer on top for the queries that run constantly.

Then the modern pipeline shape, and each stage is here for a specific reason. Ingest writes an append-only log of what happened. Immutable, so reprocessing is possible; ordered by a source timestamp rather than arrival time, because source order is the truth and arrival order is not. Transform is where the logic lives, in SQL in the warehouse, tested, and version-controlled — and the reason it is SQL rather than Spark is that a query engine can optimise it and the failure modes are familiar. Serve exposes only curated, tested outputs, which is what makes the raw layer safe: the people who use it do not query raw data, they query the tables that the transformation step produced and that someone has verified. And then the three decisions that determine whether this works in practice. How much history do you keep, and the answer is a retention policy with a reason, not "everything forever" — because the cost of the raw layer is linear in time and the value of old data is usually low. When does a table get recomputed, and the honest options are on a schedule, when the source changes, or when a consumer asks; on a schedule is predictable, on change is fresh, and asking is expensive per query and is right for expensive aggregates. And how do you know a transformation is correct, which is the discipline that separate pipelines have and sloppy ones do not: assert the things that must always be true — row counts within an expected range, no nulls in a key column, no negatives in a quantity, totals that reconcile to a source — and fail the pipeline when one does not, because a silent wrong number in a dashboard is worse than a failed job, since the first is believed and the second is noticed.

/* Why ETL lost. */
const WHY_ETL_LOST = {

  • Change Data Capture (CDC) (Debezium): watch the OLTP log and stream changes to downstream systems — no double-writing in the app.
  • Schema evolution: pick a serialisation with backward/forward compatibility (Avro with a schema registry) so a new column doesn’t break old consumers.

30.3 Batch vs streaming

Batch processing runs scheduled jobs over chunks of accumulated data, such as nightly dashboard refreshes, and is simple to make correct and cheap, with straightforward reruns. Streaming processes each event as it arrives, enabling live insights, but needs delivery guarantees such as at-least-once and more operational care. The choice trades latency against cost and complexity, and many systems combine both in a lambda architecture.

Batch versus streaming, and how to choose between them

Both are ways of getting data somewhere, and the difference is when the decision is made. Batch is a fixed schedule. Every night, or every hour, a job reads what has arrived, does the processing, and writes the result. The defining property is that the set of records is fixed at the start of the run, which makes everything else easy: the run can be retried from scratch, it can be tested against a snapshot, the output is exactly correct for the input it saw, and the resources required are known in advance because the volume is known. Streaming is continuous. Records are processed as they arrive, and each is handled independently or in small windows. The defining property is that the work is unbounded and its total volume is not known in advance, which makes the run not retryable — you cannot replay it without a record of what you already did — and makes correctness per record rather than per batch. Then the decision, and the criterion is latency, with two corollaries that people miss. If the answer to "how stale may this be" is measured in hours or days, batch is the better answer, because batch is simpler in every dimension: it is idempotent by construction, it can be inspected, it can be re-run, and a failure costs you the run rather than a continuous pipeline. If the answer is seconds or less, streaming is the only answer, and the complexity it brings is not incidental — it is inherent in the requirement. And the corollary that surprises people: a "stream" that is only consumed once a day is a batch job with extra machinery, and all of that machinery — checkpoints, exactly-once, late-event handling — is cost you are paying for nothing. Then the three failure modes unique to streaming, and each is a consequence of the unbounded, replay-free design. Late and out-of-order events. A record for 14:05 arriving at 14:07 must be handled without double-counting, which requires either idempotency keys or a windowed aggregation that can be corrected, and the second is why most streaming systems give you "at least once" rather than "exactly once" for the delivery itself. State grows. An unbounded stream with per-key state needs that state to be bounded, so windows have to expire and anything depending on all history has to be precomputed or abandoned. Failure mid-stream means partial output. A batch either completed or did not; a stream that failed after processing a million events has produced a million events' worth of output, so exactly-once semantics need either transactional writes to the sink or a reconciliation process that is effectively a batch job — which is why mature systems end up with both, running the stream for latency and the batch for correctness.

/* The difference is WHEN THE DECISION IS MADE. */
const BATCH = {
  is: 'a FIXED SCHEDULE',
  does: 'every night, or every hour, a job reads WHAT HAS ARRIVED, does the processing, and writes the result',
  definingProperty: 'the SET OF RECORDS IS FIXED AT THE START OF THE RUN',
  and: 'which makes everything else EASY',
  gains: ['the run can be RETRIED FROM SCRATCH', 'it can be TESTED AGAINST A SNAPSHOT',
    'the OUTPUT IS EXACTLY CORRECT for the input it saw',
    'the RESOURCES REQUIRED are known in advance because the VOLUME IS KNOWN'],
};
const STREAMING = {

  does: 'records are processed AS THEY ARRIVE, each independently or in SMALL WINDOWS',

const FAILURES = [

Schemas, and the decision that governs everything downstream

A warehouse schema is not a database schema and the differences are worth naming because they change what you can do. Denormalisation is the default rather than a sin, because an analytical query reads many rows and joins are the expensive part; duplicating a customer's name into a fact table means the query reads one table instead of three, and the cost is that the name exists in many places and must be refreshed when it changes. Star and snowflake are the two shapes. A star has a central fact table of measurements and dimension tables describing each dimension at that moment — the customer's region as it was on the transaction date, not as it is today — surrounded by denormalised dimensions, so a query joins one fact table to several small dimension tables. A snowflake normalises the dimensions against each other, which reduces duplication and makes cross-dimension consistency automatic at the cost of more joins. The star is usually right for a warehouse, for the same reason as the previous section's reasoning: the query is the thing you are optimising for, and a star optimises it by being flat. And then the design choices that matter most and are decided once. What is a fact and what is a dimension, and the test is whether the row records something that happened or something that describes. A sale, a page view, a temperature reading is a fact; a customer, a product, a date is a dimension. Grain, which is the single most important decision in the whole schema: what does one row represent, exactly? "One row per order line per day" and "one row per order line" are different tables and cannot be derived from each other without either a join or an aggregation, and a schema with an ambiguous grain produces every wrong number eventually. What you do with history — a slowly changing dimension of type 1 overwrites the old value, type 2 adds a row for each version, type 3 adds a new column; type 1 is wrong for anything historical because a report run today about last year will use today's values. And partitioning, which is not optional at scale and which the partition chapter's arguments apply to: partition by the column you filter on most, most often the date, so dropping old data is dropping a partition rather than deleting rows.

/* Not a database schema. */
const WAREHOUSE = {
  denormalisationIsTheDefault: true,
  because: 'an ANALYTICAL QUERY reads many rows and JOINS ARE THE EXPENSIVE PART',
  gain: 'duplicating a CUSTOMERS NAME into a fact table means the query reads ONE TABLE instead of three',
  cost: 'the name EXISTS IN MANY PLACES and must be REFRESHED WHEN IT CHANGES',
};

/* Two shapes. */
const SHAPES = [
  { s: 'STAR', has: ['a central FACT TABLE of measurements',
    'DIMENSION TABLES describing each dimension AT THAT MOMENT'],
    keyDetail: 'the CUSTOMERS REGION AS IT WAS ON THE TRANSACTION DATE, not as it is today',
    query: 'joins ONE fact table to SEVERAL SMALL dimension tables',
  },
  { s: 'SNOWFLAKE', normalises: 'the DIMENSIONS AGAINST EACH OTHER',
    gains: ['reduces DUPLICATION', 'makes CROSS-DIMENSION CONSISTENCY AUTOMATIC'],
    cost: 'MORE JOINS' },
];
const WHICH = 'the STAR is usually right for a warehouse, for the same reason as the oltp sections reasoning - the QUERY IS THE THING YOU ARE OPTIMISING FOR, and a star optimises it by being FLAT';

/* Decisions. */
const DECISIONS = [
  { d: 'WHAT IS A FACT and WHAT IS A DIMENSION',
    test: 'whether the row records SOMETHING THAT HAPPENED or SOMETHING THAT DESCRIBES',
    facts: ['a sale', 'a page view', 'a temperature reading'],
    dimensions: ['a customer', 'a product', 'a date'] },
  { d: 'GRAIN - the single most important decision in the whole schema',
    is: 'what does ONE ROW REPRESENT, exactly',
    example: 'one row per order line per day and one row per order line are DIFFERENT TABLES',
    consequence: 'and they CANNOT BE DERIVED from each other without either a JOIN or an AGGREGATION',
    failure: 'a schema with an AMBIGUOUS GRAIN produces every wrong number eventually' },
  { d: 'what you do with HISTORY', kind: 'a slowly changing dimension',
    types: [{ t: 'TYPE 1', does: 'OVERWRITES the old value', wrongFor: 'anything HISTORICAL' },
      { t: 'TYPE 2', does: 'ADDS A ROW for each version' },
      { t: 'TYPE 3', does: 'ADDS A NEW COLUMN' }],
    why1IsWrong: 'a REPORT RUN TODAY ABOUT LAST YEAR will use TODAYS VALUES' },
  { d: 'PARTITIONING', notOptional: 'at scale',
    by: 'the column you FILTER ON MOST, most often THE DATE',

  },

BatchStreaming
Unitscheduled jobs (hourly, nightly)continuous events (per-record-ish)
Latencyminutes → a dayseconds → sub-second
ToolsSpark (in-memory distributed compute), Airflow/dbtKafka (the event bus) + Flink / Kafka Streams
Great forbig transformations, ML training setsfraud alerts, live dashboards, CDC fans-out

Kafka semantics you’ll be asked about: topics (named event streams), partitions (parallel lanes; order guaranteed per partition), offsets (your place in the stream), consumer groups (a team of workers splitting partitions), and exactly/at-least-once delivery (Ch. 29.5 lessons). The "outbox pattern" (write events in the same DB transaction as the business change) makes your app its own reliable CDC source.

30.4 Data quality, governance and the "data mesh" argument

Data you cannot trust is worse than none, so teams enforce quality through contracts, schema validation, freshness checks, and lineage that shows where each value came from. Ownership is the governance core: someone is accountable per dataset, whether that lives in a central platform team or is pushed to domains in a data mesh. The data mesh debate is really about whether those contracts should sit with each business domain or with one shared central team.

  • Quality = contracts: schema tests, row-count/volume anomaly alerts, not null/uniqueness checks in the dbt layer, and a "data owner" per domain.
  • Governance = who may read what (row/column policies), retention rules, and lineage (which upstream produced this number) for audits.
  • Data mesh (the current ideology): each business domain owns its data products like a product team, instead of one central data team eating requests. Its honest status: good principles, expensive to implement — your course should teach you to evaluate it, not worship it.

The dimensions, and why completeness is the one nobody checks

Data quality has six dimensions and the reason it is worth being precise about them is that each has a different detection mechanism and a different fix. Accuracy: is it right? This is the hardest to establish and the most expensive, because ground truth often does not exist — you can know a customer's address is wrong by checking it, but you cannot know their date of birth is wrong without asking. Completeness: is anything missing? Consistency: does the same thing have the same value in two systems? Validity: does it satisfy its constraints — is that a valid date, is that column within its allowed set? Timeliness: is it current? Uniqueness: is it duplicated? Completeness is the one that gets skipped and it deserves an argument, because it is the most common real problem and the hardest to notice. A missing row is invisible. Every check you can write sees the rows that arrived and has nothing to say about the ones that did not, so a pipeline that has been dropping 5 per cent of events for a month produces plausible-looking data every day and the only symptom is that a number is a bit low. Silent drops have identifiable causes and each has a different signature: a parser that rejects malformed records and logs at a level nobody reads; a schema change that adds a required field and the ingestion code fills it with null rather than failing; a filter applied upstream that somebody narrowed; a rate limit upstream that returns fewer records and looks like a successful smaller response; a partition or shard that is read successfully by one consumer and missed by another. Only row counts catch these, and the fix is to compare the count at each hop against the previous hop, and to compare against a count from the source where one is available. Then validity, which is the cheapest to fix and the most often deferred. Validity constraints belong at the boundary, where data enters, and rejecting bad data there is far better than carrying it to every consumer: a row that violates its schema should fail loudly on arrival rather than become an empty string, a null in a non-nullable column, or a date that parsed into the wrong century. Quarantine, do not coerce. The pattern that keeps the boundary honest is: validate strictly, put rejected records somewhere with the reason, and let a human decide what to do with them — because a pipeline that coerces bad records into plausible values has converted a detectable problem into an undetectable one.

/* Six dimensions, each with a different detection and a different fix. */
const DIMENSIONS = [
  { d: 'ACCURACY', q: 'is it right', hardest: true, mostExpensive: true,
    why: 'ground truth OFTEN DOES NOT EXIST - you can check that an address is wrong, but you cannot know a date of birth is wrong WITHOUT ASKING' },
  { d: 'COMPLETENESS', q: 'is anything MISSING', skippedMost: true },
  { d: 'CONSISTENCY', q: 'does the same thing have the same value in TWO SYSTEMS' },
  { d: 'VALIDITY', q: 'does it satisfy its CONSTRAINTS - is that a valid date, is that column within its ALLOWED SET' },
  { d: 'TIMELINESS', q: 'is it CURRENT' },
  { d: 'UNIQUENESS', q: 'is it DUPLICATED' },
];

/* Why completeness is the one nobody checks. */
const COMPLETENESS = {
  mostCommonRealProblem: true,
  hardestToNotice: true,
  reason: 'A MISSING ROW IS INVISIBLE',
  detail: 'every check you can write SEES THE ROWS THAT ARRIVED and has NOTHING TO SAY about the ones that did not',
  consequence: 'a pipeline that has been dropping five per cent of events for a month produces PLAUSIBLE-LOOKING DATA EVERY DAY',
  onlySymptom: 'a NUMBER IS A BIT LOW',
  causes: [
    { c: 'a PARSER that rejects malformed records and LOGS AT A LEVEL NOBODY READS' },
    { c: 'a SCHEMA CHANGE that adds a required field and the ingestion code FILLS IT WITH NULL rather than failing' },
    { c: 'a FILTER applied UPSTREAM that SOMEBODY NARROWED' },
    { c: 'a RATE LIMIT UPSTREAM that returns FEWER RECORDS and looks like a SUCCESSFUL SMALLER RESPONSE' },
    { c: 'a PARTITION OR SHARD that is READ SUCCESSFULLY by one consumer and MISSED BY ANOTHER' },
  ],
  onlyDetection: 'ROW COUNTS CATCH THESE',
  fix: 'compare the count AT EACH HOP against the PREVIOUS HOP, and against a count FROM THE SOURCE where one is available',
};

/* Validity. */
const VALIDITY = {
  cheapestToFix: true, mostOftenDeferred: true,
  rule: 'VALIDITY CONSTRAINTS BELONG AT THE BOUNDARY, where data ENTERS',
  why: 'REJECTING BAD DATA THERE is far better than carrying it to EVERY CONSUMER',
  badRowBecomes: ['an EMPTY STRING', 'a NULL in a NON-NULLABLE column', 'a date that PARSED INTO THE WRONG CENTURY'],
  pattern: 'QUARANTINE, DO NOT COERCE',
  how: ['validate STRICTLY', 'put REJECTED RECORDS somewhere WITH THE REASON',
    'let a HUMAN DECIDE what to do with them'],
  why: 'a pipeline that COERCES BAD RECORDS into plausible values has CONVERTED A DETECTABLE PROBLEM into an UNDETECTABLE ONE',
};

Testing data, and the operations that keep it true

Data needs tests in the same way code does, and the tests are different in kind because they assert on things that are not deterministic in the way code is. Four kinds, each catching a different class. Schema tests assert the shape: the columns exist with the right types and nullability, and every table has its keys and its freshness timestamp. These are cheap and catch the most common break, which is a transformation that changed a column name and still runs because a permissive reader silently returned nulls. Expectation tests assert invariants that must always hold: a row count in a plausible range, no negative quantities, no nulls in a key column, referential integrity between the fact table and its dimensions, and totals that reconcile to a source system. The range assertion is the one that catches completeness, and it works because a real range exists — a day with 2 per cent of yesterday's traffic is either a real event or a partial ingestion, and both deserve an alert. Freshness tests assert that the data is recent, and they are the ones that catch the silent pipeline failures the previous section described: a pipeline whose last run succeeded, produced nothing, and reported success passes every other test. Consistency tests assert that the same fact agrees between the raw layer and the curated layer, which is what catches a transformation that has drifted. Then the operations, which are the difference between a pipeline that works and one that is quietly wrong. Make the pipeline idempotent, so re-running a date produces the same result rather than doubling it — which means deleting the target partition before writing, or writing to a temporary location and swapping, and the second is the one that survives a failure half way. Retain the raw layer long enough to rebuild everything from it, and treat that retention period as a hard operational requirement rather than an incidental cost setting. Monitor freshness and volume, not success, because success means the job exited zero and tells you nothing about what it produced. Make lineage visible: for any published table, be able to answer which transformation produced it, from which sources, on what schedule — and this is not bureaucracy, it is the only way to answer "why did this number change" during an incident. And have a rollback story that is not "re-run the job", because re-running a pipeline whose source data has since changed produces a different answer, so published tables need a snapshot of the run's output that can be restored while the underlying problem is diagnosed.

/* Four kinds of data test. */
const TESTS = [
  { t: 'SCHEMA tests', asserts: 'the SHAPE - the columns exist with the right TYPES AND NULLABILITY, and every table has its KEYS and its FRESHNESS TIMESTAMP',
    cost: 'CHEAP', catches: 'the most common break' },
  { t: 'EXPECTATION tests', asserts: 'INVARIANTS THAT MUST ALWAYS HOLD',
    examples: ['a ROW COUNT in a PLAUSIBLE RANGE', 'no NEGATIVE quantities',
      'no NULLS in a key column', 'REFERENTIAL INTEGRITY between the fact table and its dimensions',
      'TOTALS THAT RECONCILE to a source system'],
    theRangeOne: 'catches COMPLETENESS',
    whyItWorks: 'a REAL RANGE EXISTS - a day with two per cent of yesterdays traffic is either a REAL EVENT or a PARTIAL INGESTION, and both deserve an alert' },
  { t: 'FRESHNESS tests', asserts: 'that the data is RECENT',
    catches: 'the SILENT PIPELINE FAILURES the previous section described' },
  { t: 'CONSISTENCY tests', asserts: 'that the same fact AGREES between the RAW LAYER and the CURATED LAYER',
    catches: 'a TRANSFORMATION THAT HAS DRIFTED' },
];
const THE_ONE_THAT_MATTERS_MOST = 'a pipeline whose LAST RUN SUCCEEDED, PRODUCED NOTHING, and REPORTED SUCCESS passes EVERY OTHER TEST';

/* Operations. */
const OPERATIONS = [
  { o: 'make the PIPELINE IDEMPOTENT', gain: 're-running a date produces the SAME RESULT rather than DOUBLING it',
    how: ['DELETING the target partition before writing',
      'or writing to a TEMPORARY LOCATION and SWAPPING'],
    whichSurvives: 'the second is the one that survives a FAILURE HALF WAY' },
  { o: 'RETAIN the RAW LAYER long enough to REBUILD EVERYTHING from it',
    asA: 'a HARD OPERATIONAL REQUIREMENT rather than an INCIDENTAL COST SETTING' },
  { o: 'monitor FRESHNESS and VOLUME, not SUCCESS',
    why: 'SUCCESS MEANS THE JOB EXITED ZERO and tells you NOTHING about what it PRODUCED' },
  { o: 'make LINEAGE VISIBLE', for: 'any PUBLISHED TABLE',
    questions: 'be able to answer WHICH TRANSFORMATION produced it, FROM WHICH SOURCES, ON WHAT SCHEDULE',
    notBureaucracy: 'this is the ONLY WAY to answer why did this number change during an incident' },
  { o: 'have a ROLLBACK STORY THAT IS NOT re-run the job',
    why: 're-running a pipeline WHOSE SOURCE DATA HAS SINCE CHANGED produces a DIFFERENT ANSWER',
    therefore: 'published tables need a SNAPSHOT OF THE RUNS OUTPUT that can be restored while the underlying problem is diagnosed' },
];

  2. Compare batch vs streaming for: fraud alerts, monthly accounting reports, live sports scores — one sentence per decision.

31 · Web Engineering Deep: Performance, Rendering & Accessibility

This is the specialist web course: making pages fast on real networks by controlling exactly when bytes arrive and render steps run, and making them usable by everyone regardless of device or ability. Topics cover the critical rendering path, loading hints, cache correctness, service workers, Core Web Vitals, and accessibility against WCAG. Together they turn vague ideas of performance and inclusion into concrete budgets and checklists.

31.1 The critical rendering path31.2 Modern loading hints31.3 Cache correctness: the 100ms vs 1s story31.4 Service workers, offline and the app-like web31.5 The metrics teams actually run toward31.6 Accessibility you will actually be judged on

Ch. 17 taught you to build a frontend. This chapter is the specialist course: making it fast on real networks, understanding exactly when bytes arrive, and making it usable by everyone. These are the skills that separate "frontend developer" from "web engineer".

31.1 The critical rendering path

The browser fetches and parses HTML into the DOM and CSS into the CSSOM, builds the render tree, then lays out, paints, and composites pixels to the screen. Each blocking step delays first paint, so you remove work: inline critical CSS, defer or async scripts, and avoid render-blocking requests. Knowing where bytes and tasks sit in this path lets you target the exact step that keeps the first frame slow.

Browser: HTML bytes
  -> parse -> DOM tree
  -> CSS bytes -> parsed -> CSSOM          (render-blocking: no paint without it)   # blocks first paint
  -> combine DOM + CSSOM -> Render Tree
  -> layout (geometry) -> paint (pixels) -> composite (GPU layers)
  JS encounter: parser halts when it meets <script> (unless async/defer)   # blocks parsing
  -> which is why you put scripts at the end (or use defer)
The fastest request is the one you DON'T make; the second fastest is cache-hit.   # optimize requests

Every millisecond, and where the critical path actually goes

The path from bytes to pixels has fixed stages and the useful work is knowing which one you are paying for in each case. The network request — the browser resolves the name, opens a connection, negotiates TLS, sends the request, waits. On an existing connection this is one round trip; on a new one it is three or more, which is why connection reuse dominates and why HTTP/3's removal of the transport-level head-of-line blocking matters on a congested network. Parsing the HTML is incremental and is usually not the bottleneck, but a large HTML document does take real time to tokenise. Discovering subresources is the trap: the parser cannot know about a script or an image until it reaches the tag, so a stylesheet at the bottom of the document blocks everything that could have been discovered earlier, and this is why the stylesheet is a render-blocking resource found in the critical path while the script is not found until later. Parsing CSS and constructing the CSS object model is render-blocking and must complete before any layout can be computed, which is why an unoptimised stylesheet is disproportionately expensive. Preloading scanners exist to find subresources before the parser gets to them, which is why a preload hint for a stylesheet genuinely helps. Layout and paint is where the DOM is turned into geometry, and its cost is proportional to the number of elements the layout must consider — which is why a deeply nested page with thousands of elements is slow to lay out and why flattening the structure helps. Compositing and rasterisation is usually off the main thread, which is why animating a transform is cheap and animating a property that triggers layout is expensive. Then the four levers, in the order that actually pays, and the order is not by impact but by cost of doing. Send less. This is the largest lever by a wide margin and it is unglamorous: fewer requests through HTTP/2 multiplexing, smaller payloads through compression and by not shipping what is unused, and smaller images through the formats and sizes the responsive chapter covered. Get the critical resources earlier. A preload hint for the stylesheet, a preconnect to a third-party origin you will certainly need, HTTP/2 server push, and inlining the small amount of CSS needed for the first screen so the first paint does not wait for a stylesheet request at all. Do less JavaScript before the page is interactive. Deferred and module scripts, and the discipline of not shipping a framework's worth of code to render one page — which is where the front-end chapter's code-splitting argument lands. And do less main-thread work per event, which is what makes interactions responsive: yield to the browser between chunks of work, keep handlers short, and move computation off the main thread entirely when it is not synchronous DOM work.

/* The stages. */
const STAGES = [
  { s: 'the NETWORK REQUEST', does: 'the browser RESOLVES THE NAME, opens a connection, NEGOTIATES TLS, sends the request, waits',
    existingConnection: 'ONE ROUND TRIP', newConnection: 'THREE OR MORE',
    consequence: 'which is why CONNECTION REUSE DOMINATES',
    and: 'why HTTP/3s removal of the TRANSPORT-LEVEL HEAD-OF-LINE BLOCKING matters on a congested network' },
  { s: 'PARSING the HTML', incremental: true, usuallyNot: 'the BOTTLENECK',
    but: 'a LARGE HTML DOCUMENT does take REAL TIME to tokenise' },
  { s: 'DISCOVERING SUBRESOURCES', isTheTrap: true,
    why: 'the parser CANNOT KNOW about a script or an image UNTIL IT REACHES THE TAG',
    consequence: 'a STYLESHEET AT THE BOTTOM of the document BLOCKS EVERYTHING THAT COULD HAVE BEEN DISCOVERED EARLIER',
    and: 'which is why the stylesheet is a RENDER-BLOCKING RESOURCE found in the critical path while the script is not found until later' },
  { s: 'PARSING CSS and constructing the CSS object model',
    blocks: 'RENDER',
    because: 'it MUST COMPLETE BEFORE ANY LAYOUT CAN BE COMPUTED',
    consequence: 'which is why an UNOPTIMISED STYLESHEET is DISPROPORTIONATELY EXPENSIVE' },
  { s: 'PRELOADING SCANNERS', existTo: 'FIND SUBRESOURCES BEFORE THE PARSER GETS TO THEM',
    which: 'which is why a PRELOAD HINT for a stylesheet GENUINELY HELPS' },
  { s: 'LAYOUT and PAINT', does: 'the DOM is turned into GEOMETRY',
    costIs: 'PROPORTIONAL TO THE NUMBER OF ELEMENTS the layout must consider',
    consequence: 'which is why a DEEPLY NESTED page with THOUSANDS OF ELEMENTS is slow to lay out, and why FLATTENING THE STRUCTURE HELPS' },
  { s: 'COMPOSITING and RASTERISATION', offMainThread: 'usually',
    consequence: 'which is why animating a TRANSFORM is CHEAP and animating a property that TRIGGERS LAYOUT is EXPENSIVE' },
];

/* Four levers, in the order that pays. */
const LEVERS = [
  { n: 1, l: 'SEND LESS', largest: 'BY A WIDE MARGIN', unglamorous: true,
    how: ['FEWER REQUESTS through HTTP/2 multiplexing', 'SMALLER PAYLOADS through compression and by NOT SHIPPING WHAT IS UNUSED',
      'SMALLER IMAGES through the formats and sizes the responsive chapter covered'] },
  { n: 2, l: 'GET THE CRITICAL RESOURCES EARLIER',
    how: ['a PRELOAD HINT for the stylesheet', 'a PRECONNECT to a THIRD-PARTY ORIGIN you will certainly need',
      'HTTP/2 SERVER PUSH', 'INLINING the small amount of CSS needed for the FIRST SCREEN so the first paint does not WAIT FOR A STYLESHEET REQUEST at all'] },
  { n: 3, l: 'DO LESS JAVASCRIPT before the page is INTERACTIVE',
    how: ['DEFERRED and MODULE scripts',
      'the discipline of NOT SHIPPING A FRAMEWORKS WORTH OF CODE to render one page'],
    connectsTo: 'where the front-end chapters CODE-SPLITTING argument lands' },
  { n: 4, l: 'DO LESS MAIN-THREAD WORK per event', why: 'what makes interactions RESPONSIVE',
    how: ['YIELD TO THE BROWSER between chunks of work', 'keep HANDLERS SHORT',
      'move COMPUTATION OFF THE MAIN THREAD entirely when it is not synchronous DOM work'] },
];

It traces the browser’s path from HTML bytes to composited pixels and flags where CSS and JavaScript can block the first paint.

Three levers that dominate measurable speed: (1) fewer/smaller round trips (bundle, compress, lazy-load), (2) don’t block first paint (inline critical CSS, defer JS, loading="lazy" images), (3) cache aggressively (Ch. 14.7 headers).

31.2 Modern loading hints

Loading hints let you tell the browser to start work early: preconnect warms the connection to an origin, preload fetches a critical resource ahead of discovery, prefetch or prerender fetches likely-next pages, and defer or async change when scripts execute. Used well on the right resources they cut real latency. Used carelessly, such as preloading everything, they steal bandwidth from genuinely needed bytes, so each hint should target a measured bottleneck.

<!-- resource hints: tell the browser to start early -->
<link rel="preconnect" href="//api.example.com">  <!-- open the socket now -->
<link rel="dns-prefetch"  href="//cdn.example.com">   <!-- resolve DNS early -->
<link rel="preload" as="font" href="font.woff2" crossorigin>   <!-- current-page critical -->
<link rel="prefetch" href="/next-page-chunk.js">          <!-- idle-time grab -->

<!-- defer: fetch JS in parallel, execute after parse (the default modern choice) -->
<script defer src="app.js"></script>
<!-- async: execute ASAP when downloaded (independent widget scripts) -->
<script async src="analytics.js"></script>

These resource hints tell the browser which origins and files to fetch early, and defer versus async controls when the scripts execute.

Lazy loading, and the four ways it backfires

Deferring work is correct in principle and routinely makes pages slower, and the four ways are worth knowing because each looks like the feature working. Lazy loading below the fold shifts work into the viewport. The browser now downloads the image when it scrolls into view, which means the work happens at the moment the user is interacting — so a user who scrolls quickly triggers many downloads at once while trying to read, and a slow connection turns reading into waiting. The correct rule: lazy-load what is below the fold and unlikely to be reached, and never lazy-load anything the first screen needs, because the largest contentful element is very often the one you deferred. Deferred JavaScript moves execution rather than removing it. A deferred script runs before the DOM content is finished rather than during parsing, which unblocks the parser — but the total execution is unchanged and if it lands in the middle of the user's first interaction, the interactivity metric is worse, not better. Code-splitting is the real fix: not deferring the same work but not shipping it at all. Virtual lists trade latency for memory in a way that is invisible until it is not. A list rendering two thousand rows is slow to lay out and expensive to keep in memory; virtualising it means only the visible rows exist in the DOM, which is faster — but the height of the not-yet-rendered rows must be known or estimated, and a wrong estimate causes the scrollbar to jump as the user scrolls, which is worse than the original problem on a list of variable-height content. Deferred images without dimensions cause layout shift, which is the metrics section's third point: the space has to be reserved, which means the width and height attributes, or a fixed aspect-ratio box, and the only real fix is to specify dimensions rather than to defer. Then the two rules that make deferral safe. Defer by distance, not by section. A component is a poor unit of deferral because it appears on every page; an image or a component that appears on one page in four is a good one. And measure after. Every deferral is a guess about what matters, and a guess is worth testing: the layout and interaction metrics are the test, and the correct comparison is not "before and after adding lazy loading" but "with the image already below the fold on a fast connection", because the cases where it helps and the cases where it hurts are different cases.

/* Four ways it backfires. */
const BACKFIRES = [
  { b: 'LAZY LOADING below the fold SHIFTS WORK INTO THE VIEWPORT',
    detail: 'the browser now downloads the image WHEN IT SCROLLS INTO VIEW',
    consequence: 'the work happens AT THE MOMENT THE USER IS INTERACTING',
    so: 'a user who scrolls quickly triggers MANY DOWNLOADS AT ONCE while trying to read',
    and: 'a SLOW CONNECTION turns READING into WAITING',
    rule: 'lazy-load what is below the fold and UNLIKELY TO BE REACHED',
    never: 'never lazy-load ANYTHING THE FIRST SCREEN NEEDS, because the largest contentful element is very often the one you DEFERRED',
  },
  { b: 'DEFERRED JAVASCRIPT MOVES EXECUTION rather than REMOVING IT',
    detail: 'a deferred script runs BEFORE THE DOM CONTENT IS FINISHED rather than during parsing, which UNBLOCKS THE PARSER',
    but: 'the TOTAL EXECUTION is UNCHANGED',
    and: 'if it lands in the MIDDLE OF THE USERS FIRST INTERACTION, the interactivity metric is WORSE, not better',
    theRealFix: 'CODE-SPLITTING - not deferring the same work but NOT SHIPPING IT AT ALL' },
  { b: 'VIRTUAL LISTS trade LATENCY FOR MEMORY in a way that is INVISIBLE UNTIL IT IS NOT',
    detail: 'a list rendering two thousand rows is SLOW TO LAY OUT and EXPENSIVE TO KEEP IN MEMORY',
    good: 'virtualising it means only the VISIBLE ROWS exist in the DOM',
    but: 'the HEIGHT of the not-yet-rendered rows must be known or estimated',
    and: 'a WRONG ESTIMATE causes the SCROLLBAR TO JUMP as the user scrolls',
    which: 'is WORSE THAN THE ORIGINAL PROBLEM on a list of variable-height content' },
  { b: 'DEFERRED IMAGES WITHOUT DIMENSIONS cause LAYOUT SHIFT',
    points: 'the metrics sections third point',
    fix: ['the SPACE HAS TO BE RESERVED, which means the WIDTH and HEIGHT attributes',
      'or a FIXED ASPECT-RATIO BOX'],
    theOnlyRealFix: 'SPECIFY DIMENSIONS rather than to DEFER' },
];

/* Two rules that make it safe. */
const RULES = [
  { r: 'DEFER BY DISTANCE, not by SECTION',
    component: 'a POOR unit of deferral because it APPEARS ON EVERY PAGE',
    good: 'an image or a component that APPEARS ON ONE PAGE IN FOUR' },
  { r: 'MEASURE AFTER',
    because: 'every DEFERRAL IS A GUESS about what matters, and a guess is worth TESTING',
    theTest: 'the LAYOUT and INTERACTION metrics are the test',
    correctComparison: 'not before and after adding lazy loading, but WITH THE IMAGE ALREADY BELOW THE FOLD ON A FAST CONNECTION',
    why: 'because the cases where it HELPS and the cases where it HURTS are DIFFERENT CASES' },
];

preload vs prefetch vs preconnect are NOT synonyms — preload is for critical current-page resources, prefetch is for probable-future ones, preconnect warms origins. Using them wrongly can steal bandwidth from real needs.

31.3 Cache correctness: the 100ms vs 1s story

HTTP caching is a contract set by response headers, mainly Cache-Control with max-age plus conditional revalidation via ETag and Last-Modified, and one wrong header can serve stale content or expose private data. Assets get long immutable max-age with content hashing in the URL, HTML gets short revalidation, and API data gets policies that fit its freshness needs. Getting this contract right is the difference between a snappy site and one that is either stale or slow.

# The pragmatic caching contract for an API:
#  - immutable, fingerprinted assets (app.abc123.js):  Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable
#  - HTML:  no-cache (validate every time with ETag)   -> fresh but correct
#  - API data: vary per ownership; short TTLs or ETags
# Stale-while-revalidate lets users see cached content while it refreshes:
Cache-Control: public, max-age=0, s-maxage=31536000, stale-while-revalidate=300   # serve stale, refresh behind

Strategies, and choosing by what the content is

Four strategies, and they are not variations on one idea — each is a different answer to "how long may this be stale, and who is allowed to know that it is". Cache-first serves from the cache without checking, and only reaches the network on a miss. Stale-while-revalidate serves from the cache immediately and revalidates in the background, which is the strategy that is almost always right for read-heavy content because it makes the fast path genuinely fast and the stale window bounded by the revalidation time rather than by nothing. Network-first goes to the network and falls back to the cache, which is right when fresh data matters more than speed and you can tolerate the wait. Cache-only never goes to the network, which is right for fingerprinted immutable assets and is the strategy that makes hashed filenames work. Then the choice, which is a function of the content's properties rather than of preference. Fingerprinted assets are immutable — cache them forever and cache them first, because the filename changes when the content does, so a cached copy can never be wrong; the only cost is that the browser will not revalidate within the lifetime you set, which for a hashed file is exactly right. HTML is the hard case, because it names the assets, so a cached HTML document names old assets that may no longer exist — which is why the convention is a short lifetime with revalidation, and a deployment that changes HTML must invalidate it or users will hold a page referring to deleted assets. API responses depend on whether the endpoint is idempotent and whether a stale answer is acceptable — a stock price is close to network-first, a user's own profile should be read-your-writes, a product listing is a textbook stale-while-revalidate. And then the three things that break caching and produce the "why is it still serving the old version" report. The cache key does not include everything that varies, which is the most common bug: a query parameter, a header, a cookie, an accept-language — each of which is part of the response but not part of the key, and each of which then returns the wrong response to a user. Vary is set incorrectly or not at all, so a cache serves a compressed or localised version to a client that cannot read it. And invalidation is hard, which is why the pattern is to make keys immutable rather than to try to delete: versioned URLs, hashed filenames, and a generation counter that changes every key at once — which is what the scaling chapter's cache-invalidation section described, and it is correct by construction precisely because it never needs a delete.

/* Four strategies, each a different answer. */
const QUESTION = 'how long may THIS BE STALE, and WHO IS ALLOWED TO KNOW that it is';
const STRATEGIES = [
  { s: 'CACHE-FIRST', does: 'serves from the cache WITHOUT CHECKING, and only reaches the network on a miss' },
  { s: 'STALE-WHILE-REVALIDATE', does: 'serves from the cache IMMEDIATELY and revalidates IN THE BACKGROUND',
    whyAlmostAlwaysRight: 'for read-heavy content, because it makes the FAST PATH GENUINELY FAST',
    gain: 'and the STALE WINDOW IS BOUNDED by the revalidation time rather than by nothing' },
  { s: 'NETWORK-FIRST', does: 'goes to the network and FALLS BACK to the cache',
    rightWhen: 'FRESH DATA MATTERS MORE THAN SPEED and you can tolerate the wait' },
  { s: 'CACHE-ONLY', does: 'never goes to the network',
    rightFor: 'FINGERPRINTED IMMUTABLE ASSETS', and: 'it is the strategy that makes HASHED FILENAMES work' },
];

/* The choice, as a function of the content. */
const CHOOSE = [
  { content: 'FINGERPRINTED ASSETS', is: 'IMMUTABLE - the filename changes when the content does',
    therefore: 'CACHE THEM FOREVER AND CACHE THEM FIRST',
    why: 'a CACHED COPY CAN NEVER BE WRONG',
    onlyCost: 'the browser will not revalidate within the LIFETIME you set, which for a HASHED FILE is exactly right' },
  { content: 'HTML', isTheHardCase: true,
    why: 'it NAMES THE ASSETS, so a CACHED HTML DOCUMENT NAMES OLD ASSETS that may no longer exist',
    convention: 'a SHORT LIFETIME with revalidation',
    operational: 'a DEPLOYMENT THAT CHANGES HTML MUST INVALIDATE IT or users will hold a page referring to DELETED ASSETS' },
  { content: 'API RESPONSES', dependsOn: ['whether the endpoint is IDEMPOTENT', 'whether a STALE ANSWER IS ACCEPTABLE'],
    instances: ['a stock price is CLOSE TO NETWORK-FIRST', 'a users own profile SHOULD BE READ-YOUR-WRITES',
      'a product listing is a TEXTBOOK STALE-WHILE-REVALIDATE'] },
];

/* Three things that break caching. */
const BREAKS = [
  { b: 'the CACHE KEY does not include EVERYTHING THAT VARIES', rank: 'the MOST COMMON BUG',
    variesBy: ['a QUERY PARAMETER', 'a HEADER', 'a COOKIE', 'accept-language'],
    consequence: 'each is part of the RESPONSE but NOT part of the key, so each RETURNS THE WRONG RESPONSE TO A USER' },
  { b: 'VARY is set INCORRECTLY OR NOT AT ALL',
    consequence: 'so a CACHE SERVES A COMPRESSED or LOCALISED VERSION to a client that CANNOT READ IT' },
  { b: 'INVALIDATION is HARD',
    therefore: 'make KEYS IMMUTABLE rather than trying to delete',
    mechanisms: ['VERSIONED URLS', 'HASHED FILENAMES',
      'a GENERATION COUNTER that changes every key at once'],
    connectsTo: 'the scaling chapters cache-invalidation section',
    whyCorrectByConstruction: 'precisely because it NEVER NEEDS A DELETE' },
];

It gives the caching contract for fingerprinted assets, HTML, and API data, and shows how stale-while-revalidate keeps users unblocked while the cache refreshes.

31.4 Service workers, offline and the app-like web

A service worker is a script that runs in the browser, sits between your page and the network, and proxies requests, which enables offline use, caching, push, and installable progressive web apps. You register it, define an install step that pre-caches shell assets, a fetch handler that serves from cache with a network fallback or the reverse, and an activate step that cleans old caches. It also lets you degrade gracefully with an offline page instead of an error.

// service-worker.js -- registered once; scripts the browser's network proxy
self.addEventListener("install", (e) => {   // pre-cache the app shell
  e.waitUntil(caches.open("v1").then((c) => c.addAll(["/", "/app.js"])));
});
self.addEventListener("fetch", (e) => {   // intercept every request
  e.respondWith(
    caches.match(e.request).then((hit) => hit || fetch(e.request))
  );                                            // cache-first: instant offline
});
// Register from the page:  navigator.serviceWorker.register("/service-worker.js")
// Push notifications + background sync live behind the same "worker" idea.

Service workers, and what makes them worth the cost

A service worker is a script the browser runs in the background, separate from your page, and that separation is the whole design. It has its own lifecycle: install, waiting, activate, and then it intercepts every fetch from pages it controls. It can be stopped and restarted at any time, which is the property that makes every design rule necessary and which is worth stating first because it is the source of most service-worker bugs. Then what they are actually good at, and the list is shorter than the marketing. Offline support for an application shell — the HTML, CSS and JavaScript that make the app load at all — which is the strongest case because it is exactly what a user on a poor connection or a train needs. Eliminating the network round trip for repeated navigations, which is a genuine performance win and which is invisible as a "performance" feature because it is a reliability feature. Background synchronisation, deferring writes until connectivity returns. And push notifications. And what they are not for. They do not make a native app. The application store is a distribution mechanism, and a service worker adds a lifecycle, a caching layer, a version-migration problem and a debugging story that are all strictly more complicated than a web page, and none of which gives you what a native app gives you. They do not fix a slow first load, because everything must be downloaded and parsed once regardless. And they are not a substitute for a CDN — a service worker caches per user per device, while a CDN caches per edge location for everybody, so they solve different problems and the second one has far better economics for shared content. Then the four rules, each of which exists because of the restart property. Cache the shell, then the data, separately. Two caches with different strategies, so a data update does not invalidate the shell and a new shell version does not throw away cached data. Version your caches and clean up on activate. A new cache name per version, and the activate handler deletes the old ones — without this the storage grows without limit and users with a small quota get eviction failures that silently break the app. Handle the waiting state. A new worker installs while an old one controls the page; if you activate immediately you have two versions of the app running and the user sees a mix. The pattern is skipWaiting combined with a clients.claim for the case where you genuinely want immediate takeover, and the honest note that this is a trade rather than a free win. Never cache a response you did not create, on error, and never cache non-GET requests. A failed response cached as if it were data is the worst bug in this list, because the user gets a permanently broken page that no retry fixes; and caching anything that is not a GET can replay a mutation, which is the idempotency argument arriving again.

/* The lifecycle. */
const LIFECYCLE = {
  is: 'a SCRIPT THE BROWSER RUNS IN THE BACKGROUND, separate from your page',
  separationIsTheWholeDesign: true,
  phases: ['INSTALL', 'WAITING', 'ACTIVATE'],
  then: 'it INTERCEPTS EVERY FETCH from pages it controls',
  keyProperty: 'IT CAN BE STOPPED AND RESTARTED AT ANY TIME',
  whyFirst: 'it is the SOURCE OF MOST SERVICE-WORKER BUGS',
  and: 'which is what makes every design rule below NECESSARY',
};

/* What they are good at. */
const GOOD_AT = [
  { g: 'OFFLINE SUPPORT for an APPLICATION SHELL', is: 'the HTML, CSS and JavaScript that make the app LOAD AT ALL',
    strongest: true,
    why: 'which is exactly what a user on a POOR CONNECTION or a TRAIN needs' },
  { g: 'ELIMINATING THE NETWORK ROUND TRIP for repeated navigations',
    note: 'a GENUINE PERFORMANCE WIN that is INVISIBLE AS A PERFORMANCE FEATURE because it is a RELIABILITY FEATURE' },
  { g: 'BACKGROUND SYNCHRONISATION', does: 'DEFERRING WRITES until connectivity returns' },
  { g: 'PUSH NOTIFICATIONS' },
];

/* What they are not for. */
const NOT_FOR = [
  { n: 'they DO NOT MAKE A NATIVE APP',
    detail: 'the APPLICATION STORE is a distribution mechanism',
    and: 'a service worker adds a LIFECYCLE, a CACHING LAYER, a VERSION-MIGRATION PROBLEM and a DEBUGGING STORY that are all STRICTLY MORE COMPLICATED than a web page',
    noneOfWhich: 'gives you what a NATIVE APP gives you' },
  { n: 'they DO NOT FIX A SLOW FIRST LOAD',
    why: 'EVERYTHING MUST BE DOWNLOADED AND PARSED ONCE REGARDLESS' },
  { n: 'they are NOT A SUBSTITUTE FOR A CDN',
    contrast: ['a SERVICE WORKER caches PER USER PER DEVICE', 'a CDN caches PER EDGE LOCATION FOR EVERYBODY'],
    so: 'they solve DIFFERENT PROBLEMS', and: 'the second has far better ECONOMICS for shared content' },
];

/* Four rules, each from the restart property. */
const RULES = [
  { r: 'CACHE THE SHELL, THEN THE DATA, SEPARATELY',
    how: 'TWO CACHES with different strategies',
    gain: 'a DATA UPDATE does not invalidate the shell, and a NEW SHELL VERSION does not throw away cached data' },
  { r: 'VERSION YOUR CACHES and clean up ON ACTIVATE',
    how: 'a NEW CACHE NAME PER VERSION, and the ACTIVATE HANDLER DELETES THE OLD ONES',
    withoutIt: 'the STORAGE GROWS WITHOUT LIMIT',
    consequence: 'and users with a SMALL QUOTA get EVICTION FAILURES that SILENTLY BREAK THE APP' },
  { r: 'HANDLE THE WAITING STATE',
    detail: 'a NEW WORKER installs while an OLD ONE CONTROLS THE page',
    failure: 'if you activate IMMEDIATELY you have TWO VERSIONS OF THE APP RUNNING and the user sees A MIX',
    pattern: 'skipWaiting combined with a clients.claim for the case where you genuinely want IMMEDIATE TAKEOVER',
    honest: 'and this is A TRADE rather than a FREE WIN' },
  { r: 'NEVER CACHE a RESPONSE YOU DID NOT CREATE, a response ON ERROR, or a NON-GET REQUEST',
    worstBug: 'a FAILED RESPONSE CACHED AS IF IT WERE DATA',
    symptom: 'the user gets a PERMANENTLY BROKEN PAGE that no retry fixes',
    and: 'caching anything that is NOT A GET can REPLAY A MUTATION, which is the idempotency argument ARRIVING AGAIN' },
];

A service worker installs a cache and intercepts fetches to serve the app shell offline, showing the cache-first pattern that powers PWAs.

Service workers are the machinery of PWAs — installable, offline-capable web apps. They also give you the network-first-with-cache-fallback pattern for pages that must be fresh-or-degraded-silently (exactly the Ch. 29 "degradation, not crash" philosophy, client-side).

31.5 The metrics teams actually run toward

Core Web Vitals turn perceived speed into numbers a team can track: LCP for loading, INP for interaction responsiveness, and CLS for visual stability. You measure them in the field with the Web Vitals library or in development with Lighthouse, set a budget per metric, and guard it in CI so small regressions are caught before they compound. Treating the numbers as an enforced budget, not a report, is what keeps pages healthy.

The three metrics, and what each one is actually measuring

Web performance is a field that had no shared vocabulary for fifteen years and now has one, and the definition of each metric is more interesting than the target. Largest Contentful Paint measures when the largest image or text block finished rendering. It is the metric that approximates "when did the page look useful", and it is measured from the moment navigation started — which means it includes the server's think time, the network round trip and the browser's parsing, and that is deliberate, because a user does not care which of those is slow. The subtlety worth knowing is what counts as the candidate: the browser keeps watching for a larger element and updates the metric, so a late-loading hero image can increase LCP after the page has been interactive, and it means a large image below the fold can be picked as the candidate if it is the largest painted element on the whole page. Interaction to Next Paint measures responsiveness. It observes how long the browser takes to respond to a user interaction — it works by detecting input, then waiting for the next frame, so it measures the visible delay between your tap and the page reacting. That makes it the metric that actually corresponds to whether the page feels stuck, and it is the one whose improvement requires reducing main-thread work, since the delay is time the main thread is busy. Cumulative Layout Shift measures visual stability. The browser records every time a visible element moves without user interaction, and it is the sum of the impact fractions times the distance fractions — which is worth knowing because it explains why the metric is not "how much moved" but "how much, and how far". The biggest causes are the three the previous sections covered: an image without dimensions, a web font that swaps in, and content injected above what the reader is looking at. And then the metric deliberately excluded, with a reason. Time to First Byte is not a vital metric even though it is the most widely monitored server number, because it says almost nothing about what the user experiences — a response in fifty milliseconds that contains a stylesheet which then blocks rendering produces a page that is worse than one served in two hundred milliseconds with everything inline. The reason is the same as the front-end chapter's: a number nobody would act on is not a metric. Which is exactly the test, and it is worth applying to your own instrumentation with the same scepticism.

/* Three metrics. */
const LCP = {
  name: 'LARGEST CONTENTFUL PAINT',
  measures: 'when the LARGEST IMAGE OR TEXT BLOCK finished rendering',
  approximates: 'when did the page LOOK USEFUL',
  measuredFrom: 'the moment NAVIGATION STARTED',
  whyFromThere: 'which means it INCLUDES the servers think time, the network round trip and the browsers parsing',
  andThatIsDeliberate: 'because a user DOES NOT CARE WHICH of those is slow',
  candidateSubtlety: 'the browser KEEPS WATCHING FOR A LARGER ELEMENT and updates the metric',
  consequences: ['a LATE-LOADING HERO IMAGE can INCREASE LCP after the page has been interactive',
    'a LARGE IMAGE BELOW THE FOLD can be picked as the candidate if it is the LARGEST PAINTED ELEMENT on the whole page'],
};
const INP = {
  name: 'INTERACTION TO NEXT PAINT',
  measures: 'RESPONSIVENESS',
  how: 'it observes HOW LONG THE BROWSER TAKES TO RESPOND to a user interaction',
  mechanism: 'it detects input, then WAITS FOR THE NEXT FRAME',
  so: 'it measures the VISIBLE DELAY between your tap and the page reacting',
  corresponds: 'whether the page FEELS STUCK',
  isTheOne: 'whose improvement REQUIRES REDUCING MAIN-THREAD WORK, since the delay is time the main thread is busy',
};
const CLS = {
  name: 'CUMULATIVE LAYOUT SHIFT',
  measures: 'VISUAL STABILITY',
  rule: 'the browser records EVERY TIME A VISIBLE ELEMENT MOVES WITHOUT USER INTERACTION',
  arithmetic: 'it is the SUM OF THE IMPACT FRACTIONS TIMES THE DISTANCE FRACTIONS',
  whyWorthKnowing: 'it explains why the metric is NOT how much moved but HOW MUCH, AND HOW FAR',
  biggestCauses: ['an IMAGE WITHOUT DIMENSIONS', 'a WEB FONT THAT SWAPS IN',
    'content INJECTED ABOVE what the reader is looking at'],
};

/* The metric deliberately excluded. */
const EXCLUDED = {
  metric: 'TIME TO FIRST BYTE',
  notExcludedBecause: 'it is a bad number',
  reason: 'it says ALMOST NOTHING ABOUT WHAT THE USER EXPERIENCES',
  example: 'a response in fifty milliseconds that contains a STYLESHEET WHICH THEN BLOCKS RENDERING produces a page that is WORSE than one served in two hundred milliseconds with everything INLINE',
  connectsTo: 'the front-end chapters argument - a number NOBODY WOULD ACT ON is not a metric',
  and: 'which is exactly the test, and it is worth applying to your own instrumentation with the SAME SCEPTICISM',
};

What moves each metric, and how to know whether you improved it

A metric you cannot attribute is a metric you cannot improve, and attribution is the practical skill. Largest Contentful Paint is a loading problem. The causes, in rough order of how much they cost: the server's response time, because it is first in the chain and everything else waits for it; the stylesheet, because it is render-blocking and the browser cannot lay out without it; the largest image, because it is by definition the largest thing on the page and its size is its time; and the client-side work before the browser gets to that image, because a slow script delays discovery of it. So the levers are: make the server faster — which usually means a cache, an index or a query fix rather than a bigger machine; make the stylesheet smaller and preload it; make the largest image smaller and correctly sized, which the responsive section covered; and ship less JavaScript before the first paint. Interaction to Next Paint is a main-thread problem. The causes are long tasks — any JavaScript task over fifty milliseconds makes an input wait, and there are usually a handful of them; and expensive layout work triggered by the interaction, which is why clicking something that appends a thousand DOM nodes is slow. So the levers are break long tasks into chunks with yields, so a click is not queued behind unrelated work; do less work in the handler; make DOM updates cheap by not reading layout inside a loop, because a read after a write forces a synchronous layout and a loop with both is the classic jank pattern; and move non-urgent work to after the interaction. Cumulative Layout Shift is a reservation problem. The causes are an element that changes size after render — an image, a video, an iframe, a web font — and content inserted above what the reader is looking at, which is what an ad or a banner does. So the levers are reserve space for everything that loads late, with dimensions or a fixed ratio; avoid inserting content above the viewport; and not swap fonts late, or to swap them with a metric-compatible fallback so the change is small. Then how to know whether a change helped, and the discipline matters more than any of the techniques. Measure on a real device on a real network — a desktop on a fast connection will show you nothing, and the population you care about is disproportionately on mid-range hardware on poor connections. Measure at the 75th percentile, not the mean, because the mean of a latency distribution hides the tail where the pain is. Look at field data if you have any, because laboratory numbers are a controlled experiment and the field is the reality. And set a budget and treat it as a gate, the same discipline as the continuous-integration chapter: a performance budget that fails a build is the only kind that survives, because a budget nobody enforces is a number in a document, and the performance chapter's regression that was fast last week is the predictable outcome of that.

/* LCP is a loading problem. */
const LCP_CAUSES = [
  { c: 'the SERVERS RESPONSE TIME', first: true, because: 'it is FIRST IN THE CHAIN and everything else waits for it' },
  { c: 'the STYLESHEET', because: 'it is RENDER-BLOCKING and the browser CANNOT LAY OUT without it' },
  { c: 'the LARGEST IMAGE', because: 'it is BY DEFINITION the largest thing on the page and its SIZE IS ITS TIME' },
  { c: 'the CLIENT-SIDE WORK before the browser gets to that image',
    because: 'a SLOW SCRIPT DELAYS DISCOVERY of it' },
];
const LCP_LEVERS = [
  { l: 'make the SERVER FASTER', usually: 'means a CACHE, an INDEX or a QUERY FIX rather than a BIGGER MACHINE' },
  { l: 'make the STYLESHEET SMALLER and PRELOAD it' },
  { l: 'make the LARGEST IMAGE SMALLER and CORRECTLY SIZED', connects: 'the responsive section covered this' },
  { l: 'ship LESS JAVASCRIPT before the first paint' },
];

/* INP is a main-thread problem. */
const INP_CAUSES = [
  { c: 'LONG TASKS', detail: 'any JavaScript task over fifty milliseconds makes an input WAIT',
    and: 'there are USUALLY A HANDFUL of them' },
  { c: 'EXPENSIVE LAYOUT WORK triggered by the interaction',
    why: 'which is why clicking something that APPENDS A THOUSAND DOM NODES is slow' },
];
const INP_LEVERS = [
  { l: 'BREAK LONG TASKS INTO CHUNKS with yields', gain: 'so a click is not QUEUED BEHIND UNRELATED WORK' },
  { l: 'DO LESS WORK in the handler' },
  { l: 'make DOM UPDATES CHEAP by not READING LAYOUT INSIDE A LOOP',
    why: 'because a READ AFTER A WRITE forces a SYNCHRONOUS LAYOUT, and a loop with both is the CLASSIC JANK PATTERN' },
  { l: 'move NON-URGENT WORK to after the interaction' },
];

/* CLS is a reservation problem. */
const CLS_CAUSES = [
  { c: 'an ELEMENT THAT CHANGES SIZE after render', instances: ['an image', 'a video', 'an iframe', 'a web font'] },
  { c: 'content INSERTED ABOVE what the reader is looking at', which: 'is what AN AD or a BANNER does' },
];
const CLS_LEVERS = [
  { l: 'RESERVE SPACE for everything that loads late', how: 'with DIMENSIONS or a FIXED RATIO' },
  { l: 'avoid INSERTING CONTENT ABOVE THE VIEWPORT' },
  { l: 'do NOT SWAP FONTS LATE, or swap them with a METRIC-COMPATIBLE FALLBACK so the change is SMALL' },
];

/* How to know whether a change helped. */
const METHOD = [
  { m: 'MEASURE ON A REAL DEVICE on a real network',
    why: 'a DESKTOP ON A FAST CONNECTION WILL SHOW YOU NOTHING',
    and: 'the population you care about is DISPROPORTIONATELY on mid-range hardware on poor connections' },
  { m: 'MEASURE AT THE 75TH PERCENTILE, not the mean',
    why: 'because the MEAN OF A LATENCY DISTRIBUTION HIDES THE TAIL where the pain is' },
  { m: 'LOOK AT FIELD DATA if you have any',
    why: 'because LABORATORY NUMBERS are a CONTROLLED EXPERIMENT and the field is the REALITY' },
  { m: 'SET A BUDGET and treat it as a GATE',
    sameAs: 'the continuous-integration chapters discipline',
    why: 'a PERFORMANCE BUDGET THAT FAILS A BUILD is the only kind that SURVIVES',
    and: 'a budget NOBODY ENFORCES is a NUMBER IN A DOCUMENT',
    consequence: 'and the performance chapters REGRESSION THAT WAS FAST LAST WEEK is the PREDICTABLE OUTCOME of that' },

MetricWhat it measuresGood target
LCPlargest content paints (page "looks ready")≤ 2.5 s
INPresponse to interactions (feels responsive)≤ 200 ms
CLSlayout shift (does the page jump?)≤ 0.1
TBT / TTFBjanky blocking time / server response timeTTFB < 0.8 s; TBT < 200 ms

The "≤ X" numbers form your performance budget — commit to it like a test, and guard it in CI (Lighthouse, Playwright collects metrics on real CI). Budgets are what stop "small" regressions from compounding into a 4-с-app.

31.6 Accessibility you will actually be judged on

Day-to-day accessibility is concrete: meaningful alt text, full keyboard operability, visible focus indicators, sufficient color contrast, and labels on every control, with semantic HTML giving most of it for free. WCAG and the ARIA spec set the rules, and automated checks such as axe plus manual keyboard walks catch the common failures. Verified against screen readers, this turns an accessibility pass from a slogan into checkable behavior.

  • WCAG 2.2 is the standard; the short version is a checklist: every image alt; every interactive element keyboard-operable; focus visibly managed; colour isn’t the only signal; aria-label only where native labels fail.
  • Semantics first: a native <button> already does keyboard, focus, and screen-reader contract for free — your job is to not replace them with divs.
  • Contrast ≥ 4.5:1 for text; target sizes ≥ 24–44 px for touch; test with a screen reader (NVDA/VoiceOver) at least once — it changes how you code forever.

What assistive technology actually does, and what breaks

Accessibility failures are almost always failures of structure rather than of styling, and the reason is that assistive technology navigates by structure. A screen reader does not read the page top to bottom as a sighted person does. It presents a list of headings, a list of landmarks, a list of links, a list of form controls and a list of buttons, and the user moves among them. So the document's outline is the interface, and a page with good visual hierarchy chosen by font size and no heading structure is a page that is completely unusable with a screen reader while looking perfectly fine. It announces roles, not appearances. A <div> with a click handler is announced as a group of text; a <button> is announced as a button and appears in the button list and can be invoked by a keyboard shortcut without navigating to it. It follows the accessibility tree, which is a filtered version of the DOM tree — and the filter is why display: none and the hidden attribute remove content from that tree while visibility: hidden and opacity zero leave it present but invisible, which produces a screen reader announcing content no sighted user can see. Then the specific failures that appear in real code, and each has a fix that is not a matter of taste. Missing labels. A placeholder is not a label: it disappears on first keystroke, contrast requirements apply to it, and its support is inconsistent. Colour as the only signal. A red input border communicates error visually and communicates nothing to a colour-blind user or in a high-contrast mode; the error must be text as well as colour. Focus that cannot be seen or cannot be reached. Removing the focus outline without replacing it makes a page unusable by keyboard, and a custom control implemented as a <div> with a tabindex is reachable but announces nothing about its role or state. Timeouts and motion. A session timeout with no warning and no extension is a barrier for anyone who needs more time, and animation without a reduced-motion preference causes genuine symptoms for some people. And then what to do about it in practice, because a full audit is expensive and a partial one is not. Keyboard-only testing first, because it is free and it catches the largest class: if you cannot complete every task without a mouse, neither can many other users. Axe or an equivalent automated check in continuous integration, which catches roughly the mechanically detectable third of issues and none of the judgement-dependent ones — and its value is regression prevention rather than initial correctness. Test with a real screen reader, once, for an hour, because that converts the whole subject from theory into something you have heard. And write it into the definition of done, not into a separate initiative, because an accessibility audit after a release finds problems nobody has budget to fix and the ones that get fixed are the cheap ones.

/* How assistive technology navigates. */
const NAVIGATION = {
  doesNot: 'READ THE PAGE TOP TO BOTTOM as a sighted person does',
