  consequence: 'a SINGLE LIBRARY FUNCTION that returns nothing CORRECTLY FORCES EVERY CALLER ABOVE IT to handle it',
  and: 'that is a GENUINE CHANGE IN THE SHAPE OF CORRECT CODE' },

/* The second half. */
const MONAD = {
  is: 'a FUNCTOR THAT COMPOSES',
  distinguishingOperation: 'one that TAKES A FUNCTION RETURNING A WRAPPED VALUE and RETURNS A SINGLE WRAPPED VALUE',
  sounds: 'trivial',
  isInFact: 'the operation that lets a SEQUENCE OF WRAPPED STEPS be treated as ONE STEP',
  so: 'a chain READS AS A CHAIN rather than as NESTING',

/* Practical forms. */
const FORMS = [
  { m: 'a LIST MONAD is a LIST OF RESULTS',
    so: 'a sequence of INDEPENDENT COMPUTATIONS is expressed as a COMPREHENSION and RUN TOGETHER rather than ONE AFTER ANOTHER',
    connectsTo: 'the concurrency chapters PARALLELISM arriving in a NOTATION' },
  { m: 'an OPTIONAL MONAD is a CHAIN OF MAYBE-ABSENT VALUES',

It explains how Option and Result replace null and exceptions with explicit containers, so the compiler forces you to handle every case.

33.5 Type systems: static, inferred, structural & sum types

Type systems vary on three axes: static checks before runtime versus dynamic checks during it, how much inference fills in types for you, and whether the model can express a choice between alternatives, sum types such as an enum, as well as combinations, product types such as structs and records. Strong static typing with inference and sum types turns many runtime surprises into compile errors. Choosing how much of this machinery a codebase uses is a real design decision about safety versus speed of writing.

ConceptMeaningWhere it lives
Static vs dynamictypes checked at compile vs runtimeTS/Rust/Go vs Python/JS
Type inferencecompiler deduces types (let x = 5)Rust, TS, Kotlin
Product types"AND": a struct/record holding several fieldseverywhere
Sum types (ADTs)"OR": a value that is exactly one of several shapesOption, Result, enum-like
Pattern matchingdestructure + dispatch over every armRust match, TS discriminated unions

The career takeaway: learn ONE language with strong static types (Rust or TypeScript) well enough to feel the safety, and one dynamically-typed (Python) for speed of iteration. Teams hire people who can speak both sides of this trade-off.

What a type buys, and what it costs

A type system is a language for describing the shapes of values, and the value it provides is that some classes of mistake become impossible rather than merely unlikely. Three things, in rough order of how much they matter. It moves errors from run time to before the program runs. A type mismatch that would have been a production incident becomes a compiler message, and the difference between the two is not severity — it is whether anybody is awake. It makes the interface the contract. Once a function's signature says what it takes and what it returns, the caller can rely on it without reading the body, which means code written six months apart can be combined by people who have never spoken. And it narrows what a reader must check. If the type says a string cannot be returned where a number is required, a reader looking at a caller does not need to verify it — and that is the quiet benefit, because verification is the thing that does not scale with the size of the codebase. Then the costs, stated honestly. Expressiveness. A type system that forbids everything hard is not helpful; the work is finding where the line is. Verbosity. Annotations are words, and words cost time to read and time to maintain — though inference removes most of them in languages that have it. Friction with legitimate dynamic code. Data arriving from outside the program is not typed, so something must convert it, and that conversion is a real cost paid at every boundary. Compile time. A sophisticated checker on a large codebase is slow, and a slow checker is a checker that gets skipped. And a false sense of safety, which is the most dangerous of the six: a type system does not prove your program is correct — it proves the shapes are consistent, and it says nothing about whether a list is sorted when it needs to be, or whether a division has a zero denominator, or whether the business rule you implemented is the right one. Then the choices in practice, and the decision is mostly about what happens to data from outside. Adopt the strongest typing the ecosystem supports without ceremony, because a gradual adoption to a weaker standard than the language offers buys nothing. Make "unchecked" explicit at boundaries — a validated-parsing function that turns unknown input into a typed value — so that the unsafe surface is a list somebody can review rather than a fact about the codebase. And model the invariants the type system can express: newtypes for values that must not be interchangeable, a type that carries its unit, an opaque type that hides its representation — each of these prevents a class of mistake that a comment cannot.

/* Three things it provides. */
const PROVIDES = [

    and: 'the difference between the two is not SEVERITY - it is whether ANYBODY IS AWAKE' },

    gain: 'so code written SIX MONTHS APART can be combined BY PEOPLE WHO HAVE NEVER SPOKEN' },
  { v: 'it NARROWS WHAT A READER MUST CHECK',

  { p: 'adopt the STRONGEST TYPING the ECOSYSTEM SUPPORTS WITHOUT CEREMONY',
    why: 'because a GRADUAL ADOPTION to a WEAKER STANDARD than the language offers BUYS NOTHING' },
  { p: 'make UNCHECKED EXPLICIT AT BOUNDARIES', how: 'a VALIDATED-PARSING function that turns UNKNOWN INPUT into a TYPED VALUE',
    gain: 'so that the UNSAFE SURFACE is a LIST SOMEBODY CAN REVIEW rather than a FACT ABOUT the codebase' },
  { p: 'MODEL THE INVARIANTS the type system can express',
    instances: ['NEWTYPES for values that must NOT BE INTERCHANGEABLE', 'a TYPE THAT CARRIES ITS UNIT',
      'an OPAQUE TYPE that hides its representation'],
    gain: 'each of these prevents a CLASS OF MISTAKE that a COMMENT CANNOT' },
];

The shape of a type, and how it is checked

What a type is, in the terms that generalise across languages. A type is a set of values plus the operations permitted on them. That second half is the part beginners miss and it is the part that matters: int is not just a set of whole numbers, it is that set together with the operations that preserve them — division that truncates rather than producing a fraction, overflow that wraps or traps, a byte-sized range. Change the set without changing the operations and you have a different type; change the operations without changing the set and you have a different type with a familiar name, which is the source of a whole family of numerical bugs. Then how a checker works, because the mechanism explains why some programs are accepted and some are not. It walks the syntax tree and maintains, for each expression, the type of its value. Variables, parameters and return values carry declared types; literals have obvious ones; and every node has rules for what combinations are permitted — a binary addition requires both sides to be numeric, a comparison requires two comparable values, a call requires the argument types to match the parameter types. Where a type is not written, inference derives it from how the value is used, and the direction of inference is what makes some languages feel stricter than others despite identical guarantees. And the three consequences that follow from this mechanism. Type errors are found where types meet, which is why the error message points at the expression rather than at the mistake. Unreachable branches are detectable, because if a condition narrows a type to nothing on one branch, that branch cannot do anything. And a bidirectional boundary is where the trouble is: data from a file, a network response, a query result, an environment variable is text, and the conversion from text to a domain value is the single point where a program must handle malformed input — which is why a validation function at each boundary is not a defensive habit but the place where the type system's guarantee is established.

/* What a type is. */
const TYPE = {
  is: 'a SET OF VALUES plus THE OPERATIONS PERMITTED ON THEM',
  secondHalfIsThePoint: 'the part BEGINNERS MISS and it is the part that MATTERS',
  example: 'an integer is not just a set of whole numbers, it is that set TOGETHER WITH the operations that PRESERVE THEM',
  operations: ['DIVISION that TRUNCATES rather than producing a fraction',
    'OVERFLOW that wraps or traps', 'a BYTE-SIZED RANGE'],
  principle: ['CHANGE THE SET without changing the operations and you have a DIFFERENT TYPE',
    'CHANGE THE OPERATIONS without changing the set and you have a DIFFERENT TYPE WITH A FAMILIAR NAME'],
  and: 'which is the source of a WHOLE FAMILY OF NUMERICAL BUGS' };

/* How a checker works. */
const CHECKER = {
  mechanism: 'it WALKS THE SYNTAX TREE and maintains, for each expression, the TYPE OF ITS VALUE',
  carries: ['variables, parameters and return values carry DECLARED types',
    'literals have OBVIOUS ones'],
  nodeRules: ['a BINARY ADDITION requires BOTH SIDES TO BE NUMERIC',
    'a COMPARISON requires TWO COMPARABLE values',
    'a CALL requires the ARGUMENT TYPES TO MATCH the parameter types'],
  inference: 'where a type is not written, INFERENCE DERIVES IT from HOW THE VALUE IS USED',
  andThat: 'the DIRECTION OF INFERENCE is what makes some languages feel STRICTER than others despite IDENTICAL GUARANTEES',
};

/* Three consequences. */
const CONSEQUENCES = [
  { c: 'TYPE ERRORS ARE FOUND WHERE TYPES MEET',
    consequence: 'which is why the ERROR MESSAGE POINTS AT THE EXPRESSION rather than at the MISTAKE' },
  { c: 'UNREACHABLE BRANCHES ARE DETECTABLE',
    why: 'because if a condition NARROWS A TYPE TO NOTHING on one branch, that branch CANNOT DO ANYTHING' },
  { c: 'a BIDIRECTIONAL BOUNDARY is where the TROUBLE IS',
    detail: 'data from a FILE, a NETWORK RESPONSE, a QUERY RESULT, an ENVIRONMENT VARIABLE is TEXT',
    and: 'the CONVERSION FROM TEXT to a domain value is the SINGLE POINT where a program must handle MALFORMED INPUT',
    conclusion: 'which is why a VALIDATION FUNCTION at each boundary is not a DEFENSIVE HABIT but the PLACE WHERE THE TYPE SYSTEMS GUARANTEE IS ESTABLISHED' },
];

34 · High-Performance & Parallel Computing

Performance is governed by physics rather than preference: memory hierarchy latencies, how much work can be parallelized, and the throughput model of the hardware. Understanding causality explains why a big speedup is sometimes as cheap as reordering a loop and sometimes costs an entire architecture change. The practical toolkit is measuring with profilers, exploiting cache locality, following Amdahl’s Law, and using the right parallel hardware for the work.

34.1 The memory hierarchy is the real computer34.2 Parallelism models & Amdahl’s Law34.3 GPUs & CUDA: why deep learning rides on them34.4 Numerical hygiene: overflow, precision & stability34.5 Profiling: find O(1) gains before O(n²) rewrites

Everything scales: data, code, and computing itself. This chapter is the physics of speed — memory hierarchy, parallelism models, and GPUs — so you know why a 10× speedup occasionally costs 100 business-days.

34.1 The memory hierarchy is the real computer

A CPU reads data through a ladder of caches, L1 to L3, then main memory, with each level an order of magnitude slower, so where data sits matters more than how fast arithmetic is. Contiguous, sequential access hits cache lines and the prefetcher, while pointer-chasing and random access miss, which is why cache-friendly loops can win by orders of magnitude. Designing data layout and access order for locality is the highest-leverage optimization.

Latency ladder (rough, 2026):
   L1 cache   ~1ns     (per-core, a few dozen KB)
   L2 cache   ~4ns     (per-core, bigger but slower)
   L3 cache   ~12ns    (shared)
   RAM        ~100ns   (GBs)
   NVMe SSD   ~100µs   (fast disk)
   network    ~1-10ms  (the disk may be in a different room)
Rule: algorithms that planned for "RAM" often really run on cache;   # cache is king
 "court-sequences" beats "pointer-chasing" by 10-100x. When a program
 is mysteriously slow, first suspect: random access patterns and cache
 misses, not wrong logic.   # suspect the access pattern

It lists the approximate latency of each level of the memory hierarchy and warns that random access patterns, not wrong logic, usually cause mysterious slowness.

# Cache-friendly idea in 3 lines: iterate ROW-major (contiguous memory),
# matching how the 2D array is laid out in RAM:
for i in range(n):            # outer: rows
    for j in range(n):
        s += a[i][j]          # fast: sequential addresses
#  vs
for j in range(n):            # outer: columns
    for i in range(n):
        s += a[i][j]          # slow: striding across rows every access
# Same O(n^2), 5-50x different runtime. Profile, don't intuit.

The hierarchy, and why the access pattern decides more than the algorithm

Memory is a hierarchy of speeds rather than a single place, and the fact that it is a hierarchy rather than a flat pool of uniformly-addressable cells is what produces the entire chapter's subject. A CPU register is fastest and smallest, and a value being computed is held in one; the compiler's register allocation decides which, and it is a graph-colouring problem because registers are a limited resource that values compete for. L1 cache is next, and its defining property is that it is inside the core and the smallest — a few tens of kilobytes — which is what makes it fast and what makes it impossible to hold a working set. L2 and L3 are larger and shared, and L3 is effectively the memory the processor sees. Main memory is roughly two orders of magnitude slower, and its access time is what a cache miss costs. Storage is slower again by a large factor, and unlike memory it has a mechanical component — a rotating disk seeks, a solid-state drive does not — which is why the difference between the two storage types is measured in seeks rather than in bandwidth. Then the property that turns this hierarchy into a performance subject, and it is the single most important idea in the section. Sequential access is fast because of prefetching; random access is slow because every access is a separate trip. The hardware watches which addresses are being read, notices a pattern, and speculatively loads the next ones before the program asks. A loop reading a large array sequentially gets a large fraction of its reads satisfied by data already in flight; the same loop reading a large array with a stride that is not a power of two gets no such benefit and pays the full trip for every element. This is why two loops with identical complexity can differ by an order of magnitude in runtime, and it is why the answer to "why is my code slow" is very often "because it accesses memory in an order the hardware cannot predict" rather than because the arithmetic is expensive. And then the four things that follow, in rough order of how often they are the answer. Make the inner loop walk contiguous memory. A two-dimensional array accessed as arr[i][j] in the inner loop walks across rows with a stride of the row length, which is exactly the pattern that defeats prefetching; the same computation done with the indices transposed walks contiguously and is several times faster with identical arithmetic. Get data into cache and keep it there. A small working set is fast; a working set larger than the largest cache is not, and the boundary is the cliff from the operating-systems chapter. Get contiguous allocation right. An array of pointers is not an array of the things — it is an array of pointers followed by scattered objects, so accessing it is two dependent memory accesses per element, which is why storing values rather than references is a real optimisation when the values are small. And prefetch explicitly when the pattern is regular but not sequential, which is what a prefetch instruction is for, and which is one of the few cases where a low-level hint beats a high-level rewrite.

/* The hierarchy. */
const LEVELS = [
  { l: 'CPU REGISTER', speed: 'FASTEST', size: 'SMALLEST',
    detail: 'a value being computed is held in one',
    decision: 'the compilers REGISTER ALLOCATION decides which',
    andThatIs: 'a GRAPH-COLOURING problem because REGISTERS ARE A LIMITED RESOURCE that values COMPETE FOR' },
  { l: 'L1 CACHE', next: true,
    definingProperty: 'it is INSIDE THE CORE and the SMALLEST - a few tens of kilobytes',
    andThatIs: 'what makes it FAST and what makes it IMPOSSIBLE TO HOLD A WORKING SET' },
  { l: 'L2 and L3', larger: true, shared: true, note: 'L3 is EFFECTIVELY THE MEMORY the processor SEES' },
  { l: 'MAIN MEMORY', relativeToL1: 'roughly TWO ORDERS OF MAGNITUDE SLOWER',
    and: 'its ACCESS TIME is what a CACHE MISS COSTS' },
  { l: 'STORAGE', relative: 'SLOWER AGAIN by a large factor',
    unlike: 'memory it has a MECHANICAL COMPONENT - a rotating disk SEEKS, a solid-state drive does not',
    consequence: 'which is why the difference between the two storage types is MEASURED IN SEEKS rather than in bandwidth' },

const ACCESS_PATTERN = {
  claim: 'SEQUENTIAL ACCESS IS FAST because of PREFETCHING; RANDOM ACCESS IS SLOW because EVERY ACCESS IS A SEPARATE TRIP',

const ANSWERS = [

  { a: 'GET CONTIGUOUS ALLOCATION RIGHT',
    example: 'an ARRAY OF POINTERS IS NOT AN ARRAY OF THE THINGS - it is an array of pointers FOLLOWED BY SCATTERED OBJECTS',
    consequence: 'so accessing it is TWO DEPENDENT MEMORY ACCESSES per element',

  { a: 'PREFETCH EXPLICITLY when the PATTERN IS REGULAR BUT NOT SEQUENTIAL',

34.2 Parallelism models & Amdahl’s Law

Amdahl’s Law states that speedup is capped by the fraction of work that must remain serial: if 90 percent is parallelizable, the ceiling is ten times no matter how many cores you add. The hardware models are SIMD, one instruction on many data lanes, MIMD, many instructions on many data streams, and SIMT, the GPU model where many threads run one instruction. Matching your algorithm’s structure to the model decides what speedup is even possible.

# Amdahl's Law: if 20% of your runtime is sequential, the absolute
# ceiling of parallel speedup = 1 / (0.2 + 0) = 5x, no matter how many
# cores. The takeaway is brutal: parallelizing the 80% is capped;
# reducing the sequential 20% is what actually moves the ceiling.
#   speedup_max = 1 / (serial_fraction)
# Three guest models:
#   SIMD .. one instruction, many data (vectorized loops, numpy)
#   MIMD .. multiple cores with threads/processes (Ch.23.2)    # true parallelism
#   SIMT .. GPU-style: thousands of threads, one program (CUDA below)    # GPU model
# Scaling reality: 2x cores rarely = 2x speed (memory bandwidth,
# sync, scheduling). Measure with profilers and flamegraphs first.

Amdahl's law, and why more cores rarely helps linearly

Amdahl's law is the single most useful number in parallel programming and it is worth being able to state its implication without arithmetic. If a fraction s of a program cannot be parallelised, the maximum speedup is 1 / s no matter how many processors are added. So a program that is ten per cent inherently serial cannot go faster than ten times, ever — and a program that is fifty per cent serial cannot exceed two. This is why the interesting engineering question is not "how do I parallelise this" but "what is the serial fraction, and can it be reduced", and it is why a five per cent serial fraction caps you at twenty times while a thirty per cent one caps you at three. The corollary people find surprising: the serial fraction usually grows as you parallelise, because the parallel version needs to combine results, decide what work exists, synchronise, and communicate, and all of that is serial. Then the three execution models and the distinction that matters. SIMD — single instruction, multiple data: one instruction applied to many values simultaneously, as in a vector instruction that adds eight floats at once. It requires the data to be contiguous and the operations to be identical, which is why it is enormously effective for array arithmetic and useless for a branch. MIMD — multiple instructions, multiple data: many processors each running their own instruction stream, which is what every modern multicore machine does. SIMT — single instruction, multiple threads: many threads that execute the same instruction in lockstep and diverge only at a branch, which is the model a graphics processor uses and which is why a graphics processor is fast at exactly the workloads that have a high density of simple operations across many elements. The distinction worth internalising: a graphics processor has thousands of simple cores and a graphics processor's cores are individually far slower than a CPU's, so it wins at arithmetic throughput and loses at latency and at anything with branches, and the design of a modern accelerator library is mostly about arranging the work so that it has neither.

/* The law. */
const AMDahl = {
  says: 'if a FRACTION s of a program CANNOT BE PARALLELISED, the MAXIMUM SPEEDUP is 1 OVER s no matter how many processors are added',
  examples: [{ serialFraction: '10 per cent', ceiling: 'TEN TIMES, EVER' },
    { serialFraction: '50 per cent', ceiling: 'TWO' }],
  so: 'the interesting ENGINEERING QUESTION is not how do I parallelise this but WHAT IS THE SERIAL FRACTION, AND CAN IT BE REDUCED',
  corollary: ['a FIVE PER CENT serial fraction caps you at TWENTY TIMES',
    'a THIRTY PER CENT one caps you at THREE'],
  surprising: 'the SERIAL FRACTION USUALLY GROWS AS YOU PARALLELISE',
  why: 'because the parallel version needs to COMBINE RESULTS, DECIDE WHAT WORK EXISTS, SYNCHRONISE, and COMMUNICATE, and all of that IS SERIAL' };

/* Three execution models. */
const MODELS = [
  { m: 'SIMD', expands: 'SINGLE INSTRUCTION, MULTIPLE DATA',
    does: 'one instruction applied to MANY VALUES SIMULTANEOUSLY',
    example: 'a vector instruction that ADDS EIGHT FLOATS AT ONCE',
    requires: ['the DATA TO BE CONTIGUOUS', 'the OPERATIONS TO BE IDENTICAL'],
    therefore: 'ENORMOUSLY EFFECTIVE for array arithmetic and USELESS for a BRANCH' },
  { m: 'MIMD', expands: 'MULTIPLE INSTRUCTIONS, MULTIPLE DATA',
    does: 'many processors each running THEIR OWN INSTRUCTION STREAM',
    is: 'what EVERY MODERN MULTICORE MACHINE DOES' },
  { m: 'SIMT', expands: 'SINGLE INSTRUCTION, MULTIPLE THREADS',
    does: 'many threads that EXECUTE THE SAME INSTRUCTION IN LOCKSTEP and DIVERGE ONLY AT A BRANCH',
    usedBy: 'a GRAPHICS PROCESSOR',
    why: 'which is why a graphics processor is fast at EXACTLY THE WORKLOADS THAT HAVE A HIGH DENSITY of simple operations across many elements' },
];
const DISTINCTION = {
  a: 'a graphics processor has THOUSANDS OF SIMPLE CORES and its cores are INDIVIDUALLY FAR SLOWER THAN A CPUS',
  so: 'it WINS AT ARITHMETIC THROUGHPUT and LOSES AT LATENCY and at anything WITH BRANCHES',
  and: 'the design of a modern ACCELERATOR LIBRARY is mostly about ARRANGING THE WORK so that it has NEITHER' };

It states Amdahl’s Law that serial work caps speedup, then names the SIMD, MIMD, and SIMT execution models and warns that more cores rarely scale linearly.

34.3 GPUs & CUDA: why deep learning rides on them

GPUs trade single-thread latency for massive throughput, running thousands of small threads in parallel, which is perfect for the dense matrix multiplication neural networks are made of. CUDA is NVIDIA’s programming model: you write kernels that launch thousands of threads organized in blocks, which execute under the SIMT model with fast shared memory per block. Practical work uses libraries such as cuBLAS and cuDNN or frameworks like PyTorch that sit on top.

  • A GPU = thousands of small cores optimized for throughput (many simultaneous simple math ops), not single-thread latency.
  • That’s why matrix multiplication — thousands of independent products — is GPU-native: each core computes a small dot product.
  • CUDA/ROCm are the programming models; memory layout (coalescing, shared memory) dominates GPU performance even more than on CPU.
  • Winning frame: for embarrassingly parallel math workloads with regular structure → GPU; for irregular, branchy, latency-critical logic → CPU.

    • Why the hardware wants a different shape of program

    A graphics processor is a machine optimised for one shape of work, and understanding the shape explains every programming rule anyone has written about accelerators. Thousands of simple cores, each with the same instruction stream. A CPU has a few complex cores with a large instruction decoder, a big cache hierarchy and speculative execution, all of which exist to make one instruction stream fast; a graphics processor has thousands of cores with almost none of that, because it does not need to make any single instruction stream fast — it needs to make a very large number of identical operations fast, and the machinery for the former is wasted on the latter. Divergence is the tax. Threads in a lockstep group execute the same instruction on different data, and when they reach a conditional that some of them take and some do not, the group executes both paths with the inactive threads masked off. A branch inside a loop therefore costs the sum of all the taken paths rather than the cost of the path you took, and the practical consequence is that data-dependent branching must be hoisted out of the inner loop or the loop restructured so that all threads take the same path. Latency hiding replaces caches. Because the cores are simple, memory latency is relatively enormous compared to compute, so the design keeps many threads in flight and relies on having others ready — which is why occupancy, the number of active threads per core, is a parameter that matters, and why a kernel with high latency and low occupancy performs badly regardless of arithmetic. And the arithmetic units are specialised. There are units for floating-point multiply-add, for transcendental functions, for integer multiply, and for memory bandwidth, so an operation the hardware has no unit for is emulated at many times the cost. Then what follows for how you write for it, and the four rules are all consequences rather than conventions. Expose enough parallelism to fill the machine. A kernel using one thread on a device with thousands is using a fraction of the hardware, and this is the most common mistake because the sequential version looks correct. Avoid divergence in the inner loop, because the cost is the sum of all paths, and the fixes are to move the branch outside, to use a select rather than a branch, or to split the range so that each group of threads takes a single path. Make memory access coalesced, which means adjacent threads reading adjacent addresses — the pattern that turns many separate memory transactions into one wide one, and the pattern that a naive layout of a two-dimensional array per row defeats. Use the vectorised or matrix-multiply units explicitly where the arithmetic is dense, because a library that dispatches to them is not marginally faster but an order of magnitude faster for the same mathematical operation. And measure transfer, not just compute, because a kernel that computes fast and moves a great deal of data will be limited by bandwidth, and that is the second most common reason an accelerated program is disappointing.

    /* The shape. */
const GPU = {
  is: 'a MACHINE OPTIMISED FOR ONE SHAPE OF WORK',
  and: 'understanding the shape EXPLAINS EVERY PROGRAMMING RULE anyone has written about accelerators',
  cores: 'THOUSANDS OF SIMPLE CORES, each with the SAME INSTRUCTION STREAM',
  contrast: [
    { a: 'a CPU', has: ['a few COMPLEX CORES', 'a LARGE INSTRUCTION DECODER',
      'a BIG CACHE HIERARCHY', 'SPECULATIVE EXECUTION'],
      allExistTo: 'make ONE INSTRUCTION STREAM FAST' },
    { b: 'a graphics processor', lacksThem: true,
      reason: 'because it does NOT NEED to make any single instruction stream fast - it needs to make A VERY LARGE NUMBER OF IDENTICAL OPERATIONS fast',
      and: 'the MACHINERY FOR THE FORMER IS WASTED on the latter' },
  ],
};

/* Divergence. */

  mechanism: ['threads in a LOCKSTEP GROUP execute the SAME INSTRUCTION on different data',

/* Latency hiding. */
const LATENCY = {

    commonest: true, why: 'because the SEQUENTIAL VERSION LOOKS CORRECT' },
  { r: 'avoid DIVERGENCE in the inner loop', why: 'because the COST IS THE SUM OF ALL PATHS',
    fixes: ['MOVE THE BRANCH OUTSIDE', 'use a SELECT rather than a branch', 'SPLIT THE RANGE so that each group of threads takes a SINGLE PATH'] },
  { r: 'make MEMORY ACCESS COALESCED', means: 'ADJACENT THREADS READING ADJACENT ADDRESSES',
    gain: 'the PATTERN THAT TURNS MANY SEPARATE MEMORY TRANSACTIONS into ONE WIDE ONE',
    and: 'the pattern that a NAIVE LAYOUT of a two-dimensional array PER ROW DEFEATS' },
  { r: 'use the VECTORISED or MATRIX-MULTIPLY UNITS EXPLICITLY where the ARITHMETIC IS DENSE',
    gain: 'a LIBRARY THAT DISPATCHES TO THEM is not MARGINALLY FASTER but AN ORDER OF MAGNITUDE FASTER for the same mathematical operation' },
  { r: 'MEASURE TRANSFER, not just COMPUTE',
    why: 'a KERNEL THAT COMPUTES FAST and MOVES A GREAT DEAL OF DATA will be LIMITED BY BANDWIDTH',
    and: 'that is the SECOND MOST COMMON REASON an accelerated program is DISAPPOINTING' },
];

    Coalesced memory, and why the layout matters more than the maths

    The access pattern rule deserves its own treatment because it is the one that most often determines whether an accelerated kernel is fast or disappointing, and the reason is a property of the hardware rather than of the program. Memory is fetched in transactions covering a contiguous range, — typically thirty-two to a hundred and twenty-eight bytes — and a request for one element of a transaction retrieves the whole thing. So when adjacent threads read adjacent addresses, four threads reading four consecutive floats need one transaction, and the bandwidth is fully used. When adjacent threads read addresses far apart, each needs its own transaction, and if the addresses are spread across memory the requests cannot be combined at all: the effective bandwidth collapses to a small fraction of the hardware's, and the kernel becomes memory-bound despite doing a great deal of arithmetic. This is why a two-dimensional array read row-by-row is the canonical bad pattern — with each row contiguous but rows separated by the array's total width, the threads in a group may span a row boundary and produce a small number of transactions per row, and the second row repeats the waste. And the fixes follow directly. Store data so the access pattern is contiguous in the last dimension. In practice this usually means transposing the layout, and it means that for a computation that reads column-wise, storing it transposed is dramatically faster. Pad rows to avoid alignment problems, because if the row length is not a multiple of the transaction size, every row starts at a different offset within a transaction and a fraction of every transaction is wasted; padding each row by a few elements makes every row start at the same offset. Coalesce the reads in the algorithm, not just in the layout — if threads 0 to 31 need the same value, read it once and share it, because the hardware may cache it but you should not depend on it. And use shared memory deliberately, which is the small fast memory attached to a compute unit: load a tile of the data once cooperatively with a coalesced access, have every thread work on that tile from shared memory, then write the result out coalesced again. This is the standard structure for any computation with reuse — a matrix multiply, a stencil, a convolution — and its value is that it converts a globally-scattered access into one globally-coalesced read followed by local sharing, which is the difference between the memory system being a bottleneck and not.

    /* The hardware property. */
const MECHANISM = {
  fact: 'MEMORY IS FETCHED IN TRANSACTIONS COVERING A CONTIGUOUS RANGE - typically THIRTY-TWO TO A HUNDRED AND TWENTY-EIGHT BYTES',
  detail: 'a REQUEST FOR ONE ELEMENT of a transaction retrieves THE WHOLE THING',
  coalesced: 'when ADJACENT THREADS READ ADJACENT ADDRESSES, four threads reading four CONSECUTIVE FLOATS need ONE TRANSACTION, and the BANDWIDTH IS FULLY USED',
  scattered: 'when ADJACENT THREADS READ ADDRESSES FAR APART, EACH NEEDS ITS OWN TRANSACTION',
  collapse: 'and if the addresses are SPREAD ACROSS MEMORY the requests CANNOT BE COMBINED AT ALL: the EFFECTIVE BANDWIDTH COLLAPSES to a small fraction of the hardwares',
  consequence: 'the kernel becomes MEMORY-BOUND DESPITE DOING A GREAT DEAL OF ARITHMETIC' };

/* The canonical bad pattern. */
const BAD_PATTERN = {
  is: 'a TWO-DIMENSIONAL ARRAY READ ROW-BY-ROW',
  detail: ['each row is CONTIGUOUS', 'but rows are SEPARATED BY THE ARRAYS TOTAL WIDTH'],
  so: 'the threads in a group MAY SPAN A ROW BOUNDARY and produce A SMALL NUMBER OF TRANSACTIONS per row',
  and: 'the SECOND ROW REPEATS THE WASTE' };

/* Fixes. */
const FIXES = [
  { f: 'store data so the ACCESS PATTERN IS CONTIGUOUS in the last dimension',
    inPractice: 'this USUALLY MEANS TRANSPOSING THE LAYOUT',
    gain: 'and it means that for a computation that READS COLUMN-WISE, STORING IT TRANSPOSED is DRAMATICALLY FASTER' },
  { f: 'PAD ROWS to avoid alignment problems',
    why: 'because if the ROW LENGTH is not a MULTIPLE OF THE TRANSACTION SIZE, EVERY ROW STARTS AT A DIFFERENT OFFSET within a transaction and a FRACTION OF EVERY TRANSACTION IS WASTED',
    how: 'padding each row by A FEW ELEMENTS makes EVERY ROW START AT THE SAME OFFSET' },
  { f: 'coalesce the reads IN THE ALGORITHM, not just in the layout',
    example: 'if threads need the SAME VALUE, READ IT ONCE AND SHARE IT',
    why: 'the hardware may cache it BUT YOU SHOULD NOT DEPEND ON IT' },
  { f: 'use SHARED MEMORY DELIBERATELY', is: 'the SMALL FAST MEMORY attached to a compute unit',
    structure: ['LOAD A TILE of the data once COOPERATIVELY with a coalesced access',
      'HAVE EVERY THREAD WORK ON THAT TILE from shared memory', 'WRITE THE RESULT OUT COALESCED again'],
    standardFor: ['MATRIX MULTIPLY', 'a STENCIL', 'a CONVOLUTION'],
    and: 'ANY COMPUTATION WITH REUSE',
    value: 'it CONVERTS A GLOBALLY-SCATTERED ACCESS into ONE GLOBALLY-COALESCED READ FOLLOWED BY LOCAL SHARING',
    which: 'is the difference between the MEMORY SYSTEM being a bottleneck and not' },
];

34.4 Numerical hygiene: overflow, precision & stability

IEEE 754 floating point values are approximations, so subtracting close numbers can cancel significant digits, very large and very small magnitudes can over- or underflow, and formula order changes results. Stable, algebraically rearranged formulas, integer cents for money, and log-space sums for tiny products avoid silently wrong answers. The habit is to be suspicious of any computed difference or product near the limits of double.

# floats are approximations; large + small BYTES get swallowed:
x = 1e16                       # a huge float
print(x + 1.0 == x)            # True -- the +1 vanished!
# avoid catastrophic cancellation; prefer numerically stable formulas.
# e.g. variance: mean of squares MINUS square of mean is a famous
# instigator; use Welford's or statistics.variance instead.
# For money always integer cents; for probabilities use log-space;
# for linear algebra use the library (numpy) tuned for the model -not
# naive textbook math done in Python loops (Ch.27 warnings, reinforced).

Floating point, and the four ways it lies

The single fact that makes every floating-point surprise explicable: a finite number of bits cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly, so every arithmetic operation rounds, and the rounding accumulates. That is the whole mechanism, and the four consequences follow from it mechanically. Precision is fixed and chosen in advance. A double-precision value has about sixteen significant decimal digits, and the value stored is the nearest representable one — which for one and a tenth is not one and a tenth. So 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3, and it is not because the addition is wrong: the two operands were already rounded on the way in and the result is rounded again on the way out. Operations that should be equal are not. 0.1 + 0.7 === 0.8 is false while 0.5 + 0.5 === 1.0 is true, and the reason is which side of a representable boundary the rounding fell on — a fact about the magnitudes, not about the arithmetic. Order matters. Summing a list from smallest to largest preserves precision; summing from largest to smallest loses it, because each addition to a large accumulator discards everything smaller than the accumulator's resolution — and this is why a numerical-methods library specifies a summation order and a naive loop gets a different answer. Small values vanish. Adding one billionth to one million changes nothing at all, because the gap between representable values near one million is larger than one billionth, and no amount of arithmetic will recover it. Then the four places this bites in practice, and each has a specific answer. Money. Never a float. Store an integer number of minor units — cents — and do the arithmetic in integers, because a value in cents is exact and a value in pounds and pence is not; if you need fractional cents, use a fixed-point decimal type rather than a float. Comparisons. Do not compare floats for equality; compare with a tolerance appropriate to the magnitudes, or restructure so that the comparison is against a rounded value. Accumulating over a long sequence. Use compensated summation or accumulate in a wider type, because the error grows with the number of additions. Reproducibility. If the same computation must give the same answer on different machines, it must not depend on floating-point arithmetic at all — not because the arithmetic differs, but because different code paths, vectorisation and fused operations can produce different rounding on the same input, and this is why a build with different optimisation flags can produce a different result.

/* The one fact. */
const FACT = 'a FINITE NUMBER OF BITS CANNOT REPRESENT MOST DECIMAL FRACTIONS EXACTLY, so every arithmetic operation ROUNDS, and the rounding ACCUMULATES';

/* Four consequences, all following mechanically. */
const CONSEQUENCES = [
  { c: 'PRECISION IS FIXED AND CHOSEN IN ADVANCE',
    detail: 'a double-precision value has about SIXTEEN SIGNIFICANT DECIMAL DIGITS, and the value stored is the NEAREST REPRESENTABLE ONE',
    and: 'which for one and a tenth is NOT one and a tenth' },
  { c: 'OPERATIONS THAT SHOULD BE EQUAL are not',
    example: 'adding a tenth and a fifth is not equal to three tenths, while adding a half and a half IS equal to one',
    reason: 'which side of a REPRESENTABLE BOUNDARY the rounding fell on',
    and: 'this is a fact about the MAGNITUDES, not about the ARITHMETIC' },
  { c: 'ORDER MATTERS',
    detail: 'SUMMING FROM SMALLEST TO LARGEST PRESERVES PRECISION; SUMMING FROM LARGEST TO SMALLEST LOSES IT',
    why: 'because each addition to a LARGE ACCUMULATOR DISCARDS EVERYTHING SMALLER than the accumulators resolution',
    consequence: 'which is why a NUMERICAL-METHODS LIBRARY SPECIFIES A SUMMATION ORDER and a naive loop gets a DIFFERENT ANSWER' },
  { c: 'SMALL VALUES VANISH',
    example: 'adding one billionth to one million CHANGES NOTHING AT ALL',
    why: 'because the GAP BETWEEN REPRESENTABLE VALUES near one million is LARGER than one billionth',
    and: 'and NO AMOUNT OF ARITHMETIC WILL RECOVER IT' },
];

/* Four places it bites. */
const PRACTICE = [
  { p: 'MONEY', rule: 'NEVER A FLOAT',
    how: 'store an INTEGER NUMBER OF MINOR UNITS - CENTS - and do the arithmetic in INTEGERS',
    why: 'because a VALUE IN CENTS IS EXACT and a VALUE IN POUNDS AND PENCE IS NOT',
    ifNeeded: 'if you need FRACTIONAL CENTS, use a FIXED-POINT DECIMAL TYPE rather than a float' },
  { p: 'COMPARISONS', rule: 'do NOT COMPARE FLOATS FOR EQUALITY',
    instead: 'compare with a TOLERANCE APPROPRIATE TO THE MAGNITUDES',
    or: 'RESTRUCTURE SO THAT the comparison is AGAINST A ROUNDED VALUE' },
  { p: 'ACCUMULATING OVER A LONG SEQUENCE', do: ['COMPENSATED SUMMATION', 'accumulate in a WIDER TYPE'],
    why: 'because the ERROR GROWS WITH THE NUMBER OF ADDITIONS' },
  { p: 'REPRODUCIBILITY', rule: 'if the SAME COMPUTATION MUST GIVE THE SAME ANSWER on different machines, it MUST NOT DEPEND ON FLOATING-POINT ARITHMETIC AT ALL',
    why: ['not because the arithmetic DIFFERS',
      'but because DIFFERENT CODE PATHS, VECTORISATION and FUSED OPERATIONS can produce DIFFERENT ROUNDING on the same input'],
    consequence: 'which is why a BUILD WITH DIFFERENT OPTIMISATION FLAGS can produce a DIFFERENT RESULT' },
];

It demonstrates that adding a small number to a huge float changes nothing, then lists habits like integer cents and stable formulas that avoid precision bugs.

34.5 Profiling: find O(1) gains before O(n²) rewrites

Measure before you optimize, since intuition about where time goes is almost always wrong: a profiler such as perf, or a sampling profiler in your language, reports the actual hot functions and wait times. Fix algorithmic complexity first, an O(n squared) to O(n log n) change beats any micro-tuning, then memory layout and cache behavior, and micro-optimizations last. Baselines, a benchmark harness, and re-measuring after every change keep the work honest.

  1. Profile first (cProfile/perf, flamegraphs) — intuition about "where time goes" is wrong ~always.
  2. Optimize in this order: algorithmic change → memory layout → micro-code. Never the reverse.
  3. Measure BEFORE and AFTER with the same benchmark; keep the speedup measured, or it’s vibes.

Why profiling first, and how to read the result

Profiling is not an optimisation technique; it is the technique that tells you which optimisation to make, and skipping it is the single most common reason optimisation efforts make things slower. A profiler samples where execution actually is — periodically interrupting the program and recording the current stack — and aggregates the samples into a picture of where the time went. Two things follow and they are why the tool exists. The time is not where you think it is. In most programs the overwhelming majority of time is in a small number of places, often a third of them accounting for most of the runtime, and those places are frequently boring — a loop doing a bounds check, a property lookup, a small allocation repeated a million times. And the cost is not proportional to the complexity of the code. A function nested five calls deep with a trivial body can dominate a profile, while an algorithm that looks expensive runs once. The discipline is therefore strict: measure, find the actual hot spot, fix that, measure again. And then the four profiling tools, each answering a different question. A sampling profiler answers "where does the time go", cheaply, with low overhead, and it is the default choice because it perturbs the program least. A tracing profiler records every function entry and exit, which gives a call graph and exact inclusive and exclusive times, at the cost of a large overhead that can change the behaviour of a latency-sensitive program. A statistical profiler is a name for the sampling kind and is worth distinguishing because it can attribute time inlined and optimised code, which is its advantage over naive instrumentation. A memory profiler answers a different question — "what is allocated and what is retained" — and it is the tool for a memory leak, a growth over time, or a program that is faster when given more memory because it is thrashing. Then how to read a profile and avoid the three traps. Flat functions are not interesting; the top of the list is where the work is, and the interesting information is usually in the inclusive column and the call tree beneath it. Time spent in a function called by a hot function is not that function's fault, so the exclusive figure is the one to act on and the inclusive figure tells you the caller worth changing. And a profile taken on a different input shape is a profile of the wrong program — a function that is negligible on ten thousand records is most of the runtime on ten million, so profiles must be taken on representative data, which is the accuracy argument from the testing chapter applied to performance. Then the optimisation order, and it is worth having because the sequence matters more than the individual techniques. Fix the algorithm first, because an asymptotic improvement beats every constant-factor change by a margin no optimisation closes. Fix the data layout second, which is the memory hierarchy's answer and which is usually a larger win than anything you can do to the code. Remove work third — do not compute it, cache it, batch it, the concurrency chapter's first option. Then reduce constant factors, with vectorisation and a better algorithm for a smaller subproblem. And parallelise last, because it multiplies whatever you have, including a bad design, and because Amdahl's law means the ceiling is set by the serial fraction you have already measured.

/* Why the tool exists. */
const WHY = {
  isNot: 'an OPTIMISATION TECHNIQUE',
  is: 'the technique that TELLS YOU WHICH OPTIMISATION to make',
  and: 'skipping it is the SINGLE MOST COMMON REASON OPTIMISATION EFFORTS MAKE THINGS SLOWER',
  mechanism: 'SAMPLES WHERE EXECUTION ACTUALLY IS - periodically INTERRUPTING the program and RECORDING THE CURRENT STACK - and AGGREGATES the samples',
  follows: [
    { f: 'the TIME IS NOT WHERE YOU THINK IT IS',
      detail: 'the OVERWHELMING MAJORITY of time is in a SMALL NUMBER OF PLACES, often A THIRD of them accounting for MOST of the runtime',
      and: 'those places are FREQUENTLY BORING - a loop doing a BOUNDS CHECK, a PROPERTY LOOKUP, a small ALLOCATION repeated a million times' },
    { f: 'the COST IS NOT PROPORTIONAL to the COMPLEXITY of the code',
      detail: 'a function NESTED FIVE CALLS DEEP with a trivial body can DOMINATE a profile',
      while: 'an algorithm that LOOKS EXPENSIVE runs ONCE' },
  ],
  discipline: 'MEASURE, FIND THE ACTUAL HOT SPOT, FIX THAT, MEASURE AGAIN',
};

/* Four tools, four questions. */
const TOOLS = [
  { t: 'a SAMPLING PROFILER', q: 'where does the TIME GO',
    traits: ['CHEAP', 'LOW OVERHEAD'],
    isTheDefault: 'because it PERTURBS THE PROGRAM LEAST' },
  { t: 'a TRACING PROFILER', does: 'records EVERY FUNCTION ENTRY AND EXIT',
    gives: ['a CALL GRAPH', 'exact INCLUSIVE and EXCLUSIVE times'],
    cost: 'a LARGE OVERHEAD that can CHANGE THE BEHAVIOUR of a latency-sensitive program' },
  { t: 'a STATISTICAL PROFILER', isA: 'a NAME for the sampling kind',
    advantage: 'it can ATTRIBUTE TIME IN INLINED AND OPTIMISED CODE',
    which: 'which is its advantage over NAIVE INSTRUMENTATION' },
  { t: 'a MEMORY PROFILER', q: 'what is ALLOCATED and what is RETAINED',
    usedFor: ['a MEMORY LEAK', 'GROWTH OVER TIME',
      'a program that is FASTER WHEN GIVEN MORE MEMORY because it is THRASHING'] },
];

/* How to read it, and three traps. */
const READING = [
  { t: 'FLAT FUNCTIONS ARE NOT INTERESTING',
    detail: 'the TOP OF THE LIST is where the WORK IS',
    and: 'the INTERESTING INFORMATION is usually in the INCLUSIVE COLUMN and the CALL TREE beneath it' },
  { t: 'time spent in a function CALLED BY A HOT FUNCTION is not that functions fault',
    so: 'the EXCLUSIVE FIGURE is the one to act on',
    and: 'the INCLUSIVE FIGURE tells you the CALLER WORTH CHANGING' },
  { t: 'a PROFILE TAKEN ON A DIFFERENT INPUT SHAPE IS A PROFILE OF THE WRONG PROGRAM',
    example: 'a function that is NEGLIGIBLE ON TEN THOUSAND RECORDS is MOST OF THE RUNTIME on ten million',
    rule: 'profiles MUST BE TAKEN ON REPRESENTATIVE DATA',
    connectsTo: 'the testing chapters ACCURACY argument applied to performance' },
];

/* The optimisation order - the SEQUENCE matters more than the techniques. */
const ORDER = [
  { n: 1, a: 'fix the ALGORITHM',
    why: 'because an ASYMPTOTIC IMPROVEMENT beats every CONSTANT-FACTOR CHANGE by a margin NO OPTIMISATION CLOSES' },
  { n: 2, a: 'fix the DATA LAYOUT', which: 'is the MEMORY HIERARCHYS ANSWER',
    note: 'and it is USUALLY A LARGER WIN than anything you can do to the CODE' },
  { n: 3, a: 'REMOVE WORK', how: ['do not COMPUTE IT', 'CACHE IT', 'BATCH IT'],
    connects: 'the concurrency chapters FIRST OPTION' },
  { n: 4, a: 'then reduce CONSTANT FACTORS', how: ['VECTORISATION', 'a better algorithm for a SMALLER SUBPROBLEM'] },
  { n: 5, a: 'and PARALLELISE LAST',
    why: ['it MULTIPLIES WHATEVER YOU HAVE, including a BAD DESIGN',
      'and because AMDAHLS LAW means the CEILING IS SET BY THE SERIAL FRACTION YOU HAVE ALREADY MEASURED'] },
];

What to do when profiling says you are memory-bound

Three specific situations and their answers, because "the profile says memory" is a diagnosis and not yet a fix. Working set larger than cache. The classic fix is blocking or tiling: instead of computing over the whole array at once, process it in blocks sized to fit the cache, so each block is read from memory once and reused from cache for every pass that needs it. This is a genuine transformation of the algorithm's memory behaviour rather than a tweak, and it is the standard answer for matrix multiplication and for any operation with multiple passes over the same data. The second answer is reducing the data touched, which is usually a better algorithm: a sort that touches less data is faster than a sort that touches the same data more efficiently. Allocation churn. If a profile shows substantial time in allocation or garbage collection, the data structure is the problem: a program that allocates a small object per iteration in a tight loop will spend a large fraction of its time in the allocator, and the fix is to reuse a buffer, use a pool, or choose a flat structure. This one is worth recognising because allocation cost is invisible in the source — the code looks like a simple assignment — and the profile's "time in the allocator" line is the only place it appears. And false sharing, which is specific to multicore code: two threads writing to different fields of the same cache line invalidate each other's cache, so each write costs a coherence round trip even though no data is actually shared. The fix is padding fields so that independently-written data lands in different cache lines, and this one is worth knowing because it is invisible, it costs a great deal on a many-core machine, and it disappears on a single core, which is why it is so often attributed to something else. Then what to do when the profile says you are compute-bound, which is the easier case. The arithmetic is genuinely the cost, and the options are: a better algorithm; a cheaper formulation of the same one — replacing repeated division by a single reciprocal, hoisting an invariant out of a loop, replacing a power by repeated squaring; a fused operation where the hardware has one; or vectorisation, which is the concurrency chapter's parallel model applied within a single core's instruction set. And one thing to check before optimising anything: is the program spending its time on something that should not be computed at all? A function in a hot path that produces a value nobody reads, a repeated lookup that could be hoisted, a debug assertion left enabled in a release build, a logging call that formats its message even when the level is disabled — these are all common, all invisible in the source, and each is a larger win than any micro-optimisation available after them.

/* Memory-bound: three situations and their answers. */
const WORKING_SET = {
  problem: 'WORKING SET LARGER THAN CACHE',
  fix: 'BLOCKING or TILING',
  how: ['instead of computing over the WHOLE ARRAY AT ONCE, PROCESS IT IN BLOCKS SIZED TO FIT THE CACHE',
    'so each block is READ FROM MEMORY ONCE and REUSED FROM CACHE for every PASS that needs it'],
  kindOfChange: 'a GENUINE TRANSFORMATION of the algorithms MEMORY BEHAVIOUR rather than a TWEAK',
  standardFor: ['matrix multiplication', 'any operation with MULTIPLE PASSES over the same data'],
  betterAnswer: 'REDUCING THE DATA TOUCHED, which is USUALLY A BETTER ALGORITHM - a sort that touches less data is FASTER than a sort that touches the same data more efficiently' };
const ALLOCATION = {
  problem: 'ALLOCATION CHURN',
  symptom: 'a program that ALLOCATES A SMALL OBJECT PER ITERATION in a tight loop will spend a LARGE FRACTION OF ITS TIME in the allocator',
  fix: ['REUSE A BUFFER', 'use a POOL', 'choose a FLAT STRUCTURE'],
  worthRecognising: true,
  why: 'ALLOCATION COST IS INVISIBLE IN THE SOURCE - the code LOOKS LIKE A SIMPLE ASSIGNMENT',
  and: 'the profiles TIME IN THE ALLOCATOR line is the ONLY PLACE it appears' };
const FALSE_SHARING = {
  problem: 'two threads writing to DIFFERENT FIELDS of the SAME CACHE LINE INVALIDATE each others cache',
  cost: 'so each write costs a COHERENCE ROUND TRIP even though NO DATA IS ACTUALLY SHARED',
  fix: 'PADDING FIELDS so that INDEPENDENTLY-WRITTEN DATA LANDS IN DIFFERENT CACHE LINES',
  whyWorthKnowing: ['it is INVISIBLE', 'it COSTS A GREAT DEAL on a many-core machine',
    'and it DISAPPEARS ON A SINGLE CORE, which is why it is SO OFTEN ATTRIBUTED TO SOMETHING ELSE' } };

/* Compute-bound. */
const COMPUTE_BOUND = {
  is: 'the EASIER CASE', because: 'the ARITHMETIC IS GENUINELY THE COST',
  options: ['a BETTER ALGORITHM',
    'a CHEAPER FORMULATION of the same one - replacing REPEATED DIVISION by a single reciprocal, HOISTING AN INVARIANT out of a loop, replacing a POWER by REPEATED SQUARING',
    'a FUSED OPERATION where the hardware has one', 'VECTORISATION'],

/* Check before optimising. */
const CHECK_FIRST = {
  rule: 'is the program SPENDING ITS TIME ON SOMETHING THAT SHOULD NOT BE COMPUTED AT ALL',
  instances: ['a function in a HOT PATH that PRODUCES A VALUE NOBODY READS',
    'a REPEATED LOOKUP THAT COULD BE HOISTED',
    'a DEBUG ASSERTION LEFT ENABLED in a release build',
    'a LOGGING CALL THAT FORMATS ITS MESSAGE even when the level is disabled'],
  why: 'these are all COMMON, all INVISIBLE IN THE SOURCE, and each is a LARGER WIN than any MICRO-OPTIMISATION available after them',
};

Exercises 34

  1. Benchmark row-major vs column-major access on a 2000×2000 list-of-lists and record the ratio.
  2. Compute Amdahl’s ceiling for a workload that’s 30% serial — then state what you’d fix first.
  3. Run cProfile on a toy program, read the flamegraph, and justify the ONE fix you’d make first.

35 · Applied ML Systems: Vision, Language & LLM Engineering

The systems layer that ships models to production: versioned datasets, training and validation pipelines, embeddings, retrieval, evaluation, and serving infrastructure. Training is the fun part, but this covers the other ninety percent of real machine learning engineering, where data quality, reproducible training, latency budgets, and model monitoring decide success. Every stage is treated as software, with tests, versions, and rollback, so model changes are controlled deploys.

35.1 The ML system pipeline, end to end35.2 Embeddings & vector search: recommendation & retrieval35.3 Evals & the honest measurement of AI systems35.4 Adjacent fields: computer vision & NLP35.5 Serving, quantization & the cost cliff

Ch.28 taught the ML mechanics; this chapter is the systems layer that ships models: data pipelines, embeddings, retrieval (RAG), evals, and serving — the 90% of industry ML work that isn’t training.

35.1 The ML system pipeline, end to end

The ML pipeline runs from collection, through labeling and cleaning, to feature engineering, training, evaluation, and then serving with feedback loops that feed back into the data. Garbage labels upstream poison everything downstream no matter how good the model code is, so data quality gates the whole pipeline. Each step is versioned like code, using feature stores and experiment tracking to keep runs reproducible.

Data ----------------- training ---------------- serving ------------ feedback
collect     ->    features  ->    train/validate  ->  deploy + monitor -> drift
clean       ->    label      ->    hyperparameter  ->  A/B in prod
version     ->    augment    ->    evaluate (Hold)
gate: DATA QUALITY is 80% of model quality. Garbage labels in ->
garbage predictions out, and no architectural cleverness fixes it.
Version DATA and MODELS separately (DVC/MLflow); an ML repo should be
reproducible: same data+code+config => same eval numbers.

Reproducibility, and the three things that must be versioned separately

A machine-learning pipeline that cannot be re-run produces results you cannot trust, and reproducibility here has a specific structure that differs from a normal build. A normal build takes a source tree and produces a deterministic output; a model training run takes source, data and configuration, and produces an output that depends on the order the data was fed, the random seed, the library versions and often the hardware — so the output is reproducible only if all of those are pinned. Three things must be versioned separately and each for a specific reason. Data. The dataset is an artefact that changes independently of the code, and a result that cannot be tied to a dataset version is a result that cannot be reproduced or rolled back. This is the data-engineering chapter's load-first argument applied here: store the exact training data as an immutable snapshot, with its identifier recorded alongside every artefact produced from it, because "we retrained last month" is not an answer and the answer is frequently unavailable. Code. In source control, obviously, but the non-obvious part is that the training code and the inference code must be pinned to each other: a model evaluated with one preprocessing implementation and served with another is a different system, and this is the training-serving skew the data chapter named. Hyperparameters and the training environment. Every hyperparameter is a value that was chosen, and the environment — library versions, driver version, hardware model — is a value that was not chosen and therefore must be recorded. Then the three failure modes that this prevents, and each has produced real incidents. Silent divergence: a preprocessing change improves the reported metric and quietly worsens production, because the two code paths no longer agree. Irreproducible training: a run that cannot be repeated, so the artefact that is serving cannot be regenerated and a bug cannot be bisected. And silent data drift: the pipeline continues running, the data has changed, and the reported metric is computed on the new data so the change in output is invisible — which is why the monitoring must compare against a fixed evaluation set rather than a current one. Then the operational practices that make this hold over time. Make every training run a single command that produces a logged, versioned artefact plus a metadata record containing the seed, the data identifier, the code revision and the environment — so that a run is reproducible by reconstructing the command from the metadata rather than by remembering what was typed. Track the metric as a function of time, not just as a value, so that a change in the data shows up as a change in the curve. Keep the evaluation set frozen and separate from training, permanently, and if it must be refreshed, refresh it deliberately with a documented procedure and re-baseline. And have a rollback path: the previous model version, its data identifier and its serving configuration must all be recoverable, because the realistic incident is not "we cannot train" but "we trained something worse and are serving it" — and the fix is a rollback, which requires the previous artefacts to exist and be identifiable.

/* Reproducibility has a different structure here. */
const WHY = {
  contrast: ['a NORMAL BUILD takes a source tree and produces a DETERMINISTIC OUTPUT',
    'a MODEL TRAINING RUN takes source, data and configuration, and produces an OUTPUT THAT DEPENDS ON the order the data was fed, the RANDOM SEED, the LIBRARY VERSIONS and often the HARDWARE'],
  so: 'the output is REPRODUCIBLE ONLY IF ALL OF THOSE ARE PINNED',
};

/* Three failure modes prevented. */

    consequence: ['the ARTEFACT THAT IS SERVING cannot be regenerated', 'a BUG CANNOT BE BISECTED'] },
  { f: 'SILENT DATA DRIFT', detail: 'the PIPELINE CONTINUES RUNNING, the DATA HAS CHANGED, and the REPORTED METRIC is computed on the NEW DATA',
    consequence: 'so the CHANGE IN OUTPUT IS INVISIBLE',
    fix: 'which is why the MONITORING MUST COMPARE against a FIXED EVALUATION SET rather than a current one' },
];

/* Operational practices. */
const PRACTICE = [
  { p: 'make every TRAINING RUN A SINGLE COMMAND that produces a LOGGED, VERSIONED ARTEFACT',
    plus: 'a METADATA RECORD containing the SEED, the DATA IDENTIFIER, the CODE REVISION and the ENVIRONMENT',
    gain: 'so a run is REPRODUCIBLE BY RECONSTRUCTING THE COMMAND from the metadata RATHER THAN BY REMEMBERING WHAT WAS TYPED' },
  { p: 'track the METRIC AS A FUNCTION OF TIME, not just as a value',
    gain: 'so that a CHANGE IN THE DATA SHOWS UP AS A CHANGE IN THE CURVE' },
  { p: 'keep the EVALUATION SET FROZEN and SEPARATE from training, PERMANENTLY',
    ifRefresh: 'refresh it DELIBERATELY WITH A DOCUMENTED PROCEDURE and RE-BASELINE' },
  { p: 'have a ROLLBACK PATH',
    requires: ['the PREVIOUS MODEL VERSION', 'its DATA IDENTIFIER', 'its SERVING CONFIGURATION'],
    allRecoverable: true,
    why: 'because the REALISTIC INCIDENT is not we cannot train but WE TRAINED SOMETHING WORSE AND ARE SERVING IT',
    and: 'the fix is a ROLLBACK, which REQUIRES THE PREVIOUS ARTEFACTS TO EXIST and BE IDENTIFIABLE' },
];

An ASCII map of the whole ML lifecycle, where data quality upstream plus separate versioning of data and models keeps evals reproducible.

35.2 Embeddings & vector search: recommendation & retrieval

Embeddings map discrete and high-dimensional inputs, words, images, users, into dense vectors so that semantic similarity becomes distance in vector space, which enables search, clustering, and recommendation. Vector databases index these high-dimensional vectors with approximate nearest neighbor search such as HNSW for low-latency retrieval. Retrieval-augmented generation combines a vector lookup over your own documents with an LLM, letting products answer from data the model never saw.

  • An embedding = a dense vector capturing meaning (similar texts land near each other). It’s the primitive for search, clustering, recommendations, and dedup.
  • Vector search = "find the 10 nearest vectors". Exact (linear scan + distance) works until millions of rows; then approximate indexes (HNSW/IVF) trade ~1% recall for 100× speed. NoSQL is an odd place for this — the vector DB/Crypto— err, vector store is the new specialty.
  • RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation): chunk documents → embed → index → at query time retrieve the relevant chunks and hand them to an LLM as context. That’s how LLM products answer with your data and cite sources — grounding (Ch.31's trust lessons, Ch.28.7).

    • What an embedding is, and how one is trained

    An embedding is a fixed-length vector chosen so that proximity encodes meaning, and everything about the technique follows from how that is arranged. The training signal is a prediction task, and the trick is what the model must guess. Given a word, predict its neighbours from a large corpus — or given a sentence, predict the sentence that followed it. The model cannot do this without learning representations where words used in similar contexts are near each other, so meaning emerges from co-occurrence rather than from a definition, and this is why an embedding knows that "doctor" and "nurse" are related without anybody having said they were. Then three properties that follow, and each is a capability. Similarity becomes arithmetic: cosine similarity between vectors is a measure of semantic relatedness, so "king minus man plus woman" approximates "queen" — not because the arithmetic is learned but because the relationships between these words are approximately linear in the space. They generalise across vocabulary: a rare word appearing in eleven sentences still gets a usable vector, because it is placed by its contexts. They support ranking by meaning rather than by matching: a search for "cheap flights" can find a document about "discount airfares" with no shared vocabulary. Then the methods, and the progression is worth knowing because each solves a specific failure of the one before. Word vectors represent one word as one point, which fails for every word whose meaning depends on context — "bank" has two unrelated senses and one vector averages them. Sentence and document embeddings represent a whole text as one vector, which fixes that and loses ordering, since averaging does not distinguish "dog bites man" from "man bites dog". Transformers produce contextual embeddings, where each token's vector is computed from the sentence around it, so "bank" in "river bank" and "bank loan" receive different vectors — and this is the technique behind everything the language-model chapter described, with the consequence that embeddings are produced by a model you must run rather than looked up in a table. Then the three problems that exist with contextual embeddings and are worth knowing. They are tied to a model, so the vectors from one model cannot be compared with vectors from another — which means re-embedding a corpus is a migration, and the models chapter's evaluation discipline applies to the encoder as well as to the model built on it. They cost a forward pass per text, so indexing a large corpus is expensive and must be batched on the accelerator, and a change of encoder means re-indexing everything. And they are directional, not symmetric: a similarity score is not a distance you can threshold uniformly, and the appropriate threshold varies by corpus, which is why retrieval quality is tuned empirically rather than derived. Then how to choose, and the criterion is entirely about what you are optimising. If you need maximum quality and the corpus is small, use a transformer encoder and accept the cost — a document-level embedding from a strong model is better than a vector of averaged word vectors by a wide margin. If the corpus is large or the query rate is high, use a compact model trained for retrieval, because the quality difference is small compared with the throughput difference. If the corpus changes rarely and the vocabulary is small, a dedicated retrieval model may be entirely sufficient and will be faster and cheaper. And in every case evaluate on your own queries, because the published benchmark is measured against a general corpus and your users ask particular questions.

    /* What an embedding is. */
const EMBEDDING = {
  is: 'a FIXED-LENGTH VECTOR chosen so that PROXIMITY ENCODES MEANING',
  trainingSignal: 'a PREDICTION TASK, and the trick is WHAT THE MODEL MUST GUESS',

/* How to choose. */
const CHOOSE = [

    gain: 'a DOCUMENT-LEVEL EMBEDDING from a strong model is BETTER THAN A VECTOR OF AVERAGED WORD VECTORS by a wide margin' },

  { if: 'the CORPUS CHANGES RARELY and the VOCABULARY IS SMALL', then: 'a DEDICATED RETRIEVAL MODEL may be ENTIRELY SUFFICIENT',
    and: 'it will be FASTER AND CHEAPER' },
  { always: 'EVALUATE ON YOUR OWN QUERIES',
    why: 'because the PUBLISHED BENCHMARK is MEASURED AGAINST A GENERAL CORPUS and your users ask PARTICULAR QUESTIONS' },

    Retrieval, and why the retriever is usually the problem

    In a retrieval-augmented system the answer is almost always either present in the retrieved passages or absent from them entirely, which means the retriever decides the accuracy of the whole system and the generator only decides how it is phrased. That makes retrieval the component worth measuring first, and the failures have a specific structure. The chunk does not contain the answer because the answer spans a boundary — this is the chunking problem from the language-model chapter, and it is why overlap between adjacent chunks and keeping section structure intact are the two levers. The chunk contains the answer but does not match the query, because the query and the answer use different words — the embedding's semantic matching should handle this and does not always, and the specific case where it fails is a query using a domain term the corpus expresses differently. The retriever returns the wrong passages first, and the generator answers from them, producing a confident answer that is not in the corpus. That last one is the dangerous failure and the reason the retrieval step's output should be visible in the interface: a system that shows which sources it used can be checked, and one that does not cannot. Then the three techniques, and each fixes a different failure. Hybrid search combines a dense embedding search with a keyword index, summing or interleaving the scores, and it fixes the terminology mismatch because a keyword index finds the exact term the embedding misses; the language-model chapter's indexer argument applies here and it is why keyword search has not been replaced. Re-ranking takes the top candidates the first pass produced and applies a more expensive, more accurate model to score them properly, which recovers the cases where a cheap first pass retrieved the right documents in the wrong order — and this is nearly always worth doing because the first pass is a recall optimisation and the re-ranker is a precision optimisation, and a system with only the first pass has no precision stage at all. Query expansion rewrites the query before searching — paraphrasing it, decomposing a multi-part question into several, adding the terms a likely answer would contain — and it fixes the failure where the user's phrasing and the corpus's phrasing differ. Then the three numbers, and knowing which one is low tells you what to fix. Recall at k measures whether the correct passage is anywhere in the first k results — this is the retriever's number and it is the one to improve first. Precision at k measures the proportion of the first k that are relevant — this is what the re-ranker improves. And answer faithfulness measures whether the generated answer is supported by the retrieved passages, which is the generator's number and the one that detects the confident-wrong-answer failure. And then the operational point, which is the one that catches people out. Retrieval quality is a moving target, because the corpus changes. A system tuned against last quarter's documents is not tuned against this quarter's, and there is no alert for a retrieval system that has quietly stopped finding things — the generated answers simply get worse and there is no error. So evaluate retrieval against a fixed query set on a schedule, and monitor the distribution of retrieved scores: a shift in the typical top score is an early signal that the corpus or the queries have changed, and it arrives well before anyone complains that the answers are bad.

    /* The retriever decides the accuracy. */
const FRAMING = {
  observation: 'the ANSWER IS ALMOST ALWAYS EITHER PRESENT IN THE RETRIEVED PASSAGES OR ABSENT FROM THEM ENTIRELY',
  so: 'the RETRIEVER DECIDES THE ACCURACY of the whole system',
  and: 'the GENERATOR only decides HOW IT IS PHRASED' };

/* Retrieval failures have a structure. */

35.3 Evals & the honest measurement of AI systems

Evals are the CI/CD of AI: a golden set of examples with expected behavior, checked with task metrics before any model or prompt change is merged. They run automatically in the pipeline along with unit tests, sometimes using LLM judges to grade qualitative output where exact text cannot be checked. Without them a new prompt is an unregulated deploy whose regression you find in production.

# The eval harness is the CI/CD of AI -- without it, a model change is
# an unregulated deploy:
#  - golden set: curated input -> expected output pairs (hand-checked)
#  - task metrics: accuracy/F1 where ground truth exists, or
#    rubric scoring (judge the answer 1-5 on criteria)
#  - grading models/LLM judges: cheap & reproducible, but calibrate
#    them on hand-scored samples first
#  - drift watch: distribution of inputs/debug in prod changes; compare
#    monthly means, not vibes (Ch.30.4 lineage discipline applies)
# Gate on green: a prompt/config/tune ships only when evals + guardrail
# metrics stay green. "The model got better" is a claim, evals are proof.

Designing the evaluation, which is the actual work

Most teams build a model and then realise they have no way to tell whether a change helped, and the reason is that they never defined what "good" means for their use. The evaluation set is that definition. Collect real examples from the actual system, not from a colleague's imagination: the queries users issued, the inputs they supplied, the documents they had open. Real examples have a property synthetic ones lack, which is that their distribution is the distribution you will face, including the long tail of misspelled, ambiguous and adversarial queries that constitute a substantial fraction of real traffic. Label them by what the correct answer is, which is the expensive part and the part worth doing properly: two people independently labelling each item, disagreements resolved by discussion, and the agreement rate recorded — because a labelling scheme where the annotators agree eight times out of ten has a ceiling, and knowing it tells you which improvements are detectable. Keep the set fixed and version it. A set that changes between experiments makes results incomparable, which is the same defect as changing a test between runs and is reported as "the model improved" when the measurement changed. Then the three layers, and each answers a different question so that a failure tells you where to look. Component-level metrics — does retrieval find the right document, does generation contain the answer, is the output the right format — and their value is that a failure localises. End-to-end metrics — does the whole system give an answer a user would accept — and their value is that they measure the thing, but a failure does not localise. And human evaluation, which remains necessary for anything about quality, helpfulness or appropriateness, and which is expensive and inconsistent. Then using a model as the judge, which is genuinely useful and genuinely dangerous, and the danger is specific enough to state. Position bias: a judge prefers the answer presented first. Length bias: a judge prefers the longer answer, so a verbose system scores well. Self-preference: a judge scores its own family's output higher. Agreement is not the same as validity: a judge that agrees with humans eighty per cent of the time is a noisy measurement instrument and its noise is invisible unless you measure it. The mitigations are: always report the agreement rate between judge and human on a sample, so the number is attached to the result; randomise the presentation order; use a rubric with specific criteria rather than "is this good"; and use the judge only for relative comparisons, where its noise matters less than for absolute claims. Then the practices that make evaluation part of delivery rather than a project. Run the evaluation on every model change, in the pipeline, and block on regression — the same gate discipline as continuous integration, applied to behaviour instead of correctness. Monitor the live system with the same metrics, because the distribution shifts and a model that was evaluated on last quarter's questions is being judged on this quarter's. And watch for the failure that has no alert: a gradual decline that never crosses a threshold, which is why the dashboard should show the trend rather than only the current value.

/* The evaluation set IS the definition of good. */
const SET = {
  is: 'the DEFINITION OF WHAT GOOD MEANS for your use',
  collect: 'REAL EXAMPLES FROM THE ACTUAL SYSTEM, not from a COLLEAGUES IMAGINATION',
  instances: ['the queries users ISSUED', 'the INPUTS THEY SUPPLIED', 'the DOCUMENTS THEY HAD OPEN'],
  whyReal: 'they have a PROPERTY SYNTHETIC ONES LACK',
  which: 'their DISTRIBUTION IS THE DISTRIBUTION YOU WILL FACE',
  including: ['the LONG TAIL of MISSPELLED, AMBIGUOUS and ADVERSARIAL queries',
    'which constitute a SUBSTANTIAL FRACTION of real traffic'],
  labelling: 'by WHAT THE CORRECT ANSWER IS',
  expensivePart: 'which is the part worth doing PROPERLY',
  how: ['TWO PEOPLE INDEPENDENTLY labelling each item', 'DISAGREEMENTS RESOLVED BY DISCUSSION',
    'the AGREEMENT RATE RECORDED'],
  whyAgreementMatters: 'a labelling scheme where the annotators AGREE EIGHT TIMES OUT OF TEN has a CEILING',
  and: 'knowing it TELLS YOU WHICH IMPROVEMENTS ARE DETECTABLE',
  versionIt: 'KEEP THE SET FIXED AND VERSION IT',
  reason: 'a set that CHANGES BETWEEN EXPERIMENTS makes results INCOMPARABLE',
  sameAs: 'the same defect as CHANGING A TEST BETWEEN RUNS',
  symptom: 'and it is reported as the model improved when the MEASUREMENT CHANGED' };

  { l: 'COMPONENT-LEVEL METRICS', examples: ['does RETRIEVAL find the right document',

/* Model as judge. */

/* Making it part of delivery. */
const PRACTICE = [
  { p: 'RUN THE EVALUATION ON EVERY MODEL CHANGE, IN THE PIPELINE, and block on REGRESSION',
    sameAs: 'the same GATE DISCIPLINE as continuous integration, applied to BEHAVIOUR instead of correctness' },
  { p: 'MONITOR THE LIVE SYSTEM WITH THE SAME METRICS',
    why: 'because the DISTRIBUTION SHIFTS',
    and: 'a model that was evaluated on LAST QUARTERS QUESTIONS is being JUDGED ON THIS QUARTERS' },
