The eval harness is AI’s CI/CD: golden sets, task metrics, LLM judges, and drift watch all gate whether a model change ships.

35.4 Adjacent fields: computer vision & NLP

Computer vision applies convolutional and transformer models to pixels for classification, detection, and segmentation, while NLP handles language with embeddings, sequence models, and LLMs, and recommendation systems combine embeddings with retrieval and ranking. Each field carries its own pipeline shape and a familiar set of production gotchas, from class imbalance and label ambiguity in vision to context windows in language. The patterns of clean data, strong baselines, and honest evals transfer across all of them.

Images are tensors, and what follows from that

A vision model receives a tensor with three dimensions — height, width and channels — and almost everything about the design follows from how that tensor is used. Channels last is the convention, because it puts the spatial dimensions first and lets the arithmetic work across a contiguous block of channels per pixel, which is the layout the hardware's vector units want. Pixels are usually downscaled before the model sees them, and this is a significant decision rather than a preprocessing detail: an image classification model is trained at one resolution and evaluated at another and performs materially worse, and the reason is that the features it learned are scale-dependent. Normalisation is per channel, because each channel has a different range and a different distribution, and normalising per channel is what makes the first layer's inputs comparable. And then the three architecture families and what each is for. A classifier takes an image and produces one label, and its structure is a backbone that extracts features followed by a pooling step and a classifier head. A detection model produces boxes and labels, and the structural idea is that it must propose regions and then classify each, with the modern versions doing both in one network. A segmentation model produces a label per pixel, and the structural idea is that it must combine local detail with global context, because knowing that a road continues across the image is what distinguishes a road from a pavement. And generative models produce an image, in most cases by working in a compressed latent space rather than in pixels, which is worth understanding because it is why image generation is tractable at all: generating a thousand pixels directly is far harder than generating a small representation from which a decoder produces the pixels. Then the four things that are true across all of them, and they are the practical content. Data augmentation is the single largest source of improvement available without new labels: crop, scale, rotate, flip, colour-jitter, and — for videos — temporal sampling. It works because it enforces an invariance the model would otherwise have to learn from data it does not have, and it is worth being clear that a transformation is only valid augmentation if the label is unchanged by it — flipping a photograph of a letter does not leave the label valid. Normalisation of inputs is not optional and getting it wrong produces a model that trains and scores well and fails on real data. Train and serve with identical preprocessing, byte for byte, which is the training-serving skew of the previous section and is worth restating because it is the most common vision deployment failure — a resize done with one library in training and another in serving produces a subtly different image and a measurable accuracy loss nobody attributes to the right cause. And label quality bounds everything, because an ambiguous label — a bounding box that includes half the background, a class with two names — caps the achievable accuracy, and a model trained past that point is fitting noise, which is overfitting with a different cause.

/* Images are tensors. */
const TENSOR = {
  is: 'a TENSOR with THREE DIMENSIONS - height, width and channels',
  channelsLast: 'the CONVENTION',
  whyChannelsLast: 'it puts the SPATIAL DIMENSIONS FIRST and lets the arithmetic work ACROSS A CONTIGUOUS BLOCK of channels per pixel',
  and: 'which is the LAYOUT THE HARDWARES VECTOR UNITS WANT' };

/* Preprocessing decisions. */
const PREPROCESS = [
  { d: 'PIXELS ARE USUALLY DOWNSCALED before the model SEES THEM', isADecision: true,
    why: 'a CLASSIFICATION MODEL is trained at ONE RESOLUTION and evaluated at ANOTHER and performs MATERIALLY WORSE',
    because: 'the FEATURES IT LEARNED ARE SCALE-DEPENDENT' },
  { d: 'NORMALISATION is PER CHANNEL', why: 'each channel has a DIFFERENT RANGE and a DIFFERENT DISTRIBUTION' },
];

The two models, and the transfer-learning argument

Two architectures and the reason the second exists. A convolutional network applies learned filters across the image — a small kernel slid over the input, producing a feature map, with several layers of increasingly receptive field, so that a deep layer responds to an object rather than to an edge. The properties that follow are what matter: weights are shared across positions, so a filter that detects an edge detects it everywhere, and the parameter count does not grow with image size; and the receptive field grows with depth, so a hierarchy of increasingly complex features is built automatically. A vision transformer splits the image into patches, embeds each as a token and runs the transformer over the sequence, and the property that follows is that it has no built-in spatial prior — it must learn that neighbouring patches are related, which is a disadvantage on small datasets and an advantage on large ones, and the practical consequence is that vision transformers need substantially more data or stronger pretraining to reach convolutional performance. Then transfer learning, which is the reason vision works at all in practice, and the argument is short. A model trained on a large, generic dataset learns reusable features: edges, textures, parts, shapes. Those features are not specific to the classes it was trained on, and they transfer to a different task with a different set of labels, so the practical procedure is to take a pretrained model, replace its final classification layer, and train only that — or that plus the last few layers — on your data. That is why a modest labelled dataset is enough for a competent model, and it is why the alternative — training from scratch — is the exception reserved for very large datasets or unusual modalities. Then the four decisions, each with the reasoning that decides it. Whether to fine-tune or to train a head only. A head only preserves every pretrained feature and is right when your task differs from the pretraining task only in its labels; fine-tuning is right when the domain differs — medical images, satellite imagery, industrial surfaces all have statistics that the generic pretraining did not see, and the domain shift is the reason fine-tuning works. Which augmentation is valid, which is the augmentation section's constraint applied: only transformations that leave the label unchanged. Which metric to use, and the answer is not accuracy when the classes are imbalanced, and the section's measures are the right ones. And how much data is enough, which the honest answer is that the useful curve flattens earlier than people expect and the remaining errors are label-quality and genuinely ambiguous cases rather than model capacity. Then the failure modes in deployment, which differ from those in a notebook. Different image statistics at inference — a different camera, a different lighting regime — which shift the distribution the model saw in training and degrade accuracy without any error. A preprocessing mismatch between training and serving, the skew the pipeline section named. Classes present in production that were absent in training, which produce confident nonsense because the model has no output for them. And the model is a fixed function that does not learn from its mistakes — the fine-tuning loop has to be built separately, from collected data, reviewed, and re-evaluated, and a system with no such loop degrades quietly as the world changes.

35.5 Serving, quantization & the cost cliff

Serving models costs money proportional to memory, tokens, and compute, so engineers cut the bill with quantization that shrinks weights to fewer bits, distillation into smaller student models, caching repeated results, and batching requests. For most teams a hosted API beats self-hosting until traffic is high enough that the hardware math flips in your favor. Monitoring cost per request and latency per request keeps those choices honest.

Models are heavy; serving them is a real bill. Techniques: quantization (8/4-bit weights — 2-4× smaller/slower-free), distillation (train small model to mimic big), caching (identical requests hit quickly), and batched inference. The 2026 reality: "just call the API" often beats self-hosting until massive scale — ops cost, not pride, decides.

How compression works, and why the ratio differs so much

Every compression scheme exploits redundancy, and the ratio you achieve is a direct measurement of how much structure the data has — which is why a text file, a photograph and a database dump compress by factors of four, two and fifteen respectively. Deflate looks for repeated byte sequences and replaces each repeat with a reference. It emits a stream of literal bytes and length-distance pairs, so a run of a thousand identical bytes costs a few bytes, and it finds these matches within a sliding window of about thirty kilobytes, which is why it compresses text and structured data well and does not compress already-compressed data at all. The window size is the whole trade-off: a larger window finds longer-range matches and compresses better but requires more memory per compressor and decompressor and is slower to initialise, and a small window is faster but cannot see the repetition. Gzip and zlib are containers around deflate — the same algorithm with a header carrying metadata such as the original filename and modification time — and this is why a compressed file is often larger than the original when the input is a few hundred bytes, because the header is larger than the savings. Brotli is designed for the web and beats gzip by around fifteen to twenty per cent on text at typical settings, with the cost that it is slower to compress, which matters only if you compress on every request rather than ahead of time. Zstandard reaches the higher end — often within a few per cent of the best general-purpose compressor while being much faster — and it has a property that matters operationally: because it compresses in independent blocks with a shared dictionary, decompression can start from the middle of the stream, which is what makes seekable compressed files possible. Then the three things that change the picture in practice. Whether you compress before or after encryption, which is not a matter of preference: encrypted data is indistinguishable from random data and cannot be compressed usefully afterwards, so the order is fixed — compress, then encrypt. Whether you can afford it dynamically. Compressing on every response costs CPU proportional to size; on a small response the header dominates and the size grows; on a large one it is worth it; and the decision belongs in the code that selects a representation rather than in the application. And the dictionary question for small or repetitive payloads, which is the technique that changes the ratio for short texts: a pre-shared dictionary — a fixed list of the most common words, phrases or JSON keys for your domain — lets the compressor reference strings it has never seen in the input, and for an API with a hundred short responses it is the difference between compressing and not compressing at all. Then the two things that are worth being clear about. Compression is not encryption, and one does not imply the other — a compressed file is readable by anyone who can decompress it, and the security chapter's requirement that a secret not be in the repository applies to a compressed file containing one just as much as to a plain one. And compression hides content from inspection, which is convenient for bandwidth and inconvenient for everything else: an encrypted or compressed body cannot be scanned, cannot be logged usefully, and cannot be debugged, which is a real operational cost when something goes wrong inside a compressed response.

Choosing a format, and the failure modes that come with it

Six formats and the criteria that separate them, because the choice is made under constraints and the constraints are what decide. Gzip and zlib are what everything understands, which is their whole value: no library, no configuration and no negotiation required, and universal support in browsers, proxies and tooling. Brotli compresses text fifteen to twenty per cent better at typical settings and is supported in every current browser, at the cost of a slower compression pass — which matters if you compress per response and not if you compress at build time, so the rule is that brotli is for static assets precompressed at build and gzip is the dynamic fallback. Zstandard reaches close to the best general-purpose ratio while being much faster, and its block structure gives you the property that matters for files: you can decompress from the middle of the stream, so a compressed file remains seekable without decompressing it all, which is what makes it usable for anything that is read at arbitrary offsets. Brotli also supports this with a shared dictionary, which for small texts is the single largest available improvement. Transport-level compression is different from content compression — it exists so that a body is not resent on every hop, which makes it worth having inside a network you do not control and worthless when both ends are yours. And any compression that reduces bytes to read from a database or an API result reduces work everywhere downstream, which is why compression at the storage layer is sometimes more valuable than at the transport layer. Then the three failure modes, each of which is characteristic of a particular choice. Compression bombs: a small compressed payload that expands to gigabytes, which turns a compression-based defence into a denial-of-service vector and means a limit on the decompressed size is mandatory rather than prudent. Content-type and encoding mismatches: a client that believes a response is compressed when it is not, or the reverse, produces garbage rather than an error, and this happens through caching layers and proxies that rewrite headers. Cache interaction: a compressed response and its uncompressed equivalent are different representations with different cache keys, so a cache serving the wrong one produces content a browser cannot render. And then the practical rules, which are short. Compress text and structured data; do not compress already-compressed formats — images, video and archives, where the second compression attempt costs CPU and gains nothing. Compress responses above a size threshold, because below it the header and the work dominate and the response grows. Negotiate the encoding rather than assuming, and include the compressed size in the advertised length so a client can make progress. And precompress static assets and serve them with a content encoding, which moves the cost to build time and leaves the server doing nothing at request time.

36 · Developer Experience & Platform Engineering

Platform engineering removes friction from shipping by building and maintaining the systems developers stand on: reliable build tooling, CI/CD, environments, and clear golden paths so engineers focus on product code. Fast, safe developer velocity is a measured business metric, not a perk, because time saved for every engineer compounds. Internal platforms succeed when their interfaces are stable and boring, hiding the complexity behind a small set of blessed workflows.

36.1 Build systems & the caching gospel36.2 CI/CD mastery: pipelines as code36.3 Internal Developer Platforms: golden paths, not golden handcuffs36.4 Measuring developer experience

Developer Velocity is a business metric: the faster engineers ship safely, the faster the product ships. Platform engineering builds the "developer platform" — build systems, CI/CD, templates, golden paths — that removes friction without adding org layers.

36.1 Build systems & the caching gospel

Slow builds waste thousands of engineer-hours across a team, so build systems emphasize incrementality: rebuild only changed modules, cache artifacts, and parallelize across cores and machines. Tools such as Bazel, Buck, and Nx run hermetic builds with content-addressed caches shared between developers and CI, making builds deterministic and fast. The design goals are reproducibility, whether the same inputs produce the same output, and remote caching so a branch’s first build is already warm.

# Slow builds cost real money: 100 devs * 10 min wasted * day ≈ 100h/day.
# The fixes, cheap to expensive:
#   1 incremental: only rebuild what changed (hashes, not timestamps)
#   2 cache: share the cache across CI and machines (CI = same cache)
#   3 parallelize: independent units build in parallel (make -j / bazel)
#   4 remote cache: one shared cloud cache for every PR (bazel/nx)
# Modern rule: builds must be HERMETIC (same inputs => same output) so
# caching is safe. Wrong-language pairing: a hermetic build is also your
# most reliable reproducer (Ch.16.7).
# The 10x insight: fixing developer tooling compounds -- every saved
# minute is saved EVERY day for EVERY engineer.

The two pipelines, and why they are different jobs

Building a model is not building software, and the reason is that a model's correctness is a distribution rather than a specification. The two pipelines are designed around that. The build pipeline assembles a reproducible artefact: it checks out the data at a pinned identifier, runs training with a pinned seed and configuration, evaluates on the frozen evaluation set, and stores the result with its metadata — the data identifier, the code revision, the environment, the metrics. Every one of those pins is the reproducibility section's requirement, and the output of the pipeline is not a binary but a bundle: the weights, the preprocessing configuration, the tokeniser or image transforms, and the label mapping, because a model file without those is not deployable and reconstructing them later is a source of silent mismatch. The deployment pipeline promotes that exact bundle — the same artefact, not a rebuild, which is the continuous-integration chapter's build-once rule applied to model weights — and runs the smoke tests and the evaluation against it before traffic. And the difference in character is the reason both exist: the build pipeline is slow, expensive, and run occasionally; the deployment pipeline is fast, cheap, and run on every change. Which means a pull request that changes inference code and only the inference code should be able to ship without retraining, and a pull request that changes preprocessing must retrain or be rejected, because those are two systems that must agree. Then the four practices that make this hold, and each addresses a specific failure. Pin the data, not just the code. A run whose dataset identifier is not recorded cannot be reproduced and cannot be rolled back, and the identifier has to be an immutable snapshot rather than a query. Store the preprocessing with the weights, in the same artefact and the same version, so that a model cannot be deployed with a different transform from the one it was evaluated under — which is the training-serving skew the previous section named and which is the single most common vision and language deployment failure. Fail the pipeline on a metric regression, not only on an error, because a model change that quietly degrades quality passes every functional test. And keep a rollback path to the previous bundle with its metadata, because the realistic incident is not "the pipeline is broken" but "we shipped something worse and are serving it". Then the three things people forget, and each has cost real projects. The training data's own provenance. A dataset assembled by a script that reads from a moving source is a different dataset tomorrow, and the fix is a snapshot with a date and a checksum rather than a script that can be re-run. Compute determinism. Even with a pinned seed, a training run is not bit-reproducible across different hardware or library versions, because reduction order and fused operations vary; the honest requirement is that a run be approximately reproducible and that the evaluation set is fixed so the comparison is meaningful — the numerical section's warning applied. And the cost. A training run that costs more than a day's compute needs a cost estimate before it starts and a preemption policy, because a run killed by a preemption that leaves no checkpoint is a wasted day, and the alternative — designing for checkpointing so an interrupted run resumes — is the same defensive-engineering discipline as everything else in this book.

/* Why they are different jobs. */
const REASON = {
  claim: 'building a model is NOT BUILDING SOFTWARE',
  why: 'a models CORRECTNESS IS A DISTRIBUTION rather than a SPECIFICATION',
};

/* The build pipeline. */
const BUILD = {
  assembles: 'a REPRODUCIBLE ARTEFACT',
  steps: ['check out the DATA at a PINNED IDENTIFIER',
    'run TRAINING with a PINNED SEED and configuration',
    'evaluate on the FROZEN EVALUATION SET',
    'store the result with its METADATA - the data identifier, the code revision, the environment, the metrics'],
  outputIsNot: 'a BINARY',
  outputIs: 'a BUNDLE',
  bundleContents: ['the WEIGHTS', 'the PREPROCESSING CONFIGURATION',
    'the TOKENISER or image transforms', 'the LABEL MAPPING'],
  whyBundle: 'a MODEL FILE WITHOUT THOSE IS NOT DEPLOYABLE',
  and: 'reconstructing them later is a SOURCE OF SILENT MISMATCH' };

/* The deployment pipeline. */
const DEPLOY = {

  rule: 'which is the continuous-integration chapters BUILD-ONCE RULE applied to MODEL WEIGHTS',

Build speedups in order of rising cost, from incremental compilation to a shared remote cache, all relying on hermetic inputs so caching stays safe.

36.2 CI/CD mastery: pipelines as code

Pipelines-as-code keep the delivery workflow in the repository, so configuration is versioned and reviewed like the source: a change triggers lint, test, build, and then a staged deploy. Deployment uses feature flags, canary releases that shift a fraction of traffic, health checks, and automatic rollback to make releases boring and reversible. The goal is a deploy path so routine that nobody considers it risky.

  • Pipelines-as-code lives in the repo (GitHub Actions / GitLab CI) — reviewed like code, versioned like code, protected like code.
  • Stages: lint → unit → build → integration → (env) → deploy. Each fails fast with a clear message; artifacts flow, not recompiles.
  • Deployment safety is the real craft: canary (5% → 50% → 100%), automatic rollback on error-budget breach (Ch.22.7), and "deploys are boring" as the goal — boring means it works.
  • CI is a test of history: it should catch the regression at the PR, discouraging broken merges long before a release.

    • What to run on every change, and what not to

    A model pipeline has a natural division into fast and slow, and putting the wrong check in the wrong place is what makes a pipeline either slow or useless. Run on every change: the code's own tests, the linters, and — critically — a cheap evaluation on a small subset of the evaluation set, because a two-minute evaluation catches most regressions and the cost of running it on every push is negligible. Run on merge: the full evaluation, the offline metrics, and the model artefact build. Run on a schedule or on demand: the expensive things — a full training run, a human evaluation, a benchmark against an external model, a robustness and bias suite. And then the checks that are specific to this domain and that a normal continuous-integration setup does not have. Assert on the artefact, not only on the code — that the bundle contains everything needed to serve it, that the label mapping matches the training run's, that the tokeniser or image transforms load, that a single example can be pushed through the whole pipeline and produces the expected output shape. These are cheap, they catch the most embarrassing class of failure, and they are the checks people omit. Assert that the evaluation set has not changed, by comparing its hash, because an evaluation set that has been edited silently invalidates every comparison recorded against it and there is no symptom. Assert determinism where it holds: running the same inference twice on the same input must give the same output, which catches a model file that was overwritten by a training run that happened to share its path. And assert on the metrics with a threshold rather than a comparison to the previous run, because a comparison lets a slow decline pass — a model that loses one point of accuracy per week passes every "not worse than before" check for months. Then the three things that go wrong, and each is characteristic. The pipeline is slow, so people batch changes, which makes each run riskier and makes the pipeline slower per change, which makes batching more attractive — a feedback loop that continuous integration exists specifically to prevent. The pipeline is flaky, so people ignore it, and the fix is quarantine as the testing section argued rather than removing the check. And the pipeline tests the code but not the model, so a change to the data, the configuration or the environment passes every test and changes behaviour — which is why the metadata assertions and the artefact checks exist. Then the operational habit that ties it together. Treat the model artefact like a released binary: versioned, immutable, identified by a hash, with its metadata attached, retained for a defined period, and rollback-able. A model that exists only on one machine's disk is not an artefact; it is an incident waiting for that machine.

    /* The natural fast/slow division. */
const FAST = [
  { c: 'the CODES OWN TESTS' }, { c: 'the LINTERS' },
  { c: 'a CHEAP EVALUATION on a SMALL SUBSET of the evaluation set', whyItMatters: 'because a TWO-MINUTE EVALUATION CATCHES MOST REGRESSIONS',
    cost: 'the cost of running it on every push is NEGLIGIBLE' },
];
const ON_MERGE = ['the FULL EVALUATION', 'the OFFLINE METRICS', 'the MODEL ARTEFACT BUILD'];
const SCHEDULED = ['a FULL TRAINING RUN', 'a HUMAN EVALUATION', 'a BENCHMARK AGAINST AN EXTERNAL MODEL', 'a ROBUSTNESS and BIAS SUITE'];

/* Checks specific to this domain. */
const DOMAIN_CHECKS = [
  { c: 'assert ON THE ARTEFACT, not only on the code', what: ['the BUNDLE CONTAINS EVERYTHING needed to serve it',

/* Three things that go wrong. */
const FAILURES = [

    fix: 'QUARANTINE as the testing section argued rather than REMOVING THE CHECK' },

    symptom: 'a change to the DATA, the CONFIGURATION or the ENVIRONMENT PASSES EVERY TEST and CHANGES BEHAVIOUR',

/* The habit. */
const HABIT = {
  rule: 'treat the MODEL ARTEFACT LIKE A RELEASED BINARY',
  attributes: ['VERSIONED', 'IMMUTABLE', 'IDENTIFIED BY A HASH', 'with its METADATA ATTACHED',
    'RETAINED for a defined PERIOD', 'ROLLBACK-ABLE'],
  and: 'a model that EXISTS ONLY ON ONE MACHINES DISK is not an ARTEFACT - it is an INCIDENT WAITING FOR THAT MACHINE' },

    Model registry, and what it is for

    A model registry is a catalogue of trained models with their metadata and their lineage, and it exists because the alternative — a file on somebody's disk with a name that means something to them — fails in four specific ways. It makes a model discoverable, so the question "which model is in production and where does it come from" has an answer that does not require asking a person. It records the metadata that reproducibility requires, in one place: the data identifier, the code revision, the hyperparameters, the library versions, the hardware, the seed, and the evaluation results — which is the previous section's bundle metadata, held centrally rather than beside each artefact on somebody's machine. It tracks lineage, which is what makes a question like "this metric changed on the third of March; which data snapshot was live that day" answerable, and it is the question that arises the first time an incident requires it. And it makes promotion a state transition rather than a shell command — a model moves through stages, and promotion to production is a recorded event with an approver, which is what an audit asks for. Then the four practices that make it useful rather than a filing cabinet, and each addresses a specific failure. Every model gets an immutable identifier, and that identifier is a content hash of the artefact rather than a name you chose — because a name can be reused for different weights, and the difference between "we rolled back" and "we cannot tell what we rolled back to" is entirely this. Stages are enforced, not suggested: a model reaches production only by passing evaluation, and the enforcement is in the pipeline rather than in a convention, which is the continuous-integration chapter's argument applied to models. Every promotion is logged with who did it, when, and against which evaluation results, so that the current production version is a question with an answer. And stale models are visible. A model that has been serving for eighteen months with no re-evaluation, on data that has changed, is not a stable model — it is an unexamined one, and the registry is where a scheduled re-evaluation is tracked, because that is a task somebody must own. Then the two things the registry does not do, and both are worth stating because they are frequently attempted. It does not store the data. It stores the data's identifier; the data itself lives in object storage with its own lifecycle, and a registry that stores data becomes a data store with none of the properties of one. And it does not serve the model. It is a catalogue, and the deployment target pulls the artefact from the artefact store; conflating the two means a slow query in the registry becomes a slow request, which is the availability chapter's argument about placing coordination state on the request path.

    /* What it is for. */
const REGISTRY = {
  is: 'a CATALOGUE of trained models with their METADATA and their LINEAGE',
  alternative: 'a FILE ON SOMEBODYS DISK with a name that means SOMETHING TO THEM',
  fixes: [
    { f: 'DISCOVERABILITY',
      detail: 'so the question WHICH MODEL IS IN PRODUCTION AND WHERE DOES IT COME FROM has an answer that does not require ASKING A PERSON' },
    { f: 'the METADATA that REPRODUCIBILITY REQUIRES, in one place',
      contents: ['the DATA IDENTIFIER', 'the CODE REVISION', 'the HYPERPARAMETERS',
        'the LIBRARY VERSIONS', 'the HARDWARE', 'the SEED', 'the EVALUATION RESULTS'],
      is: 'the previous sections BUNDLE METADATA, held CENTRALLY rather than BESIDE EACH ARTEFACT on somebodys machine' },
    { f: 'LINEAGE',
      enables: 'this metric changed on the third of March, which data snapshot was live that day',
      and: 'it is the QUESTION THAT ARISES THE FIRST TIME AN INCIDENT REQUIRES IT' },
    { f: 'PROMOTION is a STATE TRANSITION rather than a SHELL COMMAND',

      why: 'which is what an AUDIT ASKS FOR' },
  ],
};

/* Four practices. */
const PRACTICES = [
  { p: 'EVERY MODEL GETS AN IMMUTABLE IDENTIFIER',

    why: 'because a NAME CAN BE REUSED for different weights',

const NOT = [

36.3 Internal Developer Platforms: golden paths, not golden handcuffs

An internal developer platform offers self-service golden paths that take an engineer from scaffold to a deployed, observable service quickly, encoding the approved way to build while hiding the underlying infrastructure. It is real only when measured: time-to-first-deploy, deploy frequency, and feedback time are tracked, and the platform improves with them. Without metrics it degenerates into scaffolding theater, generating code no one owns.

# IDP = the curated surface (portals/CATALOG, templates, self-service
# environments) on TOP of your infrastructure:
#   golden path: "scaffold a service" -> auto repo + CI + deploys +
#     observability + docs, working in <1 hour
#   self-service preview env per PR; ephemeral, cheap, prod-like
#   app catalog: which services, who owns them, what's deployed
# The trap: an IDP that's a 200-page wiki IS the old onboarding pain,
# renamed. Success = time-to-first-deploy drops & engineers stop asking
# 'where do I...' in chat. Measure it, or it's scaffolding theater.
# Governance win: golden paths ENFORCE the good defaults (Ch.20 zero-
# trust, secrets, a11y checks) by construction -- security by default.

What to build, and what to buy

Authentication is the clearest case in this book of a problem that looks small and is not, because the specification is easy — verify an identity and issue a credential — and the failure modes are where people are attacked. The token has three layers and the layer determines what a compromise of it means. An identity token says who the subject is and carries the claims about them; it is short-lived by design, because its whole purpose is to be exchanged. An access token is what the resource server checks on every request, and its design is where the trade-offs live: it must be verifiable without a network call, so it is signed; it must expire, so it has a short lifetime; it must carry enough claims to authorise with, so it carries the user's roles — and each of those three properties is a reason for a different attack. A refresh token exists to obtain new access tokens without asking the user again, and it is the most sensitive of the three, which is why the best practice is that it is opaque rather than a token — a random string the authorisation server maps to a session — so that a stolen refresh token contains no information and cannot be decoded to learn anything about the user. Then the three mechanisms that are not obvious and that get implemented wrongly. Signing and encryption are different jobs. A signed token's payload is readable by anyone holding it; the signature guarantees only that it was not altered. A token signed and encrypted — a nested token — has both properties and is what you want, and the reason many implementations use only signing is that it is simpler to inspect. Key rotation needs overlap. A verifier must accept both the current and the previous signing key for a period, because otherwise a rotation invalidates every token in flight at the moment it happens; and the design must make the rotation possible without downtime, which means the identifier of the signing key is carried in the token header so the verifier knows which key to check. And audiences must be checked, which is the attack that is missing from most implementations: a token issued for one service must not be accepted by another, and a token whose audience claim says a different service is a valid token for somebody, so "valid signature" is not sufficient — the resource server must verify that the token was issued for it. Then the four choices, and each has a real trade. Where does identity live? If your organisation has an identity provider, use it; building one is a security project, not a feature, and every organisation that has built one has regretted it. Where does the session live? Server-side is revocable; a self-contained token is not, which is the trade the authentication chapter named. How long is the access token? Long enough that a page with several requests does not refresh constantly, short enough that a stolen one has limited value — minutes to an hour, and the interaction with the refresh token is the design. And what goes in it? As little as possible, because every claim is a thing that can be wrong and a token is handed to the client; put the identifier and a version in it and look the rest up, which costs a lookup and removes an entire class of problem.

/* Three token layers. */
const LAYERS = [
  { l: 'an IDENTITY TOKEN', says: 'who the SUBJECT IS and carries the CLAIMS about them',
    lifetime: 'SHORT-LIVED BY DESIGN, because its whole purpose is to be EXCHANGED' },
  { l: 'an ACCESS TOKEN', is: 'what the RESOURCE SERVER CHECKS on every request',
    whereTradeoffsLive: true,
    mustBe: ['VERIFIABLE WITHOUT A NETWORK CALL, so it is SIGNED',
      'EXPIRE, so it has a SHORT LIFETIME',
      'carry ENOUGH CLAIMS to authorise with, so it carries the users ROLES'],
    and: 'each of those three properties is a REASON FOR A DIFFERENT ATTACK' },
  { l: 'a REFRESH TOKEN', existsTo: 'obtain NEW ACCESS TOKENS without asking the user again',
    isTheMostSensitive: 'of the three',
    bestPractice: 'it is OPAQUE rather than a token - a RANDOM STRING the authorisation server maps to a session',
    gain: 'so a stolen refresh token CONTAINS NO INFORMATION and CANNOT BE DECODED to learn anything about the user' },

const MECHANISMS = [
  { m: 'SIGNING and ENCRYPTION are DIFFERENT JOBS',

  { m: 'KEY ROTATION needs OVERLAP',

Golden paths beat wikis: curated scaffolding enforces good defaults by construction, and success is measured in time-to-first-deploy.

36.4 Measuring developer experience

Developer experience is measured, not vibes, through four lenses: speed, how fast engineers ship; safety, whether failures are contained; voice, whether engineers can influence the platform; and focus, whether the day is spent on product work rather than friction. The DORA metrics cover delivery throughput and reliability, while the SPACE framework adds human and team factors. Surveys plus objective pipeline data together keep improvement honest.

LensMetric
Fastlead time: commit → shipped
Safechange failure rate; MTTR on rollback
VoiceDX surveys (documented friction, not vibes)
Focusinterruption count — context switches are the enemy

Read one piece of "DORA metrics" and one of "SPACE framework" — the two lenses you’ll be asked about in platform interviews.

Developer experience, measured as a latency

The most useful measurement of developer experience is not a survey; it is how long it takes a change to go from being written to being live, and its components are each separately actionable. The inner loop is the time between starting an edit and seeing the effect. For web work it is dominated by a rebuild and a reload and by the browser's own cost; for a model it is dominated by nothing at all, because a model does not change when you edit the code that calls it, which is the single largest structural advantage model work has over the training-code work of a conventional application. CI time is the time from pushing to knowing whether the change is good, and it is the component most directly under engineering control. Test time in an inner loop is separate again and matters more than the total: a suite that takes forty minutes is useless for the loop even if it is tolerable in the pipeline, which is the testing section's argument about fast and slow suites restated in the context of experience. Deploy time, from merge to live. And the time to first useful result, which for a data or model task includes the time to obtain and inspect the data — often the longest component and almost never measured. Then the four things that reduce these, in the order they usually pay. Precompute and cache aggressively, because almost everything expensive in a data pipeline is deterministic given its inputs and its inputs rarely change between runs; this is the developer's counterpart to the production section's cache and it is the single biggest lever on iteration time. Work on a representative sample during development and the full data only for evaluation, because a sample that preserves the distribution — stratified if the data is imbalanced — gives the same conclusions at a fraction of the cost, and the discipline is that the sample must be fixed so results are comparable. Make the fast path the default path, which means the code should not require a flag to run against the sample and a different flag to run against the full data, because every developer will use the slower one eventually and forget. And cache aggressively and invalidate by content, so that a rerun does nothing when nothing changed — which is the same immutable-snapshot argument the reproducibility section makes, applied to the developer's loop. Then the three measurement practices that make the numbers trustworthy. Measure on the machine your team actually uses, not on the one the engineer with the fast machine uses, because the perceived experience is a distribution across the team and measuring on the best machine reports the ninety-fifth percentile as an average. Separate the components — build, test, deploy — because "CI takes twelve minutes" is not actionable and "the unit tests take two, the integration tests take eight, and the deploy step takes two" is. And track the trend rather than the value, because experience degrades gradually and a dashboard showing only the current number shows nothing until it is bad. Then the one thing that is worth saying last, and it is the continuous-integration chapter's central lesson applied here: a measured loop that nobody acts on will lengthen anyway, because every change made for another reason adds a little time, and without a gate nothing ever removes any of it.

/* The components. */
const COMPONENTS = [
  { c: 'the INNER LOOP', is: 'the time between STARTING AN EDIT and SEEING THE EFFECT',
    forWeb: 'dominated by a REBUILD AND A RELOAD and by the BROWSERS OWN COST',
    forModel: 'dominated by NOTHING AT ALL, because a model does not change when you edit the code that calls it',
    and: 'which is the SINGLE LARGEST STRUCTURAL ADVANTAGE model work has over the training-code work of a conventional application' },
  { c: 'CI TIME', is: 'the time from PUSHING to KNOWING WHETHER THE CHANGE IS GOOD',
    mostControllable: 'it is the component MOST DIRECTLY UNDER ENGINEERING CONTROL' },
  { c: 'TEST TIME in an inner loop', mattersMore: 'than the TOTAL',
    detail: 'a suite that takes FORTY MINUTES is USELESS FOR THE LOOP even if it is TOLERABLE in the pipeline',
    connects: 'the testing sections argument about FAST and SLOW SUITES restated in the context of EXPERIENCE' },
  { c: 'DEPLOY TIME', is: 'from MERGE to LIVE' },
  { c: 'the TIME TO FIRST USEFUL RESULT', includes: 'the time to OBTAIN AND INSPECT THE DATA',
    note: 'often the LONGEST COMPONENT and ALMOST NEVER MEASURED' },
];

/* Four reductions, in the order they pay. */
const REDUCE = [
  { a: 'PRECOMPUTE and CACHE AGGRESSIVELY',
    why: 'because ALMOST EVERYTHING EXPENSIVE in a data pipeline is DETERMINISTIC GIVEN ITS INPUTS and its inputs RARELY CHANGE between runs',
    rank: 'this is the DEVELOPERS COUNTERPART to the production sections cache and it is the SINGLE BIGGEST LEVER on iteration time' },
  { a: 'work on a REPRESENTATIVE SAMPLE during development and the FULL DATA only for EVALUATION',
    why: 'a sample that PRESERVES THE DISTRIBUTION - STRATIFIED if the data is imbalanced - gives the SAME CONCLUSIONS at a FRACTION OF THE COST',
    discipline: 'the sample MUST BE FIXED so results are COMPARABLE' },
  { a: 'make the FAST PATH THE DEFAULT PATH',

  connects: 'the continuous-integration chapters CENTRAL LESSON applied here' };

Golden paths, and why conventions beat documentation

A golden path is a route that is easy, well-supported and recommended, and the reason it works better than a documented convention is a structural one: a convention requires every developer to remember it, and a golden path requires nobody to. The mechanism is that the easy route and the correct route are the same route, so a developer who does the easy thing has also done the right thing — and the alternative requires a decision made correctly on a hundred occasions rather than once. What a golden path provides is a default, not a prohibition. Deviating should be possible and sometimes right, and the design question is whether the default is good enough that most people never deviate — and if most people deviate, the default is wrong rather than the people. It is enforced by construction rather than by review, which means it survives the person who wrote it, and this is the same argument as the compiler's: a check that runs automatically is a check that keeps running, and a convention that lives in a document is a document that stops being read. And it makes the fast path and the safe path identical, which is what makes it a path rather than a policy — a service template that includes the health check, the structured logging, the timeout, the deployment configuration and the test harness, so that a new service is correct by default in every one of those respects without anyone remembering any of them. Then what belongs in a golden path, and the criterion is that each item is one that is easy to get wrong and expensive to get wrong. A project skeleton with a build, a test command and a run command. A service template with the health check, graceful shutdown, structured logging, metrics and request identifiers — the observability chapter's list, delivered by default rather than remembered. A CI pipeline template with the gates already wired, so a new project is gated from its first commit. An authentication and authorisation module, which is the case where the default matters most, because every service that implements its own has a chance to get it wrong and most have. A data-access template with migrations, a seed mechanism and a query builder that parameterises — which prevents the injection class by construction. And a deployment template, which makes the operational chapter's requirements non-optional. Then the two failures, each of which is characteristic. The golden path is opinionated in ways the team outgrows. The failure mode is a framework that was right at ten services and is an obstacle at fifty, and the signs are a workaround in most repositories, a wrapper that bypasses the template, and a growing list of exceptions. The fix is to let the template have escape hatches and a documented version, and to change it deliberately rather than accumulating a de facto alternative beside it. And the golden path is never adopted, which is the more common failure and which looks like nothing: a template exists, it is correct, and every project has quietly started from an empty directory because starting from the template requires remembering it exists. The fix is to make the template the way a new project is created — the scaffolding command that a developer runs is the template, not a document that tells them it exists — and to measure adoption as a number rather than assuming it, because an unadopted golden path is indistinguishable from an unnecessary one unless you look.

37 · Embedded, Real-Time & IoT Systems

Software for the physical world runs under constraints: small memory, tight power, hard deadlines, and often no reboot button, so the discipline is about budgeting rather than allocating. Microcontrollers, interrupts, real-time scheduling, and safety processes rule, and so does proving timing rather than hoping for it. This chapter is the bridge from conventional software engineering into firmware and systems that meet real-time guarantees.

37.1 Microcontroller vs microprocessor & the constrained world37.2 Real-time: deadlines aren’t optional37.3 Peripherals, interrupts & the GPIO kiss37.4 IoT networks & the update problem37.5 Safety-critical logic & the process that backs it

Before (and beyond) the cloud lives the physical world: microcontrollers, satellites, medical devices, cars, factory floors. Different physics — constrained memory, deadlines, and no "reboot it later" luxury — make this genuinely separate discipline.

37.1 Microcontroller vs microprocessor & the constrained world

Microcontrollers combine CPU, flash, and RAM on one chip for cheap, low-power duty, while microprocessors run an OS and use larger external memory, and the distinction decides how you program: bare-metal C or Rust with no heap for the former, virtual memory and a scheduler for the latter. On a microcontroller you cannot just malloc; you budget static buffers and manage memory deterministically. Flash endurance and interrupts become first-class design inputs.

The bus, the protocol, and why they are different problems

Embedded systems fail in ways ordinary software does not, and almost all of it comes from one fact: the outside world is not under your control and does not fail cleanly. A pin floats when a wire falls off. A bus reads a bit while it is changing, producing a value that is neither the old one nor the new one. A sensor reports a plausible number when its supply has sagged. And a microcontroller has no operating system to absorb any of it, so the code that runs is the code that must detect and handle every fault. Then the four interfaces and what each one actually does, because they are not interchangeable and choosing the wrong one is a design decision that cannot be undone later. GPIO is a single bit in either direction, and its difficulty is not the bit but the electrical reality around it: an input floats to an unpredictable level when nothing drives it, so an input must have a defined state — a pull-up or pull-down, chosen so that the unconnected state is the safe one, which for an active-low device means pull-up. I2C is two wires and a conversation: a clock line and a data line, with each device addressed by a seven-bit identifier and every transfer framed by a start condition, an address, data bytes with an acknowledgement after each, and a stop condition. Its strengths are the low pin count and the ability to have many devices on the same two wires; its costs are that it has no clock of its own, so a stuck device holds the line and blocks everything, and that pull-up resistors are mandatory on both lines and somebody has to put them there. SPI is four wires and a clocked stream: a clock, a data-out, a data-in and a chip-select, with no acknowledgement and no addressing — you select a device and then read or write as many bytes as you like. It is much faster than I2C because there is no per-byte round trip and no addressing overhead, and it needs one chip-select per device, which is the cost. UART is two wires and no clock: asynchronous, with each byte framed by agreed start and stop bits and a baud rate both ends must match, and it has no notion of a device at all — it is a stream, and the framing of what is on it is entirely the protocol's problem. Then the two rules that are the whole discipline, and both exist because of specific failures. Never busy-wait on an input. Polling in a loop consumes the entire processor while producing worse latency than an interrupt, and on a battery-powered device it is the difference between hours and months. Keep interrupts microseconds long. An interrupt that does work delays every other interrupt including the one that signals an incoming byte, which turns a routine task into a dropped-message bug that appears only under load — and this is why an interrupt handler sets a flag or writes to a buffer and returns, and the actual processing happens in the main loop where it can be interrupted itself.

const FACT = 'the OUTSIDE WORLD IS NOT UNDER YOUR CONTROL and DOES NOT FAIL CLEANLY';

];

  { r: 'keep INTERRUPTS MICROSECONDS LONG',
    failure: 'an interrupt that does work DELAYS EVERY OTHER INTERRUPT including the one that signals an INCOMING BYTE',

    therefore: 'an interrupt handler SETS A FLAG or WRITES TO A BUFFER and RETURNS',

Registers, memory, and the fetch-decode-execute loop

A microcontroller executes instructions out of a small on-chip memory, and every property that matters about its performance follows from the size of that memory and the structure of the fetch cycle. Registers are the fastest memory in the machine because they are inside the arithmetic unit and are reached without addressing the memory system at all; the compiler allocates them and, as the parallel chapter's argument said, the allocation is a graph-colouring problem because there are far fewer registers than live values. Flash holds the program and is read-only, and the property that catches people is that it is not RAM: a memory-mapped write to a flash address does not write flash, and on most parts the only operation that changes flash content is a program-specific sequence that erases a block before writing it, which means flash cannot be rewritten in place and a variable cannot live there. Static RAM holds the data and loses its contents on power-down, which means a device that must remember something across a power cycle has to write to non-volatile memory explicitly. Stack and heap share that RAM, and this is the single most common cause of a device working on the bench and crashing in the field: the stack grows with call depth and, in the main thread, with the size of every local variable in every frame on the path; an interrupt that arrives deep in a call chain needs its stack frame on top of that, and the amount required is not visible in the code that causes it. Then the fetch-decode-execute cycle, and why an instruction's cycles per instruction is the number that matters. An instruction takes several cycles, not one, and the reasons are structural rather than accidental: fetching an instruction takes a memory access; a flash read takes several cycles because flash is slow to access; a taken branch flushes the pipeline, so a branch costs the pipeline depth; and a data load also takes a memory access. So the practical measurements are cycles per instruction and instructions per cycle, and both are architecture-specific numbers you look up rather than estimate. And the two that follow. A tight loop is almost always a memory access in disguise — the loop counter is being read and written on every iteration unless the compiler can keep it in a register, and whether it can depends on whether anything in the loop can modify memory it cannot prove it does not. So declare loop counters as locals, not as globals or as members of a struct accessed through a pointer, because the latter defeats the analysis and turns a two-cycle increment into a memory round trip. And the instruction set is a trade: a core with many addressing modes has short programs but variable and sometimes unpredictable cycle counts, which is bad for real-time work; a core with a simple, regular instruction set has longer programs and predictable timing, which is what real-time analysis requires. So the choice of core for a real-time application is the choice between code size and predictability, and predictability usually wins.

const MEMORIES = [

The mindset flip: you cannot "just allocate"; you budget. Heap is suspect; static buffers, interrupts, and careful lifecycle thinking dominate. This is why "write code in a VM" training under-prepares beginners for embedded interviews — and why Rust’s ownership model is loved there (no GC, provable safety).

37.2 Real-time: deadlines aren’t optional

Real-time systems must prove that every task meets its deadline, not merely run fast on average, and tasks are scheduled by priority, analyzed with approaches such as rate monotonic or earliest-deadline-first. Shared resources invite priority inversion, a lower-priority task holding a lock a higher-priority task waits on, famously implicated in the Mars Pathfinder reset. The remedies are priority inheritance, careful sharing, and worst-case execution time analysis.

// HARD real-time: missing the deadline = system failure (airbag,
// pacemaker, engine control). SOFT real-time: deadline helps but a
// miss degrades gracefully (video frame drops).
// The real-time problem ≠ "fast code"; it's SCHEDULABILITY: prove every
// task meets its deadline under the worst stack, with:
//    WCET   worst-case execution time per task
//    period + deadline  -> utilization = sum(WCET/period) <= 1
// RTOS (FreeRTOS/ThreadX): priority-based preemptive scheduling;
// priorities + priorities INVERT under shared locks (priority inversion
// is why Mars Pathfinder reset -- real bug, real story).
// Takeaway: in real-time, DETERMINISM beats average speed. Use the
// priority ceiling, small bounded queues, and measure the worst case.

Priority inversion, and what to do about it

The most instructive failure in real-time systems is one where every component is correct and the system still deadlocks, and understanding it is what teaches the subject. Setup. A low-priority task holds a shared resource. A medium-priority task is runnable and does not need that resource, so it preempts the low-priority task and runs for a long time. A high-priority task needs the resource and therefore cannot proceed, and cannot run either because the medium-priority task outranks it. The low-priority task will eventually finish and release the resource — so nothing is broken, and the high-priority task's deadline has been missed. That is priority inversion: a task's execution time depends on tasks it has no relationship to, and its latency is unbounded by its own analysis. And it caused a real mission failure. On Mars Pathfinder, a task that cleaned up after a low-priority meteorological task was preempted by a medium-priority task; the high-priority task missed its deadline; the system reset. The diagnosis was made from a log, after the fact, and it is worth reading because the same class of bug appears in every operating system and is one of the reasons priority inheritance exists. Then the fix, which is the mechanism almost every real-time system uses. Priority inheritance: when a high-priority task blocks on a resource held by a lower-priority task, the holder's priority is temporarily raised to the waiter's, so it cannot be preempted by anyone lower than the waiter, and when it releases the resource the priority is restored. The cost is that a medium-priority task can be delayed by the interaction, which is why the variant priority ceiling exists: each resource has a ceiling equal to the highest priority of any task that uses it, a task holding it is immediately raised to that ceiling, and the result is that the inheritance is bounded and deadlock is impossible by construction. Then the four things that determine whether a design is real-time, and each is a measurable quantity. Worst-case execution time, measured or proven rather than averaged — an average tells you nothing about the deadline, and a task whose average is one millisecond and whose worst case is two hundred will miss a deadline. Utilisation, the total of all worst-case execution times divided by the period, which must stay below one for a preemptive single-core system and below about eighty per cent in practice, because the analysis assumes the worst case arrives on every task simultaneously and it never does. Interrupt latency, the time from the interrupt to the first instruction of the handler, which is bounded by the architecture and is a number you look up rather than measure. And jitter, the variation in completion time, which for a hard real-time system matters more than the average and which is a property of the scheduler's policy as much as of the workload. And then the honest place to close. Most systems that think they need a real-time operating system do not, because a bare-metal loop with a timer interrupt satisfies the deadline in the great majority of cases; and the systems that genuinely need one are usually the ones where a human is harmed if a deadline is missed — a braking system, a pacemaker, an aircraft flight-control surface — which is the honest boundary between an interesting engineering problem and a safety case, and the distinction is worth stating because real-time requirements are usually introduced by a schedule rather than by a need.

/* Setup. */
const SETUP = [
  'a LOW-PRIORITY TASK holds a SHARED RESOURCE',
  'a MEDIUM-PRIORITY TASK is runnable and does not need that resource, so it PREEMPTS the low-priority task and RUNS FOR A LONG TIME',
  'a HIGH-PRIORITY TASK needs the resource and therefore CANNOT PROCEED, and CANNOT RUN either because the medium-priority task outranks it',
];
const WHY_IT_MATTERS = [
  'the low-priority task WILL EVENTUALLY FINISH and release the resource',
  'so NOTHING IS BROKEN, and the high-priority tasks DEADLINE HAS BEEN MISSED',
];
const DEFINITION = 'a tasks EXECUTION TIME DEPENDS ON TASKS IT HAS NO RELATIONSHIP TO, and its LATENCY IS UNBOUNDED BY ITS OWN ANALYSIS';

const PATHFINDER = [

];
const NOTE = 'the diagnosis was made FROM A LOG, AFTER THE FACT, and the same class of bug appears in EVERY OPERATING SYSTEM and is one of the reasons PRIORITY INHERITANCE exists';

/* The fix. */

    why: 'because the ANALYSIS ASSUMES the worst case ARRIVES ON EVERY TASK SIMULTANEOUSLY and it NEVER DOES' },
  { q: 'INTERRUPT LATENCY', is: 'the TIME FROM THE INTERRUPT to the FIRST INSTRUCTION of the handler',
    boundedBy: 'the ARCHITECTURE', and: 'it is a NUMBER YOU LOOK UP rather than MEASURE' },
  { q: 'JITTER', is: 'the VARIATION in completion time',
    mattersMore: 'for a HARD REAL-TIME SYSTEM than the average',
    property: 'a PROPERTY OF THE SCHEDULERS POLICY as much as of the workload' },
];

/* The honest place to close. */
const HONEST = {
  claim: 'MOST SYSTEMS THAT THINK THEY NEED A REAL-TIME OPERATING SYSTEM DO NOT',
  because: 'a BARE-METAL LOOP with a timer interrupt SATISFIES THE DEADLINE in the great majority of cases',
  whoNeeds: 'the SYSTEMS THAT GENUINELY NEED ONE are usually THE ONES WHERE A HUMAN IS HARMED if a deadline is missed',
  instances: ['a BRAKING SYSTEM', 'a PACEMAKER', 'an AIRCRAFT FLIGHT-CONTROL SURFACE'],
  distinction: 'which is the HONEST BOUNDARY between an INTERESTING ENGINEERING PROBLEM and a SAFETY CASE',
  why: 'and the distinction is worth stating because REAL-TIME REQUIREMENTS ARE USUALLY INTRODUCED BY A SCHEDULE rather than by a NEED' },

Real-time is schedulability, not speed: worst-case execution times and utilization prove deadlines, while priority inversion explains the Mars Pathfinder reset.

37.3 Peripherals, interrupts & the GPIO kiss

Embedded code senses the world through peripherals: GPIO pins for digital in and out, ADC for analog readings, PWM for motors and dimming, and serial buses such as I2C, SPI, and UART for chips. Interrupt service routines must stay tiny, usually setting a flag or pushing data, and defer real work to the main loop or a deferred task. Register maps, datasheets, and an RTOS with tasks and queues structure the rest.

# Embedded programs FEEL the world through peripherals; the pattern:
#   GPIO  : read a pin (button) or drive one (LED)
#   ADC   : sample a sensor (temperature -> a number)
#   PWM   : drive a "partially on" output (dim an LED, control servo)
#   I2C/SPI/UART: talk to other chips/sensors over tiny wires
#   interrupt ISR: hardware pokes the CPU when something matters;
#     ISRs must be SHORT (do the bare capture, defer the work)
# Three golden rules of newbie embedded code:
#   1 never busy-wait for a button (use interrupts/timers)
#   2 keep ISRs micro; do heavy work in the main loop with flags
#   3 every "float math in an ISR" is a review red flag

Interrupts, timers, and the discipline that makes them safe

An interrupt is the processor's attention being redirected by hardware, and everything about how one must be written follows from the same constraint: an interrupt can arrive between any two instructions of your code, including inside the code you are writing to handle the previous one. That is the whole reason the rules exist, and each rule is that one fact applied. An interrupt handler must not be preempted by another interrupt of the same or higher priority, which on a microcontroller means disabling interrupts on entry and re-enabling on exit — and the nested-interrupt case requires saving the previous state rather than simply enabling at the end, because an interrupt that arrived during the handler must still run. A handler must not wait for anything. If it waits for a hardware bit, a serial line or another peripheral, it holds the processor, and the thing it is waiting for often requires an interrupt that can no longer run — which is a deadlock created by an interrupt. Shared variables read in the handler and written in the main loop must be declared volatile, because the compiler is entitled to cache a variable in a register across a loop and the handler is invisible to that analysis; the cost of volatile is that it prevents the compiler doing useful things, which is the correct trade. And the buffer discipline, which is the pattern almost all interrupt-driven designs converge on: the handler does the minimum — read the hardware register, push the byte into a ring buffer, set a flag — and the main loop does the processing. This gives a hard bound on interrupt duration that is a property of the architecture rather than of the code's discipline, and it is worth noting that the atomicity of "push to buffer and set flag" depends on the order and on the width of the access, which is one of the few places where a one-instruction subtlety produces a real bug. Then timers, and the property that makes them more than a convenience. A timer is a counter that overflows and generates an interrupt, which gives a time base that does not depend on anything outside the processor. That enables three things. Precise periodic work — a sampling interval, a motor step rate, a protocol timeout — and the accuracy is bounded by the crystal's tolerance, which is a fixed number you should look up rather than assume. Input capture and output compare, which measure and generate a signal relative to another signal: measuring a pulse width without occupying a core in a loop, generating a precise step pulse for a stepper motor, decoding a remote-control signal — and all of these are things a loop cannot do reliably. And real-time scheduling, which the next section's subject. Then the two things that make timers dangerous, and both are the same mistake. A timer period shorter than the work it triggers. The next interrupt arrives while the previous work is unfinished, and if the handler and the work share state you have a reentrancy bug that appears only when the work takes longer than expected — which it will, under load, under debug builds, when a cache misses. Doing the work in the handler. Tempting because it is simple and avoids a queue, and wrong for the same reason as above plus the deadlock one. The discipline is: the handler is a bounded, mechanical piece that moves data out of hardware and nothing else, and everything a human would recognise as "processing" happens in a context that can be delayed, retried and reasoned about.

/* The one constraint everything follows from. */
const CONSTRAINT = 'an INTERRUPT CAN ARRIVE BETWEEN ANY TWO INSTRUCTIONS of your code, INCLUDING INSIDE THE CODE YOU ARE WRITING TO HANDLE THE PREVIOUS ONE';

/* Rules, each the constraint applied. */
const RULES = [
  { r: 'an interrupt handler must NOT be preempted by another interrupt of the SAME OR HIGHER PRIORITY',
    onAMicrocontroller: 'means DISABLING INTERRUPTS ON ENTRY and RE-ENABLING ON EXIT',
    nestedCase: 'requires SAVING THE PREVIOUS STATE rather than simply ENABLING at the end',
    because: 'an interrupt that ARRIVED DURING THE HANDLER must still run' },
  { r: 'a handler must NOT WAIT FOR ANYTHING',
    why: ['if it WAITS FOR A HARDWARE BIT, a serial line or another peripheral, it HOLDS THE PROCESSOR',
      'and the thing it is waiting for OFTEN REQUIRES AN INTERRUPT that can no longer run'],
    consequence: 'which is a DEADLOCK CREATED BY AN INTERRUPT' },
  { r: 'shared variables READ IN THE HANDLER and WRITTEN IN THE MAIN LOOP must be declared VOLATILE',
    why: 'because the COMPILER IS ENTITLED TO CACHE a variable in a register across a loop and the HANDLER IS INVISIBLE to that analysis',
    cost: 'the COST OF VOLATILE is that it PREVENTS the compiler doing USEFUL THINGS',
    verdict: 'which is the CORRECT TRADE' },
  { r: 'the BUFFER DISCIPLINE', shape: 'the pattern almost all INTERRUPT-DRIVEN DESIGNS CONVERGE ON',
    handlerDoes: ['READ THE HARDWARE REGISTER', 'PUSH THE BYTE into a ring buffer', 'SET A FLAG'],
    mainLoopDoes: 'the PROCESSING',
    gain: 'a HARD BOUND ON INTERRUPT DURATION that is a PROPERTY OF THE ARCHITECTURE rather than of the CODES DISCIPLINE',
    subtlety: 'the ATOMICITY of push to buffer and set flag DEPENDS ON THE ORDER and on the WIDTH OF THE ACCESS',
    and: 'which is one of the FEW PLACES where a ONE-INSTRUCTION SUBTLETY produces a REAL BUG' },
];

/* Timers. */
const TIMERS = {
  is: 'a COUNTER THAT OVERFLOWS and generates an INTERRUPT',
  gain: 'a TIME BASE THAT DOES NOT DEPEND on anything OUTSIDE THE PROCESSOR',
  enables: [
    { e: 'PRECISE PERIODIC WORK', instances: ['a SAMPLING INTERVAL', 'a MOTOR STEP RATE', 'a PROTOCOL TIMEOUT'],
      accuracy: 'bounded by the CRYSTALS TOLERANCE', and: 'which is a FIXED NUMBER YOU SHOULD LOOK UP RATHER THAN ASSUME' },
    { e: 'INPUT CAPTURE and OUTPUT COMPARE', does: 'MEASURE and GENERATE a signal RELATIVE TO ANOTHER SIGNAL',
      instances: ['measuring a PULSE WIDTH without occupying a core in a loop',
        'generating a PRECISE STEP PULSE for a stepper motor', 'decoding a REMOTE-CONTROL SIGNAL'],
      and: 'all of these are THINGS A LOOP CANNOT DO RELIABLY' },
    { e: 'REAL-TIME SCHEDULING', which: 'the next sections subject' },
  ],
  dangers: [
    { d: 'a TIMER PERIOD shorter than the WORK it triggers',
      detail: 'the NEXT INTERRUPT ARRIVES while the PREVIOUS WORK IS UNFINISHED',
      and: 'if the handler and the work SHARE STATE you have a REENTRANCY BUG that appears ONLY when the work takes longer than expected',

    { d: 'doing the WORK in the handler',

The peripheral tour, GPIO through UART, ending in three golden rules: no busy-waits, micro ISRs, and no float math in an interrupt.

37.4 IoT networks & the update problem

IoT devices are battery-first and mostly asleep, so radio choice is physics: protocols such as LoRaWAN, NB-IoT, Zigbee, and BLE trade range, rate, and power, and radios prefer long sleep over frequent bursts. Over-the-air updates need cryptographically signed images, staged rollouts, and rollback, because a broken firmware fleet is a crisis with no field staff. Every feature, including updates, must survive flaky links and unreachable devices.

# Field devices are mostly ASLEEP: battery-first radios, minutes of
# wake time. Protocol choices by physics:
#   MQTT : pub/sub over TCP, tiny messages, broker in the middle,
#          THE standard for fleet messaging (Ch.29 queues, lightest)
#   LoRa/NB-IoT : long-range low-power, for fields & farms, not video
#   Thread/Zigbee/matter : mesh local networks inside buildings
# The update problem: 10,000 deployed devices can't be "reboot + apt".
#   OTA: staged rollout, signature-verified images, store firmware A/B
#   (the device can roll back the moment the crash loop starts)
#   remote diagnosis first: logs/status must stream BEFORE you fly
# There is no "deploy to prod" button here; there are trucks.

Battery life, protocols, and the update you cannot afford to get wrong

IoT is embedded systems with a networking requirement and a cost constraint, and the cost constraint is what shapes every decision. Radio transmit is the most expensive thing the device does, by a wide margin — far more than the processing a transmit costs in energy — and it is a fixed cost per transmission regardless of payload size. So the design goal is send as few messages as possible, as large as possible: batch readings, tolerate latency, and let the server interpolate rather than demanding a reading per minute. And then the second-order effects of that cost, which is where the engineering actually is. Duty cycling — the device is asleep for almost all of its life and wakes on a timer or an interrupt — and the number that matters is the ratio of transmit time to sleep time. Deep sleep costs more than you expect, because the chip retains state in a small always-on domain and a longer sleep needs more of that domain retained; a device that sleeps for a week at a microamp is dominated by its wake-up and connect costs rather than by its sleep. Association costs dominate the payload. Joining a network, negotiating and keeping a connection alive takes multiple radio operations and hundreds of times the energy of a short payload, which is why protocols designed for constrained devices use long connection intervals and let the server batch rather than pushing data immediately. Then the two protocol layers, and the reason they are different jobs. MQTT is message-oriented: publish to a topic, subscribe to topics, delivered by a broker that decouples every device from every consumer. Its fit is exactly the IoT shape — many devices producing occasional readings, several services interested, no direct connection between them. Its characteristic properties are the quality-of-service levels, which are a trade rather than a guarantee — at most once loses messages, at least once duplicates them and requires an idempotent consumer, exactly-once is the strongest and the one most brokered systems cannot actually deliver end to end. CoAP is constrained-oriented: a binary protocol over UDP, designed for small payloads over unreliable links, with confirmable messages and block transfer for large bodies — and it fits the device-to-device or device-to-gateway hop where MQTT's header overhead and connection-oriented nature cost more than they return. The honest summary: CoAP from the device, MQTT to the cloud, with a bridge between, which is a very common architecture because each protocol is good at what it is for. Then the update mechanism, which is the part that has to be right before a device is in a field somewhere you cannot reach. Over the air updates are staged, signed and rollback-able, and each word is load-bearing. Staged means the new image is downloaded and verified while the old one continues running, so an interrupted update leaves a working device rather than a brick. Signed means the device verifies the signature against a key in its own storage before writing anything, because an unsigned update path is a remote code execution hole that anyone who can reach the device can use. Rollback-able means the device can return to the previous image, which requires keeping two images and a record of which is current. And battery-aware means an update never starts unless the charge level guarantees it will finish, because a device that dies mid-flash is a device that needs a human. Then the four practices that make it reliable, each from a specific failure. Progressively roll out — a percentage of the fleet, then more, then all — because a fleet update that reaches every device before anyone has watched the first few is an incident measured in thousands of devices. Report health after updating, per device, because a fleet is the only place where partial failure is visible. Have a way to reach a device that is broken, which means a physical process, and which should be an explicit decision rather than a discovery. And design for the device that never reports back, because a subset will not, and the question is whether your fleet knows that one is missing.

/* Battery. */
const BATTERY = {

  moreThan: 'far more than the PROCESSING a transmit costs in energy',

  how: ['BATCH READINGS', 'TOLERATE LATENCY', 'let the SERVER INTERPOLATE rather than DEMANDING A READING per minute'],
};
