IoT networking is physics-first: sleeping batteries, MQTT fleets, and mesh indoors, plus OTA updates that stage, sign, and roll back.

37.5 Safety-critical logic & the process that backs it

Safety-critical software turns careful code into evidenced process: requirements traced to tests, hazard analysis before code, verification of the toolchain, and certification against standards such as ISO 26262 for automotive or DO-178C for aviation. Embedded Rust plus formal methods is a rare, well-paid niche precisely because it shifts finding bugs from the field to the compiler and the proofs. The mindset difference is showing the work, not just claiming correctness.

  • Standards (ISO 26262 automotive, IEC 61508 machinery, DO-178C aviation) turn "careful code" into a process with evidence: requirements traced to tests, EI measurements, verified toolchains.
  • The mindset: safety functions must be designed with two independent paths, fail-operational or fail-safe by design, and the analysis happens BEFORE the code (FMEA/hazard analysis).
  • For a career: embedded + Rust + safety certifications is one of the least crowded, best-paid niches in software.

The safety case, and why the code is a small part of it

Safety-critical software is subject to a different engineering discipline, and the discipline has a shape that is worth understanding before the techniques. The argument is not "the code is correct" but "the risk is acceptably low", and the argument must be written down before it can be reviewed. That written argument is a safety case, and it has a structure: the claims — what must be true for the system to be safe; the arguments — why each claim is true, and this is where the evidence lives; and the evidence itself, which is not the same as a test result. The distinction matters because a claim backed by a test is weaker than a claim backed by a design property, and a system designed so that a class of fault is impossible is stronger than one designed so that the fault is unlikely to be detected late. Then three hazard classes, and each is handled differently. Catastrophic — the failure kills or maims people, an aircraft engine, a braking system, an infusion pump. The response is inherent safety by design: architecture that makes the failure mode benign or impossible, redundancy with dissimilar channels, and a design that fails safe rather than fails live. The argument is a probabilistic one and it is genuinely hard to make, which is why the systems that do it are expensive and few. Marginal — the failure causes injury or significant environmental or economic loss; a rail signalling system, a crane controller, a medical monitoring device. The response is a safety integrity level assigning hardware and software reliability targets, with the software's contribution being assessed against the fault possibilities it must handle. Non-safety — everything else, which includes almost all consumer software, where the discipline reduces to what this chapter has already said. Then the four techniques, each from a real failure and each applicable more widely than safety. Detect and handle memory errors. The system should detect an invalid memory access, an overflow, a division by zero, and place the software in a defined safe state rather than continuing with corrupted state — because on a safety system the alternative is an unpredictable later failure, and this is worth having in any system where corruption is worse than a restart. Watchdog the independent parts. A timer that must be periodically serviced by healthy code, and whose expiry resets the system — so a hang becomes a restart rather than a freeze, and the watchdog runs on independent hardware so a failure in the main processor cannot stop it working. Every safety function must be independent of the control function. A system that monitors its own actuator must do so through a different path than the one commanding it, because a shared failure defeats the monitoring entirely — and this generalises to any case where a check and the thing it checks share a dependency. And the safety state is the state that makes damage least, which is a design decision rather than a runtime one: what does the system do when it does not know? The answer must be chosen for the worst plausible case, not the most likely one. Then the two things people find uncomfortable and both are real. Certification costs money and time and buys evidence, and it is often worth it for the reasons above rather than for legal exposure, because a documented argument about why the system is safe is a design review you get for free. And the discipline improves ordinary software. Every technique in this section — bounds checking, watchdogs, defined safe states, independent verification of anything critical — is a technique that catches defects the ordinary testing chapter's argument about what tests cannot reach, and a system that would be indefensible in a safety case has defects nobody was looking for.

/* The safety case. */
const CASE = {
  argumentIsNot: 'the code is correct',
  argumentIs: 'the RISK IS ACCEPTABLY LOW',
  and: 'the argument MUST BE WRITTEN DOWN BEFORE IT CAN BE REVIEWED',

/* Two uncomfortable truths. */
const UNCOMFORTABLE = [
  { t: 'CERTIFICATION COSTS MONEY and TIME and BUYS EVIDENCE',
    worthItFor: 'the reasons above rather than for LEGAL EXPOSURE',
    because: 'a DOCUMENTED ARGUMENT about why the system is safe IS A DESIGN REVIEW YOU GET FOR FREE' },
  { t: 'the DISCIPLINE IMPROVES ORDINARY SOFTWARE',
    why: 'every technique here - BOUNDS CHECKING, WATCHDOGS, DEFINED SAFE STATES, INDEPENDENT VERIFICATION of anything critical - is a technique that catches DEFECTS the ordinary testing chapters argument about what tests cannot reach',

Standards, assurance levels, and what actually differs

Three standards, each solving a different problem, and knowing which is which prevents a great deal of confusion. IEC 61508 is the foundation — a generic safety standard for any industry, defining safety integrity levels from one to four as a measure of how rigorously the safety-related parts of the system must be developed and verified. IEC 61511 is the process-industry application of it, covering safety instrumented systems in oil and gas, chemicals and power, and adding sector-specific guidance such as proof testing intervals. ISO 26262 is automotive, with automotive-specific terminology and requirements around hardware metrics and freedom from interference between safety and non-safety software. And there is a third family worth knowing about: IEC 62304 covers medical devices and is organised around software safety classification by the consequence of a failure — from no harm possible up to the possibility of death — with the required process rigor for each class. Then what an assurance level actually changes in practice, because the abstract level means nothing without the concrete obligations. Documentation and independence. Higher levels require an independent functional safety assessment by somebody not involved in development — which is the single largest cost and the single largest source of assurance, because the assessment is what catches an assumption nobody questioned. Verification at a higher rigour, meaning not just testing but a documented argument that the verification is complete against the requirements, and independence for the people doing it at the higher levels. Failure collection and analysis, which is a quantified way of asking whether the residual failure rate of the design is below the target — and this is why the process is different in kind rather than in degree from ordinary testing, because you are reasoning about rates rather than about instances. And the life-cycle activities scale too, from management review and competence assessment of the people doing the work, which is a genuinely unusual requirement and one that reflects the observation that most safety failures trace to what a person understood rather than to what a machine did. Then the four questions to ask before claiming a system is safe, and each is the question a reviewer will ask. What is the hazard and what is the harm? A system with no identified hazard has no safety requirement, and if you cannot name the harm, the argument has no content. What safety requirement addresses it, and is it independent of the function that could produce it? Because a requirement checked by the same code that could fail it is not a safety requirement. What happens in each single failure and in combinations? Including the credible combinations, which is where the analysis becomes difficult and where independence arguments matter. And what is the evidence that this was checked? Not that it was checked — the evidence, which is a document somebody can read. Then the two things people are tempted to do that should be avoided. Treating safety as a phase at the end. Everything the safety disciplines do is cheaper and better when the design has them built in, and a safety argument constructed over a finished design is an argument that the design had no options. And using a safety standard as a checklist. The standards specify what must be demonstrated, not what to build; satisfying them produces a defensible argument, and a system that satisfies them while being unsafe is possible, which is why the hazard analysis is the part that must be done rather than the part that can be bought.

/* Three standards, different problems. */
const STANDARDS = [
  { s: 'IEC 61508', role: 'the FOUNDATION', scope: 'ANY INDUSTRY',
    defines: 'SAFETY INTEGRITY LEVELS from one to four as a measure of how RIGOROUSLY the safety-related parts must be developed and verified' },
  { s: 'IEC 61511', role: 'the PROCESS-INDUSTRY APPLICATION of it',

  { s: 'ISO 26262', role: 'AUTOMOTIVE',

  { s: 'IEC 62304', role: 'MEDICAL DEVICES',

38 · Emerging Technologies, Mapped Honestly

A sober map of whatever startups will pitch next, from distributed ledgers and quantum to AI agents and spatial computing, applied with the same tools an engineer applies to any new claim. Each appraisal is a technical estimate: what is real today, what is staged, and what cost and benefit a production decision would involve. The goal is an anti-hype toolkit you can reuse on the next new thing.

38.1 Distributed ledgers & "blockchain", an engineering view38.2 Quantum computing: what’s real in 202638.3 2026 AI agents: tool-use, loops & guardrails38.4 Spatial computing / AR / XR — and what’s postponed38.5 The anti-hype toolkit: evaluating any "next big thing"

The final chapter is a compass, not a hype machine: a sober engineering map of the technologies you’ll be pitched on in every startup meeting — what they actually are, what they change, and where they’re still vaporware.

38.1 Distributed ledgers & "blockchain", an engineering view

A distributed ledger is a tamper-evident log ordered by consensus, where each block hashes the previous one so changing history is detectable, and the log is replicated across peers without a trusted central operator. The engineering tradeoffs are real: low throughput, high latency, and heavy operational complexity, whatever the marketing says. It is the right tool only when a problem genuinely needs a shared, trusted append-only log between parties who trust no one.

# What it IS: a tamper-evident, decentralized log agreed by consensus.
#   - the immutability + consensus come at a cost: every node recomputes,
#     so throughput is tiny and cost is high (Ch.29 quorum economics)
#   - So: when is it right? (a) no trusted operator exists or is
#     acceptable, (b) auditability across parties matters more than
#     throughput, (c) permissioned consensus (Hyperledger/Quorum) for
#     enterprise consortia -- NOT one company owning it
#   - Where it's a hard NO: anything needing speed, privacy-by-default,
#     or where "we put it on the chain" is branding for a database.
# What you'll actually use: signatures/hash chains (Ch.20 crypto) in
# supply chains, licensing, and audit trails -- the technology is the
# building block; "trustless money" may or may not survive its costs.

What immutability costs, and the cases where it is worth paying

An append-only ledger removes a category of operation — the update — and the reason it is sometimes the right answer is that the update is where a great deal of harm originates. A mutable row can be changed by anyone with write access, and nothing about the change distinguishes a legitimate change from an illegitimate one unless the schema and the application are both correct, at every call site, forever. An append-only design replaces that with a different question: is this record valid? — which is decidable from the record itself. That is the whole argument, and it is a real one. But the costs are equally real and they are the reason the section's warning exists. You cannot correct a mistake. Every error becomes an additional record reversing the previous one, so a data set accumulates compensating entries; this is correct and it makes the history harder to read and the state harder to compute. Reads get slower as the log grows, because materialising current state means folding the whole history, so every read is proportional to the history length unless you maintain a derived view — which is a cache, with all the invalidation problems a cache has, and the correctness of the cache becomes the correctness of the system. Privacy deletion becomes impossible, and this is the one that is genuinely hard: a regulation that requires a person's data to be erased is in direct conflict with an immutable log, and the usual resolutions — encryption keys per record, so a deletion is destroying a key — change the append-only property into something more subtle and are a design decision that must be made deliberately rather than discovered under a request. And throughput is lower, because the workload is write-heavy with no in-place updates, which is the opposite of what a transactional system is optimised for. Then the three cases where the trade is clearly right, and the pattern is a property of the domain rather than of the technology. Where no trusted operator works. If the parties to the transaction do not trust each other — a consortium, a cross-organisational ledger, a system where the operator could profit from altering history — then a party who can alter the past can profit from the future, and the only defence is for the past to be verifiable, which means signed and linked. Where verification is the product. An audit log, a supply-chain record, a voting record: the value of the artefact is that it can be checked, and an artefact that can be edited cannot be checked. Where the correction history is itself wanted — a financial ledger, a versioned document, a configuration history — because there the append-only model is not a cost but the requirement, and a design that allowed silent edits would be the defect. And the decision rule, which is short: use immutability where an untrusted party could profit from altering history; use a normal mutable model where you trust the operator and need current-state reads to be cheap. The second case is the great majority of systems, and choosing the first out of fashion produces a system that is slower, harder to query and harder to delete from, in exchange for a guarantee nobody needed.

/* The argument. */
const ARGUMENT = {

  secondCaseIs: 'the GREAT MAJORITY OF SYSTEMS',

The honest ledger judgment: immutability costs throughput, so use it only where no trusted operator works, not as database branding.

38.2 Quantum computing: what’s real in 2026

Quantum claims split into what is arriving now and what is pending: post-quantum cryptography is shipping, with NIST-endorsed lattice and hash algorithms replacing RSA, while general quantum advantage waits on thousands of fault-tolerant qubits that likely need years of physics progress. The practical action is a crypto agility migration: inventory algorithms, adopt hybrid schemes, and test performance. Other quantum promises are best treated as staged research to monitor.

What quantum computing actually changes

Quantum computing is worth understanding precisely because it is a case where the popular framing is wrong in an instructive way. A qubit is not a bit that is secretly either zero or one. It is a two-level system in a superposition — a linear combination of two basis states — and measuring it yields one of them with probabilities given by the amplitudes' squared magnitudes. The consequence is that you cannot read a superposition: the moment you measure, the state collapses to a definite value and the other component is gone. So the value is not that a qubit holds many answers; it is that the manipulation of amplitudes can be arranged so that the probability of a useful answer is amplified before measurement. Then the three things that make it different in kind, and each has a precise consequence. Interference. Quantum operations are linear and can make amplitudes cancel or reinforce, so an algorithm can be constructed so that wrong answers cancel and right answers reinforce — which is the mechanism by which a quantum algorithm gives a speed-up, and it is why quantum algorithms are hard to invent: you are designing the cancellation. Entanglement, where the joint state of two qubits cannot be described independently, which lets an algorithm represent a correlation that has no classical counterpart and is why the state space available grows exponentially. And the measurement problem: because measurement destroys the state, a computation must be arranged so that a single measurement of a small number of bits yields the answer, and an algorithm that requires an exponential number of measurements is worthless — which is the honest reason quantum advantage is hard to demonstrate and why the useful algorithms are few. Then the three algorithms that are real, because they are the evidence that the field is not vapour and they each exploit a specific structure. Factorisation, where the classical best is sub-exponential and the quantum algorithm is polynomial — which threatens the public-key cryptography the networking chapter described, and it is worth being clear about why: the security of those schemes rests on the difficulty of exactly these problems, so a sufficiently large quantum computer breaks them, and the response has to happen now because harvest-now-decrypt-later means data recorded today can be decrypted later. Simulation of molecules, which is the strongest practical claim because a molecule's state is a quantum system and representing it classically requires exponential space — the reason the field has an application rather than only a demonstration. And certain search and optimisation problems with a quadratic rather than exponential improvement. Then the honest assessment, which is what makes this worth including in an engineering book rather than only as trivia. Nothing currently useful runs on a quantum computer outside a laboratory. The hardware is small, the noise is severe, and correcting errors requires an overhead that currently exceeds the useful computation by a large factor. The error rates mean a meaningful computation cannot complete today, because a deep circuit accumulates errors across its gates and the answer is wrong. And the useful quantum algorithms require fault-tolerant hardware with thousands of physical qubits per logical qubit, so the gap between a laboratory demonstration and a useful device is not an engineering increment but an architectural one. The practical consequence for an engineer is precise and limited: cryptography is the thing to act on, and it is the only thing. Not because quantum computing will soon make your application faster — it will not — but because the transition to post-quantum cryptography has to be completed before the capability exists, and every system that will live longer than a decade stores data whose confidentiality has to survive the transition.

/* What a qubit is not. */

Where the field actually stands, and what to watch

Three technologies, because "quantum computing" names more than one thing and conflating them is the most common error in any discussion of the subject. Quantum computing is a general-purpose machine that manipulates qubits and runs algorithms whose advantage comes from interference — and its state is far from what is needed for a general machine. Quantum annealing solves one class of problem, finding low-energy states of a graph, by running a physical system in a quantum annealing dynamics and reading out its final configuration; it is a specialised accelerator for optimisation, not a computer, and its advantage over a good classical solver on the instances people actually have is contested. Quantum simulation is the area where the application is clearest, because simulating molecules and materials is a quantum problem and doing it classically requires exponential space — which is why the chemistry use case is the one the field points at and why the error-correction threshold for simulating a useful molecule is the number being tracked. Then the single engineering fact that governs everything, and it is worth stating because it explains why the field's progress is measured in qubits rather than in applications. Physical qubits are noisy and error-prone, and a quantum computation is a circuit of them, so errors accumulate with the depth. A deep circuit produces a wrong answer. Error-correcting codes work by encoding one logical qubit across many physical ones and measuring syndromes to detect errors without measuring the data — but the overhead is large, typically a thousand physical qubits or more per logical qubit, and until that overhead is achievable the circuits that could be run are too shallow to do anything useful. The quantum advantage threshold — the size of the computation at which a fault-tolerant machine beats a classical one — has been estimated to require thousands of logical qubits for the shortest interesting algorithms, and no machine has been built at that scale. And the honest note: the classical alternatives have not stood still. Better classical algorithms, better hardware and a great deal of specialised optimisation have moved the line repeatedly, and the honest reading is that the comparison is against a moving target that is currently much better than it was five years ago. Then the four things worth watching, because they are the ones that would change an engineer's decisions. Physical qubit counts at fault-tolerance-relevant quality, not on a headline specification — the relevant number is qubits whose error rates are low enough to be usable, and a device with many poor qubits is worse than a device with few good ones. Logical qubit counts and circuit depths achieved, which is what actually determines what can be computed. Progress on error correction as a technique rather than on qubit counts, because a better code reduces the overhead and the overhead is the binding constraint. And whether the useful algorithms are changing — a new algorithm that requires far fewer logical qubits changes the timeline more than a larger device. Then the honest place to close, and it is the same one the section's warning makes. Nothing about this is an engineering decision you need to make now, with one exception, and the exception is not about computing. Post-quantum cryptography is a decision you must make now, because the transition takes years — inventory what you use, classify what must survive, replace the algorithms — and because of the harvest-now-decrypt-later property, data captured today and stored for a decade will be decryptable at the end of it unless the data itself is protected with post-quantum cryptography now. Quantify the migration: find where asymmetric cryptography is used, distinguish between key exchange and signatures because their replacements differ, and start with the data that has the longest confidentiality requirement, because it has the longest lead time. Do not panic about performance. There is nothing quantum about your application's compute requirements and no reason to expect that to change.

  and: 'because of the HARVEST-NOW-DECRYPT-LATER property, DATA CAPTURED TODAY and STORED FOR A DECADE will be DECRYPTABLE at the end of it unless the data itself is PROTECTED WITH POST-QUANTUM CRYPTOGRAPHY NOW',
  how: ['QUANTIFY THE MIGRATION', 'FIND WHERE ASYMMETRIC CRYPTOGRAPHY IS USED',
    'DISTINGUISH between KEY EXCHANGE and SIGNATURES because their REPLACEMENTS DIFFER',
    'START WITH THE DATA THAT HAS THE LONGEST CONFIDENTIALITY REQUIREMENT, because it has the LONGEST LEAD TIME'],
  doNotPanic: 'there is NOTHING QUANTUM about your applications COMPUTE REQUIREMENTS and NO REASON TO EXPECT that to change' };
ClaimReality
"Quantum will break all crypto"Shor’s algorithm would — but only with thousands of fault-tolerant qubits; today’s processors are error-prone "NISQ" and can’t yet run it at scale
"Quantum computers are fast"they’re fast at a handcrafted few problems (search, factorization, simulation); general workloads no
Post-quantum cryptographyREAL and arriving now: NIST-published PQ algorithms replacing RSA/ECC in TLS stacks — engineers should already support the transition

The honest position: learn the algorithms at a conceptual level, track fault-tolerance progress, and DO plan the crypto migration (harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks are already real for long-lived secrets).

38.3 2026 AI agents: tool-use, loops & guardrails

An agent is an LLM plus tools it can call plus a loop that decides the next action, and in 2026 that loop needs hard limits, verification, and observability: step and cost budgets, sandboxed tools, validated output, and a full audit trail. Use agents for genuinely open-ended tasks; hardcode the known journeys, since a deterministic path is cheaper and more controllable. Guardrails are the product, because an agent without limits fails in production.

# An "agent" = LLM + tools + a loop (plan -> call tool -> observe ->
# replan). The engineering is where the charm ends:
#   - reliability: an agent loop is a state machine with stochastic
#     steps; it NEEDS limits (max steps, budget, timeout) and a
#     sandbox (no raw shell access near prod data)
#   - verification: the system must VERIFY tool outputs before acting
#     on them (an agent that trusts its own web search = confabulation
#     multiplier)
#   - observability: step logs, cost per task, and abrupt-stop buttons
# Choose the "reduce to a hardcoded flow" lever whenever the loop can
# be a mere promise cascade: agents for open-ended tasks, fixed
# pipelines for known journeys. (Ch.26.2's step-cards UI went this way.)

The loop, and why it needs more scaffolding than it looks

An agent is a loop: give a model a goal and a set of tools, let it decide what to do next, execute it, feed back the result, repeat until it says it is finished. The loop is small and the engineering is not, and the reason is worth stating precisely. The loop's stopping condition is the model's judgement, and the model has no way to distinguish "the task is complete" from "I have produced something that reads like completion" — so an unbounded loop either stops too early having done half the work or never stops having spent a great deal on nothing. And each iteration is a fresh set of inputs, so an error compounds: an early mistake becomes context that the next step reasons from, and a mistake three steps in can produce a plausible and entirely wrong final answer. Then the four things that make it work, and each addresses a specific failure. Hard limits, and not only a step count. A maximum number of steps is necessary and insufficient; you also need a wall-clock limit, a token limit, and a cost limit, because the pathological case is not many steps but one step that generates a great deal of output or that retries something indefinitely. Verify every tool output before it becomes context. A tool that returns an error string, a truncated result or a value in an unexpected shape must be rejected explicitly rather than passed on, because the alternative is the model reasoning from a malformed fact as though it were a correct one — and this is the same error as the injection section's argument that input must be validated at the boundary, applied to output rather than input. Make the actions verifiable and the state inspectable, which means structured logs of every step — what was decided, what was called with what arguments, what came back — because a loop that has taken forty steps and produced a wrong answer is undebuggable without them. And keep the authority boundary explicit. A tool that reads can be called freely; a tool that writes, sends, pays or deletes needs a policy check independent of the model's judgement, because the model is not a security control and treating its confidence as one is the failure that produces the incidents. Then the honest comparison with the alternative, which is the design chapter's argument in a new place. A hardcoded pipeline is more reliable, more testable, more predictable, cheaper and faster for every task whose steps are known. The reason to prefer an agent is not that it is better at those things — it is that it handles the parts of a task that were not anticipated: an open-ended question, a document whose structure you did not expect, a request where the right sequence of operations is not knowable in advance. And the honest framing of that is that you are trading known behaviour for coverage of the unknown, which is a good trade when the unknown is the majority of the work and a bad one when the unknown is five per cent of a task whose other ninety-five per cent is a payment. Then the four failure modes with a specific mitigation each, because most of them are fixable by structure rather than by prompting. Loops that do not terminate — fixed by limits and by detecting a repeated state. Goal drift, where step fifteen is no longer serving the original objective — fixed by restating the goal periodically rather than trusting the model's memory of it. Confabulation, where a tool call is reported as having happened when it did not — fixed by making the loop's state come from the tool's return value and never from the model's own account. And cascading cost, where each step's output becomes the next step's input and the context grows — fixed by summarising rather than accumulating, and by bounding what a step can return. Then the honest place to close. If the journey is known, write the pipeline. Not because agents are not useful but because the situations where they are useful are narrower than their marketing and are characterised by the unknown, and the cost of discovering that an agent was unnecessary is a system that is harder to reason about than what it replaced.

38.4 Spatial computing / AR / XR — and what’s postponed

Spatial computing, augmented and mixed reality, overlays digital content onto the physical world and tracks the user’s head, hands, and eyes, and today the real deployments are industrial and professional, such as maintenance, training, and design review, rather than a mass-market metaverse that remains postponed. Either way, bet on transferable skills: 3D math, rendering pipelines, and interaction design, which keep their value no matter which headset wins. Evaluate hardware promises against the same evidence bar as any other technology.

  • Genuine today: AR for industrial annotations, remote assistance, spatial design tools; the hardware is niche but real.
  • Postponed (for most): consumer mass-market mixed reality, "metaverse" as a daily platform — check revenue, not trailers.
  • Transferable skill either way: 3D math (Ch.27.2 vectors/transforms), GPU pipelines (Ch.34), and new-interaction design (Ch.28.4) — bet on the skills, not the vertical.

    • What spatial computing adds, and what it changes

    A spatial computing system is one where position in physical space is a primary input rather than something you describe, and the technical consequence is that the system must know where everything is with enough accuracy to draw at it. Spatial computing is tracking plus rendering plus input. Tracking establishes where the headset, the hands and the surroundings are in space; rendering draws a scene that appears correctly placed from that viewpoint; input converts what the user does with their hands or gaze into actions. Each has a hard problem underneath. Tracking cannot be perfect, because the devices are small, the batteries are small, and the accuracy achievable in ordinary rooms is a few millimetres with occasional loss — so everything the system draws must tolerate a small error, and everything the user reaches for must tolerate a small error in their own sense of where their hand is, which is larger and varies with fatigue and attention. Anchoring is how content stays attached to the physical world across a session: the system finds a known feature, tracks its position over time, and uses that as the reference frame for everything else, and the failure modes are that an anchor is found in the wrong place, drifts when the environment changes, or is lost when the user leaves and returns. Rendering must be stable, because a virtual object that jitters relative to a real one is worse than one that is wrong in a consistent way. Then the design problems that are specific, and each has a rule. Provide escape hatches — a way out, a recentre, a way to get back to a known orientation — because a user who cannot recover their orientation cannot use the system, and there is no equivalent of closing a window. Do not require precise gestures: the field of view is limited, the user's hands are in peripheral vision at best, and precision demands are the most common reason people abandon a spatial interface, so the interaction should succeed from a large volume rather than a small one. Put content where the user expects it — the world-anchored convention is that a panel stays where it was put and is reachable from where you are, and floating content that follows the camera is disorienting because it has no stable relationship with anything. Do not require the user to look directly at everything, because looking is expensive and using peripheral vision is how people actually use the world. And respect that a spatial system has one user and is physically present: it is not a screen you can walk away from, it occupies the person's attention and their room, and an interface that demands sustained attention for routine tasks will be abandoned. Then what it is genuinely for, and the honest list is short — anything where the physical context is the information, which is the test: if the task would not improve by being done in the room where it happens, it does not need to be spatial. Training, where a dangerous or expensive procedure is practised in a simulation of the actual equipment and the physical arrangement matters. Design review, where a model at full scale can be walked through before it is built. Remote assistance, where an expert needs to see what the technician sees, and the alternative is a phone call with a description. Data visualisation, where the volume of data makes a two-dimensional representation unreadable and the third dimension is not decoration but the actual variable. And location-anchored instructions, where the instructions are only useful in that spot. And then the two limits that decide whether a project works. The field of view is small and fixed, so an interface designed as a wall of controls is unusable — which means spatial interfaces are necessarily sparse, and any design that requires a lot of visible content has to use another device or another modality. And the hardware is expensive, uncomfortable, and socially conspicuous, which is why the applications that succeeded early are largely industrial and training applications rather than consumer ones: the person wearing the device for eight hours a day is at work and is being paid for it, which changes everything about the design constraints.

    Privacy, comfort, and the practical questions to ask first

    Three areas where a spatial system differs from every other computing device you own, and each has a specific concern. The system is always mapping your room. A device that needs to know where the walls, the floor and the furniture are — continuously, and in a space you did not designate for it — has access to information about your home that no other device has, and it is capturing it to do its job. The questions worth asking are: what does it store, for how long, and who can access it; does it operate when you are not present; and is the map local to the device. A handheld device in a headset has no screen you can look away from. There is no other window to open and no notification that is not in your field of view, so the design has to assume the entire visual budget is committed, which is why the input rules about direct attention exist. Social presence. A device worn on the face is visible to everyone you meet, and the reaction of people around you is a real cost that the wearer bears and cannot avoid — which is a factor in adoption that has nothing to do with the technology and has proved decisive for consumer products. Then the questions to ask before building anything, and they are deliberately concrete. What is the user's head position and hand position error budget, because everything else — what can be hit, what must be hit, what can be missed — follows from it. How much of the user's field of view is committed and for how long, and the discipline is that a task requiring sustained attention must have a natural stopping point. What happens when tracking is lost, and the correct answer is not that content stops moving; it is that the system enters a state where nothing is anchored to the world and everything is reachable, because a virtual object that slides across the room when tracking fails is the single most disorienting failure the technology has. Can the user get out of everything, including a state they have entered accidentally, and this is the accessibility chapter's argument applied to a system with no window to close. And what does the room need to look like, because a good implementation works in an ordinary room with ordinary light and ordinary furniture, and one that needs a carefully prepared space is a laboratory demonstration. Then the four things that make an application good or bad, and they are worth naming because they are not about technology. It must be usable with one hand. Everything else in the interface has to work without a second hand, because the other hand may be holding something, or supporting the person's weight, or injured, and an application that requires two hands excludes a great many people for reasons that have nothing to do with their ability to use a computer. It must tolerate a person who cannot see well, which in this medium is not a colour or a font adjustment but the fact that a virtual object at arm's length is at the same focal distance as the real hand in front of the user's face, so it may be unfocusable by a person whose vision is otherwise adequate, and the mitigation is to place content at distances the user can actually focus on. It must not require precise continuous movement, because that is exhausting in a way that mouse use is not, and a system that requires it is used for a few minutes rather than for hours. And it must have a first-run experience that takes under a minute, because the alternative is a calibration or a scanning step, and the attrition at that step is where nearly every consumer application of this kind has lost its audience.

38.5 The anti-hype toolkit: evaluating any "next big thing"

Five questions filter any next big thing: what genuinely new capability does it enable, what is the real cost, are there production users with results, what benefit does it deliver to the user, and what does ignoring it cost you. Adoption follows evidence and measurable outcomes, not novelty or manufactured urgency. The same checklist, applied regularly, replaces FOMO with position: you know what needs action and what can wait.

# The five questions to ask before believing any tech-news headline:
#  1 What NEW capability does it provide (vs cheaper-but-same)?
#  2 What is the ACTUAL cost (time/latency/money/energy) of that
#    capability?
#  3 Who is already using it with measurable, auditable results, at
#    scale, in production (not a demo)?
#  4 What got simpler FOR THE USER, not just for the investor deck?
#  5 If I ignore it for 24 months, what do I miss? (usually: nothing)
# Velocity rule: adopt technologies that remove friction with evidence;
# ignore tech that adds novelty with a pitch. Your career compounds on
# boring, working infrastructure.

Five questions to run any headline through before adopting, because careers compound on boring, working infrastructure.

Reading a claim, and a checklist for deciding what to believe

The genuinely useful skill here is not enthusiasm or scepticism but evaluation, and it can be made mechanical. Ask what the benchmark actually measures. A number on a leaderboard means the model performs well on the distribution that benchmark uses, which is a particular set of questions written by particular people about particular topics; a model that scores highly on one and poorly on your users' questions is not better at the thing you care about. The honest version of this question is: would I expect this improvement to help on the task I have, and can I construct ten examples from my own data that would show it? If not, you have a benchmark result rather than a prediction. Ask whether the comparison is like for like. Most published comparisons are not: a different prompt, a different number of attempts, a different amount of retrieved context, a different latency budget, a model measured with retrieval and one without. Each of those changes the result and each is reported as if the only difference were the model. Ask what the failure looks like. A capability that improves something 20 per cent and is wrong in a new way can be worse than the previous version if the new wrongness is harder to detect — and the honest question is not "is it better on average" but "is it better on the cases that matter and no worse elsewhere". Ask what it displaces. A capability that replaces a deterministic step with a probabilistic one changes the system's character: something that either worked or did not now sometimes works, and every downstream assumption about correctness has to be revisited. And ask whether anyone has tried to break it. A capability demonstrated by its proponents and not by its users is a demonstration. Then the three things that are actually settled, and knowing them saves a great deal of argument. Scaling has produced predictable improvement on a wide range of tasks, and the predictability is itself remarkable — enough that the existence of a capability should be expected rather than surprised. The techniques are widely understood, and the argument that a particular approach is secret has not survived inspection. And the deployment limitations are well known and real: latency, cost, unreliable intermediate results, difficulty evaluating, and the fact that a model is a black box nobody can query for why. Then the three that are genuinely open, and these are the interesting ones. How capability scales beyond the current regime is not known, and the empirical curve has a shape that nobody can justify extrapolating. Whether reliability can be made intrinsic rather than achieved by scaffolding around it is unresolved. And the economics are unclear at scale — the cost of serving a request has been falling, and what it falls to when everyone is doing it is not something anyone can predict. And then the practical stance, which is short and is what most of this chapter is for. Use these systems where they are clearly better and the failure is survivable: drafting, summarising, classifying, extracting, translating, first-pass code. Do not use them where correctness is verifiable only by them, where the cost of being wrong is unbounded, or where the audit requirement means you must be able to state why. Evaluate on your own data, with your own examples, before believing any published number. And keep the ability to turn it off, because a dependency on a third party's model, pricing and availability is a dependency you did not design, and the operating chapter's incident chapter is full of systems that could not be changed quickly because they were deeply integrated with something they should have used loosely.

/* A mechanical evaluation checklist. */
const CHECK = [

Exercises 38

  1. Run one "next big thing" headline through the 5-question anti-hype filter and write your verdict.
  2. Identify the real engineering win hiding inside one hype tech (e.g., hash chains in audit trails) and specify it.
  3. Sketch the agent-with-guardrails architecture for a "research assistant that books trips": tools, limits, verification, undo.

Appendix · Glossaries, Answers & Roadmap

The appendix is the reference and capstone section of the guide: a survival glossary of the terms used everywhere, hints and answers for selected exercises, pinned cheat sheets for Big-O, HTTP statuses, and Git, and a full chapter-by-chapter roadmap mapped onto a real university timeline. Skim the glossary early and keep the cheat sheets handy on the job. It turns the guide from reading material into a working reference.

A.1 Survival glossaryA.2 Answers & hintsA.3 Cheat sheets (keep these pinned)A.4 The full degree roadmap (32 chapters → timeline)

A.1 Survival glossary

Quick, precise definitions for the terms that appear everywhere on the job: deadlock, idempotent, p99, regression, eventual consistency, and their neighbors, each explained in a sentence or two that shows why it matters. Skim it early to build orientation, and keep it nearby as a lookup so unfamiliar words do not stall your learning. It is written to be read out of sequence.

TermOne-line meaning
AbstractionHiding detail behind a clean interface
Crash / segfaultProgram hit an illegal operation; OS killed it
DeadlockTwo parties each wait on the other’s lock, forever
IdempotentDoing it twice = doing it once
ImmutabilityData that never changes after creation
LatencyTime for one request end-to-end
ThroughputHow many requests per second
MonolithOne application containing everything
MicroservicesMany small deployable services, talking over network
p9999% of requests are this fast or faster (the "unlucky user")
Race conditionBug caused by timing of concurrent access
RegressionA bug that re-appeared because a change broke old behaviour

A.2 Answers & hints

Hints for selected exercises, from balanced-bracket stacks to knapsack dynamic programming and merge property-based tests, give enough of a nudge to unstick you without handing over full solutions. Each hint points at the pattern or data structure the exercise is really about. The design keeps the challenge intact while making the material self-study friendly.

  • Ch 8.2 balanced brackets: stack of openers; when you see a closer )]}, the top of the stack must be its matching opener. At the end the stack must be empty. O(n).
  • Ch 9 (Knapsack): dp[w] = best value using weight ≤ w; iterate items; update backwards dp[w] = max(dp[w], dp[w - item.weight] + item.value).
  • Ch 9 LIS: tails + binary search for O(n log n); or the simpler dp[i] = 1 + max over previous smaller — O(n²) to start.
  • Ch 16 property: for merge(a,b) assert the merged list is sorted and has the same multiset as a+b.

How to read the table, and how to compress it

The table above is a mapping from stage to chapters to outside reading, and the thing worth understanding about it is what each column is for rather than what it contains. The stage column is a pacing suggestion, not a prerequisite. A stage is roughly a term, and the table assumes you can give one to each — but the dependency structure is in the chapter order, not in the stages, so if you already know the material in stage two you can start there without weakening stage three. The chapter column is the actual dependency graph, and the two places it is worth reading closely are the stage 2 to 3 boundary and the stage 7 to 8 boundary, because both are where a chapter assumes something introduced two stages earlier. Stage 3 assumes the systems thinking from stage 2 for its architecture decisions; stage 8 assumes the mathematics from stage 2 and the machine-level material from stage 3, which is why it is the elective set and why picking a stage-8 elective with a weak stage-2 background is the one combination that does not work. The outside-reading column is optional in a way the first two are not, and it is there because a degree that only reads its own chapters teaches a closed vocabulary; each entry is the standard treatment of the chapter's topic by somebody better at it than this book, and reading one per stage is enough. Then how to compress it, because a full pass is three to four years at a realistic ten hours a week and most readers will not do that. Stages 1 and 2 are not compressible. Programming skill and the systems fundamentals are the two things everything else rests on, and a compressed version of either produces a reader who can follow the later chapters and cannot build anything. If time is the constraint, cut stages 4 to 8 rather than stages 1 and 2 — the reverse is the mistake that produces a graduate who has read about transactions and has never seen a schema. Stage 3 is compressible to its first half for a web or product reader: processes, concurrency and testing are the transferable half, and the delivery and metrics material can wait until you have shipped something. Stage 7 is compressible to nothing at all, because the career material is only useful once there is something to have a career about, and reading it earlier tends to produce a plan instead of work. And stage 8 is not compressible; it is selectable. The electives exist to be chosen against a direction — the applied machine-learning systems chapters for someone moving towards data, the embedded chapters for someone towards hardware, the emerging-technology chapters for someone who wants to know what to be careful about — and a reader who takes all of them shallowly knows less than one who takes three properly. Then the one rule that governs all of this, and it is the reason the table stops at stage 8. The chapters exist to be used and the evidence of having read them is not a completion percentage. A stage is finished when you can build the thing it describes, and the exercise sets are the instrument for deciding: if you cannot do the exercises without looking at the prose again, the stage is not finished and no amount of reading will change that. The table's last row is a list of subjects rather than a list of steps precisely because the fourteen that follow are the ones with no single obvious job — and the useful way to choose among them is to choose the one whose problems you find interesting when nothing depends on the answer.

If you are not doing a degree, and what each stage produces

Two things the table does not say, and both change how you read it. If you are not pursuing a degree, treat the stages as a capability ladder rather than a schedule and the only two that matter are the bottom and the top: stages 1 and 2 are what make you someone who can be trusted with a system, and stage 3 is what makes you someone who can design one. Everything between them is domain knowledge, and domain knowledge is acquired by working rather than by reading — which means the correct version of this library for a working developer is stages 1 and 2 done properly, stage 3's first half done properly, and the rest consulted when a problem arrives rather than read in advance. Each stage has an output, and the output is what tells you whether you finished it, which is a more useful definition than having read the chapters. Stage 1 produces a program you did not write — a working tool, a game, a script that does something you wanted done — built by you, debugging included, and the debugging is the point rather than an inconvenience. Stage 2 produces a working concurrent system with a persistence layer: something with a queue, a worker pool, a real schema with foreign keys and migrations, and a web interface over it, deployed somewhere other than your own machine. Stage 3 produces a design document that changed because of something you read — the test being that you can name a decision you would not have made before the chapter that taught you why, and that is a real test because it distinguishes a chapter that informed you from a chapter you skimmed. Stage 4 produces a project with tests you trust enough to refactor under, which is a much higher bar than "has tests" and is the stage's entire content. Stage 5 produces something deployed with a rollback and monitored, because the distinguishing feature is not that it is deployed but that you have seen it fail and brought it back. Stage 6 produces something you measured — an actual measurement, before and after, of a change you made, with the number recorded and the reasoning for the change. And stage 7, the capstone, produces something with users who were not you, which is the only stage whose output cannot be produced alone, and which is why it is last and why the earlier stages are all preparation for it. Then the honest arithmetic about outside reading, because it is the column most often ignored and the one with the best ratio. A standard computer-science text covers in six hundred pages what these chapters cover in one section, so the efficient arrangement is: read this library for the shape of the problem and the vocabulary, then read the standard treatment for the depth, in that order, because reading the standard treatment first is how a person ends up able to recite a definition and unable to use it. And that order reverses for one kind of chapter — the ones where the mathematics is the argument rather than the vocabulary, the linear algebra and the computability chapters — where the standard treatment first and this library second is the better use of the same hours.

Finish line philosophy. The degree teaches you 20% of what you’ll ever use and 100% of the foundations. What makes you an engineer is what you build after the last chapter — so close this file and go ship something.
